indications: Surgery or procedures that need unconsciousness, amnesia and immobility
Procedures where regional or local anaesthesia is unsuitable or declined
Patients unable to cooperate (young children, some learning disabilities)
contraindications: Inadequate fasting for elective surgery (delay or use rapid sequence induction if urgent)
Unoptimised severe cardiorespiratory disease for elective surgery
Absence of essential monitoring, oxygen, suction or airway equipment
Known malignant hyperthermia susceptibility without trigger-free setup
equipment: Checked anaesthetic machine or draw-over apparatus with oxygen supply and backup cylinder
Airway equipment (face masks, airways, laryngoscopes, tubes, supraglottic airways, bougie)
Monitoring (ECG, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, capnography, temperature)
Induction, maintenance, muscle relaxant and emergency drugs, labelled
steps: Confirm identity, procedure, site, consent, fasting and allergies and complete the WHO sign-in.
Check the anaesthetic machine, suction, airway equipment and drugs before the patient enters.
Review the pre-anaesthetic assessment, airway plan and blood availability.
Attach monitoring and record baseline observations.
Secure intravenous access and start fluids as needed.
Preoxygenate with a tight-fitting face mask until end-tidal oxygen is adequate or for at least three minutes.
Induce anaesthesia with the planned agents, using rapid sequence induction where aspiration risk is high.
Secure the airway with the planned device and confirm placement with capnography.
Maintain anaesthesia, analgesia and relaxation as required and record observations at least every five minutes.
Position and protect pressure points, eyes and limbs, and keep the patient warm.
Manage fluids and blood loss and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol at the correct time.
Plan postoperative analgesia and antiemesis before emergence.
Reverse neuromuscular block when indicated and confirm recovery before extubation.
Extubate or remove the airway device when criteria are met and give oxygen.
Hand over to the recovery nurse with the anaesthetic chart and instructions.
aftercare: Monitor in recovery until discharge criteria are met.
Give oxygen, analgesia and antiemetics as prescribed.
Continue observations on the ward as instructed.
Review the patient within 24 hours if an anaesthetic complication occurred.
red_flags: Unexpected difficult airway or failed intubation (follow the difficult airway algorithm and call for help)
Persistent desaturation or loss of capnography trace
Severe hypotension, arrhythmia or cardiac arrest
Suspected anaphylaxis
Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide with rigidity and fever (suspect malignant hyperthermia)
Delayed awakening after anaesthesia

indications: General anaesthesia needing a definitive airway
Airway protection in reduced consciousness or high aspiration risk
Respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation
Airway obstruction or anticipated airway compromise (burns, trauma)
contraindications: Severe distorted upper airway where a surgical airway is the safer plan
Unstable cervical spine without in-line stabilisation (relative)
equipment: Oxygen, face mask and self-inflating bag or anaesthetic circuit
Laryngoscope handles and blades of suitable sizes, checked
Endotracheal tubes of the estimated size and one size above and below
10 mL syringe for cuff inflation and cuff pressure gauge if available
Induction and muscle relaxant drugs and emergency drugs
Supraglottic airway and front-of-neck access kit as rescue
steps: Confirm identity and indication, assess the airway and plan for difficulty including rescue options.
Check equipment, suction and drugs and assign team roles.
Position the patient in the sniffing position, ramped if obese, with in-line stabilisation for suspected neck injury.
Preoxygenate for at least three minutes or eight vital-capacity breaths and consider apnoeic nasal oxygen.
Give induction and neuromuscular blocking drugs as planned, with cricoid pressure per local practice in rapid sequence induction.
Insert the laryngoscope from the right, sweep the tongue left and lift to view the larynx.
Record the laryngeal view and pass the tube through the cords, using a bougie if the view is limited.
Inflate the cuff to just seal the leak and check cuff pressure if a gauge is available.
Confirm placement with a sustained capnography waveform, chest rise and bilateral breath sounds.
Note the tube depth at the teeth or lips and secure the tube.
Connect to the ventilator or circuit and set ventilation.
If intubation fails, stop after a limited number of attempts, oxygenate by mask or supraglottic airway and follow the difficult airway algorithm.
aftercare: Monitor capnography and oxygen saturation continuously.
Recheck tube position after any patient movement.
Arrange a chest X-ray for patients going to the ICU.
Provide continued sedation and analgesia in ventilated patients.
red_flags: No capnography trace after intubation (assume oesophageal intubation and remove the tube)
Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate (proceed to front-of-neck access)
Unilateral breath sounds suggesting endobronchial intubation
Severe hypotension after induction
Dental or airway trauma

indications: Oral, dental or maxillofacial surgery needing a clear oral field
Limited mouth opening
Prolonged ventilation in selected neonates and infants
contraindications: Suspected base of skull fracture
Significant coagulopathy
Nasal obstruction, polyps or recent nasal surgery
equipment: Nasal preformed or standard endotracheal tubes of suitable sizes
Topical vasoconstrictor and local anaesthetic for the nose
Fibreoptic scope or video laryngoscope if available
Capnography, oxygen and airway rescue equipment
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent and check for nasal and skull base contraindications.
Ask about the more patent nostril and prepare the nasal mucosa with topical vasoconstrictor.
Check equipment and soften the tube in warm water if appropriate.
Preoxygenate and induce anaesthesia as planned.
Lubricate the tube and pass it gently along the floor of the nose, bevel facing the septum.
Advance into the oropharynx and view the larynx with the laryngoscope.
Guide the tube into the trachea with Magill forceps, gripping the tube above the cuff, or with fibreoptic guidance.
Inflate the cuff and confirm placement with capnography and auscultation.
Secure the tube without pressure on the nostril margin and record depth at the nares.
Place a throat pack if required and record its insertion.
aftercare: Inspect the nostril for pressure injury during long cases.
Remove and count any throat pack before extubation.
Watch for epistaxis after extubation.
red_flags: Severe epistaxis obscuring the airway
Tube entering the submucosal tissue or false passage
No capnography trace
Throat pack not accounted for

indications: Thoracic surgery needing lung isolation or one-lung ventilation
Massive haemoptysis or lung abscess to protect the healthy lung
Bronchopleural fistula
contraindications: Known difficult airway where a single-lumen tube with bronchial blocker is safer
Tracheobronchial anatomy that prevents placement
equipment: Left and right double-lumen tubes of suitable sizes with stylet
Two cuff syringes and tube clamps
Laryngoscope, suction and airway rescue equipment
Capnography and ventilator able to deliver one-lung ventilation
steps: Confirm identity, side of surgery and consent, and review chest imaging for airway anatomy.
Choose tube side and size and check both cuffs and connectors.
Preoxygenate and induce anaesthesia with full muscle relaxation.
Pass the tube through the cords with the tip concave anteriorly, then remove the stylet and rotate toward the intended bronchus.
Advance until moderate resistance is felt and inflate the tracheal cuff.
Confirm bilateral ventilation, then inflate the bronchial cuff with small volumes.
Clamp each lumen in turn to confirm isolation of each lung by auscultation and chest movement.
Confirm final position with a fibreoptic bronchoscope where available.
Recheck position after turning to the lateral position.
Start one-lung ventilation when required and monitor oxygenation closely.
aftercare: Change to a single-lumen tube if postoperative ventilation is needed.
Deflate the bronchial cuff when isolation is no longer needed.
Arrange a chest X-ray after thoracic surgery.
red_flags: Persistent desaturation during one-lung ventilation
High airway pressures suggesting malposition
Loss of isolation with soiling of the healthy lung
Airway trauma or bronchial rupture

form.label: Lowest oxygen saturation during one-lung ventilation

indications: Predicted or known difficult airway
Failed direct laryngoscopy
Limited neck movement or cervical spine precautions
Teaching and routine intubation where available
contraindications: Heavy blood or secretions obscuring the camera (have direct laryngoscopy ready)
Very limited mouth opening that will not admit the blade
equipment: Charged video laryngoscope with suitable blade (standard or hyperangulated)
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent and check the device powers on with a clear image.
Apply anti-fog measures and load the tube on a stylet shaped to the blade curve.
Preoxygenate and induce anaesthesia as planned.
Insert the blade in the midline and advance under direct vision of the mouth.
Look at the screen and obtain a view of the glottis, avoiding inserting too deep.
Insert the tube alongside the blade under direct vision until the tip appears on screen.
Steer the tube through the cords, withdrawing the stylet as the tube advances.
Inflate the cuff and confirm placement with capnography.
Secure the tube and record depth.
aftercare: Check the oropharynx for injury if the tube was hard to pass.
Clean and disinfect the device per manufacturer and infection-control policy.
red_flags: Good view but unable to pass the tube after limited attempts (use a bougie or change technique)
Desaturation during attempts
Palatal or pharyngeal injury

indications: Known or predicted difficult airway where loss of spontaneous breathing is unsafe
Severely limited mouth opening or neck movement
Unstable cervical spine needing neurological checks after intubation
contraindications: Patient refusal or inability to cooperate
Imminent airway obstruction needing an immediate surgical airway
Local anaesthetic allergy
equipment: Fibreoptic bronchoscope with light source, checked and anti-fogged
Topical local anaesthetic, atomiser and nasal vasoconstrictor
Endotracheal tubes (reinforced tubes preferred) loaded on the scope
Light sedation drugs and reversal agents
steps: Explain the procedure, confirm identity and written consent, and agree a stop signal with the patient.
Attach full monitoring and give supplemental oxygen throughout.
Prepare the airway with topical local anaesthetic, staying within the maximum safe total amount.
Give light sedation only if needed, keeping the patient awake and breathing.
Load the tube on the scope and advance the scope through the nose or mouth keeping the view centred.
Identify the epiglottis and cords and spray further local anaesthetic through the working channel.
Pass the scope through the cords and identify the tracheal rings and carina.
Railroad the tube over the scope, rotating it if it catches at the arytenoids.
Confirm tube position by viewing the carina as the scope is withdrawn and by capnography.
Check limb movement if spine precautions apply, then induce general anaesthesia.
aftercare: Keep the patient nil by mouth until airway sensation returns after extubation.
Document the airway difficulty and give the patient an airway alert letter.
red_flags: Oversedation with apnoea or obstruction
Local anaesthetic toxicity signs (perioral numbness, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia)
Bleeding obscuring the view
Complete airway obstruction (proceed to front-of-neck access)

indications: Airway for short general anaesthetic in fasted patients
Rescue airway after failed intubation
Airway during resuscitation when intubation is not possible
contraindications: High aspiration risk (unfasted, bowel obstruction, late pregnancy) for elective use
Need for high airway pressures
Limited mouth opening below the device size
equipment: Supraglottic airways in the estimated size and one size either side
steps: Confirm identity, fasting status and consent and select size by weight.
Check the device and deflate the cuff fully if cuffed, then lubricate the back.
Induce adequate depth of anaesthesia to abolish airway reflexes.
Position the head in the sniffing position and open the mouth.
Press the device along the hard palate and advance until definite resistance is felt.
Inflate the cuff to the recommended pressure if cuffed and allow the device to settle.
Confirm ventilation with capnography, chest movement and absence of leak.
Insert a bite block if not built in and secure the device.
Pass a gastric tube through the drain channel if the device has one.
aftercare: Remove when the patient is awake and obeying commands, or in deep anaesthesia per plan.
Check for sore throat and blood on the device.
red_flags: Persistent leak or inability to ventilate (resize or change to intubation)
Laryngospasm
Regurgitation of gastric contents into the device

form.label: Gastric tube passed through drain channel

indications: End of anaesthesia with recovery of airway reflexes and adequate breathing
Weaning from mechanical ventilation in ICU when criteria are met
contraindications: Inadequate breathing, oxygenation or reversal of muscle relaxation
Ongoing airway swelling or haemodynamic instability
No team or equipment to reintubate if needed
equipment: Monitoring including pulse oximetry and capnography
steps: Plan the extubation and identify risk factors for failure.
Confirm reversal of neuromuscular block with a nerve stimulator where available.
Preoxygenate with high-concentration oxygen.
Suction the oropharynx under direct vision and remove any throat pack.
Position the patient sitting up or lateral as appropriate.
Insert a bite block to prevent tube occlusion.
Confirm the patient is awake, obeying commands and breathing adequately, unless a deep extubation is planned.
Deflate the cuff and remove the tube with gentle positive pressure.
Give oxygen by face mask and confirm a clear airway and breathing.
Observe closely for airway obstruction or laryngospasm.
aftercare: Continue oxygen and monitoring in recovery or ICU.
Encourage deep breathing and coughing.
Keep nil by mouth until swallow is safe in ICU patients.
red_flags: Laryngospasm or stridor
Desaturation or inadequate breathing
Negative-pressure pulmonary oedema (frothy sputum, hypoxaemia)
Need for reintubation

indications: Induction of anaesthesia in children without intravenous access
Anxious or needle-phobic children
Upper airway obstruction where spontaneous breathing must be maintained
contraindications: High aspiration risk needing rapid sequence induction
Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility (use trigger-free technique)
equipment: Anaesthetic machine with volatile vaporiser and paediatric circuit
Clear paediatric face masks of suitable sizes
Oropharyngeal airways and paediatric laryngoscopes and tubes
Paediatric monitoring and pulse oximetry probe
Suction and emergency drugs calculated by weight
steps: Confirm identity, weight, fasting, allergies and parental consent.
Check equipment and calculate emergency drugs by weight.
Allow a parent to accompany the child where local policy permits and keep the room calm.
Apply pulse oximetry and other monitoring as tolerated.
Start oxygen and nitrous oxide if used, then introduce the volatile agent.
Hold the mask gently, avoiding pressure on soft tissues of the neck.
Escort the parent out once the child is asleep.
Support the airway with jaw thrust and an oropharyngeal airway as needed.
Gain intravenous access once anaesthesia is deep enough.
Proceed to airway device insertion and maintenance as planned.
aftercare: Recover in a paediatric-equipped recovery area with a trained nurse.
Reunite the child with the parent early.
Watch for emergence agitation.
red_flags: Laryngospasm (apply CPAP, deepen anaesthesia and call for help)
Bradycardia or desaturation
Unable to gain intravenous access in a deteriorating child (consider intraosseous access)

indications: High risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting
Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
Neurosurgery or airway surgery where volatile delivery is difficult
Settings without a reliable vaporiser
contraindications: No reliable dedicated intravenous line or infusion pump
Allergy to the planned agents
equipment: Infusion pumps or target-controlled infusion pumps
Dedicated intravenous cannula with anti-reflux valves
Full monitoring, ideally with depth of anaesthesia monitoring
steps: Confirm identity, consent and fasting and explain the risk of awareness is low but present.
Site a reliable cannula that will remain visible throughout the case.
Prepare and label infusions and program pumps for the patient's weight and age.
Attach monitoring including depth of anaesthesia monitoring where available.
Start the infusions and induce anaesthesia.
Secure the airway and ventilate as planned.
Check the cannula site and infusion lines regularly for disconnection or tissue infiltration.
Adjust infusion rates to clinical signs and depth monitoring.
Plan analgesia for emergence and stop infusions at the appropriate time.
Flush the cannula after stopping infusions to clear residual drug.
aftercare: Monitor in recovery until fully awake.
Ask about awareness at follow-up.
red_flags: Infusion disconnection or cannula failure (risk of awareness)
Severe hypotension or bradycardia
Signs of awareness (tachycardia, sweating, movement, tears)

form.label: Line and cannula checked during case

indications: Painful or distressing short procedures (fracture reduction, joint relocation, burns dressing)
Imaging or endoscopy in patients unable to stay still
Cardioversion
contraindications: Inadequate fasting for elective procedures (weigh risk in emergencies)
Difficult airway or severe cardiorespiratory disease without an anaesthetist present
No trained person dedicated to monitoring the patient
equipment: Oxygen, suction, self-inflating bag and masks of suitable sizes
Airway adjuncts and intubation equipment available
Pulse oximetry, blood pressure and ideally capnography
Sedative and analgesic agents and reversal agents
steps: Confirm identity, procedure, consent, fasting status, allergies and weight.
Assess the airway and ASA class and decide whether an anaesthetist is needed.
Assign one trained person to give sedation and monitor the patient only.
Secure intravenous access and attach monitoring with supplemental oxygen.
Give the sedative agent in small titrated amounts to the target depth.
Begin the procedure once the target depth is reached.
Record sedation depth, oxygen saturation, heart rate and blood pressure at least every five minutes.
Support the airway with positioning or jaw thrust if needed.
Stop giving sedation when the procedure ends.
Observe until the patient returns to baseline and meets discharge criteria.
aftercare: Discharge only with a responsible adult and written advice.
Advise no driving, machinery or important decisions for 24 hours.
Advise on eating, drinking and pain relief at home.
red_flags: Apnoea, airway obstruction or desaturation
Laryngospasm
Severe agitation or emergence reaction
Hypotension or arrhythmia
Vomiting with reduced consciousness

indications: Caesarean section
Lower abdominal, perineal, urological and lower limb surgery
Infant hernia repair (awake spinal in experienced hands)
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the injection site or untreated sepsis or bacteraemia
Uncorrected coagulopathy or recent anticoagulant within local timing rules
Severe hypovolaemia or uncorrected shock
Raised intracranial pressure
Fixed cardiac output states (severe aortic stenosis) without expert input
equipment: Sterile spinal pack, gloves, gown, hat and mask
Local anaesthetic for skin and intrathecal local anaesthetic
Intravenous cannula, fluids and vasopressor ready
Monitoring and resuscitation equipment for conversion to general anaesthesia
steps: Confirm identity, procedure, site, consent and coagulation status and complete the time-out.
Secure intravenous access, attach monitoring and prepare a vasopressor.
Position the patient sitting or lateral with the back flexed and identify the L3–4 or L4–5 interspace.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, wear cap, mask and sterile gloves, prepare the skin and drape.
Infiltrate the skin with local anaesthetic.
Insert the introducer and spinal needle in the midline until a give is felt through the dura.
Remove the stylet and confirm free flow of clear cerebrospinal fluid.
Inject the intrathecal drug slowly after confirming aspiration of cerebrospinal fluid.
Remove the needle, apply a dressing and position the patient as required.
Measure blood pressure every 1–2 minutes initially and treat hypotension promptly.
Test the block height with cold or pinprick before surgery begins.
Supplement or convert to general anaesthesia if the block is inadequate.
aftercare: Monitor blood pressure and block regression in recovery.
Keep the patient in bed until motor function returns, then mobilise with help.
Check bladder function before discharge.
Advise to report severe headache, back pain or new weakness.
red_flags: High or total spinal (breathing difficulty, weak arms, hypotension, loss of consciousness)
Severe hypotension or bradycardia
Weakness or numbness lasting longer than expected (suspect haematoma or abscess)
Postural headache after the procedure
Fever with back pain

indications: Surgical anaesthesia for lower body procedures
Postoperative analgesia after major abdominal or thoracic surgery
Analgesia for rib fractures
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site or untreated sepsis
Uncorrected coagulopathy or anticoagulant within local timing rules
Severe hypovolaemia
No staff trained to monitor epidural infusions on the ward
equipment: Sterile epidural pack with Tuohy needle, loss-of-resistance syringe, catheter and filter
Cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves, chlorhexidine skin preparation
Local anaesthetic for skin and epidural solutions
Transparent occlusive dressing and fixation device
Infusion pump or elastomeric device labelled for epidural use
steps: Confirm identity, consent, coagulation status and the planned level and complete the time-out.
Secure intravenous access and attach monitoring.
Position sitting or lateral and identify the interspace for the planned level.
Perform full asepsis, prepare the skin and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the skin.
Advance the Tuohy needle using continuous or intermittent loss of resistance to saline or air.
Note the depth to the epidural space at loss of resistance.
Thread the catheter so that 4–5 cm lies in the space and withdraw the needle.
Aspirate the catheter to exclude blood or cerebrospinal fluid.
Give a test dose and watch for signs of intravascular or intrathecal placement.
Secure the catheter, record the mark at the skin and attach the filter.
Give incremental doses or start the infusion and test the block.
aftercare: Monitor blood pressure, sedation, block height and motor power regularly per protocol.
Inspect the catheter site daily and remove according to anticoagulation timing rules.
Check the catheter tip is intact on removal.
red_flags: New or increasing leg weakness or numbness (urgent review for haematoma or abscess)
Severe back pain or fever
Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Block rising too high or breathing difficulty
Severe hypotension

indications: Maternal request for pain relief in labour
Pre-eclampsia, cardiac disease or other conditions where pain relief helps control
Anticipated operative delivery (catheter can be topped up for caesarean)
contraindications: Maternal refusal
Uncorrected coagulopathy, low platelets below local threshold, or anticoagulant within timing rules
Infection at the site or untreated maternal sepsis
Uncorrected hypovolaemia or active haemorrhage
No midwife trained to monitor labour epidurals
equipment: Sterile epidural pack with Tuohy needle, loss-of-resistance syringe, catheter and filter
Cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves, chlorhexidine skin preparation
Local anaesthetic and low-concentration epidural solutions
Infusion pump or patient-controlled epidural pump
Fetal heart monitoring, maternal monitoring and vasopressor
steps: Confirm identity, consent, platelet count where indicated and discuss with the midwife and obstetrician.
Secure intravenous access and record baseline maternal observations and fetal heart rate.
Position the woman sitting or lateral, timing insertion between contractions.
Perform full asepsis, prepare the skin and drape.
Locate the epidural space at L2–3 or L3–4 using loss of resistance.
Thread the catheter so that 4–5 cm lies in the space and aspirate to exclude blood or cerebrospinal fluid.
Secure the catheter and record the mark at the skin.
Give the initial low-concentration dose in increments and monitor blood pressure every five minutes.
Monitor the fetal heart rate after each dose.
Assess block height and pain score after twenty minutes and start the maintenance regime.
Hand over to the midwife with written monitoring instructions.
aftercare: Record blood pressure, pain score, block height and motor power at regular intervals.
Encourage regular position changes and check bladder emptying.
Remove the catheter after delivery when no longer needed, checking the tip is intact.
Review the woman the day after delivery.
red_flags: Severe hypotension or fetal bradycardia
Dense motor block or block rising above T6
Breathing difficulty or signs of total spinal
Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Postnatal leg weakness, severe headache or back pain with fever

indications: Surgery likely to outlast a single spinal
Caesarean section where extension of block may be needed
Labour analgesia needing rapid onset
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site, uncorrected coagulopathy or anticoagulant within timing rules
Severe hypovolaemia
equipment: Combined spinal-epidural kit (needle-through-needle) or separate spinal and epidural kits
Cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves, chlorhexidine skin preparation
Local anaesthetic for skin, intrathecal and epidural solutions
steps: Confirm identity, procedure, consent and coagulation status and complete the time-out.
Secure intravenous access, attach monitoring and prepare a vasopressor.
Position the patient and identify the interspace.
Perform full asepsis, prepare the skin and drape.
Locate the epidural space with the Tuohy needle using loss of resistance.
Pass the spinal needle through the Tuohy needle until cerebrospinal fluid flows.
Inject the intrathecal dose and remove the spinal needle.
Thread the epidural catheter, withdraw the Tuohy needle and secure the catheter.
Lie the patient in the required position and monitor blood pressure closely.
Test the block before surgery and top up through the catheter when needed.
aftercare: Monitor as for spinal and epidural anaesthesia.
Remember the epidural catheter is untested until the first top-up; give it in increments.
red_flags: High block or breathing difficulty
Severe hypotension
New weakness after the block should have worn off
Postural headache

form.label: Complications
options: No cerebrospinal fluid through spinal needle

indications: Analgesia for infra-umbilical surgery in children (hernia, circumcision, orchidopexy, hypospadias)
Adjunct to general anaesthesia in infants and young children
contraindications: Parental refusal
Infection over the sacrum or pilonidal sinus
Coagulopathy
Sacral anomalies or spinal dysraphism
equipment: Short-bevel or cannula needle (22–23G) or IV cannula
steps: Confirm identity, weight, procedure and parental consent.
Induce general anaesthesia and place the child in the lateral position with hips flexed.
Palpate the sacral cornua and the sacral hiatus between them.
Prepare the skin with antiseptic and drape with full asepsis.
Insert the needle at about 45 degrees to the skin until a give is felt through the sacrococcygeal ligament.
Flatten the angle and advance a few millimetres only.
Aspirate gently to exclude blood or cerebrospinal fluid.
Inject slowly while watching for subcutaneous swelling, resistance or ECG changes.
Remove the needle and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Expect temporary leg weakness and warn parents.
Check the child passes urine before discharge.
Give regular simple analgesia as the block wears off.
red_flags: Blood or cerebrospinal fluid on aspiration (do not inject)
ECG changes or arrhythmia during injection (stop; suspect intravascular injection)
Prolonged leg weakness or urinary retention

indications: Upper limb surgery (anaesthesia or analgesia)
Analgesia for upper limb fractures and dislocations
Patients at high risk from general anaesthesia
contraindications: Patient refusal or inability to cooperate (unless under general anaesthesia in children)
Infection at the site
Severe respiratory disease (for interscalene and supraclavicular approaches, due to phrenic nerve block)
Coagulopathy for deep or non-compressible approaches
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and sterile cover, or nerve stimulator
Local anaesthetic within the maximum safe dose for weight
Lipid emulsion and resuscitation equipment immediately available
steps: Confirm identity, procedure, consent and side, and mark the limb.
Perform a stop-before-you-block check with the assistant immediately before needling.
Secure intravenous access and attach monitoring.
Position the patient for the chosen approach.
Prepare the skin and probe with asepsis and identify the plexus and nearby vessels on ultrasound.
Infiltrate the skin with local anaesthetic.
Advance the needle in plane under continuous vision toward the plexus.
Aspirate before each injection and inject in small increments, watching the spread.
Stop if there is high injection pressure, pain, paraesthesia or no visible spread.
Assess sensory and motor block after fifteen to twenty minutes.
aftercare: Protect the numb limb with a sling and warn the patient about the duration.
Start oral analgesia before the block wears off.
Advise to report persisting numbness or weakness after the expected duration.
red_flags: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity (stop, call for help, give lipid emulsion per protocol)
Breathlessness (phrenic nerve block or pneumothorax)
Hoarseness or Horner syndrome causing distress
Increasing limb pain after a fracture or in a tight cast despite the block (suspect compartment syndrome)
Persistent numbness or weakness beyond 48 hours

indications: Analgesia for hip fracture or femoral shaft fracture
Analgesia for knee and anterior thigh surgery
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site
Previous femoral vascular graft at the site
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and sterile cover, or nerve stimulator
Local anaesthetic within the maximum safe dose for weight
Lipid emulsion and resuscitation equipment available
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and baseline neurovascular status of the limb.
Perform a stop-before-you-block check.
Secure intravenous access and attach monitoring.
Position the patient supine and identify the femoral artery and nerve or the fascia iliaca on ultrasound.
Prepare the skin with antiseptic and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Advance the needle lateral to the artery to reach the nerve or beneath the fascia iliaca.
Aspirate and inject in small increments, watching the spread around the nerve or under the fascia.
Remove the needle and apply a dressing.
Assess analgesia and sensory block after twenty minutes.
aftercare: Warn about quadriceps weakness and fall risk; supervise mobilisation.
Continue regular multimodal analgesia.
red_flags: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Expanding haematoma in the groin
Increasing thigh pain or tense swelling after a fracture despite the block (suspect compartment syndrome)
Persistent numbness or weakness beyond the expected duration

indications: Foot and ankle surgery
Analgesia for ankle fractures and below-knee surgery
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site
Pre-existing sciatic neuropathy (document carefully)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and sterile cover, or nerve stimulator
Local anaesthetic within the maximum safe dose for weight
Lipid emulsion and resuscitation equipment available
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and baseline neurological function of the foot.
Perform a stop-before-you-block check.
Secure intravenous access and attach monitoring.
Position prone, lateral or supine with the leg raised.
Identify the sciatic nerve in the popliteal fossa and follow it to its division.
Prepare the skin with antiseptic and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Advance the needle in plane to the nerve sheath at or just above the division.
Aspirate and inject in small increments, watching spread around the nerve.
Add a saphenous nerve block if the medial ankle is involved in surgery.
Assess sensory and motor block.
aftercare: Protect the numb foot and heel from pressure and injury.
Use crutches and avoid weight-bearing until the block wears off.
Start oral analgesia before the block wears off.
red_flags: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Pain or paraesthesia on injection
Increasing leg pain after a fracture or in a tight cast despite the block (suspect compartment syndrome)
Persistent foot drop or numbness beyond the expected duration

indications: Analgesia after lower abdominal surgery including caesarean section
Analgesia when neuraxial techniques are contraindicated
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site
Abnormal abdominal wall anatomy at the site
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and sterile cover
Local anaesthetic within the maximum safe total dose for weight (bilateral blocks share the total)
Lipid emulsion and resuscitation equipment available
steps: Confirm identity, consent and planned sides.
Perform a stop-before-you-block check for each side.
Ensure intravenous access and monitoring.
Place the probe on the lateral abdominal wall between the costal margin and iliac crest.
Identify external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.
Prepare the skin with antiseptic.
Advance the needle in plane to the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
Aspirate and inject in increments, watching for spread that separates the muscle layers.
Repeat on the other side if bilateral, keeping within the total safe dose.
aftercare: Continue multimodal analgesia.
Monitor for signs of local anaesthetic toxicity for at least thirty minutes after injection.
red_flags: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Abdominal pain or distension suggesting peritoneal or bowel puncture
Transient leg weakness (femoral nerve spread)

indications: Analgesia for rib fractures
Analgesia after thoracic, breast, spinal or upper abdominal surgery
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site
Severe coagulopathy (relative)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear or curvilinear probe and sterile cover
Block needle (80–100 mm) and catheter kit if continuous
Local anaesthetic within the maximum safe dose for weight
Lipid emulsion and resuscitation equipment available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and level.
Perform a stop-before-you-block check.
Ensure intravenous access and monitoring.
Position the patient sitting, lateral or prone.
Identify the transverse process at the target level with a parasagittal ultrasound view.
Prepare the skin with antiseptic and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Advance the needle in plane until it contacts the transverse process deep to erector spinae.
Aspirate and inject in increments, watching for linear spread lifting the muscle.
Thread a catheter if continuous analgesia is planned and secure it.
aftercare: Monitor pain scores and breathing.
Manage any catheter infusion per local protocol and check the site daily.
red_flags: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Breathlessness or chest pain (pneumothorax)
Leg weakness (neuraxial spread)

indications: Analgesia for rib fractures
Analgesia for chest drain insertion or thoracic incisions
Herpes zoster pain (selected cases)
contraindications: Patient refusal
Infection at the site
Severe respiratory reserve limitation where pneumothorax would be dangerous (consider alternatives)
equipment: Local anaesthetic within the maximum safe total dose (multiple levels share the total)
Lipid emulsion and resuscitation equipment available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and levels to be blocked.
Ensure intravenous access and monitoring.
Position sitting leaning forward or lateral with the affected side up.
Identify the lower border of each rib at the posterior angle.
Prepare the skin with antiseptic.
Insert the needle onto the rib, then walk it off the lower edge and advance a few millimetres.
Aspirate for blood or air and inject a small volume.
Repeat at each level, keeping within the total safe dose.
Listen to the chest after the procedure.
aftercare: Observe oxygen saturation and breathing for at least an hour.
Arrange a chest X-ray if breathlessness develops.
Encourage deep breathing and coughing.
red_flags: Breathlessness, chest pain or falling oxygen saturation (pneumothorax)
Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity

indications: Repair of finger or toe lacerations
Nail removal, paronychia drainage and ingrown toenail surgery
Reduction of finger or toe dislocations
contraindications: Infection at the injection site
Severely compromised circulation to the digit
equipment: Local anaesthetic without adrenaline unless local guidance supports it
steps: Confirm identity, the digit, consent and allergy history.
Check and record sensation and circulation of the digit.
Clean the base of the digit with antiseptic.
Insert the needle at the dorsolateral base of the digit and inject as it is advanced toward the palmar side.
Repeat on the other side of the digit.
Aspirate before injecting and avoid a large circumferential volume.
Wait five to ten minutes and test for numbness before starting the procedure.
aftercare: Protect the numb digit from injury until sensation returns.
Check capillary refill after the procedure.
red_flags: Pale or dusky digit that does not recover
Persisting numbness beyond a day
Signs of infection at the site

indications: Circumcision (neonates, children and adults)
Analgesia after penile surgery such as hypospadias repair
Paraphimosis reduction
contraindications: Infection at the site
Bleeding disorder
Penile anomalies where anatomy is uncertain
steps: Confirm identity, procedure and consent (parental consent for children).
Position supine and prepare the skin with antiseptic.
Identify the base of the penis below the pubic symphysis.
Insert the needle at the 10 and 2 o'clock positions just below the pubic bone into Buck's fascia.
Aspirate to exclude blood and inject slowly on each side.
Alternatively infiltrate a subcutaneous ring at the base of the penis.
Wait for the block to take effect and test before the procedure.
aftercare: Check the glans colour and for bleeding after the procedure.
Advise parents about oral analgesia as the block wears off.
red_flags: Dusky or pale glans
Expanding haematoma
Inability to pass urine

indications: Manipulation of distal forearm fractures
Short hand and forearm procedures under one hour
contraindications: Sickle cell disease or trait (tourniquet)
Severe peripheral vascular disease or Raynaud's disease
Uncontrolled hypertension preventing reliable cuff occlusion
Local anaesthetic allergy
Unreliable tourniquet or no trained second person
equipment: Purpose-made double-cuff tourniquet with pressure gauge, checked for leaks
Two intravenous cannulas (one in each arm)
Local anaesthetic suitable for IVRA (not bupivacaine)
Full monitoring, resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, weight and that sickle cell status is known.
Site a cannula in the hand of the affected limb and another in the other arm.
Attach monitoring and check the tourniquet.
Elevate and exsanguinate the limb where fracture pain allows.
Inflate the proximal cuff above systolic pressure and confirm absent radial pulse.
Inject the local anaesthetic slowly into the affected limb cannula and remove the cannula.
Inflate the distal cuff once anaesthesia is established and deflate the proximal cuff.
Perform the procedure while one person watches the tourniquet pressure continuously.
Keep the cuff inflated for at least twenty minutes after injection.
Deflate the cuff gradually or in cycles and observe for toxicity.
aftercare: Observe for at least thirty minutes after cuff deflation.
Check the limb circulation and neurovascular status.
Elevate and immobilise the limb as needed.
red_flags: Early cuff failure or deflation (risk of local anaesthetic toxicity)
Tinnitus, perioral numbness, seizures or arrhythmia
Limb pain or discolouration after the procedure

indications: Minor procedures such as wound repair, abscess drainage and excision of small lesions
Wound infiltration for postoperative analgesia
Before cannulation or other needle procedures
contraindications: Allergy to the local anaesthetic class
Infection at the injection site (infiltrate around, not into, infected tissue)
Total dose needed would exceed the safe maximum for weight
equipment: 25–27G needle for skin and longer needle for deeper tissue
Local anaesthetic with or without adrenaline per site
steps: Confirm identity, site, consent and allergy history.
Calculate the maximum safe total amount for the patient's weight.
Clean the skin with antiseptic.
Insert the needle into the skin or wound edge and raise a small bleb.
Aspirate before injecting and inject slowly while advancing or withdrawing.
Re-enter through already numb skin to extend the field.
Wait a few minutes and test for numbness before starting.
Record the total amount given.
aftercare: Protect the numb area from injury until sensation returns.
Give simple analgesia as the effect wears off.
red_flags: Perioral numbness, ringing in the ears, confusion, seizures or arrhythmia (local anaesthetic toxicity)
Allergic reaction
Tissue blanching that persists (especially at end-arteries)

indications: Closed reduction of distal radius fractures
Closed reduction of other accessible closed fractures
contraindications: Open fracture
Infection or broken skin at the injection site
Fracture more than a few days old (haematoma organised)
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and neurovascular status of the limb.
Review the X-ray and identify the fracture site.
Prepare the skin over the fracture with antiseptic.
Insert the needle into the fracture haematoma, usually from the dorsal side.
Confirm position by aspirating dark blood.
Inject the local anaesthetic slowly into the haematoma.
Wait about ten minutes for the block to work before manipulation.
Proceed with reduction and immobilisation.
aftercare: Check neurovascular status after reduction and splinting.
Arrange a check X-ray.
Elevate the limb.
red_flags: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity
Increasing pain, numbness or tight cast (compartment syndrome)
Signs of infection at the site

indications: Administration of vasopressors, irritant drugs or parenteral nutrition
Central venous pressure monitoring
Lack of peripheral venous access
Haemodialysis or plasma exchange (dialysis catheter)
contraindications: Infection at the insertion site
Thrombosis of the target vein
Uncorrected severe coagulopathy (choose a compressible site)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and sterile cover
Central venous catheter kit (catheter, guidewire, dilator, needle, scalpel)
Cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves and large drape
Local anaesthetic, saline flushes and syringes
Suture or securement device and transparent dressing
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent and coagulation status and complete the checklist.
Choose the site and scan the vein for patency.
Position the patient (head-down for neck veins) and attach ECG monitoring.
Perform full asepsis with cap, mask, gown, gloves and full-body drape.
Prepare the skin with chlorhexidine and flush all lumens of the catheter.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Puncture the vein under real-time ultrasound guidance and aspirate dark non-pulsatile blood.
Pass the guidewire without force, watching the ECG for ectopics, and confirm the wire in the vein on ultrasound.
Nick the skin, dilate the tract and pass the catheter over the wire, keeping hold of the wire at all times.
Remove the guidewire and confirm it is complete.
Aspirate and flush every lumen.
Secure the catheter and apply a sterile transparent dressing.
Confirm tip position by chest X-ray for neck and chest sites before use.
aftercare: Review the line daily for need, site infection and dressing integrity.
Use aseptic non-touch technique for all access.
Remove the line with the patient flat or head-down to prevent air embolism.
red_flags: Arterial puncture or pulsatile blood (do not dilate)
Breathlessness or desaturation (pneumothorax)
Guidewire not retrieved
Fever or redness at the site (line infection)
Arm or neck swelling (thrombosis)

indications: Beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring in unstable patients or major surgery
Frequent arterial blood gas sampling
Vasopressor titration
contraindications: Poor collateral circulation or vascular disease at the site
Infection at the site
Arteriovenous fistula in the same limb
equipment: Arterial cannula (20–22G adult; 22–24G child) or Seldinger arterial kit
Pressure transducer set with flush bag and pressure bag
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent and assess collateral circulation of the hand.
Prime and zero the transducer set and check the pressure bag.
Position the wrist slightly extended over a roll and tape it.
Clean the skin with antiseptic and put on sterile gloves.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic over the artery in an awake patient.
Palpate or scan the artery and insert the cannula at a shallow angle until arterial flashback.
Advance the cannula off the needle or over the guidewire into the artery.
Connect the transducer, flush and check for a good arterial waveform.
Secure the cannula and label the line clearly as arterial.
Level the transducer at the phlebostatic axis and zero it.
aftercare: Check hand perfusion regularly.
Never inject drugs through the arterial line.
Remove when no longer needed and press firmly for at least five minutes.
red_flags: Pale, cold or painful hand (remove the line)
Bleeding from disconnection
Damped or absent waveform
Signs of infection

indications: Intravenous therapy for more than a week (antibiotics, chemotherapy, nutrition)
Poor peripheral venous access
contraindications: Infection or thrombosis of the arm veins
Patient on or planned for haemodialysis (preserve arm veins)
Lymphoedema or recent axillary clearance on the side
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and sterile cover
PICC kit with micro-introducer, guidewire and measuring tape
Cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves and large drape
Chlorhexidine skin preparation and local anaesthetic
Saline flushes, securement device and transparent dressing
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent and choose the non-dominant arm where possible.
Scan the upper arm veins and choose a vein large enough for the catheter.
Measure the length from the insertion site to the right sternoclavicular joint and down to the third intercostal space.
Perform full asepsis and drape widely.
Apply the tourniquet and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Puncture the vein under ultrasound and pass the guidewire.
Release the tourniquet, nick the skin and insert the micro-introducer sheath.
Trim the catheter if required and advance it to the measured length, turning the head toward the arm.
Remove the sheath and guidewire and aspirate and flush the catheter.
Secure with a securement device and transparent dressing.
Confirm tip position by chest X-ray or ECG method before use.
aftercare: Flush and change the dressing per local protocol.
Measure arm circumference if swelling develops.
Teach the patient line care if going home with it.
red_flags: Arm swelling or pain (thrombosis)
Fever or redness at the site
Catheter blocked or migrated

indications: Difficult peripheral venous access after failed landmark attempts
Obesity, oedema, chronic illness or drug use with poor visible veins
contraindications: Infection, burns or injury at the site
Arteriovenous fistula or lymphoedema in the limb
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear probe and probe cover or clean barrier
Long peripheral cannula (at least 45 mm) or extended-dwell catheter
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent.
Apply a tourniquet and scan the arm to find a vein that is compressible, not pulsatile and not too deep.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the skin with antiseptic and cover the probe.
Centre the vein on the screen in a transverse view.
Insert the cannula at the probe midpoint and follow the needle tip into the vein.
Confirm flashback and advance the needle a little further inside the vein under vision.
Advance the cannula off the needle, release the tourniquet and remove the needle.
Flush with saline, checking for swelling on ultrasound.
Secure with a transparent dressing.
aftercare: Check the site regularly for infiltration, as deep cannulas can tissue without visible swelling early.
Remove when no longer needed.
red_flags: Swelling or pain on flushing (infiltration)
Arterial puncture
Redness, pain or fever (phlebitis or infection)

indications: Every patient before anaesthesia or sedation
Pre-assessment clinic for elective surgery
contraindications: None (in emergencies a focused assessment is done)
equipment: Blood pressure monitor, pulse oximeter, weighing scale and tape
steps: Confirm identity and planned procedure and introduce yourself.
Take a history of medical conditions, previous anaesthetics, family anaesthetic problems and functional capacity.
Record current medicines, allergies, smoking, alcohol and drug use.
Record last food and fluid intake and confirm fasting instructions.
Examine the cardiovascular and respiratory systems and record vital signs, weight and height.
Assess the airway (mouth opening, Mallampati, neck movement, teeth, thyromental distance).
Review investigations and order further tests only if they will change management.
Check sickle cell status, pregnancy status and blood availability where relevant.
Assign the ASA class and identify risks.
Discuss the anaesthetic options, risks and postoperative pain plan and record the patient's choice.
Give instructions on medicines to continue or stop and on fasting.
Escalate to a senior or postpone if the patient is not optimised.
aftercare: Communicate the plan and any concerns to the surgical team.
Review again on the day of surgery if circumstances change.
red_flags: Predicted difficult airway without appropriate equipment or skills
Uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure, active chest infection or severe anaemia in elective cases
Recent heart attack, unstable angina or arrhythmia
Previous serious anaesthetic reaction or malignant hyperthermia family history

indications: Every patient after general anaesthesia, regional anaesthesia or sedation
contraindications: None
equipment: Oxygen supply, face masks and nasal cannulae
steps: Receive a structured handover from the anaesthetist including the airway, drugs given and plan.
Check airway, breathing and circulation on arrival and give oxygen.
Attach monitoring and record observations every five minutes initially.
Keep one nurse with the patient until they can maintain their own airway.
Assess and treat pain, nausea and shivering per the anaesthetist's instructions.
Check the surgical site, drains and blood loss.
Monitor regional block regression and motor power where relevant.
Check the temperature and warm the patient if cold.
Score the patient against discharge criteria (such as the Aldrete score).
Call the anaesthetist if criteria are not met or the patient deteriorates.
Hand over to the ward nurse with the recovery chart.
aftercare: Continue ward observations at the frequency instructed.
Ensure analgesia, antiemetics and fluids are prescribed.
red_flags: Airway obstruction or oxygen saturation not maintained
Respiratory depression or excessive sedation
Hypotension, tachycardia or bleeding
Uncontrolled pain
Failure to wake or new neurological deficit

indications: Moderate to severe postoperative pain expected to need parenteral opioid
Severe pain from trauma, burns or sickle cell crisis in suitable patients
contraindications: Patient unable to understand or use the button
No staff trained to monitor PCA or no programmable pump
Severe respiratory disease or obstructive sleep apnoea without extra monitoring
equipment: Dedicated PCA pump with lockable syringe holder
Standard pre-filled or prepared opioid syringe per local protocol, labelled
Dedicated intravenous line with anti-reflux and anti-siphon valves
Opioid reversal agent and antiemetic prescribed
steps: Confirm identity, allergies and that the patient understands and agrees to PCA.
Prescribe the PCA regime from the local standard protocol.
Prepare and label the syringe and have a second practitioner check it.
Program the pump and have the programming independently checked.
Connect through a dedicated line with an anti-reflux valve and lock the pump.
Teach the patient that only they should press the button.
Start the PCA and record baseline sedation score, respiratory rate and pain score.
Prescribe the reversal agent and antiemetic as needed.
aftercare: Record pain, sedation, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation hourly at first, then per protocol.
Review daily by the pain team or anaesthetist and step down to oral analgesia when possible.
Check pump totals and syringe volume at each shift change.
red_flags: Increasing sedation or respiratory rate below the protocol threshold (stop PCA and give reversal agent)
Someone other than the patient pressing the button
Uncontrolled pain despite use
Severe nausea, itching or confusion

indications: Post-dural puncture headache that is severe or persists despite conservative treatment
contraindications: Patient refusal
Fever, sepsis or infection at the site
Coagulopathy or anticoagulant within timing rules
Headache with features suggesting another cause (needs neurological assessment)
equipment: Sterile epidural pack with Tuohy needle and loss-of-resistance syringe
Separate sterile pack and 20 mL syringes for blood collection
Cap, mask, sterile gowns and gloves for two operators
Chlorhexidine skin preparation and local anaesthetic
steps: Confirm the diagnosis, exclude other causes of headache and obtain written consent.
Check temperature, white cell count where indicated and coagulation status.
Position the patient lateral or sitting.
Operator one prepares the back and locates the epidural space at or below the original puncture level.
Operator two prepares the arm with full asepsis and draws venous blood.
Inject the blood slowly through the Tuohy needle until the patient feels back or leg pressure or the target volume is reached.
Remove the needle and apply a dressing.
Keep the patient lying flat for one to two hours.
Reassess the headache before discharge.
aftercare: Advise avoiding heavy lifting and straining for a few days.
Warn about mild back pain for a few days.
Arrange follow-up and a repeat patch if headache returns.
red_flags: Fever, severe back pain or new leg weakness or numbness
Headache not relieved or changing in character (seek neurological review)
Confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness

indications: Chest pain, palpitations, syncope or breathlessness
Suspected arrhythmia, ischaemia or electrolyte disturbance
Hypertension, diabetes or heart disease assessment
Pre-operative assessment when indicated
Monitoring of drugs that affect the QT interval
contraindications: None absolute; delay only if it holds up emergency treatment
equipment: ECG machine with 10 lead cables, calibrated
Disposable electrodes (paediatric size for small children)
Skin preparation (alcohol swab, gauze, razor if needed)
steps: Confirm patient identity, explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and provide privacy, exposing the chest, wrists and ankles.
Lie the patient supine and relaxed, with arms by the sides.
Clean and dry the skin, removing hair where it prevents contact.
Place limb electrodes on the wrists and ankles, or on the proximal limbs if needed.
Place V1 and V2 in the fourth intercostal space either side of the sternum.
Place V4 in the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, V3 between V2 and V4, then V5 and V6 level with V4 at the anterior and mid-axillary lines.
Check that the machine is at standard speed and gain and that the filter settings are recorded.
Ask the patient to stay still and breathe normally, then record the tracing.
Check the tracing for artefact, lead reversal and quality, and repeat if needed.
Label the tracing with name, ID, date, time and symptoms at the time of recording.
Remove electrodes, help the patient dress and pass the tracing for interpretation without delay.
aftercare: Show urgent abnormal tracings to the doctor immediately.
Keep the tracing in the record for comparison with later ECGs.
red_flags: Act immediately on ST elevation, new left bundle branch block or ischaemic changes with chest pain.
Escalate at once for ventricular tachycardia, complete heart block, very fast or very slow rates.
Escalate for a long QT interval or signs of severe hyperkalaemia.

indications: Intermittent palpitations not captured on a resting ECG
Unexplained syncope or presyncope
Atrial fibrillation rate control assessment
Suspected silent arrhythmia after stroke
contraindications: Skin condition or allergy preventing electrode placement
Patient unable to keep the recorder on or return it
equipment: Charged ambulatory recorder with lead set and memory card
steps: Confirm patient identity and explain the purpose, duration and care of the recorder.
Obtain verbal consent and check the recorder battery, memory and time setting.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the chest skin by cleaning and shaving where needed.
Place electrodes in the recommended positions avoiding bone and muscle bulk.
Connect the leads, loop and tape them to reduce pull on the electrodes.
Check the signal quality on the device or software before the patient leaves.
Give the diary and ask the patient to record activities, symptoms and times.
Advise the patient to avoid bathing the device and to continue normal activities.
On return, remove the recorder, collect the diary and download the recording.
Analyse the recording and correlate events with diary symptoms before reporting.
aftercare: Keep the recorder dry and do not remove the electrodes.
Write every symptom in the diary with the time.
Return the recorder on the agreed day.
red_flags: Seek urgent care for fainting, chest pain or sustained palpitations during monitoring, rather than waiting for the result.
Escalate the report promptly if it shows pauses, high-grade heart block or ventricular tachycardia.

indications: Confirming a diagnosis of hypertension
Suspected white-coat or masked hypertension
Assessing treatment response or resistant hypertension
Suspected nocturnal hypertension or hypotensive symptoms
contraindications: Severe uncontrolled hypertension needing immediate treatment
Arm on the side of an arteriovenous fistula or lymphoedema
Bleeding disorder with risk of bruising from repeated cuff inflation (relative)
equipment: Cuffs in correct sizes, including paediatric and large adult
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Measure the arm circumference and choose the correct cuff size, usually on the non-dominant arm.
Take clinic readings in both arms and use the arm with the higher reading if they differ significantly.
Programme the monitor for day and night reading intervals and check the clock.
Fit the cuff with the artery marker over the brachial artery and secure the tubing.
Take a test reading and compare it with a manual reading.
Advise the patient to keep the arm still and relaxed during each reading.
Give the diary for sleep times, activities and symptoms.
On return, remove the device and download the readings.
Check the number of valid readings and report day, night and 24-hour averages and dipping.
aftercare: Carry on usual activities but keep the arm still when the cuff inflates.
Do not shower with the monitor on.
Return the device on the agreed day.
red_flags: Remove the cuff and seek care for arm pain, numbness, swelling or extensive bruising.
Escalate very high averages or symptoms of hypertensive emergency such as severe headache, chest pain or visual loss.

indications: Assessment of suspected stable coronary artery disease
Risk stratification after myocardial infarction
Assessment of exercise capacity or exercise-related symptoms
Evaluation of exercise-induced arrhythmia
contraindications: Acute coronary syndrome within the last few days or unstable angina
Uncontrolled arrhythmia or decompensated heart failure
Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis
Acute myocarditis, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection
Severe uncontrolled hypertension
Inability to walk on a treadmill
equipment: Treadmill or bicycle ergometer with ECG stress system
Trained staff with advanced life support skills
steps: Confirm identity, indication, contraindications and medicines that affect the test, and obtain written consent.
Check that resuscitation equipment and a defibrillator are ready.
Prepare the skin and place electrodes in the exercise configuration.
Record a resting 12-lead ECG and blood pressure standing.
Explain how to walk on the treadmill and how to report symptoms.
Start the chosen protocol and increase the stage at set intervals.
Monitor the ECG continuously and record blood pressure and symptoms at each stage.
Stop the test at target, at patient request, or for ischaemia, arrhythmia, falling blood pressure or severe symptoms.
Record ECG and blood pressure during recovery until they return near baseline.
Remove the electrodes and report exercise time, workload, symptoms, ECG changes and the reason for stopping.
aftercare: Rest until symptoms and observations settle before leaving.
Restart usual medicines as instructed.
Attend clinic for the result and next steps.
red_flags: Stop immediately for chest pain with ST changes, ventricular tachycardia, a fall in systolic BP, or signs of poor perfusion.
Return urgently for chest pain, breathlessness or fainting after the test.

indications: Suspected heart failure or cardiomyopathy
Heart murmur or suspected valve disease, including rheumatic heart disease
Suspected congenital heart disease
Pericardial effusion or suspected tamponade
Suspected endocarditis or cardiac source of embolism
Hypertension with suspected target-organ damage
contraindications: None absolute
equipment: Echocardiography machine with cardiac probe (paediatric probe for small children)
steps: Confirm identity and indication, explain the scan and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and position the patient in the left lateral position with the left arm raised.
Attach the machine ECG leads and enter the patient details.
Obtain parasternal long- and short-axis views.
Obtain apical four-, two- and three-chamber views.
Obtain subcostal and suprasternal views as needed.
Assess chamber sizes, wall thickness and left and right ventricular function.
Assess each valve with colour, pulsed and continuous wave Doppler.
Look for pericardial effusion, intracardiac masses and estimate pulmonary pressure.
Store images and measurements and write a structured report.
Clean the probe and the patient's skin after the scan.
aftercare: Discuss urgent findings with the referring doctor the same day.
Attend clinic for the report and management plan.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for tamponade, very poor ventricular function, large vegetations, intracardiac thrombus or suspected aortic dissection.

indications: Suspected endocarditis or valve abscess with non-diagnostic transthoracic study
Exclusion of left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion or balloon valvotomy
Assessment of prosthetic valve dysfunction
Suspected aortic dissection
Assessment of atrial septal defect before device closure
contraindications: Oesophageal stricture, tumour, perforation, varices or recent oesophageal surgery
Unstable airway or inability to cooperate without airway support
Severe cervical spine disease (relative)
equipment: Echocardiography machine with disinfected TOE probe
Topical throat anaesthetic and sedation per local protocol
Pulse oximeter, blood pressure and ECG monitoring
steps: Confirm identity, indication, fasting status and contraindications, and obtain written consent.
Check probe integrity and disinfection record and test the probe controls.
Insert an intravenous cannula and start continuous monitoring and oxygen.
Remove dentures and apply topical throat anaesthetic.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, procedure and allergies.
Give sedation per local protocol and place the patient in the left lateral position with a bite guard.
Pass the lubricated probe gently through the bite guard while the patient swallows, never forcing it.
Obtain mid-oesophageal, transgastric and upper oesophageal views relevant to the question.
Withdraw the probe gently in neutral position and check it for blood.
Monitor the patient until sedation has worn off and record findings.
Clean and disinfect the probe per protocol and record the cycle.
aftercare: Nothing to eat or drink until the throat numbness has gone.
Do not drive or sign legal papers for the rest of the day after sedation.
Go home with an adult escort.
red_flags: Stop if there is resistance to probe passage, desaturation, arrhythmia or severe distress.
Return urgently for chest or neck pain, vomiting blood, fever or difficulty swallowing after the test.

indications: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with shock, syncope, ischaemia or heart failure
Elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation or flutter
Supraventricular or ventricular tachycardia with a pulse not responding to drugs
contraindications: Digoxin toxicity or severe hypokalaemia (correct first unless life-threatening)
Atrial fibrillation over 48 hours or unknown duration without anticoagulation or thrombus exclusion (elective cases)
Sinus tachycardia or multifocal atrial tachycardia
equipment: Defibrillator with synchronisation mode and ECG monitoring
Self-adhesive defibrillation pads (paediatric pads for small children)
Oxygen, suction, bag-valve-mask and airway equipment
Sedation or anaesthesia drugs per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity and rhythm on a 12-lead ECG where time allows, check potassium and anticoagulation status (and fasting in elective cases), and obtain written consent where possible.
Insert an intravenous cannula, attach monitoring and give oxygen.
Apply pads in anterolateral or anteroposterior position on clean, dry skin.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, rhythm and plan.
Give sedation or anaesthesia with a clinician skilled in airway management present.
Select synchronised mode and confirm sync markers fall on each R wave.
Choose the energy per current resuscitation guidance for the rhythm and the patient's size.
Announce charging, ensure everyone is clear, check oxygen is away from the chest and deliver the shock.
Check the rhythm and pulse, and if still in tachycardia re-synchronise and repeat with increased energy.
Record a 12-lead ECG after the procedure and monitor until fully awake.
aftercare: Continue anticoagulation as prescribed when the indication is atrial fibrillation.
Do not drive or operate machinery for the rest of the day after sedation.
Use simple skin care for any pad burns.
red_flags: If ventricular fibrillation or pulseless rhythm follows, switch off sync and defibrillate per resuscitation guidance.
Escalate for airway compromise, hypotension or bradycardia after the shock.
Return urgently for palpitations, chest pain, weakness of the face or limbs, or speech problems.

indications: Cardiac tamponade
Large pericardial effusion with haemodynamic compromise
Diagnostic sampling of a pericardial effusion, including suspected tuberculous or purulent pericarditis
contraindications: Aortic dissection or traumatic haemopericardium needing surgery (relative; surgery preferred)
Uncorrected coagulopathy or low platelets (relative)
Small, posterior or loculated effusion unsuitable for needle drainage
equipment: Ultrasound or echocardiography machine with sterile probe cover
Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Pericardiocentesis needle or kit with guidewire and pigtail drain
Three-way tap, drainage bag and specimen containers
ECG, blood pressure and pulse oximeter monitoring
steps: Confirm identity, indication and effusion size on echo, and obtain written consent unless in extremis.
Insert intravenous access, attach monitoring and position the patient semi-recumbent.
Use echo to choose the entry site and direction with the largest fluid depth and no intervening structures.
Perform a time-out and prepare the skin with antiseptic under full aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic along the planned track.
Advance the needle slowly along the planned path with continuous aspiration, usually subxiphoid toward the left shoulder or apical.
Stop when fluid is aspirated and confirm position by echo or agitated saline contrast.
Pass the guidewire, dilate the track and place the pigtail drain over the wire.
Aspirate fluid in stages, sending samples for biochemistry, cell count, microbiology including tuberculosis tests, and cytology.
Secure the drain, attach to a closed drainage bag and apply a sterile dressing.
Repeat echo to confirm reduction of the effusion and record observations.
aftercare: Monitor observations and drain output closely in a monitored bed.
Repeat echo before drain removal.
Keep the dressing clean and dry.
red_flags: Stop if the ECG shows ST elevation or arrhythmia, or if aspirate is heavily bloodstained and clots.
Escalate for worsening hypotension, suspected cardiac or vessel puncture, or pneumothorax.
Return urgently for breathlessness, chest pain, fever or fainting after discharge.

indications: Symptomatic bradycardia with poor perfusion not responding to drug treatment
High-grade heart block with instability while awaiting transvenous pacing
contraindications: Asystole without P waves as routine treatment (not effective)
Severe hypothermia-related bradycardia (relative)
equipment: Self-adhesive pacing pads (paediatric pads for small children)
ECG monitoring leads connected to the defibrillator
Analgesia and sedation per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity and bradycardia on the monitor, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent if the patient is able.
Attach the device ECG leads and apply pads in anteroposterior or anterolateral position on clean, dry skin.
Give analgesia and sedation per local protocol if conscious.
Select demand pacing mode and set the rate per current guidance.
Increase current gradually until electrical capture is seen with a wide QRS after each pacing spike.
Confirm mechanical capture by a palpable femoral pulse at the paced rate.
Set the output a little above the capture threshold.
Monitor capture, skin, pain and observations continuously.
Arrange definitive transvenous pacing or referral as soon as possible.
aftercare: Keep the patient in a monitored area with a trained staff member present.
Check the skin under the pads regularly.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for loss of capture, cardiac arrest or worsening shock.
Do not mistake muscle twitching or artefact for capture; always confirm with a pulse.

indications: Symptomatic high-grade heart block or bradycardia not controlled by drugs or transcutaneous pacing
Bradycardia after acute myocardial infarction with instability
Bridge to permanent pacemaker implantation
Overdrive pacing of recurrent tachyarrhythmia
contraindications: Mechanical tricuspid valve
Uncorrected coagulopathy (relative; choose a compressible site)
Active bloodstream infection (relative)
equipment: Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Central venous sheath kit and local anaesthetic
Bipolar temporary pacing wire (balloon-tipped where available)
External pacing box with fresh battery and connecting cable
ECG monitoring and defibrillator with pacing pads
steps: Confirm identity, indication and access site, and obtain written consent unless in an emergency.
Attach monitoring and transcutaneous pacing pads as back-up.
Perform a time-out and prepare the site under full aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and insert a venous sheath, preferably with ultrasound guidance.
Advance the pacing wire to the right ventricular apex or septum under fluoroscopy or echo guidance.
Connect the wire to the pacing box and set demand mode at the chosen rate.
Measure the capture threshold and set the output with a safety margin above it.
Check sensing and confirm a stable position by asking the patient to cough and breathe deeply.
Secure the wire and sheath with sutures and a sterile dressing.
Obtain a chest X-ray to check position and exclude pneumothorax, and record the settings.
aftercare: Check threshold, sensing and the insertion site at least daily.
Keep the patient on continuous ECG monitoring and on bed rest as advised.
Plan permanent pacing or removal as soon as appropriate.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for loss of capture, rising threshold or ventricular arrhythmia.
Escalate for chest pain, hypotension or new pericardial effusion suggesting perforation.
Escalate for fever or site infection.

indications: Symptomatic sinus node dysfunction
Complete or high-grade second-degree heart block
Symptomatic bradycardia with atrial fibrillation
Selected heart failure patients needing cardiac resynchronisation
contraindications: Active infection or fever
Reversible cause of bradycardia not yet corrected
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Pacemaker generator and leads chosen for the indication
Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Local anaesthetic and sedation per local protocol
Introducer sheaths, surgical instruments, sutures and dressing
Defibrillator, back-up pacing and resuscitation trolley
steps: Confirm identity, indication, device type and side, check anticoagulation and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and attach monitoring with back-up pacing available.
Perform a time-out, prepare the skin and drape under full aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and make an infraclavicular incision.
Gain venous access by cephalic cut-down or axillary or subclavian puncture.
Advance the lead or leads to the target position under fluoroscopy.
Measure sensing, threshold and impedance with the analyser and reposition if values are unsatisfactory.
Secure the leads to the muscle with sleeves and sutures.
Form a pocket, connect the leads to the generator and confirm pacing.
Achieve haemostasis, close the wound in layers and apply a dressing.
Programme the device and check a chest X-ray for lead position and pneumothorax.
aftercare: Keep the wound dry and covered as advised and attend wound review.
Avoid lifting the arm above the shoulder on the implant side for the advised period.
Carry the device card and attend the first device check.
Inform staff before MRI and keep phones away from the device.
red_flags: Return urgently for wound swelling, discharge, fever or redness.
Return urgently for dizziness, fainting, persistent hiccups or muscle twitching.
Return for chest pain or breathlessness.

indications: Survived cardiac arrest from ventricular arrhythmia without a reversible cause
Sustained ventricular tachycardia with structural heart disease
Primary prevention in severe left ventricular dysfunction despite optimal treatment
Inherited arrhythmia syndromes at high risk of sudden death
contraindications: Reversible cause of the arrhythmia
Active infection
Life expectancy too short to benefit, or patient does not want the device
equipment: ICD generator and defibrillation lead (plus other leads as needed)
Pacing system analyser and device programmer
Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Local anaesthetic, sedation and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol
Sheaths, surgical instruments, sutures and dressing
steps: Confirm identity, indication, device and side, discuss shocks and driving rules, and obtain written consent.
Apply external defibrillator pads, give prophylactic antibiotic per protocol and attach monitoring.
Perform a time-out, prepare and drape under full aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic, make the incision and gain venous access.
Position the defibrillation lead in the right ventricle under fluoroscopy and add other leads as needed.
Test sensing, threshold, pacing impedance and shock impedance.
Secure the leads, form the pocket and connect the generator.
Perform defibrillation testing only if indicated by local practice, with the anaesthetist present.
Close the wound in layers and apply a dressing.
Programme therapy zones and check a chest X-ray for lead position and pneumothorax.
aftercare: Follow wound and arm movement advice as for a pacemaker.
Carry the device card and attend device clinic follow-up.
Follow driving restrictions as advised.
Teach family what to do if a shock happens.
red_flags: Call for help after more than one shock or a shock with chest pain, breathlessness or collapse.
Return urgently for wound swelling, discharge, redness or fever.

indications: Routine follow-up of a pacemaker or ICD
Symptoms suggesting device malfunction such as dizziness or syncope
After an ICD shock
Before and after surgery, MRI or radiotherapy
contraindications: None absolute
equipment: Device card and previous check records
steps: Confirm identity and device make and model from the device card, and obtain verbal consent.
Attach ECG monitoring and ensure a defibrillator is available.
Place the wand over the device and interrogate it.
Review battery status, lead impedances and stored events or alerts.
Measure sensing and capture thresholds for each lead.
Review pacing percentages and stored arrhythmias or therapies.
Adjust settings if needed and confirm changes are saved.
Print or save the report and record the next check date.
aftercare: Attend the next device check on the date given.
Report dizziness, fainting or shocks promptly.
red_flags: Escalate for battery at elective replacement, lead fracture, loss of capture or recurrent ventricular arrhythmia.
Escalate when the patient is pacing-dependent and a lead problem is found.

indications: Acute coronary syndrome needing invasive assessment
Stable angina with high-risk non-invasive tests or symptoms despite treatment
Assessment of coronary arteries before valve surgery
Unexplained left ventricular dysfunction or survived cardiac arrest
contraindications: Active bleeding or severe uncorrected coagulopathy (relative)
Severe kidney impairment without preparation (relative)
Previous severe contrast reaction without premedication (relative)
Decompensated heart failure, unless the procedure is to treat the cause
equipment: Cardiac catheterisation laboratory with radiation protection
Arterial sheath, guidewires and diagnostic catheters
Contrast medium and manifold with pressure monitoring
Local anaesthetic and sedation per local protocol
Radial compression band or femoral closure device
