Defibrillator, resuscitation trolley and emergency drugs
steps: Confirm identity, indication, allergies, kidney function, anticoagulation and fasting status, and obtain written consent.
Check access pulses, insert an intravenous cannula and attach monitoring.
Perform a time-out and prepare the access site under full aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and insert the arterial sheath, preferably radial and with ultrasound if available.
Give anticoagulation and vasodilator through the radial sheath per local protocol.
Advance the catheter over a guidewire to the aortic root under fluoroscopy.
Engage each coronary artery and take angiograms in standard views while watching pressure.
Perform left ventriculography or measure pressures if indicated.
Remove the catheters and sheath and achieve haemostasis with a band, closure device or manual pressure.
Record findings, contrast volume, radiation dose and the management plan.
aftercare: Rest the access limb and check the site and distal pulse as advised.
Drink fluids to help clear contrast unless restricted.
Avoid heavy lifting with the access limb for a few days.
red_flags: Escalate for chest pain, ST changes, arrhythmia or hypotension during or after the procedure.
Apply pressure and call for help for access site bleeding or expanding swelling.
Return urgently for a cold, painful or numb limb, or reduced urine output.

indications: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (primary PCI)
High-risk non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
Stable angina with significant stenosis despite medical therapy
contraindications: Unable to take antiplatelet therapy after stenting
Active major bleeding
Anatomy better treated by surgery (decided by the heart team)
equipment: Cardiac catheterisation laboratory with radiation protection
Arterial sheath, guiding catheter, coronary guidewires
Balloons and stents of suitable sizes
Inflation device, contrast and manifold with pressure monitoring
Antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs per local protocol
Defibrillator, temporary pacing and resuscitation equipment
Cardiac surgical back-up or a referral pathway
steps: Confirm identity, indication, allergies, kidney function and bleeding risk, and obtain written consent including stent and antiplatelet implications.
Ensure antiplatelet loading has been given per protocol and attach monitoring.
Perform a time-out and obtain arterial access under aseptic technique.
Give anticoagulation per protocol and check its effect where required.
Engage the target artery with a guiding catheter and cross the lesion with a guidewire.
Pre-dilate the lesion with a balloon if needed.
Deploy a stent of suitable size and post-dilate to achieve good expansion.
Take final angiograms to confirm flow and exclude dissection or perforation.
Remove equipment and achieve haemostasis at the access site.
Record lesions treated, devices used, contrast, radiation dose and antiplatelet plan.
aftercare: Never stop antiplatelet medicines without speaking to the cardiologist.
Check the access site and attend cardiac rehabilitation and follow-up.
Stop smoking and follow diet, exercise and risk factor advice.
red_flags: Escalate for recurrent chest pain or ST elevation, suggesting stent thrombosis.
Escalate for hypotension, new pericardial effusion or access site bleeding.
Return urgently for chest pain, breathlessness, black stools or a cold limb.

indications: Confirmation and classification of pulmonary hypertension
Assessment of shunts and heart failure haemodynamics
Assessment before heart transplant or complex valve surgery
Vasoreactivity testing in selected pulmonary hypertension
contraindications: Right heart thrombus or mass
Mechanical tricuspid or pulmonary valve
Active infection or uncorrected coagulopathy (relative)
Left bundle branch block (relative; risk of complete heart block, have pacing ready)
equipment: Catheterisation laboratory with fluoroscopy and pressure recording
Venous sheath and balloon-tipped pulmonary artery catheter
Pressure transducers zeroed at mid-chest level
Blood gas syringes for oxygen saturation runs
Thermodilution or Fick cardiac output equipment
Local anaesthetic, sterile drapes and antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity and indication, review anticoagulation and obtain written consent.
Attach monitoring, perform a time-out and prepare the access site aseptically.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and place a venous sheath with ultrasound guidance.
Zero the transducers at the level of the left atrium.
Advance the balloon-tipped catheter through the right atrium, ventricle and pulmonary artery to wedge position.
Record pressures at each position at end-expiration.
Take blood samples for oxygen saturation in the venous system and pulmonary artery to look for shunts.
Measure cardiac output by thermodilution or Fick method.
Perform vasoreactivity testing if indicated, per local protocol.
Remove the catheter and sheath and apply pressure until haemostasis.
Calculate resistances and record the haemodynamic report.
aftercare: Rest and check the access site as advised.
Attend clinic to discuss results and treatment.
red_flags: Escalate for sustained arrhythmia, haemoptysis suggesting pulmonary artery injury, or hypotension.
Return urgently for bleeding, swelling at the access site, or breathlessness.

indications: Haemodynamic assessment of congenital heart disease before surgery
Assessment of pulmonary vascular resistance and operability
Anatomy not clear on echocardiography
contraindications: Active infection or sepsis
Severe uncorrected anaemia, coagulopathy or electrolyte disturbance
Clinical instability that can first be improved medically
equipment: Paediatric catheterisation laboratory with radiation protection
Pressure transducers and blood gas syringes
Contrast medium dosed by weight per local protocol
Paediatric anaesthesia, warming and airway equipment
Paediatric defibrillator and resuscitation drugs calculated by weight
steps: Confirm identity, weight, diagnosis and fasting, review echo findings and obtain written consent from a parent or guardian.
Check haemoglobin, electrolytes and blood group, and mark the plan with the anaesthetist.
Give anaesthesia or sedation and keep the child warm with monitoring throughout.
Perform a time-out and prepare the groin aseptically.
Insert venous and arterial sheaths with ultrasound guidance where available.
Record pressures and oxygen saturations in each chamber and great vessel.
Perform angiograms in the views needed to define the anatomy.
Calculate shunts and resistances and test with oxygen if needed.
Remove sheaths and apply pressure until haemostasis, then check limb pulses.
Record findings and discuss the plan at the joint cardiology and surgery meeting.
aftercare: Keep the leg straight and check the groin and foot pulses as advised.
Restart feeds when awake and tolerating fluids.
Watch for fever and bleeding at home.
red_flags: Escalate for a cold, pale or pulseless leg after the procedure.
Escalate for arrhythmia, hypotension, desaturation or bleeding.
Return urgently for fever, poor feeding, breathing difficulty or groin swelling.

name: Device closure of patent ductus arteriosus

indications: Haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus with left heart volume overload
Symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus with heart failure or poor growth
Small audible duct for endocarditis prevention per local policy
contraindications: Pulmonary vascular disease with right-to-left ductal shunt
Duct-dependent circulation
Patient too small for the available devices (consider surgical ligation)
Active infection or sepsis
equipment: Sheaths, catheters, guidewires and delivery system
Occlusion devices or coils in a range of sizes
steps: Confirm identity, weight and echo diagnosis, check for infection and obtain written consent from a parent or guardian.
Give anaesthesia or sedation with full monitoring and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform a time-out and obtain femoral venous and, if needed, arterial access.
Record pressures and perform an aortogram to measure duct size and shape.
Choose a device size based on the narrowest duct diameter.
Cross the duct and position the delivery sheath in the descending aorta.
Deploy the device and confirm position by angiography and echo before release.
Release the device and check for residual shunt and obstruction of the aorta or left pulmonary artery.
Remove sheaths, achieve haemostasis and check limb pulses.
Record device type and size and arrange echo follow-up.
aftercare: Keep the leg straight and check the groin as advised.
Avoid strenuous activity for the advised period.
Attend echo follow-up to confirm closure.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for suspected device embolisation, haemolysis (dark urine) or a cold leg.
Return urgently for fever, breathing difficulty or groin swelling.

indications: Secundum atrial septal defect with right heart volume overload
Selected muscular or perimembranous ventricular septal defects suitable for devices
Patent foramen ovale after cryptogenic stroke in selected patients
contraindications: Severe pulmonary vascular disease with right-to-left shunt
Defect with insufficient rims or unsuitable type (primum, sinus venosus) for device closure
Intracardiac thrombus or active infection
equipment: Sizing balloon, sheaths, delivery system and guidewires
Septal occluder devices in a range of sizes
Anticoagulant and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, defect type, rims and size on echo, and obtain written consent.
Give anaesthesia, prophylactic antibiotic and anticoagulation per protocol.
Perform a time-out and obtain femoral venous access aseptically.
Record pressures and measure the defect by echo and, where used, balloon sizing.
Choose a device size suitable for the defect and rims.
Advance the delivery sheath across the defect.
Deploy the left-sided disc, then the right-sided disc, under echo and fluoroscopy guidance.
Perform push-pull testing and check for residual shunt and valve interference before release.
Release the device and confirm a stable position.
Remove the sheath, achieve haemostasis and record device type and size.
aftercare: Take antiplatelet medicines for the advised period.
Avoid contact sports for the advised period.
Attend echo follow-up and keep good dental hygiene.
red_flags: Escalate for suspected device embolisation, new heart block, pericardial effusion or arrhythmia.
Return urgently for chest pain, fainting, breathlessness, palpitations or fever.

indications: Symptomatic moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with favourable valve anatomy
Severe mitral stenosis in pregnancy with symptoms despite medical treatment
contraindications: Left atrial or appendage thrombus
Moderate or severe mitral regurgitation
Heavily calcified valve or commissures, or unfavourable anatomy score
Other severe valve disease or coronary disease needing surgery
equipment: Catheterisation laboratory with fluoroscopy and pressure monitoring
Mitral valvotomy balloon catheter with sizing and inflation equipment
Defibrillator, pericardiocentesis set and surgical back-up or referral pathway
steps: Confirm identity, valve anatomy score and absence of left atrial thrombus on transoesophageal echo, and obtain written consent.
Attach monitoring, give sedation or anaesthesia per protocol and perform a time-out.
Obtain femoral venous and arterial access under aseptic technique.
Record baseline left atrial, ventricular and pulmonary pressures and the mitral gradient.
Perform transseptal puncture under fluoroscopy and echo guidance and give anticoagulation.
Advance the balloon across the mitral valve.
Inflate the balloon in steps, checking the gradient and regurgitation by echo after each inflation.
Stop when the valve area is adequate or regurgitation increases.
Remove the balloon and record final pressures and valve area.
Remove sheaths, achieve haemostasis and check echo for effusion.
aftercare: Continue prophylaxis against rheumatic fever as prescribed.
Continue anticoagulation if in atrial fibrillation.
Attend echo follow-up and antenatal care if pregnant.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for hypotension or effusion suggesting tamponade.
Escalate for severe new mitral regurgitation or signs of stroke.
Return urgently for breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations or weakness.

form.label: Left atrial thrombus excluded on TOE

indications: Moderate or severe valvar pulmonary stenosis
Critical pulmonary stenosis in the newborn
contraindications: Dysplastic valve or supravalvar stenosis unlikely to respond (relative)
Pulmonary atresia without a suitable route (specialist decision)
Active infection
equipment: Sheaths, catheters, guidewires and valvuloplasty balloons in a range of sizes
Anaesthesia, warming and paediatric resuscitation equipment
Prostaglandin infusion available for critical neonatal cases per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, weight and echo diagnosis, and obtain written consent from a parent or guardian.
Give anaesthesia or sedation with monitoring and keep the child warm.
Perform a time-out and obtain femoral venous access aseptically.
Record right ventricular and pulmonary artery pressures.
Perform right ventricular angiography and measure the valve annulus.
Choose a balloon slightly larger than the annulus per current guidance.
Cross the valve with a guidewire and position the balloon across it.
Inflate the balloon briefly until the waist disappears, then deflate quickly.
Repeat pressure measurement and record the residual gradient.
Remove equipment, achieve haemostasis and check limb pulses.
aftercare: Keep the leg straight and check the groin as advised.
Attend echo follow-up.
red_flags: Escalate for hypotension, arrhythmia, severe desaturation or effusion.
Return urgently for fever, breathing difficulty or a cold leg.

indications: Recurrent or loculated pericardial effusion
Purulent pericarditis needing open drainage
Pericardial effusion needing tissue biopsy, such as suspected tuberculosis or malignancy
contraindications: Constrictive pericarditis needing pericardiectomy instead
Patient too unstable for anaesthesia without first needle drainage
equipment: Major or minor surgical set with sternal retractors
Suction, diathermy and drainage tube with underwater seal or bag
Specimen containers for fluid and tissue
Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity, indication and echo findings, and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic and induce anaesthesia carefully, prepared for haemodynamic collapse in tamponade.
Perform a time-out and prepare and drape the chest and abdomen.
Make a subxiphoid incision and excise the xiphoid if needed.
Dissect to the pericardium and open it under direct vision.
Drain the fluid slowly and send samples for biochemistry, microbiology including tuberculosis tests, and cytology.
Excise a piece of pericardium for histology.
Break down loculations gently and wash out if purulent.
Place a drain in the pericardial space and bring it out through a separate stab incision.
Close the wound in layers and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Monitor drain output and observations and repeat echo before drain removal.
Keep the wound clean and attend for the histology result.
red_flags: Escalate for heavy bleeding from the drain, hypotension or recurrence of tamponade.
Return urgently for fever, wound discharge, breathlessness or chest pain.

indications: Symptomatic chronic constrictive pericarditis, including after tuberculosis
Recurrent effusive-constrictive pericarditis not responding to medical treatment
contraindications: Very advanced disease with severe myocardial involvement where risk outweighs benefit (relative)
Active untreated tuberculosis (start treatment first per protocol)
equipment: Cardiac theatre with general anaesthesia and invasive monitoring
Diathermy, suction and cell salvage if available
Chest drains, sternal wires and sutures
Blood products and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis by imaging and haemodynamics, and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic, induce anaesthesia and insert invasive monitoring.
Perform a time-out and prepare and drape the chest.
Perform a median sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy.
Dissect the thickened pericardium off the heart, starting over the ventricles.
Remove pericardium widely between the phrenic nerves, protecting the nerves and coronary vessels.
Release the inferior vena cava and right atrium where constricted, with bypass on standby.
Send pericardium for histology and tuberculosis culture.
Achieve haemostasis, place chest drains and close the chest.
Transfer to intensive care with monitoring.
aftercare: Complete tuberculosis treatment if prescribed.
Follow sternal precautions and attend wound and clinic review.
Follow fluid and salt advice.
red_flags: Escalate for heavy drain output, low cardiac output or arrhythmia after surgery.
Return urgently for fever, wound discharge, sternal clicking, breathlessness or swelling.

indications: Severe symptomatic rheumatic mitral or aortic valve disease
Severe aortic stenosis or regurgitation with symptoms or ventricular dysfunction
Infective endocarditis with heart failure, abscess or uncontrolled infection
Failed previous valve repair or prosthetic valve
contraindications: Severe irreversible pulmonary hypertension or ventricular failure (relative)
Inability to take or monitor anticoagulation when a mechanical valve is planned (choose a tissue valve)
Active untreated dental sepsis or other infection (elective cases)
equipment: Cardiac theatre with cardiopulmonary bypass and perfusion team
Mechanical or tissue prostheses with sizers
Cardioplegia and myocardial protection per local protocol
Blood products, chest drains, pacing wires and sternal wires
steps: Confirm identity, valve(s) to be replaced and prosthesis type, and obtain written consent including anticoagulation and pregnancy implications.
Give prophylactic antibiotic, induce anaesthesia and insert invasive monitoring and a TOE probe.
Perform a time-out and prepare and drape the chest.
Perform a median sternotomy and open the pericardium.
Cannulate, start cardiopulmonary bypass and arrest the heart with cardioplegia.
Open the atrium or aorta, excise the diseased valve and debride calcium or infected tissue.
Size the annulus and implant the prosthesis with interrupted sutures.
Close the atrium or aorta, de-air the heart and wean from bypass.
Check prosthesis function and leaks on TOE.
Place pacing wires and chest drains, achieve haemostasis and close the chest.
Transfer to intensive care with monitoring.
aftercare: Take anticoagulation exactly as prescribed and attend INR checks as instructed.
Continue rheumatic fever prophylaxis if prescribed.
Keep good dental hygiene and tell dentists about the valve.
Seek advice before pregnancy.
red_flags: Escalate for heavy drain output, tamponade, low cardiac output or arrhythmia after surgery.
Return urgently for fever, breathlessness, a change in valve clicks, stroke symptoms or bleeding.

indications: Left main or three-vessel coronary disease, especially with diabetes or reduced ventricular function
Coronary disease unsuitable for PCI
Coronary disease needing surgery at the time of valve surgery
contraindications: No suitable target vessels or conduits
Severe comorbidity where risk outweighs benefit (heart team decision)
equipment: Cardiac theatre with cardiopulmonary bypass and perfusion team (or off-pump stabilisers)
Sternotomy set and coronary microsurgical instruments
Conduit harvesting instruments for internal mammary artery, vein and radial artery
Fine sutures, shunts and magnification loupes
Blood products, chest drains, pacing wires and sternal wires
steps: Confirm identity, angiogram and graft plan, and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic, induce anaesthesia and insert invasive monitoring.
Perform a time-out and prepare and drape the chest and legs.
Perform a median sternotomy and harvest the internal mammary artery.
Harvest vein or radial artery conduits at the same time.
Cannulate and start bypass with cardioplegic arrest, or stabilise the heart for off-pump surgery.
Perform distal anastomoses to each target coronary artery.
Perform proximal anastomoses to the aorta and de-air the grafts.
Wean from bypass and check graft flow where possible and ventricular function on TOE.
Place pacing wires and chest drains, achieve haemostasis and close the chest and leg wounds.
Transfer to intensive care with monitoring.
aftercare: Take antiplatelet, statin and other heart medicines as prescribed.
Follow sternal precautions and attend cardiac rehabilitation.
Stop smoking and control blood pressure, diabetes and diet.
red_flags: Escalate for heavy drain output, new ST changes, low cardiac output or arrhythmia after surgery.
Return urgently for chest pain, breathlessness, fever, wound discharge or sternal clicking.

name: Surgical ligation of patent ductus arteriosus

indications: Significant patent ductus arteriosus in a preterm infant after failed or contraindicated medical closure
Large patent ductus arteriosus with heart failure where device closure is unavailable or unsuitable
contraindications: Duct-dependent circulation
Pulmonary vascular disease with right-to-left shunt
equipment: Theatre or neonatal unit set-up with paediatric anaesthesia
Warming, monitoring and pre- and post-ductal pulse oximetry
Blood available and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, weight and echo diagnosis, and obtain written consent from a parent or guardian.
Give anaesthesia with warming and monitoring including pre- and post-ductal saturations.
Perform a time-out and position the baby right side down.
Perform a left posterolateral thoracotomy and retract the lung.
Identify the aorta, left pulmonary artery, recurrent laryngeal nerve and the duct.
Test-occlude the duct and confirm the descending aortic pulse and saturations are maintained.
Ligate or clip the duct, protecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Re-expand the lung, insert a drain if needed and close the chest in layers.
Check for pneumothorax on chest X-ray and record the procedure.
aftercare: Monitor breathing, feeding and the wound.
Watch for hoarse cry or feeding problems.
Attend echo follow-up.
red_flags: Escalate for low blood pressure, rising oxygen need or pneumothorax after surgery.
Escalate for a weak cry, stridor or choking on feeds.
Return urgently for fever, wound redness or breathing difficulty.

name: Total correction of tetralogy of Fallot

indications: Tetralogy of Fallot, usually electively in infancy
Older child or adult with uncorrected or palliated tetralogy of Fallot
contraindications: Severely hypoplastic pulmonary arteries (staged palliation first)
Active infection or brain abscess
equipment: Paediatric cardiac theatre with cardiopulmonary bypass and perfusion team
Sternotomy set and paediatric cardiac instruments
Patch material for ventricular septal defect and outflow tract
Hegar dilators for pulmonary valve and arteries
Blood products, drains and pacing wires
steps: Confirm identity, weight, anatomy on echo or catheter, and obtain written consent from a parent or guardian.
Give prophylactic antibiotic and anaesthesia, avoiding triggers for hypercyanotic spells.
Perform a time-out and prepare and drape the chest.
Perform median sternotomy, take down any previous shunt and start cardiopulmonary bypass.
Arrest the heart and resect obstructing right ventricular outflow muscle.
Close the ventricular septal defect with a patch, avoiding the conduction tissue.
Relieve pulmonary valve stenosis by valvotomy or a transannular patch as needed.
Close the atrial communication if present, de-air and wean from bypass.
Measure right ventricular and left ventricular pressures and check for residual defect on echo.
Place pacing wires and drains, achieve haemostasis and close the chest.
Transfer to paediatric intensive care.
aftercare: Attend long-term cardiology follow-up into adulthood.
Keep good dental hygiene and follow endocarditis advice.
Follow sternal precautions and wound care.
red_flags: Escalate for low cardiac output, junctional tachycardia or heart block after surgery.
Return urgently for fever, breathlessness, poor feeding, palpitations or fainting.

form.label: RV to LV pressure ratio after repair

indications: Cyanotic congenital heart disease with reduced pulmonary blood flow not suitable for early repair
Duct-dependent pulmonary circulation in the newborn
contraindications: Pulmonary arteries too small for a shunt
Anatomy suitable for primary complete repair
equipment: Paediatric cardiac theatre with anaesthesia and monitoring
Thoracotomy or sternotomy set with fine vascular instruments
Synthetic graft tubes in suitable sizes
steps: Confirm identity, weight and anatomy, and obtain written consent from a parent or guardian.
Give anaesthesia with careful monitoring of oxygen saturation and blood pressure.
Perform a time-out and prepare and drape the chest.
Approach by thoracotomy or median sternotomy.
Dissect the subclavian or innominate artery and the branch pulmonary artery.
Give anticoagulation per protocol and apply clamps.
Sew the graft end-to-side to the systemic artery and then to the pulmonary artery.
Release the clamps and check the thrill and rise in oxygen saturation.
Stop any ductal prostaglandin as planned, achieve haemostasis and close.
Transfer to intensive care and start antiplatelet treatment per protocol.
aftercare: Give antiplatelet medicine every day as prescribed.
Watch for a drop in oxygen levels or blue spells.
Attend cardiology review and plan for complete repair.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for sudden fall in saturation, suggesting shunt blockage.
Escalate for pulmonary over-circulation with low diastolic blood pressure or poor perfusion.
Return urgently for increased blueness, breathlessness, poor feeding, vomiting or diarrhoea.

indications: ST-elevation myocardial infarction or new left bundle branch block within the treatment window when timely primary PCI is not available
contraindications: Any previous intracranial haemorrhage or recent ischaemic stroke
Known intracranial tumour or vascular malformation
Suspected aortic dissection
Active bleeding or bleeding disorder
Recent major surgery, head injury or trauma
Severe uncontrolled hypertension (relative)
Previous streptokinase exposure or allergy (do not use streptokinase again)
equipment: Two intravenous cannulas and infusion pump
Fibrinolytic agent and adjunctive antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, symptom onset time and ST elevation on the 12-lead ECG.
Work through the contraindication checklist and explain benefits and bleeding risk to obtain verbal consent.
Attach continuous ECG monitoring with a defibrillator at the bedside.
Insert intravenous cannulas and take blood for tests without delaying treatment.
Give antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment per local protocol.
Give the fibrinolytic agent per local protocol, recording the door-to-needle time.
Monitor blood pressure, rhythm and for bleeding or allergic reaction throughout.
Repeat the ECG at the time set in the protocol to assess ST resolution.
Refer for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails, or for routine angiography where available.
aftercare: Stay on the monitored ward or coronary care unit.
Take heart medicines as prescribed and attend cardiac rehabilitation.
Report any bleeding or black stools.
red_flags: Stop the infusion and escalate for sudden headache, confusion, weakness or reduced consciousness.
Stop and escalate for major bleeding, anaphylaxis or severe hypotension.
Escalate for ongoing chest pain or less than half ST resolution for rescue PCI.

indications: Stable narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia
Diagnosis of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability (use synchronised cardioversion)
Carotid sinus massage in children, or with a carotid bruit, recent stroke or transient ischaemic attack
Valsalva with recent myocardial infarction, severe aortic stenosis or glaucoma (relative)
equipment: Continuous ECG monitoring with rhythm strip recording
Couch that can be laid flat with leg raise
Bag of iced water for the diving reflex in infants
steps: Confirm identity and a narrow-complex tachycardia with a stable patient, and obtain verbal consent.
Attach continuous ECG monitoring and record a rhythm strip throughout.
For the modified Valsalva, sit the patient semi-recumbent and ask them to blow into a syringe to move the plunger for about 15 seconds.
Immediately lie the patient flat and raise the legs for about 15 seconds.
In infants, apply a bag of iced water briefly to the face without blocking the airway.
In adults only, if used, perform carotid sinus massage on one side only for a few seconds after auscultating for bruits.
Watch the monitor for slowing or termination and record the rhythm.
Repeat once if unsuccessful, then move to drug treatment or cardioversion per protocol.
aftercare: Record a 12-lead ECG after termination.
Learn the Valsalva manoeuvre for future episodes.
Attend cardiology follow-up if episodes recur.
red_flags: Stop and escalate for pauses, bradycardia, hypotension or neurological symptoms.
Escalate for broad-complex tachycardia or deterioration.
Return urgently for palpitations with chest pain, fainting or breathlessness.

indications: Recurrent unexplained syncope with suspected reflex (vasovagal) cause
Suspected orthostatic hypotension or postural tachycardia syndrome
Distinguishing syncope from seizures or psychogenic attacks
contraindications: Severe aortic stenosis or left ventricular outflow obstruction
Severe coronary disease or recent myocardial infarction
Severe cerebrovascular disease
Pregnancy
equipment: Motorised tilt table with foot board and safety straps
Continuous ECG and beat-to-beat or frequent blood pressure monitoring
Defibrillator, resuscitation trolley and emergency drugs
steps: Confirm identity, indication, fasting and medicines, and obtain written consent.
Insert an intravenous cannula, attach monitoring and secure the patient with straps.
Record baseline heart rate and blood pressure after a period lying flat.
Tilt the table head-up to the protocol angle.
Record heart rate, blood pressure and symptoms at regular intervals during the passive phase.
Give provocation per local protocol if the passive phase is negative.
Return the table flat immediately at syncope or severe symptoms and record the response.
Monitor until heart rate, blood pressure and symptoms recover.
Classify the response and write the report.
aftercare: Rest and drink fluids before leaving.
Do not drive for the rest of the day.
Follow advice about fluids, salt and counter-pressure manoeuvres if given.
red_flags: Return flat at once for loss of consciousness, prolonged asystole or severe hypotension.
Escalate for chest pain, arrhythmia or failure to recover quickly when flat.

indications: Tooth unrestorable from caries or fracture
Advanced periodontal disease with hopeless mobility
Retained or over-retained primary tooth
Orthodontic extraction as planned
Source of infection not treatable by root canal treatment or not affordable to the patient
contraindications: Uncontrolled bleeding disorder or anticoagulation not reviewed
Recent head and neck radiotherapy or antiresorptive therapy without specialist plan
Uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes, or recent myocardial infarction
Acute spreading infection with trismus or airway risk (treat infection and refer)
equipment: Local anaesthetic cartridges, dental syringe and needles
Elevators and extraction forceps suited to the tooth
steps: Confirm identity, the tooth to be removed against the chart and radiograph, medical history and written consent.
Check blood pressure and ask about bleeding disorders, anticoagulants and allergies.
Perform hand hygiene, wear protective equipment and have the patient rinse with antiseptic mouthwash.
Perform a time-out to confirm the correct tooth and side.
Give topical then local anaesthetic by infiltration or nerve block and confirm numbness.
Detach the gingival cuff around the tooth with an elevator or periosteal instrument.
Luxate the tooth with an elevator, using a finger rest and supporting the alveolus.
Apply forceps well apically and remove the tooth with controlled movements suited to the root form.
Inspect the tooth to confirm the roots are complete.
Inspect the socket, remove debris and squeeze the socket walls together.
Place a gauze pack and ask the patient to bite firmly for at least 30 minutes.
Confirm haemostasis before discharge and give written aftercare advice.
aftercare: Bite on the gauze for 30 minutes and do not rinse vigorously for the first day.
From the next day rinse gently with warm salt water after meals.
Avoid smoking, alcohol and sucking through straws for at least two days.
Eat soft cool foods and chew on the other side.
Take pain relief as advised.
If bleeding restarts, bite on a clean folded gauze or cloth for 20 minutes.
red_flags: Stop and reassess or refer if the root fractures deep or close to the sinus or nerve canal.
Escalate if bleeding continues despite pressure and sutures.
Return for bleeding that does not stop, swelling of the face or neck, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or fever.
Return for severe pain starting two to four days after extraction (possible dry socket).
Return if fluid passes from mouth to nose after an upper back tooth extraction.

indications: Retained root or fractured tooth not removable with forceps
Tooth with curved, divergent or ankylosed roots
Failed simple extraction
Heavily restored or root-filled brittle tooth
contraindications: Uncontrolled bleeding disorder or anticoagulation not reviewed
Recent head and neck radiotherapy or antiresorptive therapy without specialist plan
Unstable systemic illness
equipment: Local anaesthetic cartridges, dental syringe and needles
Scalpel handle with blade, periosteal elevator and retractors
Surgical handpiece with sterile irrigation, or chisel and mallet
Needle holder, scissors and resorbable sutures
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, radiograph, medical history and written consent.
Perform hand hygiene, surgical asepsis and a time-out confirming tooth and side.
Give local anaesthetic and confirm numbness.
Raise a mucoperiosteal flap with a scalpel incision and periosteal elevator.
Remove buccal bone as needed with a bur under saline irrigation.
Section the tooth into roots if needed to allow separate delivery.
Elevate and deliver the tooth or root fragments.
Check the fragments are complete and compare with the radiograph.
Smooth sharp bone edges, irrigate the socket and remove debris.
Replace the flap and close with sutures.
Place a pressure pack and confirm haemostasis before discharge.
aftercare: Bite on the gauze for 30 minutes and avoid rinsing on the first day.
Use cold packs on the face for the first day to reduce swelling.
Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals from the next day.
Avoid smoking for at least two days.
Take pain relief and any prescribed medicines as advised.
Return for suture removal or review if non-resorbable sutures were used.
red_flags: Stop and refer if the root is displaced into the sinus or soft tissues or lies close to the nerve canal.
Return for bleeding that will not stop, spreading swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or fever.
Return for numbness of the lip or tongue that persists after the anaesthetic has worn off.
Return if fluids pass from mouth to nose.

name: Surgical removal of impacted third molar

indications: Recurrent pericoronitis
Caries in the third molar or distal caries of the second molar
Cyst, tumour or resorption associated with the impacted tooth
Periodontal disease distal to the second molar
Tooth in a fracture line or before radiotherapy
contraindications: Acute pericoronitis with trismus (treat first, operate later)
Asymptomatic deeply impacted tooth with high nerve injury risk
Uncontrolled bleeding disorder or unstable systemic illness
equipment: Panoramic radiograph showing relation to the inferior alveolar canal
Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Scalpel, periosteal elevator, Ward or Minnesota retractor and lingual retractor
Surgical handpiece with burs and sterile saline irrigation
Elevators (Coupland, Warwick James, Cryer) and forceps
Needle holder, scissors and resorbable sutures
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, radiograph assessment of impaction and nerve relation, and written consent including nerve injury risk.
Perform surgical hand antisepsis, drape and carry out a time-out.
Give inferior alveolar, lingual and long buccal anaesthesia and confirm numbness.
Raise a buccal mucoperiosteal flap and protect the lingual tissues.
Remove buccal and distal bone with a bur under constant saline irrigation.
Section the crown and roots as needed according to the impaction pattern.
Elevate and deliver the tooth segments with controlled force.
Check all segments are removed and the follicle is curetted.
Smooth bone edges, irrigate thoroughly and inspect for nerve exposure.
Replace the flap and close with sutures.
Place a pressure pack and confirm haemostasis.
Record the procedure and give written aftercare advice.
aftercare: Bite on gauze for 30 minutes and avoid rinsing on the first day.
Apply cold packs for the first day then warm salt water rinses after meals.
Expect swelling and stiffness peaking around day two to three.
Eat soft foods and avoid smoking for at least two days.
Take pain relief and any prescribed medicines as advised.
Attend review in about one week.
red_flags: Stop and refer if the root is intimately related to the nerve canal and full removal risks nerve injury (consider coronectomy).
Return urgently for swelling spreading to the neck or floor of mouth, difficulty swallowing or breathing.
Return for bleeding that will not stop, fever or worsening pain after day three.
Return for numbness of the lip, chin or tongue persisting beyond the next day.

indications: Calculus and plaque deposits
Gingivitis
Periodontal maintenance
Before other dental treatment or prosthesis
contraindications: Ultrasonic scaler in patients with older unshielded cardiac pacemakers (use hand scaling)
Uncontrolled bleeding disorder (hand scaling with care after review)
equipment: Ultrasonic scaler with water supply, or hand scalers and curettes
Mouth mirror, probe and periodontal probe
Low-speed handpiece with prophylaxis cup or brush and polishing paste
Protective eyewear for patient and operator
steps: Confirm identity, medical history and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment, and ask the patient to rinse with antiseptic mouthwash to reduce aerosol load.
Record a basic periodontal examination score for each sextant.
Remove supragingival calculus systematically sextant by sextant with the ultrasonic or hand scaler.
Remove accessible subgingival calculus with light overlapping strokes.
Check all surfaces with a probe for remaining calculus.
Polish the teeth with a cup and paste to remove stain and plaque.
Rinse and suction debris.
Give oral hygiene instruction with brushing and interdental cleaning.
aftercare: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and clean between the teeth.
Expect mild gum tenderness or sensitivity for a few days.
Attend recall as advised.
red_flags: Stop if there is excessive bleeding and check for a bleeding disorder.
Refer for specialist periodontal care if deep pockets or bone loss are found.
Return if gums swell, bleed persistently or a gum abscess develops.

indications: Caries in posterior teeth where amalgam is the agreed material
Replacement of a failed restoration in a load-bearing posterior site
contraindications: Known amalgam allergy
Pregnancy, breastfeeding or children under 15 where alternatives exist (follow national Minamata guidance)
Anterior teeth where appearance matters
equipment: High- and low-speed handpieces with burs, or hand excavators
Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Cotton rolls, suction or rubber dam
Matrix band and retainer with wedges
Amalgam carrier, condensers, carvers and burnisher
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, diagnosis with radiograph if available, and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment.
Give local anaesthetic if needed and isolate the tooth.
Gain access and remove caries, keeping the cavity within amalgam retention principles.
Check for pulp exposure and place a liner in deep cavities.
Place a matrix band and wedge for cavities involving contact surfaces.
Triturate encapsulated amalgam and condense it in small increments.
Carve the anatomy, remove the matrix and check the margins.
Check and adjust the occlusion with articulating paper.
Dispose of amalgam waste in the sealed mercury container.
aftercare: Avoid chewing hard food on the filling for a few hours.
Expect mild sensitivity to cold for a few days.
Return for polishing if advised.
red_flags: Stop and plan pulp treatment if there is a carious pulp exposure in a symptomatic tooth.
Return for persistent or spontaneous pain, pain on biting or a high feeling filling.

indications: Caries or fracture in anterior or posterior teeth
Replacement of failed restorations
Repair of non-carious tooth wear or small fractures
contraindications: Inability to achieve moisture control
Very large posterior cavities with heavy load (consider other options)
Allergy to resin components
equipment: High- and low-speed handpieces with burs
Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Rubber dam or cotton rolls with suction
Etchant, bonding agent and composite resin of matched shade
Matrix strips or sectional matrix with wedges
Finishing burs, discs and polishing strips
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, diagnosis and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment.
Select the shade before isolation while the tooth is moist.
Give local anaesthetic if needed and isolate the tooth.
Remove caries and prepare the cavity conservatively.
Place a liner over very deep areas if needed.
Place a matrix for proximal cavities.
Etch, rinse, dry and apply bonding agent per the manufacturer and light cure.
Place composite in small increments and light cure each layer.
Remove the matrix, finish margins and polish.
Check and adjust the occlusion.
aftercare: Expect mild sensitivity for a few days.
Avoid staining foods and drinks for the first day.
Keep up good oral hygiene to protect the margins.
red_flags: Stop and plan pulp treatment if there is a pulp exposure in a symptomatic tooth.
Return for persistent pain, pain on biting, a high bite or a lost filling.

indications: Caries in primary teeth
Atraumatic restorative treatment where electricity or handpieces are not available
Root surface or cervical caries
Interim restoration in high-caries-risk patients
contraindications: Large load-bearing posterior cavities in permanent teeth needing a definitive restoration
Tooth with signs of irreversible pulpitis or abscess (needs pulp treatment or extraction)
equipment: Hand excavators and enamel hatchet (ART), or handpieces and burs
Petroleum jelly or varnish for surface protection
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, diagnosis and verbal consent from the patient or parent.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment.
Isolate the tooth with cotton rolls and keep it dry.
Widen the opening and remove soft caries with hand excavators, starting at the enamel-dentine junction.
Leave firm affected dentine over the pulp where removal risks exposure.
Wash and condition the cavity, then rinse and dry without desiccating.
Mix the glass ionomer and fill the cavity and adjacent pits and fissures.
Press with a gloved finger coated in petroleum jelly and remove excess.
Check the bite and adjust high spots.
Coat the surface with petroleum jelly or varnish.
aftercare: Do not eat for at least one hour.
Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and reduce sugary snacks.
Attend review to check the restoration.
red_flags: Stop and reassess if there is pulp exposure, swelling or a sinus (needs pulp treatment or extraction).
Return for pain, swelling or loss of the filling.

indications: Irreversible pulpitis
Pulp necrosis or periapical periodontitis in a restorable tooth
Elective treatment before a post-retained crown
contraindications: Unrestorable tooth or inadequate periodontal support
Vertical root fracture
Patient unable to attend multiple visits or afford the final restoration (discuss extraction)
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Endodontic files (hand or rotary) and apex locator if available
Irrigation syringes with side-vented needles and irrigant per protocol
Intracanal medicament and temporary filling material
Spreaders or pluggers and heat source
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, diagnosis with radiograph, prognosis and written consent including cost and number of visits.
Perform hand hygiene, give local anaesthetic and isolate with rubber dam.
Remove caries and existing restorations and prepare an access cavity.
Locate all canal orifices.
Establish working length with an apex locator if available and confirm with a radiograph.
Shape the canals with files while irrigating generously between instruments.
Dry the canals with paper points.
If symptoms or exudate persist, place an intracanal medicament and temporary seal and complete at a later visit.
Obturate the canals with gutta-percha and sealer to working length.
Take a radiograph to check the quality of the root filling.
Seal the access with a temporary or definitive coronal restoration.
aftercare: Expect tenderness on biting for a few days.
Avoid chewing hard foods on the tooth until the final restoration is placed.
Return for the definitive restoration or crown as planned, as unrestored teeth fracture.
red_flags: Stop and refer if a file separates, a perforation occurs or canals cannot be negotiated.
Stop immediately if irrigant is extruded with severe pain or swelling and manage as an emergency.
Return for facial swelling, fever or severe persistent pain.

indications: Carious or traumatic pulp exposure in a vital primary molar without signs of irreversible pulpitis
Vital young permanent tooth with open apex and limited exposure (partial pulpotomy)
contraindications: Spontaneous or night pain, swelling, sinus or abnormal mobility
Radiographic root resorption or furcation radiolucency
Pulp bleeding that cannot be controlled after amputation
Unrestorable tooth
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Rubber dam or cotton rolls with suction
High- and low-speed handpieces with burs
Pulpotomy medicament (MTA or similar per local protocol)
Glass ionomer or zinc oxide eugenol base
Preformed metal crown kit for primary molars
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, diagnosis with radiograph and written consent from the parent.
Perform hand hygiene, give local anaesthetic and isolate the tooth.
Remove all caries and unroof the pulp chamber.
Amputate the coronal pulp with a sterile excavator or slow-speed round bur.
Apply a moist sterile cotton pellet with light pressure to achieve haemostasis.
Abandon pulpotomy and plan pulpectomy or extraction if bleeding does not stop within a few minutes.
Place the pulpotomy medicament over the radicular pulp stumps.
Seal with a base material.
Restore the tooth, preferably with a preformed metal crown.
Check the occlusion.
aftercare: Avoid chewing on the numb side until feeling returns, and watch that the child does not bite the lip.
Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste.
Attend clinical and radiographic review at the advised intervals.
red_flags: Stop if pulp bleeding is uncontrolled or the pulp is necrotic, and change the treatment plan.
Return for pain, swelling, a gum boil or increasing mobility.

indications: Irreversible pulpitis or pulp necrosis in a restorable primary tooth with adequate root length
Failed pulpotomy where the tooth can be kept
contraindications: Advanced root resorption or permanent successor close to eruption
Extensive furcation bone loss or perforated pulp floor
Unrestorable tooth
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Rubber dam or cotton rolls with suction
Irrigation syringes and irrigant per protocol
Resorbable root canal filling paste for primary teeth
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, radiograph and written consent from the parent.
Perform hand hygiene, give local anaesthetic and isolate the tooth.
Remove caries and gain access to the pulp chamber.
Locate the canals and remove the pulp tissue with files.
Establish working length short of the radiographic apex to protect the successor.
Clean the canals gently with files and irrigation.
Dry the canals with paper points.
Fill the canals with a resorbable paste using a lentulo spiral or syringe.
Seal the chamber and restore with a preformed metal crown or other durable restoration.
Take a radiograph to check the fill.
aftercare: Expect mild tenderness for a few days.
Watch that the child does not bite the numb lip or cheek.
Attend review at the advised intervals.
red_flags: Stop and plan extraction if the floor is perforated or roots are largely resorbed.
Return for swelling, fever, gum boil or pain.

indications: Caries-free or early non-cavitated pits and fissures in permanent molars and premolars of high-risk patients
Deep fissures in primary molars of high-risk children
contraindications: Cavitated caries into dentine (needs restoration)
Partially erupted tooth where moisture control is impossible (consider glass ionomer sealant)
equipment: Cotton rolls, dry guards and suction
Resin sealant or glass ionomer sealant
steps: Confirm identity, the teeth to seal and verbal consent from the patient or parent.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment.
Clean the fissures with a dry brush or pumice.
Isolate the tooth and keep it completely dry.
Etch the fissures, rinse thoroughly and dry until frosty white.
Re-etch if saliva contaminates the surface.
Apply sealant into the fissures without air bubbles.
Light cure for the recommended time.
Check retention with a probe and adjust the occlusion.
aftercare: Eat and drink normally after leaving.
Continue brushing with fluoride toothpaste.
Attend recall for sealant check.
red_flags: Stop and restore instead if a cavity into dentine is found.
Return if the sealant feels rough or comes off.

indications: Children and adults at moderate or high caries risk
Early enamel caries (white spot lesions)
Dentine hypersensitivity
Patients with orthodontic appliances or dry mouth
contraindications: Ulcerative gingivitis or stomatitis
Known allergy to varnish components (for example colophony)
steps: Confirm identity, caries risk and verbal consent from the patient or parent.
Perform hand hygiene and wear gloves.
Position a young child knee-to-knee with the parent if needed.
Wipe the teeth dry with gauze, one area at a time.
Paint a thin layer of varnish on all tooth surfaces, focusing on at-risk areas.
Use only the single-use pack amount appropriate to the dentition.
Allow the varnish to set on contact with saliva.
Give oral hygiene and diet advice.
aftercare: Do not eat or drink for 30 minutes and eat soft food for the rest of the day.
Do not brush the teeth until the next morning.
Repeat application at the advised interval.
red_flags: Stop if the patient has an allergic reaction or is distressed and wipe off the varnish.
Return if mouth swelling or rash develops.

form.label: Diet and oral hygiene advice given

indications: Arrest of cavitated caries in primary teeth in young or uncooperative children
Root caries in older adults
Caries management where restorative care is not available
contraindications: Silver allergy
Ulcerative gingivitis or stomatitis
Tooth with pulpal involvement, swelling or sinus
equipment: Petroleum jelly to protect lips and gingiva
steps: Confirm identity, teeth to treat and verbal consent, showing the parent that treated caries turns permanently black.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment.
Protect the lips and adjacent gingiva with petroleum jelly.
Isolate the tooth with cotton rolls and dry the lesion.
Apply the solution to the lesion only with a microbrush for about one minute.
Remove excess with gauze or cotton.
Optionally cover with glass ionomer or fluoride varnish.
Record treated lesions on the chart.
aftercare: Avoid eating or drinking for 30 minutes.
Expect the treated area to turn black, which shows the caries is arrested.
Attend review for reapplication as advised.
red_flags: Stop and plan other treatment if the tooth has pain, swelling or a sinus.
Return for gum irritation that does not settle in a few days.

name: Incision and drainage of dental abscess

indications: Fluctuant dentoalveolar or periodontal abscess
Localised facial swelling of dental origin with pus collection
contraindications: Spreading cellulitis involving the floor of mouth, neck or orbit (admit, secure airway and refer to maxillofacial surgery)
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Sterile saline and syringe for irrigation
Corrugated or rubber drain and suture
steps: Confirm identity, the causative tooth, airway status and written consent.
Assess for trismus, difficulty swallowing, breathing difficulty, fever and floor-of-mouth swelling and escalate if present.
Perform hand hygiene and wear protective equipment.
Give local anaesthetic around rather than into the abscess.
Incise the most dependent fluctuant point parallel to nerves and vessels.
Open the cavity with artery forceps to break loculations and drain pus.
Send a pus swab for culture if available.
Irrigate the cavity with saline.
Place a drain and secure it with a suture if the cavity is large.
Remove the cause by extraction or opening the pulp chamber when possible.
aftercare: Rinse with warm salt water frequently.
Take prescribed medicines and pain relief as advised.
Return in one to two days for drain removal and review.
Complete definitive treatment of the causative tooth.
red_flags: Stop and refer urgently if swelling extends to the floor of mouth, neck or eye, or the patient cannot swallow or breathe easily.
Return immediately for spreading swelling, high fever, voice change or drooling.
Return if swelling does not reduce within two days.

indications: Severe throbbing pain two to four days after extraction with an empty socket and bare bone
contraindications: Signs of spreading infection, retained root or fracture needing other treatment
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Sterile saline or antiseptic irrigant in a blunt syringe
Socket dressing material (resorbable or iodoform-based per local protocol)
Periapical radiograph if a retained fragment is suspected
steps: Confirm identity, extraction history and symptoms, and obtain verbal consent.
Examine the socket and exclude retained root, fracture or infection.
Give local anaesthetic if needed.
Irrigate the socket gently with warm saline or antiseptic to remove debris.
Avoid vigorous curettage of the socket walls.
Dry the socket gently and pack loosely with the dressing material.
Give pain relief advice and instructions for home irrigation.
aftercare: Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals.
Take pain relief as advised.
Avoid smoking until healed.
Return for dressing change in two to three days if pain persists.
red_flags: Refer or investigate if pain persists beyond two weeks or there is numbness, swelling or exposed dead bone.
Return for fever, spreading swelling or pus.

indications: Bleeding from an extraction socket not controlled by biting on gauze
contraindications: None absolute; if bleeding is severe or the patient is shocked, resuscitate and escalate first
equipment: Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor per local protocol, dental syringe and needles
Oxidised cellulose, gelatin sponge or other haemostatic dressing
Needle holder, scissors and resorbable sutures
Tranexamic acid mouthwash if per local protocol
Blood tubes for full blood count and clotting tests
steps: Confirm identity, check pulse and blood pressure, and assess blood loss and airway.
Ask about bleeding disorders, liver disease, anticoagulants and alcohol use.
Seat the patient upright, perform hand hygiene and clear clots with suction.
Identify the bleeding source (soft tissue or bone) under good light.
Apply firm pressure with folded gauze for 15 to 20 minutes.
If bleeding continues, give local anaesthetic and place a haemostatic dressing in the socket.
Close the socket with horizontal mattress sutures across the margins.
Apply pressure again and confirm bleeding has stopped.
Send blood tests and seek medical review if a bleeding disorder is suspected.
Keep the patient for observation until bleeding has stopped for at least 30 minutes.
aftercare: Rest with the head raised and avoid hot drinks and vigorous rinsing for a day.
Bite on folded gauze for 20 minutes if oozing restarts.
Avoid smoking and alcohol.
red_flags: Escalate urgently for signs of shock, airway compromise or bleeding not controlled by sutures and packing.
Refer for haematology review if a bleeding disorder or anticoagulant excess is suspected.
Return immediately if heavy bleeding restarts.

name: Splinting of avulsed or mobile teeth

indications: Avulsed permanent tooth suitable for replantation
Luxated or mobile permanent teeth after trauma
Root fracture with mobile coronal fragment
contraindications: Avulsed primary teeth (do not replant)
Severely damaged or non-viable tooth or alveolus
Severe medical condition or immunosuppression where replantation risk outweighs benefit
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Extraction forceps for holding the crown
Flexible wire or nylon line splint material
Etchant, bonding agent and composite resin
Suture kit for soft tissue lacerations
steps: Confirm identity, mechanism and time of injury, extra-oral time and storage medium, tetanus status and consent.
Exclude head injury, other facial fractures and inhaled or swallowed teeth.
Hold an avulsed tooth by the crown only and rinse the root gently with saline without scrubbing.
Give local anaesthetic and irrigate the socket with saline.
Replant the avulsed tooth with gentle finger pressure, or reposition luxated teeth.
Confirm position clinically and with a radiograph.
Bond a flexible splint to the injured tooth and one or two healthy teeth on each side.
Suture gingival lacerations.
Check the occlusion and adjust if needed.
Plan the splint duration and endodontic review according to injury type.
aftercare: Eat a soft diet and avoid biting on the splinted teeth.
Brush gently with a soft toothbrush and use antiseptic mouthwash.
Take prescribed medicines and confirm tetanus protection.
Return for splint removal and pulp vitality checks as scheduled.
red_flags: Refer for head injury signs, facial fractures or a missing tooth that may have been inhaled.
Return for pain, swelling, discolouration of the tooth or loosening of the splint.

indications: Extensively restored or weakened tooth
Root-treated posterior tooth
Fractured tooth with adequate remaining structure
Severe discolouration or wear
contraindications: Untreated caries, pulpal or periodontal disease
Insufficient tooth structure for retention without a core
Poor oral hygiene not yet controlled
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
High-speed handpiece with crown preparation burs
Impression trays and material or digital scanner
Temporary crown material and temporary cement
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, treatment plan, cost, laboratory time and written consent.
Check the tooth is restorable, root canal treated if needed, and has a sound core.
Select the shade and take a pre-preparation impression for the temporary crown.
Give local anaesthetic if the tooth is vital.
Reduce the tooth to the required thickness for the crown material with a defined finish line.
Place retraction cord and take a definitive impression.
Record the bite and send laboratory instructions.
Make and cement a temporary crown.
At the fit visit, remove the temporary and try in the crown for fit, contacts, margins and occlusion.
Cement the crown, remove excess cement and floss the contacts.
Check the occlusion again.
aftercare: Avoid sticky or hard foods on the temporary crown.
Clean around the crown margin with brushing and floss.
Return if the temporary crown comes off.
Attend regular reviews.
red_flags: Stop and plan root canal treatment if the tooth shows pulpal symptoms during preparation.
Return for persistent pain, a loose crown or a high bite.

indications: Replacement of one or two missing teeth with healthy adjacent abutment teeth
contraindications: Abutment teeth with poor periodontal support, untreated caries or poor prognosis
Long spans or poor oral hygiene
Active periodontal disease
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Shade guide and bite registration material
Temporary bridge material and temporary cement
steps: Confirm identity, the span, abutment teeth, plan, cost and written consent.
Check abutments clinically and radiographically and treat any disease first.
Select the shade and take a pre-preparation impression for the temporary.
Give local anaesthetic and prepare the abutments with a common path of insertion.
Place retraction cord and take a definitive impression and bite record.
Fit a temporary bridge.
At the fit visit, try in the bridge for fit, margins, pontic contact and occlusion.
Cement the bridge and remove excess cement.
Teach cleaning under the pontic with superfloss or threaders.
Check the occlusion.
aftercare: Clean under the pontic daily with superfloss or threaders.
Avoid very hard or sticky foods.
Attend regular reviews.
red_flags: Return for a loose bridge, pain in an abutment tooth or bleeding gums around the bridge.

indications: Complete loss of teeth in one or both arches
contraindications: Unhealed extraction sockets or untreated oral lesions
Patient unable to tolerate or care for a denture
equipment: Stock impression trays and impression material
Bite registration aids, Willis gauge or ruler
Shade and mould guide for teeth
Pressure indicating paste and acrylic burs
steps: Confirm identity, examine the ridges and soft tissues, and agree the plan, cost and number of visits.
Take primary impressions in stock trays.
Take secondary impressions in special trays with border moulding.
Record the occlusal vertical dimension, centric relation and lip support with wax rims.
Select tooth shade and mould with the patient.
Try in the waxed denture to check appearance, speech, occlusion and patient approval.
At the fit visit, insert the dentures and check retention, stability and extensions.
Use pressure indicating paste to find and relieve pressure areas.
Check and adjust the occlusion.
Teach insertion, removal, cleaning and night-time removal.
aftercare: Remove dentures at night and keep them in water.
Clean dentures daily with a brush and soap or denture cleaner, and brush the gums.
Expect some soreness and difficulty speaking and eating for the first weeks.
Return for easing at the scheduled review.
red_flags: Return for an ulcer that does not heal within two weeks after easing (needs examination for other causes).
Return for severe soreness, a broken denture or a loose fit.

indications: Missing teeth in an arch where fixed options are unsuitable or unaffordable
contraindications: Untreated caries or periodontal disease in remaining teeth
Poor oral hygiene not yet controlled
equipment: Stock impression trays and impression material
Acrylic burs and pressure indicating paste
steps: Confirm identity, examine the remaining teeth and soft tissues, and agree the plan, cost and visits.
Treat caries and periodontal disease first.
Take primary impressions and survey the study models to plan the design.
Prepare rest seats and guide planes if the design needs them.
Take definitive impressions and record the bite.
Select the tooth shade.
Try in the framework or wax try-in and check fit and appearance.
At the fit visit, insert the denture and check retention, clasps and pressure areas.
Adjust the occlusion.
Teach insertion, removal and cleaning of the denture and abutment teeth.
aftercare: Remove the denture at night and clean it daily.
Brush the natural teeth carefully, especially those the clasps touch.
Return for review and easing.
red_flags: Return for ulcers not healing in two weeks after easing.
Return for a broken clasp, loose denture or pain in clasped teeth.

indications: Malocclusion needing correction (crowding, spacing, overjet, crossbite, open bite) with an agreed treatment plan
contraindications: Poor oral hygiene or active caries
Active periodontal disease
Patient or parent not committed to long-term attendance
equipment: Records (photographs, study models, panoramic and cephalometric radiographs)
Brackets, bands and archwires, or removable appliance from laboratory
steps: Confirm identity, treatment plan, duration, cost and written consent from the patient and parent.
Check oral hygiene and caries status and delay if poor.
For a fixed appliance, clean the tooth surfaces with pumice, isolate and dry.
Etch, prime and bond brackets in the planned positions and light cure.
Fit bands if planned and cement them.
Insert the initial archwire and ligate.
For a removable appliance, try it in, adjust clasps and springs, and check comfort.
Check that nothing traumatises the soft tissues and provide wax.
Teach oral hygiene, diet restrictions and appliance care.
aftercare: Expect aching for a few days after fitting and each adjustment.
Brush carefully around brackets after every meal and use fluoride mouthwash if advised.
Avoid hard, sticky and sugary foods.
Wear a removable appliance as instructed.
Attend adjustment appointments regularly.
red_flags: Return for a broken bracket, poking wire or ulcer.
Return if a removable appliance no longer fits or is lost.

indications: Early loss of a primary molar where the space is likely to close before the successor erupts
contraindications: Successor absent or erupting soon
Poor oral hygiene or high caries activity not controlled
Child or parent unable to attend review
equipment: Pliers and scaler for cement removal
steps: Confirm identity, the space, successor development on radiograph and verbal consent from the parent.
Select and fit a band on the abutment tooth.
Take an impression with the band in place and send to the laboratory, or use a prefabricated design.
At the fit visit, try in the appliance and check the loop does not impinge on gingiva.
Dry the abutment and cement the band with glass ionomer.
Remove excess cement and check the occlusion.
Teach cleaning around the appliance.
aftercare: Avoid sticky sweets and hard foods.
Brush carefully around the band.
Attend review every few months until the successor erupts.
red_flags: Return if the appliance becomes loose, bent or digs into the gum.

indications: Persistent periapical lesion after adequate root canal treatment where retreatment is not possible
Post or crown that cannot be removed with ongoing periapical disease
Biopsy of a periapical lesion
contraindications: Tooth with poor periodontal support or vertical root fracture
Root end close to the inferior alveolar nerve or sinus without specialist skills
Uncontrolled systemic disease
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Surgical handpiece and burs with sterile saline irrigation
steps: Confirm identity, tooth, radiographs and written consent.
Perform surgical asepsis and a time-out.
Give local anaesthetic.
Raise a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap.
Locate the root apex and remove overlying bone under irrigation.
Curette the periapical lesion and send tissue for histology.
Resect about 3 mm of the root end perpendicular to the long axis.
Prepare a root-end cavity and place a root-end filling.
Take a radiograph to confirm the resection and filling.
Irrigate, replace the flap and suture.
aftercare: Apply cold packs for the first day.
Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals.
Take pain relief and any prescribed medicines as advised.
Return for suture removal and review with radiographs.
red_flags: Stop and refer if the sinus is entered widely or the nerve is at risk.
Return for spreading swelling, fever, persistent numbness or bleeding.

indications: Gingival overgrowth from drugs, hereditary fibromatosis or chronic inflammation
False pockets not resolving after scaling
Aesthetic crown lengthening where bone level allows
contraindications: Inadequate attached gingiva or pockets extending beyond the mucogingival junction
Bony defects needing flap surgery
Poor oral hygiene not yet controlled
equipment: Periodontal probe and pocket marking forceps
Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Gingivectomy knives or scalpel, or electrosurgery unit
steps: Confirm identity, area, medical and drug history and written consent.
Perform hand hygiene and give local anaesthetic.
Probe and mark the pocket depths with bleeding points.
Make a continuous external bevel incision apical to the marks.
Remove the excised tissue and send it for histology if the cause is unclear.
Scale and plane the exposed root surfaces.
Recontour the gingiva to a natural scalloped form.
Control bleeding with pressure.
Place a periodontal dressing if used.
aftercare: Avoid brushing the area for the first days and use antiseptic mouthwash as advised.
Eat soft food and avoid hot spicy food.
Return for dressing removal and review in about one week.
red_flags: Stop if bone is exposed widely or the incision goes beyond attached gingiva.
Return for bleeding that will not stop, fever or severe pain.

indications: Thick or low labial frenum causing a persistent midline diastema after canine eruption
Frenum pulling on the gingival margin with recession
Frenum interfering with denture stability or oral hygiene
contraindications: Diastema in young children before permanent canines erupt (review later)
Bleeding disorder not reviewed
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
steps: Confirm identity, indication and written consent from the patient or parent.
Perform hand hygiene and give local anaesthetic infiltration around the frenum.
Retract the lip to tense the frenum.
Clamp the frenum with artery forceps at its depth.
Excise the frenum above and below the forceps.
Release fibres attached to the periosteum between the central incisors.
Undermine the wound edges and close with sutures.
Control bleeding with pressure.
aftercare: Eat soft food and keep the lip still for a day.
Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals.
Return for review and orthodontic follow-up if a diastema is being closed.
red_flags: Return for bleeding that will not stop, swelling or fever.

indications: Sharp or irregular alveolar ridge after extractions
Bony undercuts or prominences preventing denture fit
contraindications: Thin ridge where bone removal would compromise denture support
Recent head and neck radiotherapy or antiresorptive therapy without specialist plan
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
Rongeurs, bone file and surgical handpiece with burs
steps: Confirm identity, area, denture plan and written consent.
Perform surgical asepsis and give local anaesthetic.
Raise a mucoperiosteal flap over the ridge.
Remove sharp edges and undercuts conservatively with rongeurs, file or bur under irrigation.
Palpate through the flap to check the ridge is smooth.
Irrigate, trim excess soft tissue and close with sutures.
Apply pressure for haemostasis.
aftercare: Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals from the next day.
Do not wear dentures over the area until advised.
Return for suture removal and denture planning.
red_flags: Stop if the sinus or nerve canal is approached.
Return for bleeding, spreading swelling, fever or numbness.

indications: Diagnosis of caries, periapical or periodontal disease
Assessment before extraction, root canal treatment or surgery
Trauma, impacted teeth or jaw pathology
contraindications: Possible pregnancy where the image is not clinically justified
No clear clinical justification (avoid routine screening exposures)
equipment: Intraoral X-ray unit or panoramic unit
Digital sensor, phosphor plate or film with processing facilities
Lead apron or thyroid collar per local rules
Barrier covers for sensors and holders
steps: Confirm identity, clinical justification and the views requested.
Ask female patients of childbearing age about pregnancy.
Remove glasses, earrings, dentures and metal objects from the head and neck.
Apply a thyroid collar where it will not obstruct the view.
Position the sensor with a holder and align the tube, or position the patient in the panoramic unit using the guide lights.
Ask the patient to keep still and stand clear behind the barrier while exposing.
Process the image and check quality.
Repeat only if the image is non-diagnostic, recording the reason.
Report the findings in the record.
aftercare: No special aftercare is needed.
red_flags: Refer or escalate urgently if the image shows a suspected tumour, fracture or large cyst.

indications: Oral ulcer, lump or white or red patch persisting beyond two to three weeks
Suspected oral cancer or potentially malignant disorder
Diagnosis of mucosal disease
contraindications: Suspected vascular lesion (needs imaging first)
Bleeding disorder not reviewed
Highly suspicious lesion where direct referral to a cancer team is available
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion, its photograph and measurement, and written consent.
Perform hand hygiene and give local anaesthetic around, not into, the lesion.
Choose the most representative area including the margin with normal tissue.
Take an elliptical incisional sample of adequate depth, or excise a small lesion completely.
Handle the tissue gently without crushing.
Place the specimen in formalin and label it at the chairside.
Close the wound with sutures.
Control bleeding with pressure.
Complete the request form with history and clinical diagnosis.
Arrange follow-up for the result.
aftercare: Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals.
Eat soft food and avoid spicy food for a few days.
Return for the result and suture review.
red_flags: Refer urgently to a maxillofacial or cancer team for a malignant result or a lesion highly suspicious of cancer.
Return for bleeding that will not stop or spreading swelling.

indications: Anterior dislocation of the mandibular condyle with an open locked jaw
contraindications: Associated mandibular or condylar fracture (image first and refer)
equipment: Panoramic radiograph if fracture is suspected or reduction fails
Barrel or crepe bandage for jaw support
Sedation and monitoring equipment if needed
steps: Confirm identity, history of the dislocation and verbal consent, and exclude trauma-related fracture.
Reassure the patient and seat them upright and low with the head supported.
Wrap the thumbs in gauze and place them on the lower molars or external oblique ridges, fingers under the jaw.
Press firmly downward and then backward to move the condyles over the eminence.
Reduce one side at a time if both sides do not reduce together.
Withdraw the thumbs quickly to the side as the jaw closes.
If muscle spasm prevents reduction, use local anaesthetic into the joint area or sedation, and refer if still not reduced.
Confirm normal occlusion and mouth closure.
Apply a supporting bandage if advised.
aftercare: Avoid wide mouth opening and support the chin when yawning for several weeks.
Eat a soft diet.
Take pain relief as advised.
red_flags: Stop and refer if a fracture is suspected or reduction fails after sedation.
Refer recurrent dislocations to a maxillofacial surgeon.
Return if the jaw locks open again.

indications: Closed treatment of mandibular or maxillary fractures
Temporary occlusal fixation during open reduction
contraindications: Airway compromise or inability to protect the airway with jaws wired
Uncontrolled seizures, severe vomiting or psychiatric illness without supervision
Insufficient teeth for fixation (consider other methods)
Head injury with reduced consciousness or unexcluded cervical spine injury (stabilise first)
equipment: Arch bars or eyelet wires and stainless steel wire
Wire cutters, wire twisters and needle holders
Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles, or general anaesthesia
Suction (including portable suction for the ward)
Wire cutters to stay with the patient
steps: Confirm identity, fracture type on radiographs, airway assessment and written consent.
Perform a time-out and secure anaesthesia, with nasal intubation if under general anaesthesia.
Clean the teeth and remove debris.
Adapt the arch bars to the upper and lower arches.
Fix the arch bars to the teeth with circumdental wires, twisting them tight.
Reduce the fracture and bring the teeth into the patient's normal occlusion.
Apply fixation wires or elastics between the arch bars.
Check occlusion and fracture reduction.
Turn wire ends away from the soft tissues.
Confirm reduction with a post-procedure radiograph.
Attach wire cutters to the bedside and teach staff when to cut the wires.
aftercare: Keep wire cutters with the patient at all times.
Take a fluid or blended diet and maintain nutrition.
Clean the mouth with brushing and antiseptic mouthwash after meals.
Attend weekly review and planned removal date.
red_flags: Cut the fixation wires or elastics immediately if the patient vomits with airway risk or cannot breathe.
Return for loose wires, malocclusion, swelling, fever or weight loss.

indications: Completed fracture healing period after intermaxillary fixation
Infection, loosening or complications needing early removal
contraindications: Clinically non-united fracture (review and image first)
equipment: Local anaesthetic, dental syringe and needles
steps: Confirm identity, healing time and fracture union clinically and on radiograph, and obtain verbal consent.
Remove the inter-arch wires or elastics and check fracture stability and occlusion.
Give local anaesthetic if needed.
Cut each circumdental wire and unwind it carefully.
Remove the arch bars.
Check that all wire fragments are removed.
Inspect the gingiva and teeth and clean the mouth.
Assess mouth opening and give exercises.
aftercare: Eat a soft diet for a few more weeks.
Do mouth-opening exercises as shown.
Brush and use antiseptic mouthwash.
red_flags: Return for mobility at the fracture site, change in bite, swelling or pus.

name: Open reduction and internal fixation of mandible

indications: Displaced or unstable mandibular fracture
Fracture unsuitable for closed treatment
Edentulous or comminuted fractures needing fixation
contraindications: Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
Severe uncontrolled infection at the fracture site (drain and stabilise first)
equipment: Panoramic radiograph and CT if available
Mandibular plating set with miniplates and screws
Arch bars or IMF screws for temporary occlusion
Scalpel, periosteal elevators, retractors and bone clamps
steps: Confirm identity, fracture pattern on imaging, head and cervical spine injury excluded, written consent and anaesthetic review.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist and nasal intubation.
Prepare and drape the face and mouth.
Apply temporary intermaxillary fixation to establish the occlusion.
Expose the fracture through an intraoral or extraoral approach, protecting the mental nerve and facial nerve branches.
Clean the fracture ends and remove teeth in the fracture line only if indicated.
Reduce the fracture anatomically.
Fix with miniplates along the lines of ideal osteosynthesis.
Release temporary fixation and confirm the occlusion is correct.
