Irrigate and close in layers.
Obtain a post-operative radiograph.
aftercare: Eat a soft diet for several weeks.
Clean the mouth carefully and use antiseptic mouthwash.
Take prescribed medicines as advised.
Attend review for wound check and radiograph.
red_flags: Escalate for airway swelling, bleeding or haematoma after surgery.
Return for change in bite, wound discharge, exposed plate, fever or numbness getting worse.

indications: Displaced zygomatic complex or arch fracture with cosmetic deformity
Restricted mouth opening from arch impingement on the coronoid
Altered sensation or visual disturbance from displacement
contraindications: Undiagnosed eye injury or reduced vision (ophthalmology review first)
Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
steps: Confirm identity, imaging, eye examination including visual acuity, and written consent.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist under general anaesthesia.
Shave if needed and make a temporal incision within the hairline.
Dissect down to the deep temporal fascia and incise it.
Pass the elevator deep to the fascia beneath the arch or zygoma.
Lift the fragment outward and forward while protecting the skull with the other hand.
Palpate the contour and check reduction.
Fix with plates if the fracture is unstable.
Close the wound in layers.
Check eye movements and pupils on waking.
aftercare: Avoid pressure on the cheek and sleep on the other side.
Avoid nose blowing if the sinus is involved.
Take prescribed medicines as advised.
Attend review with eye check.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for reduced vision, eye pain, increasing proptosis or a tense eye (retrobulbar haemorrhage).
Return for double vision, swelling increasing or wound discharge.

indications: Unilateral or bilateral cleft lip, usually at about three months of age when well and gaining weight
contraindications: Child unwell, anaemic or not gaining weight
Unassessed associated anomalies (cardiac or syndromic)
equipment: General anaesthesia with paediatric airway equipment
Cleft lip set with fine scalpels, scissors, hooks and tweezers
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, cleft type, weight, haemoglobin, feeding status and written consent from the parents.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist and secure the airway.
Mark the repair landmarks with calipers and pen.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor.
Incise along the markings and release the abnormal muscle attachments.
Repair the nasal floor and correct the nasal deformity as planned.
Repair the orbicularis oris muscle to restore continuity.
Close the mucosa and skin in layers, aligning the vermilion border precisely.
Clean the wound and apply ointment.
Apply arm splints if the unit uses them.
aftercare: Resume feeding as advised by the cleft team using the recommended method.
Keep the wound clean and apply ointment as advised.
Stop the child from rubbing or putting objects in the mouth.
Attend the cleft team review, including hearing, speech and dental follow-up.
red_flags: Escalate for breathing difficulty, bleeding or poor feeding with dehydration.
Return for wound breakdown, fever or discharge.

indications: Cleft palate, usually repaired at about 9 to 12 months of age before speech develops
contraindications: Child unwell, anaemic or not gaining weight
Airway problems such as Pierre Robin sequence not yet assessed
equipment: General anaesthesia with oral RAE tube
Cleft palate set with elevators, fine scissors and needle holders
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, cleft type, weight, haemoglobin, airway assessment and written consent from the parents.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist and intubate.
Place the mouth gag and check ventilation remains good.
Place a throat pack and record that it is in, to be removed and counted before extubation.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor.
Incise and raise mucoperiosteal flaps, protecting the palatine vessels.
Release and reposition the velar muscles to form a muscle sling.
Close the nasal layer, then the muscle, then the oral layer.
Pack lateral releasing incisions if used.
Check for bleeding and release the gag periodically.
Place a tongue stitch if airway support is needed after extubation.
aftercare: Feed fluids and soft food as advised and avoid hard objects in the mouth.
Rinse with water after feeds.
Monitor breathing closely the first night.
Attend speech therapy and cleft team follow-up.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for airway obstruction, desaturation or significant bleeding.
Return for poor feeding, fever, bleeding or a hole in the palate.

indications: Benign aggressive jaw tumour such as ameloblastoma or myxoma
Malignant tumour of the jaw or oral cavity invading bone
contraindications: Patient unfit for major surgery
Unresectable disease or distant spread (palliative pathway)
equipment: General anaesthesia with secured airway (tracheostomy set available)
Major head and neck set with oscillating saw and drill
Reconstruction plate and screws or graft materials
steps: Confirm identity, histology, imaging, multidisciplinary plan, cross-match and written consent including reconstruction and appearance.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist and secure the airway, with tracheostomy if planned.
Pre-bend the reconstruction plate on the intact jaw before resection if using one.
Expose the tumour through the planned intraoral or extraoral approach.
Resect the jaw with planned margins in healthy bone and soft tissue.
Orient and label the specimen and send it for histology.
Achieve haemostasis.
Reconstruct with plate, graft or flap as planned, or place an obturator for maxillectomy.
Close in layers over drains.
Plan post-operative airway care and nutrition.
aftercare: Feed by the planned route, often tube feeding initially.
Keep the mouth clean with careful rinses.
Attend review for histology, reconstruction and obturator or prosthetic planning.
Attend long-term follow-up for recurrence.
red_flags: Escalate for airway compromise, bleeding, flap colour change or haematoma.
Return for wound breakdown, plate exposure, fever or a new swelling.

indications: Radicular, dentigerous or other jaw cysts confirmed or suspected on radiograph
contraindications: Very large cyst where enucleation risks jaw fracture or damage to vital structures (consider marsupialisation first)
Suspected vascular lesion before aspiration
equipment: Surgical handpiece with burs and sterile saline irrigation
steps: Confirm identity, imaging, plan and written consent including nerve injury and fracture risk.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist or time-out.
Aspirate the lesion to exclude a vascular lesion before opening.
Raise a mucoperiosteal flap.
Remove bone to create a window over the cyst.
Separate the cyst lining from the bone and remove it intact where possible.
Remove or treat the associated tooth as planned.
Inspect the cavity for remnants and irrigate.
Send the lining for histology.
Close the flap, or suture the lining to the mucosa and pack the cavity if marsupialising.
aftercare: Rinse gently with warm salt water after meals.
Eat soft food and avoid hard chewing to protect the jaw.
Attend review with radiographs to confirm bone healing.
red_flags: Stop and pack if aspiration shows fresh blood under pressure (suspected vascular lesion) and refer.
Return for jaw pain on chewing, change in bite, swelling, discharge or numbness.

indications: Necrotic tissue and sequestrated bone in acute or subacute noma once the patient is resuscitated
contraindications: Unresuscitated or severely malnourished child (stabilise, feed and treat infection first)
equipment: Anaesthesia appropriate to the child's condition
Scissors, tweezers, curettes and bone rongeurs
Specimen pots for culture if available
steps: Confirm identity, nutritional status, HIV and malaria status, and written consent from the guardian.
Ensure fluids, nutrition and prescribed antimicrobials have been started per national noma guidelines.
Perform hand hygiene and full protective precautions.
Give appropriate anaesthesia or analgesia.
Remove only clearly dead soft tissue conservatively, preserving viable tissue.
Remove loose sequestra and loose teeth in the necrotic area.
Irrigate the wound thoroughly.
Apply moist dressings.
Start mouth-opening physiotherapy early to prevent trismus.
Notify the case to noma surveillance per national reporting.
aftercare: Clean the wound and change dressings as instructed.
Continue nutritional rehabilitation and feeding support.
Continue jaw exercises daily.
Attend the noma or maxillofacial team for reconstruction planning.
red_flags: Escalate for shock, worsening sepsis, bleeding or airway compromise.
Return for spreading necrosis, fever, refusal to feed or worsening jaw stiffness.

indications: Facial defects after healed noma
Trismus or ankylosis from noma scarring
contraindications: Active noma or unhealed wounds
Malnutrition or anaemia not yet corrected
Difficult airway without advanced airway support available
equipment: Fibreoptic or awake intubation capability and tracheostomy set
Clinical photographs and CT if available
Flap planning materials and Doppler if available
Bone cutting instruments for ankylosis release
steps: Confirm identity, healed status, nutrition, haemoglobin, plan and written consent including staged surgery.
Plan the airway with the anaesthetist, including fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy.
Perform the WHO surgical safety checklist.
Release scar bands and any bony ankylosis to restore mouth opening.
Excise scar tissue at the defect margins.
Reconstruct inner lining, bone support and outer cover with planned local, regional or free flaps.
Achieve haemostasis and check flap perfusion.
Close donor sites and place drains.
Place mouth props if trismus was released.
aftercare: Watch flap colour and warmth as advised.
Follow tube or liquid feeding as planned.
Do mouth-opening exercises with props for months to prevent relapse.
Attend staged surgery and follow-up.
red_flags: Escalate for airway compromise, flap colour change, bleeding or haematoma.
Return for wound breakdown, fever or loss of mouth opening.

indications: Gaping tongue lacerations, those through the edge or tip, or with ongoing bleeding
Flaps or lacerations larger than about 1 cm
contraindications: Small non-gaping lacerations which heal well without sutures
Uncooperative child where safe repair needs general anaesthesia (refer)
equipment: Gauze for holding the tongue, or a traction suture
steps: Confirm identity, mechanism, airway, other injuries (teeth, jaw, head) and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and position with good light and suction.
Place a mouth prop to protect the operator.
Give local anaesthetic by infiltration or lingual nerve block.
Hold the tongue with gauze or a traction suture.
Irrigate and inspect for foreign bodies such as tooth fragments.
Close full-thickness wounds in layers, taking deep bites through muscle.
Align the tongue edge accurately.
Confirm haemostasis.
aftercare: Eat soft food and rinse with warm salt water after meals.
Expect the sutures to dissolve within one to two weeks.
Take pain relief as advised.
red_flags: Escalate for airway swelling, uncontrolled bleeding or a large haematoma.
Return for swelling, fever, pus or wound opening.

indications: Diagnosis of inflammatory skin disease (rash of unclear cause)
Suspected skin tumour or pigmented lesion where excision is not practical
Suspected cutaneous infection needing tissue culture
Diagnosis of blistering disease (with perilesional sample for immunofluorescence)
contraindications: Active infection at the biopsy site unless infection is the diagnosis
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Suspected melanoma where excisional biopsy is possible
Sites over superficial nerves or arteries without experience
equipment: Local anaesthetic, 2-5 mL syringe and 25-30 G needle
Antiseptic solution, sterile gloves, drape and gauze
Fine-toothed forceps, curved iris scissors or scalpel
Specimen pot with formalin and labelled request form (saline or transport medium for culture)
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion to be sampled and verbal consent, and ask about bleeding disorders and anticoagulants.
Choose the most representative active lesion and mark it, avoiding the face, shin and joints where possible.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the site with antiseptic and put on sterile gloves.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic under the site and wait for it to take effect.
Stretch the skin perpendicular to the relaxed skin tension lines so the defect becomes elliptical.
Press the punch into the skin with a twisting motion down to subcutaneous fat.
Lift the core gently by its base with forceps or a needle without crushing it and cut it free at the fat.
Place the specimen in the labelled pot straight away.
Control bleeding with pressure and close the defect with one or two sutures, or leave small defects to heal.
Apply a dressing and complete the histology request with a clear clinical history.
aftercare: Keep the dressing dry for 24-48 hours, then wash gently daily.
Remove sutures at 5-7 days on face, 10-14 days on trunk and limbs.
Give the date and route for collecting the histology result.
red_flags: Bleeding that does not stop with 15 minutes of firm pressure
Increasing redness, pain, swelling or pus at the site
Fever after the procedure
Histology showing malignancy (arrange prompt review)

indications: Raised (exophytic) lesions such as seborrhoeic keratosis or intradermal naevus
Suspected superficial basal cell carcinoma or actinic keratosis
Removal of benign raised lesions for diagnosis and cosmetic reasons
contraindications: Suspected melanoma (needs full-thickness excision)
Flat or deep lesions where the diagnosis depends on depth
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Scalpel with size 15 blade or flexible razor blade
Local anaesthetic, 2 mL syringe and 30 G needle
Specimen pot with formalin and request form
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion and verbal consent, and check that the lesion is not suspicious for melanoma.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the area with antiseptic and put on gloves.
Inject local anaesthetic just beneath the lesion to raise it above the surrounding skin.
Hold the blade almost parallel to the skin and shave beneath the lesion with a smooth sawing motion.
Remove the lesion in one piece at the level of the mid dermis.
Place the specimen in formalin and label it.
Achieve haemostasis with pressure, a topical haemostatic agent or light electrocautery.
Apply a non-adherent dressing.
aftercare: Keep the wound covered and moist with petroleum jelly until healed (usually 1-2 weeks).
Warn that a flat pale or dark mark may remain, especially in dark skin.
Arrange review with the histology result.
red_flags: Persistent bleeding despite pressure
Signs of infection (spreading redness, pus, fever)
Lesion regrowth or histology showing malignancy at the deep margin

indications: Suspected melanoma or changing pigmented lesion
Small lesion where complete removal is diagnostic and curative
Suspected skin cancer needing full-depth assessment
Deep lesions such as panniculitis needing a fat sample
contraindications: Lesion too large to close primarily (refer for flap or graft)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Local infection at the site
Keloid-prone patient at high-risk sites unless benefit outweighs risk
equipment: Sterile minor surgery set (scalpel handle, size 15 blade, toothed forceps, skin hook, scissors, needle holder)
Local anaesthetic (with or without adrenaline per site), 5-10 mL syringe and 25-27 G needle
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gloves and gauze
Absorbable sutures for deep layer and non-absorbable sutures for skin
Specimen pot with formalin and request form
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion, site marking and written consent, and ask about anticoagulants and keloid history.
Mark an ellipse three times as long as wide along the relaxed skin tension lines with a 2 mm margin around the lesion.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare the skin with antiseptic and drape it.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the ellipse.
Do a time-out confirming patient, site and procedure.
Incise along the marking vertically through the full dermis into subcutaneous fat.
Lift the ellipse with a skin hook and excise it at an even depth in the fat.
Orient the specimen with a suture if margins matter and place it in formalin.
Undermine the wound edges if needed and secure haemostasis.
Close deep dead space with absorbable sutures and the skin with interrupted or subcuticular sutures.
Apply a dressing and complete the histology request with the clinical details.
aftercare: Keep the dressing dry for 48 hours, then clean gently daily.
Give simple analgesia and advise rest of the area to reduce tension on the wound.
Remove sutures at 5-7 days on the face and 10-14 days on trunk and limbs.
Review with the histology result and plan further treatment if margins are involved.
red_flags: Expanding swelling or bleeding through the dressing (haematoma)
Wound opening, pus or spreading redness
Fever or severe pain
Histology showing melanoma or other malignancy (refer urgently)

indications: Symptomatic or disfiguring keloid not responding to intralesional steroid alone
Earlobe keloid after piercing
Pedunculated or bulky keloid suitable for debulking
contraindications: No plan for adjuvant therapy to prevent recurrence (recurrence is very high after excision alone)
Active infection or ulceration of the keloid
Unrealistic expectations after counselling
Very large chest or shoulder keloids at a primary-care level (refer)
equipment: Sterile minor surgery set with size 15 blade, fine forceps, skin hook and scissors
Local anaesthetic, 5-10 mL syringe and 25-27 G needle
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gloves and gauze
Fine non-absorbable sutures (5/0-6/0 for ear) and absorbable deep sutures
Intralesional corticosteroid and syringe for adjuvant injection
steps: Confirm identity, the keloid site and written consent, including the high risk of recurrence and need for adjuvant treatment.
Photograph the keloid with consent for follow-up comparison.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare with antiseptic and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around and beneath the keloid.
Do a time-out confirming patient, side and site.
Excise the keloid, keeping within the keloid margin (intramarginal) or just at its edge, with minimal trauma to normal skin.
Preserve a skin flap from the keloid surface where useful to close without tension.
Secure haemostasis and close in layers with fine sutures avoiding tension.
Give adjuvant intralesional corticosteroid into the wound edges per local protocol.
Send the tissue for histology if the diagnosis is uncertain and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Remove sutures at 7-10 days and start pressure therapy (pressure earring or garment) once healed.
Repeat intralesional steroid injections at intervals per local protocol for several months.
Review every 4-6 weeks for early signs of recurrence.
Advise against further piercing or elective skin trauma.
red_flags: Bleeding, haematoma or wound infection
Early thickening, itching or redness at the scar suggesting recurrence
Skin thinning or pale patches after steroid injections

indications: Keloids and hypertrophic scars
Alopecia areata patches
Localised chronic plaques (lichen planus, discoid lupus, lichen simplex, psoriasis)
Acne cysts and nodules
contraindications: Infection at the injection site
Known allergy to the preparation
Lesions on the eyelids or near the eye without specialist skill
Previous atrophy at the site from steroid injection
equipment: Intralesional corticosteroid suspension (strength per indication and local protocol)
1 mL luer-lock syringe and 27-30 G needle (needle-free injector if available)
Topical anaesthetic cream or ice for comfort
steps: Confirm identity, the lesions to inject and verbal consent, and warn about skin thinning and pale patches.
Apply topical anaesthetic or ice to reduce pain if needed.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the lesion with antiseptic.
Draw up the steroid at the strength chosen for the indication and shake the suspension well.
Insert the needle into the upper dermis or body of the lesion, not into fat.
Inject slowly until the lesion blanches slightly, moving the needle about every 1 cm.
Stop if there is high resistance or the needle is in fat, and reposition.
Apply pressure with gauze and record the volume and strength used.
aftercare: Expect mild soreness for a day or two.
Repeat at intervals per local protocol, usually every 4-6 weeks.
Combine with pressure therapy or silicone for keloids where possible.
red_flags: Skin thinning, depression or white patches at the site (pause treatment)
Signs of infection
Raised blood glucose symptoms in diabetic patients after injection
Visual symptoms after injection near the eye (urgent referral)

indications: Viral warts
Actinic keratoses and seborrhoeic keratoses
Molluscum contagiosum in older children and adults
Small skin tags and some superficial benign lesions
contraindications: Undiagnosed pigmented lesion or suspected melanoma
Cold urticaria, cryoglobulinaemia or Raynaud disease at the treatment site
Poor circulation at the site (e.g. foot in peripheral arterial disease)
Caution in dark skin because of lasting hypopigmentation; discuss first
equipment: Liquid nitrogen in a cryospray canister or a cotton-tipped applicator with a flask
Otoscope cones or neoprene cone to confine the spray (optional)
steps: Confirm identity, the lesions to treat and verbal consent, warning about blistering and pale marks.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Pare thick hyperkeratotic warts first to improve freezing.
Hold the spray nozzle about 1-1.5 cm from the lesion or press the soaked applicator onto it.
Freeze until a white ice ball covers the lesion with a 1-2 mm rim of normal skin.
Hold the freeze for the time appropriate to the lesion and allow it to thaw fully.
Repeat a second freeze-thaw cycle for warts if needed.
Record the number of lesions, freeze time and cycles.
aftercare: Expect redness, swelling and possibly a blister within 24 hours.
Leave blisters intact; if they burst, clean and cover with a plaster.
Repeat treatment every 2-4 weeks if needed, up to the number of sessions agreed.
red_flags: Large painful blood blisters or spreading redness
Signs of infection (pus, fever)
Numbness or colour change of a finger or toe after treatment
Lesion that persists or changes after several sessions (consider biopsy)

indications: Skin tags, dermatosis papulosa nigra and small seborrhoeic keratoses
Viral warts not responding to other treatment
Haemostasis after shave or curettage
Small spider naevi and telangiectases
contraindications: Undiagnosed or suspected malignant lesion without tissue for histology
Cardiac pacemaker or implanted defibrillator (use bipolar or seek advice)
Alcohol-based antiseptic still wet on the skin (fire risk)
Keloid tendency at the site, after discussion
equipment: Electrocautery or hyfrecator unit with sterile tips
Earthing plate if the unit needs one
Local anaesthetic, syringe and 30 G needle or topical anaesthetic cream
Smoke evacuator or mask (wart plume can carry virus)
steps: Confirm identity, the lesions and verbal consent, and ask about pacemakers.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and a mask, and clean with non-alcohol antiseptic.
Give topical or local anaesthetic as needed for the size and number of lesions.
Set the unit to the lowest effective power.
Touch or hold the tip just above the lesion until it desiccates or chars lightly.
Wipe away the treated tissue with gauze and treat any remaining base lightly.
Avoid deep burns to reduce scarring and pigment change.
Apply petroleum jelly or a simple dressing.
aftercare: Keep the area clean and apply petroleum jelly until crusts fall off (1-2 weeks).
Avoid picking crusts and protect from sun.
Warn about temporary dark or pale marks, especially in dark skin.
red_flags: Spreading redness, pus or fever
Bleeding that does not stop with pressure
Raised, thickened scar forming (possible keloid)

indications: Seborrhoeic keratoses
Viral warts and molluscum contagiosum
Small, well-defined superficial basal cell carcinoma or Bowen disease (after histological diagnosis)
Pyogenic granuloma (with cautery to the base)
contraindications: Suspected melanoma
Recurrent or poorly defined tumours, or tumours on high-risk facial sites (refer for excision)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Ring or spoon curettes of assorted sizes
Local anaesthetic, syringe and 27-30 G needle
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the area with antiseptic and put on gloves.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic under the lesion.
Stretch the surrounding skin firmly between finger and thumb.
Scrape the lesion with the curette using firm strokes in several directions until a firm, gritty normal dermis is felt.
Send the curetted tissue for histology.
Control bleeding with electrocautery or a topical haemostatic agent to the base.
Repeat curettage and cautery cycles for tumours as per local protocol.
Apply a dressing.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and moist with petroleum jelly until healed.
Warn of a flat pale scar.
Review with histology and check for recurrence.
red_flags: Persistent bleeding
Signs of infection
Regrowth at the scar

indications: Skin tags that catch on clothing or jewellery, bleed or are irritated
Cosmetic removal at patient request
contraindications: Lesion that is not clearly a skin tag (consider biopsy)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder for broad-based tags
Perianal tag that may be a sign of Crohn disease or a sentinel pile without assessment
equipment: Sterile fine curved scissors or scalpel
Local anaesthetic, syringe and 30 G needle for larger tags
steps: Confirm identity, the tags to remove and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean with antiseptic.
Give local anaesthetic at the base for tags larger than a few millimetres.
Hold the tag with forceps to stretch the stalk gently.
Snip the tag at its base flush with the skin using curved scissors.
Apply pressure, a topical haemostatic agent or light cautery to stop bleeding.
Send unusual or large tags for histology.
Cover with a plaster.
aftercare: Keep the area clean and dry for a day.
Small scabs fall off within 1-2 weeks.
red_flags: Bleeding that does not stop with pressure
Signs of infection

indications: Cosmetically troubling dermatosis papulosa nigra on the face and neck
Lesions that are irritated or catch on clothing
contraindications: Keloid tendency (discuss risk)
Active facial infection or eczema
Unrealistic expectations of complete permanent clearance
equipment: Fine curved scissors, curette or hyfrecator with fine tip
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, explaining that new lesions may appear and pigment change can occur.
Apply topical anaesthetic cream and wait for it to work.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean with non-alcohol antiseptic.
Treat a test area first if the patient has not been treated before.
Snip pedunculated lesions flush with the skin with fine scissors.
Lightly desiccate flat lesions at the lowest effective hyfrecator setting or remove with light curettage.
Wipe away treated tissue and avoid going deeper than the lesion.
Apply petroleum jelly.
aftercare: Apply petroleum jelly twice daily until crusts fall off.
Use sun protection on treated areas.
Review in 4-6 weeks before treating further areas.
red_flags: Dark or pale patches that persist beyond a few months
Raised scars at treated sites
Signs of infection

indications: Suspected tinea of the skin, scalp or nails
Suspected pityriasis versicolor
Suspected cutaneous candidiasis
Suspected scabies (scraping for mites)
contraindications: Recent topical antifungal use may give false negatives (note it on the form)
Badly excoriated or bleeding areas (choose a different area)
equipment: Blunt scalpel blade or glass slide edge
Black paper, folded or a sterile container
Nail clippers for nail samples and toothbrush or forceps for scalp samples
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and ask about recent antifungal treatment.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Clean the area with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry.
Scrape scale from the active edge of the lesion with the blunt blade onto black paper or a slide.
For nails, clip the affected nail and scrape debris from under the nail plate near the cuticle.
For scalp, pluck broken hairs and scrape scale or brush the area into a container.
Add potassium hydroxide to a portion on a slide, add a coverslip and wait for keratin to clear.
Examine under the microscope for hyphae, spores or yeasts, or send to the laboratory with a request form.
aftercare: Explain when culture results will be available (often 2-4 weeks).
Start or continue treatment per clinical findings and microscopy.
red_flags: Widespread or deep fungal infection in an immunosuppressed patient (refer)
Kerion with pus and lymph nodes in a child (needs systemic treatment)

indications: Suspected leprosy where smear services are available
Classifying leprosy as paucibacillary or multibacillary when clinically unclear
Suspected relapse after treatment
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Diagnosis should not be delayed if smear is unavailable (clinical diagnosis per national guidelines)
equipment: New sterile single-use scalpel blade for each patient
Ziehl-Neelsen staining reagents and microscope (or transport to laboratory)
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Choose sites per national protocol (usually both earlobes and one or two active lesions).
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean each site with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry.
Pinch the skin firmly between thumb and finger to squeeze out blood until the area is pale.
Make a small cut about 5 mm long and 2-3 mm deep while keeping the pinch, using a new sterile blade for each patient (never re-use or flame-sterilise blades between patients).
Turn the blade and scrape the edges and base of the cut to collect tissue fluid and pulp, not blood.
Spread the material in a small circle on the labelled slide, one site per smear.
Apply pressure with gauze to stop bleeding and cover each site.
Air-dry and fix the slides and send for Ziehl-Neelsen staining and bacterial index.
aftercare: Keep the sites clean; they heal within a few days.
Give the date for the result and start or continue treatment per national leprosy programme.
Notify the case per national programme rules.
red_flags: Painful or tender nerves, new weakness or loss of sensation (leprosy reaction - urgent review)
Infection at smear sites

indications: Assessing extent and activity of vitiligo and other pigment disorders
Suspected tinea capitis (some species fluoresce)
Suspected pityriasis versicolor or erythrasma
Assessing depth of melasma
contraindications: None absolute; avoid shining the lamp into the eyes
equipment: Wood's lamp (long-wave UV light, about 365 nm)
Eye protection for patient and examiner when examining the face
steps: Confirm identity and explain the examination to the patient.
Ask the patient not to wash or apply creams to the area just before the examination if possible.
Darken the room fully and let the examiner's eyes adjust for a minute.
Switch on the lamp and let it warm up.
Hold the lamp 10-20 cm from the skin and examine the affected and normal areas.
Note the colour of any fluorescence and whether pigment loss is accentuated.
Record the findings and extent, using a body chart or photograph if possible.
aftercare: Explain that a negative result does not exclude infection; arrange microscopy if needed.
red_flags: Rapidly spreading depigmentation with other autoimmune symptoms (investigate)
Inflamed boggy scalp swelling with hair loss in a child (kerion - treat promptly)

indications: Suspected allergic contact dermatitis
Chronic hand or facial eczema not explained otherwise
Suspected allergy to hair dye, cosmetics, rubber, metals or topical medicines
contraindications: Active widespread eczema or eczema on the back
Pregnancy (usually deferred)
Recent strong topical steroid on the back, systemic immunosuppression or recent sun exposure to the back
Previous severe reaction to a test allergen (exclude it)
equipment: Standard allergen series and any relevant patient-supplied products (diluted as per guidelines)
steps: Confirm identity, take a full exposure history and written consent, explaining the three visits and keeping the back dry.
Check the back is free of eczema and that the patient has stopped interfering medicines per protocol.
Load the chambers with the allergens in the order on the recording sheet.
Apply the strips to the upper back, avoiding the spine, and press firmly.
Mark the position of each strip with a skin marker.
Ask the patient to keep the back dry and avoid exercise and sun until the reading visits.
Remove the strips at about 48 hours, mark the sites and do the first reading after 30 minutes.
Do the second reading at about 96 hours and grade each reaction per international criteria.
Decide the relevance of each positive result to the patient's exposures.
aftercare: Give written information on any allergens found and how to avoid them.
Advise to report late reactions that appear after the last reading.
red_flags: Severe blistering or spreading reaction at test sites (remove strip and treat)
Widespread flare of eczema
Shortness of breath or swelling of face or lips (anaphylaxis - emergency)

indications: Assessment of pigmented lesions and suspected melanoma (including acral and nail lesions)
Suspected basal cell carcinoma or other skin tumours
Scalp and hair disorders (trichoscopy)
Scabies, warts and other inflammatory or infectious conditions
contraindications: None; clean the device between patients
equipment: Handheld dermatoscope (polarised or non-polarised) or smartphone adapter
Alcohol gel or immersion fluid for non-polarised contact
Alcohol wipes to clean the lens
Camera or phone for images (with consent)
steps: Confirm identity and explain the examination.
Perform hand hygiene and clean the dermatoscope lens.
Apply immersion fluid if using non-polarised contact mode.
Place the lens on or just above the lesion and examine it systematically.
Assess pattern, colours, structures and symmetry using a recognised algorithm.
Examine acral lesions for parallel ridge versus furrow patterns and nails for band features.
Capture images with consent for comparison and record the impression.
Clean the device after use.
aftercare: Arrange biopsy, excision or monitoring based on the findings.
Give a date for repeat dermoscopy if monitoring.
red_flags: Features suggestive of melanoma (urgent excision or referral)
Lesion changing on serial imaging
Pigmented band on a nail that is widening or involves the nail fold

indications: Melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
Mild acne and acne marks
Superficial photodamage and uneven skin texture
contraindications: Active infection, herpes simplex or open wounds in the area
Use of oral isotretinoin in the last 6 months
Pregnancy for some agents
Keloid tendency, unrealistic expectations or inability to avoid sun
Medium and deep peels in dark skin (high risk of pigment change; superficial peels only)
equipment: Peeling agent at the concentration chosen (superficial agents only in dark skin)
Neutraliser if required by the agent
Degreasing cleanser, gauze and fan brush or cotton applicators
Petroleum jelly to protect eyes, nostrils and lip corners
Gloves and eye protection for the patient
steps: Confirm identity, skin type, indication and written consent, and check the pre-peel skin preparation was done.
Photograph the area with consent.
Cleanse and degrease the skin and protect the eye area, nostrils and lip corners with petroleum jelly.
Apply the peel evenly in a set order across cosmetic units with a brush or applicator.
Time the application and watch closely for erythema or frosting.
Neutralise or remove the peel at the end time or earlier if there is intense redness or frosting.
Rinse with cool water and apply cool compresses.
Apply a bland moisturiser and broad-spectrum sunscreen.
aftercare: Expect redness and peeling for several days; do not pick the skin.
Use bland moisturiser and daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, and avoid sun.
Avoid other active topical products until peeling has settled.
Repeat sessions at intervals of 2-4 weeks as agreed.
red_flags: Blistering, crusting or oozing (possible burn)
Dark or white patches developing after the peel
Cold sores or pustules (infection)

indications: Persistent open or closed comedones not responding to topical treatment
Macrocomedones
contraindications: Inflamed pustules, nodules or cysts (treat medically)
Active facial infection
Keloid tendency (gentle technique only)
equipment: Sterile 25-27 G needle or fine lancet for closed comedones
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and explain that extraction does not replace ongoing acne treatment.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Apply a warm compress for a few minutes to soften the plugs.
Clean the skin with antiseptic.
Open closed comedones with a tiny nick from the needle tip at the surface.
Centre the extractor loop over the comedone and press down gently and evenly.
Stop after two attempts if the plug does not come out to avoid scarring.
Clean the area and apply a soothing moisturiser.
aftercare: Continue prescribed acne treatment daily.
Avoid squeezing spots at home.
red_flags: Spreading redness or swelling
Dark marks or scarring developing

form.label: Needle used to open closed comedones

indications: Molluscum contagiosum that is symptomatic, spreading or causing distress
Lesions in immunocompromised patients (consider HIV testing in adults with extensive lesions)
contraindications: Very young or distressed child where watchful waiting is reasonable
Lesions on the eyelid margin (refer)
Inflamed lesions showing natural resolution
equipment: Small ring curette or sterile needle and fine forceps
Topical anaesthetic cream applied in advance
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, explaining that lesions often resolve on their own.
Apply topical anaesthetic cream under occlusion and wait for it to work.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the area with antiseptic.
Stretch the skin and remove each lesion with a quick scoop of the curette, or nick and express the core.
Apply pressure to stop bleeding.
Cover larger areas with plasters.
Dispose of materials safely because the cores are infectious.
aftercare: Keep treated areas clean and covered until healed.
Avoid sharing towels and scratching to limit spread.
Review new lesions in 4-6 weeks if needed.
red_flags: Signs of secondary bacterial infection
Extensive or giant lesions in an adult (check for immunosuppression)
Lesions on the eyelid with red eye

indications: Longitudinal pigmented band suspicious for subungual melanoma
Nail dystrophy of unclear cause after negative fungal tests
Suspected nail unit tumour
contraindications: Peripheral arterial disease or poor digital circulation
Uncontrolled diabetes or local infection
Inexperience with nail surgery (refer to dermatology or hand surgery)
equipment: Sterile nail surgery set (nail elevator, nail splitter, fine scalpel, skin hooks, punch tools)
Local anaesthetic without adrenaline (or per local protocol), syringe and 27-30 G needle for digital block
Specimen pot with formalin and flat card for orientation
steps: Confirm identity, the digit, written consent and site marking, and explain possible permanent nail deformity.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare the digit with antiseptic and drape it.
Give a digital block with local anaesthetic and wait for full numbness.
Do a time-out confirming patient, digit and side.
Apply a digital tourniquet and note the time.
Lift the proximal nail fold or avulse part of the nail plate to expose the target area.
Take the biopsy from the matrix or bed by punch, transverse or longitudinal excision as indicated.
Place the specimen flat on card, orient it and fix in formalin.
Repair the bed or matrix with fine absorbable sutures and replace the nail plate as a splint if possible.
Remove the tourniquet, check the digit pinks up and apply a bulky dressing.
aftercare: Keep the hand or foot elevated for 48 hours and give analgesia.
Change the dressing at 48 hours and keep clean and dry.
Warn that the nail may grow abnormally for months or permanently.
Review with histology.
red_flags: Digit pale, blue or cold after surgery (check tourniquet is off - urgent)
Severe throbbing pain, pus or fever
Histology showing melanoma (urgent referral)

indications: Vitiligo
Moderate to severe psoriasis
Atopic eczema not controlled with topical treatment
Chronic itch, lichen planus and early mycosis fungoides
contraindications: Photosensitive disorders (lupus, porphyria, xeroderma pigmentosum)
History of skin cancer or melanoma
Photosensitising medicines without review
Inability to stand in the cabinet or attend regularly
equipment: Calibrated narrowband UVB cabinet or hand-and-foot unit
UV-protective goggles for patient and staff
Genital shields and face protection if the face is unaffected
steps: Confirm identity, skin type, indication, medicines and written consent, and explain the course of 2-3 sessions per week.
Decide the starting dose from skin type or minimal erythema dose per unit protocol.
Ask the patient to remove creams and perfumes and to wear goggles and genital protection.
Check the response and any redness from the previous session before treating.
Set the dose for this session, adjusting up or holding per protocol and the previous reaction.
Position the patient in the cabinet in the standard position and start the treatment.
Supervise the session and stop it if the patient becomes unwell.
Record the dose delivered and the cumulative dose.
aftercare: Moisturise after treatment and avoid extra sun exposure on treatment days.
Report any burning or redness at the next session.
Review progress every 10-20 sessions and keep a lifetime count of treatments.
red_flags: Painful redness or blistering after a session (hold treatment)
New or changing moles or skin lesions
Eye pain or visual changes

indications: Atypical or changing naevus
Naevus that is repeatedly traumatised or irritated
Cosmetic removal at patient request
Medium congenital naevi where removal is planned
contraindications: Large congenital naevus (refer to plastic surgery)
Local infection
Keloid tendency at high-risk sites without counselling
equipment: Sterile minor surgery set with size 15 blade
Local anaesthetic, 5 mL syringe and 25-27 G needle
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gloves and gauze
steps: Confirm identity, the naevus, site marking and written consent, and explain the scar will be longer than the mole.
Mark an ellipse along relaxed skin tension lines with a 2 mm margin.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare with antiseptic and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the ellipse.
Do a time-out confirming patient, side and site.
Excise the ellipse full thickness into subcutaneous fat.
Place the specimen in formalin with a clear label.
Secure haemostasis and close in layers.
Apply a dressing and complete the histology request.
aftercare: Keep dry for 48 hours, then clean daily.
Remove sutures at 5-7 days on face and 10-14 days elsewhere.
Review the histology result and arrange wider excision if atypia or melanoma is reported.
red_flags: Bleeding, swelling or wound opening
Signs of infection
Histology showing melanoma (urgent referral)

indications: Primary, well-defined nodular or superficial basal cell carcinoma at a low-risk site
Histologically confirmed BCC where excision can be closed primarily
contraindications: Recurrent, morphoeic or poorly defined tumours, or tumours on high-risk facial sites (refer for specialist or Mohs surgery)
Defect too large for primary closure (refer for flap or graft)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Sterile minor surgery set with size 15 blade, skin hooks and fine instruments
Local anaesthetic, 5-10 mL syringe and 25-27 G needle
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gloves and gauze
Specimen pot with formalin and orientation suture
steps: Confirm identity, histology or clinical diagnosis, site marking and written consent including recurrence risk.
Mark the visible tumour edge under good light, then a peripheral margin of 4 mm for well-defined small tumours.
Draw an ellipse around the margin along relaxed skin tension lines.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare with antiseptic and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and do a time-out.
Excise full thickness into subcutaneous fat, keeping an even deep margin.
Mark orientation with a suture and place the specimen in formalin.
Secure haemostasis, undermine if needed and close in layers without tension.
Apply a dressing and record the margin taken and orientation on the histology request.
aftercare: Keep dry for 48 hours, then clean daily, and remove sutures at the usual time for the site.
Review histology; arrange re-excision or referral if margins are involved.
Teach sun protection and skin self-checks, and arrange follow-up for new lesions.
red_flags: Bleeding, haematoma or wound infection
Involved or close margins on histology
New lesion or regrowth at the scar

indications: Histologically confirmed melanoma needing wide local excision (including acral lentiginous melanoma of sole or palm)
Squamous cell carcinoma including Marjolin ulcer in chronic scars or ulcers
Other confirmed skin cancers needing margin clearance
contraindications: Unconfirmed diagnosis (biopsy first)
Unstaged disease where nodal or distant spread is suspected (stage and discuss at a multidisciplinary meeting)
Defect needing reconstruction or amputation beyond the facility's capacity (refer)
Patient unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Major or minor surgery set as appropriate to the site
Anaesthesia as planned (local, regional or general)
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gowns and gloves
Sutures, skin graft equipment (dermatome or knife) if planned
Specimen pot with formalin and orientation sutures
steps: Confirm identity, histology report, staging, site marking and written consent including reconstruction, amputation risk and recurrence.
Examine and record regional lymph nodes before surgery.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare and drape the site, and do a time-out.
Mark the scar or tumour and the surgical margin based on tumour thickness per current guidelines.
Excise the tissue down to the deep fascia or as indicated, keeping the specimen intact.
Orient the specimen with sutures and send it in formalin with a full history.
Achieve haemostasis.
Close primarily if possible or reconstruct with a flap or split-skin graft.
Apply a pressure dressing and splint if a graft is on a weight-bearing or mobile area.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and give analgesia; keep graft dressings in place until first inspection.
Review histology margins and discuss at a multidisciplinary meeting for further staging or treatment.
Arrange long-term follow-up with node and skin examination.
red_flags: Graft failure, bleeding or wound infection
New lumps in the scar, nearby skin or lymph nodes
Weight loss, bone pain, cough or headache (possible spread)

indications: Confirmed or clinically diagnosed scabies
Treatment of household and close contacts at the same time
Mass treatment in institutions (schools, prisons, care homes) per public health advice
contraindications: Known allergy to the chosen scabicide (choose another)
Agents unsuitable for infants, pregnancy or breastfeeding (choose per local guidance)
Broken, heavily crusted skin needing specialist management (crusted scabies)
equipment: Topical scabicide chosen for the patient's age and pregnancy status
Written instructions for the patient and contacts
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis and verbal consent, and identify all household and close contacts for treatment.
Choose a scabicide suitable for age, pregnancy and breastfeeding status per local guidance.
Ask the patient to have a bath and dry the skin, then wait until the skin is cool.
Apply the scabicide to the whole body from the neck down, including between fingers and toes, under nails, the genitals and soles.
In infants, young children, the elderly and the immunocompromised include the scalp, face and ears, avoiding eyes and mouth.
Reapply to hands after each hand wash during the contact time.
Leave on for the time stated for the product, then wash off.
Wash clothes, towels and bedding used in the past 3 days in hot water or seal in a bag for 72 hours.
Repeat the application after 7 days.
aftercare: Explain itching can last 2-4 weeks after successful treatment and is not a sign of failure.
Give a soothing emollient or antihistamine for itch per local protocol.
Treat secondary bacterial infection if present.
red_flags: New burrows or lesions after 4 weeks (treatment failure or reinfection)
Thick crusted plaques on hands and feet (crusted scabies - refer)
Pus, fever, facial or leg swelling, or dark urine (infection or post-streptococcal kidney disease)

indications: Confirmed or suspected Buruli ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans) nodule, plaque, oedema or ulcer
Wound care alongside antibiotic treatment per WHO and national programme
contraindications: Do not delay antibiotic treatment or programme notification for wound care
Avoid extensive surgical debridement without specialist input
equipment: Sterile dressing pack, gloves and normal saline or clean water
Non-adherent dressings, gauze and crepe bandage
Swabs and fine-needle aspirate or biopsy kit for PCR confirmation
Ruler or wound tracing sheet and camera
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis or suspicion and verbal consent, and check antibiotic treatment has started per national programme.
Collect samples from the undermined edge for PCR before or at the start of treatment if not yet confirmed.
Give analgesia before the dressing if the wound is painful.
Perform hand hygiene and use clean or aseptic technique.
Remove the old dressing gently, soaking it if it sticks.
Clean the wound and surrounding skin with saline or clean water.
Remove loose necrotic tissue gently without cutting healthy tissue.
Measure the wound and the undermined edges and photograph it.
Apply a non-adherent dressing and secure with a bandage, not too tight.
Position and splint the joint in a functional position if the wound crosses a joint, and start exercises.
aftercare: Change dressings every 1-3 days depending on exudate.
Do range-of-movement exercises daily to prevent contractures.
Complete the full antibiotic course and attend follow-up for at least a year.
red_flags: Wound enlarging despite treatment or new lesions (paradoxical reaction or failure - review)
Joint stiffness or contracture developing
Spreading redness, fever or bone pain (secondary infection or osteomyelitis)

indications: Venous leg ulcer with adequate arterial supply
Sickle cell leg ulcer with oedema (with caution and good padding)
Chronic leg oedema with ulceration
contraindications: Ankle-brachial pressure index below 0.8 or absent foot pulses without Doppler (reduced or no compression; refer)
Acute cellulitis or deep vein thrombosis until treated
Severe diabetic neuropathy or heart failure without review
equipment: Handheld Doppler and sphygmomanometer for ankle-brachial pressure index
Dressing pack, gloves, normal saline or clean water
Non-adherent primary dressing and absorbent pad
Padding, crepe and cohesive or elastic compression bandages (or layered system)
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and check the ankle-brachial pressure index recorded within the last 3 months.
Perform hand hygiene and remove the old bandage and dressing.
Wash the leg and clean the ulcer with saline or clean water.
Measure the ulcer and assess the bed, edges, exudate and surrounding skin.
Apply emollient to the surrounding dry skin, avoiding the ulcer.
Apply the non-adherent primary dressing and absorbent pad.
Pad the ankle and shin, protecting the bony prominences.
Apply the compression bandage from the base of the toes to below the knee with the foot at a right angle, overlapping by half.
Check toes for colour, warmth and movement and ask about comfort.
aftercare: Elevate the legs above heart level when resting and keep walking.
Return for re-bandaging once or twice a week or if the bandage slips.
Use compression stockings after healing to prevent recurrence.
red_flags: Toes cold, blue, numb or painful under the bandage (remove the bandage and return)
Spreading redness, fever or increasing pain
Ulcer not reducing in size after 12 weeks or with rolled edges (biopsy to exclude cancer)

indications: Bleeding or bothersome pyogenic granuloma of skin or lip
Lesion of uncertain nature needing histology
contraindications: Lesion that may be amelanotic melanoma or other malignancy (send for histology; excise properly)
Pregnancy-related gum lesions (often resolve after delivery; refer to dental)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Curette or scalpel with size 15 blade
Local anaesthetic, syringe and 27-30 G needle
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion and verbal consent, and warn of possible recurrence.
Perform hand hygiene, clean with antiseptic and put on gloves.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the base.
Shave or curette the lesion off at its base, or excise it with an ellipse for recurrent lesions.
Place the specimen in formalin for histology.
Cauterise the base thoroughly to stop bleeding and reduce recurrence.
Close an excision with sutures or apply a pressure dressing.
aftercare: Keep the wound covered and clean until healed.
Review with histology.
red_flags: Brisk bleeding not stopped by 15 minutes of pressure
Rapid regrowth
Histology showing malignancy

indications: Lymphatic filariasis lymphoedema
Podoconiosis
Chronic lymphoedema of any cause with skin changes or recurrent attacks of cellulitis
contraindications: Acute attack (acute dermatolymphangioadenitis) with fever - rest, cool and treat infection first, then resume
Deep vein thrombosis suspected
equipment: Basin, clean water at room temperature and plain soap
Topical antifungal or antiseptic for entry lesions per local protocol
Comfortable shoes and socks or bandages
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and involve the family member who will help at home.
Measure the limb circumference at set points and record the lymphoedema stage.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves if there are open wounds.
Wash the whole limb gently with soap and clean water, including between the toes and in skin folds.
Dry carefully with a clean cloth, especially between the toes and in skin folds.
Look for entry lesions (cracks, fungal infection, wounds) and treat them per local protocol.
Apply emollient to dry, thickened skin, avoiding between the toes.
Teach and observe exercises and leg elevation, and advise on footwear.
Teach the patient and family to recognise an acute attack and what to do.
aftercare: Wash and dry the limb daily at home.
Elevate the limb at night and do exercises several times a day.
Wear shoes and socks outdoors to prevent injury and soil exposure.
Take mass drug administration for filariasis when offered.
red_flags: Fever, chills, painful hot swollen limb (acute attack - seek care)
Open wounds that do not heal or smell
Rapid increase in swelling

indications: Embedded Tunga penetrans fleas in the feet, hands or other sites
contraindications: Heavy infestation with severe secondary infection (treat infection and consider topical treatment first)
Do not use shared, unsterile needles or thorns
equipment: Sterile needle or lancet (one per patient) and fine forceps
Soap, water and basin for soaking
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and count the lesions.
Soak and wash the feet with soap and water.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the site with antiseptic.
Widen the opening of the pore around the black dot gently with the sterile needle.
Ease the whole flea out without rupturing it, using the needle or fine forceps.
Check the cavity is empty and clean it with antiseptic.
Cover with a dressing and dispose of the flea and sharps safely.
Check tetanus vaccination status.
aftercare: Keep the feet clean, wear closed shoes and keep floors swept or sealed.
Treat the household and animals if infested.
Return if new lesions appear.
red_flags: Spreading redness, swelling, pus or fever (secondary infection)
Lockjaw or muscle spasms (tetanus - emergency)
Loss of nails or difficulty walking from many lesions

indications: Furuncular myiasis (boil-like lesion with a central pore, e.g. tumbu fly)
Wound myiasis
contraindications: Myiasis of the eye, nose, ear or deep cavities (refer to specialist)
Do not squeeze firmly without first loosening the larva (may rupture it)
equipment: Petroleum jelly or liquid paraffin to occlude the pore
Local anaesthetic, syringe and needle if a small incision is needed
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and count the lesions.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the area with antiseptic.
Cover the central pore with petroleum jelly for 30-60 minutes so the larva moves up for air.
Grasp the emerging larva with fine forceps and remove it whole with steady traction.
If it does not emerge, give local anaesthetic and widen the pore with a small incision, then remove the larva.
For wound myiasis, irrigate with saline and remove all visible larvae.
Check that each larva is intact and clean the cavity.
Apply a dressing and dispose of larvae safely.
aftercare: Iron clothes and dry laundry indoors or off the ground to prevent tumbu fly eggs.
Keep the wound clean until healed.
Check tetanus vaccination status.
red_flags: Spreading redness, pus or fever
Lesion that remains painful or discharging after removal (retained larva)
Lesions near the eye, nose or ear

indications: Recurrent painful nodules or sinus tracts of hidradenitis suppurativa at the same site
Hurley stage I-II disease not controlled by medical treatment
contraindications: Extensive Hurley stage III disease (refer for wide excision under general anaesthesia)
Acute abscess with cellulitis (drain and treat first)
Uncontrolled diabetes or bleeding disorder
equipment: Sterile minor surgery set with scalpel, scissors and blunt probe
Local anaesthetic, 10 mL syringe and 25 G needle
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gloves and gauze
Specimen pot with formalin if needed
steps: Confirm identity, the area, site marking and written consent, explaining open wound healing and recurrence risk.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare with antiseptic and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the lesion.
Do a time-out confirming patient, side and site.
Pass a blunt probe through the sinus tracts to map their full extent.
Remove the roof of each tract over the probe with scissors or electrocautery.
Curette the gelatinous material from the floor of the tract.
Secure haemostasis and leave the wound open to heal by secondary intention.
Apply a non-adherent and absorbent dressing.
aftercare: Change dressings daily and shower to clean the wound.
Give analgesia; healing usually takes 2-4 weeks.
Continue medical treatment, weight and smoking advice, and review for new lesions.
red_flags: Bleeding through the dressing
Fever, spreading redness or increasing pain
New lesions at other sites (review medical treatment)

indications: Stable segmental or focal vitiligo not responding to medical treatment or phototherapy
Stable patches with no new lesions or spread for at least 12 months
contraindications: Active or spreading vitiligo
Koebner phenomenon or keloid tendency
Bleeding disorder or local infection
Unrealistic expectations
equipment: Sterile punch biopsy tools (1-2 mm; recipient punch slightly smaller than donor punch)
Local anaesthetic, syringes and 30 G needles
Antiseptic solution, sterile drapes, gloves and gauze
Fine forceps and saline-soaked gauze to hold grafts
steps: Confirm identity, stability of the vitiligo, site marking and written consent including the risk of cobblestoning and partial repigmentation.
Photograph the recipient area with consent.
Perform surgical hand hygiene, prepare the donor site (usually the outer thigh or buttock) and recipient site with antiseptic and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic at both sites and do a time-out confirming patient and sites.
Make recipient holes with the punch 5-8 mm apart across the patch, slightly smaller than the donor punches.
Harvest donor grafts with the punch and keep them on saline-soaked gauze.
Place each graft into a recipient hole, flush with the skin and the right way up.
Cover the grafts with non-adherent dressing and film to hold them in place.
Dress the donor site.
aftercare: Keep the dressings dry and undisturbed for a week, then remove at review.
Start phototherapy or sun exposure per plan 2-4 weeks after grafting to spread pigment.
Review at 3 and 6 months with photographs.
red_flags: Grafts lost or displaced in the first week
Signs of infection at donor or recipient sites
New vitiligo at the donor site (Koebner)

indications: Impacted ear wax causing hearing loss, discomfort or blocking the view of the drum
Soft foreign material such as debris in the ear canal
contraindications: Known or suspected tympanic membrane perforation
Grommet in place, previous ear surgery or ear discharge in the past (possible perforation)
Active otitis externa or otitis media
Vegetable foreign body (may swell) or button battery
Only hearing ear
equipment: Electronic ear irrigator or metal ear syringe
Water or saline at body temperature
Otoscope or head mirror with light
Kidney dish, waterproof cape and towel
Wax softening drops for prior use
steps: Confirm identity, take an ear history and check there is no perforation, grommet or previous ear surgery.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, and check the patient used wax softening drops for several days.
Perform hand hygiene and examine both ears with the otoscope.
Check the water is at body temperature to avoid dizziness.
Seat the patient with the cape and kidney dish held under the ear.
Pull the pinna up and back in adults or down and back in young children to straighten the canal.
Direct the jet along the posterior-superior canal wall, never straight at the drum.
Irrigate in short bursts and inspect the canal regularly.
Stop if pain, dizziness or bleeding occurs or after a few unsuccessful attempts.
Dry the canal with a cotton-tipped probe and re-examine the canal and drum.
Document the result and the appearance of the drum.
aftercare: Keep the ear dry for a day if the canal is irritated.
Use wax softening drops and repeat irrigation another day if wax remains.
Refer for microsuction if irrigation fails twice.
red_flags: Sudden pain, bleeding or hearing loss during irrigation - stop and inspect
Vertigo, nausea or nystagmus that does not settle
Perforation seen after irrigation - refer to ENT
Ear discharge or pain in the following days

indications: Impacted wax when irrigation is contraindicated or failed
Discharge and debris in otitis externa or chronic suppurative otitis media
Mastoid cavity cleaning
Removal of small foreign bodies
contraindications: Uncooperative patient where the ear cannot be kept still (consider general anaesthesia)
Severe canal swelling preventing safe view
equipment: Operating microscope or endoscope with light source
Suction machine with fine ear suction tips of assorted sizes
Jobson-Horne probe, crocodile forceps and wax hook
Cotton wool and swabs for culture
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent, and warn the patient the suction is noisy.
Perform hand hygiene and position the patient lying or seated with the head turned and supported.
Choose the largest comfortable speculum and focus the microscope on the canal.
Set the suction to the lowest effective pressure.
Remove wax or debris under direct vision, keeping the tip away from the drum.
Use a probe or forceps to lift hard wax before suctioning.
Take a swab for culture if there is discharge.
Pause if the patient feels dizzy and let it settle.
Inspect the canal and drum fully after clearing.
Insert an ear wick with drops if the canal is very swollen.
Document findings including the state of the drum and any cavity.
aftercare: Keep the ear dry until reviewed if there is infection or perforation.
Use prescribed topical ear drops as directed.
Arrange regular aural toilet for chronic discharge or mastoid cavities.
red_flags: Severe pain, bleeding or sudden hearing loss
Facial weakness, severe vertigo or vomiting
Persistent discharge despite treatment (consider cholesteatoma, refer)
Fever with spreading swelling around the ear

name: Removal of foreign body from ear

indications: Foreign body in the external ear canal
Live insect in the ear canal
contraindications: Uncooperative child after one failed attempt (arrange removal under general anaesthesia)
Foreign body medial to the canal isthmus or embedded in the drum (refer to ENT)
Irrigation is contraindicated for vegetable matter, button batteries and perforated drums
equipment: Otoscope or headlight, ideally operating microscope
Crocodile forceps, wax hook, right-angled hook and Jobson-Horne probe
Oil or local anaesthetic solution to kill a live insect
Restraint sheet or assistant for children
steps: Confirm identity, take a history of the object type and time, and obtain verbal consent.
Treat a button battery as an emergency and arrange urgent removal without irrigation.
Perform hand hygiene and examine both ears and both nostrils for other foreign bodies.
Drown a live insect with oil before removal.
Position the patient with the head well supported and a child held securely by an assistant.
Use forceps for soft or graspable objects and a hook passed beyond the object for round hard objects.
Use suction for small light objects.
Use irrigation only for small inert objects with an intact drum.
Limit attempts and stop if the patient cannot keep still or the canal bleeds.
Inspect the canal and drum after removal for injury or retained material.
aftercare: Give topical antibiotic drops if the canal is abraded, per local protocol.
Keep the ear dry for a few days.
Review if pain, discharge or hearing loss persists.
red_flags: Button battery or object pushed deeper - refer urgently
Bleeding from the middle ear, vertigo or facial weakness
Retained fragments or perforation seen
Ear discharge, fever or swelling in the following days

name: Removal of foreign body from nose

indications: Foreign body seen or suspected in the nasal cavity
Unilateral foul-smelling nasal discharge in a child
contraindications: Posteriorly placed object with airway risk in an uncooperative child (remove under general anaesthesia)
Mother's kiss technique not suitable if the object is not occluding the nostril
equipment: Topical decongestant and topical anaesthetic per local protocol
Crocodile forceps, Tilley forceps and right-angled hook
Foley catheter of small size for balloon technique
steps: Confirm identity, the object type and time, and obtain verbal consent from the parent or patient.
Treat a button battery or magnets as an emergency and remove them without delay.
Perform hand hygiene and examine both nostrils, ears and the chest for signs of aspiration.
Apply topical decongestant and anaesthetic to shrink the mucosa where available.
Try positive pressure first in children, with the parent blowing into the mouth while occluding the other nostril.
Seat the child on the parent's lap with the head held firmly by an assistant.
Use forceps for graspable objects and pass a hook behind round objects to roll them forward.
Use a balloon catheter passed behind the object, inflated and withdrawn, as an alternative.
Avoid pushing the object backwards towards the airway.
Re-examine the nose after removal for retained objects or mucosal injury.
aftercare: Expect minor bleeding for a short time.
Treat residual infection with saline douches and antibiotics only if clinically indicated.
Advise parents on keeping small objects away from children.
red_flags: Coughing, choking or breathing difficulty (possible aspiration) - examine chest and refer
Button battery - risk of septal perforation, urgent ENT review
Heavy nosebleed that does not stop with pressure
Persistent one-sided discharge after removal

indications: Fish bone or other foreign body seen in the tonsil, tongue base or vallecula
Persistent foreign body sensation after swallowing a bone
contraindications: Object below the view of indirect laryngoscopy or in the oesophagus (needs endoscopy)
Airway compromise (manage the airway first)
Uncooperative patient with a deep object (remove under general anaesthesia)
equipment: Headlight, tongue depressor and laryngeal mirror
Tilley forceps or angled laryngeal forceps
Lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray request form
steps: Confirm identity, the object type, timing and symptoms, and obtain verbal consent.
Check for drooling, stridor, chest pain or neck swelling that suggest a deeper or complicated object.
Perform hand hygiene and examine the tonsils, tongue base and pharynx with a headlight and depressor.
Use a laryngeal mirror or nasendoscope to inspect the vallecula and piriform fossae.
Apply topical anaesthetic spray to reduce gagging.
Grasp the visible object with forceps under direct vision and remove it gently.
Re-inspect the site for a second object or retained fragment.
Request a lateral neck X-ray or refer for endoscopy if the object is not seen and symptoms persist.
Advise nil by mouth until the anaesthetic wears off.
aftercare: Start oral fluids when the throat sensation returns.
Expect mild scratch sensation for a day or two.
Return if symptoms persist beyond two days.
red_flags: Unable to swallow saliva, drooling or chest pain (possible oesophageal object)
Stridor or breathing difficulty
Fever, neck swelling or neck pain (possible perforation or abscess)
Blood-stained saliva that persists

indications: Anterior epistaxis not controlled by pressure and cautery
Bleeding after nasal surgery or trauma
contraindications: Suspected base of skull fracture with cerebrospinal fluid leak (avoid blind packing, seek senior advice)
Bleeding controlled by simpler measures
equipment: Personal protective equipment including eye protection
Topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor per local protocol
Nasal tampon or ribbon gauze impregnated with antiseptic paste such as BIPP
IV cannula, blood tubes and fluids
steps: Confirm identity and obtain verbal consent, and start first aid with the patient sitting forward pinching the soft nose.
Check pulse, blood pressure and airway, and insert an IV cannula and take bloods if bleeding is heavy.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves, apron and eye protection.
Clear clots by asking the patient to blow the nose or with suction.
Apply topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor on cotton pledgets for a few minutes.
Lubricate the tampon and insert it along the floor of the nose, parallel to the palate.
Expand the tampon with sterile water or saline as directed by the maker.
For ribbon gauze, layer it from the floor upwards in folds using Tilley forceps, filling the cavity.
Tape the strings to the cheek and check the back of the throat for continued bleeding.
Pack the other side if bleeding continues, and plan posterior packing if blood still runs down the throat.
aftercare: Admit or observe according to severity and local policy, especially the elderly.
Remove the pack after the planned interval, usually one to two days.
Check blood pressure, haemoglobin and clotting if indicated.
Advise no nose blowing, heavy lifting or hot drinks for a week after removal.
red_flags: Blood still running down the throat after packing
Signs of shock, fainting or falling haemoglobin
Fever, rash or low blood pressure while pack in place (toxic shock)
Pack displaced into the throat or breathing difficulty

indications: Posterior epistaxis not controlled by anterior packing
contraindications: Suspected base of skull fracture (high risk of intracranial placement)
Bleeding that can be controlled by anterior packing
equipment: Personal protective equipment including eye protection
12-14 Fr Foley catheter or dual-balloon epistaxis catheter
Saline or water in a syringe for inflation
Umbilical clamp or padding to protect the nostril
IV cannula, blood tubes, fluids and pulse oximeter
steps: Confirm identity, obtain written consent and resuscitate with IV access and bloods.
Perform hand hygiene and put on full protective equipment.
Apply topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor to the nose.
Pass the lubricated Foley catheter along the nasal floor until the tip is seen behind the soft palate.
Inflate the balloon slowly with water or saline, stopping if the patient has pain.
Pull the catheter gently forward until the balloon lodges in the posterior choana.
Place an anterior pack in front of the balloon while maintaining traction.
Secure the catheter with an umbilical clamp over padding so the nostril skin is not pressed.
Check the throat for continued bleeding and repeat on the other side if needed.
Start oxygen saturation monitoring and admit the patient.
aftercare: Admit to a ward with oxygen saturation monitoring and close observation.
Give analgesia and consider prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Check the nostril skin regularly for pressure necrosis.
Remove after the planned interval under ENT supervision, ready to treat rebleeding.
red_flags: Low oxygen saturation, apnoea or breathing difficulty
Continued bleeding (consider surgical ligation or embolisation, refer)
Signs of shock
Fever, rash or low blood pressure (toxic shock)
Pain or ulceration of the nostril or palate

indications: Recurrent anterior epistaxis from a visible vessel in Little's area
Active anterior bleeding point that can be seen
contraindications: Bleeding point not visible
Same area on both sides of the septum cauterised at the same visit (risk of perforation)
Uncontrolled heavy bleeding (pack first)
equipment: Topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor on cotton pledgets
steps: Confirm identity, the side and history of bleeding, and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and inspect both sides of the septum with a headlight.
Apply topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor for a few minutes.
Identify the bleeding vessel or prominent vessels.
Apply the silver nitrate stick around the vessel first and then to the vessel itself.
Hold each application for a few seconds only, without rubbing.
Treat only one side of the septum at a time.
Wipe away excess and check that bleeding has stopped.
aftercare: Apply antiseptic nasal cream to the area as advised.
Avoid nose picking, blowing, hot drinks and heavy lifting for a week.
Treat the other side at a later visit if needed.
red_flags: Recurrent heavy bleeding
Bleeding with easy bruising or other bleeding (check clotting)
Unilateral nasal blockage or mass (possible tumour)

indications: Persistent otitis media with effusion with hearing loss
Recurrent acute otitis media
Eustachian tube dysfunction with retraction
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia
Cholesteatoma or suspected middle ear tumour
equipment: Grommets or ventilation tubes of chosen type
steps: Confirm identity, side, audiogram and tympanogram results and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Turn the head and insert the largest speculum that fits the canal.
Clear wax and debris and inspect the drum.
Make a radial incision in the anterior-inferior quadrant of the drum.
Suction the middle ear fluid and record its type.
Insert the grommet into the incision with forceps and seat it with a needle.
Check that the grommet is in place and patent.
Instil topical antibiotic drops if the ear was wet or bloody, per local protocol.
Repeat on the other side if planned.
aftercare: Keep water out of the ears when swimming or washing hair as advised locally.
Expect slight discharge for a day or two.
Arrange hearing test and review at about six to eight weeks.
Review regularly until the grommets extrude.
red_flags: Persistent ear discharge (treat with topical drops and review)
Ear pain with fever
Grommet seen in the canal soon after surgery
Facial weakness or severe vertigo

indications: Dry chronic tympanic membrane perforation with conductive hearing loss
Recurrent discharge through a perforation
Ossicular chain reconstruction with drum repair
contraindications: Actively discharging ear (treat first)
Only hearing ear (relative)
Cholesteatoma needing mastoid surgery (plan combined procedure)
Poorly controlled nasal or eustachian tube disease
equipment: Operating microscope and ear instrument set
Fine suction tips and drill if canalplasty is needed
Graft material (temporalis fascia, tragal perichondrium or cartilage)
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor for infiltration
steps: Confirm identity, side, recent audiogram and written consent, and mark the operative ear.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Infiltrate the canal and incision sites with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Harvest the graft through a postauricular or tragal incision and let it dry.
Approach the drum through the canal, endaurally or postauricularly.
Freshen the edges of the perforation by removing the rim.
Raise a tympanomeatal flap and inspect the middle ear and ossicles.
Repair the ossicular chain if needed and possible.
Place the graft underlay or overlay to cover the perforation, supported with gelatin sponge.
Replace the flap and pack the canal.
Close the incision and apply a mastoid dressing.
Check facial nerve function on waking.
aftercare: Keep the ear dry and avoid nose blowing for several weeks.
Remove the canal pack at the planned outpatient visit.
Arrange audiogram at about three months.
red_flags: Facial weakness
Severe vertigo, vomiting or sudden hearing loss
Fever, wound redness or offensive discharge
Bleeding soaking the dressing

indications: Cholesteatoma
Acute mastoiditis not responding to medical treatment or with subperiosteal abscess
Chronic suppurative otitis media with mastoid disease
Access for cochlear implantation
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia (drain abscess under local and refer)
Intracranial complication needing neurosurgery first (manage jointly)
equipment: Operating microscope and otological drill with cutting and diamond burrs
Mastoid retractors and ear instrument set
Gelatin sponge, ribbon gauze and BIPP
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging, audiogram and written consent, and mark the ear.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established and position the head turned away.
Infiltrate the postauricular area with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Make a postauricular incision and raise a periosteal flap to expose the mastoid cortex.
Drain any subperiosteal abscess and send pus for culture.
Drill the mastoid cortex within the landmarks of the suprameatal triangle.
Identify the antrum, tegmen, sigmoid sinus and lateral semicircular canal.
Remove diseased air cells and cholesteatoma while protecting the facial nerve.
Take down the posterior canal wall and fashion a meatoplasty if a canal wall down procedure is planned.
Irrigate, check haemostasis and pack the cavity as planned.
Close the incision in layers and apply a mastoid dressing.
Check facial nerve function on waking.
aftercare: Give antibiotics as indicated and analgesia.
Remove the dressing after a day and the pack at outpatient review.
Arrange regular cavity cleaning and long-term follow-up for cholesteatoma.
