red_flags: Facial weakness
Severe headache, neck stiffness, drowsiness or fits (intracranial infection)
Severe vertigo or vomiting
Clear fluid leak from wound or ear
Fever with wound swelling

name: Incision and drainage of peritonsillar abscess

indications: Peritonsillar abscess with trismus, uvula deviation and bulging soft palate
contraindications: Airway compromise (secure airway first)
Uncooperative young child (drain under general anaesthesia)
Suspected aneurysm or vascular malformation
Parapharyngeal extension (needs imaging and theatre)
equipment: Headlight, tongue depressor and suction with Yankauer tip
Topical anaesthetic spray and local anaesthetic for infiltration
Wide-bore needle and 10 mL syringe for aspiration
Scalpel with blade guarded to limit depth
steps: Confirm identity and obtain consent, and assess the airway, hydration and trismus.
Seat the patient upright with the head supported and suction ready.
Perform hand hygiene and put on protective equipment.
Spray topical anaesthetic and infiltrate the most fluctuant point with local anaesthetic.
Aspirate with a wide-bore needle at the point of maximum bulge, staying lateral to the uvula and no deeper than about one centimetre.
Send pus for culture.
If pus is found and a larger collection remains, make a small guarded incision at the same point.
Open the cavity gently with sinus forceps and let the patient spit out pus.
Suction blood and check the airway.
aftercare: Give IV or oral antibiotics and analgesia per local protocol.
Encourage oral fluids and admit if unable to swallow.
Plan interval tonsillectomy if recurrent.
red_flags: Stridor or breathing difficulty
Heavy bleeding from the throat
Neck swelling, neck stiffness or chest pain (deep neck spread)
Fever or trismus not improving within 24 hours

indications: Recurrent acute tonsillitis meeting local frequency criteria
Obstructive sleep apnoea from tonsillar enlargement
Recurrent or severe peritonsillar abscess
Suspected tonsillar malignancy or asymmetry
contraindications: Acute tonsillitis at the time of surgery
Bleeding disorder not corrected
Anaemia or unfit for anaesthesia
Cleft or submucous cleft palate (relative)
equipment: Boyle-Davis mouth gag with tongue blades and Draffin rods
Tonsil holding forceps, dissector and snare
Bipolar diathermy or ties with ligature carrier
steps: Confirm identity, indication, haemoglobin, sickle cell status, bleeding history, recent infection status and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia with a protected airway is established.
Position with neck extended and insert the mouth gag, checking the tube is not kinked.
Grasp the tonsil and retract it medially.
Incise the mucosa at the anterior pillar and find the capsule plane.
Dissect the tonsil from the fossa in the capsular plane from upper pole to lower pole.
Remove the tonsil with dissection or snare at the lower pole.
Control bleeding with pressure, bipolar diathermy or ties.
Repeat on the other side.
Release the gag for a short time and recheck both fossae for bleeding before ending.
Suction the postnasal space and pharynx and count swabs.
Send tissue for histology if malignancy is suspected or per local policy.
aftercare: Nurse in the recovery position and watch for frequent swallowing, which can mean bleeding.
Give regular analgesia and encourage normal diet and fluids early.
Expect throat pain and referred ear pain for about ten days.
Advise the patient to return immediately if any bleeding occurs in the first two weeks.
red_flags: Any fresh bleeding from the mouth or vomiting blood
Frequent swallowing, rising pulse or pallor in recovery
Unable to drink with signs of dehydration
Fever with worsening pain after the first week
Breathing difficulty or snoring with pauses in young children after surgery

indications: Adenoid hypertrophy with nasal obstruction or mouth breathing
Obstructive sleep apnoea from adenoids
Recurrent otitis media with effusion with grommet insertion
Recurrent adenoiditis or sinusitis in children
contraindications: Cleft or submucous cleft palate (risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency)
Bleeding disorder not corrected
Atlanto-axial instability, for example in Down syndrome (seek senior advice)
Acute upper respiratory infection
equipment: Laryngeal mirror and palate retractor or catheters
Adenoid curettes of assorted sizes or suction diathermy
steps: Confirm identity, indication, haemoglobin, sickle cell status, bleeding history, palate examination and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Insert the mouth gag and palpate the palate for a submucous cleft.
Retract the soft palate and inspect the adenoids with a mirror.
Remove the adenoids with a curette in a single sweep or with suction diathermy under vision.
Avoid the eustachian tube openings and the prevertebral tissues.
Insert a postnasal pack for a few minutes to control bleeding.
Remove the pack and confirm haemostasis with the mirror.
Suction the postnasal space and pharynx and remove the gag.
aftercare: Nurse in the recovery position and watch for bleeding from the nose or mouth.
Give regular analgesia and a normal diet.
Expect temporary nasal voice and mild neck stiffness.
red_flags: Fresh bleeding from the nose or mouth
Severe neck pain or reduced neck movement
Persistent nasal speech or fluid coming from the nose when drinking
Breathing difficulty

indications: Obstructive sleep apnoea in children from adenotonsillar hypertrophy
Recurrent tonsillitis with adenoid obstruction
contraindications: Acute tonsillitis or upper respiratory infection
Bleeding disorder not corrected
Submucous cleft palate (avoid adenoidectomy or do partial)
Severe sleep apnoea without access to postoperative monitoring (refer to a centre with HDU)
equipment: Boyle-Davis mouth gag with tongue blades
Tonsil instruments, adenoid curettes and laryngeal mirror
steps: Confirm identity, indication, haemoglobin, sickle cell status, bleeding history, sleep study or history severity and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Insert the gag and palpate the palate for a submucous cleft.
Perform the adenoidectomy and insert a postnasal pack.
Dissect both tonsils in the capsular plane and secure haemostasis.
Remove the postnasal pack and confirm haemostasis in the nasopharynx.
Release the gag, recheck both tonsil fossae and count swabs.
Suction the pharynx and postnasal space before waking.
aftercare: Monitor oxygen saturation overnight in children with significant sleep apnoea.
Give regular analgesia and encourage early eating and drinking.
Advise the family to return immediately for any bleeding in the first two weeks.
red_flags: Any fresh bleeding from the mouth or nose
Low oxygen saturation, apnoea or noisy breathing
Refusing fluids with signs of dehydration
Fever with worsening pain

indications: Deviated nasal septum causing nasal obstruction
Access for sinus surgery or to control epistaxis
contraindications: Active nasal infection or uncontrolled rhinitis
Bleeding disorder not corrected
Cocaine use or granulomatous disease (risk of perforation)
equipment: Septoplasty set with Freer elevator, Cottle elevator, swivel knife and Jansen-Middleton forceps
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor for infiltration
steps: Confirm identity, findings and written consent, and photograph the nose if external deformity exists.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Decongest the nose topically and infiltrate the septum with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Make a hemitransfixion or Killian incision.
Raise the mucoperichondrial flap on one side in the correct plane.
Cross through the cartilage and raise the opposite flap as needed.
Remove or reposition the deviated cartilage and bone, keeping a dorsal and caudal strut of at least one centimetre.
Replace straightened cartilage if needed and check the airway is open.
Close the incision with absorbable sutures and place quilting sutures or splints.
Insert packs if needed and check for septal haematoma.
aftercare: Sleep with the head raised and avoid nose blowing for a week.
Remove packs after one day and splints at about one week.
Use saline nasal douches as advised.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding
Increasing nasal blockage with pain or swelling (septal haematoma or abscess)
Fever or offensive discharge
Clear watery discharge (cerebrospinal fluid leak)

indications: Displaced nasal bone fracture with cosmetic deformity or obstruction
Best done within about two weeks of injury once swelling settles (within about a week in children)
contraindications: Septal haematoma not yet drained (drain first)
Fracture older than about three weeks in adults or about ten days in children (bones have set; needs formal rhinoplasty later)
Other facial fractures or head injury needing priority care
equipment: Walsham and Asch forceps or blunt elevator
Topical anaesthetic and local anaesthetic for infiltration
Nasal packs and external splint or plaster
Photographs or mirror to compare before and after
steps: Confirm identity, the date of injury, the patient's view of the deformity and written consent.
Examine for septal haematoma, CSF leak and other facial injuries.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia or local block is established.
Measure the elevator against the outside of the nose so it does not go above the inner canthus.
Elevate the depressed nasal bone with the elevator inside the nose while guiding it with the other hand outside.
Use forceps to disimpact and realign the bones if needed.
Straighten the septum with Asch forceps if it is displaced.
Check the alignment from above and from the front.
Place nasal packs if bleeding or the septum is unstable, and apply an external splint.
aftercare: Keep the splint on for about one week and avoid contact sport for six weeks.
Sleep with the head raised and use cold compresses.
Review at one week to remove the splint and assess the result.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding
Clear fluid from the nose (CSF leak)
Increasing nasal blockage with pain (septal haematoma)
Double vision or eye swelling

indications: Septal haematoma or abscess after nasal trauma or surgery
contraindications: None absolute - this is an urgent procedure to prevent cartilage loss
equipment: Topical anaesthetic and local anaesthetic for infiltration
Nasal packs or quilting sutures and splints
steps: Confirm identity and written consent, and explain the urgency to the patient or parent.
Examine both sides of the septum for a soft, boggy swelling.
Perform hand hygiene and apply topical and local anaesthetic, or use general anaesthesia in children.
Aspirate with a needle to confirm the diagnosis if unsure.
Make a horizontal incision over the most dependent part of the swelling on one side.
Evacuate the clot or pus with suction and send a swab for culture.
Inspect for damaged cartilage and treat both sides if bilateral, with incisions at different levels.
Place packs or quilting sutures on both sides to prevent recollection.
aftercare: Give antibiotics per local protocol, especially if an abscess was found.
Review in one to two days to remove packs and check for recollection.
Follow up for late nasal deformity.
red_flags: Swelling returning after drainage
Fever, increasing pain or eye swelling
Headache, vomiting or drowsiness (intracranial spread)
Loss of nasal height (saddle deformity)

indications: Chronic rhinosinusitis not responding to maximal medical treatment
Nasal polyps
Recurrent acute sinusitis
Complications of sinusitis such as orbital abscess or mucocoele
Fungal sinusitis
contraindications: No CT scan of the sinuses reviewed before surgery
Bleeding disorder not corrected
Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Rigid endoscopes (0 and 30 degree), camera, monitor and light source
FESS instrument set with sickle knife, backbiters, Blakesley forceps and microdebrider if available
Topical vasoconstrictor and local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor
Suction with fine tips and bipolar diathermy
steps: Confirm identity, side, CT findings and written consent, and review the CT for risk anatomy.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established, with the eyes uncovered and taped.
Decongest the nose and infiltrate the lateral wall with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Medialise the middle turbinate gently and perform uncinectomy.
Identify and widen the natural maxillary ostium.
Open the ethmoid bulla and anterior ethmoid cells as needed.
Proceed to posterior ethmoids, sphenoid and frontal recess only as the disease requires.
Keep the dissection medial to the orbit and below the skull base.
Check the eye regularly for swelling or proptosis.
Remove polyps and send tissue for histology and fungal culture.
Secure haemostasis and place packs if needed.
aftercare: Sleep with the head raised and avoid nose blowing for a week.
Use saline nasal douches regularly and continue topical steroid sprays.
Review for endoscopic cleaning at about two to three weeks.
red_flags: Eye swelling, double vision, eye pain or reduced vision (orbital injury) - urgent review
Clear watery nasal discharge (CSF leak)
Heavy bleeding
Headache, fever, neck stiffness or drowsiness

indications: Nasal polyps causing obstruction despite medical treatment
Antrochoanal polyp
contraindications: Unilateral polyp or mass not yet assessed (suspect tumour, image and biopsy first)
Polyp in a child that may be an encephalocoele (image first)
Bleeding disorder not corrected
equipment: Headlight or rigid endoscope with camera
Nasal speculum, polyp snare and Tilley-Henckel or Blakesley forceps
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Decongest the nose and infiltrate the base of the polyps where reachable.
Remove polyps under endoscopic or direct vision with forceps, snare or microdebrider.
Keep removal medial to the orbit and below the skull base.
Remove an antrochoanal polyp completely including its antral part.
Secure haemostasis and place packs if needed.
Send all tissue for histology.
aftercare: Avoid nose blowing for a week and sleep with the head raised.
Use saline douches and topical steroid sprays long term to reduce recurrence.
Review histology and arrange follow-up.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding
Eye swelling or visual disturbance
Clear watery nasal discharge
Histology showing tumour or inverted papilloma

indications: Acute or chronic maxillary sinusitis not responding to treatment where endoscopic surgery is not available
Obtaining maxillary sinus pus for culture
contraindications: Children with undeveloped maxillary sinus
Suspected maxillary tumour
Bleeding disorder not corrected
equipment: Topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor on pledgets
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging and written consent.
Perform hand hygiene and place topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor under the inferior turbinate.
Sit the patient up with the head slightly forward, or use general anaesthesia if planned.
Pass the trocar under the inferior turbinate about two centimetres behind its front end.
Direct the trocar towards the outer canthus of the same eye and puncture the thin bone with firm controlled pressure.
Remove the trocar and aspirate to confirm the cannula is in the sinus before irrigating.
Irrigate gently with warm saline while the patient leans forward with the mouth open.
Collect the returning fluid for culture and note its appearance.
Stop immediately if there is pain, swelling of the cheek or around the eye.
Remove the cannula and check for bleeding.
aftercare: Expect mild nasal bleeding for a short time.
Complete antibiotics guided by culture.
Review in one to two weeks.
red_flags: Swelling of the cheek or eye, pain or air in the tissues (false passage)
Visual disturbance
Heavy bleeding
Signs of air embolism such as sudden collapse (never inject air)

indications: Chronic maxillary sinus disease where endoscopic access is not available or not adequate
Removal of antrochoanal polyp or foreign body or dental root from the antrum
Biopsy of maxillary sinus lesion
Oroantral fistula repair access
contraindications: Children with developing teeth (risk to tooth buds)
Bleeding disorder not corrected
equipment: Headlight, cheek retractors and periosteal elevator
Chisel and mallet or burr, and Kerrison punches
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor for infiltration
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Infiltrate the gingivolabial sulcus with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Make an incision in the sulcus above the canine and premolar roots, leaving a cuff of mucosa for closure.
Raise the periosteum to expose the canine fossa, protecting the infraorbital nerve.
Open the anterior wall of the antrum and enlarge the opening with punches.
Remove the diseased mucosa, polyp or foreign body and send tissue for histology.
Create an intranasal antrostomy under the inferior turbinate if drainage is needed.
Secure haemostasis and place a pack if needed.
Close the sulcus incision with absorbable sutures.
aftercare: Apply cold compresses to the cheek and expect facial swelling for a few days.
Use soft diet and salt water mouth rinses.
Avoid nose blowing for two weeks.
red_flags: Persistent cheek numbness or tooth numbness (report and review)
Fever, wound breakdown or fluid passing from mouth to nose (oroantral fistula)
Eye swelling or visual change
Heavy bleeding

indications: Inferior turbinate hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction despite medical treatment
contraindications: Atrophic rhinitis or dry nose
Untreated allergic rhinitis without trial of medical treatment
Bleeding disorder not corrected
equipment: Submucosal diathermy needle, coblation or radiofrequency probe, or turbinectomy scissors
steps: Confirm identity, findings, side and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Decongest the nose and infiltrate the turbinate with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Outfracture the turbinate laterally with an elevator if planned.
Reduce the turbinate by submucosal diathermy, radiofrequency or partial resection of the lower edge.
Preserve the overlying mucosa where possible to keep nasal function.
Secure haemostasis and place packs if partial resection was done.
Repeat on the other side if planned.
aftercare: Expect crusting and blockage for two to three weeks.
Use saline nasal douches regularly.
Avoid nose blowing and strenuous activity for a week.
red_flags: Heavy or recurrent bleeding, especially at about one week
Fever or offensive discharge
Persistent dryness and crusting (consider empty nose syndrome)

indications: Evaluation of laryngeal or hypopharyngeal lesion
Biopsy when flexible endoscopy is not possible
Assessment of stridor or airway in children
Staging of head and neck cancer
contraindications: Unstable cervical spine
Severe trismus preventing access
Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Rigid operating laryngoscopes of suitable sizes with light source
Suspension or chest support if available
Difficult airway and tracheostomy set available
steps: Confirm identity, symptoms, imaging and written consent, including possible tracheostomy if the airway is narrow.
Plan the airway jointly with the anaesthetist and perform the time-out.
Place a tooth guard and position the head extended on a flexed neck.
Introduce the laryngoscope along the right side of the tongue and lift the epiglottis.
Inspect the oropharynx, vallecula, supraglottis, glottis, subglottis and piriform fossae systematically.
Take biopsies from suspicious areas and send them for histology.
Control bleeding with pressure or topical vasoconstrictor.
Remove the scope and check the teeth and lips.
aftercare: Keep nil by mouth until fully awake and swallowing safely.
Give voice rest if the cords were biopsied.
Arrange follow-up with histology results.
red_flags: Stridor or breathing difficulty after the procedure
Coughing up significant blood
Neck swelling, crackling under the skin or chest pain (perforation)
Dental injury

form.label: Indication
options: Staging of head and neck cancer

indications: Vocal cord lesion needing biopsy or excision (nodule, polyp, cyst, leukoplakia)
Suspected laryngeal cancer
Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis debulking
contraindications: Unstable cervical spine or severe trismus
Critical airway narrowing without a tracheostomy plan
Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Operating microscope with long focal-length lens
Small endotracheal tube or jet ventilation system
steps: Confirm identity, voice and airway assessment, imaging and written consent including possible tracheostomy.
Agree the airway plan with the anaesthetist and perform the time-out.
Place the tooth guard, insert the laryngoscope and suspend it to expose the vocal cords.
Position the microscope and inspect the larynx systematically.
Grasp the lesion with cup forceps and excise or biopsy it, protecting the underlying vocal ligament.
Avoid injury to the anterior commissure on both sides at once (risk of web).
Control bleeding with pledgets soaked in topical vasoconstrictor.
Send all tissue for histology, orientated if excised.
Remove the laryngoscope and check the teeth and lips.
aftercare: Give voice rest as advised, usually a few days, then gentle use.
Refer to speech therapy for voice care if available.
Arrange review with histology.
red_flags: Stridor or breathing difficulty
Coughing up significant blood
Persistent loss of voice beyond expected recovery
Malignant histology (urgent oncology referral)

name: Rigid oesophagoscopy and foreign body removal

indications: Foreign body impacted in the oesophagus (coin, bone, food bolus)
Button battery in the oesophagus (emergency)
Inspection or biopsy of upper oesophagus when flexible endoscopy is not available
contraindications: Unstable cervical spine
Suspected perforation with mediastinitis needing open surgery (resuscitate and refer)
Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Rigid oesophagoscopes of suitable sizes with light source
Foreign body forceps of assorted types
Chest and lateral neck X-ray available
Flexible endoscope as alternative if available
steps: Confirm identity, the object, time of ingestion, X-ray position and written consent.
Treat a button battery as an emergency and remove it as soon as possible.
Repeat the X-ray just before surgery if the object may have passed.
Agree the airway plan with the anaesthetist and perform the time-out.
Place the tooth guard and position the head extended.
Pass the oesophagoscope under direct vision behind the cricoid and advance only when the lumen is seen.
Locate the object, grasp it securely and withdraw it together with the scope.
Reinspect the oesophagus for mucosal injury, a second object or perforation.
Withdraw slowly while inspecting and check the teeth.
aftercare: Keep nil by mouth for a few hours, then start clear fluids if there is no pain or fever.
Observe for chest pain, fever and neck crackling.
Arrange follow-up for oesophageal narrowing after a button battery or caustic injury.
red_flags: Chest pain, fever or rising pulse after the procedure (perforation)
Crackling under the skin of the neck
Vomiting blood
Difficulty swallowing that persists

indications: Suspected or confirmed inhaled foreign body (history of choking, unilateral wheeze, X-ray signs)
contraindications: None absolute when foreign body is suspected - proceed as soon as a skilled team is available
Complete obstruction at the larynx needs immediate airway rescue first
equipment: Rigid ventilating bronchoscopes of assorted sizes for age with light source
Optical forceps or foreign body forceps (peanut, alligator)
Oxygen, anaesthesia circuit connector and pulse oximetry
Chest X-ray and drugs for bronchospasm available
steps: Confirm identity, history, examination, X-ray findings and written consent including possible tracheostomy.
Check all scopes, telescopes and forceps fit and work before induction.
Agree the airway plan with the anaesthetist, keeping spontaneous ventilation where possible, and perform the time-out.
Position the head extended and protect the teeth.
Pass the bronchoscope through the cords under direct vision and connect the ventilation.
Inspect the normal side first, then the suspected side.
Grasp the object securely with suitable forceps, using optical forceps if available.
Withdraw the object, forceps and scope together if it is larger than the scope lumen.
Re-inspect both bronchial trees for remaining fragments and suction secretions.
Stop and ventilate if oxygen saturation falls, and resume when stable.
Request a chest X-ray after the procedure if fragments may remain or there was a difficult extraction.
aftercare: Monitor oxygen saturation and breathing closely for several hours.
Treat airway oedema or infection as clinically indicated.
Educate the family on keeping nuts and small objects away from young children.
red_flags: Stridor, breathing difficulty or falling oxygen saturation
Signs of pneumothorax (sudden breathlessness, reduced breath sounds)
Persistent wheeze or fever (retained fragment or pneumonia)
Coughing up blood

indications: Upper airway obstruction (tumour, infection, trauma, bilateral vocal cord palsy)
Prolonged mechanical ventilation
Poor protection of the airway or difficulty clearing secretions
Planned as part of major head and neck surgery
contraindications: Infection or tumour over the operative site (relative)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder (relative, correct if time allows)
Complete airway obstruction needing immediate cricothyroidotomy first
equipment: Tracheostomy set with retractors, tracheal hook and dilator
Tracheostomy tubes of the planned size and one size smaller, cuffed or uncuffed for age
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor for infiltration
Oxygen, catheter mount and pulse oximetry
steps: Confirm identity, indication and written consent, or proceed in an emergency under best interests.
Agree the airway plan with the anaesthetist and perform the time-out.
Position the patient with the neck extended on a shoulder roll.
Infiltrate the skin with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Make a horizontal skin incision about two finger breadths above the sternal notch.
Separate the strap muscles in the midline and divide or retract the thyroid isthmus.
Secure haemostasis before opening the trachea.
Open the trachea at the second to fourth rings with a window in adults or a vertical slit with stay sutures in children.
Ask the anaesthetist to withdraw the tube to just above the opening, then insert the tracheostomy tube.
Inflate the cuff, connect ventilation and confirm placement with capnography and chest movement.
Secure the tube with sutures and tapes, and label stay sutures in children.
Request a chest X-ray if indicated.
aftercare: Nurse with humidified oxygen, regular suction and inner tube cleaning.
Keep a spare tube, obturator and tracheal dilator at the bedside.
Do not change the tube for the first few days unless needed, until a track forms.
Teach the patient or carer tracheostomy care and communication methods.
red_flags: Tube displaced or blocked - follow the emergency tracheostomy algorithm
Bleeding from the stoma or coughing blood (consider tracheo-innominate fistula)
Surgical emphysema or pneumothorax
Falling oxygen saturation or breathing difficulty

form.label: Indication
options: Part of head and neck surgery

indications: Prolonged mechanical ventilation in intensive care
Weaning from ventilation
contraindications: Children
Emergency airway
Difficult neck anatomy (short or obese neck, large goitre, previous neck surgery)
Unstable cervical spine or high oxygen or ventilation requirements
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Percutaneous tracheostomy kit with introducer needle, guidewire and dilator
Ultrasound for vessel assessment if available
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting and written consent or best-interest decision.
Perform the time-out with the anaesthetist managing the airway and bronchoscope.
Pre-oxygenate fully, position the neck extended and scan the neck for vessels if possible.
Clean and drape the neck and infiltrate the skin with local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor.
Withdraw the endotracheal tube under bronchoscopic view to just below the cords.
Insert the needle between the first and second or second and third tracheal rings in the midline under bronchoscopic view.
Pass the guidewire and dilate the track using the kit technique.
Insert the tracheostomy tube over the dilator and confirm position with the bronchoscope and capnography.
Inflate the cuff, connect ventilation and secure the tube.
Remove the endotracheal tube once placement is confirmed.
aftercare: Keep emergency tracheostomy equipment at the bedside.
Provide humidification, suction and stoma care.
Request a chest X-ray if indicated.
red_flags: Tube displaced or blocked - follow the emergency algorithm
Bleeding from the stoma
Surgical emphysema or pneumothorax
Falling oxygen saturation

indications: Routine change after the track has formed
Blocked, damaged or wrong-size tube
Change to a different type of tube for weaning or speech
contraindications: Fresh tracheostomy before the track is mature (change only by experienced staff with full backup)
Patient unstable or needing high ventilation support (relative)
equipment: New tracheostomy tube of the same size and one size smaller, checked before use
Obturator, tracheal dilator and water-based lubricant
Tracheostomy tapes or holder and dressing
Syringe for cuff deflation and inflation
steps: Confirm identity, the tube type and size and obtain verbal consent.
Prepare equipment, check the new tube cuff, insert the obturator and lubricate the tube.
Perform hand hygiene and position the patient with the neck extended on a shoulder roll.
Pre-oxygenate and suction the tube and mouth.
Have an assistant hold the tube while the tapes are cut.
Deflate the cuff and remove the old tube with an outward and downward curved movement.
Insert the new tube along the track in a smooth curved movement and remove the obturator.
Insert the inner tube, inflate the cuff and confirm breathing through the tube.
Check capnography or chest movement and oxygen saturation.
Secure the tube with tapes allowing one finger under them and apply a clean dressing.
aftercare: Keep a spare tube and obturator at the bedside.
Clean the inner tube regularly and humidify air.
Document the date of the next planned change.
red_flags: Unable to insert the new tube - try the smaller tube, then oxygenate via the face or stoma and call for help
Falling oxygen saturation or no air flow through the tube
Bleeding from the stoma
Surgical emphysema around the neck

indications: Hoarseness or voice change lasting more than three weeks
Suspected upper aerodigestive tract tumour or neck lump
Stridor or airway assessment
Dysphagia or swallowing assessment
Postnasal space examination
contraindications: Severe bleeding disorder (relative)
Impending airway obstruction where the procedure may precipitate laryngospasm (do in theatre)
equipment: Flexible nasolaryngoscope with light source and, if available, camera
Disinfection system for the scope per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, symptoms and verbal consent, and explain what the patient will feel.
Perform hand hygiene and spray the nose with topical anaesthetic and decongestant.
Seat the patient upright with the head supported.
Pass the lubricated scope along the floor of the nose or between the middle and inferior turbinates.
Inspect the postnasal space and eustachian tube openings.
Advance behind the soft palate to view the tongue base, vallecula, epiglottis and larynx.
Ask the patient to breathe, say "ee" and cough to assess vocal cord movement.
Inspect the piriform fossae and postcricoid area.
Record images or video if available and withdraw slowly.
Clean and disinfect the scope according to protocol and record its identification.
aftercare: Avoid eating or hot drinks until the throat numbness wears off, usually about an hour.
Expect mild nasal discomfort.
red_flags: Mass, ulcer or fixed cord seen (urgent referral pathway for cancer)
Stridor or breathing difficulty during or after the procedure
Persistent nosebleed

indications: Hearing loss or tinnitus assessment
Assessment before and after ear surgery
Monitoring for ototoxic medicines or noise exposure
Hearing screening in school-age children and adults
contraindications: Children too young to cooperate (use age-appropriate tests such as play or visual reinforcement audiometry)
Ear canal occluded by wax or discharge (clear first)
equipment: Calibrated audiometer with headphones and bone conductor
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test, obtain verbal consent, take a short hearing history and check the audiometer calibration is current.
Examine both ear canals with an otoscope and clear wax if needed.
Explain the test and ask the patient to respond to every tone heard however faint.
Fit the headphones correctly and test the better ear first.
Start at 1 kHz, then test 2, 4, 8 kHz, then 500 and 250 Hz, and retest 1 kHz.
Find each threshold using the down 10, up 5 method.
Test bone conduction where air conduction thresholds are raised.
Apply masking when the difference between ears or air-bone gap is large enough to need it.
Plot the results on the audiogram with standard symbols.
Interpret the type and degree of hearing loss and explain the result to the patient.
aftercare: Refer for ENT review, hearing aids or further tests as indicated.
Advise on hearing protection if there is noise exposure.
red_flags: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (urgent ENT referral, same day if possible)
Unilateral or asymmetric sensorineural loss (refer for imaging)
Results inconsistent with behaviour (consider non-organic loss, retest)

indications: Suspected otitis media with effusion
Assessment of eustachian tube function or middle ear pressure
Checking for perforation or grommet patency
Part of hearing assessment with audiometry
contraindications: Acute painful otitis externa or otitis media
Discharging ear or recent ear surgery
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Examine the ear canal and drum with an otoscope.
Choose a probe tip that seals the canal comfortably.
Pull the pinna gently to straighten the canal and insert the probe to get a seal.
Ask the patient to keep still and not swallow during the test.
Run the test and record the trace, middle ear pressure, compliance and canal volume.
Repeat on the other ear.
Classify the trace and correlate with the otoscopy.
aftercare: Explain the result and plan, such as watchful waiting or ENT referral.
red_flags: Flat trace with hearing loss persisting beyond three months in a child (refer)
Flat trace with large canal volume (perforation)
Unilateral effusion in an adult (examine the postnasal space)

indications: Benign parotid tumour in the superficial lobe (for example pleomorphic adenoma)
Selected malignant parotid tumours
Chronic recurrent parotitis not responding to treatment
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia
Lymphoma suspected on cytology (biopsy rather than excise)
equipment: Major head and neck surgery set
Facial nerve monitor or nerve stimulator if available
Bipolar diathermy and fine artery forceps
steps: Confirm identity, side, fine needle cytology and imaging, facial nerve function and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established without long-acting muscle relaxants.
Position with the head turned and expose the face so movement can be seen.
Make a modified Blair incision and raise the skin flap over the parotid fascia.
Separate the gland from the sternomastoid and cartilage of the ear canal.
Identify the facial nerve trunk using landmarks (tragal pointer, posterior belly of digastric, tympanomastoid suture).
Follow the branches forward and lift the superficial lobe and tumour off the nerve.
Remove the tumour with a cuff of normal tissue without rupturing the capsule.
Stimulate the nerve to confirm function and secure haemostasis.
Place a suction drain and close in layers.
Send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Check facial nerve function on waking and record it.
Remove the drain when output is low.
Warn about earlobe numbness and possible gustatory sweating later.
red_flags: Facial weakness not present before surgery
Rapidly enlarging neck swelling (haematoma)
Clear fluid collection under the flap (sialocoele)
Fever or wound redness

indications: Recurrent sialadenitis or stones in the gland
Submandibular gland tumour
Part of neck dissection
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia
Stone accessible in the duct that can be removed through the mouth
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging, cytology and written consent, warning about nerve injuries.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Make a skin incision in a neck crease about two to three finger breadths below the jaw line.
Divide platysma and raise the fascia over the gland to protect the marginal mandibular nerve.
Ligate and divide the facial vein and artery as needed.
Free the gland from the mylohyoid and identify the lingual nerve and submandibular ganglion.
Divide the ganglion branches and the duct, protecting the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
Remove the gland and send it for histology.
Secure haemostasis, place a drain and close in layers.
aftercare: Check lower lip movement, tongue movement and tongue sensation after surgery.
Remove the drain when output is low.
Review with histology.
red_flags: Rapid neck swelling or breathing difficulty (haematoma) - open the wound and call for help
Lower lip weakness, tongue numbness or deviation
Fever or wound discharge

indications: Thyroglossal duct cyst or sinus
Recurrent infection of a midline neck cyst
contraindications: Active infection (treat first, operate when settled)
Ectopic thyroid as the only functioning thyroid tissue (confirm a normal thyroid on ultrasound first)
steps: Confirm identity, ultrasound showing a normal thyroid gland, thyroid function if indicated and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Position with the neck extended and make a skin crease incision over the cyst, including any sinus opening.
Raise subplatysmal flaps and dissect the cyst free from the strap muscles.
Follow the tract to the hyoid bone.
Excise the central part of the hyoid bone in continuity with the cyst.
Follow the tract towards the foramen caecum and excise a core of tongue base muscle with it.
Close the tongue base defect and check haemostasis.
Place a drain if needed and close in layers.
Send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Watch for neck swelling and breathing difficulty.
Remove the drain when output is low.
Review histology for rare carcinoma.
red_flags: Neck swelling or breathing difficulty (haematoma or oedema)
Fever or wound infection
Recurrence of a lump or sinus

indications: Branchial cleft cyst, sinus or fistula in the lateral neck
Recurrent infection of a lateral neck cyst
contraindications: Active infection (treat first)
Lateral neck cyst in an adult over about 40 years until cystic nodal metastasis is excluded
equipment: Lacrimal probe or fine catheter for sinus tracts
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging, cytology and written consent, warning about nerve injury.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Position with the head turned away and make a skin crease incision over the cyst, including any sinus opening.
Raise subplatysmal flaps and retract the sternomastoid backwards.
Dissect the cyst wall free, protecting the internal jugular vein, carotid vessels, accessory, hypoglossal and vagus nerves.
Follow any tract upwards with a probe, using a second higher incision if needed.
Remove the cyst and tract completely to prevent recurrence.
Secure haemostasis, place a drain and close in layers.
Send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Remove the drain when output is low.
Check shoulder, tongue and voice function.
Review histology, especially in adults.
red_flags: Neck swelling or breathing difficulty (haematoma)
Shoulder weakness, tongue deviation or hoarseness
Fever or wound discharge
Malignant histology (refer to head and neck oncology)

indications: Recurrent infection or discharge from a preauricular sinus
Abscess formation that has been treated and settled
contraindications: Asymptomatic sinus (no surgery needed)
Active infection (drain and treat first)
equipment: Lacrimal probe and methylene blue dye
steps: Confirm identity, side, history of infections and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Inject dye gently into the sinus opening and probe the tract if possible.
Make an elliptical incision around the opening, extended upwards if needed.
Dissect deep to the temporalis fascia and remove the tract and all branches in one piece with the attached cartilage if involved.
Excise any old abscess scar with the tract.
Secure haemostasis and close in layers, obliterating dead space.
Apply a pressure dressing.
aftercare: Keep the dressing dry and in place for a few days.
Remove skin sutures at about one week.
Warn that recurrence can happen if any tract remains.
red_flags: Swelling under the wound (haematoma or seroma)
Fever, redness or discharge
Recurrent discharge from the wound later

indications: Lymph node metastasis from head and neck cancer
Elective treatment of the neck at high risk of hidden metastasis
Part of resection of a primary head and neck cancer
contraindications: Unresectable disease or distant metastasis (consider palliative care)
Unfit for major surgery
No histological diagnosis (relative)
equipment: Major head and neck surgery set
Bipolar diathermy, ties and vascular clips
Specimen containers with labels for neck levels
steps: Confirm identity, side, histology, imaging, multidisciplinary plan and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established, with blood available.
Position with the head turned away on a head ring with the shoulder raised.
Make the planned incision and raise subplatysmal flaps.
Identify and protect the marginal mandibular nerve.
Dissect the nodal levels planned, removing the fibrofatty tissue in one block.
Identify and preserve the accessory nerve, internal jugular vein and sternomastoid unless they must be removed.
Protect the vagus, hypoglossal and phrenic nerves, the brachial plexus and the carotid artery.
Ligate the thoracic duct carefully on the left side and check for chyle leak.
Label and orientate the specimen by level for histology.
Secure haemostasis, place suction drains and close in layers.
aftercare: Nurse head-up and watch the drains and the neck for swelling.
Remove the drains when output is low.
Start shoulder physiotherapy early.
Arrange multidisciplinary review of histology for further treatment.
red_flags: Rapid neck swelling or breathing difficulty (haematoma) - open the wound and call for help
Milky drain fluid (chyle leak)
Flap necrosis, fever or wound breakdown
Shoulder droop or weakness

indications: Advanced laryngeal or hypopharyngeal cancer
Recurrent laryngeal cancer after radiotherapy
Severe non-functional larynx with persistent aspiration
contraindications: Distant metastasis or unresectable disease
Unfit for major surgery
Patient not prepared for permanent stoma after counselling
equipment: Major head and neck surgery set
Bipolar diathermy, ties and vascular clips
Laryngectomy tubes and stoma care equipment
Nasogastric feeding tube or voice prosthesis set if planned
steps: Confirm identity, histology, imaging, multidisciplinary plan, nutrition and written consent with counselling on the stoma and speech.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established, often through a tracheostomy.
Make the planned apron or U-shaped incision and raise subplatysmal flaps.
Perform neck dissection as planned.
Free the larynx by dividing the strap muscles, thyroid isthmus and constrictor muscles, preserving thyroid tissue as possible.
Divide the hyoid attachments and the trachea below the tumour.
Enter the pharynx away from the tumour and remove the larynx with clear margins.
Perform a primary puncture for a voice prosthesis if planned.
Close the pharynx in layers over a feeding tube.
Suture the trachea to the skin to form the end stoma.
Place suction drains and close the skin.
Send the specimen orientated for histology.
aftercare: Provide humidified air, stoma suction and laryngectomy tube care.
Feed through the nasogastric tube until the pharynx has healed as planned.
Check calcium and thyroid function.
Refer to speech therapy and teach stoma care before discharge.
red_flags: Stoma blockage or breathing difficulty - remove the tube and suction
Saliva leaking through the wound (pharyngocutaneous fistula)
Bleeding from the neck or stoma
Low calcium symptoms such as tingling or cramps

indications: Parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal or submandibular space abscess
Ludwig's angina with collection or not improving on antibiotics
contraindications: None absolute when the airway is threatened - secure the airway first
equipment: Difficult airway equipment, flexible scope and tracheostomy set
steps: Confirm identity, airway status, imaging and written consent including possible tracheostomy.
Keep the patient sitting up and plan the airway with the anaesthetist, considering awake fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy under local anaesthesia.
Perform the surgical time-out once the airway is secured.
Drain a retropharyngeal abscess through the mouth with the head down and suction ready, if suitable.
Make an external incision over the collection, usually below the jaw line or along the sternomastoid.
Open the fascial spaces bluntly with sinus forceps, protecting the great vessels.
Break down loculations and send pus for culture.
Remove the cause such as an infected tooth if identified and safe.
Irrigate the cavity and place drains.
Leave the wound loosely closed or open.
aftercare: Continue IV antibiotics per local protocol and culture results.
Monitor the airway closely, ideally in a high-dependency area.
Remove drains as discharge settles and control blood sugar if diabetic.
red_flags: Stridor, drooling or breathing difficulty
Chest pain or widening mediastinum (mediastinitis)
Bleeding from the wound or mouth (possible vessel erosion)
Persistent fever or spreading swelling

indications: Haematoma of the pinna after blunt trauma, ideally within a few days
contraindications: Old organised haematoma (consider surgical excision later)
Bleeding disorder not corrected (relative)
equipment: Local anaesthetic and syringe with fine needle
Wide-bore needle or scalpel with size 15 blade
Bolster or dental rolls, or silicone splint
steps: Confirm identity, side, time since injury and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the ear with antiseptic and give a local anaesthetic ear block.
Aspirate a small early haematoma with a wide-bore needle.
For larger or recurrent collections, incise along the helical rim fold and evacuate the clot.
Irrigate the space with saline.
Apply bolsters on both sides of the pinna with through-and-through sutures, or a firm splint, to stop reaccumulation.
Apply a head bandage.
aftercare: Review in one day to check for reaccumulation.
Keep the bolster in place for about one week.
Give antibiotics per local protocol if the wound is contaminated.
Advise headgear for contact sports.
red_flags: Swelling returning
Increasing pain, redness or fever (perichondritis)
Skin colour change under the bolster

indications: Partial or complete split earlobe from earrings or trauma
Acute earlobe laceration
contraindications: Active infection
History of keloid at the ear (counsel carefully and plan keloid prevention)
equipment: Minor plastic surgery set with fine scissors and skin hooks
Local anaesthetic with syringe and fine needle
Fine non-absorbable or absorbable skin sutures
steps: Confirm identity, side, keloid history and written consent.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the ear with antiseptic and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Excise the epithelium lining the cleft edges to create raw surfaces.
Shape the edges with a straight line, Z-plasty or notch to avoid a notch deformity.
Close the front and back skin and the lobe edge with fine sutures.
Apply a light dressing.
aftercare: Keep the ear clean and dry for a few days.
Remove sutures at about one week.
Wait about six to eight weeks before repiercing at a different site.
red_flags: Redness, swelling or discharge
Thick raised scar developing (keloid) - review early
Wound breakdown

indications: Suspected nasopharyngeal carcinoma or lymphoma
Nasal or postnasal mass needing tissue diagnosis
Unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult with postnasal space abnormality
contraindications: Suspected juvenile angiofibroma (risk of severe bleeding - image first, do not biopsy)
Pulsatile or vascular mass
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Rigid endoscope (0 and 30 degree) with light source and camera
Specimen containers for histology and fresh tissue if lymphoma suspected
steps: Confirm identity, imaging, clotting and written consent.
Perform the time-out and apply topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor, or use general anaesthesia.
Pass the endoscope along the nasal floor to the postnasal space.
Inspect the fossa of Rosenmüller, eustachian tube openings and the roof.
Take several biopsies from the abnormal area, or the fossae on both sides if the area looks normal.
Control bleeding with pressure, vasoconstrictor pledgets or bipolar diathermy.
Place a pack if bleeding persists.
Send tissue for histology, and fresh tissue if lymphoma is suspected.
aftercare: Avoid nose blowing for a few days.
Expect blood-stained mucus for a day or two.
Arrange review with histology results.
red_flags: Heavy or persistent nosebleed
Malignant histology (urgent oncology referral)
Neck lump or cranial nerve symptoms

indications: Posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo confirmed by a positive Dix-Hallpike test
contraindications: Unstable or severe cervical spine disease, recent neck injury
Carotid or vertebral artery disease, or unstable heart disease (relative)
Atypical nystagmus or neurological signs (needs neurological assessment)
equipment: Examination couch that allows the head to hang over the edge
steps: Confirm identity, the diagnosis and verbal consent, and warn that vertigo will be provoked.
Check neck movement and ask about neck or vascular problems.
Sit the patient on the couch and turn the head 45 degrees towards the affected ear.
Lie the patient back quickly with the head hanging about 20 degrees below horizontal and observe the nystagmus.
Hold until the nystagmus and vertigo settle, then for about another 30 seconds.
Turn the head 90 degrees to the opposite side and hold.
Roll the patient onto that side with the head turned to look at the floor and hold.
Bring the patient slowly up to sitting with the head tilted down.
Wait in the sitting position until any dizziness settles before standing.
Repeat once or twice at the same visit if the vertigo persists.
aftercare: Advise care on standing and avoiding sudden head movements for a day.
Teach home Brandt-Daroff exercises or self-Epley if suitable.
Review in one to two weeks and repeat if needed.
red_flags: Neurological signs such as double vision, slurred speech, weakness or inability to walk (urgent stroke assessment)
Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus not typical of BPPV
Hearing loss or persistent severe vertigo

indications: Otosclerosis with conductive hearing loss and good cochlear reserve
contraindications: Only hearing ear
Active middle or outer ear infection or perforation
Active otosclerosis phase or Meniere's disease (relative)
Patient who prefers a hearing aid after counselling
equipment: Operating microscope and middle ear instrument set
Perforator or skeeter drill or laser if available
steps: Confirm identity, side, audiogram with tuning fork tests and written consent with counselling about dead ear risk.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia or local infiltration is established.
Infiltrate the canal and raise a tympanomeatal flap.
Remove bone from the posterior-superior canal wall to see the stapes and the facial nerve.
Confirm stapes fixation and normal mobility of the malleus and incus.
Measure the distance from the incus to the footplate.
Divide the stapedius tendon and stapes superstructure.
Make a small opening in the footplate with a perforator, drill or laser.
Place the prosthesis through the opening and crimp it onto the incus.
Seal around the prosthesis with fat or vein if used and replace the flap.
Pack the canal.
aftercare: Avoid nose blowing, straining, heavy lifting and flying for several weeks.
Expect mild dizziness for a day or two.
Arrange audiogram at follow-up.
red_flags: Severe vertigo, vomiting or nystagmus
Sudden loss of hearing after initial improvement (perilymph fistula or reparative granuloma)
Facial weakness
Fever or ear discharge

indications: Bilateral severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss with little benefit from hearing aids
Children with congenital deafness, as early as practicable
Post-meningitis deafness (urgent before cochlear ossification)
contraindications: Absent cochlea or cochlear nerve on imaging
Active middle ear infection
Unable to commit to rehabilitation and follow-up
Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Cochlear implant device and backup device from the programme
Operating microscope, otological drill and facial nerve monitor
steps: Confirm identity, side, imaging, audiology, team assessment, vaccination status and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established, checking the device and side.
Make a postauricular incision and fashion a bed and tie-down for the receiver-stimulator.
Perform a cortical mastoidectomy.
Open the facial recess between the facial nerve and chorda tympani to see the round window.
Open the round window or make a cochleostomy.
Insert the electrode array gently and fully into the scala tympani.
Seal around the electrode and secure the receiver-stimulator.
Perform intraoperative device and nerve response testing.
Close in layers and apply a pressure dressing.
Request postoperative imaging to confirm electrode position if per protocol.
aftercare: Check facial nerve function on waking.
Keep the wound dry until healed and review the wound at one week.
Activate and programme the device at a few weeks and begin auditory rehabilitation.
Ensure pneumococcal vaccination is complete.
red_flags: Facial weakness
Fever, headache or neck stiffness (meningitis)
Swelling, redness or exposure of the device
Severe vertigo

indications: Bilateral choanal atresia in a newborn (airway emergency)
Unilateral choanal atresia with symptoms, usually repaired electively later
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia because of associated anomalies (secure airway with oral airway or McGovern nipple first)
CT not done to confirm the diagnosis and bony anatomy
equipment: Paediatric rigid endoscopes with camera and monitor
Paediatric nasal instruments and curved urethral sounds or dilators
Drill with long fine burrs and backbiters
Oral airway or McGovern nipple for the newborn
steps: Confirm identity, CT findings, assessment for associated anomalies such as CHARGE and written consent from the parents.
Secure the newborn airway with an oral airway or McGovern nipple until surgery.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Decongest the nose and view the atretic plate with the endoscope.
Perforate the plate gently in the inferior-medial part along the nasal floor, never directing the instrument upwards towards the skull base.
Enlarge the opening with dilators, drill or backbiters.
Remove the back of the vomer to make a single wide opening.
Preserve mucosal flaps to cover raw bone where possible.
Place stents if planned and secure them.
Check the airway by passing a suction catheter through each side.
aftercare: Suction the nose and stents regularly and use saline drops.
Monitor breathing and feeding closely.
Plan endoscopic review and dilatation if the opening narrows.
red_flags: Breathing difficulty, cyanosis with feeding or stent blockage
Heavy bleeding
Clear watery discharge (CSF leak)
Return of noisy breathing or nasal blockage (restenosis)

indications: Long-acting reversible contraception requested
Emergency contraception within the eligible window after unprotected sex
Intolerance of or contraindication to hormonal methods
contraindications: Pregnancy or pregnancy not reasonably excluded
Current purulent cervicitis, chlamydia or gonorrhoea, or pelvic inflammatory disease
Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation
Known cervical or endometrial cancer awaiting treatment
Distorted uterine cavity (large fibroids, congenital anomaly)
Puerperal sepsis or post-abortion sepsis
equipment: Copper IUD in sterile pack (check expiry)
Local anaesthetic and syringe if a paracervical block is used
steps: Confirm identity, counselling completed, medical eligibility and written consent.
Exclude pregnancy using a pregnancy test or the pregnancy checklist.
Ask the client to empty her bladder and position her in lithotomy.
Perform hand hygiene and a bimanual examination to determine uterine size and position.
Put on sterile gloves, insert the speculum and inspect the cervix for discharge or lesions.
Clean the cervix and vagina with antiseptic using a no-touch technique.
Apply the tenaculum gently to the anterior lip of the cervix and apply traction to straighten the uterus.
Sound the uterus slowly to measure depth and direction, stopping at the fundus.
Load the IUD in the sterile pack and set the depth gauge to the sounded length.
Insert the loaded inserter through the cervix to the fundus, then withdraw the inserter tube to release the arms.
Push the tube gently up to the fundus again, then remove the plunger and tube.
Cut the strings to about 3 cm from the external os.
Remove the tenaculum, check for bleeding at the puncture sites and remove the speculum.
Observe the client for pain, dizziness or fainting before she sits up and leaves.
aftercare: Explain how to feel for the strings and when to check them.
Warn that heavier, longer or crampy periods are common in the first months.
Give a card with the device type, insertion date and removal date.
Book a check visit after the next period or within six weeks.
Advise condoms as well if there is a risk of sexually transmitted infection.
red_flags: Stop if the sound or inserter meets sudden loss of resistance or passes beyond expected depth (possible perforation).
Stop and refer if severe pain, vasovagal collapse that does not settle, or heavy bleeding occurs.
Return urgently for severe lower abdominal pain, fever, foul discharge or pain during sex.
Return if the strings cannot be felt, feel longer, or the IUD is felt in the vagina.
Return if a period is missed or pregnancy is suspected.

indications: Client wishes to become pregnant or stop the method
Device due for replacement
Side effects not tolerated
Partial expulsion or malposition
Pelvic infection not responding to treatment
Pregnancy with strings visible
contraindications: Strings not visible (use the missing-strings procedure instead)
equipment: Long artery forceps or sponge-holding forceps
New device if replacement is planned
steps: Confirm identity, reason for removal and verbal consent.
Discuss the need for another method if pregnancy is not wanted, and plan for immediate start.
Perform hand hygiene and position the client in lithotomy.
Insert the speculum and identify the strings at the cervical os.
Clean the cervix with antiseptic.
Grasp the strings close to the os with long forceps.
Apply slow, steady traction to remove the device, asking the client to breathe out.
Inspect the device to confirm it is complete and show it to the client.
Insert a new device or start another method now if planned.
Remove the speculum and observe the client briefly.
aftercare: Advise that fertility returns quickly after removal.
Use condoms or another method straight away if pregnancy is not wanted.
Light spotting for a day or two is expected.
red_flags: Stop if there is strong resistance; do not pull hard, refer for assisted removal.
Stop and refer if strings break or the device is incomplete.
Return for heavy bleeding, fever or severe pain after removal.
If pregnant with the IUD in place, refer for review of pregnancy location and risk.

indications: Client counselled antenatally or in early labour and chooses an IUD after delivery
Insertion within 10 minutes of placenta delivery or within 48 hours postpartum
Insertion at caesarean section through the uterine incision
contraindications: Chorioamnionitis or fever in labour
Prolonged rupture of membranes beyond local threshold
Unresolved postpartum haemorrhage
Extensive genital trauma that would be disrupted
Puerperal sepsis
More than 48 hours and less than four weeks since delivery
equipment: Postpartum IUD inserter or copper IUD
Kelly placental forceps (long, curved) for vaginal insertion
steps: Confirm prior counselling, eligibility and written consent before or early in labour, and reconfirm after delivery.
Confirm the placenta is complete and bleeding is controlled after active management of the third stage.
Change to new sterile gloves and drape the perineum.
Clean the cervix and vagina with antiseptic.
Grasp the anterior lip of the cervix with ring forceps.
Hold the IUD with the postpartum inserter or Kelly forceps so the arms are horizontal.
Insert the IUD through the cervix into the lower uterus, avoiding touching the vaginal walls.
Place the other hand on the abdomen and push the uterus upward to straighten the lower segment.
Advance the IUD to the fundus, confirming position with the abdominal hand.
Open the forceps, release the IUD at the fundus and withdraw the forceps along the uterine side wall.
Check that the IUD is not visible at the cervix; do not cut the strings.
At caesarean, place the IUD at the fundus through the incision, direct the strings toward the cervix, then close the uterus.
Continue routine postpartum monitoring of uterine tone and bleeding.
aftercare: Explain that expulsion is more likely than with interval insertion and how to recognise it.
Strings may need trimming at the postnatal check.
Book a check at six weeks postpartum.
Give a card with device type, date and removal date.
red_flags: Stop if postpartum haemorrhage begins; manage the bleeding first.
Do not insert if the client has fever, foul liquor or signs of infection.
Return for fever, foul lochia, severe abdominal pain or heavy bleeding.
Return if the device is felt or seen in the vagina.

indications: Long-acting contraception requested
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Endometrial protection with oestrogen therapy
Dysmenorrhoea or adenomyosis symptom control
contraindications: Pregnancy or pregnancy not reasonably excluded
Current pelvic infection or purulent cervicitis
Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation
Current breast cancer
Distorted uterine cavity
Severe active liver disease or liver tumour
equipment: Hormonal IUS in sterile pack with its inserter
Cervical dilators and local anaesthetic available
steps: Confirm identity, counselling, eligibility and written consent.
Exclude pregnancy and check the timing in the cycle.
Perform hand hygiene and a bimanual examination for uterine size and position.
Insert the speculum, inspect and clean the cervix with antiseptic.
Apply the tenaculum and gentle traction to align the uterus.
Sound the uterus to measure depth and direction.
Prepare the inserter following the manufacturer's instructions and set the flange to the sounded depth.
Advance the inserter until the flange is about 1.5 to 2 cm from the os, then release the arms and wait a few seconds.
Advance the inserter gently to the fundus, release the device and withdraw the inserter.
Cut the threads to about 3 cm and remove the tenaculum and speculum.
Observe for pain, bleeding or fainting before the client leaves.
aftercare: Explain that irregular spotting is common for the first months and periods often become lighter or stop.
Teach string checks.
Give a card with device type, insertion date and replacement date.
Book a check visit at about six weeks.
Use condoms for seven days if not inserted in the first days of the cycle.
red_flags: Stop if perforation is suspected (sudden loss of resistance, depth beyond expected).
Return for severe abdominal pain, fever or foul discharge.
Return if the strings are missing or the device is felt.
Return if pregnancy is suspected.

indications: Long-acting reversible contraception requested, including adolescents and postpartum clients
contraindications: Pregnancy or pregnancy not reasonably excluded
Current breast cancer
Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation
Severe active liver disease or liver tumour
equipment: Implant in sterile pre-loaded applicator (check expiry and type)
Local anaesthetic, syringe and fine needle
Scalpel and trocar if a non-preloaded system is used
Adhesive plaster or skin closure strip
steps: Confirm identity, counselling, eligibility and verbal consent (and assent with guardian involvement for minors per local policy).
Exclude pregnancy.
Ask the client to lie down with the non-dominant arm flexed and externally rotated.
Mark the insertion site on the inner upper arm over the triceps, away from the sulcus between biceps and triceps.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the site with antiseptic.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic along the planned track.
Insert the applicator needle bevel up just under the skin at a shallow angle.
Tent the skin upward while advancing the needle along its full length in the subdermal plane.
Release the implant according to the device instructions and withdraw the applicator.
Palpate to confirm the implant (or both rods) is in place and ask the client to feel it.
Close the site with an adhesive strip and apply a pressure bandage.
Fill in the user card and the clinic record with type, batch, site and date.
aftercare: Keep the pressure bandage on for a day and the small dressing for a few days, kept dry.
Bruising and tenderness are common for a few days.
Explain expected changes in bleeding pattern.
Use condoms for seven days if not inserted in the first days of the cycle or straight after removal of another method.
Give the removal date and advise return any time for removal.
red_flags: Stop if the implant cannot be felt after insertion; check placement before the client leaves and refer for imaging if still not palpable.
Return for pus, increasing redness or pain at the site.
Return if the implant comes out or cannot be felt.
Return for arm numbness or tingling, severe headache, or suspected pregnancy.

indications: Client request for any reason
Implant expired or due for replacement
Side effects not tolerated
Wants pregnancy
contraindications: Implant not palpable (use deep implant removal pathway)
equipment: Local anaesthetic, syringe and fine needle
steps: Confirm identity, reason for removal and verbal consent, and plan the next method.
Palpate and mark both ends of each rod.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the site with antiseptic.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic under the end of the implant nearest the elbow.
Push the far end of the implant so the near end bulges, and make a small incision over the tip.
Push the implant toward the incision until the tip is visible, then grasp it with forceps.
Free any fibrous sheath with gentle dissection and remove the implant.
Repeat for the second rod if present and confirm each rod is whole and its full length.
Insert a new implant through the same incision if requested.
Close the incision with skin closure strips and apply a pressure bandage.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry for a few days.
Fertility returns quickly; start another method now if pregnancy is not wanted.
Bruising is common and settles.
red_flags: Stop and refer if a rod cannot be located or breaks and part remains; do not dig blindly.
Return for pus, spreading redness or increasing pain at the wound.
Return for numbness or weakness of the hand or forearm.

indications: Implant not palpable or deeply placed and removal required
Failed routine removal
contraindications: Implant not localised by ultrasound or X-ray (localise first)
No trained operator or imaging available (refer)
equipment: High-frequency linear ultrasound probe or prior imaging report
Scalpel, fine forceps, modified vasectomy clamp or U-forceps
steps: Confirm identity, localisation report, indication and written consent including risk of nerve or vessel injury.
Localise the implant with ultrasound and mark its position, depth and relation to nerves and vessels.
Perform hand hygiene, gown and glove, and prepare and drape the arm.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic carefully around the implant track without displacing it.
Make a small incision over the implant at the most accessible point under ultrasound guidance.
Dissect bluntly toward the implant, keeping away from the neurovascular bundle.
Grasp the implant with a clamp, free its sheath and remove it whole.
Confirm the full length is removed and, if two rods, remove the second the same way.
Close the wound and apply a pressure bandage.
Document findings and send the implant for inspection if required.
aftercare: Keep the dressing dry and in place for a few days.
Review the wound in a week or for suture removal.
Start another method now if pregnancy is not wanted.
red_flags: Stop if the implant lies against the brachial artery or a major nerve and refer to a vascular or surgical specialist.
Stop after a reasonable time without success rather than extending dissection blindly.
Return for numbness, weakness, cold hand, swelling or wound infection.
Implant not found on imaging may have migrated; refer for chest imaging and specialist review.

indications: Client chooses a progestogen-only injectable for contraception
Repeat injection due
contraindications: Pregnancy or pregnancy not reasonably excluded
Current breast cancer
Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation
Multiple cardiovascular risk factors or severe uncontrolled hypertension per eligibility criteria
equipment: Injectable contraceptive vial or prefilled syringe (check expiry)
Sterile syringe and needle for intramuscular injection
Alcohol swab or clean water and cotton wool
steps: Confirm identity, method choice, eligibility and verbal consent.
Check the date of the last injection and whether the client is within the grace period; exclude pregnancy if late.
Check blood pressure.
Perform hand hygiene.
Shake the vial well and draw up the full contents, or prepare the prefilled syringe.
Clean the site (deltoid or upper outer buttock) and inject deep intramuscularly (or subcutaneously for DMPA-SC).
Do not massage the site.
Dispose of the needle in the sharps container immediately.
Record the drug, date, site and next due date on the client card and register.
aftercare: Give the return date and explain the grace period.
Explain that irregular bleeding or no periods are common and not harmful.
Explain that return of fertility can be delayed after stopping.
Use condoms for seven days if not given in the first days of the cycle.
red_flags: Return for very heavy or prolonged bleeding.
Return for severe headache with visual change, or severe abdominal pain.
Return if pregnancy is suspected.
Return for pus or a painful lump at the injection site.

indications: Client chooses DMPA-SC and wishes to self-inject at home
contraindications: Same medical eligibility limits as other progestogen-only injectables
Client unable to demonstrate safe technique after training (provider-administer instead)
equipment: DMPA-SC prefilled injection devices (one for demonstration, supply for home)
Client instruction leaflet and reinjection calendar
Sharps disposal container or puncture-proof container advice
Alcohol swabs or soap and water
steps: Confirm identity, method choice, eligibility and verbal consent.
Exclude pregnancy and check blood pressure.
Explain the device parts, how to check the expiry date and how to store it at room temperature.
Demonstrate hand washing, choosing a site on the abdomen or front of the thigh, and cleaning the skin.
Show how to mix the device by shaking and activate it by pushing the needle cap and port together.
Show how to pinch the skin, insert the needle straight in and squeeze the reservoir slowly.
Watch the client give her own first injection under supervision and correct technique.
Teach safe disposal of used devices.
Mark the next due dates on a calendar and supply devices for home use.
aftercare: Reinject every three months; use the calendar or phone reminders.
Explain the grace period and what to do if late.
Explain expected bleeding changes.
Return any time with questions or problems.
red_flags: Stop and provider-inject if the client cannot perform the steps safely.
Return for very heavy bleeding, severe headache or suspected pregnancy.
Return for a painful, red or pus-filled injection site.

indications: Client chooses combined or progestogen-only pills
contraindications: Combined pill - migraine with aura, history of venous thromboembolism, smoker aged 35 or over, uncontrolled hypertension, breastfeeding under six weeks
Combined pill - ischaemic heart disease, stroke, severe liver disease or major surgery with prolonged immobilisation
Current breast cancer
Pregnancy
steps: Confirm identity and method choice after counselling.
Take a history for medical eligibility, including migraine, clotting history, smoking and breastfeeding.
Check blood pressure and weight.
Exclude pregnancy or use a quick start with back-up advice.
Choose the pill type (combined or progestogen-only) based on eligibility and preference.
Explain when to start, how to take the pill daily and what to do with missed pills.
Explain common side effects and interactions, including enzyme-inducing medicines.
Supply pill packs and record the type and quantity given.
aftercare: Use condoms for seven days if not started at the beginning of the cycle (two days for progestogen-only pills).
Follow the missed pill rules given.
Return for review and resupply as booked.
Use condoms as well if there is a risk of sexually transmitted infection.
red_flags: Return urgently for calf pain or swelling, chest pain, breathlessness, sudden severe headache, vision loss or weakness.
Return for very heavy bleeding or suspected pregnancy.
Return for jaundice.

indications: Unprotected sex, contraceptive failure or sexual assault within the eligible time window
contraindications: Established pregnancy (no benefit)
equipment: Copper IUD and insertion kit if the IUD option is chosen
steps: Confirm identity, offer privacy and take verbal consent (with safeguarding approach for minors).
Establish the time since unprotected sex and the date of the last period.
Ask about sexual assault and follow the sexual assault care pathway if present.
Explain the options, copper IUD (most effective) or emergency pills.
Check for enzyme-inducing medicines or high body weight, which reduce pill effectiveness, and adjust the choice per local protocol.
Give the pills to take now, or arrange copper IUD insertion.
Offer an ongoing contraceptive method and a quick start where appropriate.
Offer sexually transmitted infection and HIV testing and post-exposure prophylaxis if indicated.
aftercare: Take a repeat dose if vomiting occurs soon after the pill, per instructions.
Expect the next period around the usual time; it may be early or late.
Do a pregnancy test if the period is more than a week late or unusually light.
Use condoms until an ongoing method is effective.
red_flags: Return for lower abdominal pain or a missed or abnormal period (exclude ectopic pregnancy).
Refer immediately to the sexual assault pathway if assault is disclosed.
Report safeguarding concerns for minors per local policy.

indications: Woman requesting permanent contraception after full counselling
contraindications: Pregnancy
Acute pelvic infection
Uncertainty about the decision or coercion suspected
Unfit for anaesthesia without optimisation
equipment: Minilaparotomy set (small retractors, Babcock forceps, artery forceps, scissors, needle holder)
Sterile gowns, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Local anaesthetic and sedation or anaesthesia set-up with resuscitation equipment
Urinary catheter or bladder empty before procedure
steps: Confirm identity, counselling on permanence and alternatives, voluntary written consent and pregnancy test.
Perform the surgical safety checklist and time-out.
Ensure the bladder is empty and position the client supine.
Give anaesthesia per plan, scrub and glove, prepare and drape the abdomen, and place the uterine elevator.
Make a small transverse suprapubic incision and open the layers to the peritoneum.
Use the uterine elevator to bring each tube into view.
Grasp the tube with Babcock forceps and follow it to the fimbrial end to confirm it is the tube.
Ligate and excise a segment of each tube using the modified Pomeroy or Parkland technique.
Check for bleeding from the cut ends and mesosalpinx.
Close the peritoneum, fascia and skin in layers.
Remove the uterine elevator and check for vaginal bleeding.
Send the tubal segments for histology if available.
Complete the sign-out with instrument and swab count.
aftercare: Observe vital signs until fully recovered and able to walk and pass urine.
Keep the wound clean and dry and return for wound review in about a week.
Avoid heavy lifting for a week and sex until comfortable.
Explain that the method is effective immediately but rare failure can occur.
red_flags: Stop and convert or refer if tubes cannot be identified with certainty or bleeding cannot be controlled.
Return urgently for fever, increasing abdominal pain, wound discharge or fainting.
Return for a missed period or pregnancy symptoms (exclude ectopic pregnancy).

indications: Woman who chose permanent contraception during antenatal counselling, within seven days of delivery or at caesarean
contraindications: Consent given only during labour or under duress
Puerperal sepsis, fever or chorioamnionitis
Severe anaemia or haemorrhage not yet corrected
Uncertain wellbeing of the newborn per local policy
equipment: Sterile gowns, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity, antenatal counselling, voluntary written consent and wellbeing of mother and baby.
Perform the surgical safety checklist and time-out.
Give anaesthesia per plan with the bladder emptied.
Make a small infraumbilical incision over the fundus (or use the caesarean incision).
Bring each tube out and confirm it by following it to the fimbria.
Tie a loop of the mid-tube with absorbable suture and excise the loop (Pomeroy technique).
Check the cut ends for bleeding.
Repeat on the other side.
Close the abdominal layers.
Send the segments for histology if available.
Complete the sign-out with instrument and swab count.
aftercare: Continue routine postnatal care, including uterine tone and bleeding checks.
Keep the wound clean and review in about a week.
Support breastfeeding as usual.
red_flags: Stop and refer if a tube cannot be confidently identified.
Return urgently for fever, wound discharge, increasing abdominal pain or heavy bleeding.
Return if pregnancy is suspected later.

indications: Woman requesting permanent contraception after counselling, with laparoscopy available
contraindications: Pregnancy
Acute pelvic infection
Previous extensive abdominal surgery or adhesions (consider minilaparotomy)
Cardiorespiratory disease unsuitable for pneumoperitoneum
