equipment: Laparoscopy stack, insufflator and carbon dioxide supply
Clip or ring applicator with Filshie clips or Falope rings
General anaesthesia set-up with resuscitation equipment
Sterile gowns, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Instruments for conversion to open surgery
steps: Confirm identity, counselling, voluntary written consent and negative pregnancy test.
Perform the surgical safety checklist and time-out.
Give anaesthesia, empty the bladder and place the uterine manipulator.
Create pneumoperitoneum and insert the umbilical port and camera.
Inspect the pelvis and identify each tube by following it to the fimbria.
Insert the secondary port and the clip or ring applicator.
Apply a clip across the isthmic part of each tube at right angles, including the full width.
Confirm correct placement on both tubes.
Check for bleeding, release the gas and remove the ports under vision.
Close the port sites.
Complete the sign-out with instrument and swab count.
aftercare: Shoulder tip pain and bloating are common for a day or two.
Keep the port sites clean and dry.
Return to normal activity in a few days.
Explain the rare risk of failure and ectopic pregnancy.
red_flags: Convert to open surgery if visceral or vascular injury is suspected.
Abandon and use another method if tubes cannot be seen clearly.
Return urgently for increasing abdominal pain, fever, vomiting or distension after discharge.
Return for a missed period or pregnancy symptoms.

indications: Man requesting permanent contraception after counselling
contraindications: Uncertainty about the decision or coercion suspected
Scrotal infection, large hydrocele, varicocele or hernia (treat or refer)
Undescended testis or vas not palpable
Bleeding disorder not managed
equipment: Local anaesthetic, syringe and fine needle
Absorbable suture or diathermy for vas occlusion
steps: Confirm identity, counselling on permanence and the need for back-up contraception, and written consent.
Perform the time-out and confirm both vasa are palpable.
Perform hand hygiene, prepare the scrotum with antiseptic and drape.
Fix the right vas under the median raphe using the three-finger technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the skin and along the vas.
Grasp the vas through the skin with the ringed clamp.
Puncture the skin and vas sheath with the dissecting forceps and spread to expose the vas.
Deliver a loop of vas and occlude it by ligation or cautery with fascial interposition, excising a segment if used.
Return the vas and repeat on the left side through the same puncture.
Check for bleeding; the puncture usually needs no sutures.
Apply gauze and a scrotal support.
aftercare: Rest for a day, wear scrotal support and avoid heavy work for a few days.
Use another contraceptive method until semen analysis confirms no sperm (about three months).
Mild swelling and discomfort are common.
Book semen analysis.
red_flags: Stop and refer if a vas cannot be identified with confidence.
Return urgently for rapidly enlarging scrotal swelling (haematoma).
Return for fever, wound pus or severe pain.
Return if a partner becomes pregnant.

indications: Contraception
Dual protection against sexually transmitted infections and HIV
Back-up method while starting another method
contraindications: Latex allergy (offer non-latex condoms)
equipment: Male condoms (latex and non-latex if available)
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, ensure privacy and use non-judgemental language.
Check the expiry date and package integrity with the client.
Show how to open the packet carefully without teeth or sharp objects.
Demonstrate pinching the tip and rolling the condom onto the erect penis model before any contact.
Explain using only water- or silicone-based lubricant with latex condoms.
Demonstrate withdrawal while holding the rim, and safe disposal.
Ask the client to demonstrate on the model and correct errors.
Explain what to do if a condom breaks, including emergency contraception and PEP.
Supply condoms.
aftercare: Use a new condom for every act of sex.
Store away from heat and sunlight.
Return for more supplies or another method at any time.
red_flags: Seek emergency contraception and HIV PEP promptly if a condom breaks or slips.
Return for genital sores, discharge or pain.

indications: Client seeking contraception or a change of method
Postpartum or post-abortion contraception
Adolescent sexual and reproductive health visit
contraindications: None
steps: Greet the client, ensure privacy and confidentiality, and take verbal consent.
Ask about reproductive goals, previous methods, partner and health history.
Tell the client about all available methods, including effectiveness, use and side effects.
Help the client choose a method, respecting her or his own decision free of pressure.
Check medical eligibility for the chosen method, including blood pressure where relevant.
Explain how to use the chosen method, side effects and when to return.
Exclude pregnancy where needed before starting.
Offer HIV and STI testing and dual protection.
Arrange the method start today or a return visit.
aftercare: Return any time to change or stop a method.
Return on the scheduled date for resupply or check.
red_flags: Refer if coercion, intimate partner violence or child abuse is disclosed, per safeguarding policy.
Refer if a medical condition makes most methods unsuitable.

form.label: Complications
options: Not medically eligible for preferred method

indications: Client prefers a natural method for avoiding or achieving pregnancy
contraindications: Cycles outside the 26 to 32 day range for the standard days method
Recent childbirth, breastfeeding or stopping hormonal methods until cycles are regular
Situation where pregnancy would be dangerous (offer more effective methods)
steps: Confirm identity and verbal consent, and involve the partner if the client wishes.
Take a menstrual history and confirm cycle length and regularity.
Explain how the fertile window is identified with the chosen method.
Teach use of CycleBeads or the calendar, starting on the first day of the period.
Explain the need to avoid sex or use condoms on fertile days.
Check understanding by asking the client to explain the method back.
Supply condoms for fertile days if wanted.
aftercare: Record cycles and return if two cycles in a year fall outside the range.
Return for review in about three months.
red_flags: Return if a period is late or pregnancy is suspected.
Return if cycles become irregular or the partner will not cooperate.

name: Retrieval of IUD with missing strings

indications: IUD removal needed and strings not visible, with intrauterine position confirmed by ultrasound
contraindications: Pregnancy (refer for specialist management)
IUD not seen in the uterus on ultrasound (see translocated IUD)
Acute pelvic infection
steps: Confirm identity, ultrasound showing intrauterine IUD, negative pregnancy test and written consent.
Perform hand hygiene and position the client in lithotomy.
Insert the speculum and clean the cervix with antiseptic.
Try to draw the strings out of the canal using a cytobrush or thread retriever.
If unsuccessful, give a paracervical block and apply the tenaculum.
Sound the uterus gently to locate the device.
Use alligator forceps or an IUD hook to grasp the device, ideally under ultrasound guidance.
Withdraw the device gently and check it is complete.
If blind attempts fail, stop and arrange hysteroscopic removal.
Insert a new device or start another method if wanted.
aftercare: Expect cramping and light bleeding for a day or two.
Start another method if pregnancy is not wanted.
red_flags: Stop after a limited number of gentle attempts; do not persist blindly.
Stop if perforation is suspected.
Return for fever, severe pain or heavy bleeding.

indications: IUD located outside the uterus on imaging
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia without optimisation
equipment: Imaging (plain abdominal X-ray and ultrasound) report
Laparoscopy stack and instruments or laparotomy set
General anaesthesia set-up with resuscitation equipment
Sterile gowns, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity, imaging location of the IUD, negative pregnancy test and written consent including possible bowel or bladder repair.
Perform the surgical safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and catheterise the bladder.
Enter the abdomen laparoscopically, or by laparotomy if laparoscopy is unavailable or unsafe.
Inspect the pelvis and abdomen to find the device, often in omentum or adherent to bowel.
Free adhesions carefully and grasp the device.
Remove the device and check that it is complete.
Inspect the uterus, bowel and bladder for injury and repair if needed.
Achieve haemostasis and close the wounds.
Complete the sign-out with instrument and swab count.
aftercare: Routine postoperative observations and analgesia per protocol.
Start another contraceptive method before discharge if wanted.
Review the wound in about a week.
red_flags: Call a general surgeon if bowel or bladder is involved.
Return urgently for fever, vomiting, distension or increasing pain after discharge.

indications: Client chooses a vaginal ring for contraception
Progesterone-only ring for breastfeeding women where available
contraindications: Combined ring - same as combined pill contraindications
Pregnancy
Uterine prolapse or vaginal conditions that prevent retention
steps: Confirm identity, method choice, medical eligibility and verbal consent.
Exclude pregnancy and check blood pressure for the combined ring.
Explain timing of insertion and removal for the ring type.
Teach the client to wash hands, squeeze the ring and insert it high into the vagina.
Let the client insert the first ring herself, with help if needed.
Confirm it is comfortable; if felt, push it higher.
Explain what to do if the ring comes out or removal is delayed.
aftercare: Use condoms for seven days if not started on the first day of the period.
Rinse a ring that falls out in cool water and reinsert promptly.
Return for resupply as scheduled.
red_flags: Return urgently for calf pain, chest pain, breathlessness, sudden severe headache or vision loss.
Return for vaginal discharge, irritation or suspected pregnancy.

indications: Client chooses a female barrier method
contraindications: Recurrent urinary tract infections
Uterine prolapse or poor vaginal muscle tone
Within six weeks of childbirth or second-trimester abortion
Latex allergy for latex diaphragms
History of toxic shock syndrome
equipment: Fitting rings or diaphragms in a range of sizes, or single-size diaphragm
steps: Confirm identity, method choice and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and a vaginal examination to assess the cervix and vaginal length.
Estimate size by measuring from the posterior fornix to behind the pubic bone.
Insert a fitting ring of that size and check it covers the cervix and sits snugly behind the pubic bone.
Ask the client to walk, squat and cough to check comfort and stability.
Teach the client to insert, check cervix coverage and remove the diaphragm.
Watch the client insert and check it herself.
Explain leaving it in for at least six hours after sex and the maximum wear time.
aftercare: Practise at home and use another method until confident.
Wash with mild soap and water, dry and store in its case.
Refit after childbirth, pelvic surgery or a large weight change.
red_flags: Remove and return for fever, rash, vomiting or diarrhoea while wearing it (possible toxic shock).
Return for urinary burning or frequency.
Return if pregnancy is suspected.

indications: Dyspepsia with alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, anaemia, persistent vomiting, age over local threshold)
Upper gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis or melaena)
Dysphagia or odynophagia
Suspected portal hypertension and variceal screening
Biopsy for coeliac disease, Helicobacter pylori or suspected malignancy
Removal of foreign body or therapeutic intervention
contraindications: Suspected perforated viscus
Haemodynamic instability not yet resuscitated
Uncooperative patient without adequate sedation or anaesthesia
Recent myocardial infarction or severe cardiorespiratory instability (weigh risk and benefit)
equipment: Flexible gastroscope (paediatric or ultrathin scope for small children) checked and high-level disinfected
Light source, processor and monitor, with suction and air or CO2 insufflation
Biopsy forceps, specimen pots with formalin and request forms
Topical pharyngeal anaesthetic spray and sedation drugs per local protocol
Pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor and oxygen supply
Resuscitation trolley with reversal agents and airway equipment
Gloves, apron, eye protection and lubricant gel
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication, fasting status, allergies, anticoagulant use and written consent.
Perform a safety time-out with the team and check the scope, suction and monitoring.
Site an intravenous cannula if sedation is planned and attach oxygen saturation and blood pressure monitoring.
Apply topical pharyngeal anaesthetic and give sedation per local protocol if required.
Position the patient in the left lateral position and insert the mouth guard.
Pass the scope under direct vision through the upper oesophageal sphincter as the patient swallows.
Examine the oesophagus, noting the Z-line and the distance of any lesion from the incisors.
Advance into the stomach, insufflate gently and examine the body, antrum and pylorus.
Pass into the duodenum to the second part and examine the mucosa.
Retroflex in the stomach to inspect the cardia and fundus.
Take biopsies or perform therapy as indicated and label specimens at the bedside.
Aspirate air and fluid from the stomach before withdrawing the scope.
Monitor the patient in recovery until awake and observations are stable.
Explain findings to the patient and give a written report and follow-up plan.
aftercare: Nothing to eat or drink until the throat numbness wears off (usually about one hour).
If sedated, do not drive, operate machinery or sign legal documents for the rest of the day and go home with an adult.
Mild throat soreness and bloating are common and settle within a day.
Restart medicines as advised, including anticoagulants per the plan given.
Biopsy results will be reviewed at the follow-up appointment.
red_flags: Stop if oxygen saturation falls persistently, there is significant arrhythmia or the patient cannot tolerate the procedure.
Escalate urgently for suspected perforation (chest, neck or abdominal pain, surgical emphysema).
Return for vomiting blood, black stools, worsening chest or abdominal pain, fever or difficulty breathing.

indications: Rectal bleeding or iron deficiency anaemia
Change in bowel habit or chronic diarrhoea
Suspected colorectal cancer or abnormal imaging
Inflammatory bowel disease assessment and surveillance
Polyp surveillance or family history of colorectal cancer
Therapeutic intervention (polypectomy, haemostasis, decompression)
contraindications: Suspected perforation or peritonitis
Severe acute colitis or toxic megacolon (limited examination only by an experienced endoscopist)
Recent bowel anastomosis
Haemodynamic instability not resuscitated
equipment: Colonoscope (paediatric scope for children) checked and high-level disinfected
Light source, processor, monitor, suction and insufflation (CO2 if available)
Biopsy forceps, snares, clips and specimen pots
Sedation and analgesia per local protocol, with reversal agents
Pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor and oxygen
steps: Confirm identity, indication, bowel preparation taken, allergies, anticoagulant plan and written consent.
Perform a safety time-out and check equipment and monitoring.
Site an intravenous cannula, attach monitoring and give sedation and analgesia per protocol.
Position the patient in the left lateral position.
Inspect the perianal area and perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated colonoscope and advance under direct vision using minimal insufflation.
Use torque, withdrawal, abdominal pressure and position changes to reduce loops.
Confirm caecal intubation by the appendiceal orifice and ileocaecal valve, and intubate the terminal ileum if indicated.
Withdraw slowly over at least six minutes, inspecting behind folds and cleaning the mucosa.
Take biopsies or remove polyps as indicated and label specimens.
Retroflex in the rectum to inspect the distal rectum and aspirate air before removal.
Monitor in recovery until awake and stable, then explain findings and the follow-up plan.
aftercare: Bloating and wind are common and settle within hours.
Eat normally unless told otherwise.
If sedated, do not drive or operate machinery for the rest of the day and go home with an adult.
A small amount of blood in the stool is possible after biopsies or polyp removal.
Restart anticoagulants and other medicines as advised.
red_flags: Stop if the patient has severe pain, desaturation, arrhythmia or suspected perforation.
Return urgently for severe or worsening abdominal pain, a swollen tender abdomen or fever.
Return for heavy rectal bleeding, passing clots, dizziness or fainting.

indications: Bright red rectal bleeding
Assessment of distal colitis or proctitis
Evaluation of left-sided lesion seen on imaging
Diagnostic assessment of suspected sigmoid volvulus or pseudo-obstruction (therapeutic deflation is documented under the decompression entry, with a mucosal viability check)
Surveillance of rectal or sigmoid disease
contraindications: Suspected perforation or peritonitis
Toxic megacolon
Haemodynamic instability not resuscitated
equipment: Flexible sigmoidoscope or colonoscope checked and disinfected
Light source, processor, suction and insufflation
Pulse oximeter and blood pressure monitor if sedation is used
steps: Confirm identity, indication, enema preparation given, anticoagulant use and consent.
Perform a time-out and check the scope and suction.
Position the patient in the left lateral position with knees flexed.
Inspect the perianal area and perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated scope and advance under direct vision with minimal insufflation.
Advance to the splenic flexure or as far as safely possible.
Withdraw slowly, inspecting the mucosa and taking biopsies as indicated.
Retroflex in the rectum if safe and aspirate air before removal.
Record the distance reached and findings and explain them to the patient.
aftercare: Mild bloating and cramps settle quickly.
Eat and drink normally.
A little blood in the stool may occur after biopsies.
red_flags: Stop if the patient has severe pain or the scope will not advance without force.
Return for severe abdominal pain, abdominal swelling, fever or heavy rectal bleeding.

indications: Rectal bleeding assessment in clinic
Assessment and biopsy of rectal mass
Assessment of proctitis
Measuring the height of a rectal tumour from the anal verge
contraindications: Acute painful anal condition (fissure, thrombosed haemorrhoid, abscess) without anaesthesia
Suspected perforation
Anal stenosis preventing passage of the instrument
equipment: Rigid sigmoidoscope with obturator, light source and bellows insufflator (disposable or sterilised)
Long biopsy forceps and specimen pots
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent and explain the procedure with a chaperone present.
Position the patient in the left lateral position with knees drawn up.
Inspect the perianal area and perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated sigmoidoscope with obturator, directed towards the umbilicus, for about 4–5 cm.
Remove the obturator, attach the light and window, and advance under direct vision with gentle insufflation.
Follow the lumen posteriorly into the sacral curve and advance as far as comfortable, usually 15–20 cm.
Withdraw slowly, inspecting the mucosa circumferentially.
Take biopsies if indicated, avoiding the anterior wall above the peritoneal reflection.
Record the distance of any lesion from the anal verge and explain findings.
aftercare: Mild discomfort and wind settle quickly.
A small amount of bleeding may follow biopsy.
red_flags: Stop if there is severe pain or the lumen cannot be seen.
Return for severe abdominal pain, fever or heavy rectal bleeding.

form.label: Lowest edge of lesion from anal verge

indications: Rectal bleeding with suspected anal cause
Assessment of haemorrhoids
Anal pain, discharge or itching
Before haemorrhoid banding or injection
contraindications: Acute anal fissure or thrombosed haemorrhoid causing severe pain (examine under anaesthesia instead)
Anal stenosis
equipment: Proctoscope with obturator (sterile or disposable) and light source
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent and ensure a chaperone is present.
Position the patient in the left lateral position with knees drawn up.
Inspect the perianal skin and perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated proctoscope with obturator gently towards the umbilicus.
Remove the obturator and inspect the anorectal mucosa with the light.
Ask the patient to strain gently while withdrawing slowly to show haemorrhoids.
Note the position and grade of haemorrhoids and any fissure, polyp or mass.
Record findings using clock positions with the patient in the lithotomy convention.
aftercare: Mild discomfort settles quickly.
Follow the treatment plan given for haemorrhoids or other findings.
red_flags: Stop if there is severe pain.
Refer for sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy if bleeding is not explained or there are alarm features.

indications: Acute oesophageal variceal bleeding
Secondary prophylaxis after variceal bleeding
Primary prophylaxis of large or high-risk oesophageal varices
contraindications: Unprotected airway with massive haematemesis (intubate first)
Haemodynamic instability not yet resuscitated
Isolated gastric fundal varices (consider other therapy)
equipment: Gastroscope compatible with the banding device
Suction with large-bore tubing and spare suction
Vasoactive drug and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol for acute bleeding
Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tube available for rescue
steps: Confirm identity, indication, resuscitation status, blood availability and written consent.
Ensure vasoactive therapy and antibiotics are started per protocol in acute bleeding.
Protect the airway with intubation if there is massive bleeding or reduced consciousness.
Perform a time-out and carry out a diagnostic gastroscopy to confirm the source and assess the varices.
Withdraw the scope, attach the banding device and reinsert under vision.
Start at the gastro-oesophageal junction and work upwards in a spiral pattern.
Suction each varix into the cap until the view is red and fire a band.
Place bands on the bleeding point or stigmata first in acute bleeding.
Record the number of bands placed and confirm haemostasis.
Withdraw the scope and monitor closely in recovery or high-dependency care.
aftercare: Chest discomfort and difficulty swallowing are common for a few days.
Take fluids and soft food as advised for the first day or two.
Continue medicines prescribed for portal hypertension.
Attend repeat banding sessions until the varices are eradicated.
red_flags: Escalate for re-bleeding, haemodynamic instability or failure of haemostasis (consider balloon tamponade or referral).
Return urgently for vomiting blood, black stools, dizziness or severe chest pain.
Return for confusion, abdominal swelling or fever.

indications: Bleeding oesophageal varices when band ligation is not possible or not available
Gastric varices (tissue adhesive injection where available)
Small residual varices after banding
contraindications: Unprotected airway with massive bleeding
Haemodynamic instability not yet resuscitated
Known allergy to the sclerosant
equipment: Sclerosant or tissue adhesive per local protocol
Eye protection for all staff when using tissue adhesive
Blood products, monitoring and resuscitation trolley
Balloon tamponade tube available for rescue
steps: Confirm identity, indication, resuscitation status and written consent.
Ensure vasoactive therapy and antibiotics are started per protocol in acute bleeding.
Protect the airway if there is massive bleeding or reduced consciousness.
Perform a time-out and carry out a diagnostic gastroscopy to identify the bleeding varix.
Prime the injection needle with the agent and pass it through the working channel.
Inject into or beside the varix starting near the gastro-oesophageal junction, as per protocol.
Flush and withdraw the needle carefully after each injection.
Check for haemostasis and record the sites and number of injections.
Withdraw the scope and monitor closely in recovery or high-dependency care.
aftercare: Chest pain, fever and difficulty swallowing may occur for a few days.
Take soft food and fluids as advised.
Attend follow-up endoscopy as booked.
red_flags: Escalate for re-bleeding or failed haemostasis (consider balloon tamponade or referral).
Return urgently for vomiting blood, black stools, severe chest pain or breathlessness.
Return for fever, painful or difficult swallowing that worsens.

indications: Bleeding peptic ulcer with active bleeding or a non-bleeding visible vessel
Adherent clot over an ulcer after removal attempt
Mallory-Weiss tear with active bleeding
Bleeding after polypectomy or other endoscopic therapy
Dieulafoy lesion
contraindications: Unprotected airway with massive haematemesis
Haemodynamic instability not yet resuscitated
Suspected perforation
equipment: Therapeutic gastroscope with large working channel if available
Injection needle and diluted vasoconstrictor per local protocol
Thermal coagulation probe (heater probe or bipolar) if available
Blood products, monitoring and resuscitation trolley
steps: Confirm identity, risk score, resuscitation status, blood availability and written consent.
Protect the airway if there is massive bleeding or reduced consciousness.
Perform a time-out and carry out a diagnostic gastroscopy, washing away blood to find the source.
Classify the lesion and stigmata of recent haemorrhage.
For high-risk stigmata, inject around the bleeding point to slow bleeding.
Apply a second modality such as clips or thermal coagulation, as injection alone is not enough.
Use haemostatic powder as a bridge if bleeding persists and other methods fail.
Wash and observe the site to confirm haemostasis.
Record the lesion, stigmata, methods used and result.
Withdraw the scope and arrange monitoring, acid suppression per protocol and a re-bleeding plan.
aftercare: Stay in hospital for monitoring as advised.
Continue acid-reducing medicine and any Helicobacter pylori treatment as prescribed.
Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers unless a doctor advises otherwise.
Attend follow-up endoscopy if booked to confirm ulcer healing.
red_flags: Escalate for failed haemostasis or re-bleeding to repeat endoscopy, interventional radiology or surgery.
Escalate urgently for suspected perforation (severe abdominal pain, peritonism).
Return for vomiting blood, black stools, dizziness or fainting.

indications: Angiodysplasia causing bleeding or anaemia
Gastric antral vascular ectasia
Radiation proctitis with bleeding
Ablation of residual polyp tissue after resection
Tumour debulking or bleeding control
contraindications: No electrosurgical unit or argon supply
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Poor bowel preparation in the colon (risk of gas explosion)
equipment: Electrosurgical unit with argon module and APC probe
Suction and CO2 insufflation if available
steps: Confirm identity, indication, bowel preparation for colon work, anticoagulant plan and written consent.
Check for implanted cardiac devices and follow the local electrosurgery policy.
Apply the return electrode and set the unit per manufacturer and local settings.
Perform a time-out and insert the endoscope to the target lesion.
Pass the APC probe beyond the scope tip and hold it a few millimetres from the mucosa without touching.
Apply short pulses until the lesion is coagulated, working systematically.
Aspirate excess gas regularly to avoid overdistension.
Record the number and sites of lesions treated.
Withdraw the scope and monitor in recovery.
aftercare: Bloating and mild discomfort settle quickly.
Continue iron or other treatment as advised.
Attend repeat sessions if needed.
red_flags: Stop if there is marked distension or suspected perforation.
Return for severe abdominal pain, fever or heavy bleeding.

indications: Colorectal or gastric polyp found at endoscopy
Juvenile polyp causing rectal bleeding in a child
Polyposis surveillance
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or anticoagulation not managed per plan
Polyp with features of deep invasion (biopsy, tattoo and refer for surgery)
Poor bowel preparation
equipment: Cold and hot snares of suitable sizes
Polyp retrieval net or trap, specimen pots
Tattoo ink for lesions that may need surgery
steps: Confirm identity, indication, anticoagulant plan, bowel preparation and written consent.
Perform a time-out and check the snares, electrosurgical unit and return electrode.
Assess the polyp size, shape and surface to choose the resection method.
Position the polyp at the five to six o'clock position in the endoscopic view.
Inject a submucosal lift beneath sessile or large polyps if needed.
Close the snare around the polyp with a small margin of normal tissue.
Resect by cold snaring for small polyps or with electrosurgical current for larger ones.
Inspect the base for residual tissue or bleeding and treat with clips if needed.
Retrieve the polyp and send it in labelled formalin.
Tattoo the site if the polyp is suspicious or may need surgical removal.
Record the size, morphology, location, method and completeness of resection.
aftercare: Small amounts of blood in the stool are common for a few days.
Avoid heavy lifting and long-distance travel for a few days after large polyp removal.
Restart anticoagulants as advised.
Histology results will set your next surveillance date.
red_flags: Stop and treat if there is uncontrolled bleeding or a visible perforation (clip and escalate).
Return urgently for heavy rectal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, abdominal swelling or fever, up to two weeks later.

indications: Large sessile or flat colorectal polyp without signs of deep invasion
Early superficial neoplasia in the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum
Barrett's oesophagus with visible nodular lesion
contraindications: Features of deep submucosal invasion (non-lifting sign, ulceration)
Uncorrected coagulopathy
No experienced endoscopist or surgical back-up available
equipment: Therapeutic endoscope with transparent cap if needed
Injection needle and lifting solution with dye
Snares, electrosurgical unit and return electrode
Retrieval net and specimen pots with pins and board for orientation
steps: Confirm identity, lesion assessment, anticoagulant plan and written consent including perforation risk.
Perform a time-out and check equipment and electrosurgical settings.
Assess and mark the lesion margins, examining surface pattern for features of invasion.
Inject the submucosa to lift the lesion fully.
Resect with the snare en bloc or piecemeal in a planned sequence.
Re-inject as needed to keep the lesion lifted.
Inspect the resection defect for residual tissue, bleeding vessels or muscle injury.
Treat edges and residual tissue and close the defect with clips if indicated.
Retrieve all pieces and pin the specimen for histology.
Record lesion size, location, method and completeness, with photographs.
Monitor in recovery and give written advice about delayed bleeding and perforation.
aftercare: Some blood in the stool can occur in the first two weeks.
Follow the diet advice given.
Restart anticoagulants as advised.
Attend the scar check endoscopy as booked.
red_flags: Stop and escalate for perforation not closable with clips or uncontrolled bleeding.
Return urgently for severe abdominal pain, fever, abdominal swelling or heavy bleeding.

indications: Common bile duct stones causing jaundice or cholangitis
Malignant or benign biliary obstruction needing drainage
Bile leak after surgery or trauma
Selected pancreatic duct disease
contraindications: Diagnostic purpose only when MRCP or EUS is available
Uncorrected coagulopathy if sphincterotomy planned
Haemodynamic instability not resuscitated
Pregnancy without radiation protection planning
equipment: Stone extraction balloons and baskets, mechanical lithotripter
Contrast medium, electrosurgical unit and return electrode
Lead aprons, thyroid shields and dosimeters
Prophylactic antibiotic and post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, indication, imaging, coagulation, allergies, pregnancy status and written consent.
Give prophylaxis per local protocol and ensure intravenous access and monitoring.
Perform a time-out including radiation safety checks.
Position the patient prone or left lateral and give sedation or anaesthesia.
Pass the duodenoscope to the second part of the duodenum and identify the papilla.
Cannulate the bile duct selectively using a guidewire.
Inject contrast under fluoroscopy to define the anatomy and pathology.
Perform sphincterotomy if needed for stone removal or stenting.
Clear stones with a balloon or basket and confirm clearance with an occlusion cholangiogram.
Insert a stent if the duct cannot be cleared or there is a stricture.
Record findings, interventions and fluoroscopy time, and save images.
Monitor in recovery and for signs of pancreatitis, bleeding or perforation.
aftercare: Stay for observation as advised and eat only when allowed.
Some upper abdominal discomfort is common.
Do not drive for the rest of the day after sedation.
Attend for stent change or removal if a stent was placed.
red_flags: Stop and escalate for suspected perforation, uncontrolled bleeding or failed cannulation with cholangitis (arrange alternative drainage).
Return urgently for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, fever with rigors, worsening jaundice or black stools.

indications: Malignant distal biliary obstruction for palliation or before surgery
Bile duct stones that cannot be cleared
Benign biliary stricture
Bile leak
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy if sphincterotomy is needed
Inaccessible papilla (consider percutaneous drainage)
Haemodynamic instability not resuscitated
equipment: Plastic stents of suitable lengths and diameters, or self-expanding metal stents
steps: Confirm identity, indication, imaging, coagulation and written consent including stent occlusion risk.
Perform a time-out and radiation safety checks.
Perform ERCP with selective biliary cannulation and cholangiography.
Pass a guidewire across the stricture or stones into the proximal duct.
Measure the stricture length to choose stent length.
Perform sphincterotomy if indicated.
Advance the stent over the wire until it bridges the stricture, with the distal end in the duodenum.
Confirm position and drainage of contrast and bile on fluoroscopy and endoscopy.
Record stent type, length, diameter and date due for change.
aftercare: Jaundice and itch should improve over one to two weeks.
Plastic stents need changing, usually every three months; keep the date.
Take antibiotics if prescribed.
red_flags: Return urgently for fever, rigors, returning jaundice, dark urine or pale stools (possible stent blockage).
Return for severe abdominal pain or vomiting.

indications: Long-term enteral feeding need (more than four weeks) with a functioning gut
Unsafe swallow after stroke or neurological disease
Head and neck cancer before or during treatment
Children with neurodisability and feeding difficulty
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy
Inability to transilluminate or indent the stomach
Gross ascites, peritonitis or active abdominal sepsis
Gastric outlet obstruction (unless for decompression)
Limited life expectancy where feeding will not help
equipment: PEG kit (tube of suitable French size, needle, guidewire or loop, external fixation device)
Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity, indication, multidisciplinary decision, coagulation, fasting and written consent from patient or legal representative.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per protocol and perform a time-out.
Perform gastroscopy to exclude obstruction and insufflate the stomach.
Identify the site by transillumination and finger indentation, usually in the left upper quadrant.
Clean and drape the skin and infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the stomach.
Make a small skin incision and pass the needle into the stomach under endoscopic view.
Pass the guidewire through the needle and grasp it with a snare.
Withdraw the scope and wire through the mouth and attach the PEG tube to the wire.
Pull the tube through the mouth, oesophagus and stomach out through the abdominal wall.
Optionally re-scope to confirm the internal bumper position without excess tension.
Fit the external fixator with slight free play and record the external length marking.
Apply a dry dressing and document tube size and markings.
aftercare: Nil by tube for a few hours, then start water and feeds per the dietitian plan.
Keep the site clean and dry, and check it daily.
After about two weeks, rotate the tube and move it in and out daily to prevent buried bumper.
Flush the tube before and after each feed and medicine.
red_flags: Stop if a safe site cannot be found.
Escalate urgently for pain on feeding, leakage around the tube, peritonism or fever (stop feeding).
Return for tube displacement (cover the stoma and come immediately so the tract does not close), bleeding or site redness and pus.

indications: Blocked, damaged or worn gastrostomy tube
Planned conversion to a balloon tube or low-profile button
Tube no longer needed
Dislodged tube with a mature tract
contraindications: Immature tract (less than about four to six weeks) for blind replacement
Suspected buried bumper (needs endoscopic assessment)
Signs of peritonitis
equipment: Replacement balloon gastrostomy tube or button of correct size
Sterile water and syringes for balloon inflation
Endoscope and snare if an internal bumper must be removed endoscopically
steps: Confirm identity, tube type, tract age and verbal consent (written if endoscopy is needed).
Check the tube type, size and how it is retained (balloon or internal bumper).
For a balloon tube, deflate the balloon fully and withdraw the tube gently.
For a bumper PEG, remove by firm traction only if the manufacturer allows, otherwise remove endoscopically.
Inspect the stoma and clean around it.
Insert the lubricated new tube into the tract at the same angle.
Inflate the balloon with sterile water to the volume printed on the tube.
Pull back gently until resistance is felt and position the external fixator.
Aspirate gastric contents and confirm acidic pH before use.
If the tube is being removed for good, apply a dressing and expect the stoma to close within days.
Record tube type, size, balloon volume and position check.
aftercare: Check the balloon water volume weekly as instructed.
Rotate and clean the tube daily.
Keep a spare tube and know who to call if it falls out.
red_flags: Stop if there is resistance or pain on insertion; do not force (risk of false tract).
Do not feed if position cannot be confirmed; escalate for contrast check.
Return for pain with feeds, leakage, fever or a tube that falls out.

indications: Benign oesophageal stricture (peptic, anastomotic, post-radiotherapy)
Caustic stricture in children or adults
Schatzki ring or oesophageal web
Eosinophilic oesophagitis with stricture
contraindications: Recent caustic ingestion (usually avoid dilatation in the first few weeks)
Suspected perforation
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Malignant stricture where stenting is the better option
equipment: Through-the-scope balloons with inflation device and manometer, or Savary-Gilliard bougies with guidewire
Fluoroscopy if available for complex strictures
steps: Confirm identity, stricture details from previous endoscopy or contrast study and written consent.
Perform a time-out and give sedation or anaesthesia.
Perform gastroscopy to assess the stricture length, diameter and appearance; biopsy if not yet done.
For balloon dilatation, pass the balloon across the stricture and inflate in stages to the target diameter.
For bougie dilatation, place a guidewire beyond the stricture and pass bougies of increasing size.
Once moderate resistance is first felt, pass no more than three bougies of increasing size in one session.
Re-inspect the stricture for mucosal tear depth and bleeding.
Record the starting and final diameter achieved.
Monitor in recovery for chest pain, fever or surgical emphysema before oral intake.
aftercare: Start fluids when advised, then a soft diet.
Mild chest discomfort is common for a day.
Repeat dilatations may be needed; attend as booked.
red_flags: Stop and escalate urgently for severe chest pain, neck swelling, breathlessness or fever (suspected perforation); keep nil by mouth.
Return for vomiting blood or inability to swallow saliva.

indications: Confirmed achalasia (by manometry or barium swallow and endoscopy)
Recurrent symptoms after previous dilatation or myotomy
contraindications: Malignancy not excluded (pseudoachalasia)
Patient unfit for surgery if perforation occurs
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Achalasia balloon dilators (graded sizes) and inflation device with manometer
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis, fasting (often a liquid diet for one to two days before) and written consent including perforation risk.
Perform a time-out and give sedation.
Perform gastroscopy, clear retained food and exclude a tumour at the cardia.
Place a guidewire in the stomach and withdraw the scope.
Pass the balloon over the wire and position it across the gastro-oesophageal junction under fluoroscopy.
Inflate gradually until the waist on the balloon disappears and hold for the set time.
Deflate and remove the balloon and check for blood on the balloon.
Re-scope or arrange a contrast swallow if perforation is suspected.
Observe for several hours before starting fluids.
aftercare: Start fluids when advised and build up to a normal diet.
Eat upright and chew well.
Symptoms may recur; report any return of difficulty swallowing.
red_flags: Escalate urgently for severe chest pain, fever, tachycardia or surgical emphysema after the procedure (suspected perforation, keep nil by mouth).
Return for vomiting blood or chest pain after discharge.

indications: Malignant dysphagia from inoperable oesophageal or cardia cancer
Tracheo-oesophageal fistula from malignancy
Selected benign perforation or leak (covered stent)
contraindications: Tumour too close to the upper oesophageal sphincter (relative)
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Very limited life expectancy where stent will not improve comfort
Airway compression risk without airway assessment
equipment: Self-expanding metal stent (covered or partially covered) of suitable length
Fluoroscopy unit, contrast and radio-opaque skin markers
Balloon or bougie dilators if needed
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis, multidisciplinary decision and written consent.
Perform a time-out and give sedation.
Perform gastroscopy and measure the upper and lower tumour margins from the incisors.
Mark the tumour margins with skin markers or contrast under fluoroscopy.
Pass a stiff guidewire into the stomach and withdraw the scope.
Choose a stent at least a few centimetres longer than the tumour.
Deploy the stent over the wire under fluoroscopic guidance across the stricture.
Confirm position and expansion on fluoroscopy and endoscopically if safe.
Record stent type, length and position.
aftercare: Start fluids after a few hours, then soft and moist food; chew well and sit upright.
Drink fizzy or warm drinks with meals to help keep the stent clear.
Chest discomfort is common for a few days.
Sleep propped up if the stent crosses into the stomach, to reduce reflux.
red_flags: Escalate for severe chest pain, fever or breathlessness (perforation or airway compression).
Return if swallowing becomes difficult again (food blockage, tumour overgrowth or stent migration).
Return for vomiting blood or black stools.

indications: Food bolus obstruction in the oesophagus
Button battery in the oesophagus (emergency) or stomach with symptoms
Sharp or long objects in the oesophagus or stomach
Magnets (more than one) or any object causing symptoms
Coins retained in the oesophagus
contraindications: Signs of perforation (needs surgical review)
Packets of drugs (body packers; do not remove endoscopically, risk of rupture)
Unprotected airway in a child or patient unable to handle secretions
equipment: Overtube or protective hood for sharp objects
Retrieval devices (rat-tooth forceps, alligator forceps, net, snare, basket, cap)
Endotracheal intubation equipment and anaesthetist where needed
Neck, chest and abdominal X-ray to locate the object
steps: Confirm identity, object type, time of ingestion, X-ray location and written consent.
Treat a button battery in the oesophagus as an emergency for removal within two hours.
Secure the airway with intubation for children and for high-risk objects.
Perform a time-out and choose the retrieval device after inspecting the object.
Pass the scope and examine the object and surrounding mucosa.
Use an overtube or hood for sharp objects to protect the oesophagus.
Grasp the object securely and withdraw it with the scope, keeping sharp ends trailing.
Push a soft food bolus gently into the stomach only when the path beyond is clear, otherwise remove piecemeal.
Re-examine the mucosa for injury, perforation or underlying stricture or eosinophilic oesophagitis.
Take biopsies for food bolus cases if indicated and record findings.
aftercare: Start fluids when advised.
After a button battery, watch closely for delayed injury and attend follow-up as arranged.
Store batteries, magnets and small objects out of children's reach.
red_flags: Stop and escalate for perforation or failed retrieval of a dangerous object (surgical referral).
Return urgently for chest or neck pain, fever, vomiting blood, breathing difficulty or refusal to eat.

indications: Uncontrolled variceal bleeding despite drug therapy, as a bridge to endoscopy, TIPS or surgery
Variceal bleeding where endoscopy is not available, while arranging transfer
contraindications: Recent oesophageal or gastric surgery
Known oesophageal stricture
Unprotected airway (intubate first where possible)
equipment: Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tube (checked by inflating balloons under water)
Water-soluble lubricant and local anaesthetic spray
Traction system (weight and pulley or helmet fixation) or tape
Suction for the gastric and oesophageal aspiration ports
Scissors at the bedside to cut the tube if it migrates
Intubation equipment and chest X-ray access
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent (from patient or as an emergency) and inform the senior.
Protect the airway with endotracheal intubation if possible.
Check both balloons for leaks and fully deflate them.
Lubricate the tube and pass it orally (or nasally) to at least the 50 cm mark.
Confirm gastric position by aspiration and inflate the gastric balloon with a small volume of air.
Check the gastric balloon is in the stomach with an X-ray before full inflation where possible.
Inflate the gastric balloon fully per the manufacturer and pull back gently until resistance is felt.
Apply gentle traction and secure the tube, marking its position at the mouth.
Inflate the oesophageal balloon to the set pressure only if bleeding continues.
Aspirate the gastric and oesophageal ports regularly and record output.
Deflate the oesophageal balloon periodically as per protocol and plan removal within 24 hours.
Arrange definitive therapy (endoscopy, TIPS or transfer) as soon as possible.
aftercare: The patient stays in high-dependency or intensive care with continuous monitoring.
Nil by mouth with mouth care and suction of secretions.
Keep scissors at the bedside.
red_flags: Cut and remove the tube immediately for respiratory distress (balloon migration into the airway).
Escalate for continued bleeding despite tamponade or chest pain (oesophageal rupture).
Do not leave balloons inflated longer than the protocol allows (pressure necrosis).

indications: Unexplained abnormal liver tests or hepatomegaly
Staging of chronic hepatitis B or C where non-invasive tests are unclear
Suspected autoimmune hepatitis, storage or infiltrative disease
Focal liver lesion when tissue diagnosis changes management
Neonatal cholestasis in children (specialist setting)
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or low platelets per local thresholds
Uncooperative patient unable to hold breath (consider sedation or another route)
Tense ascites (drain first or use transjugular route)
Suspected hydatid cyst or vascular tumour
Extrahepatic biliary obstruction
equipment: Liver biopsy needle (core cutting needle of suitable gauge) and guide
Sterile gloves, gown, drapes and skin antiseptic
Local anaesthetic, needles and syringes, scalpel blade
Formalin specimen pots and other media as needed
Dressing, observation chart and blood group and save
steps: Confirm identity, indication, recent full blood count, clotting and written consent.
Check blood group and save and that anticoagulants and antiplatelets have been stopped as per plan.
Perform a time-out and position the patient supine with the right arm above the head.
Mark the site by ultrasound, avoiding vessels, gallbladder and lung.
Clean and drape the skin and infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the liver capsule.
Make a small skin nick.
Ask the patient to hold the breath in expiration and pass the needle to take the core.
Repeat passes only as needed for an adequate sample.
Place the core in formalin and check its length.
Apply pressure and a dressing and lie the patient on the right side for the first hour.
Monitor pulse and blood pressure frequently for several hours.
aftercare: Rest for the rest of the day and avoid heavy lifting for a week.
Mild right shoulder or side pain is common and settles with simple painkillers (avoid anti-inflammatories).
Restart blood thinners only when advised.
red_flags: Stop if the patient cannot cooperate with breath holding.
Escalate for falling blood pressure, rising pulse, increasing pain or abdominal distension (bleeding).
Return urgently for severe abdominal or chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or fever.

indications: Assessing liver fibrosis in chronic hepatitis B or C
Fatty liver disease risk stratification
Alcohol-related liver disease
Monitoring known chronic liver disease
contraindications: Ascites (invalid readings)
Pregnancy (relative)
Implanted cardiac device (check manufacturer advice)
Recent meal, acute hepatitis, heart failure or biliary obstruction (falsely high readings; interpret with caution)
equipment: Transient elastography machine with suitable probe (M or XL)
steps: Confirm identity, indication, fasting for at least two to three hours and verbal consent.
Position the patient supine with the right arm fully raised behind the head.
Locate an intercostal space over the right lobe of the liver at the mid-axillary line.
Select the probe according to skin-to-capsule distance or body build.
Apply gel and hold the probe perpendicular to the skin with steady pressure.
Take at least ten valid measurements.
Check reliability using the interquartile range to median ratio.
Record the median stiffness and controlled attenuation parameter if available.
Interpret results against the cause of liver disease and clinical context.
aftercare: No special care is needed after the test.
Results will be discussed at your clinic visit.
red_flags: Repeat or use another test if readings are unreliable.
Refer high readings suggesting cirrhosis for variceal and liver cancer surveillance.

indications: Detecting Helicobacter pylori during gastroscopy
Peptic ulcer disease
Gastritis or dyspepsia investigated by endoscopy
contraindications: Proton pump inhibitor in the last two weeks or antibiotics or bismuth in the last four weeks (false negatives; interpret with caution)
Active bleeding where biopsy is unsafe
equipment: Rapid urease test kit (in date, stored correctly)
steps: Confirm identity and that the test is part of the consented gastroscopy.
Check recent use of acid suppressants, antibiotics and bismuth.
Warm the test kit to room temperature and label it with patient details.
Take biopsies from the antrum and the gastric body.
Place the biopsies fully into the test gel and reseal the kit.
Read the colour change at the times stated by the manufacturer.
Record the result and reading time in the endoscopy report.
aftercare: Take eradication treatment if prescribed when positive.
A test of cure may be planned after treatment.
red_flags: Consider histology or breath test if the result is negative but suspicion remains high.

form.label: Acid suppressant in last two weeks
Antibiotic or bismuth in last four weeks

indications: Non-invasive diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori in dyspepsia without alarm features
Confirming eradication after treatment
contraindications: Proton pump inhibitor in the last two weeks or antibiotics or bismuth in the last four weeks (false negatives)
Inability to follow breathing instructions (young children need adapted technique)
Recent upper gastrointestinal surgery (relative)
equipment: Urea breath test kit (labelled urea and collection tubes or bags)
Analyser or arrangement to send samples
steps: Confirm identity, fasting per kit instructions and recent drug history and give verbal consent.
Label baseline and post-dose breath tubes or bags.
Collect a baseline breath sample by gentle exhalation through the straw.
Give the test drink and labelled urea per kit instructions.
Keep the patient seated and resting during the waiting time.
Collect the post-dose breath sample at the set time.
Seal and send samples or analyse them on site.
Record the result as positive or negative with the delta value if given.
aftercare: Eat and drink normally after the test.
Results will be given with the treatment plan.
red_flags: Refer for gastroscopy if there are alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding, anaemia, persistent vomiting).

form.label: Acid suppressant in last two weeks
Antibiotic or bismuth in last four weeks

indications: Suspected small bowel bleeding after normal gastroscopy and colonoscopy
Suspected small bowel Crohn's disease
Small bowel tumour or polyposis surveillance
Refractory coeliac disease
contraindications: Known or suspected bowel obstruction, stricture or fistula (use patency capsule first)
Swallowing disorder (capsule may need endoscopic placement)
Pregnancy
Planned MRI before capsule has passed
equipment: Capsule, recorder, sensor belt or patch array
Patency capsule if stricture is suspected
steps: Confirm identity, indication, bowel preparation, fasting and written consent including retention risk.
Check for strictures and implanted devices, and use a patency capsule if indicated.
Fit the sensor belt or patches and recorder and check they are working.
Ask the patient to swallow the capsule with water.
Confirm the capsule has left the stomach using real-time view if available.
Advise clear fluids after two hours and a light meal after four hours.
Return the recorder after the set recording time.
Download and review the recording and record findings and transit times.
aftercare: Avoid MRI scanners and strong magnetic fields until the capsule has passed.
Watch for the capsule in the stool; it is disposable.
Avoid strenuous activity while wearing the recorder.
red_flags: Return urgently for abdominal pain, vomiting or bloating (possible capsule retention or obstruction).
Report if the capsule has not been seen passed after two weeks; an X-ray may be needed.

indications: Staging of oesophageal, gastric, pancreatic or rectal cancer
Evaluation of pancreatic mass, cyst or chronic pancreatitis
Suspected bile duct stones when other imaging is unclear
Subepithelial lesion assessment
Tissue sampling by fine-needle aspiration or biopsy
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy if sampling is planned
Suspected perforation
Oesophageal stricture preventing passage (relative)
equipment: Radial or linear echoendoscope and ultrasound processor
Slides, fixative and specimen pots, with on-site cytology if available
Sedation per local protocol, monitoring and resuscitation trolley
Prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol for cyst sampling
steps: Confirm identity, indication, imaging, coagulation and written consent.
Perform a time-out and give sedation with monitoring.
Insert the echoendoscope and advance to the target area.
Fill the balloon or instil water for acoustic coupling.
Perform a systematic ultrasound survey and identify the lesion and surrounding structures.
Stage tumours by depth and nodal involvement where relevant.
Sample the lesion with the needle under real-time guidance, avoiding vessels with Doppler.
Prepare and send samples correctly labelled.
Record findings, staging and sampling details with images.
Monitor in recovery.
aftercare: Throat soreness and bloating settle within a day.
Do not drive for the rest of the day after sedation.
Results will be reviewed at clinic or multidisciplinary meeting.
red_flags: Escalate for severe abdominal pain, fever, bleeding or suspected perforation.
Return for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, fever or black stools.

indications: Need for post-pyloric feeding in gastric outlet delay or gastroparesis
Severe acute pancreatitis where gastric feeding is not tolerated
High aspiration risk with gastric feeding
contraindications: Base of skull fracture or severe facial trauma (nasal route)
Complete bowel obstruction
Recent upper GI surgery without surgical agreement
Uncorrected severe coagulopathy (relative)
equipment: Nasojejunal feeding tube of suitable size with stylet
Endoscope (for endoscopic placement) or fluoroscopy (radiological placement)
Tape or nasal bridle for securing
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent and choose bedside, endoscopic or fluoroscopic method.
Measure and note the expected length.
Apply local anaesthetic spray to the nostril and lubricate the tube.
Pass the tube through the nose into the stomach.
Advance beyond the pylorus using endoscopic guidance, fluoroscopy or bedside technique per local practice.
For endoscopic placement, carry the tube or guidewire into the jejunum and withdraw the scope leaving the tube.
Remove the stylet and flush with water.
Confirm the tip position on abdominal X-ray or fluoroscopy before feeding.
Secure the tube and record the length at the nostril.
aftercare: Do not feed until position is confirmed.
Flush regularly to prevent blockage.
Check the length mark at the nostril every shift.
red_flags: Stop if there is coughing, choking or breathing difficulty during insertion (possible airway placement).
Do not use the tube if position is uncertain; recheck with X-ray.
Escalate for abdominal pain, vomiting or distension during feeds.

indications: Sigmoid volvulus after endoscopic or rigid decompression to keep it deflated
Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (with other measures)
Neonatal or infant abdominal distension in suspected Hirschsprung disease (rectal washouts by trained staff)
contraindications: Signs of perforation, peritonitis or gangrenous bowel
Recent rectal surgery or rectal tumour
Severe neutropenia (relative)
equipment: Flatus tube or soft rectal catheter of suitable size
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent and ensure privacy and a chaperone.
Position the patient in the left lateral position with knees flexed.
Perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated tube gently with a twisting motion, never forcing it.
Advance until there is a rush of gas and liquid stool.
Connect to a drainage bag and secure the tube to the buttock.
Reassess the abdomen for reduction in distension.
Record the length inserted and the volume and nature of drainage.
aftercare: The tube is usually left for a period set by the team and checked regularly.
Keep skin around the anus clean and dry.
red_flags: Stop if there is resistance, pain or fresh bleeding.
Escalate urgently for blood-stained or foul drainage, fever, tachycardia or peritonism (possible ischaemia or perforation).
Escalate if distension recurs after removal.

indications: Sigmoid volvulus without signs of gangrene or perforation
Temporising measure before planned sigmoid colectomy
contraindications: Peritonitis, perforation or clinical signs of gangrene (needs emergency laparotomy)
Haemodynamic instability not resuscitated
Dark, ulcerated or necrotic mucosa seen at endoscopy (stop and refer for surgery)
equipment: Flexible sigmoidoscope or colonoscope, or rigid sigmoidoscope where flexible is not available
Flatus tube for leaving in place
Lubricant, gloves, gowns and absorbent pads
steps: Confirm identity, X-ray diagnosis, absence of peritonitis, resuscitation and written consent.
Inform the surgical team and perform a time-out.
Position the patient in the left lateral position with protective pads.
Insert the scope and advance gently with minimal insufflation to the twist point.
Pass gently through the twist with minimal air until gas and stool rush out.
Inspect the mucosa for ischaemia, ulceration or necrosis.
Aspirate gas and fluid to decompress the loop.
Leave a flatus tube beyond the twist if possible and secure it.
Confirm reduction clinically and with repeat abdominal X-ray if needed.
Record mucosal appearance and plan for definitive surgery.
aftercare: Keep the flatus tube in place as advised.
Most patients need planned surgery during the same admission to prevent recurrence.
red_flags: Stop and refer for emergency surgery if the mucosa is dark, ulcerated or necrotic, or decompression fails.
Escalate for fever, rising pulse, peritonism or blood in the drainage.
Return urgently for recurrent abdominal swelling, pain or no passage of stool or gas.

indications: Bleeding grade 1 or 2 internal haemorrhoids not responding to diet and fibre
Patients on anticoagulants where banding carries higher bleeding risk (specialist decision)
contraindications: External haemorrhoids, thrombosed haemorrhoids or anal fissure
Perianal sepsis
Inflammatory bowel disease of the rectum
Rectal bleeding not yet investigated where colorectal cancer risk is present
equipment: Haemorrhoid injection needle (Gabriel type) and syringe
steps: Confirm identity, indication, prior investigation of bleeding and written consent.
Position the patient in the left lateral position with a chaperone present.
Insert the proctoscope and identify the haemorrhoidal pedicles.
Insert the needle into the submucosa at the base of each pedicle above the dentate line.
Inject the sclerosant slowly, checking that the mucosa swells and blanches without pain.
Stop and reposition if the patient feels sharp pain (needle too low or too deep).
Repeat for each pedicle being treated.
Withdraw the proctoscope and record the sites injected.
aftercare: A dull ache for a day is normal; use simple painkillers.
Eat a high-fibre diet and drink plenty of water to avoid straining.
Treatment may need repeating after a few weeks.
red_flags: Stop if there is sharp pain on injection.
Return urgently for fever, severe pain, difficulty passing urine or heavy bleeding.

indications: Dysphagia with normal endoscopy (suspected achalasia or motility disorder)
Before anti-reflux or achalasia surgery
Non-cardiac chest pain
Locating the lower oesophageal sphincter for pH catheter placement
contraindications: Obstructing oesophageal lesion or recent oesophageal surgery
Severe coagulopathy (relative)
Unable to cooperate with swallows
equipment: Manometry catheter (high-resolution solid state or water-perfused) and system, calibrated
steps: Confirm identity, fasting, stopping of motility-altering medicines as instructed and verbal consent.
Calibrate the system per manufacturer.
Apply local anaesthetic to the nostril and pass the catheter through the nose into the stomach while the patient sips water.
Confirm that the catheter spans the upper sphincter, oesophagus and lower sphincter on the display.
Secure the catheter and allow the patient to settle.
Record a baseline period without swallowing.
Give a series of small water swallows at set intervals per protocol.
Add provocative tests such as multiple rapid swallows if indicated.
Remove the catheter and analyse according to the current Chicago classification.
aftercare: A sore nose or throat settles within a day.
Restart any stopped medicines unless told otherwise.
red_flags: Stop if there is coughing, breathing difficulty, nosebleed that does not settle or the patient cannot tolerate the catheter.

indications: Reflux symptoms not responding to acid suppression with normal endoscopy
Before anti-reflux surgery
Atypical reflux symptoms (chronic cough, hoarseness, chest pain)
contraindications: Obstructing oesophageal lesion
Recent oesophageal surgery
Base of skull fracture or nasal obstruction (nasal route)
equipment: pH or pH-impedance catheter, calibrated, with data recorder
steps: Confirm identity, stopping of acid-suppressing medicines as instructed and verbal consent.
Calibrate the catheter in buffer solutions.
Pass the catheter through the nose so the sensor sits about 5 cm above the lower oesophageal sphincter.
Use manometry results or a standard formula to set the correct depth.
Secure the catheter to the nose and cheek and connect the recorder.
Teach the patient to press event buttons and complete the diary for meals, lying down and symptoms.
Advise normal eating and activity during the recording.
Remove the catheter after the recording period and download the data.
Analyse acid exposure time and symptom association.
aftercare: Keep to normal diet and activity so the study reflects daily life.
Do not shower while wearing the recorder.
Restart medicines after the study unless told otherwise.
red_flags: Remove the catheter and seek help for breathing difficulty, severe nosebleed or vomiting.

indications: Chronic constipation with suspected dyssynergic defaecation
Faecal incontinence assessment
Screening for Hirschsprung disease (absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex) in children
Before or after anorectal surgery
contraindications: Acute painful anal condition (fissure, abscess)
Recent anorectal surgery
Uncooperative patient (children may need sedation or adapted protocol)
equipment: Anorectal manometry catheter with balloon and system, calibrated
steps: Confirm identity, preparation per protocol and verbal consent (parental for children) with a chaperone.
Calibrate the system per manufacturer.
Position the patient in the left lateral position and perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated catheter into the rectum so sensors span the anal canal.
Allow a short rest period and record resting anal pressure.
Ask the patient to squeeze and record squeeze pressure and duration.
Ask the patient to push as if to defaecate and record the push pattern.
Inflate the rectal balloon to test the rectoanal inhibitory reflex and rectal sensation thresholds.
Perform a balloon expulsion test if indicated.
Remove the catheter and analyse findings.
aftercare: Resume normal activity and diet.
Results will guide treatment such as biofeedback or further tests.
red_flags: Stop if there is severe pain or bleeding.
Refer for rectal biopsy if the rectoanal inhibitory reflex is absent in a child.

indications: Faecal impaction not responding to laxatives, suppositories or enemas
Patients with spinal cord injury or neurogenic bowel needing routine digital removal
Impaction causing overflow diarrhoea, urinary retention or delirium
contraindications: Rectal or anal surgery or trauma, active bleeding or recent radiotherapy to the area (relative)
Severe painful anal condition without analgesia
Bleeding disorder or severe neutropenia (relative)
Children unless under specialist guidance, often under sedation or anaesthesia
equipment: Gloves (two pairs), apron and lubricant gel
Absorbent pads, bedpan or commode, and waste bag
Pulse and blood pressure monitoring equipment
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent, and explain the risk of vagal reaction.
Check pulse and blood pressure before starting, especially in spinal cord injury (autonomic dysreflexia risk).
Position the patient in the left lateral position with pads beneath and ensure privacy and a chaperone.
Apply lubricant and local anaesthetic gel to the anus and wait a few minutes.
Insert a lubricated gloved finger gently into the rectum.
Break up hard stool and remove it in small pieces using a gentle hooking movement.
Pause regularly and check the patient's comfort, pulse and colour.
Continue until the rectum is clear or the patient cannot tolerate more.
Clean the skin, check pulse and blood pressure and record the amount and type of stool.
Start a regular bowel regimen to prevent recurrence.
aftercare: Take prescribed laxatives regularly and drink enough fluid.
Eat more fibre where possible and keep active.
Report if bowels have not opened for three days.
red_flags: Stop if there is bradycardia, fainting, sweating, severe pain or bleeding.
Stop and treat urgently if blood pressure rises sharply with headache in spinal cord injury (autonomic dysreflexia).
Escalate for abdominal distension, vomiting or suspected obstruction.

indications: Unresponsive patient with absent or abnormal (agonal) breathing
No definite pulse felt within 10 seconds
contraindications: Valid documented do-not-resuscitate decision
Obvious signs of death incompatible with life (decapitation, rigor mortis, decomposition)
Scene unsafe for rescuers
equipment: Gloves and other personal protective equipment
Bag-valve-mask with reservoir and oxygen source
IV or IO access kit and fluids
Resuscitation drugs per local cardiac arrest protocol
Watch or timer and a recorder
steps: Check the scene is safe, then check responsiveness by speaking to and gently shaking the patient.
Shout for help, activate the resuscitation team and ask for the defibrillator.
Open the airway with head tilt-chin lift (jaw thrust if trauma suspected) and check breathing and pulse for no more than 10 seconds.
If no normal breathing or pulse, start chest compressions in the centre of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute and 5 to 6 cm depth.
Allow full chest recoil and minimise interruptions in compressions.
Give 2 ventilations with the bag-valve-mask and oxygen after every 30 compressions, each breath just enough to see the chest rise.
Attach defibrillator pads as soon as available while compressions continue.
Check the rhythm and shock if ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, then resume compressions immediately.
Obtain IV or IO access and give adrenaline and other drugs per the local cardiac arrest protocol.
Once an advanced airway is placed, give continuous compressions with one breath every 6 seconds.
Swap compressors every 2 minutes at rhythm checks to keep compressions effective.
Look for and treat reversible causes (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyper or hypokalaemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis).
Record times of arrest, shocks, drugs and rhythm checks throughout.
On return of spontaneous circulation, check airway, breathing and circulation and start post-resuscitation care.
If resuscitation is stopped, the team leader confirms the decision, the time is recorded and the family is informed.
aftercare: Maintain oxygen saturation 94 to 98 percent and avoid hyperventilation
Obtain 12-lead ECG, blood glucose and blood tests
Treat hypotension and seizures, and avoid hyperthermia
Transfer to ICU or HDU, or refer to a higher centre with escort
Debrief the team and support the family
red_flags: Re-arrest or loss of pulse after ROSC
Persistent hypotension despite fluids
Hypoxia despite oxygen and ventilation
Rib fractures or pneumothorax after compressions
Seizures or failure to wake after ROSC

indications: Ventricular fibrillation
Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
contraindications: Organised rhythm with a pulse (use synchronised cardioversion instead if indicated)
Asystole or pulseless electrical activity (not shockable)
Patient lying in water or touching metal that others are touching
equipment: Adult and paediatric pads or paddles with gel
Razor or towel to clear and dry the chest
steps: Confirm cardiac arrest and continue CPR while the defibrillator is brought.
Remove clothing, dry the chest, shave heavy hair and remove medication patches from the pad sites.
Place pads in the right infraclavicular and left mid-axillary positions, or anterior-posterior in small children.
Select paediatric pads or energy settings for children per the device and local protocol.
Pause compressions briefly to analyse the rhythm.
If shockable, resume compressions while the device charges.
Remove oxygen from the immediate area and shout a clear warning that everyone stands clear.
Check visually that nobody is touching the patient or bed, then deliver the shock.
Restart chest compressions immediately without checking for a pulse.
Reassess the rhythm after 2 minutes of CPR and repeat the cycle as indicated.
Record the time, energy and rhythm before and after each shock.
aftercare: Continue post-resuscitation care if ROSC is achieved
Inspect the skin under the pads for burns
Check and restock the defibrillator and pads after use
red_flags: Recurrent ventricular fibrillation (refractory arrest)
Skin burns or arcing at the pads
Device failure to charge or deliver shock
Shock delivered with someone in contact with the patient

form.label: Rhythm after last shock
options: Sinus or organised rhythm with pulse

indications: Apnoea or inadequate breathing
Hypoxia not corrected by oxygen with spontaneous breathing
Pre-oxygenation before intubation
During cardiopulmonary resuscitation
contraindications: Severe facial trauma preventing a mask seal (consider surgical airway)
Complete upper airway obstruction until cleared
equipment: Self-inflating bag of the right size (adult, child or infant) with reservoir
steps: Choose a mask that covers the nose and mouth without pressing on the eyes.
Connect the bag to oxygen at high flow with the reservoir attached.
Position the head (sniffing position in adults, neutral in infants) and clear the airway with suction.
Insert an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway if the airway is hard to keep open.
Hold the mask with a C-E grip, or use a two-person technique with both hands if the seal is poor.
Squeeze the bag just enough to see the chest rise, over about one second.
Ventilate at the rate for age, or 2 breaths per 30 compressions during CPR.
Watch the chest rise, oxygen saturation and the abdomen for gastric distension.
Reposition the head and mask if the chest does not rise.
Continue until spontaneous breathing is adequate or an advanced airway is placed.
aftercare: Monitor breathing, oxygen saturation and level of consciousness
Consider a nasogastric tube if the stomach is distended
Plan definitive airway or ventilation if still needed
red_flags: Chest does not rise despite repositioning
Falling oxygen saturation or bradycardia
Vomiting or aspiration
Signs of pneumothorax

indications: Unconscious patient with airway obstruction by the tongue
To aid bag-valve-mask ventilation
contraindications: Intact gag reflex or semi-conscious patient
Recent oral trauma or oral surgery
equipment: Tongue depressor or laryngoscope for children
steps: Confirm the patient is unconscious with no gag reflex.
Size the airway from the centre of the incisors to the angle of the jaw.
Suction the mouth to clear secretions, blood or vomit.
In adults, insert the airway upside down along the hard palate and rotate it 180 degrees as it reaches the soft palate.
In children, use a tongue depressor and insert the airway the right way up without rotation.
Check the flange sits at the lips and the airway is not pushing the tongue back.
Confirm improved airflow and chest movement, and give oxygen.
Remove the airway at once if the patient gags or coughs.
aftercare: Keep monitoring airway, breathing and level of consciousness
Remove when the patient wakes or tolerates it poorly
red_flags: Gagging, vomiting or laryngospasm
Persistent obstruction despite the airway
Bleeding from the mouth

indications: Airway obstruction in a patient with reduced consciousness who still has a gag reflex
Trismus or clenched jaw preventing an oral airway
To aid bag-valve-mask ventilation
contraindications: Suspected base of skull fracture or severe midface injury
Severe nasal obstruction or nasal bleeding disorder
equipment: Safety pin if the airway has no flange
steps: Check for signs of base of skull fracture before choosing this airway.
Size the airway from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, with a diameter that fits the nostril.
Lubricate the airway well.
Insert into the larger nostril with the bevel toward the septum, passing straight back along the floor of the nose.
Rotate gently if resistance is met, and try the other nostril rather than forcing it.
Advance until the flange rests at the nostril.
Confirm airflow and chest movement and give oxygen.
Secure the airway so it cannot slip into the nose.
aftercare: Monitor airway, breathing and for nasal bleeding
Suction through the airway as needed
red_flags: Epistaxis that does not settle
Persistent obstruction or laryngospasm
Deterioration in consciousness

indications: Choking with ineffective cough, inability to speak or cry, or cyanosis
Witnessed inhalation of a foreign body with severe airway obstruction
contraindications: Effective cough present (encourage coughing and observe instead)
Abdominal thrusts in infants under 1 year (use chest thrusts)
steps: Ask the patient if they are choking and assess whether the cough is effective.
If the cough is effective, encourage coughing and watch closely.
For an ineffective cough in a conscious adult or child, give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the patient leaning forward.
If back blows fail, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts standing behind the patient (chest thrusts in pregnancy or obesity).
In infants, hold face down along the forearm with the head lower and give 5 back blows, then turn face up and give 5 chest thrusts with two fingers.
Alternate back blows and thrusts until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unconscious.
If the patient becomes unconscious, lower them to the ground, call for help and start CPR.
Look in the mouth before giving breaths and remove a visible object, but do not do blind finger sweeps.
If trained, use a laryngoscope and Magill forceps to remove an object seen in the pharynx.
If the airway cannot be cleared and ventilation fails, proceed to a surgical or needle airway.
aftercare: Examine for injury after abdominal thrusts
Arrange chest X-ray if aspiration or a retained object is possible
Refer for bronchoscopy if a foreign body may remain in the airway
red_flags: Persistent cough, wheeze or stridor after the episode
Abdominal pain after abdominal thrusts
Fever or breathlessness in the following days
Loss of consciousness during the event

indications: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate situation
Complete upper airway obstruction above the larynx not relieved by other means
Emergency surgical airway in children under about 10 to 12 years
contraindications: Ability to oxygenate by less invasive means
Transection of the trachea or major laryngeal fracture
equipment: Large-bore cannula (12 to 14 G) on a 5 mL or 10 mL syringe
Oxygen source with jet ventilation device or oxygen tubing with a Y-connector or side hole
3.0 mm ETT adaptor or 3 mL syringe barrel with 7.0 mm ETT connector
