steps: Call for help and continue attempts to oxygenate from above while preparing.
Extend the neck if there is no suspected cervical spine injury.
Identify the cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
Clean the skin quickly and stabilise the larynx with the non-dominant hand.
Insert the cannula on the syringe through the membrane at 45 degrees aimed toward the feet, aspirating as you advance.
Confirm free aspiration of air, then advance the cannula off the needle and remove the needle.
Reconfirm air aspiration and hold the cannula securely at all times.
Connect to the oxygen system and give intermittent insufflation, about one second on and four seconds off.
Watch chest rise and fall and allow exhalation through the upper airway.
Secure the cannula and arrange an urgent definitive airway.
aftercare: Treat as a temporary measure lasting only minutes
Arrange definitive airway (surgical cricothyroidotomy, tracheostomy or intubation) immediately
Monitor oxygen saturation, chest movement and neck swelling
red_flags: Surgical emphysema or neck swelling
Rising carbon dioxide or poor chest deflation (barotrauma risk)
Kinking or dislodgement of the cannula
Bleeding into the airway

indications: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate situation in an adult or older child
Severe facial or upper airway trauma preventing intubation
contraindications: Children under about 10 to 12 years (use needle cricothyroidotomy)
Laryngeal fracture or tracheal transection
Less invasive airway still possible
equipment: Cuffed tracheal tube 6.0 mm, or small tracheostomy tube
Tracheal hook and dilator if available
Bag-valve-mask, oxygen and capnography if available
steps: Declare the emergency, call for help and continue oxygenation attempts from above.
Extend the neck and identify the cricothyroid membrane, using a vertical skin incision if landmarks cannot be felt.
Stabilise the larynx with the non-dominant hand.
Make a transverse stab incision through the skin and cricothyroid membrane with the blade facing you.
Rotate the blade 90 degrees so the sharp edge faces the feet and pull it toward you to open the hole.
Slide a bougie along the blade into the trachea.
Remove the scalpel and railroad the lubricated cuffed tube over the bougie into the trachea.
Inflate the cuff, remove the bougie and ventilate.
Confirm placement with capnography, chest rise and breath sounds.
Secure the tube and control bleeding.
aftercare: Chest X-ray to confirm tube position
Admit to ICU or HDU and arrange formal tracheostomy by ENT or surgery
Monitor for bleeding, surgical emphysema and tube blockage
red_flags: Loss of capnography trace or chest rise (tube displacement)
Significant bleeding
Surgical emphysema
Pneumothorax

form.label: Technique
options: Open surgical with hook and dilator

indications: Clinical tension pneumothorax with respiratory distress and haemodynamic compromise
Suspected tension pneumothorax in traumatic cardiac arrest
contraindications: No clinical signs of tension (confirm with imaging first if stable)
equipment: Large-bore cannula (14 G, at least 5 cm long in adults; shorter in children)
Chest drain set ready to follow
steps: Recognise tension clinically (distress, hypoxia, hypotension, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation) and do not wait for an X-ray.
Give high-flow oxygen and call for help.
Identify the site, which is the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line in adults, or the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line in children.
Clean the skin quickly.
Insert the cannula just above the rib below, perpendicular to the chest wall.
Listen for a rush of air or watch for bubbles in the syringe.
Withdraw the needle and leave the cannula in place, securing it.
Reassess breathing, oxygen saturation and blood pressure.
Proceed promptly to formal intercostal chest drain insertion.
aftercare: Insert a chest drain as soon as possible
Chest X-ray after the drain
Monitor for re-accumulation if the cannula kinks or blocks
red_flags: No improvement after decompression (wrong diagnosis, blocked cannula or too short a needle)
Re-accumulation of tension
Bleeding from the site

indications: Pneumothorax (after needle decompression or large or symptomatic)
Haemothorax
Large pleural effusion or empyema
Penetrating chest trauma before ventilation or transfer
contraindications: Coagulopathy (correct where possible, unless life-threatening)
Uncertain diagnosis (for example large bulla) without imaging
Lung adherent to the chest wall at the site
equipment: Sterile gloves, gown, drapes and antiseptic
Local anaesthetic with needles and syringes
Scalpel, curved artery forceps and blunt dissecting forceps
Chest drain of suitable size (larger 28 to 32 Fr for haemothorax in adults)
Underwater seal bottle with sterile water, or a flutter valve
Heavy suture for securing, and a dressing
steps: Confirm the side with examination and imaging and check identity, consent and time-out.
Position the patient semi-reclined with the arm behind the head.
Mark the safe triangle, which is the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the mid to anterior axillary line.
Clean and drape the site using full aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the pleura, aspirating to confirm air or fluid.
Make a 2 to 3 cm incision along the upper border of the rib below.
Bluntly dissect over the rib and through the pleura with the artery forceps.
Sweep a gloved finger into the pleural space to confirm entry and free adhesions.
Insert the drain directed upward for air or downward and back for fluid, without using a sharp trocar.
Connect to the underwater seal and confirm swinging and bubbling or drainage.
Secure the drain with a suture and apply a dressing.
Obtain a chest X-ray to confirm position.
aftercare: Keep the drain bottle below chest level and upright at all times
Record drainage, swinging and bubbling regularly
Give analgesia and encourage deep breathing
Never clamp a bubbling drain
Remove when lung is re-expanded and drainage is low, per senior review
red_flags: Blood loss more than 1,500 mL at insertion or more than 200 mL per hour (consider thoracotomy or refer)
Sudden breathlessness or surgical emphysema
Drain falls out or disconnects
Fever or pus at the site

indications: Cardiac arrest or severe shock when IV access fails or would be delayed
Emergency in children after failed peripheral cannulation (two attempts or 90 seconds)
contraindications: Fracture of the target bone
Infection or burn over the site
Previous IO attempt in the same bone within 48 hours
Osteogenesis imperfecta or severe osteoporosis
equipment: IO needle (manual, spring-loaded or powered driver) of suitable length
Extension set and pressure bag or syringe for push
steps: Choose the site, usually the proximal tibia 1 to 2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity; alternatives are the distal tibia or proximal humerus in adults.
Clean the skin and use aseptic technique.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic to the periosteum if the patient is conscious.
Stabilise the limb and insert the needle perpendicular to the bone with a twisting motion or driver until there is a loss of resistance.
Remove the stylet and check that the needle stands firmly without support.
Aspirate marrow to confirm placement and send samples if needed.
Flush with saline and watch for swelling around the site.
Connect the extension set and secure the needle.
Give fluids and drugs by push or pressure bag, as flow by gravity is slow.
Record the time of insertion on the limb and in the notes.
aftercare: Check the limb often for swelling, colour and compartment syndrome
Replace with IV access as soon as possible and remove within 24 hours
Apply a dressing after removal
red_flags: Swelling or tense calf (extravasation or compartment syndrome)
Redness, pus or fever (osteomyelitis)
Needle dislodged

indications: Trauma with neck pain, tenderness or neurological symptoms
Dangerous mechanism of injury (fall from height, road traffic crash, diving)
Reduced consciousness or intoxication after trauma
contraindications: Penetrating neck injury without neurological deficit (collar may hide bleeding or airway problems)
Fixed neck deformity such as ankylosing spondylitis (immobilise in the patient's own position)
Collar worsening airway compromise or raised intracranial pressure
equipment: Rigid cervical collar of correct size, or towel rolls and tape if no collar
Second trained person for manual in-line stabilisation
steps: Explain the procedure and ask the patient not to move their head.
Have one person hold manual in-line stabilisation from behind the head.
Assess the neck, airway and limb neurology before applying the collar.
Size the collar using the distance from the shoulder to the jaw angle per the manufacturer's guide.
Slide the back of the collar behind the neck without moving the head.
Bring the front of the collar up under the chin and fasten it snugly.
Check the airway is clear and the patient can open their mouth for vomiting.
Add head blocks and tape if the patient is on a board or stretcher.
Recheck neurology after application and record it.
Clear the spine clinically using a validated rule or arrange imaging before removing the collar.
aftercare: Keep the patient supine with log roll precautions until the spine is cleared
Check skin under the collar for pressure sores
Have suction ready in case of vomiting
Refer to orthopaedics or neurosurgery if injury is confirmed
red_flags: New weakness, numbness or loss of bladder control
Airway compromise or vomiting
Increasing agitation (may need manual stabilisation instead of a collar)
Pressure sores under the collar

name: Spinal board immobilisation and log roll

indications: Suspected spinal injury needing transfer or examination of the back
Turning a trauma patient for back examination, sheet change or pressure care
contraindications: Prolonged lying on a hard board (remove as soon as possible)
Unstable pelvic fracture needing minimal movement (use a scoop and minimise rolls)
equipment: At least four trained people (five for a large patient)
steps: Explain the procedure to the patient and check the cervical collar is fitted.
Assign the person at the head as leader, who gives all commands.
Place helpers at the chest, pelvis and legs on one side, with arms crossed for a firm hold.
Check limb neurology before the roll.
On the leader's count, roll the patient as one unit toward the helpers, keeping the head, neck and spine in line.
A further person examines the back, removes debris and checks for spinal tenderness or step.
Slide the board or clean sheet under the patient if needed.
Roll the patient back onto the board on the leader's count.
Secure straps across the chest, pelvis and thighs, then tape the head last.
Recheck neurology, airway and breathing.
aftercare: Remove the board as soon as the patient reaches a firm trolley or bed
Continue log roll every 2 hours for pressure care until the spine is cleared
Keep suction at hand and monitor breathing
red_flags: New neurological deficit after movement
Breathing difficulty from tight straps
Vomiting while immobilised
Pressure sores

indications: Any patient with significant trauma
Mechanism suggesting serious injury even without obvious signs
contraindications: None (adapt order to life threats found)
equipment: Two large-bore IV cannulas and warmed fluids
Blood tubes for group and crossmatch
Point-of-care ultrasound and X-ray if available
steps: Prepare the team and assign roles before the patient arrives if warned.
Control catastrophic external bleeding first with direct pressure or a tourniquet.
Assess and secure the airway with cervical spine protection.
Assess breathing and treat tension pneumothorax, open chest wounds and flail chest.
Assess circulation, insert two large-bore cannulas, send blood and look for bleeding in chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and on the floor.
Assess disability with the AVPU or GCS score, pupils and blood glucose.
Fully expose the patient, examine front and back with a log roll and then prevent hypothermia.
Reassess ABCDE after each intervention and whenever the patient deteriorates.
Use adjuncts such as chest and pelvis X-ray, FAST scan, urinary catheter and nasogastric tube where indicated and safe.
Take an AMPLE history (allergies, medicines, past history, last meal, events).
Perform a head-to-toe secondary survey once the patient is stable.
Decide on definitive care, theatre, admission or transfer, and document all findings.
aftercare: Repeat the survey regularly and after any change
Give analgesia and tetanus prophylaxis
Arrange tertiary survey within 24 hours to find missed injuries
Communicate with the receiving team and family
red_flags: Airway compromise or falling GCS
Persistent hypotension or tachycardia despite fluids
Expanding abdomen or pelvic instability
Unequal pupils
Injuries beyond local capacity (refer early)

indications: Clean laceration less than 12 hours old (up to 24 hours on the face) needing closure
Gaping wound over a mobile area
contraindications: Heavily contaminated, crushed or infected wound (consider delayed closure)
Animal bite wounds except on the face (seek advice)
Tendon, nerve, vessel or joint injury needing specialist repair
Retained foreign body not removed
equipment: Sterile suture pack with needle holder, toothed forceps and scissors
Suture material (non-absorbable 3-0 to 5-0 for skin, smaller on face)
Antiseptic solution and sterile saline for irrigation
steps: Confirm identity, take the history of the injury and check tetanus status and any allergy to local anaesthetic.
Examine the wound for depth, foreign bodies and distal nerve, tendon and blood supply before anaesthesia.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Wash hands, put on sterile gloves and clean the skin around the wound.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic through the wound edges and wait for it to work.
Irrigate the wound thoroughly with sterile saline or clean tap water.
Explore the wound base and remove debris or foreign material.
Place interrupted sutures, entering the skin at 90 degrees, equal depth and distance from each side, with edges slightly everted.
Tie knots without strangulating the tissue and place them to one side of the wound.
Space sutures evenly, usually as far apart as the bite distance.
Clean and dry the wound and apply a dressing.
Count and dispose of sharps safely.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry for 48 hours
Remove sutures at 5 days on the face, 7 to 10 days on the scalp and trunk, 10 to 14 days on limbs and over joints
Give analgesia advice and tetanus prophylaxis as needed
red_flags: Increasing pain, redness, swelling or pus
Fever
Wound opens up
Numbness or weakness beyond the wound

indications: Deep laceration through dermis into fat or fascia with tension or dead space
Laceration needing deep sutures to reduce scarring
contraindications: Grossly contaminated or infected wound
Injury to tendon, nerve, major vessel or joint needing specialist repair
Large tissue loss needing skin graft or flap
equipment: Sterile suture pack with needle holder, toothed forceps, scissors and skin hooks
Absorbable suture for deep layer and non-absorbable or absorbable suture for skin
Sterile saline for irrigation and antiseptic
Sterile gloves, drapes, gauze and good lighting
steps: Confirm identity, take the history and check tetanus status.
Examine and record distal neurovascular and tendon function before anaesthesia.
Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Clean the skin, drape and infiltrate local anaesthetic or give a regional block.
Irrigate thoroughly and explore the full depth of the wound under good light.
Trim ragged or devitalised edges minimally with a scalpel.
Close the deep layer with buried interrupted absorbable sutures, knots placed deep.
Make sure the dead space is closed and the skin edges come together without tension.
Close the skin with interrupted or subcuticular sutures, everting the edges.
Align landmarks such as skin creases first if present.
Clean the wound and apply a dressing.
Document the layers closed and suture materials used.
aftercare: Keep the wound dry for 48 hours, then gentle washing
Elevate limb wounds to reduce swelling
Remove skin sutures at the usual time for the site
Advise sun protection of the scar for months
red_flags: Spreading redness, pus or fever
Wound breakdown
Increasing swelling or tense limb
New numbness or weakness

indications: Contaminated or dirty wound
Wound with small areas of dead or devitalised tissue
Preparation of a wound before closure or dressing
contraindications: Large or deep wound needing theatre debridement
Wound near major vessels, nerves or the face needing specialist care
equipment: Sterile dressing pack with forceps, scissors and scalpel
Large volume of sterile saline or clean drinking water for irrigation
20 mL or larger syringe or irrigation set
Antiseptic solution, sterile gloves and gauze
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and check tetanus status.
Give analgesia and infiltrate local anaesthetic around the wound if needed.
Wash hands and put on gloves, using sterile technique.
Irrigate the wound under pressure with a syringe or running clean water until visibly clean.
Remove grit, soil and foreign material with forceps and gauze.
Trim dead or clearly devitalised tissue with scissors or scalpel back to bleeding tissue.
Avoid removing healthy skin, especially on the face and hands.
Control bleeding with pressure.
Decide on primary closure, delayed closure or healing by secondary intention.
Apply a suitable dressing.
aftercare: Change dressing daily or as advised, or return to the dressing clinic
Give tetanus prophylaxis as needed
Antibiotics only if indicated per local protocol
Review in 48 hours for heavily contaminated wounds
red_flags: Spreading redness, swelling or foul smell
Fever or feeling unwell
Crepitus under the skin or rapidly spreading pain
Bleeding through the dressing

indications: Short, clean, straight laceration with edges that come together easily
Low-tension wounds, especially in children on the face or scalp
contraindications: Wounds under tension, over joints or on hands
Contaminated, infected, bite or crush wounds
Mucosal surfaces, close to the eye or over the eyebrows
Deep wounds needing deep sutures
equipment: Petroleum jelly to protect nearby areas if needed
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and check the wound is suitable.
Clean and irrigate the wound and dry it thoroughly.
Stop any bleeding with pressure before applying glue.
Hold the wound edges together with fingers or forceps, slightly everted.
Apply thin layers of adhesive over the surface of the closed wound, not into it.
Extend the adhesive about 5 mm beyond each side of the wound.
Hold the edges together for about 30 seconds while each layer sets.
Apply two to three layers and allow to dry fully.
Protect the eyes with gauze when working on the face and keep the patient's head tilted away.
aftercare: Keep the wound dry for 5 days and avoid soaking or scrubbing
Do not apply ointment over the glue
Glue peels off by itself in 5 to 10 days
red_flags: Wound edges open
Redness, swelling or discharge
Glue in the eye

indications: Small superficial lacerations with low tension
Skin tears in elderly patients with fragile skin
Support after suture removal
contraindications: Wounds under high tension or over joints
Hairy areas or wet, oozing wounds
Contaminated or bite wounds
equipment: Adhesive skin closure strips of suitable width
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and check the wound is suitable.
Clean and irrigate the wound and dry the surrounding skin thoroughly.
Apply skin adhesive tincture to the skin beside the wound if available, avoiding the wound itself.
Attach half of the first strip to one side across the middle of the wound.
Push the edges together and attach the other half on the opposite side.
Place further strips about 3 mm apart along the wound.
For skin tears, gently roll the skin flap back into place before applying the strips.
Place two strips parallel to the wound across the strip ends to stop them lifting.
Cover with a light dressing if needed.
aftercare: Keep dry for 48 hours
Leave strips to fall off by themselves, usually in 7 to 10 days
Do not pull strips off; soak gently if they need removal
red_flags: Redness, swelling or discharge
Wound gaping
Skin tear flap turning dark

name: Removal of foreign body from skin or soft tissue

indications: Visible or palpable superficial foreign body
Foreign body causing pain, infection or reduced function
contraindications: Deep foreign body near nerves, vessels, tendons or joints (refer)
Foreign body in the eye, or in the hand with uncertain depth (seek advice)
Suspected bullet or blast fragment near vital structures
equipment: Sterile minor procedure pack with fine forceps, scalpel and scissors
Needle (19 G to 21 G) for lifting small splinters
Antiseptic solution, sterile gloves and gauze
X-ray or ultrasound for radio-opaque or deep objects if available
steps: Confirm identity, ask about the object type and time, and check tetanus status.
Locate the object by examination and imaging if it is glass, metal or deep.
Explain the procedure, risks and that removal may fail.
Clean the skin and infiltrate local anaesthetic around the site.
For a superficial splinter, grasp the end with fine forceps and pull along the line of entry.
If not graspable, make a small incision along the track or over the object and lift it out.
Limit the search time to about 15 to 20 minutes, and stop if the object is not found.
Check the object is complete and the wound has no further fragments.
Irrigate the wound and leave small wounds open or close loosely.
Apply a dressing.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry
Review if signs of infection
Refer if part of the object remains
red_flags: Persistent pain or a lump at the site (retained fragment)
Redness, swelling or pus
Numbness or weakness beyond the site

indications: Ring stuck on a swollen finger after injury, infection, burn or allergy
Ring needing removal before imaging, surgery or because of swelling risk
contraindications: Cutting a ring the patient refuses to have cut, unless circulation is at risk
equipment: String, umbilical tape or thick suture material
steps: Explain the options and that the ring may need to be cut, and record the patient's agreement.
Check circulation and sensation of the finger.
Elevate the hand and apply cold for a few minutes to reduce swelling.
Lubricate the finger and try twisting the ring off gently.
If that fails, pass string under the ring and wrap it tightly around the finger from the ring toward the fingertip.
Unwind the string from the ring end so the ring moves over the wrapped part.
If still stuck, protect the finger with the cutter guard and cut through the ring at its narrowest point.
Spread the cut ring apart with forceps and slide it off.
Recheck the finger for injury, circulation and sensation.
Return the ring or pieces to the patient.
aftercare: Elevate the hand and treat the underlying injury
Advise not to wear rings until swelling settles
red_flags: Pale, blue or numb finger
Increasing pain or swelling
Skin breakdown under the ring site

indications: Suspected or confirmed snakebite
contraindications: Tight arterial tourniquets, cutting, sucking or burning the wound (harmful, do not do)
Pressure bandage for cytotoxic bites with local swelling (carpet viper, puff adder) per local guidance
equipment: Clean water or saline for wound cleaning
steps: Reassure the patient, keep them still and lying down.
Remove rings, bracelets and tight clothing from the bitten limb.
Ask about the time of the bite and the snake description, without trying to catch the snake.
Remove any tourniquet applied before arrival slowly and only once antivenom and resuscitation are ready.
Clean the bite gently with water and cover with a clean dry dressing.
Immobilise the limb with a splint at heart level and avoid moving it.
Mark the edge of swelling and measure the limb circumference at set points with the time.
Insert an IV cannula in an unaffected limb and send blood for the 20-minute whole blood clotting test.
Monitor vital signs, bleeding, ptosis and breathing closely.
Arrange antivenom if there are signs of envenoming, or refer urgently if not available.
aftercare: Observe for at least 24 hours even if no early signs of envenoming
Repeat clotting test and swelling measurements regularly
Give tetanus prophylaxis; do not give antibiotics routinely
Elevate the limb once antivenom started and avoid intramuscular injections
red_flags: Bleeding from gums, wounds or urine, or non-clotting blood
Drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing or breathing
Rapidly spreading swelling or blistering
Dark urine or reduced urine output
Collapse or low blood pressure

indications: Bite or scratch from a dog, cat, monkey, bat or other mammal
Human bite including fight bite to the knuckles
contraindications: Primary closure of most bite wounds except facial ones (risk of infection)
Deep hand bites or joint involvement without specialist review
equipment: Soap and running water or large volume of saline
steps: Confirm identity, take the history including animal type, provocation and the animal's vaccination and status.
Wash the wound immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes.
Apply antiseptic solution after washing.
Examine for depth, tendon, joint or bone involvement and record a diagram.
Debride devitalised tissue under local anaesthetic if needed.
Leave most wounds open; close facial wounds loosely after thorough cleaning if cosmetically needed.
Apply a non-adherent dressing.
Classify rabies exposure category and start rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin per national guidelines.
Give tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics per local protocol for high-risk wounds, and for human bites assess HIV and hepatitis B exposure.
Report the bite to the local surveillance officer and advise observation of the animal if possible.
aftercare: Review in 24 to 48 hours for infection
Complete the rabies vaccine schedule on the dates given
Elevate bitten limbs
red_flags: Redness, swelling, pus or fever
Pain on moving a finger or joint
Animal dies or behaves strangely (tell the clinic)
Tingling, fear of water or confusion (possible rabies)

indications: Superficial and small partial-thickness burns suitable for outpatient care
Dressing change of a healing burn
contraindications: Burns needing referral (over 10 percent body surface in adults or 5 percent in children, full thickness, face, hands, feet, genitals, joints, circumferential, electrical, chemical or inhalation)
Suspected non-accidental injury without safeguarding review
equipment: Clean running water or saline for cooling and cleaning
Topical antimicrobial dressing per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, take the history including cause, time and first aid, and check tetanus status.
Cool the burn with cool running water for 20 minutes if within 3 hours of injury, keeping the patient warm.
Give analgesia before handling the wound.
Estimate depth and body surface area using the rule of nines or a Lund and Browder chart.
Clean the burn gently with saline or clean water.
Leave small intact blisters, and remove large, tense or broken blisters with sterile scissors.
Apply a non-adherent dressing and topical agent per local protocol.
Cover with absorbent gauze and a loose bandage, separating fingers or toes.
Elevate burnt limbs.
Arrange review and dressing change in 48 hours.
aftercare: Keep the dressing clean and dry
Return for dressing change in 48 hours, then every 2 to 3 days
Refer if not healed in 2 weeks
Moisturise healed skin and protect from sun
red_flags: Fever, foul smell, increasing redness or pain
Dressing soaked through
Burn not healed after 14 days
Child drowsy, vomiting or with rash (toxic shock)

indications: Rarely, a potentially life-threatening ingestion within about 1 hour, where no better treatment exists, on senior or poison centre advice
contraindications: Unprotected airway with reduced consciousness (intubate first)
Corrosive (acid or alkali) ingestion
Hydrocarbon ingestion such as kerosene or petrol
Risk of bleeding or perforation of the gut
Non-toxic ingestion or more than 1 hour after ingestion in most cases
equipment: Large-bore orogastric tube (36 to 40 Fr adult, 22 to 28 Fr child)
Warm water or saline in measured aliquots
Bite block, lubricant, gloves, apron and eye protection
steps: Confirm the indication with a senior or poison centre and obtain consent.
Make sure the airway is protected; intubate first if consciousness is reduced.
Place the patient in the left lateral head-down position.
Measure the tube from the mouth to the ear lobe to below the xiphisternum.
Lubricate and pass the tube through the mouth with a bite block in place.
Confirm position in the stomach by aspiration and testing.
Aspirate stomach contents and keep the first sample for toxicology.
Instil small warm aliquots of fluid by funnel and let them drain out by gravity.
Repeat until the returning fluid is clear, keeping a record of volumes in and out.
Give activated charcoal down the tube before removal if indicated.
Pinch the tube and remove it.
aftercare: Monitor airway, breathing and vital signs
Observe for aspiration
Continue specific poisoning treatment and psychiatric assessment if intentional
red_flags: Coughing, breathlessness or falling oxygen saturation (aspiration)
Blood in the returning fluid
Abdominal pain or distension
Falling consciousness

indications: Ingestion of a toxic substance that binds charcoal, usually within 1 hour
Selected poisonings where repeat doses are advised by poison centre
contraindications: Unprotected airway or reduced consciousness
Corrosives, hydrocarbons, alcohols, iron, lithium or heavy metals
Bowel obstruction or perforation risk
Vomiting that cannot be controlled
equipment: Water or juice to mix and a cup with a lid and straw
Nasogastric tube and syringe if the patient cannot drink
steps: Confirm the substance, time and that charcoal is useful for it.
Check the patient is alert with a protected airway.
Explain that it tastes gritty and may cause vomiting or black stools.
Prepare the charcoal per the product instructions and weight-based dosing in the drug list.
Sit the patient upright.
Give it to drink through a covered cup and straw, or down a confirmed nasogastric tube.
Watch for vomiting and keep suction nearby.
Record the time given.
aftercare: Monitor level of consciousness and breathing
Watch for constipation, especially with repeated doses
Continue specific poisoning treatment
red_flags: Vomiting with reduced consciousness (aspiration risk)
Coughing or breathlessness after the dose
Abdominal distension or no bowel movement

indications: Suspected unstable pelvic fracture after high-energy trauma with signs of shock
High-energy mechanism with pelvic pain in an unconscious or haemodynamically unstable patient
contraindications: Isolated hip or acetabular fracture without pelvic ring injury (not helpful)
equipment: Commercial pelvic binder, or a folded bed sheet and clamps or ties
steps: Suspect pelvic injury from mechanism and shock, and do not spring or rock the pelvis.
Remove objects from pockets and slide the binder under the knees and up under the buttocks with minimal movement.
Centre the binder over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests.
Bring the ankles and knees together and tie or pad them.
Tighten the binder evenly until the device locks, or tie the sheet firmly and clamp it.
Check distal pulses and breathing after application.
Record the time of application.
Arrange imaging and definitive care, and refer urgently if no orthopaedic or interventional service.
aftercare: Leave the binder in place until the fracture is assessed by a specialist
Check skin and pressure points every few hours
Cut holes in the sheet if access to the groin or catheter is needed rather than removing the binder
Avoid urethral catheter if blood at the meatus without specialist advice
red_flags: Persistent shock despite binder (needs surgical or interventional control)
Blood at urethral meatus or rectal bleeding
Pressure sores or skin necrosis
Loss of distal pulses

indications: Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure
Traumatic amputation
Mass casualty or unsafe setting where direct pressure cannot be kept up
contraindications: Bleeding controllable with direct pressure or packing
Junctional bleeding at the groin, axilla or neck (pack and press instead)
equipment: Improvised option of a wide band (at least 4 cm) and a rigid rod if no device
steps: Apply direct firm pressure while the tourniquet is prepared.
Place the tourniquet 5 to 7 cm above the wound, not over a joint, or high on the limb if the wound site is unclear.
Pull the strap tight and fasten it.
Turn the windlass until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is lost.
Lock the windlass and secure the strap.
Write the time of application on the tourniquet and the patient's forehead or chart.
Apply a second tourniquet above the first if bleeding continues.
Do not cover the tourniquet so it stays visible.
Treat shock and arrange urgent surgical care.
aftercare: Do not loosen the tourniquet to check the wound except under surgical supervision
Aim for definitive surgical control within 2 hours
Give analgesia, and monitor distal limb and vital signs
red_flags: Bleeding restarts (tighten or add second tourniquet)
Tourniquet in place longer than 2 hours
Patient remains in shock

form.label: Tourniquet time until release or handover

indications: Deep bleeding wounds where a tourniquet cannot be used (groin, axilla, neck, buttock)
Limb bleeding not controlled by pressure while waiting for a tourniquet or surgery
contraindications: Penetrating chest or abdominal cavity wounds (do not pack into body cavities)
Bleeding controlled with simple pressure
equipment: Haemostatic gauze or plain roller gauze
steps: Expose the wound and find the source of bleeding.
Remove excess blood and clots from the wound with gauze.
Push gauze firmly into the wound directly onto the bleeding point with fingers.
Keep packing until the wound cavity is tightly filled.
Apply firm direct pressure over the packed wound for at least 3 minutes (10 minutes for plain gauze).
Check for continued bleeding and add more gauze if needed without removing the first pack.
Secure with a pressure bandage.
Treat shock and arrange urgent surgical care.
aftercare: Leave packing in place for removal in theatre
Monitor for further bleeding and vital signs
Record the number of gauze rolls used
red_flags: Bleeding through the dressing
Expanding swelling (haematoma)
Persistent shock
Neck wound with breathing difficulty

indications: Snakebite with systemic envenoming (non-clotting blood on 20WBCT, bleeding, neurotoxic signs, shock)
Snakebite with severe or rapidly spreading local swelling
contraindications: No signs of envenoming (observe instead)
Previous severe reaction to antivenom (give only with full anaphylaxis readiness if life-threatening)
equipment: Antivenom specific to local snakes (polyvalent or monovalent), checked for expiry
IV cannula, giving set and infusion fluid
Adrenaline and anaphylaxis kit drawn up and ready
steps: Confirm envenoming signs and record baseline vital signs and the 20WBCT result.
Explain the benefits and risk of reaction and obtain consent.
Check the product, expiry and dosing in the product insert and drug list.
Have adrenaline and resuscitation equipment ready at the bedside.
Reconstitute and dilute the antivenom as the manufacturer directs.
Give by slow IV injection or infusion over the time stated by the manufacturer, never intramuscularly.
Watch the patient closely through the infusion for itching, rash, fever, wheeze or low blood pressure.
Stop the infusion and treat anaphylaxis at once if a severe reaction occurs.
Repeat the 20WBCT 6 hours after the dose and give further doses if blood still does not clot.
Record the batch number, amount and time.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, bleeding and urine output
Repeat 20WBCT every 6 hours until clotting returns
Watch for late serum sickness at 5 to 24 days
red_flags: Anaphylaxis (wheeze, hypotension, swelling)
Continued bleeding or non-clotting blood after the dose
Worsening paralysis needing ventilation
Reduced urine output

indications: Suspected viper snakebite to detect venom-induced coagulopathy
Monitoring response to antivenom every 6 hours
contraindications: None (use another site if the limb is bitten)
equipment: New, clean, dry glass test tube (plastic tubes give false results)
steps: Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Use a new, clean, dry glass tube that has not been washed with detergent.
Draw a few millilitres of venous blood from an unbitten limb.
Gently place 2 mL blood into the glass tube.
Leave the tube undisturbed upright at room temperature for 20 minutes.
After 20 minutes, tip the tube once gently to see if the blood has clotted.
Record clotted if the blood is solid, or not clotted if it still runs.
Repeat every 6 hours after antivenom until the blood clots.
aftercare: Act on a non-clotting result with antivenom or urgent referral
Press firmly on the puncture site for longer than usual
red_flags: Blood not clotting at 20 minutes (venom coagulopathy)
Prolonged bleeding from the puncture site
Spontaneous bleeding from gums, wounds or urine

indications: Heat stroke with core temperature above 40 degrees C and confusion
Severe hyperthermia from drugs, exertion or neuroleptic or serotonin syndromes
contraindications: Fever from infection alone (treat with antipyretics and cause instead)
Cold water immersion in an unstable patient who cannot be monitored safely
equipment: Tub or tarpaulin for cold water immersion if available
steps: Confirm high temperature and assess ABCDE, giving oxygen and treating seizures.
Move the patient to a cool, shaded or air-conditioned area.
Remove clothing while keeping dignity.
Start cooling immediately and do not wait for tests.
Use cold water immersion up to the neck when available and the patient can be safely monitored.
Otherwise spray the skin with cool water and fan continuously for evaporation.
Place ice packs or cold wet towels in the neck, armpits and groin.
Give cool IV fluids if dehydrated or hypotensive, guided by vital signs.
Measure temperature every 5 to 10 minutes.
Stop active cooling when the core temperature reaches about 38.5 to 39 degrees C to avoid overshoot.
Check blood glucose, electrolytes, kidney function and look for the cause.
aftercare: Monitor temperature, urine output and consciousness
Check for rhabdomyolysis, kidney injury and clotting problems
Admit for observation, and to ICU if organ failure
red_flags: Shivering (slow cooling) or temperature falling below 37 degrees C
Seizures or falling consciousness
Dark urine or low urine output
Bleeding or bruising

indications: Core temperature below 35 degrees C
Cold, wet trauma patients or neonates at risk of heat loss
contraindications: None for passive rewarming (avoid rough handling in severe hypothermia)
equipment: Warm blankets, foil blankets or forced-air warmer
Warmed IV fluids (fluid warmer or warm water bath)
Hot water bottles wrapped in cloth if no other means
steps: Confirm low temperature with a low-reading thermometer and assess ABCDE.
Handle the patient gently and keep them horizontal to avoid triggering arrhythmia.
Remove wet clothing and dry the skin.
Move to a warm room and cover the head and body with blankets.
For mild hypothermia, use passive rewarming with blankets and warm sweet drinks if alert.
For moderate hypothermia, add active external warming such as forced-air warmers or wrapped warm packs on the trunk.
Give warmed IV fluids and humidified warm oxygen if available.
Monitor the heart rhythm continuously.
Check temperature every 15 to 30 minutes and aim to rise slowly.
Refer for active core rewarming if the temperature is below 30 degrees C or the patient is unstable.
In cardiac arrest, continue resuscitation until the patient is warmed.
aftercare: Check blood glucose and electrolytes
Look for the cause (exposure, sepsis, hypoglycaemia, hypothyroidism, drugs)
Keep warm and monitor for rewarming shock
red_flags: Arrhythmia or cardiac arrest
Falling blood pressure during rewarming
No rise in temperature
Burns from warm packs

indications: Patient who has died in hospital or is brought in dead
Expected death needing confirmation by a clinician
contraindications: Possible reversible cause with resuscitation still appropriate (hypothermia, drug overdose)
steps: Confirm the identity of the patient with the wristband, records or relatives.
Check for any do-not-resuscitate decision and the circumstances of death.
Observe for at least 5 minutes to confirm absence of breathing and circulation.
Confirm no central pulse and no heart sounds on auscultation for at least 1 minute.
Confirm absence of breath sounds for at least 1 minute.
Check that the pupils are fixed and do not react to light.
Check there is no response to pain such as supraorbital pressure.
Look for an implanted device such as a pacemaker and record it.
Record the date and time of verification and any signs of injury.
Inform the relatives sensitively and offer support.
Inform the police or coroner if the death is sudden, unnatural, violent or unexplained.
aftercare: Complete the medical certificate of cause of death if appropriate
Arrange last offices respecting religious and cultural practice (including early burial requests)
Release the body to the mortuary or family per local process
red_flags: Any sign of life during the check (restart resuscitation)
Suspected unnatural death (medicolegal referral, do not wash the body)
Infectious disease needing special handling (for example Lassa fever or Ebola)

indications: Patient reporting sexual assault who agrees to examination
Child with suspected sexual abuse, examined by a trained clinician with a guardian or social worker
contraindications: Patient declines (respect the decision and still offer medical care)
Life-threatening injuries (treat first and preserve evidence where possible)
equipment: Private room and a trained chaperone
Sexual assault evidence kit (swabs, envelopes, labels, seal tape)
Body diagrams and camera if consent for photos
Blood tubes for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis testing
Change of clothes for the patient
steps: Ensure safety, privacy and a chaperone, and treat urgent injuries first.
Explain each part of the examination and that the patient can stop at any time.
Obtain written consent separately for examination, evidence collection, photographs and release of information to police.
For a child, obtain consent from a parent or guardian who is not a suspect, with the child's assent, and involve child protection services without delaying care.
Take a history of the assault, timing, acts and actions since (washing, changing, urinating) without leading questions.
Collect clothing and evidence in paper bags, labelling and sealing each item.
Perform a general top-to-toe examination and record all injuries on body diagrams with size and description.
Perform the anogenital examination appropriate to age, with speculum only in adults and when acceptable.
Take forensic swabs as indicated by the history before any medical swabs.
Keep the chain of custody with signatures for every handover of evidence.
Offer emergency contraception, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, STI prophylaxis and hepatitis B vaccination per national guidelines.
Assess for safety, suicide risk and safeguarding, especially in children.
Refer to counselling and support services and give a follow-up plan.
aftercare: Follow-up at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months for tests and support
Complete the medicolegal report and police form if requested
Ensure child protection referral where needed
red_flags: Suicidal thoughts or ongoing risk of harm
Significant genital injury or bleeding
Signs of pregnancy or infection at follow-up
Child in an unsafe home

indications: Injury from assault, domestic violence, road traffic crash or work incident where a legal report may be needed
Police or court request for medical examination
contraindications: Patient declines examination or release of information (record and treat clinically)
steps: Treat urgent injuries before documentation.
Explain the purpose and obtain written consent for examination, photographs and release of the report.
Record the patient's account in their own words with the date, time and place of the incident.
Examine systematically from head to toe in good light with a chaperone.
Describe each injury by type, site, size, shape, colour and pattern using correct terms (abrasion, bruise, laceration, incised wound, stab wound).
Measure injuries with a ruler and mark them on body diagrams.
Take photographs with a scale where consented.
Record findings objectively and avoid guessing the weapon or the age of bruises beyond your expertise.
Record investigations, treatment and referrals.
Write and sign the report with name, qualification, date and time, keeping a copy.
aftercare: Treat injuries and arrange follow-up review of evolving bruises if needed
Screen for domestic violence and safeguarding concerns
Store the records securely
red_flags: Ongoing threat to safety (refer for protection)
Child or vulnerable adult at risk
Injuries worse than the account explains

indications: Urgent venous access in shock when percutaneous and intraosseous access have failed or are not available
contraindications: Other access is possible (IO or percutaneous is faster)
Injury, infection or fracture proximal to the site
Coagulopathy (relative)
equipment: Sterile cutdown or minor procedure set (scalpel, curved artery forceps, scissors, vein lifter)
steps: Confirm need, identity and consent (emergency consent if unconscious) and do a time-out.
Choose the great saphenous vein 2 cm anterior and superior to the medial malleolus.
Clean and drape the site and infiltrate local anaesthetic if the patient is conscious.
Make a transverse skin incision about 2 to 3 cm across the line of the vein.
Bluntly dissect with curved forceps parallel to the vein to lift it free.
Pass two ties under the vein, one distal and one proximal.
Tie off the distal end and keep the proximal tie loose for control.
Make a small venotomy and insert the cannula into the vein toward the heart.
Tie the proximal tie around the vein and cannula to secure it.
Connect the drip, check free flow and close the skin and dress.
aftercare: Replace with percutaneous access as soon as possible
Remove within 24 to 48 hours and observe for infection
red_flags: Swelling or leak at the site
Redness, tenderness along the vein (phlebitis) or fever
Bleeding

indications: Urgent venous access when peripheral arm veins have failed and the external jugular is visible
contraindications: Suspected cervical spine injury needing neck turning
Local infection, trauma or haematoma
Vein not visible
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent if the patient is conscious.
Place the patient head-down (Trendelenburg) and turn the head away from the side used.
Clean the skin over the vein.
Press lightly above the clavicle to distend the vein, without compressing the carotid.
Stretch the skin and insert the cannula along the line of the vein toward the clavicle at a shallow angle.
Watch for flashback and advance the cannula off the needle.
Withdraw the needle while occluding the vein to prevent air entry.
Attach the flush or giving set and check free flow.
Secure the cannula firmly and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Return the patient to normal position once secured
Check the site often, as the cannula dislodges easily with movement
Replace with a peripheral or central line when possible
red_flags: Swelling of the neck (extravasation or haematoma)
Breathlessness or chest pain (air embolism or pneumothorax)
Arterial blood flashback

indications: Skin of the penis, foreskin or other area trapped in a zip
contraindications: Deep tissue injury or urethral injury (refer to urology or surgery)
equipment: Bone cutters, wire cutters or strong scissors
steps: Explain the procedure, reassure the patient and parent, and obtain verbal consent.
Give analgesia and a penile block or local infiltration if needed.
Apply mineral oil over the trapped skin and zipper and wait a few minutes.
Try gently unzipping in the direction that releases the skin.
If stuck, cut across the median bar (diamond) of the zipper slider with bone or wire cutters so the two halves fall apart.
Alternatively, cut the zip fabric below the slider and separate the teeth.
Gently free the skin from the teeth.
Inspect the skin for laceration and clean it.
Apply a light dressing or leave open.
aftercare: Keep the area clean and dry
Check that the patient passes urine normally
red_flags: Difficulty passing urine
Increasing swelling or redness
Discharge or fever

indications: Skin contact with acid, alkali or other corrosive chemicals
Acid attack injury
contraindications: Water on elemental metals such as sodium or potassium (brush off and cover with oil instead)
Neutralising the chemical on the skin (causes heat injury, do not do)
equipment: Personal protective equipment for staff (gloves, apron, goggles)
Large amounts of running clean water or saline
Shower or hose with low pressure
steps: Protect yourself with gloves, apron and eye protection before touching the patient.
Remove contaminated clothing and jewellery and seal them in a bag.
Brush off dry powder chemicals before wetting the skin.
If the eyes are involved, irrigate them first with running water or saline, as this takes priority over skin irrigation.
Irrigate the affected skin with large amounts of running water at low pressure, starting straight away.
Let the water run off away from unaffected skin and away from the eyes.
Continue irrigation for at least 20 minutes for acids and longer for alkalis, often an hour or more.
Check skin pH with paper and continue until it is neutral.
Continue eye irrigation until the pH is neutral and arrange urgent eye review.
Keep the patient warm during prolonged irrigation.
Assess burn depth and area and apply a dressing.
Identify the chemical and contact a poison centre for specific advice.
aftercare: Treat as a burn with dressings and review
Refer burns of face, hands, genitals or large area to a burns unit
Report assaults to police and offer psychological support
red_flags: Eye involvement or reduced vision
Breathing difficulty or hoarse voice (inhaled chemical)
Hydrofluoric acid exposure (risk of low calcium, seek specialist help)
Deep or extensive burns

indications: Skin or clothing contamination with organophosphate or carbamate pesticide (including Sniper/DDVP)
Patient with pesticide poisoning arriving in soiled clothing or vomit
contraindications: Delaying airway, breathing or antidote treatment for decontamination (resuscitate in parallel)
equipment: Personal protective equipment for staff (nitrile gloves, apron, eye protection, mask)
steps: Put on gloves, apron and eye protection before contact; avoid latex gloves which pesticides can pass through.
Start ABC resuscitation and antidote treatment at the same time as decontamination, with suction for secretions.
Move the patient to a well-ventilated area.
Remove all contaminated clothing, shoes and jewellery and seal them in bags.
Wash the skin and hair thoroughly with soap and water, including skin folds, nails and behind the ears.
Irrigate the eyes with water or saline if contaminated.
Wipe away vomit and secretions and dispose of them as contaminated waste.
Rinse and dry the patient and move them to a clean bed.
Clean contaminated surfaces and change gloves after the procedure.
Monitor staff for symptoms such as headache, sweating or blurred vision.
aftercare: Continue antidote treatment and close monitoring of breathing, pupils, heart rate and secretions
Admit for observation; ICU if respiratory failure
Offer psychiatric assessment if intentional
red_flags: Increasing secretions, wheeze or breathing difficulty
Muscle weakness or falling consciousness
Slow heart rate or seizures
Staff developing symptoms

form.label: Decontamination done
options: Skin washed with soap and water

indications: External bleeding from a wound controlled or partly controlled by direct pressure
Ooze after venepuncture, wound repair or minor surgery
contraindications: Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure (use tourniquet)
Suspected compartment syndrome
equipment: Crepe or elastic bandage or commercial emergency bandage
steps: Explain the procedure and expose the wound.
Apply firm direct pressure with gauze over the bleeding point for at least 10 minutes without lifting to check.
Elevate the limb above heart level if possible.
Keep the gauze in place and add more on top if blood soaks through.
Wrap the bandage firmly over the gauze, starting below the wound and moving up.
Make sure the bandage is firm but does not cut off circulation.
Check the colour, warmth, capillary refill and sensation beyond the dressing.
Mark the edge of any blood on the dressing with the time.
aftercare: Recheck circulation beyond the dressing every 15 to 30 minutes at first
Leave in place for the time advised, then review the wound
Loosen if fingers or toes become numb, cold or pale
red_flags: Blood soaking through despite the dressing
Numb, pale, cold or blue fingers or toes
Increasing pain or swelling under the dressing

indications: Scalp laceration needing closure
Bleeding scalp wound
contraindications: Underlying depressed or open skull fracture (refer to neurosurgery)
Signs of significant head injury needing assessment or CT first
equipment: Sterile saline, antiseptic, gloves and gauze
Scissors or clippers for hair trimming (avoid shaving)
steps: Assess for head injury, level of consciousness and neurological signs before repair.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Control bleeding with firm pressure.
Trim hair around the wound only if needed, without shaving.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the wound edges.
Irrigate the wound and palpate the skull through the wound for a fracture or step.
Close the galea with absorbable sutures if it is torn.
Close the skin with interrupted sutures or staples, taking full-thickness bites to control bleeding.
For small wounds in children, consider the hair apposition technique with twisted hair strands and tissue adhesive.
Clean the area and check bleeding has stopped.
aftercare: Hair can be washed gently after 48 hours
Remove sutures or staples in 7 to 10 days
Give head injury advice in writing
red_flags: Vomiting, worsening headache, drowsiness or confusion
Fits or weakness
Clear fluid from the nose or ears
Swelling, redness or pus at the wound

indications: Lip laceration crossing the vermilion border
Full-thickness or gaping lip wounds
contraindications: Large tissue loss or complex wounds needing plastic or maxillofacial surgery
Uncooperative child needing sedation or general anaesthesia (refer or arrange)
equipment: Fine suture pack with needle holder, fine forceps and scissors
Non-absorbable 6-0 suture for skin and absorbable 5-0 for muscle and mucosa
Local anaesthetic and dental needle for infraorbital or mental nerve block
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain consent, and check for dental injuries or retained tooth fragments.
Mark the vermilion border with a pen before giving anaesthetic, as swelling hides it.
Give an infraorbital or mental nerve block, or infiltrate carefully to avoid distorting the border.
Irrigate the wound and remove debris.
Place the first skin suture exactly at the vermilion border to align it.
Close the orbicularis oris muscle with absorbable sutures in full-thickness wounds.
Close the mucosa with absorbable sutures.
Close the skin with fine non-absorbable sutures.
Check the alignment of the lip line and symmetry.
Clean and apply a thin layer of ointment.
aftercare: Soft diet and rinse mouth after meals
Remove skin sutures in 5 days
Avoid sun on the scar
red_flags: Swelling, pus or fever
Wound reopening
Visible step in the lip line

indications: Acute paronychia with pus collection at the nail fold
contraindications: Herpetic whitlow (do not incise)
Felon or deep pulp space infection or tendon sheath infection (needs formal surgical drainage)
equipment: Digital block equipment with local anaesthetic (without adrenaline unless local policy allows)
Size 11 scalpel blade or blunt instrument
steps: Confirm identity, examine the finger and exclude herpetic whitlow and felon.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Clean the finger and give a digital block.
Lift the nail fold gently away from the nail with a blade held flat or a blunt instrument to release pus.
If pus is under the nail, remove the affected part of the nail.
Take a swab of the pus for culture if recurrent or spreading.
Irrigate the cavity with saline.
Place a small gauze wick if needed and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Soak the finger in warm water two to three times a day starting the next day
Remove the wick after 24 to 48 hours
Antibiotics only if cellulitis is present per local protocol
red_flags: Spreading redness up the hand or arm
Swelling of the whole finger or pain on moving it
Fever
No improvement in 48 hours

indications: Painful subungual haematoma with intact nail and nail edges, usually within 48 hours
contraindications: Nail disrupted or nail fold torn (consider nail removal and nail bed repair)
Acrylic nails (flammable with cautery)
equipment: Battery cautery device, or 18 G needle or heated paperclip
X-ray to check for tuft fracture if crush injury
steps: Confirm identity, examine the finger and check the nail and edges are intact.
Explain the procedure and that it is usually painless.
Clean the nail with antiseptic and allow it to dry (alcohol is flammable).
Hold the finger steady on a firm surface.
Place the cautery tip or needle over the centre of the haematoma.
Make a hole through the nail with gentle pressure or a twisting motion until blood comes out, stopping at once to avoid the nail bed.
Make a second hole if drainage is poor.
Press gently to drain blood and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Keep the finger elevated and clean, and change the dressing if wet
The nail may fall off later and regrow over months
red_flags: Redness, swelling or pus
Pain returns
Fever

indications: Nail bed injury needing repair
Ingrown toenail (partial avulsion)
Severe fungal or damaged nail, or pus under the nail
contraindications: Poor circulation to the toe or uncontrolled diabetes (seek review first)
Bleeding disorder (relative)
equipment: Digital block equipment with local anaesthetic
Finger tourniquet or a glove finger
Nail elevator or fine artery forceps
steps: Confirm identity, digit and consent, and check circulation and sensation.
Clean the digit and give a digital block.
Apply a digit tourniquet and record the time.
Slide the elevator under the nail plate from the free edge toward the base to separate it from the nail bed.
Free the nail folds from the nail plate with the elevator.
For partial avulsion, cut the nail lengthwise to the base and remove only the affected strip.
Grasp the nail or strip with forceps and remove it with a gentle rolling motion.
Inspect the nail bed and repair lacerations with fine absorbable sutures if needed.
Remove the tourniquet and check colour returns.
Apply paraffin gauze and a dressing.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and keep the dressing on for 48 hours
Then wash daily and redress until healed
Expect regrowth of the nail over months
red_flags: Digit pale or dusky after tourniquet removal
Spreading redness, pus or fever
Heavy bleeding through the dressing

indications: Recurrent or persistent ingrown toenail despite conservative care
Chronic infected nail fold with hypergranulation
contraindications: Peripheral arterial disease or poor foot circulation
Uncontrolled diabetes without foot specialist review
Acute severe cellulitis (treat first)
equipment: Digital block equipment with local anaesthetic
Nail elevator, straight scissors or nail splitter, artery forceps
Chemical matrix ablation agent per local protocol, or equipment for surgical matrix excision
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, drapes and dressings
steps: Confirm identity, side, toe and consent, check foot pulses and do a time-out.
Clean the toe and give a digital block.
Apply a tourniquet and record the time.
Separate the affected edge of the nail from the nail bed and fold with an elevator.
Cut the nail lengthwise about 3 to 4 mm from the affected edge back to under the nail fold.
Remove the nail strip with forceps, including the part under the fold.
Destroy the matrix in that strip by chemical ablation per protocol, protecting the skin, or by excising the matrix wedge with a scalpel.
Curette away granulation tissue from the nail fold.
Irrigate, remove the tourniquet and check bleeding and toe colour.
Apply a non-adherent dressing and bulky bandage.
aftercare: Elevate the foot for 24 to 48 hours and give analgesia
Remove the dressing at 48 hours, then soak and redress daily until healed
Wear open or loose footwear and cut nails straight across in future
red_flags: Pale or blue toe
Spreading redness, pus or fever
Ongoing discharge after 4 to 6 weeks
Regrowth of the nail spike

indications: Wound with possible foreign body, tendon, nerve or vessel injury
Penetrating wound where depth is uncertain
Wound over a joint with possible capsule breach
contraindications: Penetrating wounds of the neck deep to platysma, chest, abdomen or eye (refer to surgery, do not probe)
Active major bleeding or haemodynamic instability (resuscitate and take to theatre)
equipment: Sterile minor procedure set with retractors, forceps, scissors and needle holder
Local anaesthetic or regional block equipment
Limb tourniquet for a bloodless field if needed
Sterile saline, antiseptic, gloves and drapes
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site, and do a time-out.
Examine and record distal circulation, sensation, motor function and tendon function before anaesthesia.
Clean, drape and give local or regional anaesthesia.
Use a tourniquet for a bloodless field if needed, recording the time.
Irrigate the wound thoroughly.
Extend the wound slightly if needed for a clear view, along skin lines.
Examine the full depth and the structures through their range of movement.
Remove foreign bodies and devitalised tissue.
Refer injuries to tendons, nerves, vessels or joints to the right specialist if not repaired.
Close the wound if clean, or leave open for delayed closure if contaminated.
Release the tourniquet, check bleeding and circulation, and dress the wound.
aftercare: Elevate and splint if tendon involvement suspected
Review in 48 hours for contaminated wounds
Tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics per local protocol
red_flags: Numbness, weakness or loss of movement
Pale, cold limb beyond the wound
Spreading infection or fever

name: Removal of superficial bullet or pellet

indications: Bullet or pellet palpable just under the skin causing pain or irritation
Superficial pellet that is infected or in a hand or foot causing problems
contraindications: Deep fragments near vessels, nerves, joints, chest, abdomen, neck or eye (refer)
Fragments that are not easily palpable (most can be left in place)
Unstable patient or other gunshot injuries not yet assessed
equipment: Sterile minor procedure set with scalpel and fine artery forceps
steps: Complete a full trauma assessment first and record entry and exit wounds.
Locate the object by palpation and X-ray in two views, and mark the skin.
Explain that removal may fail and many fragments are safely left in place, and obtain written consent.
Clean, drape and infiltrate local anaesthetic over the object.
Make a small incision directly over the object along skin lines.
Fix the object between two fingers and grasp it with fine forceps.
Limit the search to about 15 to 20 minutes and stop if not found.
Irrigate the track and close loosely or leave open.
Place the object in a labelled container and hand it over with a signed chain of custody if police request.
Apply a dressing and record the procedure.
aftercare: Wound review in 48 hours
Tetanus prophylaxis
Inform police per Nigerian law on gunshot injuries (treat first; police report is not a condition of care)
red_flags: Signs of infection
Numbness or weakness beyond the wound
Expanding swelling or pulsatile mass
Joint pain or swelling (fragment in joint)

form.label: Evidence handed to police
options: Handed over with chain of custody

indications: Fluctuant skin or subcutaneous abscess
Abscess not resolving with antibiotics alone
Pyomyositis with confirmed pus collection
contraindications: Cellulitis without a pus collection
Pulsatile swelling or suspected aneurysm or vascular malformation
Deep neck, perianal-complex, hand or breast abscess needing a specific approach or theatre
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Ribbon gauze or wick for packing
steps: Confirm patient identity, site and consent and check for diabetes and HIV status where relevant.
Mark the point of maximal fluctuance and confirm with needle aspiration if in doubt.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, clean the skin and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the abscess or use sedation or general anaesthesia for large abscesses and children.
Make an adequate incision over the point of maximal fluctuance along skin creases where possible.
Collect pus with a swab or syringe for microscopy, culture and sensitivity.
Break down all loculi gently with a finger or artery forceps.
Irrigate the cavity with normal saline until the return is clear.
Take a biopsy of the wall if the abscess is recurrent or looks atypical.
Pack the cavity loosely or place a wick so the wound drains.
Apply an absorbent dressing and record the size of the cavity.
aftercare: Change the dressing and pack after 24-48 hours, then as needed until the cavity closes.
Give analgesia and antibiotics per local protocol if there is surrounding cellulitis or systemic illness.
Check blood glucose in recurrent abscesses.
Review culture results and adjust treatment.
red_flags: Fever, spreading redness or crepitus suggesting necrotising infection.
Brisk bleeding from the cavity.
Abscess recollecting despite drainage.
Signs of sepsis such as confusion, fast breathing or low blood pressure.

indications: Symptomatic or enlarging lipoma
Cosmetic concern
Diagnostic uncertainty about a soft tissue lump
contraindications: Lump with features of sarcoma (deep, fixed, larger than 5 cm, rapidly growing) until imaged and biopsied
Uncontrolled bleeding disorder
Local skin infection at the site
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Scalpel, dissecting scissors, toothed forceps and artery forceps
steps: Confirm identity, consent, site marking and that the lump is superficial and mobile.
Perform hand hygiene, clean and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the lump, or arrange general anaesthesia for large or deep lumps and young children.
Make a skin incision along skin lines over the lump, about two thirds of its diameter.
Dissect in the plane between the lipoma capsule and surrounding fat using blunt and sharp dissection.
Deliver the lipoma with gentle pressure and finger dissection, keeping the capsule intact.
Check that no lobules remain in the cavity.
Secure haemostasis with pressure, ligation or diathermy.
Obliterate dead space with absorbable sutures if the cavity is large.
Close the skin and apply a pressure dressing.
Send the specimen for histology if atypical, deep or large.
aftercare: Keep the dressing dry for 48 hours.
Remove skin sutures at 7-14 days depending on the site.
Give simple analgesia.
Review histology if sent.
red_flags: Expanding swelling under the wound suggesting haematoma.
Fever, redness or discharge from the wound.
Histology showing liposarcoma, which needs specialist referral.

indications: Symptomatic or enlarging epidermoid cyst
Recurrent infection of a cyst once inflammation has settled
Cosmetic concern
contraindications: Acutely infected cyst, which needs incision and drainage first
Uncontrolled bleeding disorder
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Scalpel, fine scissors, toothed forceps and artery forceps
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site, and check the cyst is not acutely infected.
Perform hand hygiene, clean and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the cyst, avoiding injection into it.
Make an elliptical incision around the punctum along skin lines.
Dissect around the cyst wall with fine scissors, keeping it intact.
Deliver the cyst with the ellipse of skin attached.
If the cyst ruptures, remove all wall fragments to reduce recurrence.
Secure haemostasis.
Close dead space if needed and close the skin.
Apply a dressing and send the specimen for histology if indicated.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry for 48 hours.
Remove sutures at 5-7 days on the face and 10-14 days elsewhere.
Give simple analgesia.
red_flags: Wound infection with redness, swelling or pus.
Haematoma.
Recurrence at the same site.

indications: Congenital dermoid cyst, commonly at the outer brow or midline
Enlarging or infected dermoid cyst after inflammation settles
contraindications: Midline nasal, scalp or neck cyst not yet imaged for intracranial or deep extension
Acute infection at the site
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Local anaesthetic, or general anaesthesia set-up for children
Fine scalpel, scissors, forceps and skin hooks
Bipolar or fine diathermy if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site, and review imaging for midline lesions.
Give general anaesthesia for children or local anaesthetic for cooperative adults.
Perform hand hygiene, clean and drape the area, protecting the eye for brow lesions.
Make an incision in a skin crease or within the eyebrow line over the cyst.
Dissect around the cyst carefully, which often lies deep to muscle and may sit in a bony depression.
Protect nearby nerves such as branches of the facial nerve.
Remove the cyst intact.
Secure haemostasis.
Close in layers with fine sutures for a good cosmetic result.
Send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry.
Remove facial skin sutures at 5-7 days.
Review histology.
red_flags: Swelling around the eye or reduced eye opening.
Wound infection.
Clear fluid leak from a midline wound, suggesting intracranial connection.

indications: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy
Suspected lymphoma
Suspected tuberculous lymphadenitis when aspiration is not diagnostic
Suspected metastatic disease with unknown primary
contraindications: Uncontrolled bleeding disorder
Node adherent to major vessels without imaging and senior input
Suspected head and neck squamous carcinoma before ENT examination of the upper airway
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Local anaesthetic, or general anaesthesia for deep nodes and children
Scalpel, fine dissecting scissors, forceps and retractors
Two specimen pots, one with formalin and one dry or saline for culture
steps: Confirm identity, consent and the node to be removed, and mark it before anaesthesia.
Give local or general anaesthesia as planned.
Perform hand hygiene, clean and drape the area.
Make a skin incision along skin lines over the node.
Divide the subcutaneous tissue and platysma or fascia as needed.
Dissect close to the node capsule, protecting nearby nerves such as the spinal accessory nerve in the neck.
Ligate or coagulate feeding vessels and remove the node intact without crushing it.
Divide the specimen as required, sending part fresh for TB culture if indicated and part in formalin for histology.
Secure haemostasis.
Close in layers and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry.
Remove sutures at 7-10 days.
Follow up histology and culture results and plan treatment.
red_flags: Shoulder weakness after neck node biopsy, suggesting accessory nerve injury.
Expanding neck swelling or breathing difficulty.
Wound infection or persistent discharge, which may suggest TB sinus.

indications: Fibroadenoma that is large, growing or worrying the patient
Benign breast lump with uncertain core biopsy result
Phyllodes tumour on core biopsy (needs a margin)
contraindications: Suspected breast cancer without triple assessment, which needs core biopsy first
Acute breast infection
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Scalpel, scissors, tissue forceps, skin hooks and retractors
Absorbable sutures for breast tissue and subcuticular skin closure
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and site, and mark the lump with the patient sitting up.
Review the triple assessment (examination, imaging and core biopsy where available).
Give local or general anaesthesia.
Perform hand hygiene, clean and drape the breast.
Make a circumareolar or curvilinear skin-line incision with the best cosmetic result.
Dissect down to the lump and grasp it with tissue forceps.
Excise the lump with a rim of normal tissue, or with a wider margin if phyllodes is suspected.
Orient the specimen with sutures if malignancy is possible.
Secure haemostasis carefully.
Close breast tissue with absorbable sutures and the skin with a subcuticular suture.
Apply a dressing and a supportive bra.
aftercare: Wear a supportive bra day and night for a week.
Give simple analgesia.
Review histology at follow-up and plan further treatment if needed.
red_flags: Expanding painful breast swelling suggesting haematoma.
Wound infection.
Histology showing malignancy or phyllodes tumour with close margins.

indications: Palpable breast lump needing tissue diagnosis
Suspicious lesion on ultrasound or mammogram
Confirming receptor status before cancer treatment
contraindications: Uncontrolled bleeding disorder
Patient unable to stay still
Very small lesion that cannot be targeted without image guidance
equipment: Scalpel with size 11 blade for a skin nick
Trucut or automated core biopsy needle (14 G)
Gauze, adhesive dressing and ultrasound if available
steps: Confirm identity, side and consent, check for bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use, and examine to locate the lump.
Position the patient lying with the arm raised on the side of the lesion.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the skin.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the skin and along the planned needle track.
Make a small skin nick with the blade.
Fix the lump between the fingers or under ultrasound guidance.
Advance the needle parallel to the chest wall into the lump and fire it.
Remove the needle, place the core in formalin and check it is solid tissue.
Repeat to obtain three to five good cores from different parts of the lump.
Apply firm pressure for several minutes and then a dressing.
aftercare: Keep the dressing on for 24 hours.
Expect mild bruising and give simple analgesia.
Arrange a results visit and multidisciplinary review.
red_flags: Expanding swelling or bruising suggesting haematoma.
Breathlessness or chest pain after the biopsy, suggesting pneumothorax.
Fever or redness at the site.

indications: Breast abscess confirmed clinically or on ultrasound
Lactational or non-lactational abscess not settling with antibiotics
contraindications: Mastitis without a collection
Suspected inflammatory breast cancer, which needs a biopsy
equipment: Sterile gloves, drapes and skin antiseptic
Wide-bore needle (18 G or 19 G) and 20 mL syringe for aspiration
Scalpel, artery forceps and ribbon gauze for open drainage
steps: Confirm identity, side and consent, and assess whether the woman is breastfeeding.
Perform hand hygiene, clean and drape the breast.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic over the abscess.
For smaller abscesses, aspirate pus with a wide-bore needle under ultrasound guidance where available.
For larger or pointing abscesses, make a radial or circumareolar incision away from the nipple.
Send pus for culture and sensitivity.
Break down loculi gently with a finger.
Irrigate the cavity with normal saline.
Biopsy the cavity wall if the woman is not lactating or the appearance is unusual.
Pack loosely or leave a small drain and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Encourage continued breastfeeding or expressing from the affected breast.
Give antibiotics per local protocol and analgesia.
Review in 2-3 days and repeat aspiration if the collection reforms.
Review in 4-6 weeks to confirm resolution and exclude underlying cancer in non-lactating women.
red_flags: Recurrent abscess, especially in a non-lactating woman.
Spreading redness, fever or signs of sepsis.
Milk fistula with persistent leakage.

indications: Breast cancer where axillary clearance is not needed or has been done
Large or recurrent phyllodes tumour
Palliative toilet mastectomy for fungating tumour
Risk-reducing surgery in selected high-risk women
contraindications: Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
Incomplete staging for cancer without multidisciplinary agreement
equipment: Specimen pot with formalin and orientation sutures
Grouped and saved or cross-matched blood available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and site marking, and complete the surgical safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position the patient supine with the arm on an arm board.
Clean and drape the chest wall and axilla.
Mark and make an elliptical incision that includes the nipple-areola complex and any skin involved by tumour.
Raise skin flaps in the plane superficial to the breast tissue to the clavicle, sternum, inframammary fold and latissimus dorsi.
Remove the breast from the pectoralis major muscle including its fascia.
Orient the specimen with sutures for the pathologist.
Secure haemostasis and irrigate the wound.
Insert a closed suction drain under the flaps.
Close the skin without tension and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Record drain output daily and remove when output is low.
Encourage early arm and shoulder exercises.
Give analgesia and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Discuss histology at the multidisciplinary meeting and plan adjuvant treatment.
Offer counselling and a breast prosthesis.
red_flags: Rapid swelling or high blood drain output suggesting haematoma.
Flap necrosis or wound breakdown.
Fever or wound infection.
Recurring seroma needing repeated aspiration.

indications: Operable breast cancer with involved or clinically positive axillary nodes
Locally advanced breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy
Breast cancer where breast-conserving surgery is not suitable or radiotherapy is not available
contraindications: Distant metastases unless done for local control after multidisciplinary review
Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
Inflammatory breast cancer before systemic treatment
equipment: Skin hooks and breast and axillary retractors
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and staging results, mark the site and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position supine with the arm abducted on an arm board, clean and drape the chest and axilla.
Make an elliptical incision that includes the nipple-areola complex and the skin over the tumour.
Raise skin flaps to the clavicle, sternum, inframammary fold and latissimus dorsi.
Remove the breast with the pectoralis major fascia from medial to lateral.
Continue into the axilla, identifying the axillary vein, long thoracic nerve and thoracodorsal bundle.
Clear the axillary nodes in continuity with the breast to the level planned, preserving the named nerves.
Orient the specimen and label the axillary tail for the pathologist.
