Secure haemostasis and irrigate.
Place drains under the flaps and in the axilla.
Close the skin without tension and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Record drain outputs daily and remove when output is low.
Start arm exercises early and teach lymphoedema prevention.
Avoid injections, drips and blood pressure cuffs on the operated arm.
Give analgesia and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Plan adjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy and hormone treatment at the multidisciplinary meeting.
red_flags: Swelling with high blood drain output suggesting haematoma.
Winged scapula suggesting long thoracic nerve injury.
Wound infection or flap necrosis.
Arm swelling suggesting lymphoedema or venous thrombosis.

indications: Early breast cancer suitable for breast conservation
Tumour small relative to breast size
Radiotherapy available after surgery
contraindications: Radiotherapy not available or not accessible to the patient
Multicentric disease or diffuse suspicious calcification
Persistently involved margins after re-excision
Pregnancy in the first or second trimester where radiotherapy would be delayed
equipment: Wire or marker localisation for impalpable lesions if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side, imaging and site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position supine with the arm abducted and clean and drape the breast and axilla.
Make an incision over the tumour or at the areolar edge for the best cosmetic result.
Excise the tumour with a rim of normal tissue down to the pectoral fascia.
Orient the specimen with sutures in at least two planes.
Inspect the specimen and take extra shaves from any margin that looks close.
Place clips in the cavity walls to guide radiotherapy.
Secure haemostasis.
Reshape the breast tissue to fill the defect where possible.
Close the skin with a subcuticular suture and apply a dressing and supportive bra.
Perform axillary staging as planned and record it under its own entry.
aftercare: Wear a supportive bra and give analgesia.
Review histology and margin status at the multidisciplinary meeting.
Refer for radiotherapy and any systemic treatment.
red_flags: Involved or close margins needing re-excision or mastectomy.
Breast haematoma or infection.
Patient unable to access radiotherapy, which should prompt a change of plan.

indications: Breast cancer with clinically or biopsy-proven axillary node involvement
Positive sentinel node where further clearance is planned
Melanoma or skin cancer with axillary node metastases
contraindications: Patient unfit for anaesthesia
Clinically node-negative breast cancer where sentinel node biopsy is available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position supine with the arm abducted and clean and drape the axilla.
Make a transverse incision in the axillary skin crease below the hair-bearing area, or extend the mastectomy incision.
Raise skin flaps and identify the lateral borders of pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi.
Identify the axillary vein as the upper limit of dissection.
Identify and preserve the long thoracic nerve on the chest wall and the thoracodorsal bundle.
Preserve the intercostobrachial nerve where possible.
Clear the nodal fat to the planned level, clipping or tying lymphatics and small vessels.
Label the specimen by level for the pathologist.
Secure haemostasis, place a suction drain and close in layers.
aftercare: Record drain output daily and remove when output is low.
Start shoulder exercises early.
Teach lymphoedema prevention and avoid procedures on the operated arm.
Aspirate seroma if symptomatic.
red_flags: Winged scapula or arm weakness.
Arm swelling, numbness or colour change.
Haematoma or infection.

indications: Persistent symptomatic gynaecomastia after causes are treated
Adolescent gynaecomastia lasting more than 2 years
Psychological distress from breast enlargement in males
contraindications: Untreated underlying cause such as a testicular tumour, liver disease or a medicine cause
Pubertal gynaecomastia of short duration that may resolve
Suspected male breast cancer, which needs a biopsy first
equipment: Minor or major general surgery set
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and check that causes have been looked for.
Mark the extent of breast tissue with the patient sitting up.
Give general or local anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Clean and drape the chest.
Make an inferior periareolar incision.
Dissect the glandular tissue off the skin, leaving a disc of tissue under the areola to prevent a crater.
Dissect the tissue off the pectoral fascia and remove it.
Secure haemostasis carefully.
Place a drain if the dissection is large.
Close the incision and apply a compression dressing.
Send the tissue for histology.
aftercare: Wear a compression garment for 4-6 weeks.
Remove the drain when output is low.
Review histology.
red_flags: Haematoma under the flaps.
Nipple-areola discolouration suggesting necrosis.
Wound infection.

indications: Large multinodular goitre causing pressure symptoms or cosmetic concern
Thyroid cancer
Toxic goitre not controlled or not suitable for medical or radioiodine treatment
Retrosternal goitre
contraindications: Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, which risks thyroid storm
Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
No pre-operative vocal cord assessment where it can be obtained
equipment: Thyroid or major general surgery set
steps: Confirm identity, consent and that the patient is euthyroid, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Confirm the pre-operative vocal cord check and serum calcium where available.
Give general anaesthesia with tracheal intubation and extend the neck with a sandbag under the shoulders.
Make a collar incision two fingerbreadths above the sternal notch and raise subplatysmal flaps.
Separate the strap muscles in the midline, dividing them if the gland is large.
Mobilise the lobe and ligate the middle thyroid vein and superior pole vessels close to the gland.
Identify and preserve the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the parathyroid glands with their blood supply.
Ligate the inferior thyroid vessels close to the gland.
Remove the lobe and isthmus completely for total thyroidectomy, or leave a small remnant for subtotal thyroidectomy.
Repeat on the other side.
Secure haemostasis with the anaesthetist performing a Valsalva manoeuvre.
Close strap muscles and platysma, with a drain if needed, and close the skin.
Check vocal cord movement at extubation where possible.
aftercare: Nurse sitting up and observe the neck for swelling.
Keep suture or clip removers at the bedside in case of neck haematoma.
Check serum calcium after surgery and watch for tingling or cramps.
Start thyroid hormone replacement after total thyroidectomy per local protocol.
Check the voice and refer for laryngoscopy if hoarse.
red_flags: Neck swelling, stridor or breathing difficulty, which needs immediate wound opening at the bedside.
Tingling around the mouth, cramps or a positive Chvostek sign.
Hoarse or weak voice or noisy breathing.
Fever, tachycardia and agitation suggesting thyroid storm.

indications: Solitary thyroid nodule with indeterminate or suspicious cytology
Toxic solitary nodule
Large benign unilateral nodule causing symptoms
Low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer where lobectomy is enough
contraindications: Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism
Bilateral disease needing total thyroidectomy
Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
equipment: Thyroid or major general surgery set
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and thyroid status, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Confirm the pre-operative vocal cord check where available.
Give general anaesthesia with tracheal intubation and extend the neck.
Make a collar incision and raise subplatysmal flaps.
Separate the strap muscles in the midline and retract them on the affected side.
Ligate the middle thyroid vein and superior pole vessels close to the gland.
Identify and preserve the recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid glands.
Divide the inferior vessels close to the gland and free the lobe from the trachea.
Divide the isthmus at the opposite side and oversew the cut edge.
Secure haemostasis and close in layers with or without a drain.
Send the lobe for histology, marking the side.
aftercare: Nurse sitting up and observe the neck for swelling.
Check the voice and refer for laryngoscopy if hoarse.
Review histology, which may show cancer needing completion thyroidectomy.
Check thyroid function at 6 weeks.
red_flags: Neck swelling or breathing difficulty, which needs urgent wound opening.
Hoarse voice.
Histology showing cancer needing further treatment.

indications: Symptomatic inguinal hernia in an adult
Irreducible or previously incarcerated inguinal hernia
Strangulated inguinal hernia as an emergency
contraindications: Patient unfit for surgery with a small symptom-free hernia, where watchful waiting may be used
Active skin infection in the groin for elective repair
Mesh should be avoided in a contaminated field such as strangulation with gangrenous bowel
equipment: Polypropylene mesh, or sterilised mosquito-net mesh where approved locally
Non-absorbable monofilament sutures for mesh or tissue repair
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate and insert a nasogastric tube and catheter first if the hernia is strangulated.
Give local, spinal or general anaesthesia, and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol if mesh is used.
Clean and drape the groin and make an incision above and parallel to the inguinal ligament.
Open the external oblique aponeurosis along its fibres and protect the ilioinguinal nerve.
Mobilise the spermatic cord or round ligament and identify the hernia sac.
For an indirect sac, free it from the cord to the deep ring, check its contents, then transfix and excise it.
For a direct sac, invert it and plicate the transversalis fascia.
Place mesh over the posterior wall fixed to the pubic tubercle, inguinal ligament and conjoint tendon without tension (Lichtenstein).
Where mesh is not used, perform a tissue repair such as Shouldice or Bassini.
If the hernia was incarcerated, check bowel viability with warm packs and resect non-viable bowel, then avoid mesh if the field is contaminated.
Check the deep ring is snug but not tight around the cord.
Close the external oblique, subcutaneous tissue and skin.
Check that the testis is in the scrotum at the end.
aftercare: Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Avoid heavy lifting for 4-6 weeks.
Review the wound at 1-2 weeks.
red_flags: Scrotal swelling or groin haematoma.
Testicular pain and swelling suggesting ischaemic orchitis.
Urinary retention.
Wound infection, especially with mesh.
Recurrence of the lump.

indications: Bilateral inguinal hernias
Recurrent hernia after open repair
Primary inguinal hernia where laparoscopic expertise is available
contraindications: Unfit for general anaesthesia
Previous extensive lower abdominal or pelvic surgery, for the TEP approach
Strangulated hernia with suspected gangrene
Bleeding disorder
equipment: Laparoscopy tower, camera, light source and insufflator
Balloon dissector for TEP if available
Polypropylene mesh and tacks or glue
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder or insert a urinary catheter.
Give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Enter the preperitoneal space (TEP) or the peritoneal cavity (TAPP) through an umbilical port.
Insert the working ports under vision.
For TAPP, open a peritoneal flap above the hernia defect.
Identify landmarks including the pubic bone, inferior epigastric vessels, cord structures and iliac vessels.
Reduce the hernia sac fully, avoiding injury to the vas and testicular vessels.
Place a large mesh covering the direct, indirect and femoral spaces.
Fix the mesh if required, avoiding the triangle of doom and the triangle of pain.
For TAPP, close the peritoneal flap.
Release gas under vision and close the fascia and skin at the port sites.
aftercare: Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Return to light activity within days and avoid heavy lifting for 2-4 weeks.
Review at 2 weeks.
red_flags: Abdominal pain, distension or vomiting suggesting bowel injury or obstruction.
Groin or scrotal haematoma.
Urinary retention or blood in the urine.
Fever or wound infection.

indications: Symptomatic paraumbilical or umbilical hernia in an adult
Incarcerated or strangulated paraumbilical hernia
Hernia with thinning or ulcerated overlying skin
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia with a small symptom-free hernia
Uncontrolled ascites, which should be treated first where possible
Mesh should be avoided in a contaminated field
equipment: Non-absorbable or slowly absorbable sutures for fascial repair
Polypropylene mesh for defects larger than about 2 cm
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give local, spinal or general anaesthesia, and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol if mesh is used.
Clean and drape and make a curved infraumbilical or transverse incision.
Dissect the sac free from the umbilical skin and subcutaneous fat.
Clear the fascial edges around the defect.
Open the sac, check and reduce the contents and assess bowel viability if incarcerated.
Excise excess sac and close the peritoneum.
Repair small defects with interrupted sutures, or overlap the fascia for a Mayo repair.
Place onlay, sublay or preperitoneal mesh for larger defects.
Reattach the umbilical skin to the fascia.
Close the skin and apply a pressure dressing.
aftercare: Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Avoid heavy lifting for 4-6 weeks.
Encourage weight loss where relevant to reduce recurrence.
red_flags: Wound infection or discharge, especially with mesh.
Seroma or haematoma.
Abdominal pain, vomiting or distension.
Recurrence.

indications: Painful or enlarging epigastric hernia
Incarcerated epigastric hernia
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia with a small symptom-free hernia
Divarication of the recti without a true defect, which does not need repair
equipment: Non-absorbable or slowly absorbable sutures for fascia
steps: Confirm identity, consent and the site, which is best marked with the patient standing.
Complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give local or general anaesthesia, using general anaesthesia in children.
Clean and drape and make a vertical or transverse incision over the hernia.
Dissect down to the herniated preperitoneal fat and the fascial defect.
Reduce or excise the extraperitoneal fat and check there is no bowel in a sac.
Look for other small defects along the linea alba.
Close the defect with interrupted non-absorbable sutures or use mesh for larger defects.
Close the subcutaneous tissue and skin.
Apply a dressing.
aftercare: Give simple analgesia.
Avoid heavy lifting for 2-4 weeks.
Review the wound at 1-2 weeks.
red_flags: Wound infection.
Haematoma or seroma.
Recurrence of the lump.

indications: Symptomatic or enlarging incisional hernia
Incarcerated or strangulated incisional hernia
Hernia with skin thinning or ulceration
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia, where an abdominal binder may be used instead
Active wound or mesh infection, for elective repair
Very large hernia with loss of domain without specialist planning
Uncontrolled diabetes or active smoking where elective surgery can be delayed
equipment: Slowly absorbable or non-absorbable looped sutures for fascia
Cross-matched blood available for large repairs
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site, review previous operation notes and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general or regional anaesthesia, with prophylactic antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Clean and drape and excise the old scar.
Dissect the hernia sac and define the fascial edges of the whole defect.
Open the sac, divide adhesions carefully and check the bowel.
Look for and include any additional defects along the scar.
Close the fascia without tension where possible, with component separation if needed and the skills are available.
Place mesh in the retromuscular (sublay) or onlay position with good overlap beyond the defect.
Secure haemostasis and place suction drains as needed.
Close the subcutaneous tissue and skin.
Apply a dressing and an abdominal binder.
aftercare: Record drain output and remove drains when output is low.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Wear an abdominal binder for 4-6 weeks and avoid heavy lifting.
Encourage weight loss, stopping smoking and diabetes control.
red_flags: Abdominal distension, vomiting or no passage of flatus.
Wound infection or discharge, especially with mesh.
Breathlessness or low urine output after closing a large hernia, suggesting raised abdominal pressure.
Large or recurring seroma.

indications: Any femoral hernia, because the risk of strangulation is high
Incarcerated or strangulated femoral hernia as an emergency
contraindications: Patient unfit for any anaesthesia, after senior review
Mesh plug should be avoided in a contaminated field
equipment: Polypropylene mesh plug or roll if used
Laparotomy set available for bowel resection
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate with fluids and insert a nasogastric tube and catheter if the hernia is strangulated.
Give local, spinal or general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Choose a low (Lockwood) approach for elective cases or a high (Lotheissen or McEvedy) approach if strangulation is suspected.
Dissect the sac out of the femoral canal, protecting the femoral vein laterally.
Open the sac and check the contents, assessing bowel viability with warm packs if needed.
Resect non-viable bowel through a preperitoneal or abdominal approach and record it.
Reduce the contents, transfix and excise the sac.
Close the femoral canal by suturing the inguinal ligament to the pectineal ligament, or place a mesh plug, without narrowing the femoral vein.
Close the wound in layers.
aftercare: Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Monitor bowel function closely if bowel was resected.
Avoid heavy lifting for 4-6 weeks.
red_flags: Abdominal distension, vomiting or fever after bowel resection, suggesting leak.
Leg swelling suggesting femoral vein compression or thrombosis.
Groin haematoma or wound infection.

indications: Incarcerated inguinal or umbilical hernia without signs of strangulation
Incarcerated inguinal hernia in an infant or child, as a bridge to early repair
contraindications: Signs of strangulation such as fever, skin redness, severe tenderness, peritonitis or blood in stool
Incarceration for more than 12 hours in adults, or bowel obstruction with toxicity
Femoral hernia, which should go straight to surgery
equipment: Analgesia and sedation set-up with monitoring
Pillow or bed able to tilt head-down
steps: Confirm identity, verbal consent and that there are no signs of strangulation.
Give adequate analgesia or sedation with monitoring, especially in children.
Position the patient head-down with the hip flexed and rotated outwards on the side of an inguinal hernia.
Allow a few minutes for the patient to relax.
Hold the neck of the hernia with one hand to guide it toward the defect.
Apply steady gentle pressure to the fundus with the other hand to push contents back through the defect.
Stop if reduction is not achieved after gentle attempts and do not use force.
After reduction, examine the abdomen for peritonitis.
Observe for at least 6-12 hours for signs of reduced non-viable bowel.
Plan surgical repair, usually within 24-48 hours in infants.
aftercare: Observe pulse, temperature, abdominal signs and bowel function.
Keep the patient fasted if surgery is planned soon.
Book repair at the earliest suitable time.
red_flags: Failure to reduce, which needs emergency surgery.
Abdominal pain, tenderness, vomiting or fever after reduction, suggesting dead bowel was reduced.
Reduction en masse, where the lump goes but obstruction continues.

indications: Acute appendicitis
Perforated appendicitis with localised or general peritonitis
Appendix mass that fails to settle, or interval appendicectomy
contraindications: Appendix mass that is settling on conservative treatment
Haemodynamic instability needing resuscitation first
equipment: Suction and warm saline for lavage
steps: Confirm identity, consent and diagnosis, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate with fluids and give prophylactic or treatment antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general or spinal anaesthesia and examine under anaesthesia for a mass.
Make a gridiron or Lanz incision centred on McBurney's point, or a midline incision for generalised peritonitis.
Split the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus muscles along their fibres.
Open the peritoneum, collect any pus for culture and find the caecum and taenia coli.
Deliver the appendix and divide its mesentery between ligatures.
Crush, ligate and divide the appendix base, burying the stump with a purse-string if preferred.
Check for a Meckel's diverticulum and other pathology if the appendix looks normal.
Suction and wash out pus locally or fully if there is generalised peritonitis.
Close the peritoneum and muscles in layers.
Close the skin, or leave it for delayed closure if heavily contaminated.
aftercare: Start oral fluids when bowel sounds return, often within 24 hours.
Continue antibiotics for perforated appendicitis per local protocol.
Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Review histology.
red_flags: Persisting fever, pain or ileus after day 3, suggesting pelvic or wound abscess.
Wound redness, discharge or breakdown.
Faecal discharge from the wound suggesting stump leak or fistula.
Signs of sepsis.

indications: Acute appendicitis where laparoscopy is available
Diagnostic uncertainty in right iliac fossa pain, especially in women of childbearing age
Obese patients where an open incision would be large
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability
Unfit for pneumoperitoneum, for example severe cardiorespiratory disease
No laparoscopic equipment or trained team, where open surgery is used
equipment: Laparoscopy tower, camera, light source and insufflator
Atraumatic graspers, scissors, Maryland dissector and diathermy
steps: Confirm identity, consent and diagnosis, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder or insert a urinary catheter.
Give general anaesthesia and antibiotics per local protocol.
Insert the umbilical port by open technique and create the pneumoperitoneum.
Insert working ports under vision in the suprapubic and left iliac fossa positions.
Inspect the whole abdomen and pelvis.
Lift the appendix and divide the mesoappendix with diathermy or clips.
Secure the appendix base with two endoloops or clips and divide it.
Remove the appendix in a retrieval bag through the umbilical port.
Suction pus and irrigate locally if contaminated.
Release gas under vision and close the umbilical fascia and the skin.
aftercare: Start oral intake early and mobilise the same day.
Continue antibiotics for complicated appendicitis per local protocol.
Give analgesia and review histology.
red_flags: Persisting fever, pain or ileus suggesting intra-abdominal abscess.
Increasing abdominal pain or distension suggesting bowel injury.
Port site infection or hernia.

indications: Generalised peritonitis
Penetrating abdominal injury with peritonism or instability
Blunt abdominal trauma with instability or positive FAST in an unstable patient
Intestinal obstruction not settling or with signs of strangulation
Undiagnosed acute abdomen after appropriate assessment
contraindications: Patient not resuscitated where delay is safe
Moribund patient where surgery would not change the outcome, after senior discussion
equipment: Bowel clamps and staplers if available
Absorbable and non-absorbable sutures, including looped sutures for mass closure
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate, insert a nasogastric tube and urinary catheter, and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and clean and drape from nipples to mid-thigh.
Make a midline incision and open the peritoneum carefully.
In trauma, pack all four quadrants to control bleeding, then remove packs one area at a time.
Control contamination quickly with clamps or sutures.
Examine all abdominal organs systematically, including the whole bowel from the duodenojejunal flexure to the rectum.
Treat the cause found, or perform damage control surgery if the patient is unstable.
Wash out the abdomen thoroughly with warm saline.
Place drains where needed.
Close the abdomen with mass closure, or leave it temporarily open if swelling is severe or a relook is planned.
Close the skin or leave it open in heavy contamination.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output and fluid balance closely, in high dependency if available.
Keep the nasogastric tube on free drainage until bowel function returns.
Give analgesia, antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Mobilise early and start chest physiotherapy.
Arrange a relook laparotomy if planned.
red_flags: Falling blood pressure, rising pulse or low urine output.
Increasing abdominal distension or pain after day 3.
Wound discharge or burst abdomen.
Fever or new peritonitis suggesting leak or collection.

indications: Undiagnosed abdominal pain after non-invasive tests
Suspected abdominal tuberculosis needing peritoneal biopsy
Staging of abdominal cancer before major surgery
Stable penetrating trauma to assess peritoneal breach
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability
Severe cardiorespiratory disease limiting pneumoperitoneum
Gross abdominal distension or multiple previous laparotomies without senior input
equipment: Laparoscopy tower, camera, light source and insufflator
Specimen pots for histology and culture
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder or insert a catheter.
Give general anaesthesia and position the patient supine.
Insert the first port by open technique at the umbilicus and create the pneumoperitoneum.
Insert extra ports under vision as needed.
Inspect all four quadrants, the liver, peritoneum, bowel, pelvis and omentum systematically.
Take peritoneal fluid for cytology or culture and biopsies of abnormal tissue.
Proceed to a therapeutic procedure or convert to laparotomy if needed and consented.
Release gas under vision and close port sites.
aftercare: Start oral intake when awake and mobilise early.
Give analgesia and explain that shoulder-tip pain is common.
Review biopsy and culture results.
red_flags: Increasing abdominal pain, fever or distension suggesting missed bowel injury.
Bleeding from a port site.
Port site hernia or infection.

indications: Peritonitis with suspected or confirmed typhoid ileal perforation
contraindications: No absolute contraindication once resuscitated, as the condition is fatal without surgery
equipment: Large volumes of warm saline for lavage
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate aggressively with fluids, insert a nasogastric tube and urinary catheter, and start antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and open the abdomen through a midline incision.
Collect peritoneal fluid for culture.
Find the perforation or perforations, usually on the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum.
Examine the whole small bowel, as there may be several perforations or impending perforations.
Freshen the edges and close single perforations in two layers or one layer transversely.
Resect the affected segment with anastomosis, or bring out an ileostomy, for multiple perforations or very friable bowel.
Wash out the abdomen thoroughly with warm saline until clear.
Place a drain in the pelvis if needed.
Close the abdomen with mass closure and consider leaving the skin open for delayed closure.
aftercare: Continue antibiotics per local protocol for enteric fever.
Monitor vital signs, urine output and fluid balance closely.
Keep the nasogastric tube on drainage until bowel function returns.
Give nutritional support early.
Watch the wound closely, as infection is common.
red_flags: Faecal discharge from the wound or drain suggesting fistula or leak.
Persisting fever or new peritonitis.
Burst abdomen.
Signs of septic shock.

form.label: Distance of nearest perforation from ileocaecal junction

indications: Perforated duodenal or gastric ulcer with peritonitis
contraindications: Sealed perforation in a stable patient managed conservatively after senior review
Suspected gastric cancer perforation, where biopsy or resection is also needed
equipment: Major laparotomy set, or laparoscopy set where expertise exists
Absorbable sutures for the omental patch
Large volumes of warm saline for lavage
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate, insert a nasogastric tube and catheter, and start antibiotics and acid suppression per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and open the abdomen through an upper midline incision.
Suction the peritoneal fluid and find the perforation, usually on the anterior duodenum or lesser curve.
Biopsy the edge of a gastric ulcer to exclude cancer.
Place full-thickness sutures across the perforation without tying them.
Lay a pedicle of omentum over the perforation and tie the sutures over it gently.
Check the repair is watertight.
Wash out the whole abdomen with warm saline, including both subphrenic spaces and the pelvis.
Place a drain near the repair if needed.
Close the abdomen.
aftercare: Keep the nasogastric tube on drainage until bowel function returns.
Continue acid suppression and give Helicobacter pylori eradication per local protocol.
Advise stopping NSAIDs, smoking and alcohol.
Arrange endoscopy at 6-8 weeks for gastric ulcers to confirm healing.
red_flags: Bilious drain output or peritonitis suggesting leak.
Persisting fever suggesting subphrenic or pelvic abscess.
Vomiting suggesting gastric outlet obstruction.

indications: Strangulated or gangrenous small bowel
Multiple typhoid perforations or bowel trauma
Small bowel tumour or stricture
Intussusception that cannot be reduced or is gangrenous
contraindications: Unstable patient where damage control without anastomosis is safer
Severe peritonitis with poor nutrition, where a stoma may be safer than anastomosis
equipment: Linear and circular staplers if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate, insert a nasogastric tube and catheter, and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and perform a laparotomy.
Assess viability with colour, peristalsis and mesenteric pulsation after warming, and mark the margins.
Divide the mesentery in a V shape, ligating the vessels.
Place non-crushing clamps on the healthy ends and crushing clamps on the specimen side.
Divide the bowel and remove the specimen.
Join the ends with a hand-sewn single- or two-layer anastomosis or with a stapler.
Check the anastomosis is patent, well perfused and without tension.
Close the mesenteric defect.
Measure and record the length of remaining small bowel if much was removed.
Wash out and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Keep the nasogastric tube on drainage until bowel function returns.
Monitor fluid balance and electrolytes.
Give nutritional support and watch for short bowel if a long segment was removed.
Mobilise early with thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
red_flags: Fever, tachycardia, peritonitis or bowel contents in a drain suggesting anastomotic leak.
Prolonged ileus or vomiting.
High stoma or stool output with dehydration.
Wound infection or burst abdomen.

indications: Adhesive small bowel obstruction with signs of strangulation
Adhesive obstruction failing to resolve after a trial of conservative treatment
Complete obstruction with closed loop on imaging
contraindications: Partial adhesive obstruction improving with conservative treatment
Unresuscitated patient
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate, decompress with a nasogastric tube, insert a catheter and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and enter the abdomen carefully, away from the old scar if possible.
Find collapsed bowel and follow it back to the point of obstruction.
Divide the obstructing band or adhesions with sharp dissection, avoiding injury to the bowel.
Divide other adhesions only as needed to free the bowel fully.
Check the whole small bowel for viability, enterotomies and serosal tears.
Repair serosal tears and enterotomies, and resect non-viable bowel.
Milk bowel contents back to the stomach for aspiration if the bowel is very distended.
Wash out and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Keep the nasogastric tube on drainage until bowel function returns.
Monitor fluid balance and electrolytes.
Mobilise early with thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
red_flags: Peritonitis or fever suggesting a missed enterotomy.
Return of obstructive symptoms.
Wound infection or burst abdomen.

indications: Cancer of the caecum, ascending colon or hepatic flexure
Ileocaecal tuberculosis with obstruction or mass
Caecal volvulus or gangrene
Complicated appendix mass or caecal perforation
contraindications: Unfit for major surgery
Widespread metastatic disease where a bypass or stent may be better, after multidisciplinary review
Unstable patient where an ileostomy without anastomosis is safer
equipment: Absorbable sutures or staplers for anastomosis
steps: Confirm identity, consent and staging, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia with prophylactic antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol, and insert a catheter.
Perform a midline or transverse laparotomy and check the liver and peritoneum for spread.
Mobilise the right colon by dividing the lateral peritoneal attachment.
Lift the colon medially, protecting the right ureter, gonadal vessels and duodenum.
Mobilise the hepatic flexure and separate the omentum as needed.
Divide and ligate the ileocolic and right colic vessels, and the right branch of the middle colic for cancer, close to their origin.
Divide the terminal ileum and transverse colon at the planned margins.
Join the ileum to the transverse colon with a hand-sewn or stapled anastomosis.
Check the anastomosis is well perfused and tension-free, and close the mesenteric defect.
Wash out and close the abdomen.
Send the specimen for histology with lymph nodes.
aftercare: Start oral fluids early under an enhanced recovery approach where suitable.
Monitor fluid balance, bowel function and wound.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Discuss histology at the multidisciplinary meeting and plan chemotherapy if needed.
red_flags: Fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain or peritonitis around days 3-7, suggesting anastomotic leak.
Prolonged ileus or vomiting.
Wound infection or burst abdomen.
Bleeding per rectum.

Perform a midline laparotomy and check the liver and peritoneum for spread.
Mobilise the descending colon by dividing the lateral peritoneal attachment.
Identify and protect the left ureter and gonadal vessels.
Mobilise the splenic flexure carefully to avoid splenic injury.
Divide the left colic vessels, or the inferior mesenteric vessels for cancer, close to their origin.
Divide the colon at the planned margins.
Join the colon ends with a hand-sewn or stapled anastomosis.
Check the anastomosis is well perfused and tension-free.
Wash out and close the abdomen.
Send the specimen for histology with lymph nodes.
aftercare: Start oral fluids early where suitable.
Monitor fluid balance, bowel function and wound.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Discuss histology at the multidisciplinary meeting.
red_flags: Fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain or peritonitis suggesting anastomotic leak.

Prolonged ileus.
Wound infection.

indications: Sigmoid volvulus with gangrene or perforation
Sigmoid volvulus that cannot be decompressed endoscopically or with a rectal tube
Elective resection after successful decompression to prevent recurrence
contraindications: Unstable patient with gangrenous bowel, where a Hartmann's procedure is safer than anastomosis
Unfit for surgery, after senior review of decompression and other options
equipment: Absorbable sutures or staplers for anastomosis
steps: Confirm identity, consent and indication, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate, insert a nasogastric tube and catheter, and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and open the abdomen through a lower or full midline incision.
Deliver the twisted sigmoid loop carefully and assess viability.
Untwist the loop if viable and decompress it through a rectal tube passed by an assistant.
If gangrenous, avoid untwisting before clamping, to reduce release of toxins into the circulation.
Divide the sigmoid mesentery, ligating vessels close to the bowel for benign disease.
Divide the bowel at healthy, well-perfused levels.
Join the ends with a primary anastomosis if the patient is stable and the bowel healthy, otherwise perform a Hartmann's procedure.
Check for other gangrenous bowel, including ileosigmoid knotting.
Wash out and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Keep the nasogastric tube on drainage until bowel function returns.
Monitor fluid balance, vital signs and electrolytes closely.
Mobilise early with thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Review histology.
red_flags: Fever, peritonitis or tachycardia suggesting anastomotic leak.
Shock or low urine output.
Dusky or retracted stoma if a Hartmann's was done.
Wound infection or burst abdomen.

indications: Perforated diverticulitis with purulent or faecal peritonitis
Gangrenous sigmoid volvulus in an unstable patient
Obstructing or perforated rectosigmoid cancer where anastomosis is unsafe
Rectosigmoid trauma with heavy contamination
contraindications: Stable patient with healthy bowel where primary anastomosis is safe
equipment: Linear stapler or sutures to close the rectal stump
Non-absorbable marking sutures for the stump
steps: Confirm identity, consent and stoma site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Resuscitate, insert a nasogastric tube and catheter, and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia, position in lithotomy-Trendelenburg if possible and perform a midline laparotomy.
Wash out contamination and identify the diseased segment.
Mobilise the sigmoid colon, protecting the left ureter.
Divide the mesentery and the bowel above and below the diseased segment.
Close the rectal stump with a stapler or two layers of sutures and mark it with long non-absorbable sutures.
Mobilise the descending colon enough to reach the abdominal wall without tension.
Bring the proximal end out through a trephine in the left iliac fossa at the marked site.
Wash out and close the abdomen.
Mature the end colostomy by suturing it to the skin, and apply a stoma bag.
aftercare: Check stoma colour and output daily.
Refer to a stoma nurse or trained nurse for stoma care teaching.
Monitor fluid balance and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Plan reversal after 3-6 months if the patient recovers well.
red_flags: Dark, black or retracted stoma.
No stoma output with vomiting or distension.
Pelvic pain, fever or rectal discharge suggesting rectal stump leak.
Peristomal skin breakdown.

indications: Patient recovered from a previous Hartmann's procedure who wishes to have continuity restored
contraindications: Unfit for major surgery
Residual or recurrent cancer
Poor anal sphincter function
Less than about 3 months since the original operation, unless senior decision
equipment: Circular stapler and sizers if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent and that the rectal stump and remaining colon were checked by contrast study or endoscopy.
Give bowel preparation per local protocol.
Complete the safety checklist and time-out and give general anaesthesia with prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy-Trendelenburg and insert a urinary catheter.
Take down the colostomy by dissecting it free from the abdominal wall.
Perform a midline laparotomy and divide adhesions to find the rectal stump, using the marking sutures and a sigmoidoscope.
Mobilise the proximal colon, including the splenic flexure if needed, to reach the pelvis without tension.
Join the colon to the rectal stump with a circular stapler or a hand-sewn anastomosis.
Test the anastomosis for leaks by filling the pelvis with saline and insufflating air through the rectum.
Consider a covering loop ileostomy for low or difficult anastomoses.
Close the old stoma site and the abdomen.
aftercare: Start oral intake early and monitor bowel function.
Mobilise early with thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Expect frequent bowel actions at first.
red_flags: Fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain or peritonitis suggesting anastomotic leak.
Bleeding per rectum.
No bowel action with distension.
Wound infection at the old stoma site.

indications: Cancer of the upper or middle rectum or rectosigmoid
Selected lower rectal cancer where the sphincter can be preserved
contraindications: Tumour involving the anal sphincter
Poor sphincter function
Unfit for major surgery

steps: Confirm identity, consent, staging, neoadjuvant treatment and stoma site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia with prophylactic antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol, catheterise and position in lithotomy-Trendelenburg.
Perform a midline laparotomy and check the liver and peritoneum for spread.
Mobilise the sigmoid and descending colon, and the splenic flexure as needed, protecting the left ureter.
Divide the inferior mesenteric vessels close to their origin.
Perform total mesorectal excision in the plane outside the mesorectal fascia, protecting the pelvic nerves.
Divide the rectum below the tumour with an adequate distal margin.
Join the colon to the rectum with a circular stapler or a hand-sewn anastomosis.
Test the anastomosis for leaks.
Create a covering loop ileostomy for low anastomoses or after radiotherapy.
Place a pelvic drain and close the abdomen.
Check the specimen for completeness of the mesorectum and send for histology.
aftercare: Monitor fluid balance, stoma output and bowel function.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Teach stoma care if an ileostomy was made.
Discuss histology at the multidisciplinary meeting.
Explain low anterior resection syndrome and bladder or sexual function changes.
red_flags: Fever, pelvic pain, peritonitis or rectal discharge suggesting anastomotic leak.
High ileostomy output with dehydration.
Urinary retention or difficulty passing urine.
Bleeding per rectum or from the drain.

indications: Low rectal cancer involving or very close to the anal sphincter
Anal canal cancer after failed chemoradiotherapy
Poor sphincter function with low rectal cancer
contraindications: Unfit for major surgery
Disseminated disease, unless done for symptom control after multidisciplinary review
equipment: Major laparotomy set with deep pelvic retractors and long instruments
steps: Confirm identity, consent, staging and stoma site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia with prophylactic antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol, catheterise and position in lithotomy-Trendelenburg.
Close the anus with a purse-string suture.
Perform a midline laparotomy and check the liver and peritoneum for spread.
Mobilise the sigmoid colon, protect the left ureter and divide the inferior mesenteric vessels.
Perform total mesorectal excision down to the pelvic floor, protecting the pelvic nerves.
Divide the sigmoid colon and bring the proximal end out as an end colostomy in the left iliac fossa.
Through an elliptical perineal incision around the anus, dissect through the ischioanal fat and levator muscles to join the abdominal dissection.
Remove the specimen through the perineum, avoiding perforation of the tumour.
Secure haemostasis in the pelvis and place drains.
Close the perineal wound in layers, using a flap if the defect is large and expertise is available.
Close the abdomen and mature the colostomy.
aftercare: Check stoma colour and output daily and teach stoma care.
Care for the perineal wound and avoid prolonged sitting at first.
Remove the catheter after several days and check voiding.
Discuss histology at the multidisciplinary meeting.
red_flags: Perineal wound breakdown, discharge or abscess.
Dark or retracted stoma.
Urinary retention or sexual dysfunction.
Pelvic bleeding with falling blood pressure.

indications: Large bowel obstruction from an unresectable or distal tumour
Anorectal malformation or Hirschsprung disease in children before definitive surgery
Complex perianal sepsis, fistula or trauma needing faecal diversion
Protection of a distal anastomosis or repair
contraindications: Situation where definitive resection or stenting is safer and available
equipment: Stoma rod or bridge for loop colostomy
Stoma appliance sized for the patient
steps: Confirm identity, consent and stoma site marking with the patient sitting and standing, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general or regional anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Make a circular skin incision at the marked site, or perform a laparotomy if needed.
Incise the rectus sheath in a cruciate fashion and split the muscle to make a trephine admitting two fingers.
Open the peritoneum and identify the correct segment of colon, using the taenia and omentum and confirming direction for loop stomas.
Bring the colon through the trephine without tension or twisting.
For a loop colostomy, pass a rod under the bowel and open it along the taenia.
For an end colostomy, close or bring out the distal end as planned.
Close any laparotomy wound before maturing the stoma.
Suture the bowel edge to the skin with absorbable sutures.
Check the stoma is pink and fit a stoma bag.
aftercare: Check stoma colour and output daily.
Teach the patient or parents stoma care and bag changing before discharge.
Remove a loop rod after 5-7 days if used.
Refer to stoma support and plan closure when appropriate.
red_flags: Dark, black or retracted stoma.
No output with vomiting or distension.
Prolapse, herniation or bleeding of the stoma.
Peristomal skin breakdown or abscess.

indications: Loop colostomy no longer needed after healing of the distal repair or definitive surgery

contraindications: Distal obstruction, leak or unhealed repair on distal contrast study or examination

Active peristomal infection
equipment: Absorbable sutures for bowel repair or anastomosis
steps: Confirm identity, consent and that the distal bowel is healthy and patent on contrast study or examination.
Give bowel preparation of the distal limb per local protocol.
Complete the safety checklist and time-out and give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Make an elliptical incision around the stoma at the mucocutaneous junction.
Dissect the colon free from the skin, fat, rectus sheath and peritoneum.
Trim the edges back to healthy bowel.
Close the defect transversely in one or two layers, or resect and anastomose if the bowel is damaged.
Check the repair is patent, well perfused and watertight.
Return the bowel to the abdomen.
Close the rectus sheath and loosely close the skin, or use purse-string closure to reduce infection.
aftercare: Start oral intake when bowel sounds return.
Monitor for bowel action and abdominal signs.
Care for the wound, as infection is common.
Continue anal dilatation or bowel management in children as planned.
red_flags: Fever, peritonitis or faecal discharge from the wound suggesting leak.
Vomiting and distension without bowel action.
Wound infection.
Incisional hernia at the old stoma site later.

indications: Protection of a low colorectal or ileal anastomosis

Necrotising enterocolitis or neonatal bowel pathology needing diversion

Ileostomy appliance sized for the patient
steps: Confirm identity, consent and stoma site marking, and complete the safety checklist and time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Make a circular skin incision at the marked site, usually in the right iliac fossa.
Incise the rectus sheath and split the muscle to make a trephine.
Select the loop of ileum and mark the proximal and distal limbs.
Bring the ileum through the trephine without tension or twisting.
For a loop ileostomy, pass a rod under the loop and open the distal side of the bowel.
For an end ileostomy, bring out the divided end of the ileum.
Close any laparotomy wound first.
Evert the proximal limb to form a spout and suture it to the skin.
Check the stoma is pink and fit an ileostomy bag.
aftercare: Check stoma colour and measure output daily.
Replace fluid and electrolytes, as high output causes dehydration quickly.
Teach the patient or parents stoma care and skin protection.
Plan closure when the distal bowel has healed.
red_flags: Stoma output high enough to cause dehydration, weakness or low urine output.
Dark or retracted stoma.
No output with vomiting or distension.
Peristomal skin breakdown.

indications: Symptomatic gallstones
Acute or recurrent cholecystitis
Gallstone pancreatitis after recovery
Gallbladder polyp or suspected gallbladder cancer
Conversion from laparoscopic cholecystectomy
contraindications: Unfit for general anaesthesia
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Suspected advanced gallbladder cancer needing specialist resection
equipment: Cholangiogram catheter and contrast if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, fasting, blood group and save, and ultrasound findings.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia and position the patient supine.
Prepare and drape the abdomen and make a right subcostal or upper midline incision.
Pack the bowel away and retract the liver and duodenum to expose the gallbladder.
Dissect Calot's triangle to achieve the critical view of safety before dividing any structure.
If the anatomy stays unclear, do not divide any structure; go fundus-first or do a subtotal cholecystectomy and call a senior surgeon.
Perform an intraoperative cholangiogram through the cystic duct, before dividing it, if stones in the duct are suspected.
Ligate and divide the cystic artery and cystic duct close to the gallbladder.
Dissect the gallbladder off the liver bed and remove it.
Secure haemostasis in the liver bed and check for bile leak.
Open the gallbladder on a side table, inspect the mucosa and send it for histology.
Place a drain if there is concern about bleeding or bile leak.
Complete swab and instrument counts and close the wound in layers.
aftercare: Analgesia and early mobilisation
Oral fluids when awake and diet as tolerated
Monitor drain output and character
Chest physiotherapy and incentive spirometry
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol
Review histology at follow-up
red_flags: Jaundice, fever or rising abdominal pain after surgery
Bile in the drain or wound
Signs of haemorrhage or shock
Unclear biliary anatomy at operation: stop and call a senior surgeon

steps: Confirm identity, consent including possible conversion to open, fasting and imaging.
Check the laparoscopic equipment and gas supply before induction.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia, insert a urinary catheter if needed, and prepare and drape the abdomen.
Establish pneumoperitoneum by open (Hasson) or Veress technique and insert the camera port.
Insert the working ports under direct vision.
Retract the gallbladder fundus cephalad and the infundibulum laterally.
Dissect Calot's triangle to obtain the critical view of safety.
Clip and divide the cystic artery and cystic duct.
Dissect the gallbladder off the liver bed with diathermy and check haemostasis.
Convert to open surgery at any point if anatomy is unclear, bleeding is uncontrolled or progress stalls.
Remove the gallbladder in a retrieval bag through the umbilical or epigastric port.
Release the gas, close the fascia at ports of 10 mm or larger, and close the skin.
aftercare: Analgesia including for shoulder-tip pain
Early mobilisation and oral intake
Usually discharged within 24 to 48 hours
Port-site wound care
Review histology at follow-up
red_flags: Increasing abdominal pain, fever or jaundice after day one
Persistent vomiting or abdominal distension
Tachycardia or hypotension
Bile or blood from a port site

indications: Common bile duct stones not cleared by endoscopy
Duct stones found at cholecystectomy where ERCP is unavailable
Obstructive jaundice from stones
contraindications: Unfit for general anaesthesia

T-tube (12–16 Fr) and fine absorbable sutures
steps: Confirm identity, consent, fasting, clotting status and blood availability.
Correct coagulopathy before surgery per local protocol.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia, open the abdomen and perform cholecystectomy if the gallbladder is present.
Mobilise the duodenum (Kocher manoeuvre) and expose the supraduodenal bile duct.
Place stay sutures and make a longitudinal choledochotomy.
Remove stones with forceps, irrigation and balloon catheter, and check with choledochoscope if available.
Confirm free flow into the duodenum with a dilator or cholangiogram.
Close the duct over a T-tube or by primary closure with fine absorbable sutures.
Perform a completion cholangiogram through the T-tube if available.
Place a drain near the duct, complete counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Record T-tube and drain output daily
Monitor liver function and jaundice
T-tube cholangiogram before clamping and removal, usually after 10 to 14 days
Fluid and electrolyte balance
red_flags: Bile peritonitis or rising abdominal pain
Fever with rigors suggesting cholangitis
T-tube dislodged before tract has formed
Persistent high T-tube output or rising bilirubin

steps: Confirm identity, consent and cross-matched blood; in elective cases confirm vaccinations given at least two weeks before.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia and insert a nasogastric tube.
Open the abdomen through an upper midline or left subcostal incision.
In trauma, pack all quadrants and control bleeding by manual compression of the splenic hilum.
Mobilise the spleen by dividing the lienorenal and splenophrenic ligaments and deliver it into the wound.
Divide the short gastric vessels carefully, avoiding the stomach wall.
Identify the tail of the pancreas, then ligate and divide the splenic artery and vein separately.
Check the splenic bed and stomach for bleeding and injury.
Look for and record accessory spleens.
Place a drain if the pancreatic tail was disturbed, complete counts and close.
aftercare: Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus if not done before surgery
Lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis advice per local protocol, especially in children
Malaria prophylaxis and bed nets in endemic areas
Monitor platelet count for thrombocytosis
Give a splenectomy card or written advice
red_flags: Fever or rigors at any time after splenectomy: urgent antibiotics and review
Drain output rising or bloody, or signs of shock

indications: Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic stricture

Duodenal obstruction
contraindications: Unfit for general anaesthesia

steps: Confirm identity, consent and fasting; decompress the stomach and correct fluids and electrolytes before surgery.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia and open the abdomen through an upper midline incision.
Assess the cause of obstruction and take biopsy if malignancy is suspected.
Select a jejunal loop near the duodenojejunal flexure.
Bring the loop to the dependent part of the stomach, antecolic or retrocolic.
Place non-crushing clamps and fashion a two-layer or single-layer side-to-side anastomosis.
Check the anastomosis for patency and leaks.
Position the nasogastric tube and close the mesenteric defect if retrocolic.
Complete counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Nasogastric drainage until output falls
Fluids and electrolytes, then graded oral feeding
Nutritional support
Review histology and plan oncology referral if malignant

Uncontrolled gastric bleeding

steps: Confirm identity, consent, staging investigations, nutrition and cross-matched blood.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia and open the abdomen through an upper midline incision.
Assess resectability, including liver and peritoneum, before committing to resection.
Mobilise the stomach by dividing the omentum and ligating the gastric vessels.
Perform lymph node dissection appropriate to the disease.
Divide the duodenum and close or prepare it for anastomosis.
Divide the stomach (partial) or oesophagus (total) with adequate margins.
Restore continuity by Billroth I, Billroth II or Roux-en-Y reconstruction.
Check anastomoses for leaks and haemostasis.
Place a feeding jejunostomy if prolonged poor intake is expected.
Place drains, complete counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: High dependency monitoring in the first 24 to 48 hours
Nasogastric drainage and early jejunal feeding if placed
Fluid, electrolyte and nutritional support
Long-term vitamin B12 and iron replacement after total gastrectomy
Review histology and oncology referral

steps: Confirm identity, consent, fasting and the plan for long-term feeding.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Give general or local anaesthesia and make a short left upper midline or left paramedian incision.
Identify the stomach and choose a site on the anterior wall of the body away from the pylorus.
Place two concentric purse-string sutures.
Open the stomach inside the purse-strings and insert the tube.
Tie the purse-strings to invert the gastric wall around the tube.
Bring the tube out through a separate stab incision in the left upper quadrant.
Fix the stomach to the anterior abdominal wall around the tube exit.
Close the wound and secure the tube to the skin.
aftercare: Start water then feeds through the tube after 24 hours if bowel sounds present
Flush the tube after every feed and medicine
Clean the stoma site daily
Teach the patient or carer tube care and blended feeding

Fever, wound redness or discharge

steps: Confirm identity, consent and the indication for distal feeding.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Identify a jejunal loop about 20 to 30 cm from the duodenojejunal flexure.
Place a purse-string suture on the antimesenteric border.
Make an enterotomy and pass the tube distally into the jejunum.
Tie the purse-string and bury the tube in a short serosal tunnel (Witzel).
Bring the tube out through a separate stab incision in the left abdomen.
Fix the jejunum to the abdominal wall around the exit to prevent leakage and volvulus.
Flush the tube to confirm free flow and secure it to the skin.
aftercare: Start slow continuous feeds and increase gradually
Flush with water regularly to prevent blockage
Daily site care
Watch for diarrhoea and abdominal distension
red_flags: Abdominal pain, distension or vomiting during feeds
Leak of feed around the tube or peritonism
Tube dislodged or blocked

indications: Resectable carcinoma of the pancreatic head
Periampullary or distal bile duct carcinoma
Duodenal carcinoma
Selected benign or premalignant pancreatic head tumours
contraindications: Distant metastases or major vascular encasement
Poor performance status or unfit for major surgery
No HDU or ICU support available (refer to a specialist centre)
equipment: Major hepatobiliary set with fixed retractor
Fine absorbable sutures for pancreatic and biliary anastomoses
steps: Confirm identity, consent, staging imaging, biliary drainage status, nutrition and blood.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia with invasive monitoring and open the abdomen.
Exclude metastatic disease and assess resectability before any irreversible step.
Perform a Kocher manoeuvre and assess the superior mesenteric vein and portal vein.
Perform cholecystectomy and divide the common hepatic duct.
Divide the stomach or duodenum, the jejunum beyond the ligament of Treitz and the pancreatic neck.
Dissect the uncinate process off the superior mesenteric vessels and remove the specimen.
Reconstruct with pancreatic, biliary and gastric or duodenal anastomoses to the jejunum.
Secure haemostasis, place drains near the pancreatic and biliary anastomoses and close.
aftercare: ICU or HDU care in the early postoperative period
Monitor drain output and drain amylase
Glucose monitoring and pancreatic enzyme replacement when eating
Nutritional support including enteral feeding
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol
red_flags: Pancreatic fistula: high-amylase or cloudy drain fluid
Bleeding from drains or haematemesis, especially after day five
Delayed gastric emptying with persistent vomiting
Sepsis or rising abdominal pain

indications: Ruptured or impending rupture of liver abscess
Abscess not responding to antibiotics and needle or catheter drainage
Left lobe abscess at risk of pericardial rupture where percutaneous drainage is not possible
Multiloculated or thick-pus abscess
contraindications: Uncomplicated amoebic abscess responding to medical treatment
Abscess suitable for ultrasound-guided aspiration or catheter drainage
steps: Confirm identity, consent and ultrasound findings including abscess size and site.
Resuscitate with fluids and start antibiotics and amoebicide per local protocol.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and induce general anaesthesia.
Open the abdomen through a right subcostal or upper midline incision.
Protect the peritoneal cavity with packs around the abscess.
Aspirate the abscess with a needle to confirm pus and send samples for microscopy and culture.
Open the abscess cavity and evacuate pus and necrotic material with suction.
Break down loculations gently with a finger and irrigate with warm saline.
Lavage the peritoneal cavity thoroughly if the abscess had ruptured.
Place large drains into the cavity and bring them out through separate stab incisions.
Complete counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Continue antibiotics and amoebicide per local protocol
Record drain output daily and remove when output is minimal
Repeat ultrasound to confirm resolution
Nutritional support
red_flags: Persistent fever or rising white count
Bile in the drain
Chest pain or breathlessness suggesting pleural or pericardial spread
Signs of generalised peritonitis

indications: Third- or fourth-degree haemorrhoids
Haemorrhoids failing banding or other office treatment
Mixed internal and external haemorrhoids with symptoms
Thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoids
contraindications: Inflammatory bowel disease of the anorectum
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Rectal bleeding not yet investigated for cancer where indicated
Portal hypertension with rectal varices
equipment: Anorectal set with proctoscope and anal retractor
steps: Confirm identity, consent and that rectal bleeding has been investigated where indicated.
Give bowel preparation with an enema per local protocol.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give spinal, caudal or general anaesthesia and place the patient in lithotomy position.
Examine the anal canal and identify the main haemorrhoidal cushions.
Grasp the external skin and internal component of each haemorrhoid with forceps.
Dissect each haemorrhoid off the internal sphincter with scissors or diathermy.
Transfix and ligate the pedicle and excise the haemorrhoid.
Preserve skin and mucosal bridges between excision sites to prevent stenosis.
Check haemostasis and apply a light anal dressing.
aftercare: Regular analgesia and stool softeners
Warm sitz baths two to three times daily
High-fibre diet and plenty of fluids
Check the patient passes urine before discharge
red_flags: Heavy rectal bleeding or passage of clots
Unable to pass urine
Fever, increasing pain or perineal swelling
Difficulty passing stool or narrowing weeks later

indications: Symptomatic first- to third-degree internal haemorrhoids
Bleeding internal haemorrhoids failing conservative treatment
contraindications: External haemorrhoids or band site below the dentate line
Anticoagulation or bleeding disorder
Anorectal sepsis or inflammatory bowel disease
Immunosuppression (higher risk of pelvic sepsis)
equipment: Haemorrhoid band ligator (Barron or suction type)
steps: Confirm identity and explain the procedure, expected discomfort and risk of bleeding.
Obtain verbal consent and check the patient is not on anticoagulants.
Place the patient in left lateral position and perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the lubricated proctoscope and identify the internal haemorrhoids.
Grasp or suction the haemorrhoid above the dentate line and check the patient feels no sharp pain.
Release the band onto the base of the haemorrhoid.
Band no more than two or three haemorrhoids in one session.
Withdraw the proctoscope and observe the patient for vasovagal symptoms before discharge.
aftercare: Simple analgesia for dull ache
Stool softeners, high-fibre diet and fluids
Expect the banded tissue to fall off in 7 to 10 days with slight bleeding
Review in 6 to 8 weeks for repeat banding if needed
red_flags: Severe pain immediately after banding: remove the band
Fever, severe pelvic pain or urinary retention (pelvic sepsis): return urgently
Heavy rectal bleeding

indications: Chronic anal fissure failing medical treatment
Recurrent anal fissure
contraindications: Pre-existing faecal incontinence or weak sphincter
Fissure from Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, HIV ulcer or cancer
Low-pressure fissure (for example after childbirth)
equipment: Anorectal set with Eisenhammer or Parks retractor
steps: Confirm identity, consent and that atypical causes of fissure have been considered.
Explain the small risk of incontinence to flatus or stool.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general, spinal or local anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Examine under anaesthesia to confirm the fissure and exclude other pathology.
Insert the anal retractor and palpate the intersphincteric groove laterally.
Divide the internal sphincter from its lower edge up to the height of the dentate line or fissure apex.
Avoid dividing the external sphincter.
Apply pressure for haemostasis and close or leave the small wound open.
Excise a sentinel tag or fibrous polyp if present and send it for histology if atypical.
aftercare: Analgesia and stool softeners
Sitz baths
High-fibre diet
Review at 6 weeks for healing and continence
red_flags: Bleeding or perianal haematoma
Perianal abscess or fistula formation
New incontinence to stool or flatus
Fissure not healed at review

indications: Low intersphincteric or low trans-sphincteric anal fistula
Seton drainage of high or complex fistula
Recurrent perianal sepsis from a fistula
contraindications: High fistula crossing much of the external sphincter (fistulotomy alone unsafe)
Active Crohn's proctitis without specialist input
Uncontrolled acute sepsis needing drainage first
equipment: Hydrogen peroxide or dilute methylene blue to find the internal opening
Seton material (silastic loop or non-absorbable suture)
steps: Confirm identity, consent and any imaging; explain the risk of recurrence and incontinence.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and place the patient in lithotomy or prone jack-knife position.
Examine under anaesthesia and identify the external opening.
Identify the internal opening gently with a probe or by injecting dye through the external opening.
Assess how much sphincter lies above the track.
For a low fistula, lay open the track over the probe and curette the granulation tissue.
For a high or uncertain fistula, place a loose draining seton instead of dividing muscle.
Marsupialise the wound edges if needed and send tissue for histology.
Check haemostasis and apply a light dressing.
aftercare: Analgesia and stool softeners
Sitz baths after each bowel action
Regular wound review until healed from the base
Seton review and planned definitive surgery if a seton was placed
red_flags: Bleeding from the wound
Fever or new perianal swelling
Incontinence of stool
Wound not healing after several weeks (consider TB, Crohn's or cancer)

indications: Perianal abscess
Ischiorectal abscess
Intersphincteric abscess
contraindications: Supralevator abscess needing imaging and specialist drainage route
Uncorrected coagulopathy (correct first)
steps: Confirm identity and consent and check for diabetes or immunosuppression.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general, spinal or ketamine anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Examine under anaesthesia to define the abscess and any fistula.
Make a cruciate or radial incision over the point of maximum fluctuance close to the anal verge.
Drain pus, take a culture swab and break down loculations with a finger.
Excise skin edges to create a wide opening that will not close early.
Look for a fistula gently but do not probe forcefully.
Lightly pack or leave the cavity open to drain and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Analgesia
Remove pack after 24 hours and start sitz baths
Daily wound care until healed
Check blood glucose and HIV status if not known
Follow-up to check for fistula
red_flags: Spreading redness, crepitus or black skin (Fournier's gangrene)
Fever or sepsis after drainage
Recurrent abscess or persistent discharge suggesting fistula

indications: Chronic or recurrent pilonidal sinus
Pilonidal sinus with recurrent abscesses
contraindications: Acute pilonidal abscess (drain first)
Uncontrolled diabetes or poor wound-healing state not optimised
steps: Confirm identity and consent, including options of open healing or flap closure.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Give anaesthesia and place the patient prone with buttocks taped apart.
Shave the area and inject dye into the sinus openings to mark the tracks.
Excise all sinus tracks and pits down to the presacral fascia while saving healthy tissue.
Secure haemostasis.
Leave the wound open, or close it off the midline with an advancement or rotation flap.
Place a suction drain under a flap if used.
Apply a pressure dressing.
aftercare: Daily dressings if left open until healed
Keep the area clean and dry
Regular hair removal around the natal cleft
Avoid prolonged sitting for two weeks after flap closure
red_flags: Fever, wound redness or pus
Wound breakdown after flap closure
Recurrence of a discharging pit

indications: Full-thickness rectal prolapse
Recurrent prolapse after previous repair
Incarcerated prolapse not reducible
contraindications: Unfit for chosen approach (choose perineal procedure for frail patients)
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Anorectal or laparotomy set depending on approach
Mesh if abdominal rectopexy is planned
Thiersch wire or tape if used
steps: Confirm identity, consent, bowel preparation and the chosen approach.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Give anaesthesia and position in lithotomy or prone for perineal approach, or supine for abdominal approach.
For Delorme repair, strip the mucosa off the prolapse and plicate the muscle wall before suturing the mucosa.
For perineal rectosigmoidectomy, resect the full-thickness prolapse and form a coloanal anastomosis.
For abdominal rectopexy, mobilise the rectum and fix it to the sacral promontory with sutures or mesh.
For a Thiersch procedure, place an encircling suture around the anus tied over a finger.
Check haemostasis and the anastomosis or repair.
Close the wound and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Analgesia and stool softeners
Avoid straining; treat constipation
Monitor for urinary retention
Follow-up for recurrence and continence
red_flags: Rectal bleeding or pelvic sepsis
Fever or abdominal pain suggesting anastomotic leak
Early recurrence of prolapse

indications: Acute rectal prolapse that is reducible
Prolapse in children with diarrhoea, constipation or worms
contraindications: Gangrenous or ulcerated prolapse (needs surgery)
Suspected intussusception through the anus (child unwell, prolapse with a groove you can enter)
equipment: Granulated sugar to reduce oedema if needed
steps: Confirm identity and explain the procedure to the patient or carer and gain verbal consent.
Check the prolapse is pink and viable and that you cannot pass a finger alongside it (to exclude intussusception).
Position the patient knee-chest or left lateral, or a child prone over the carer's lap.
If the prolapse is swollen, apply granulated sugar and wait for the oedema to settle.
Lubricate the prolapse and apply steady gentle pressure, reducing the tip first.
Confirm full reduction with a gentle digital examination.
Strap the buttocks together with tape for a few hours if prolapse recurs immediately.
Treat the underlying cause such as constipation, diarrhoea or worms.
aftercare: Avoid straining and treat constipation
Deworming and nutrition review in children
Teach the carer to reduce recurrent prolapse
Surgical referral for recurrent or full-thickness adult prolapse
red_flags: Prolapse cannot be reduced or becomes dark or black
Severe pain, bleeding or fever
Child unwell with vomiting or abdominal pain (consider intussusception)

indications: Healthy granulating wound too large to close
Burns after excision
Large skin loss after trauma or debridement
Chronic ulcers with clean granulation
contraindications: Infected wound or heavy bacterial load (for example streptococcal or pseudomonas)
Exposed bone without periosteum, tendon without paratenon or cartilage
Unfit for anaesthesia or severe anaemia not corrected
equipment: Skin graft knife (Humby or Watson) or dermatome
Graft mesher if available or scalpel for fenestration
Liquid paraffin for the donor site and blade
Paraffin gauze, gauze and crepe bandages
Staples or sutures to secure graft
steps: Confirm identity, consent, haemoglobin and that the wound bed is clean and granulating.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general, spinal or regional anaesthesia and prepare the recipient and donor sites.
Prepare the recipient bed by scraping or excising excess granulation and securing haemostasis.
Lubricate the donor site, usually the thigh, and stretch it flat with boards.
Harvest a thin graft with smooth even strokes of the knife.
Mesh or fenestrate the graft to allow fluid to escape and to expand cover if needed.
Lay the graft on the bed with its raw dermal side down and secure it with staples, sutures or dressings.
Apply a tie-over or pressure dressing to stop movement and prevent haematoma.
Dress the donor site with paraffin gauze and a firm dressing.
Splint the joint if the graft is across it.
aftercare: Keep the grafted area still and elevated
First graft inspection at 3 to 5 days, earlier if smell or fever
Leave the donor dressing for 10 to 14 days unless soaked or smelly
Moisturise healed grafts and protect from sun
Pressure garments and physiotherapy where needed
red_flags: Fever, smell or pus under the dressing
Graft lifted by blood or fluid
Graft turning white or dark and not adherent

indications: Small defects on the face, hands or fingers
Release of contracture where good-quality skin is needed
Defects after excision of skin tumours
contraindications: Poorly vascularised or infected recipient bed
Large defects beyond the donor skin available
Exposed bone, tendon or cartilage without vascular cover
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site marking.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local or general anaesthesia and prepare recipient and donor sites.
Prepare the recipient bed and make a template of the defect.
Mark the template on a donor site such as the groin, postauricular or supraclavicular skin.
Excise the full-thickness graft as an ellipse and close the donor site directly.
Defat the graft completely with fine scissors.
Suture the graft into the defect without tension.
Place a tie-over bolster dressing to keep the graft in contact with the bed.
aftercare: Keep the bolster on for 5 to 7 days
Elevate and rest the part
Massage and moisturise once healed
Remove donor-site sutures at 7 to 14 days
red_flags: Fever, pain or pus under the bolster
Graft dark or blistered after bolster removal
Donor-site bleeding or infection

indications: Defects that cannot be closed directly
Cover of exposed bone, tendon or vessels
Reconstruction after tumour excision
Pressure sore reconstruction
contraindications: Active infection in the defect
Damaged or irradiated local tissue unsuitable for a flap
Smoking or poor vascularity not addressed (relative)
equipment: Plastic surgery set with skin hooks
steps: Confirm identity, consent and the flap plan, and mark the flap with the patient awake if possible.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local or general anaesthesia and prepare the area.
Excise or debride the defect to healthy margins.
Re-check the flap design against the final defect size, keeping a safe length-to-width ratio.
Raise the flap in the correct plane, preserving its blood supply.
Move the flap into the defect by rotation, advancement or transposition without tension.
Close the donor defect directly or with a skin graft.
Check the flap colour and capillary refill before dressing.
Place a drain under large flaps and apply a light, non-compressive dressing.
aftercare: Flap observation for colour, warmth and capillary refill regularly in the first 48 hours
Avoid pressure on the flap and its base
Elevate the part
Remove sutures at 7 to 14 days
red_flags: Flap pale, cold or slow refill (arterial problem)
Flap dusky, purple or swollen (venous congestion)
Haematoma under the flap
Fever or pus

indications: Burn scar contracture limiting joint movement
Neck contracture affecting airway, eating or appearance
Contracture affecting hand function or growth in children
contraindications: Immature, still-active scar (unless function is threatened)
Infected or unhealed wounds in the area
Poor nutrition or anaemia not corrected
steps: Confirm identity and consent, and record joint range of movement before surgery.
Plan the airway with the anaesthetist for neck contractures.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prepare the area and graft donor site.
Mark Z-plasties for narrow bands or an incisional release for broad contractures.
Incise the scar across the line of tension and release until full or near-full movement is achieved.
Protect nerves, vessels and tendons that may be tight or displaced.
