Transpose Z-plasty flaps or cover the defect with skin graft or a local flap.
Apply a bulky dressing and splint the joint in the fully released position.
aftercare: Keep the splint on as instructed, usually for several weeks at night
Physiotherapy to maintain range of movement
Pressure garments and scar massage once healed
Long-term follow-up in growing children
red_flags: Fever, smell or pus from the dressing
Graft or flap failure
Numbness or weakness beyond the operated area
Recurrence of tightness

indications: Circumferential full-thickness burn of a limb with impaired circulation
Circumferential chest or abdominal burn restricting breathing
Rising compartment pressure under eschar
contraindications: Partial-thickness burns that remain pliable
Non-circumferential burns without circulatory compromise
equipment: Doppler or pulse oximeter to check distal flow
steps: Confirm identity and gain consent, or proceed in an emergency if consent cannot be obtained.
Assess distal pulses, capillary refill and oxygen saturation, or chest movement and ventilation.
Give analgesia or sedation; the full-thickness eschar is usually insensate.
Clean the area and mark incision lines along the mid-medial and mid-lateral lines of the limb.
Incise through the eschar only, down to bleeding fat, along the full length of the burn.
For the chest, incise along both anterior axillary lines joined by a costal margin incision.
Extend incisions across joints and into the hand along finger sides if needed.
Re-check pulses or ventilation, and add incisions or consider fasciotomy if not improved.
Control bleeding with pressure or diathermy and dress the wounds.
aftercare: Elevate limbs and recheck circulation hourly
Monitor ventilation after chest escharotomy
Dress as part of the burn wound
Plan excision and grafting
red_flags: Pulses or perfusion do not return (consider fasciotomy)
Persistent bleeding from incision lines
Worsening ventilation or rising airway pressures

indications: Deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns
Burns not expected to heal within 2 to 3 weeks
Granulating burn wounds needing cover
contraindications: Patient not resuscitated or haemodynamically unstable
Blood not available for large excisions
Superficial burns expected to heal on their own
equipment: Skin graft knife or dermatome and mesher
Diathermy and topical haemostatic packs per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, consent, resuscitation status, haemoglobin and blood availability.
Plan the area to excise, usually limited per session to control blood loss.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and keep the theatre warm.
Give general anaesthesia and prepare burn and donor sites.
Apply a tourniquet on limbs where possible.
Excise the burn tangentially in thin layers until punctate bleeding shows a viable bed, or excise to fascia if deep.
Control bleeding with pressure packs and diathermy.
Harvest split-thickness grafts and mesh as needed.
Apply grafts to the excised areas and secure them.
Dress grafts and donor sites and splint joints in a safe position.
aftercare: Monitor haemoglobin and transfuse per protocol
Keep the patient warm and continue nutrition support
Graft check at 3 to 5 days
Physiotherapy and splinting to prevent contracture
Plan further sessions for remaining burns
red_flags: Ongoing bleeding or falling haemoglobin
Hypothermia
Fever, sepsis or graft loss

indications: Necrotising soft-tissue infection
Contaminated or crushed traumatic wounds
Infected wounds with dead tissue
Diabetic foot sepsis
contraindications: None absolute in life-threatening infection; resuscitate in parallel
equipment: Major or minor set depending on extent
Large volumes of saline for irrigation
steps: Confirm identity and consent, including possible amputation or repeat operations.
Resuscitate and start antibiotics per local protocol without delaying surgery for necrotising infection.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prepare widely beyond the affected area.
Open the wound and excise all dead and infected tissue until healthy bleeding tissue is reached.
Test the fascia; easy finger dissection and dishwater fluid suggest necrotising fasciitis.
Send tissue for culture and histology.
Irrigate the wound thoroughly with saline.
Leave the wound open and dress it, planning a second look within 24 to 48 hours.
aftercare: Continue antibiotics and sepsis care
Return to theatre for repeat debridement as needed
Daily wound review and dressing
Control blood glucose and support nutrition
red_flags: Spreading redness, crepitus or new necrosis
Worsening sepsis or shock
Bleeding from the wound

indications: Contaminated wounds left open after initial surgery
War, gunshot or bite wounds after debridement
Laparotomy wounds left open for contamination
contraindications: Ongoing infection or necrosis in the wound
Wound edges cannot be brought together without tension (consider grafting)
steps: Confirm identity and consent.
Inspect the wound at 3 to 5 days to confirm it is clean, with no pus or dead tissue.
Perform the time-out and give local or general anaesthesia.
Clean the wound and freshen the edges if needed.
Irrigate with saline.
Close the skin loosely with interrupted sutures, leaving gaps or a drain if concerned.
Apply a dry dressing.
aftercare: Wound review at 48 hours
Remove sutures at 7 to 14 days
Continue antibiotics only if indicated
red_flags: Redness, pus or wound breakdown: open sutures
Fever or increasing pain

indications: Full-thickness abdominal wound dehiscence (burst abdomen)
Evisceration of bowel through the wound
contraindications: Severe intra-abdominal sepsis where temporary abdominal closure is safer
Unable to close without excessive tension (consider laparostomy)
equipment: Strong slowly-absorbable or non-absorbable looped sutures
Tension sutures and bolsters if used
Mesh or temporary closure device if needed
steps: Cover exposed bowel immediately with warm saline-soaked packs and reassure the patient.
Resuscitate, insert a nasogastric tube and confirm consent.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Induce general anaesthesia and remove old sutures and dead tissue.
Inspect the abdomen for a leak or collection that may have caused the dehiscence.
Wash out the abdomen with warm saline.
Close the abdomen with mass closure using a long suture, with or without tension sutures.
Leave the skin open or loosely closed if contaminated.
Use temporary abdominal closure if tension is too great.
aftercare: Treat the cause such as infection, malnutrition or coughing
Abdominal binder and support when coughing
Nutritional support
Wound care and observation
red_flags: Repeat dehiscence or discharge from wound
Signs of sepsis or anastomotic leak
Breathing difficulty from tight closure

indications: Gunshot wound to a limb or soft tissue needing debridement
Suspected vascular or nerve injury from a gunshot
Retained fragment causing problems
contraindications: Gunshot wound to the abdomen, chest or head needs laparotomy, thoracotomy or neurosurgery instead
Haemodynamic instability needing damage-control resuscitation first
equipment: Major or minor set depending on site
steps: Follow ABCDE trauma assessment and control haemorrhage first.
Confirm identity, consent, tetanus status and X-rays.
Inform police per local regulations and document wounds carefully as medico-legal evidence.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet if a limb wound.
Extend entry and exit wounds along the axis of the limb.
Excise dead muscle, foreign material and loose bone fragments; leave fragments that are deep and harmless.
Explore and repair or ligate injured vessels and tag injured nerves.
Irrigate the wound thoroughly.
Leave the wound open and dressed, planning delayed primary closure.
aftercare: Second look and delayed primary closure at 3 to 5 days
Check distal circulation and neurology
Stabilise fractures by splint or external fixation
Psychological support
red_flags: Loss of distal pulse or rising compartment pressure
Fever, gas gangrene signs or foul smell
Ongoing bleeding

indications: Large open wounds after debridement
Securing skin grafts
Open abdomen management
Chronic wounds slow to heal
contraindications: Untreated osteomyelitis or cancer in the wound
Exposed blood vessels or organs without protective layer
Uncontrolled bleeding
Non-enteric unexplored fistula
equipment: NPWT machine or improvised wall suction with regulator
Suction tubing (or nasogastric tube for improvised system)
steps: Confirm identity, explain the device and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic technique.
Clean and debride the wound and secure haemostasis.
Protect the surrounding skin with a barrier film or hydrocolloid.
Cut the foam or gauze to fit the wound without overlapping onto healthy skin.
Place a protective non-adherent layer over exposed vessels, tendons or bowel.
Cover with adhesive drape, sealing well beyond the wound edge.
Make a small hole in the drape and attach the tubing pad or embedded tube.
Connect to suction and set the pressure per protocol, usually -75 to -125 mmHg.
Confirm the dressing collapses and holds a seal without leaks.
aftercare: Change the dressing every 48 to 72 hours
Check the seal and canister regularly
Record output volume and character
Do not leave the dressing off suction for more than two hours
red_flags: Fresh blood in the tubing or canister: stop suction and review
Foul smell, fever or spreading redness
Loss of seal not fixable
Pain at the wound not controlled

indications: Pyomyositis with pus collection (suppurative stage)
Muscle abscess confirmed by ultrasound or aspiration
contraindications: Early invasive stage without pus (treat with antibiotics)
Psoas abscess where guided percutaneous drainage is available and suitable
equipment: Minor or major set depending on depth
steps: Confirm identity, consent and ultrasound findings.
Perform the time-out and give antibiotics per local protocol.
Give general or ketamine anaesthesia and prepare the area.
Aspirate with a needle to confirm pus and its depth.
Incise the skin along the line of the muscle fibres over the abscess.
Split the muscle bluntly and open the abscess cavity.
Drain pus, send it for culture and break down loculations with a finger.
Irrigate with saline and place a drain.
Close loosely or leave open and dress.
aftercare: Continue antibiotics per culture results
Daily dressings and drain removal when output stops
Check for other abscesses, HIV and sickle cell status
Physiotherapy to restore movement
red_flags: Persistent fever or new swelling elsewhere
Septic shock
Joint pain or swelling (septic arthritis)

indications: Carbuncle with multiple sinuses and necrosis
Carbuncle not responding to antibiotics
Large carbuncle in a diabetic patient
contraindications: Early carbuncle without necrosis responding to antibiotics
Facial carbuncle in the danger triangle (manage medically and refer)
steps: Confirm identity and consent and check blood glucose.
Perform the time-out and give anaesthesia.
Clean the area and make a cruciate incision over the carbuncle.
Excise the necrotic tissue and the roof of the sinuses (saucerisation).
Remove all slough down to healthy bleeding tissue.
Take a swab or tissue for culture.
Pack the wound lightly and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Daily dressing until healed
Tight glucose control and diabetes review
Antibiotics per local protocol and culture
Consider skin graft for large wounds
red_flags: Spreading redness or fever
Very high or low blood glucose
Wound not improving in a week

indications: Symptomatic varicose veins with saphenous reflux
Venous ulcer or skin changes from superficial reflux
Recurrent thrombophlebitis or bleeding varices
contraindications: Deep vein thrombosis or deep venous obstruction
Peripheral arterial disease
Pregnancy
equipment: Varicose vein set with vein strippers
Doppler or duplex ultrasound for mapping
steps: Mark the varicose veins with the patient standing and confirm reflux by Doppler or duplex.
Confirm identity, consent and side.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and position with the legs slightly elevated.
Make a groin incision and identify the saphenofemoral junction.
Ligate and divide all tributaries and ligate the great saphenous vein flush with the femoral vein.
Strip the great saphenous vein to just below the knee.
Remove marked varicosities through small stab incisions (avulsions).
Close the groin wound and apply compression bandages from foot to thigh.
aftercare: Walk early and often
Keep compression on for one to two weeks
Elevate legs when resting
Thromboprophylaxis per local risk assessment
red_flags: Calf pain or swelling suggesting deep vein thrombosis
Groin swelling or bleeding
Numbness along the shin or foot
Chest pain or breathlessness

indications: Acute limb ischaemia from embolism
Acute thrombosis of a recently patent artery
contraindications: Irreversible limb ischaemia (fixed mottling, rigid muscles) - consider amputation
Patient too unwell for any intervention (palliation)
equipment: Vascular set with vascular clamps and slings
steps: Confirm identity, consent and the time of onset, and assess limb viability.
Give systemic anticoagulation as soon as the diagnosis is made per local protocol.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local or general anaesthesia and expose the common femoral or brachial artery bifurcation.
Control the artery and its branches with slings and clamps.
Make a transverse arteriotomy.
Pass the balloon catheter up and down each vessel, inflate gently and withdraw clot until good inflow and backflow.
Flush the vessels with heparinised saline.
Close the arteriotomy with fine vascular sutures.
Check distal pulses or Doppler signals and consider fasciotomy if ischaemia was prolonged.
aftercare: Hourly limb checks for colour, warmth, pulses and sensation
Continue anticoagulation per protocol
Look for the source of embolism, such as atrial fibrillation
Monitor urine output and potassium for reperfusion injury
red_flags: Return of limb pain, pallor or loss of pulses
Tense, painful calf (compartment syndrome)
Wound bleeding or haematoma
Dark urine or reduced urine output

indications: Penetrating or blunt arterial injury with hard signs
Pulsatile bleeding or expanding haematoma
Distal ischaemia after trauma
Iatrogenic arterial injury
contraindications: Unsalvageable limb (primary amputation may be safer)
Patient in extremis (damage control with shunt or ligation)
equipment: Vascular set with clamps and slings
Temporary shunt (or sterile nasogastric or feeding tube)
steps: Control bleeding with direct pressure or tourniquet and resuscitate.
Confirm identity, consent and associated injuries.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Prepare the injured limb and the opposite leg for vein harvest.
Gain proximal and distal control of the artery before opening the haematoma.
Debride damaged artery back to healthy intima.
Pass a balloon catheter to clear thrombus and flush with heparinised saline.
Repair by lateral suture, end-to-end anastomosis or reversed vein interposition graft.
Use a temporary shunt first if bone fixation is needed or the patient is unstable.
Cover the repair with healthy soft tissue and check distal pulses.
Perform fasciotomy if ischaemia was prolonged or the limb is swollen.
aftercare: Hourly limb circulation checks
Keep the limb warm and avoid tight dressings
Watch for compartment syndrome
Antibiotics and tetanus cover per local protocol
red_flags: Loss of distal pulse or Doppler signal
Bleeding or expanding swelling at the repair
Tense compartments or pain on passive stretch

name: Burr hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma

indications: Symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma on CT
Chronic subdural haematoma with mass effect or reduced consciousness
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or antiplatelet effect where time allows
Acute subdural haematoma (needs craniotomy)
No CT confirmation of side and site
equipment: Burr hole set with hand drill (Hudson brace) or perforator
Soft irrigation catheter and warm saline
steps: Confirm identity, consent and the side on the CT scan, and mark the side.
Correct clotting and stop antiplatelets or anticoagulants where possible.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out with explicit side confirmation.
Give local anaesthesia with sedation or general anaesthesia and position with the head turned.
Shave and prepare the scalp and mark one or two burr hole sites over the collection.
Incise the scalp and make the burr hole, waxing bone edges.
Coagulate and open the dura in a cruciate fashion.
Let the haematoma drain and irrigate gently with warm saline until clear.
Place a subdural drain if used and close the scalp in layers.
aftercare: Neurological observations including GCS and pupils regularly
Nurse flat or as per surgeon while drain is in place
Remove drain at 24 to 48 hours
Restart anticoagulants only after senior review
red_flags: Falling GCS, new weakness or seizures
Unequal pupils or severe headache
Wound leak of clear fluid or infection

name: Craniotomy for evacuation of intracranial haematoma

indications: Extradural haematoma with mass effect or reduced consciousness
Acute subdural haematoma with mass effect
Intracerebral haematoma causing deterioration
contraindications: Non-survivable brain injury after senior review
Small haematoma without mass effect in a stable patient (observe)
equipment: Craniotomy set with perforator and craniotome or Gigli saw
Bipolar diathermy, bone wax and haemostatic agents
steps: Confirm identity, consent (or emergency proceed) and side on CT, and mark the side.
Secure the airway and protect the brain with oxygenation, blood pressure control and head-up position.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out with explicit side confirmation.
Induce general anaesthesia and position with the head supported.
Shave and prepare the scalp and fashion a scalp flap over the haematoma.
Make burr holes and connect them to raise a bone flap.
Evacuate the extradural clot, or open the dura and evacuate the subdural clot gently.
Find and control the bleeding source with bipolar diathermy or haemostatic material.
Close or patch the dura and place dural hitch stitches.
Replace the bone flap, or leave it out if the brain is swollen, then close the scalp over a drain.
aftercare: ICU or HDU neurological monitoring
Keep head up and avoid hypoxia and hypotension
Seizure prophylaxis and analgesia per local protocol
Repeat CT if deterioration
red_flags: Falling GCS or new pupil change
Seizures
CSF leak or wound infection
High drain output

indications: Compound depressed skull fracture
Depression greater than the skull thickness
Underlying haematoma or brain compression
Cosmetic deformity in the forehead
contraindications: Fracture over a major venous sinus without blood and expertise available
Closed simple depressed fracture without other indication (observe)
equipment: Craniotomy set with perforator and elevators
steps: Confirm identity, consent and CT findings, and mark the side.
Give antibiotics and tetanus cover per local protocol for compound fractures.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Induce general anaesthesia, shave and prepare the scalp.
Debride the scalp wound and extend it to expose the fracture.
Make a burr hole next to the depressed bone.
Elevate or remove the depressed fragments with elevators.
Inspect the dura, repair tears and remove devitalised brain and foreign material.
Wash thoroughly, replace clean bone fragments if suitable and close the scalp over a drain.
aftercare: Neurological observations
Continue antibiotics if compound
Seizure precautions
Plan cranioplasty later if bone was removed
red_flags: Falling GCS or new weakness
Seizures
CSF leak or wound infection

indications: Massive haemothorax or ongoing chest drain bleeding after trauma
Penetrating chest injury with instability
Lung resection for tumour, bronchiectasis or abscess
Oesophageal surgery or repair
contraindications: Unfit for single-lung anaesthesia without proper support
Lack of thoracic or ICU support for elective cases (refer)
equipment: Chest drains and underwater seal bottles
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and imaging, and cross-match blood.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out with explicit side confirmation.
Induce general anaesthesia, with lung isolation where available.
Position in lateral decubitus for posterolateral thoracotomy, or supine for anterolateral in emergencies.
Incise along the chosen rib space, divide the muscles and enter the pleura above the rib.
Insert the rib spreader and open slowly.
Explore the chest and control bleeding or perform the planned procedure.
Check for air leaks under saline with the lung inflated.
Place one or two chest drains through separate stab incisions.
Approximate the ribs, close the muscles in layers and close the skin.
aftercare: Analgesia including regional block where available
Chest physiotherapy and early mobilisation
Record drain output and air leak
Chest X-ray after surgery
red_flags: Drain blood output high or rising
Persistent large air leak or breathlessness
Fever or pus from the drain
Hypotension or tachycardia

indications: Chronic empyema with trapped lung
Organised haemothorax with lung entrapment
Failed chest drain treatment of empyema
contraindications: Underlying lung destroyed beyond re-expansion (consider other options)
Active untreated tuberculosis (treat first where possible)
Unfit for thoracotomy
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and imaging, and cross-match blood.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Induce general anaesthesia and position lateral.
Open the chest by posterolateral thoracotomy.
Evacuate pus and debris and send samples for culture and TB testing.
Incise the thickened visceral peel down to the lung surface.
Peel the fibrous layer off the lung with blunt dissection, allowing the lung to expand.
Free the diaphragm and remove the parietal peel if needed.
Inflate the lung to confirm re-expansion and check for air leaks.
Place two chest drains, close the chest and connect to underwater seal.
aftercare: Chest physiotherapy and incentive spirometry
Antibiotics or TB treatment per culture
Monitor drain output and air leak
Chest X-ray for lung expansion
red_flags: High blood loss from drains
Persistent air leak or collapse on X-ray
Fever returning or pus in drains

name: Open drainage of empyema with rib resection

indications: Chronic empyema with thick pus not drained by chest tube
Patient unfit for decortication
Bronchopleural fistula with empyema
contraindications: Acute empyema with thin fluid (chest drain first)
Free unadherent lung where open drainage would cause collapse
equipment: Rib resection set with periosteal elevator and rib shears
Large-bore chest tube (28–36 Fr) or open-window dressing
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and imaging, and mark the lowest part of the cavity.
Confirm the lung is adherent (chronic empyema) before planning open drainage.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general or local anaesthesia and position lateral.
Make an incision over the rib at the lowest point of the empyema.
Strip the periosteum and resect a short segment of rib.
Aspirate to confirm pus, then open the pleura and evacuate pus and debris.
Send pus and pleura for culture, TB testing and histology.
Insert a large-bore tube or suture skin to pleura to create an open window.
Secure the tube and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Daily dressing or tube care
Gradual shortening of the tube when the cavity shrinks
Antibiotics or TB treatment per culture
Nutrition and chest physiotherapy
red_flags: Breathlessness or lung collapse
Bleeding from the wound
Fever not settling

indications: Incomplete miscarriage up to 12-14 weeks uterine size
Missed or delayed miscarriage in the first trimester
Endometrial sampling
Post-abortion care after unsafe abortion
contraindications: Uterine size above 14 weeks (refer for surgical or medical management)
Suspected uterine perforation or bowel injury
Haemodynamic instability before resuscitation
Suspected molar pregnancy without facility for suction and histology
equipment: MVA aspirator and cannulae of assorted sizes
Sterile speculum, tenaculum and sponge forceps
Local anaesthetic, spinal needle or long needle and 10 mL syringe for paracervical block
Strainer, bowl and clear container for tissue inspection
Sterile gloves, drapes and light source
Uterotonic and IV cannula with fluids available
steps: Confirm identity, gestation, indication and written consent, and check vital signs and haemoglobin.

Give analgesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol, and ask the patient to empty her bladder. If fever or sepsis is suspected, resuscitate and start treatment antibiotics before evacuating.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and do a bimanual examination to confirm uterine size and position.
Insert the speculum and clean the cervix and vagina with antiseptic solution.
Give a paracervical block with local anaesthetic.
Apply the tenaculum to the anterior lip of the cervix and apply gentle traction to straighten the canal.
Dilate the cervix gently if needed to admit a cannula matching the uterine size.
Prepare the aspirator, close the valves and create the vacuum.
Insert the cannula through the cervix to just short of the fundus, connect the aspirator and release the valves.
Evacuate the uterus by rotating the cannula and moving it gently back and forth.
Stop when the signs of completion appear (red or pink foam, gritty feel, uterus contracting around the cannula).
Inspect the tissue in water or saline to confirm products of conception and exclude molar tissue.
Check for bleeding from the cervix and tenaculum site, then remove the instruments.
Offer family planning counselling and a method before discharge.
aftercare: Observe vital signs and bleeding for at least 1 hour.
Give analgesia and anti-D immunoglobulin if Rh-negative per local protocol.
Advise that light bleeding and cramps may last a few days.
Offer contraception and arrange follow-up in 1-2 weeks.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding soaking more than two pads an hour
Fever, foul-smelling discharge or worsening abdominal pain
Cannula passing further than expected (suspected perforation) - stop and observe
No products seen on inspection (consider ectopic pregnancy)
Fainting, dizziness or fast pulse

name: Evacuation of retained products of conception

indications: Incomplete or missed miscarriage
Retained products after delivery or termination
Failed medical management of miscarriage
contraindications: Uncorrected haemodynamic instability
Suspected ectopic pregnancy
Suspected uterine perforation
equipment: Sterile D&C set with speculum, tenaculum, sponge forceps and dilators
Suction machine and cannulae or MVA kit
Antiseptic solution, gauze, drapes and sterile gloves
steps: Confirm identity, indication, ultrasound findings and written consent, and group and save blood.
Resuscitate if needed and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol. If fever or sepsis is suspected, start treatment antibiotics before evacuating.
Perform the surgical time-out once anaesthesia is established.
Place the patient in lithotomy, clean and drape, and empty the bladder if full.
Perform bimanual examination to confirm uterine size and position.
Insert the speculum, grasp the cervix with a tenaculum and dilate gently if the os is closed.
Remove products in the canal with ovum forceps.
Evacuate the uterus with a suction cannula sized to gestation, using gentle rotation.
Check for completion with gentle suction or a blunt curette without vigorous curettage.
Give a uterotonic per local protocol if bleeding is heavy.
Check haemostasis at the cervix, remove instruments and count swabs.
Send tissue for histology and record the findings.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs and vaginal bleeding until stable.
Give analgesia and anti-D if Rh-negative per local protocol.
Offer contraception and counselling, and arrange follow-up.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding or falling blood pressure
Fever, foul discharge or severe abdominal pain
Instrument passing beyond expected depth (perforation)
Persistent bleeding or positive pregnancy test after 3 weeks

indications: Abnormal uterine bleeding needing tissue diagnosis when hysteroscopy is not available
Postmenopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium
Removal of endometrial polyp when hysteroscopy is not available
contraindications: Possible viable intrauterine pregnancy
Acute pelvic infection
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Sterile D&C set with speculum, tenaculum, uterine sound and Hegar dilators
Sharp and blunt curettes and polyp forceps
steps: Confirm identity, indication, negative pregnancy test and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out after anaesthesia.
Place in lithotomy, clean and drape, and perform bimanual examination.
Insert the speculum and grasp the anterior lip of the cervix with the tenaculum.
Sound the uterus gently to confirm direction and record the length.
Dilate the cervix sequentially to the size needed.
Curette all walls of the cavity systematically, including the fundus and cornua.
Explore the cavity with polyp forceps to remove any polyp.
Collect all tissue and place it in formalin for histology.
Check haemostasis, remove instruments and complete the swab count.
aftercare: Observe vital signs and bleeding before discharge.
Give analgesia and advise that light bleeding may last a few days.
Arrange review of the histology result.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding or fainting
Fever or foul-smelling discharge
Severe or increasing abdominal pain (possible perforation)

indications: Ultrasound or clinical diagnosis of complete or partial hydatidiform mole
contraindications: Uncorrected severe anaemia or haemodynamic instability (resuscitate first)
Uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis or severe pre-eclampsia until stabilised
equipment: Electric suction machine with large-bore cannulae (MVA if not available)
Sterile D&C set with dilators and blunt curettes
Two large-bore IV cannulae and crossmatched blood
steps: Confirm diagnosis, identity and written consent, and check haemoglobin, blood group, thyroid status and baseline beta-hCG.
Crossmatch blood and insert two large-bore IV lines.
Ensure a senior clinician is present and perform the surgical time-out.
Place in lithotomy, clean, drape and empty the bladder.
Dilate the cervix gently to admit a cannula suited to the uterine size.
Evacuate with suction, keeping the cannula moving, until the cavity is empty.
Start an infusion of uterotonic only after the uterus has been emptied, per local protocol.
Check gently that the cavity is empty, avoiding vigorous curettage of the soft uterus.
Send all tissue for histology, labelled as suspected molar pregnancy.
Check haemostasis and remove instruments.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, bleeding and urine output closely for several hours.
Give anti-D if Rh-negative per local protocol.
Register for beta-hCG follow-up until normal and as advised by the trophoblastic disease service.
Advise reliable contraception (avoid IUD until hCG normal) and avoid pregnancy during follow-up.
red_flags: Massive haemorrhage - call for help and activate blood transfusion
Breathlessness or low oxygen saturation (trophoblastic embolisation)
Plateau or rise of beta-hCG on follow-up - refer to oncology
Persistent vaginal bleeding after evacuation

indications: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemoperitoneum
Unruptured tubal ectopic unsuitable for or failing medical management
contraindications: None absolute in ruptured ectopic (resuscitate and operate)
equipment: Major laparotomy set or laparoscopy stack
Suction with large reservoir and swabs
Two large-bore IV cannulae, crossmatched blood and autotransfusion set where available
steps: Confirm identity, positive pregnancy test, scan findings and written consent (urgent consent if unstable).
Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood, and do not delay surgery in a patient who is bleeding.
Perform the surgical time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Open the abdomen through a Pfannenstiel or midline incision, or establish laparoscopic ports in a stable patient.
Remove blood and clots with suction and identify the affected tube.
Clamp the mesosalpinx and the tube close to the uterus to control bleeding.
Excise the tube and ligate the pedicles, or perform salpingostomy if the other tube is absent or damaged.
Inspect the contralateral tube and both ovaries and record their state.
Wash out the pelvis, check haemostasis and complete the swab count.
Close the abdomen in layers.
Send the tube for histology.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output and haemoglobin.
Give anti-D if Rh-negative per local protocol.
Follow up beta-hCG to zero if salpingostomy was done.
Counsel on future fertility and early scan in the next pregnancy.
red_flags: Ongoing hypotension or falling haemoglobin after surgery
Rising beta-hCG after salpingostomy (persistent trophoblast)
Fever or wound discharge

indications: Symptomatic fibroids not suitable for myomectomy
Abnormal uterine bleeding failing other treatment
Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia or early endometrial cancer
Adenomyosis or endometriosis with completed family
contraindications: Desire for future fertility
Uncorrected anaemia or medical illness (optimise first)
equipment: Major laparotomy set with hysterectomy clamps
steps: Confirm identity, indication, haemoglobin, crossmatch and written consent including ovaries and fertility.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out and insert a urinary catheter.
Open the abdomen, explore it and place a self-retaining retractor.
Clamp, divide and ligate the round ligaments and open the broad ligaments.
Divide the infundibulopelvic ligaments (if removing ovaries) or the utero-ovarian pedicles.
Reflect the bladder down off the lower uterus and cervix.
Identify the ureters and clamp, divide and ligate the uterine vessels close to the uterus.
Clamp, divide and ligate the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments in steps.
Enter the vagina, remove the uterus and cervix, and close the vault, securing the angles.
Check all pedicles for haemostasis, check bladder integrity and complete the swab count.
Close the abdomen in layers and send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output and drain if placed.
Encourage early mobilisation and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Remove the catheter per protocol and check voiding.
Advise no intercourse or heavy lifting for 6 weeks.
red_flags: Falling blood pressure, rising pulse or abdominal distension (bleeding)
Reduced urine output, haematuria or leakage of urine from the vagina
Fever, wound discharge or foul vaginal discharge
Calf swelling or breathlessness

indications: Hysterectomy where removal of the cervix is difficult or unsafe (dense adhesions, bleeding)
Benign uterine disease with normal cervical screening and patient preference
contraindications: Cervical premalignant or malignant disease
Endometrial cancer
equipment: Major laparotomy set with hysterectomy clamps
Crossmatched blood and specimen container with formalin
steps: Confirm identity, indication, recent normal cervical screening and written consent.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out and insert a urinary catheter.
Open the abdomen, explore it and place a retractor.
Divide and ligate the round ligaments and the adnexal pedicles as planned.
Reflect the bladder and identify the ureters.
Clamp, divide and ligate the uterine vessels at the level of the internal os.
Amputate the uterus above the cervix and close the cervical stump.
Check haemostasis and complete the swab count.
Close the abdomen in layers and send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output and wound.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Advise that cervical screening must continue.
red_flags: Signs of intra-abdominal bleeding
Urine leakage, reduced output or flank pain
Fever or wound infection
Cyclical bleeding from the cervical stump

indications: Uterovaginal prolapse with completed family
Benign uterine disease with a small mobile uterus
contraindications: Large or fixed uterus
Suspected ovarian or uterine malignancy
Previous extensive pelvic surgery or severe endometriosis
equipment: Vaginal hysterectomy set with weighted speculum and Sims retractors
Heaney or similar clamps and needle holders
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor for infiltration per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, indication, normal cervical screening and written consent.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, place in lithotomy, clean, drape and catheterise.
Infiltrate the cervicovaginal junction to reduce bleeding.
Make a circumferential incision around the cervix and push up the bladder and rectum.
Open the posterior then the anterior peritoneum.
Clamp, divide and ligate the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments.
Clamp, divide and ligate the uterine vessels, then the upper pedicles.
Deliver and remove the uterus and check all pedicles for bleeding.
Close the peritoneum and attach the uterosacral ligaments to the vault for support.
Close the vaginal vault and perform any planned repair.
Insert a vaginal pack if needed and complete the swab count.
aftercare: Remove pack and catheter per protocol and check voiding.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Advise no intercourse or heavy lifting for 6 weeks.
red_flags: Heavy vaginal bleeding or signs of internal bleeding
Inability to pass urine or urine leaking from the vagina
Fever or foul discharge

indications: Benign uterine disease needing hysterectomy where laparoscopic skills and equipment are available
Early endometrial cancer in suitable centres
contraindications: Very large uterus beyond the operator's laparoscopic capability
Unable to tolerate pneumoperitoneum or steep head-down position
equipment: Laparoscopy stack with camera, insufflator and light source
Ports, uterine manipulator and vaginal occluder
Laparoscopic needle holders and absorbable sutures
steps: Confirm identity, indication and written consent including risk of conversion to open surgery.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy with arms tucked and catheterise.
Insert the uterine manipulator.
Establish pneumoperitoneum and insert the ports under vision.
Inspect the pelvis and upper abdomen and identify the ureters.
Seal and divide the round ligaments and the adnexal pedicles as planned.
Develop the bladder flap and push the bladder down.
Seal and divide the uterine vessels at the level of the cervix.
Perform the colpotomy on the manipulator cup and remove the uterus vaginally.
Close the vaginal vault and check haemostasis at low pressure.
Remove ports under vision and close port sites.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs and urine output.
Mobilise early and remove the catheter per protocol.
Advise no intercourse for 6 weeks.
red_flags: Increasing abdominal pain, distension or fever (possible bowel injury)
Urine leakage or flank pain (possible ureteric or bladder injury)
Signs of bleeding or shoulder-tip pain beyond 48 hours

indications: Early-stage cervical cancer (stage IA2 to IB2 or as decided by the tumour board)
Selected endometrial cancer with cervical involvement
contraindications: Locally advanced cervical cancer (refer for chemoradiation)
Medically unfit for major surgery
equipment: Major laparotomy set with long instruments and deep retractors
steps: Confirm staging, tumour board decision, identity and written consent including bladder and sexual effects.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol, and crossmatch blood.
Perform the surgical time-out and insert a urinary catheter.
Open the abdomen through a midline incision and explore for spread beyond the pelvis.
Open the retroperitoneum and identify the ureters and iliac vessels.
Perform pelvic lymphadenectomy and send nodes labelled by side.
Ligate the uterine arteries at their origin and dissect the ureters through the tunnel.
Divide the parametrium and uterosacral ligaments wide of the cervix.
Remove the uterus with an adequate upper vaginal cuff.
Close the vault, check haemostasis and the integrity of ureters and bladder.
Place drains as needed, complete the swab count and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Care in high-dependency setting if available, monitoring vital signs and urine output.
Keep the urinary catheter for a prolonged period and check residual volume after removal.
Continue thromboprophylaxis and review histology at the tumour board.
red_flags: Urine leaking from the vagina or wound (ureteric or bladder fistula)
Signs of internal bleeding
Leg swelling or lymphocyst symptoms
Fever or sepsis

indications: Symptomatic uterine fibroids (bleeding, pressure, pain) with wish to keep the uterus
Fibroids thought to contribute to infertility or recurrent miscarriage
contraindications: Pregnancy
Suspected uterine sarcoma or malignancy
Uncorrected severe anaemia (correct first)
equipment: Major laparotomy set and self-retaining retractor
Myoma screw, tenacula and bone hooks
Vasoconstrictor for uterine infiltration or uterine tourniquet per local protocol
Absorbable sutures for layered myometrial closure
Crossmatched blood (at least two units) and cell saver if available
steps: Confirm identity, fibroid mapping on scan, haemoglobin, crossmatch and written consent including possible hysterectomy.
Give prophylactic antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out and insert a urinary catheter.
Open the abdomen and deliver the uterus into the wound.
Apply a tourniquet around the lower uterus or infiltrate the myometrium to reduce bleeding.
Make as few uterine incisions as possible, preferably anterior and vertical.
Enucleate the fibroids along the cleavage plane, removing as many as safely possible through each incision.
Close the dead space and myometrium in layers with absorbable sutures.
Close the serosa and release the tourniquet, then check haemostasis.
Record the number and size of fibroids and whether the cavity was entered.
Apply an adhesion barrier where available, complete the swab count and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, haemoglobin and urine output.
Mobilise early and continue thromboprophylaxis.
Advise on timing of conception and that caesarean birth may be advised if the cavity was entered.
red_flags: Falling haemoglobin, abdominal distension or rising pulse
Fever beyond 48 hours or wound infection
Severe abdominal pain or vomiting

indications: Submucous fibroid (type 0, 1 or selected type 2) causing bleeding or infertility
contraindications: Pregnancy or active pelvic infection
Suspected uterine or cervical malignancy
Fibroid mostly intramural and beyond hysteroscopic reach
equipment: Operative hysteroscope with resectoscope loop or tissue removal device
Camera, light source and fluid management system with deficit monitoring
Distension medium suited to the energy type (saline for bipolar)
steps: Confirm identity, negative pregnancy test, scan mapping of the fibroid and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Place in lithotomy, clean, drape and examine bimanually.
Dilate the cervix to admit the resectoscope.
Insert the hysteroscope under vision with distension fluid running and inspect the cavity and ostia.
Resect the fibroid in strips from the surface towards the base, keeping the loop moving towards you.
Monitor the fluid deficit continuously and stop at the agreed limit.
Remove chips regularly to keep a clear view.
Inspect the cavity at low pressure for bleeding and residual fibroid.
Send all chips for histology.
aftercare: Observe vital signs and check fluid deficit and electrolytes if the deficit was high.
Advise that watery or light bloody discharge may last 2-3 weeks.
Arrange follow-up with histology and plan a second stage if resection was incomplete.
red_flags: Fluid deficit above the safety limit - stop, check sodium and watch for fluid overload
Confusion, headache, breathlessness or seizures (fluid overload or hyponatraemia)
Heavy bleeding, fever or severe pain (perforation or infection)

indications: Symptomatic subserous or intramural fibroids of suitable number and size with wish to keep the uterus
contraindications: Many or very large fibroids beyond laparoscopic capability
Suspected uterine sarcoma
Pregnancy
equipment: Laparoscopy stack with insufflator, camera and light source
Ports, myoma screw and laparoscopic graspers
Monopolar hook or harmonic device and bipolar forceps
Laparoscopic needle holders and barbed or absorbable sutures
Containment bag for tissue extraction and morcellation where available
Uterine manipulator and open conversion set
steps: Confirm identity, fibroid mapping, crossmatch and written consent including conversion to laparotomy.
Give prophylactic antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position, catheterise and insert a uterine manipulator.
Establish pneumoperitoneum and insert ports under vision.
Infiltrate the myometrium over the fibroid with vasoconstrictor per local protocol.
Incise the serosa over the fibroid and enucleate it with traction and counter-traction.
Close the myometrium in layers with laparoscopic suturing.
Extract the fibroid through an enlarged port or mini-laparotomy, always using a containment bag if morcellating, and do not morcellate if malignancy is suspected.
Irrigate, check haemostasis at low pressure and apply an adhesion barrier if available.
Remove ports under vision and close the sites.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs and haemoglobin.
Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Advise on interval before conception and mode of future delivery.
red_flags: Signs of intra-abdominal bleeding
Increasing pain, fever or distension after 48 hours (bowel injury)
Wound redness or discharge

indications: Abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding
Suspected polyp, submucous fibroid or intrauterine adhesions
Infertility or recurrent miscarriage work-up
Lost IUD threads with device not retrievable otherwise
contraindications: Pregnancy
Active pelvic infection
Heavy active bleeding obscuring the view
equipment: Rigid or flexible hysteroscope with sheath
Normal saline distension medium with pressure bag or pump
steps: Confirm identity, negative pregnancy test, indication and written consent.
Offer analgesia before the procedure and explain that she can ask to stop at any time.
Perform the time-out, position in lithotomy and clean the vulva and vagina.
Use a vaginoscopic approach without speculum where possible, or insert a speculum and steady the cervix.
Pass the hysteroscope through the canal under vision with saline flowing.
Inspect the cervical canal, cavity, both ostia and the endometrium systematically.
Take a directed biopsy or remove small polyps or a device if indicated.
Withdraw the scope, inspecting the canal again.
Record the findings with photographs if possible.
aftercare: Observe for vasovagal symptoms before discharge.
Advise that cramps and light bleeding may last a few days.
Arrange follow-up for results.
red_flags: Severe pain or fainting during the procedure - stop
Fever or foul discharge after the procedure
Heavy bleeding

indications: Intrauterine adhesions causing amenorrhoea, hypomenorrhoea, infertility or recurrent miscarriage
contraindications: Pregnancy or active pelvic infection
Genital tuberculosis not yet treated
equipment: Operative hysteroscope with scissors or bipolar electrode
Fluid management system with deficit monitoring
Ultrasound for guidance in severe adhesions where available
Intrauterine balloon or IUD as barrier per local practice
steps: Confirm identity, negative pregnancy test, previous findings and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out and position in lithotomy.
Dilate the cervix carefully and insert the hysteroscope under vision.
Identify the landmarks and the remaining normal cavity.
Divide central filmy adhesions first, then work towards the lateral walls and fundus.
Use ultrasound guidance in dense adhesions to reduce perforation risk.
Monitor fluid deficit throughout.
Restore the cavity shape and open both tubal ostia if possible.
Insert an anti-adhesion barrier such as a balloon or device if per local practice.
Record the adhesion grade and final cavity appearance.
aftercare: Give hormonal therapy and follow-up per local protocol.
Arrange a second-look hysteroscopy to check for re-forming adhesions.
Advise that adhesions can recur.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding or severe abdominal pain (possible perforation)
Fever or foul discharge
Persistent amenorrhoea after treatment

form.label: Tubal ostia seen at the end

indications: Assessment of tubal patency in infertility
Chronic pelvic pain or suspected endometriosis
Suspected pelvic adhesions
contraindications: Pregnancy
Active pelvic infection
Unable to tolerate pneumoperitoneum
equipment: Laparoscopy stack with insufflator, camera and light source
Veress needle or open-entry set and ports
Uterine cannula or manipulator for dye injection
Methylene blue dye diluted per local protocol and syringe
steps: Confirm identity, negative pregnancy test, timing in the follicular phase and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out and position in lithotomy with head-down tilt available.
Empty the bladder and insert the uterine cannula.
Enter the abdomen with Veress needle or open technique and establish pneumoperitoneum.
Insert the telescope and a secondary port under vision.
Inspect the uterus, tubes, ovaries, pouch of Douglas, peritoneum and upper abdomen.
Inject dye through the cervix and watch for spill from each fimbrial end.
Record any endometriosis, adhesions or hydrosalpinx with photographs.
Release the gas, remove ports under vision and close the port sites.
aftercare: Give analgesia and warn about shoulder-tip pain for 1-2 days.
Advise that blue vaginal discharge or urine is expected.
Discuss findings and fertility plan at follow-up.
red_flags: Increasing abdominal pain, fever or vomiting after 24 hours (bowel injury)
Signs of bleeding or fainting
Port-site redness or discharge

indications: Persistent or symptomatic benign ovarian cyst (dermoid, endometrioma, cystadenoma)
Ovarian cyst with torsion after detorsion
contraindications: Features suspicious of malignancy (refer to gynae-oncology and plan staging)
equipment: Atraumatic graspers, scissors and bipolar forceps
steps: Confirm identity, imaging, tumour markers if indicated, and written consent including possible oophorectomy.
For a child or adolescent, confirm parental consent and the young person's assent.
Perform the surgical time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Enter the abdomen by laparoscopy or laparotomy and inspect the pelvis, peritoneum and upper abdomen.
Take peritoneal washings if there is any doubt about malignancy.
Incise the ovarian capsule over the cyst away from the hilum.
Strip the cyst wall from the ovary with traction and counter-traction, trying to keep it intact.
Place the cyst in a retrieval bag and remove it, avoiding spillage.
Achieve haemostasis with minimal energy to preserve ovarian tissue, and suture the ovary if needed.
Irrigate the pelvis, especially after any dermoid spill.
Close the wounds and send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Give analgesia and mobilise early.
Review histology at follow-up.
Arrange repeat ultrasound if indicated.
red_flags: Signs of internal bleeding
Fever or peritonitis (chemical peritonitis after dermoid spill)
Histology showing borderline or malignant tumour - refer to gynae-oncology

indications: Ovarian mass where cystectomy is not possible or appropriate
Risk-reducing surgery in high genetic risk
Non-viable ovary after torsion
Tubo-ovarian abscess not responding to treatment
contraindications: Suspected ovarian cancer without plan for staging (refer to gynae-oncology)
equipment: Bipolar or vessel-sealing device, or clamps and ties
steps: Confirm identity, imaging, tumour markers if indicated and written consent including menopause effects if bilateral.
Perform the surgical time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Enter the abdomen and inspect the pelvis, peritoneum, omentum and upper abdomen.
Take peritoneal washings if malignancy is possible.
Identify the ureter on the pelvic side wall before clamping.
Divide the infundibulopelvic ligament above the ureter.
Divide the broad ligament and the utero-ovarian ligament and tube close to the uterus.
Place the specimen in a retrieval bag and remove it intact.
Check haemostasis and complete the swab count.
Close the wounds and send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Give analgesia and mobilise early.
Discuss menopausal symptoms and hormone therapy if both ovaries were removed.
Review histology at follow-up.
red_flags: Signs of internal bleeding
Flank pain or reduced urine output (possible ureteric injury)
Fever or wound infection

indications: Clinical or ultrasound suspicion of ovarian or adnexal torsion
contraindications: None (surgical emergency; do not delay for imaging if suspicion is high)
steps: Confirm identity and urgent written consent, with parental consent and assent for a child.
Give analgesia and keep nil by mouth.
Perform the surgical time-out.
Enter the abdomen by laparoscopy or laparotomy and identify the twisted adnexa.
Untwist the ovary and tube gently with atraumatic graspers.
Conserve the ovary even if it looks dark, unless it is clearly necrotic and falling apart.
Remove an underlying cyst by cystectomy or drain it if safe.
Consider oophoropexy for recurrent torsion or a long ligament.
Inspect the other ovary and record its state.
Close the wounds.
aftercare: Give analgesia and observe for fever.
Arrange repeat ultrasound in 6-12 weeks to check ovarian recovery.
Counsel about the risk of recurrence.
red_flags: Persistent fever or worsening pain (necrosis or infection)
Return of sudden severe pain (re-torsion)
Signs of bleeding

indications: Tubal factor infertility with distal or mild disease where IVF is not accessible or not chosen
Peritubal adhesions
contraindications: Severe bilateral tubal damage (IVF is the better option)
Active pelvic infection or untreated genital tuberculosis
equipment: Laparoscopy stack or laparotomy set with microsurgical instruments
Uterine cannula and dilute dye for chromotubation
steps: Confirm identity, semen analysis, ovulation status, prior tubal tests and written consent.
Counsel on success rate, ectopic risk and IVF as an alternative.
Perform the surgical time-out and insert a uterine cannula.
Enter the abdomen and assess the tubes, ovaries and adhesions.
Divide adhesions around the tubes and ovaries with fine instruments, keeping tissue moist.
Open the blocked distal tube with a cruciate incision and evert the mucosa, or free the fimbriae.
Test patency with dye through the cervix.
Use minimal energy and fine sutures to reduce new adhesions.
Irrigate and close the wounds.
aftercare: Give analgesia and mobilise early.
Advise trying to conceive soon and an early scan in pregnancy because of ectopic risk.
Refer for IVF if no pregnancy within an agreed time.
red_flags: Missed period with pain or bleeding (possible ectopic pregnancy)
Fever or increasing pain after surgery

indications: Polycystic ovary syndrome with anovulation resistant to ovulation induction medicines
contraindications: Pregnancy
Unable to tolerate laparoscopy
Low ovarian reserve
equipment: Laparoscopy stack with insufflator, camera and light source
Uterine cannula and dye if tubal testing planned
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis, semen analysis, tubal status plan and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out and insert a uterine cannula.
Establish pneumoperitoneum and insert ports.
Inspect the pelvis and perform a dye test if planned.
Hold the ovary away from the bowel by the utero-ovarian ligament.
Make a small number of punctures on each ovary away from the hilum with the electrode.
Cool the ovaries with irrigation fluid.
Check haemostasis and remove ports under vision.
aftercare: Give analgesia and warn about shoulder-tip pain.
Track menstrual cycles and ovulation over the next months.
Continue fertility follow-up.
red_flags: Increasing abdominal pain, fever or vomiting (bowel injury)
Signs of bleeding

indications: Postmenopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium
Abnormal uterine bleeding over 40-45 years or with risk factors
Persistent intermenstrual bleeding
contraindications: Pregnancy
Acute pelvic infection
Cervical stenosis preventing entry (arrange hysteroscopy)
equipment: Endometrial sampler (Pipelle or similar) or MVA syringe with small cannula
steps: Confirm identity, indication, negative pregnancy test if premenopausal and verbal consent.
Offer analgesia beforehand and explain the expected cramp.
Perform hand hygiene and a bimanual examination to find uterine position.
Insert the speculum and clean the cervix.
Steady the cervix with a tenaculum if needed.
Pass the sampler through the os to the fundus and note the depth.
Withdraw the piston to create suction and move the sampler in and out while rotating.
Withdraw the sampler and expel the tissue into formalin.
Repeat once if the sample is scanty, then check for bleeding and remove instruments.
aftercare: Advise that light bleeding and cramps are common for 1-2 days.
Arrange follow-up for the histology result.
red_flags: Severe pain or fainting - stop the procedure
Heavy bleeding, fever or foul discharge afterwards
Insufficient sample with ongoing bleeding (arrange hysteroscopy)

indications: Abnormal cervical cytology or positive high-risk HPV test
Positive visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or Lugol's iodine (VILI)
Suspicious-looking cervix or postcoital bleeding
Follow-up after treatment of cervical precancer
contraindications: Heavy menstrual bleeding at the time (rebook)
Untreated acute cervicitis (treat first)
equipment: Cusco speculum of suitable size and lateral wall retractor if needed
Dilute acetic acid and Lugol's iodine solutions
Punch biopsy forceps, endocervical speculum and specimen containers
Haemostatic agent (silver nitrate or Monsel's paste)
steps: Confirm identity, referral reason, pregnancy status, last cytology and verbal consent.
Position in lithotomy and insert the speculum to expose the whole cervix.
Inspect the cervix at low magnification before applying solutions.
Apply dilute acetic acid and wait about 1 minute.
Identify the squamocolumnar junction and record the transformation zone type.
Look for acetowhite areas, punctation, mosaic and atypical vessels and map them on a diagram.
Apply Lugol's iodine to outline non-staining areas if helpful.
Give a colposcopic impression (normal, low-grade, high-grade, suspicious of invasion).
Take directed biopsies from the worst areas if indicated.
Control bleeding with a haemostatic agent and remove the speculum.
aftercare: Advise that dark discharge may follow if haemostatic paste was used.
Advise no intercourse or tampons for a few days after biopsy.
Arrange follow-up for histology and treatment planning.
red_flags: Lesion suspicious of invasive cancer - biopsy and refer urgently to gynae-oncology
Heavy bleeding after biopsy
Fever or foul-smelling discharge

indications: Abnormal area seen at colposcopy or VIA
Visible cervical lesion suspicious of cancer
contraindications: Bleeding disorder not corrected
Pregnancy needs senior decision (biopsy only if invasion suspected)
equipment: Haemostatic agent (silver nitrate or Monsel's paste) and gauze for packing
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent, and explain possible bleeding.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Insert the speculum to expose the cervix and apply acetic acid to show the lesion.
Take the biopsy from the worst-looking area, starting with the lowest site so blood does not obscure others.
Place each sample in a labelled container.
Apply haemostatic agent or pressure to the biopsy sites.
Check for ongoing bleeding and pack lightly if needed.
Remove the speculum and any pack before the patient leaves unless told otherwise.
aftercare: Advise light bleeding or dark discharge for a few days.
Avoid intercourse and tampons until bleeding settles.
Arrange follow-up for histology.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding soaking pads
Fever or foul discharge
Histology showing invasion - refer to gynae-oncology urgently

name: Loop electrosurgical excision procedure
synonyms: large loop excision of the transformation zone

indications: High-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 2-3)
Screen-positive lesion in see-and-treat programmes
Unsatisfactory colposcopy with abnormal cytology
contraindications: Suspected invasive cancer (biopsy and refer)
Pregnancy (defer unless invasion suspected)
Acute cervicitis (treat first)
equipment: Electrosurgical unit with loop and ball electrodes and return plate
Colposcope, acetic acid and Lugol's iodine
Local anaesthetic with vasoconstrictor per local protocol and dental syringe
Haemostatic agent and specimen container with formalin
steps: Confirm identity, indication, negative pregnancy test and written consent.
Attach the return plate and set the generator per manufacturer guidance.
Insert the insulated speculum and outline the lesion with acetic acid or iodine.
Infiltrate the cervix with local anaesthetic.
Choose a loop that will remove the whole transformation zone in one pass if possible.
Excise the transformation zone with a smooth steady pass, keeping the loop perpendicular.
Take a second top-hat pass if the lesion extends into the canal.
Achieve haemostasis with the ball electrode and haemostatic paste.
Orientate and place the specimen in formalin.
Remove the speculum and check the patient before she sits up.
aftercare: Advise discharge for up to 4 weeks and avoid intercourse, tampons and swimming for 4 weeks.
Arrange follow-up with histology and test of cure per local protocol.
Counsel about small increased risk of preterm birth.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding (especially days 5-14 after treatment)
Fever, pelvic pain or foul discharge
Positive margins or invasion on histology - senior review

indications: Glandular abnormality (adenocarcinoma in situ) of the cervix
Suspected microinvasion needing a clear specimen
Type 3 transformation zone with high-grade disease where LEEP is unsuitable
contraindications: Obvious invasive cancer (biopsy and refer for staging)
Pregnancy unless invasion must be excluded (senior decision)
equipment: Minor gynaecology set with speculum, tenacula and scalpel with long handle
Vasoconstrictor for cervical infiltration per local protocol
Specimen container with formalin and orientation suture
steps: Confirm identity, indication, negative pregnancy test and written consent including fertility effects.
Perform the surgical time-out after anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Paint the cervix with Lugol's iodine to define the lesion.
Place lateral haemostatic sutures at 3 and 9 o'clock and infiltrate the cervix.
Cut a cone with the knife around the lesion and canal, leaving clear margins.
Mark the specimen at 12 o'clock with a suture for orientation.
Achieve haemostasis with diathermy and sutures.
Insert a vaginal pack if needed and record when it must be removed.
aftercare: Remove the pack and catheter per instructions.
Advise no intercourse or tampons for 4-6 weeks.
Arrange follow-up with histology and test of cure.
Counsel about cervical stenosis and preterm birth risk.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding, especially 1-2 weeks after surgery
Fever or foul discharge
Absent periods with cyclical pain (cervical stenosis)

indications: Visible cervical polyp causing bleeding or discharge
Cervical polyp found at screening
contraindications: Broad-based polyp or polyp arising high in the uterus (arrange hysteroscopy)
Lesion suspicious of cancer (biopsy and refer)
equipment: Cotton swabs and haemostatic agent (silver nitrate or Monsel's paste)
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Insert the speculum and identify the polyp and its stalk.
Grasp the polyp at the base with polyp forceps.
Twist the forceps slowly until the polyp separates.
Apply haemostatic agent or pressure to the base.
Inspect the cervix for any remaining lesion.
Place the polyp in formalin for histology.
aftercare: Advise light bleeding or discharge for a few days.
Arrange follow-up for histology.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding that does not settle
Ongoing abnormal bleeding (arrange further assessment of the uterus)
Abnormal histology

indications: Routine cervical screening in the eligible age group per national guideline
Follow-up after abnormal result or treatment
contraindications: Heavy menstrual bleeding at the time (rebook)
Visible suspicious lesion (examine and biopsy rather than rely on cytology)
equipment: Cusco speculum of suitable size and light source
Cervical broom or spatula and endocervical brush
Glass slide with fixative or liquid-based cytology vial
Gloves and water-based lubricant if needed
steps: Confirm identity, screening history, last menstrual period and verbal consent.
Offer a chaperone and explain each step.
Position the patient and insert the speculum to see the whole cervix.
Note the appearance of the cervix and any discharge or lesion.
Rotate the broom five times in the same direction over the transformation zone.
Smear and fix the sample immediately on the slide, or rinse the broom into the vial.
Remove the speculum gently.
Label the sample and complete the request form with the clinical details.
aftercare: Explain how and when the result will be given.
Record the next screening due date.
red_flags: Visible lesion, contact bleeding or ulcer - arrange colposcopy or biopsy
Postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding needs further assessment even with a normal result

indications: Vaginal discharge, bleeding or pain
Pelvic mass or suspected pelvic pathology
Taking swabs or cervical screening
Check of IUD threads
contraindications: Patient declines or withdraws consent
Virgo intacta or child (do not perform routinely; consider alternatives or examination under anaesthesia)
Antepartum haemorrhage with possible placenta praevia (no digital examination until excluded)
equipment: Cusco and Sims speculums in assorted sizes
steps: Confirm identity, explain the examination and obtain verbal consent.
Offer a chaperone and record their name, and ask the patient to empty her bladder.
Position the patient in dorsal or left lateral position with privacy maintained.
Inspect the vulva and perineum.
Insert the warmed, lubricated speculum gently and open to see the cervix.
Inspect the cervix and vaginal walls and take any swabs needed.
Close and remove the speculum, inspecting the vaginal walls as you withdraw.
Perform bimanual examination to assess the cervix, uterus and adnexa.
Stop at once if the patient asks.
Explain the findings to the patient.
aftercare: Explain what samples were taken and when results will be available.
Plan management based on findings.
red_flags: Cervical lesion suspicious of cancer - biopsy and refer
Cervical excitation with fever (pelvic inflammatory disease or ectopic)
Pelvic mass with weight loss or ascites

indications: Clinical staging of cervical cancer
Pelvic examination not possible awake (child, severe pain, vaginismus)
Vaginal bleeding or foreign body in a child
Assessment of genital trauma including sexual assault
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Minor gynaecology set with speculums of assorted sizes
Swabs and forensic kit where relevant
Cystoscope and sigmoidoscope for cancer staging
steps: Confirm identity, indication and written consent, with parental consent and child assent where relevant.
In suspected abuse, involve the safeguarding team and use a forensic kit with chain of custody.
Perform the surgical time-out after anaesthesia.
Position in lithotomy or frog-leg position for a child and clean if required.
Inspect the vulva, perineum and anus and document injuries.
Examine the vagina and cervix with a speculum or vaginoscope.
Perform bimanual and rectovaginal examination to assess parametria and pelvic side walls.
Perform cystoscopy and proctoscopy if needed for staging.
Take biopsies, swabs or remove a foreign body as indicated.
Record findings on a diagram, including clinical stage where relevant.
aftercare: Recover from anaesthesia per protocol.
Discuss findings and plan with the patient or parents.
Arrange follow-up for histology or safeguarding actions.
red_flags: Unexplained genital injury in a child - safeguarding referral
Heavy bleeding after biopsy
Bladder or rectal involvement (upstage and refer)

indications: Bartholin's abscess
Symptomatic or recurrent Bartholin's cyst
contraindications: Firm or irregular mass in a woman over 40 (biopsy to exclude cancer)
equipment: Minor surgical set with scalpel, artery forceps and scissors
steps: Confirm identity, side and written consent.
Perform the time-out and position in lithotomy.
Clean and drape the vulva and give anaesthesia.
Make a vertical incision on the inner side of the labium minus over the cyst, near the hymenal ring.
Drain the contents and send a swab for culture.
Break up loculations gently with a finger or forceps and irrigate the cavity.
Evert the cyst wall and suture it to the vestibular skin with interrupted absorbable sutures.
Check haemostasis and apply a pad.
aftercare: Advise warm sitz baths and analgesia.
Give antibiotics only if cellulitis or sexually transmitted infection is suspected, per local protocol.
Test for and treat sexually transmitted infections if indicated.
red_flags: Spreading redness, fever or severe pain
Recurrence of the swelling
Heavy bleeding from the wound

indications: Bartholin's cyst or abscess suitable for office treatment
contraindications: Deep or very small cyst not suitable for catheter placement
Irregular firm mass in a woman over 40 (biopsy)
equipment: Word catheter (or small Foley catheter as a low-cost alternative)
Sterile water and 3 mL syringe for balloon inflation
steps: Confirm identity, side and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the area and infiltrate local anaesthetic over the cyst.
Make a small stab incision inside the hymenal ring on the vestibular side of the cyst.
Drain the contents and take a swab for culture.
Break up loculations gently with artery forceps.
Insert the catheter into the cavity and inflate the balloon with sterile water until secure.
Tuck the free end of the catheter into the vagina.
Record the volume used to inflate the balloon and the planned removal date.
aftercare: Leave the catheter in place for about 4 weeks to form a tract.
Advise sitz baths and analgesia, and that the catheter may fall out.
Deflate and remove the catheter at the planned visit.
red_flags: Fever, spreading redness or severe pain
Catheter falling out early with swelling returning
Recurrent abscess (consider marsupialisation)

indications: Vulval lesion of uncertain diagnosis
Suspected lichen sclerosus, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer
Non-healing vulval ulcer
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Punch biopsy instrument of suitable size or scalpel
steps: Confirm identity, site and verbal consent, and offer a chaperone.
Photograph or draw the lesion and mark the biopsy site.
Perform hand hygiene and clean the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic under the site.
Take the biopsy from the most abnormal area, including the edge of an ulcer.
Lift the core with forceps and cut the base with scissors.
Control bleeding with pressure, a haemostatic agent or a suture.
Place the sample in labelled formalin.
aftercare: Keep the area clean and dry, using salt water baths.
Arrange follow-up for histology.
red_flags: Persistent bleeding
Signs of infection
Histology showing cancer - refer to gynae-oncology

indications: Vulval cancer (radical excision as decided by the tumour board)
Extensive vulval intraepithelial neoplasia not suitable for other treatment
contraindications: Medically unfit for major surgery
Unresectable disease (refer for chemoradiation)
equipment: Specimen containers labelled by site, with orientation sutures
steps: Confirm biopsy diagnosis, staging, tumour board decision, identity and written consent including body image and sexual effects.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy and catheterise.
Mark the excision margins around the lesion with adequate clearance.
Excise the vulval tissue to the planned depth, protecting the urethra and anus.
Perform inguinofemoral lymph node dissection or sentinel node biopsy if planned.
Orientate the specimen with sutures.
Achieve haemostasis and close the defect primarily or with a flap.
Place drains in the groin wounds if dissected.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry and give careful perineal care.
Keep the catheter until mobile and the wound allows.
Monitor drains and watch for groin wound breakdown and lymphocyst.
Review histology at the tumour board.
red_flags: Wound breakdown or infection
Leg swelling or groin collection
Heavy bleeding

indications: Extensive or bulky genital warts not responding to topical treatment
Warts in pregnancy obstructing the birth canal (senior decision)
contraindications: Uncertain diagnosis (biopsy first)
equipment: Minor surgical set with fine scissors and forceps
Electrocautery with smoke evacuation, or cryotherapy unit
steps: Confirm identity, extent of warts and written consent, with parental consent for a child.
In a child, consider possible sexual abuse and involve the safeguarding team.
Perform the time-out and position in lithotomy.
Clean the area and give local or general anaesthesia.
Excise warts at skin level with scissors, or destroy them with cautery, avoiding deep burns.
Send a representative sample for histology.
Achieve haemostasis with pressure or cautery.
Apply a non-adherent dressing or barrier ointment.
aftercare: Advise salt water baths and analgesia.
Offer HIV and sexually transmitted infection screening and partner notification.
Advise that warts may recur and arrange review.
red_flags: Wound infection or severe pain
Urinary retention from pain
Rapid regrowth or atypical lesion (biopsy to exclude neoplasia)

indications: Symptomatic anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) failing or declining pessary
contraindications: Asymptomatic prolapse
Plans for further pregnancy (relative)
equipment: Vaginal surgery set with Sims speculum and Allis forceps
Vasoconstrictor or saline for hydrodissection per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, prolapse assessment, urinary symptoms and written consent.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy, clean, drape and catheterise.
Infiltrate the anterior vaginal wall to aid dissection.
Make a midline incision in the anterior vaginal wall.
Dissect the vaginal skin off the underlying fascia and bladder on both sides.
Plicate the fascia in the midline with buried sutures to support the bladder.
Trim excess vaginal skin conservatively and close the vaginal wall.
Insert a vaginal pack and leave the catheter in place.
aftercare: Remove the pack and catheter per protocol and check post-void residual.
Advise avoiding heavy lifting, straining and intercourse for 6 weeks.
Treat constipation and chronic cough to protect the repair.
red_flags: Inability to pass urine or large residual volume
Heavy bleeding or vaginal haematoma
Fever or foul discharge

indications: Symptomatic posterior vaginal wall prolapse (rectocele)
Deficient perineal body with symptoms
contraindications: Asymptomatic prolapse
Active perineal infection
equipment: Vaginal surgery set with Allis forceps and scissors
Vasoconstrictor or saline for hydrodissection per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, bowel symptoms, prolapse assessment and written consent including dyspareunia risk.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy, clean, drape and catheterise.
Infiltrate the posterior vaginal wall and perineum.
Make a triangular perineal incision and a midline incision up the posterior wall.
Dissect the vaginal skin off the rectovaginal fascia and rectum.
Plicate the fascia in the midline, avoiding a tight ridge, with a finger in the rectum if needed.
Repair the perineal body muscles and trim vaginal skin conservatively.
Close the vaginal skin and perineum and do a rectal examination to check for sutures in the rectum.
Insert a vaginal pack if needed.
aftercare: Remove pack and catheter per protocol.
Give stool softeners per local protocol and avoid straining.
Advise no intercourse or heavy lifting for 6 weeks.
red_flags: Severe perineal pain or swelling (haematoma)
Passage of stool or wind through the vagina (fistula)
Fever or wound breakdown

indications: Vault prolapse after hysterectomy
Apical prolapse at vaginal hysterectomy with poor uterosacral support
Uterine prolapse for uterine-sparing repair (sacrospinous hysteropexy)
contraindications: Short vagina where fixation would cause tension
Medically unfit for surgery (consider pessary or colpocleisis)
equipment: Vaginal surgery set with long instruments and deep retractors
steps: Confirm identity, prolapse assessment and written consent including buttock pain and nerve injury risk.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy and catheterise.
Open the posterior vaginal wall and enter the right pararectal space.
Palpate the ischial spine and identify the sacrospinous ligament.
Place sutures through the ligament about two finger-breadths medial to the spine, avoiding the pudendal vessels and nerve.
Attach the sutures to the vaginal apex or cervix.
Tie the sutures to bring the vault to the ligament without a suture bridge.
Close the vaginal wall and perform any other repair.
Perform a rectal examination and insert a vaginal pack.
aftercare: Remove pack and catheter per protocol and check voiding.
Give analgesia and warn that buttock pain is common and usually settles.
Avoid heavy lifting and straining for 6 weeks.
red_flags: Severe or worsening buttock or leg pain (nerve entrapment) - urgent review
Signs of bleeding or haematoma
Urinary retention or fever

indications: Vault prolapse, especially recurrent or in sexually active women
Apical prolapse where durable repair is needed
contraindications: Unfit for abdominal surgery
Active pelvic infection or bowel disease making mesh unsafe
equipment: Permanent sutures or tacks for sacral fixation
steps: Confirm identity, prolapse assessment and written consent including mesh risks and alternatives.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position and catheterise, and insert a vaginal probe.
Enter the abdomen and pack the bowel away.
Open the peritoneum over the sacral promontory, identifying the right ureter, iliac vessels and middle sacral vessels.
Dissect the bladder off the anterior vault and the rectum off the posterior vault.
Attach the mesh to the anterior and posterior vaginal walls with sutures.
Fix the mesh to the anterior longitudinal ligament on the promontory without tension.
