Close the peritoneum over the mesh.
Check haemostasis, complete the swab count and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Mobilise early and remove the catheter per protocol.
Avoid heavy lifting and straining for 6 weeks.
Review for mesh exposure at follow-up.
red_flags: Severe bleeding from presacral vessels (pack and call for senior help)
Vaginal discharge or bleeding months after surgery (mesh exposure)
Fever, back pain or signs of infection (discitis)

indications: Uterine prolapse with cervical elongation in a woman who wishes to keep her uterus
contraindications: Wish for future pregnancy (relative; cervical incompetence risk)
Uterine or cervical disease needing hysterectomy
equipment: Vaginal surgery set with tenacula and dilators
Vasoconstrictor for infiltration per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, normal cervical screening, prolapse assessment and written consent.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy and catheterise.
Dilate the cervix and sample the endometrium.
Make a circumferential incision around the cervix and reflect the bladder upwards.
Clamp, divide and ligate the cardinal ligaments on each side.
Amputate the elongated cervix.
Bring the cardinal ligaments together in front of the cervix to support and lift it.
Cover the cervical stump with vaginal skin using Sturmdorf sutures.
Perform an anterior repair and posterior repair if needed.
Insert a vaginal pack.
aftercare: Remove pack and catheter per protocol.
Avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for 6 weeks.
Counsel on cervical stenosis and future pregnancy risks.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding
Urinary retention or fever
Absent periods with cyclical pain (cervical stenosis)

indications: Symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse in a woman who prefers not to have or is unfit for surgery
Temporary relief while awaiting surgery
contraindications: Active vaginal infection or unexplained bleeding (assess first)
Patient unable to attend for regular changes
equipment: Ring pessaries in a range of sizes (or fitting set)
steps: Confirm identity, prolapse assessment and verbal consent.
Ask the patient to empty her bladder and examine to estimate the size needed.
Inspect the vagina for ulceration or atrophy.
Lubricate the pessary and fold it gently.
Insert it along the posterior vaginal wall, then lift the front edge behind the pubic bone.
Check that a finger can pass between the pessary and the vaginal wall.
Ask the patient to stand, walk, cough and strain to check it stays in and is comfortable.
Ask her to pass urine before she leaves.
aftercare: Review in a few weeks, then change or clean the pessary every 3-6 months.
Consider vaginal oestrogen per local protocol in atrophy.
Teach self-management if suitable.
red_flags: Vaginal bleeding or offensive discharge (ulceration)
Difficulty passing urine or stool
Pain or pessary falling out
Missed reviews (risk of a forgotten pessary and fistula)

indications: Vesicovaginal fistula after obstructed labour, surgery or trauma
contraindications: Tissues still inflamed or sloughing (wait until healthy, usually about 3 months)
Malignant fistula or after radiotherapy (refer to specialist centre)
Untreated urinary tract infection or severe malnutrition (correct first)
equipment: Fistula repair set with fine instruments and long-handled scalpel
Dye for leak test (methylene blue) and syringe
Foley catheter (16-18 Fr) and vaginal pack
steps: Confirm identity, fistula classification, urine culture, haemoglobin and written consent.
For an adolescent, involve parents or guardian and assess for safeguarding needs.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in exaggerated lithotomy and prepare.
Examine under anaesthesia to define the fistula size, site and relation to the ureters.
Catheterise the ureters if the fistula is near the ureteric openings.
Infiltrate and incise around the fistula, and mobilise the vaginal wall widely off the bladder.
Close the bladder in one or two tension-free layers with fine delayed absorbable sutures.
Test the repair by filling the bladder with dilute dye and look for leakage.
Add a flap such as a Martius graft if tissue is poor.
Close the vaginal wall and insert a vaginal pack and urethral catheter.
aftercare: Keep the catheter draining freely for 10-14 days and check it frequently.
Encourage high oral fluid intake.
Advise no intercourse for 3 months and plan caesarean birth in future pregnancies.
Offer pelvic floor exercises and social and nutritional support.
red_flags: Blocked catheter or reduced drainage - flush or replace immediately
Urine leaking again from the vagina
Fever, flank pain or haematuria with clots

indications: Rectovaginal fistula after obstetric injury, surgery or trauma
contraindications: Active inflammation, Crohn's disease flare or malignancy (refer)
Tissues not yet healthy after injury
equipment: Fistula repair set with fine instruments
steps: Confirm identity, fistula assessment, anal sphincter status and written consent.
Prepare the bowel and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out and position in lithotomy or prone jack-knife.
Examine under anaesthesia and define the fistula with a probe.
Incise around the fistula and separate the vaginal wall from the rectum.
Excise the fistula tract and close the rectal wall in layers without tension.
Repair the anal sphincter if it is damaged.
Close the vaginal wall separately.
Consider a protective colostomy for complex or recurrent fistulas.
aftercare: Give stool softeners and a low-residue diet per local protocol.
Keep the perineum clean with salt water baths.
Advise no intercourse for 3 months.
red_flags: Passage of stool or wind through the vagina again
Fever or perineal abscess
Severe constipation or faecal impaction

indications: Stress urinary incontinence failing pelvic floor muscle training
contraindications: Predominant urge incontinence or overactive bladder
Plans for further pregnancy (relative)
Untreated urinary tract infection
equipment: Retropubic or transobturator sling kit where approved
Cystoscope with 70-degree lens for retropubic route
Local anaesthetic or saline for hydrodissection
steps: Confirm identity, urodynamic or clinical diagnosis and written consent including mesh risks and alternatives.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Perform the surgical time-out, position in lithotomy and empty the bladder.
Infiltrate under the mid-urethra and the planned exit points.
Make a small midline incision under the mid-urethra and dissect laterally.
Pass the trocars on each side by the chosen route, keeping close to the bone.
Perform cystoscopy to exclude bladder perforation for the retropubic route.
Adjust the tape so it lies flat under the urethra without tension.
Remove the plastic sheaths and trim the tape at the skin.
Close the vaginal incision and check the patient voids after the procedure.
aftercare: Check post-void residual before discharge.
Avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for 6 weeks.
Review for voiding problems, pain and tape exposure.
red_flags: Urinary retention or large residual volume
Groin or thigh pain that persists
Vaginal discharge, bleeding or felt tape (exposure)

indications: Imperforate hymen with haematocolpos or mucocolpos
Microperforate or septate hymen causing obstruction
contraindications: Uncertain diagnosis - exclude transverse vaginal septum or vaginal agenesis with ultrasound first
equipment: Minor surgical set with scalpel, fine scissors and forceps
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis on ultrasound and written parental consent with the girl's assent.
Explain privacy, the effect on the hymen and cultural concerns sensitively.
Perform the surgical time-out after anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Catheterise the bladder to identify the urethra.
Make a cruciate or circular incision in the bulging hymen.
Let the retained blood drain without pressing on the abdomen or irrigating the uterus.
Excise the hymenal flaps to leave an adequate opening.
Suture the mucosal edges with fine absorbable sutures for haemostasis.
aftercare: Give analgesia and advise sitz baths.
Expect dark discharge for a few days.
Review in a few weeks to check the opening has stayed patent and periods are normal.
red_flags: Fever or offensive discharge (infection of retained blood)
Recurrence of cyclical pain without bleeding (re-closure or other obstruction)
Urinary retention

indications: Type 3 female genital mutilation (infibulation) causing urinary, menstrual or sexual problems
Infibulation in pregnancy, ideally before labour (second trimester)
contraindications: Patient declines (counsel and document)
equipment: Minor surgical set with scissors and forceps
steps: Confirm identity, FGM type and written consent, with parental consent and assent for a minor.
Discuss the law on FGM, that re-infibulation will not be done, and offer psychological support.
Complete safeguarding assessment, including for any daughters.
Perform the time-out and position in lithotomy.
Give local anaesthetic, or spinal or general if preferred.
Insert a finger or forceps under the scar and divide it in the midline towards the pubis until the urethral meatus is seen.
Stop before the area where the clitoris lies if it cannot be seen.
Oversew each cut edge with fine absorbable sutures for haemostasis.
Check that the urethra and vaginal opening are clear.
aftercare: Advise salt water baths, analgesia and passing urine in a warm bath if it stings.
Arrange follow-up and psychological support.
Record FGM in the notes and report per national guidance.
red_flags: Urinary retention or bleeding
Signs of infection
Significant distress (offer counselling)

indications: Longitudinal vaginal septum causing dyspareunia, tampon problems or obstruction
Transverse vaginal septum with haematocolpos
Obstructed hemivagina (OHVIRA)
contraindications: Anatomy not yet defined - get MRI or ultrasound and examination under anaesthesia first
equipment: Vaginal surgery set with fine instruments
Vaginal dilators or mould for transverse septum
steps: Confirm identity, anatomy on imaging, renal tract assessment and written consent, with parental consent and assent for a minor.
Perform the surgical time-out after anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Catheterise the bladder and perform a careful examination to define the septum.
Clamp and excise a longitudinal septum close to the vaginal walls, avoiding bladder and rectum.
For a transverse septum, identify the upper vagina with a needle aspirate, then excise the septum.
Join the upper and lower vaginal mucosa with fine absorbable sutures.
Check haemostasis.
Insert a mould or plan dilator use after transverse septum resection.
aftercare: Give analgesia and advise sitz baths.
Teach dilator use when advised to prevent narrowing.
Arrange follow-up to check for stenosis.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding
Recurrent cyclical pain or obstruction (stenosis)
Fever or offensive discharge

indications: Suspected or confirmed ovarian, tubal or primary peritoneal cancer
Interval debulking after neoadjuvant chemotherapy
contraindications: Medically unfit for major surgery (consider biopsy and chemotherapy)
Disease clearly unresectable on imaging (biopsy and refer for chemotherapy)
equipment: Major laparotomy set with long instruments and self-retaining retractor
Diathermy and vessel-sealing device if available
Suction, warm saline and large swabs
steps: Confirm imaging, tumour markers, tumour board decision, identity and written consent including stoma possibility.
Give thromboprophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol, and crossmatch blood.
Perform the surgical time-out and catheterise.
Open the abdomen through a midline incision extending above the umbilicus.
Collect ascites or peritoneal washings for cytology.
Inspect and palpate the whole peritoneal cavity, diaphragm, liver, bowel and nodes and record disease.
Remove the uterus, both tubes and ovaries intact where possible.
Perform infracolic omentectomy.
Take peritoneal biopsies and sample nodes per staging protocol, or remove all visible disease in debulking.
Record the size of residual disease.
Check haemostasis, complete the swab count and close with a mass closure.
aftercare: Care in high-dependency setting if available.
Monitor fluids, urine output and bowel function.
Continue extended thromboprophylaxis.
Discuss histology and chemotherapy at the tumour board.
red_flags: Signs of bleeding or shock
Fever, distension or vomiting (anastomotic leak or ileus)
Wound dehiscence
Calf swelling or breathlessness

indications: Tubo-ovarian abscess not improving after 48-72 hours of IV antibiotics
Ruptured abscess with peritonitis (emergency)
Large abscess where early drainage is advised
contraindications: Uncorrected sepsis without resuscitation (resuscitate and operate in parallel)
equipment: Ultrasound with guided drainage kit, or laparotomy or laparoscopy set
Suction with large reservoir and warm saline
steps: Confirm identity, imaging and written consent including possible removal of tube and ovary.
Resuscitate, take blood cultures and continue IV antibiotics per local protocol.
Perform the surgical or procedure time-out.
For image-guided drainage, insert the needle or drain into the abscess transvaginally or abdominally under ultrasound.
For surgery, open the abdomen, free the adhesions gently and open the abscess cavity.
Send pus for microscopy, culture and sensitivity.
Remove necrotic tissue or perform salpingectomy or oophorectomy only if needed, preserving fertility where possible.
Wash out the abdomen with warm saline and place a drain.
Close the abdomen with mass closure, leaving skin open if heavily contaminated.
aftercare: Continue antibiotics per sensitivities and local protocol.
Monitor temperature, white cell count and drain output.
Screen and treat for sexually transmitted infections, including partner treatment.
red_flags: Persistent fever or rising inflammatory markers
Signs of septic shock
Bowel or bladder injury symptoms

indications: Suspected haemoperitoneum (ruptured ectopic) where ultrasound is not available
Drainage of pelvic abscess pointing into the pouch of Douglas (posterior colpotomy)
contraindications: Ultrasound available and diagnostic (prefer it)
Fixed retroverted uterus or mass filling the pouch of Douglas
equipment: Sims or Cusco speculum and tenaculum
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent, and start resuscitation if the patient is unstable.
Position in lithotomy with head slightly up so fluid collects in the pouch.
Clean the vagina and insert the speculum.
Grasp the posterior lip of the cervix and lift it up.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the posterior fornix.
Insert the needle through the posterior fornix in the midline parallel to the cervix and aspirate.
Note the aspirate (non-clotting blood, clear fluid, pus or nothing).
Remove the needle and check for bleeding.
aftercare: Act on the result at once (non-clotting blood suggests haemoperitoneum - prepare for laparotomy).
Send pus for culture if obtained.
red_flags: Non-clotting blood aspirated - urgent laparotomy
Worsening shock
Dry tap does not exclude ectopic pregnancy

indications: Mild male factor infertility
Unexplained infertility
Cervical factor or sexual dysfunction preventing intercourse
Donor sperm insemination
contraindications: Blocked fallopian tubes on both sides
Active pelvic infection
Severe male factor (refer for IVF or ICSI)
equipment: Prepared washed sperm sample with labelled container
steps: Confirm identity of the woman and partner or donor, written consent and timing of ovulation.
Check the sperm sample label against both patients with a second person (witness check).
Record the post-wash sperm concentration and motility.
Position the patient and insert the speculum to see the cervix.
Clean the cervix gently with saline.
Load the sample into the catheter without air bubbles.
Pass the catheter gently through the cervical canal to just short of the fundus.
Inject the sample slowly and withdraw the catheter.
Let the patient rest briefly before getting up.
aftercare: Advise normal activity and that light spotting may occur.
Arrange a pregnancy test about 2 weeks later.
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain, bloating or breathlessness (ovarian hyperstimulation)
Fever or foul discharge
Positive pregnancy test with pain or bleeding (early scan for ectopic)

indications: Controlled ovarian stimulation for IVF or ICSI
Oocyte freezing or donation
contraindications: Ovaries not reachable transvaginally (consider transabdominal route)
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Transvaginal ultrasound probe with needle guide and sterile cover
Oocyte aspiration needle and suction pump at set pressure
Heated test tube block and culture medium per laboratory protocol
Sterile speculum and saline (no antiseptic in the vagina before retrieval)
steps: Confirm identity, trigger injection timing and written consent, and label tubes with a witness check.
Give sedation with monitoring per local protocol.
Perform the time-out and position in lithotomy.
Clean the vagina with saline and insert the covered probe.
Identify both ovaries and the iliac vessels on ultrasound.
Pass the needle through the vaginal wall into each follicle and aspirate, rotating to empty it.
Hand tubes to the embryologist in sequence and confirm oocytes found.
Repeat on the other ovary, keeping punctures to a minimum.
Check the vaginal wall for bleeding and the pelvis for free fluid at the end.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs and pain until fully recovered from sedation.
Advise about signs of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
Confirm the number of oocytes and the plan for embryo transfer.
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain, distension or breathlessness (ovarian hyperstimulation)
Fainting, fast pulse or falling blood pressure (internal bleeding)
Fever (pelvic infection)

indications: Transfer of embryos after IVF or ICSI (fresh or frozen)
contraindications: Severe ovarian hyperstimulation (freeze all and defer)
Uterine cavity abnormality not corrected
equipment: Sterile speculum and culture medium for cleaning the cervix
steps: Confirm identity of the patient and partner, written consent and the number of embryos to transfer.
Perform a witness check of patient identity against the embryo dish with the embryologist.
Ask the patient to come with a comfortably full bladder for ultrasound guidance.
Insert the speculum and clean the cervix with culture medium.
Perform a mock passage with the outer sheath if the canal is difficult.
Load the embryos into the catheter as per laboratory protocol.
Pass the catheter under ultrasound guidance to the upper mid cavity without touching the fundus.
Expel the embryos gently and withdraw the catheter slowly.
Hand the catheter to the embryologist to check no embryos remain.
aftercare: Allow normal activity and continue luteal support per local protocol.
Arrange a pregnancy test at the scheduled date.
Counsel about multiple pregnancy and ectopic risk.
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain, bloating or breathlessness (ovarian hyperstimulation)
Heavy bleeding or fever
Positive pregnancy test with pain or bleeding (early scan)

indications: Suspected meningitis or encephalitis
Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with normal CT
Measurement of CSF opening pressure (e.g. cryptococcal meningitis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
Suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome or CNS malignancy
Intrathecal drug administration by trained staff
contraindications: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or focal neurology without prior imaging
Uncorrected coagulopathy or low platelet count
Infection of the skin over the puncture site
Haemodynamic instability or active seizures
equipment: Sterile LP pack with drapes, gauze and dressing
Spinal needles (20-22 G, paediatric sizes as needed)
Sterile CSF bottles (at least three, labelled in order) and a fluoride bottle for glucose
Antiseptic solution, sterile gloves, mask and gown
Glucometer or blood glucose bottle for paired serum glucose
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent, and review imaging, platelet count and clotting results where needed.
Position the patient in the lateral decubitus position with knees to chest, or sitting leaning forward.
Identify the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace using the line between the iliac crests.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the skin and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the skin and interspinous tissue.
Insert the spinal needle with the stylet in, bevel parallel to the spine, aiming slightly towards the umbilicus.
Advance slowly, withdrawing the stylet periodically until CSF flows.
Measure the opening pressure with the manometer with the patient lying relaxed and legs extended.
Collect CSF into the numbered bottles for microscopy, culture, protein, glucose and other tests as indicated.
Take a paired blood glucose sample at the same time.
Replace the stylet, withdraw the needle and apply a sterile dressing.
Label samples at the bedside and send them to the laboratory promptly.
aftercare: Rest lying flat or comfortably for a short period if preferred and drink fluids.
Take simple analgesia for back pain or headache.
Keep the dressing dry and remove it after 24 hours.
red_flags: Stop if the patient develops new neurological signs, severe pain radiating down a leg or becomes unstable.
Escalate urgently for reduced consciousness, new weakness or a fall in pulse with rising blood pressure.
Return for severe headache not relieved by lying down, fever, neck stiffness, leg weakness or leakage at the site.

indications: New-onset ascites needing diagnosis
Suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Tense or symptomatic ascites needing drainage
contraindications: Acute abdomen needing surgery
Severe uncorrected coagulopathy with active bleeding
Skin infection, distended bowel or surgical scars at the chosen site
Pregnancy (use ultrasound-guided site if essential)
equipment: Sterile dressing pack, drapes and gloves
Paracentesis catheter or large-bore cannula (14-16 G) with drainage tubing
Collection bag or sterile container and specimen bottles, including blood culture bottles
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent, and review clotting, platelet count and kidney function.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder and lie supine or slightly tilted to the side of the tap.
Choose a site in the left or right lower quadrant lateral to the rectus sheath, confirmed by percussion or ultrasound.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, clean and drape the site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the peritoneum.
Insert the needle or catheter using a Z-track technique, aspirating as you advance until fluid returns.
Collect fluid for cell count, albumin, protein, Gram stain and culture, inoculating blood culture bottles at the bedside.
For therapeutic drainage, connect the catheter to the drainage bag and secure it.
Monitor pulse and blood pressure during drainage and give albumin replacement per local protocol for large volumes.
Remove the catheter when drainage is complete or the prescribed volume is reached.
Apply an occlusive dressing and record the volume and appearance of the fluid.
aftercare: Lie on the opposite side for a few hours if the site leaks.
Keep the dressing clean and dry.
Follow fluid and salt restriction advice and take diuretics as prescribed.
red_flags: Stop drainage if the patient becomes hypotensive, dizzy or develops abdominal pain.
Escalate for bloodstained fluid that increases, falling blood pressure or confusion.
Return for persistent leakage, fever, abdominal pain or redness at the puncture site.

indications: Unexplained cytopenias or abnormal blood film
Suspected leukaemia, lymphoma infiltration, myeloma or myelodysplasia
Staging of haematological malignancy and response assessment
Pyrexia of unknown origin with suspected marrow infection (e.g. visceral leishmaniasis, TB)
contraindications: Infection or radiotherapy at the chosen site
Severe uncorrected coagulopathy (low platelets alone is not a contraindication)
Sternal site in children (use the iliac crest; the tibia only in infants)
equipment: Bone marrow aspiration needle (e.g. Salah or Islam needle) of suitable size
Sterile pack, drapes, gloves and gown
Glass slides, spreader and EDTA bottles
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent, and review blood count and clotting.
Offer analgesia or sedation per local protocol, especially for children.
Position the patient lateral with knees drawn up for the posterior iliac crest, or supine for sternum or tibia.
Identify the posterior superior iliac spine and mark the site.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, clean and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to and over the periosteum.
Insert the aspiration needle with stylet through the skin to the bone and advance with a twisting motion until it is fixed in the marrow cavity.
Remove the stylet, attach a syringe and aspirate a small volume of marrow briskly.
Make smears immediately at the bedside and place further aspirate in EDTA or other bottles as required.
Remove the needle and apply firm pressure followed by a pressure dressing.
Label slides and samples and send them with the clinical details and a recent blood film.
aftercare: Keep the dressing on and dry for 24 hours.
Take simple analgesia for soreness.
Lie on the site for a short time if advised to help pressure.
red_flags: Stop if the patient becomes faint or the needle position is uncertain over the sternum.
Escalate for continued bleeding through the dressing.
Return for swelling, increasing pain, fever or redness at the site.

indications: Dry tap on aspiration
Staging of lymphoma and solid tumours
Suspected myelofibrosis, aplastic anaemia or marrow infiltration
Assessment of marrow cellularity
contraindications: Infection or radiotherapy at the posterior iliac crest
Severe uncorrected coagulopathy
Patient unable to stay still without sedation where sedation is unavailable
equipment: Trephine biopsy needle (e.g. Jamshidi) of suitable size
Sterile pack, drapes, gloves and gown
Formalin container and labelled request form
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent, and review blood count and clotting.
Offer analgesia or sedation per local protocol.
Position the patient lateral with knees drawn up and mark the posterior superior iliac spine.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and gown, clean and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic generously down to the periosteum.
Make a small skin nick with the scalpel.
Advance the trephine needle with stylet to the bone and then into the cortex with a rotating motion.
Remove the stylet and advance the needle further with rotation to obtain a core of adequate length.
Rock the needle gently to free the core and withdraw it with rotation.
Remove the core with the probe from the hub end and place it in formalin.
Apply firm pressure, then a pressure dressing.
Label the specimen and send it with clinical details.
aftercare: Keep the dressing on and dry for 24 hours.
Take simple analgesia for soreness.
Avoid strenuous activity for the rest of the day.
red_flags: Stop if the patient becomes faint or distressed despite analgesia.
Escalate for bleeding that does not settle with pressure or a growing haematoma.
Return for fever, increasing pain, swelling or discharge at the site.

indications: Acute chest syndrome
Acute stroke or transient ischaemic attack in sickle cell disease
Multi-organ failure or severe sickle crisis
Priapism not responding to initial treatment
Preparation for major surgery when advised by haematology
contraindications: No compatible blood available
Haemoglobin already high, so the target post-procedure haemoglobin must not be exceeded (hyperviscosity risk)
Haemodynamic instability without monitoring capacity
equipment: Cross-matched sickle-negative red cells (phenotyped where available)
Two large-bore cannulas or a central line
Blood giving sets and venesection bags or syringes
Monitor for pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation
Blood count, HbS percentage and electrolyte bottles
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent, and check the pre-exchange Hb, haematocrit and HbS percentage.
Calculate the volume of blood to remove and replace per haematology protocol and body weight.
Insert two large-bore cannulas, one for removal and one for infusion, or use a central line.
Perform bedside blood checks with two staff before each unit is started.
Record baseline pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation.
Remove an aliquot of blood from the patient into a venesection bag or syringe.
Replace with an equal volume of saline or donor red cells per the cycle in the protocol.
Repeat removal and replacement cycles, keeping the patient's volume balanced.
Monitor observations frequently and slow or pause if the patient becomes unstable.
Check Hb and haematocrit midway and at the end to avoid hyperviscosity.
Record total volumes removed and transfused and the units used.
Send post-exchange Hb and HbS percentage and document the result.
aftercare: Continue hydration, oxygen and analgesia as prescribed.
Keep the cannula sites clean and report swelling.
Attend haematology follow-up and repeat exchanges if planned.
red_flags: Stop and assess for a transfusion reaction if there is fever, rigors, rash, back pain, breathlessness or hypotension.
Escalate for rising Hb above the target, worsening hypoxia or new neurological signs.
Return for fever, dark urine, jaundice or new pain in the days after transfusion.

indications: Polycythaemia vera to keep haematocrit within target
Haemochromatosis or iron overload
Secondary polycythaemia with symptoms of hyperviscosity, as advised
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability or significant anaemia
Severe heart failure or cyanotic heart disease without specialist advice
Poor venous access
equipment: Venesection pack or blood donation bag with large-bore needle (16 G)
Weighing scale for the collection bag
Normal saline and giving set for replacement if prescribed
steps: Confirm identity, indication and the prescribed volume to remove, and check the latest haematocrit or ferritin.
Record baseline pulse and blood pressure and ask about dizziness or chest pain.
Lay the patient supine or semi-reclined.
Perform hand hygiene, apply the tourniquet and select a large antecubital vein.
Clean the skin and insert the needle, then release the tourniquet partly to allow steady flow.
Collect blood into the bag on the scale until the prescribed volume is reached.
Monitor the patient for faintness and stop if they become unwell.
Remove the needle, apply pressure and a plaster.
Give oral fluids or saline replacement per prescription.
Recheck pulse and blood pressure before the patient stands.
Dispose of the blood as clinical waste and record the volume removed.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids for the rest of the day.
Avoid heavy lifting with that arm and strenuous exercise for 24 hours.
Sit or lie down if dizzy.
red_flags: Stop if the patient becomes faint, hypotensive or develops chest pain.
Escalate for chest pain or breathlessness that does not settle.
Return for persistent dizziness, bleeding from the site or arm swelling.

name: Insulin initiation and injection technique training

indications: Starting insulin for type 1 or type 2 diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy
Poor glucose control linked to injection technique or lipohypertrophy
Change of insulin device or regimen
contraindications: None absolute; delay training if the patient is acutely unwell or unable to take in information
equipment: Insulin pen or vial and syringes as prescribed (training device if available)
Pen needles or insulin syringes of suitable length
Sharps container or safe alternative (thick plastic bottle)
Written or pictorial instructions in the patient's language
steps: Confirm identity, the prescribed insulin regimen and who will give the injections (patient or carer).
Explain what insulin does and the importance of regular meals and glucose monitoring.
Demonstrate hand hygiene and checking the insulin type, expiry date and appearance.
Show how to mix cloudy insulin by rolling, attach a needle and prime the pen, or draw up from a vial using a syringe that matches the vial strength (U-40 or U-100).
Teach injection sites (abdomen, thigh, upper arm, buttock) and rotation to avoid lumps.
Demonstrate injecting at 90 degrees, with a skin lift where needed, and holding the needle in for ten seconds.
Ask the patient or carer to give the first injection under supervision.
Teach home glucose testing and how to record results in the diary.
Explain recognition and treatment of hypoglycaemia with fast-acting sugar and when to call for help.
Explain sick-day rules and never stopping insulin without advice.
Teach safe needle disposal and insulin storage without a fridge (cool clay pot or cool place out of sunlight).
Check understanding with teach-back and arrange follow-up.
aftercare: Check blood glucose as advised and bring the diary to every visit.
Always carry sugar or a sweet drink.
Rotate sites and check for lumps.
Keep insulin cool and out of direct sunlight.
red_flags: Return urgently or call for help for repeated hypoglycaemia, confusion or fits.
Return for persistently high glucose, vomiting, abdominal pain or fast breathing (possible DKA).
Return if insulin cannot be obtained or stored safely.

indications: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state as directed by protocol
contraindications: Starting insulin before potassium is known and adequate (correct potassium first if low)
equipment: Infusion pump or syringe driver (or burette and drip counting if no pump)
Two IV cannulas and fluid giving sets
Short-acting insulin and potassium per protocol
Glucometer and ketone meter or urine ketone strips
Blood gas, electrolyte and kidney function sample bottles
Fluid balance and DKA monitoring chart
steps: Confirm identity and diagnosis with glucose, ketones and blood gas or bicarbonate.
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, consciousness and hydration, and weigh children.
Insert IV access and send glucose, electrolytes, kidney function, blood gas, a malaria test and a septic screen as needed.
Start IV fluids per adult or paediatric DKA protocol.
Check potassium and add potassium replacement to fluids per protocol before or with insulin.
Prepare the insulin infusion per local protocol, label it clearly and start it at the weight-based rate, with no insulin bolus; in children start once fluids are running.
Continue long-acting insulin if the patient already takes it, per protocol.
Check capillary glucose hourly and ketones and electrolytes as the protocol directs.
Add glucose-containing fluid when glucose falls to the protocol threshold, keeping the insulin running.
Monitor fluid balance, consciousness and observations, watching children closely for cerebral oedema.
Identify and treat the precipitating cause such as infection or missed insulin.
Switch to subcutaneous insulin only when ketoacidosis has resolved and the patient is eating, overlapping before stopping the infusion.
aftercare: Review insulin doses, injection technique and supplies before discharge.
Teach sick-day rules and when to test ketones.
Arrange diabetes clinic follow-up.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for headache, falling consciousness, bradycardia or rising blood pressure in a child (possible cerebral oedema).
Escalate for hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia or arrhythmia on the monitor.
Escalate if acidosis or ketones are not improving at the expected rate.
Return after discharge for vomiting, abdominal pain, fast breathing or high glucose.

indications: Annual screening of every person with diabetes
New foot symptoms, deformity or skin changes in diabetes
contraindications: None; avoid monofilament testing over ulcers, callus or scars
steps: Confirm identity and ask about foot symptoms, previous ulcers, amputation and footwear.
Remove shoes and socks from both feet and perform hand hygiene.
Inspect both feet, including between the toes, for skin breaks, callus, fungal infection, deformity and colour change.
Check the footwear for fit, foreign objects and wear.
Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses on both sides.
Demonstrate the monofilament on the patient's hand, then test the standard sites on each foot with eyes closed.
Test vibration sense at the great toe with the tuning fork.
Classify foot risk using the local risk categories.
Give foot-care education and plan follow-up and referral according to the risk.
aftercare: Inspect your feet daily, using a mirror or a relative if needed.
Wash and dry the feet carefully, especially between the toes.
Never walk barefoot and wear well-fitting shoes.
Do not cut corns or use chemical treatments yourself.
red_flags: Refer the same day for an ulcer with infection, spreading redness, gangrene or a hot swollen foot.
Return immediately for any new wound, blister, colour change or swelling of the foot.

indications: Diabetic foot ulcer with slough, callus or non-viable tissue
Ulcer needing assessment of depth and probe-to-bone
contraindications: Critical limb ischaemia without vascular assessment (avoid aggressive debridement)
Severe spreading infection or gas gangrene needing surgical debridement in theatre
Uncontrolled bleeding risk
equipment: Sterile dressing pack, scalpel (size 10 or 15 blade), forceps and scissors
Wound swab or tissue sample container
Ruler or wound measuring guide and camera if allowed
steps: Confirm identity and consent, and check pulses, glucose control and any recent imaging.
Perform hand hygiene, position the foot with good light and put on protective equipment.
Remove the old dressing and inspect the ulcer and the surrounding skin.
Measure the ulcer length, width and depth and probe for bone.
Clean the wound with saline.
Remove callus around the edge and slough or dead tissue with the scalpel until bleeding healthy tissue is reached.
Stop debridement if the patient feels pain or tissue appears ischaemic.
Take a deep tissue sample for culture if infection is suspected, after cleaning.
Control bleeding with pressure.
Apply a suitable moist dressing and an offloading device or shoe.
Record the ulcer size, grade and plan, and arrange the next review.
aftercare: Keep weight off the foot and use the offloading device as advised.
Keep the dressing clean and dry and attend dressing changes.
Keep glucose under control and take antibiotics if prescribed.
red_flags: Stop and refer if bone, tendon or pus tracking is found, or the foot looks ischaemic.
Refer urgently for spreading redness, fever, crepitus, black tissue or a foul smell.
Return for increasing pain, swelling, discharge or bleeding.

indications: Suspected peripheral arterial disease
Assessment before compression bandaging for leg ulcers
Diabetic foot risk assessment
contraindications: Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Severe pain or ulceration where the cuff would be placed
equipment: Handheld Doppler probe (8 MHz) and ultrasound gel
steps: Confirm identity and explain the test, asking the patient to avoid smoking beforehand.
Lay the patient flat and rest for at least ten minutes.
Measure the brachial systolic pressure in both arms with the Doppler and use the higher value.
Place the cuff just above the ankle on the first leg.
Locate the dorsalis pedis signal with gel and Doppler, inflate the cuff until the signal disappears, then deflate slowly and record when it returns.
Repeat for the posterior tibial artery.
Repeat on the other leg.
Calculate ABPI for each leg as the higher ankle pressure divided by the higher brachial pressure.
Interpret the result, noting that calcified vessels in diabetes can give falsely high readings.
Clean the gel off and explain the result and plan to the patient.
aftercare: Stop smoking and keep walking as advised.
Attend follow-up for the result and any vascular referral.
red_flags: Refer urgently if ABPI is very low or there is rest pain, gangrene or a cold pale foot.
Return for new rest pain, a non-healing wound or colour change in the foot.

indications: Suspected peripheral neuropathy
Suspected entrapment neuropathy such as carpal tunnel syndrome
Suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome or other demyelinating disease
Nerve injury assessment
contraindications: Broken skin or infection at stimulation sites
Caution with implanted cardiac devices near stimulation sites (follow local policy)
equipment: Conductive gel and skin preparation wipes
steps: Confirm identity, the clinical question and any pacemaker or bleeding risk.
Explain that brief electric pulses will be felt as tingling or a tap.
Position the patient comfortably and expose the limbs to be tested.
Check limb temperature and warm the limb if cold.
Clean the skin and place recording, reference and ground electrodes over the muscle or nerve.
Stimulate the nerve at standard points and record latency, amplitude and conduction velocity.
Measure distances between stimulation points with the tape.
Record sensory and motor responses and F-waves as indicated.
Test the opposite limb for comparison where needed.
Remove the electrodes and clean the skin.
Interpret the findings and write the report.
aftercare: Resume normal activity straight away.
Attend the clinic for the result.
red_flags: Stop if the patient cannot tolerate the stimulation or becomes unwell.
Escalate urgently if rapidly progressive weakness or breathing difficulty is noted (possible Guillain-Barre syndrome).

indications: Suspected epilepsy or classification of seizure type
Unexplained altered consciousness or suspected non-convulsive status
Encephalopathy assessment
contraindications: Scalp infection or open wounds at electrode sites
Avoid hyperventilation in sickle cell disease, recent stroke, raised intracranial pressure or significant heart or lung disease
equipment: EEG machine with electrodes and cap or paste electrodes
Measuring tape and skin preparation gel
steps: Confirm identity, the clinical question and medications, and ask whether the patient was sleep deprived if requested.
Explain the test and ask that hair is clean and free of oil or braids where possible.
Measure the head and mark electrode positions using the 10-20 system.
Prepare the skin and attach electrodes, checking impedances.
Record with the patient resting with eyes closed, then open and closed on request.
Perform hyperventilation for a few minutes unless contraindicated.
Perform photic stimulation at a range of frequencies.
Record drowsiness or sleep if it occurs or is required.
Note any clinical events with time marks.
Remove the electrodes and clean the paste from the hair.
Report the findings and correlate with the clinical history.
aftercare: Wash the hair to remove the paste.
Do not drive home if sleep deprived or after a seizure.
Attend the clinic for the result.
red_flags: Stop activation and give seizure first aid if a prolonged seizure occurs, escalating per protocol.
Escalate if the recording suggests non-convulsive status epilepticus.

indications: Suspected myopathy or motor neurone disease
Radiculopathy or plexopathy assessment
Neuromuscular junction disorder workup (with repetitive stimulation)
contraindications: Bleeding disorder or anticoagulation (relative; avoid deep muscles)
Skin infection over the muscles to be tested
Lymphoedema in the limb to be tested
steps: Confirm identity, the clinical question and bleeding risk.
Explain that a fine needle will be inserted into several muscles.
Position the patient and identify the muscles to be tested.
Perform hand hygiene, wear gloves and clean the skin.
Insert the needle into the muscle and record insertional and spontaneous activity at rest.
Ask the patient to contract the muscle gently, then strongly, and record motor unit potentials and recruitment.
Repeat in each selected muscle.
Remove the needle and apply pressure to each site.
Dispose of needles safely.
Interpret findings with any nerve conduction results and write the report.
aftercare: Expect mild soreness or small bruises for a day or two.
Take simple analgesia if needed.
red_flags: Stop if bleeding is persistent or the patient cannot tolerate the test.
Return for a swelling muscle, increasing pain or signs of infection at needle sites.

indications: Prescribed systemic anticancer treatment per an approved regimen
contraindications: Blood counts, kidney or liver function outside the regimen limits
Active uncontrolled infection
Pregnancy unless specifically planned by the oncology team
No signed prescription by an authorised prescriber
equipment: Prescribed chemotherapy prepared in a safety cabinet and labelled
Infusion pump and compatible giving sets
IV cannula or access to a central or port line
Personal protective equipment (chemotherapy gloves, gown, eye protection)
Spill kit and cytotoxic waste bin
steps: Confirm identity, consent, regimen, cycle number, weight, height and the signed prescription.
Check that blood counts, kidney and liver function meet the regimen criteria.
Confirm premedication such as antiemetics has been given as prescribed.
Perform an independent two-person check of drug, dose, route, rate, volume and expiry against the prescription.
Put on protective equipment.
Secure venous access and confirm good blood return and free flow with saline.
Administer each drug in the order and at the rate prescribed, using the pump.
For vesicant drugs, check blood return frequently and watch the site throughout.
Monitor observations and watch for infusion reactions, especially with the first doses.
Flush the line between drugs and at the end as prescribed.
Dispose of all equipment as cytotoxic waste.
Record drugs given, times and any reactions, and give the patient written advice and contact numbers.
aftercare: Take antiemetics and other take-home medicines as prescribed.
Drink plenty of fluids and avoid people with infections.
Use separate or carefully cleaned toilets and wash hands after body fluids for 48 hours.
Attend for the next blood test and cycle.
red_flags: Stop the infusion immediately for pain, burning or swelling at the cannula site (possible extravasation) and follow the extravasation protocol.
Stop and treat for rash, breathlessness, chest tightness or hypotension (infusion reaction).
Return immediately for fever or feeling shivery and unwell (possible neutropenic sepsis).
Return for persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers, bleeding or bruising.

form.label: Blood results checked and within limits

indications: Guillain-Barre syndrome or myasthenic crisis
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Hyperviscosity syndrome
Selected autoimmune kidney or neurological diseases as advised by specialists
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability or uncontrolled sepsis
No suitable vascular access
Known allergy to replacement fluids without an alternative
equipment: Apheresis machine or dialysis machine with plasma filter, or manual centrifugation setup
Large-bore dual-lumen catheter or two large peripheral cannulas
Replacement fluid (albumin or fresh frozen plasma per indication)
Monitor for pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent and the exchange prescription, including volume and replacement fluid.
Check blood count, clotting, calcium and fibrinogen before the session.
Secure vascular access and check that it flows well.
Prime the circuit per the machine protocol.
Record baseline observations.
Start the exchange, removing plasma and returning cells with replacement fluid at the set ratio.
Monitor observations frequently and ask about tingling around the mouth or fingers (low calcium).
Give calcium replacement per protocol and slow the procedure if symptoms occur.
Complete the prescribed exchange volume and return blood from the circuit.
Lock and dress the catheter aseptically.
Record exchange volume, fluids used and any reactions.
aftercare: Rest after the session.
Look after the catheter and keep the dressing dry.
Report any bleeding, fever or new weakness.
red_flags: Stop for hypotension, chest pain, breathlessness, rash or severe tingling and cramps.
Escalate for suspected line infection, bleeding or allergic reaction to plasma.
Return for fever, rigors or redness at the catheter site.

indications: Iron deficiency anaemia not responding to or not tolerating oral iron
Need for rapid iron replacement (e.g. late pregnancy, before surgery, chronic kidney disease)
contraindications: Anaemia not due to iron deficiency or iron overload
Previous serious reaction to IV iron
First trimester of pregnancy
Active infection or bacteraemia
equipment: IV cannula and infusion set or pump
Normal saline for dilution and flushing
steps: Confirm identity, the prescription, the iron deficiency results and any previous reactions.
Check the patient has not taken oral iron today and is not acutely unwell.
Ensure staff and resuscitation equipment are available.
Record baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and oxygen saturation.
Insert an IV cannula and check it flushes freely.
Prepare the infusion per the product instructions and local protocol.
Start the infusion at the prescribed rate.
Monitor observations during and for at least 30 minutes after the infusion.
Watch the cannula site for leakage, which can stain the skin.
Flush the line and remove the cannula once observations are stable.
Record the product, batch, volume and any reaction.
aftercare: Stop oral iron unless told to continue.
Expect mild aches or headache for a day or two.
Attend for a blood count recheck as advised.
red_flags: Stop the infusion for rash, breathlessness, chest tightness, facial swelling or hypotension and treat as a reaction.
Stop if there is pain or brown discolouration at the cannula site.
Return for fever, rash or breathlessness after leaving.

indications: Immune thrombocytopenia with bleeding or before procedures
Guillain-Barre syndrome or myasthenic crisis
Kawasaki disease
Primary immunodeficiency replacement therapy
contraindications: Previous anaphylaxis to immunoglobulin
IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (use IgA-depleted product)
Caution with kidney impairment, heart failure or thrombosis risk
equipment: IV cannula and normal saline flush
steps: Confirm identity, consent, indication, prescription and weight.
Check kidney function and hydration status and give fluids if prescribed.
Give any prescribed premedication.
Bring the product to room temperature and check name, batch and expiry with a second staff member.
Record baseline observations.
Start the infusion slowly and increase the rate stepwise per the product schedule if tolerated.
Check observations at each rate change and regularly through the infusion.
Slow or stop the infusion if the patient develops headache, chills, flushing or back pain.
Flush the line at the end and observe the patient after completion.
Record product, batch number, volume, rates and any reactions.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids for the next day.
Take simple analgesia for mild headache.
Attend follow-up blood tests as advised.
red_flags: Stop and treat for breathlessness, wheeze, hypotension or facial swelling (anaphylaxis).
Return urgently for severe headache with neck stiffness, chest pain, leg swelling, weakness or reduced urine output.

indications: Transfusional iron overload (e.g. thalassaemia, sickle cell disease on chronic transfusion)
contraindications: Known severe allergy to desferrioxamine
Active infection (pause chelation during febrile illness per specialist advice, especially with suspected Yersinia)
equipment: Prescribed desferrioxamine prepared per pharmacy instructions
Portable infusion pump or balloon infuser
Subcutaneous butterfly needle or infusion set
Alcohol swabs, gloves and transparent dressing
steps: Confirm identity, the prescription and the latest ferritin, and ask about eye or hearing problems.
Teach the patient or carer hand hygiene and preparation of the infusion per pharmacy instructions.
Load the syringe or infuser and connect the infusion set, priming the line.
Choose a site on the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, rotating sites each night.
Clean the skin, insert the needle subcutaneously and secure it with a transparent dressing.
Start the pump and set the infusion over the prescribed number of hours.
Check the site for redness or swelling during the infusion.
Remove the needle when the infusion ends and dispose of it safely.
Supervise the first self-administered infusion and check understanding.
Arrange regular eye, hearing and ferritin monitoring.
aftercare: Rotate infusion sites and report painful lumps.
Keep the chelation diary and bring it to clinic.
Stop the infusion and seek advice if you develop fever.
red_flags: Stop and seek advice urgently for fever, abdominal pain or diarrhoea (possible Yersinia infection).
Return for changes in vision or hearing.
Stop and return for a rash, breathlessness or facial swelling.

indications: Suspected adrenal insufficiency (primary or secondary)
Assessment of adrenal recovery after long-term steroid therapy
contraindications: Known allergy to tetracosactide
Suspected adrenal crisis (treat first, do not delay treatment for the test)
Caution in asthma or other allergic disorders
equipment: IV cannula, syringes and saline flush
Serum cortisol bottles labelled with timed samples
Request form noting time of each sample
steps: Confirm identity and the request, and check whether the patient takes steroids or oestrogen-containing medicines that affect results.
Arrange the test in the morning if possible and hold steroids per specialist instructions.
Insert an IV cannula and take a baseline cortisol sample (and ACTH if requested).
Give tetracosactide IV or IM as prescribed and record the exact time.
Observe the patient for allergic reactions.
Take cortisol samples at 30 and 60 minutes after the injection as per local protocol.
Label each sample with the exact time and send them to the laboratory together.
Remove the cannula and restart steroids as advised.
aftercare: Restart steroids if they were held, as instructed.
Carry a steroid card if already on steroids.
Attend for the result.
red_flags: Treat immediately and do not wait for results if the patient becomes hypotensive, vomiting or confused (possible adrenal crisis).
Stop and treat for rash, wheeze or facial swelling.

indications: Polyuria and polydipsia with suspected diabetes insipidus
Distinguishing cranial from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and primary polydipsia
contraindications: Serum sodium already high or dehydration at baseline (diagnosis may be made without the test)
Untreated adrenal or thyroid insufficiency
Unable to supervise the patient closely throughout
equipment: Urine collection containers and measuring jug
Blood bottles for sodium and osmolality
Prescribed desmopressin for the second phase
Monitoring chart for weight, urine volume, pulse and blood pressure
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent and that adrenal and thyroid function have been checked.
Start in the morning in a supervised unit after any overnight fluid plan per protocol.
Weigh the patient and take baseline blood and urine samples for sodium and osmolality.
Stop all fluid intake and supervise the patient continuously to prevent hidden drinking.
Record weight, urine volume and urine osmolality at regular intervals per protocol.
Check plasma sodium and osmolality at the set times.
Stop the deprivation phase if weight falls by the protocol limit, sodium rises above the limit or the patient becomes unwell.
Give desmopressin as prescribed at the end of the deprivation phase.
Allow measured fluids and continue urine osmolality sampling per protocol.
Record all results on the chart and interpret them with the endocrine team.
aftercare: Drink normally once the test is complete unless advised otherwise.
Follow any new treatment instructions carefully to avoid low sodium.
red_flags: Stop the test for weight loss beyond the protocol limit, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion or high sodium.
Return for headache, confusion or vomiting after starting treatment (possible low sodium).

form.label: Urine osmolality at end of deprivation

indications: Suspected Cushing's syndrome
Adrenal incidentaloma assessment
contraindications: Acute illness, severe stress or alcohol excess that can give false results (defer)
Medicines that alter dexamethasone metabolism or cortisol binding (review first)
equipment: Serum cortisol bottles and request form
steps: Confirm identity and indication and review medicines such as oral contraceptives, anticonvulsants and rifampicin that affect results.
Give clear written instructions for the timing of the tablet and the blood test.
The patient takes the prescribed dexamethasone late in the evening (overnight test) or at set times (two-day test).
Take the serum cortisol sample the next morning at the time stated in the protocol.
Record the exact time the tablet was taken and the time of the blood sample.
Send the sample to the laboratory with the timing details.
Interpret the result with the endocrine team.
aftercare: Resume usual medicines as normal.
Attend for the result.
red_flags: Repeat the test if the tablet was missed or taken at the wrong time.
Return for severe headache, very high blood pressure or high glucose symptoms while waiting.

indications: Suspected inflammatory myopathy
Suspected muscular dystrophy or metabolic myopathy
Suspected vasculitis involving muscle
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy
Infection over the chosen site
Muscle recently tested by needle EMG at the same site (choose another site)
equipment: Minor operation pack or muscle biopsy needle
Specimen containers (formalin, saline-moist gauze, and frozen sample transport as the lab requires)
steps: Confirm identity, consent and the laboratory requirements for sample handling before starting.
Choose a moderately affected muscle (commonly quadriceps or deltoid) not recently needled.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and gown, clean and drape the site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into skin and subcutaneous tissue, avoiding the muscle itself.
Make a skin incision along the muscle fibres and open the fascia.
Remove a small block of muscle along the fibre direction, or take cores with the biopsy needle.
Handle the sample gently and divide it for histology, frozen section and other tests as required.
Achieve haemostasis and close the fascia and skin.
Apply a dressing and label the samples.
Send samples promptly with clinical details.
aftercare: Keep the wound dry for 48 hours.
Avoid strenuous exercise of the limb for a few days.
Return for suture removal as advised.
red_flags: Escalate for bleeding through the dressing or an expanding haematoma.
Return for fever, increasing pain, redness or discharge from the wound.

indications: Type 1 diabetes or insulin-treated diabetes needing closer glucose monitoring
Recurrent or unrecognised hypoglycaemia
Diabetes in pregnancy where available
contraindications: Skin infection, scarring or lipohypertrophy at the site
Planned MRI or CT while wearing the sensor (remove first)
equipment: Sensor and applicator kit within expiry
steps: Confirm identity and that the patient or carer has a reader or compatible phone.
Choose the site recommended by the manufacturer (back of the upper arm or abdomen), away from injection sites.
Perform hand hygiene and clean the skin with an alcohol wipe and let it dry.
Prepare the applicator per the manufacturer's instructions.
Apply the sensor firmly to the skin and release the applicator.
Check the sensor is secure and apply an overpatch if needed.
Start the sensor with the reader or app and explain the warm-up period.
Teach how to scan or read results, set alarms and confirm unusual readings with a finger-prick test.
Record the insertion date and planned removal date.
aftercare: Confirm symptoms of low glucose with a finger-prick test.
Remove the sensor before MRI or CT scans.
Replace the sensor on the date advised by the manufacturer.
red_flags: Remove the sensor and seek advice for redness, pain, swelling or discharge at the site.
Treat hypoglycaemia immediately and seek help for repeated low readings.

indications: Acute ischaemic stroke with disabling deficit within the licensed time window and haemorrhage excluded on CT
contraindications: Intracranial haemorrhage on CT or history suggesting subarachnoid haemorrhage
Onset time beyond the treatment window or unknown (unless imaging criteria met)
Recent major surgery, head injury, stroke or gastrointestinal bleeding
Uncontrolled high blood pressure despite treatment
No CT scanner, or no stroke unit or monitored bed for the following 24 hours (refer instead)
Low platelets, anticoagulation with abnormal clotting or very abnormal glucose
equipment: Infusion pump and two IV cannulas
Accurate weighing scale or weight estimate method
Cardiac monitor and blood pressure machine
NIHSS chart and stroke thrombolysis checklist
Antihypertensives and emergency trolley per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, the exact time last seen well and the stroke diagnosis using a stroke scale.
Check glucose and send urgent blood count, clotting and kidney function without delaying CT.
Obtain an urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage.
Work through the thrombolysis inclusion and exclusion checklist.
Discuss benefits and bleeding risks with the patient or family and record consent.
Lower blood pressure to within protocol limits if needed before treatment.
Calculate the dose by weight per protocol and have it checked by a second clinician.
Give the bolus and infusion per protocol and record the start time.
Monitor neurological status and blood pressure frequently per protocol during and after treatment.
Avoid antiplatelets, anticoagulants, arterial punctures and urinary catheters for the protocol period.
Repeat CT head before starting antithrombotic treatment, usually at 24 hours.
aftercare: Stay on the stroke unit or high-dependency area for close monitoring.
Swallow screen before eating or drinking.
Start stroke prevention treatment after the follow-up scan if advised.
red_flags: Stop the infusion and get urgent CT for worsening neurology, severe headache, vomiting or sudden high blood pressure.
Stop and treat for tongue or lip swelling (angio-oedema) or anaphylaxis.
Escalate for any significant bleeding.

indications: Acute stroke before any oral intake or medicines
Reduced consciousness recovering, neurological disease or suspected dysphagia
contraindications: Drowsy or unable to sit upright and stay alert
Absent cough or unable to manage own secretions (keep nil by mouth and refer)
steps: Confirm identity and that the patient is alert and can sit upright at 90 degrees.
Check oral hygiene, ability to manage saliva, voice quality and voluntary cough.
Give a teaspoon of water and watch for coughing, choking, wet voice or breathlessness.
Repeat with teaspoons of water up to three times if safe.
If teaspoons are passed, give a small cup of water to drink in sips.
Watch for delayed coughing and a wet or gurgly voice for a minute after each trial.
Stop immediately at any sign of aspiration.
Record the result and set the diet and medicine route accordingly.
Refer to speech and language therapy or a trained clinician if failed, and consider nasogastric feeding.
aftercare: Sit fully upright to eat and drink and for 30 minutes after.
Follow the diet texture advised and do not give food or drink if nil by mouth.
Check the mouth is clear after meals.
red_flags: Stop and keep nil by mouth for coughing, choking, wet voice or fall in oxygen saturation.
Escalate for fever, new cough or breathlessness (possible aspiration pneumonia).

form.label: Alert and able to sit upright

indications: Suspected IgE-mediated food, inhalant or insect allergy
Allergic rhinitis or asthma with suspected triggers
contraindications: Recent antihistamine use (stop for the advised period before testing)
Widespread eczema or dermographism at test sites
Unstable asthma or recent anaphylaxis
Pregnancy (defer unless essential)
equipment: Standardised allergen extracts with positive (histamine) and negative (saline) controls
steps: Confirm identity, the history and that antihistamines have been stopped for the required time.
Check for current wheeze and record a peak flow in asthmatic patients.
Seat the patient with the forearm (or back in young children) exposed and clean the skin.
Mark and number test sites at least 2 cm apart.
Place a drop of each allergen and the controls at the marked sites.
Prick through each drop with a new lancet, then blot excess solution.
Wait the recommended time, usually 15 minutes, observing the patient.
Measure the wheal diameter for each site and record it.
Interpret results against the controls and the clinical history.
Observe the patient for a period after the test before they leave.
aftercare: Avoid scratching the sites; itching settles within a few hours.
Restart antihistamines after the test if needed.
Follow the allergen avoidance advice given.
red_flags: Stop and treat immediately for wheeze, throat tightness, widespread hives or faintness (anaphylaxis).
Return for delayed swelling or breathing difficulty after leaving.

indications: Blood tests requested for diagnosis or monitoring
Pre-operative or pre-transfusion blood work
Therapeutic drug level monitoring
contraindications: Limb with an arteriovenous fistula or on the side of an axillary node clearance
Arm with an infusion running (sample from the other arm)
Infected, burnt, oedematous or scarred skin at the site
equipment: Vacuum tube holder and needle or 21-23 G needle and syringe
23-25 G butterfly set for small or fragile veins and children
Correct sample tubes for the tests requested
Gauze or cotton wool and plaster
steps: Check the request, confirm patient identity with two identifiers and check fasting status if required.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, and for a child involve the carer and plan holding and distraction.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Position the arm supported and extended and apply the tourniquet a hand's width above the site.
Palpate to select a straight, bouncy vein and avoid sites listed as contraindications.
Clean the skin and let it dry completely without touching it again.
Anchor the vein below the site by stretching the skin with the non-dominant thumb.
Insert the needle bevel up at a shallow angle in line with the vein.
Fill tubes in the correct order of draw and invert each gently as it fills.
Release the tourniquet before withdrawing the needle and keep total tourniquet time to about one minute.
Withdraw the needle, apply pressure with gauze and activate the safety device.
Dispose of sharps immediately into the sharps container.
Label every tube at the bedside before leaving the patient and check against the request form.
Check the site for bleeding, apply a plaster and send samples to the laboratory promptly.
aftercare: Advise pressure for a few minutes and longer if the patient is on anticoagulants.
Advise the patient to report swelling, numbness or pain at the site.
Document the attempts, site and any problems.
red_flags: Fainting or vasovagal collapse during sampling
Severe shooting pain or numbness suggesting nerve injury (stop immediately)
Bright red pulsatile blood suggesting arterial puncture
Expanding haematoma or compartment-type swelling
Needlestick injury to staff (follow post-exposure protocol)

form.label: Labelling
options: Labelled and checked by second person

indications: Suspected sepsis or bacteraemia
Fever with no clear source, including suspected typhoid fever
Suspected endocarditis or line infection
Fever in a neonate or immunocompromised patient
contraindications: None absolute; avoid sampling through an existing line unless line infection is suspected
equipment: Aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles (paediatric bottle for small children)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation and separate wipe for bottle tops
Sterile gloves or non-touch technique supplies
Butterfly set with culture holder or needle and syringe
Request form with clinical details and antibiotic history
steps: Confirm identity, the indication and whether antibiotics have been started, and ideally sample before the first dose.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Check bottle expiry dates and mark the fill line on each bottle.
Perform hand hygiene, remove bottle caps and disinfect the tops and let them dry.
Apply the tourniquet and select a vein, and do not use a site above an infusion.
Clean the skin with chlorhexidine-alcohol for about thirty seconds and let it dry fully without repalpating.
Perform venepuncture with an aseptic non-touch technique.
Inoculate the aerobic bottle first with a butterfly set or the anaerobic bottle first with a syringe.
Fill each bottle to the recommended volume for adult or paediatric bottles and do not overfill.
Collect any other blood tubes only after the culture bottles.
Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, apply pressure and dispose of sharps.
Label bottles with patient details, site, date and time without covering the barcode.
Collect a second set from a separate site if two sets are requested.
Send bottles to the laboratory promptly at room temperature and do not refrigerate.
aftercare: Start or continue empirical antibiotics without delay in suspected sepsis.
Follow up the culture result and adjust antibiotics to sensitivities.
Document the number of sets, sites and time of collection.
red_flags: Signs of septic shock (escalate immediately; do not delay antibiotics to obtain cultures)
Neonate with fever, poor feeding or lethargy
Positive culture reported by the laboratory (review the patient the same day)

form.label: Antibiotics before sampling
options: On antibiotics for more than 24 hours

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Assessment of oxygenation and ventilation in respiratory failure
Assessment of acid-base status in sepsis, DKA, poisoning or renal failure
Monitoring of a patient on oxygen or ventilation
contraindications: Abnormal modified Allen test at the radial site
Infection, burn or arteriovenous fistula at the site
Severe coagulopathy (relative; use a compressible site and senior operator)
equipment: Pre-heparinised arterial blood gas syringe with cap
Rolled towel to support wrist extension
Sharps container and ice if analysis is delayed
steps: Confirm identity, indication and current oxygen therapy, and note the inspired oxygen.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, warning that it may be painful.
Perform a modified Allen test at the radial artery and choose another site if it is abnormal.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and extend the wrist over a rolled towel.
Clean the skin and consider local anaesthetic infiltration if time allows.
Palpate the radial pulse with two fingers and insert the needle bevel up at about 45 degrees towards the pulse.
Allow the syringe to fill by arterial pressure and stop once the required volume is reached.
Withdraw the needle and apply firm pressure for at least five minutes, longer if anticoagulated.
Remove the needle safely, expel any air bubbles and cap the syringe.
Roll the syringe gently to mix and label it with patient details, time and oxygen delivery.
Analyse within fifteen minutes or send on ice if there will be a delay.
Check the distal circulation and the puncture site before leaving.
aftercare: Interpret results in light of the inspired oxygen and clinical picture.
Check the site again for haematoma after thirty minutes.
Advise the patient to report hand pain, coldness or numbness.
red_flags: Pale, cold or painful hand after puncture (urgent review)
Expanding haematoma at the site
Severe hypoxaemia, hypercapnia or acidosis on the result (escalate immediately)
Repeated failed attempts (stop and call a senior)

indications: Planned or possible blood transfusion
Pre-operative preparation for surgery with expected blood loss
Antenatal blood group and antibody screen
Major haemorrhage
contraindications: None; never pre-label tubes or take samples from two patients at the same time
equipment: EDTA tube or tube specified by the blood bank
Pen for handwritten label if required by local policy
steps: Confirm the indication and the number and type of units needed.
Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth and check against the identity band and request form, or use the band and a second person if the patient cannot respond.
Explain the procedure, obtain verbal consent and ask about previous transfusions and pregnancies.
Collect blood from one patient only, with no unlabelled tubes from other patients nearby.
Perform venepuncture into the correct tube and invert gently.
Label the tube at the bedside immediately with full name, hospital number, date of birth, date, time and your signature.
Do not pre-label tubes or use addressograph labels unless local policy allows.
Complete the request form fully including indication, urgency and transfusion history.
Recheck the label against the identity band and form before leaving the bedside.
Send the sample and form to the blood bank and inform them directly if urgent.
aftercare: Confirm with the blood bank that units are ready before the procedure or transfusion.
Ask relatives about donor availability where the blood bank requires replacement donors.
Record the sample time because samples are valid only for a limited period.
red_flags: Any doubt about identity or labelling (repeat the sample)
Blood bank reports antibodies or difficulty finding compatible blood (inform senior)
Active major bleeding (activate the major haemorrhage protocol)

form.label: Identity check
options: Patient stated name and DOB and band matched
Band checked - patient unable to state

indications: Screening for sickle cell disease or trait
Premarital or antenatal genotype screening
Child with anaemia, dactylitis, recurrent pain or jaundice
Family screening of a known sickle cell patient
contraindications: Recent blood transfusion within about three months (result may be unreliable; defer or note)
equipment: EDTA tube (small paediatric tube for infants)
steps: Confirm identity and the reason for the test, and ask about transfusion in the last three months.
Explain the test and its implications, including for family planning, and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Collect venous blood into the EDTA tube, or a heel-prick sample in small infants if the laboratory accepts it.
Invert the tube gently several times to mix.
Label the tube at the bedside and record transfusion history and age on the request form.
Send to the laboratory, noting that results in infants under six months may need repeating.
aftercare: Arrange post-test counselling when the result is ready.
Refer patients with sickle cell disease to the sickle cell clinic.
Offer screening to partners and family members where appropriate.
red_flags: Child with suspected sickle cell crisis (treat now; do not wait for the result)
Fever, severe pain, chest symptoms or pallor in a known sickle cell child
Result unclear or unexpected (send for confirmatory testing)

form.label: Labelling
options: Labelled and checked by second person

indications: Monitoring of warfarin therapy (INR)
Bleeding, bruising or suspected coagulopathy
Pre-procedure assessment in liver disease or sepsis
Suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation
contraindications: Do not sample from a heparinised line or above an infusion
equipment: Sodium citrate tube (light blue) within expiry
Discard tube if a butterfly set is used
steps: Confirm identity and record any anticoagulant the patient takes and the time of the last dose.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and apply the tourniquet for as short a time as possible.
Draw a discard tube first if using a butterfly set to remove air from the tubing.
Fill the citrate tube exactly to the fill line because under-filled tubes give false results.
Draw the citrate tube before serum or EDTA tubes in the order of draw.
Invert gently three to four times and do not shake.
Withdraw the needle and apply pressure, longer if the patient is anticoagulated.
Label at the bedside and send to the laboratory for analysis within four hours.
aftercare: Act on the INR or clotting result the same day for patients on warfarin.
Advise the patient to report prolonged bleeding from the site.
red_flags: Prolonged bleeding or large haematoma at the puncture site
Very high INR or abnormal clotting with active bleeding (urgent senior review)
Signs of DIC such as oozing from several sites

form.label: Labelling
options: Labelled and checked by second person

indications: Fever or history of fever in a malaria-endemic area
Suspected severe malaria
Confirmation of a rapid diagnostic test or monitoring parasite clearance
contraindications: None; do not delay treatment of severe malaria while waiting for the film
equipment: Clean grease-free glass slides with frosted end
Slide box or tray for air drying
Gloves, cotton wool and sharps container
Malaria rapid diagnostic test kit if available
steps: Confirm identity and ask about fever duration and any antimalarial already taken.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and label the slide with pencil.
Clean the side of the fingertip (heel in infants) and let it dry.
Prick firmly with the lancet and wipe away the first drop.
Place a small drop near the centre for the thin film and a larger drop or three drops towards the end for the thick film.
Spread the thin film with a spreader at about 45 degrees in one smooth movement.
Spread the thick drop into a circle the size of a small coin, thin enough to read print through.
Apply pressure to the puncture site and dispose of the lancet.
Air dry the slide flat, protected from flies and dust, and do not heat it.
Fix only the thin film if the laboratory requires it and keep fixative away from the thick film.
Send the slide to the laboratory for staining and reading, or perform an RDT alongside where used.
aftercare: Treat according to national malaria guidelines once confirmed, or immediately if severe.
Review results the same day.
Advise return if fever persists or the patient worsens.
red_flags: Signs of severe malaria such as prostration, convulsions, reduced consciousness, respiratory distress, jaundice, dark urine or severe anaemia
High parasite density reported
Pregnant woman or young child with malaria
Negative film with ongoing fever (repeat film and look for other causes)

form.label: Labelling
options: Labelled and checked by second person

indications: Unexplained anaemia, cytopenia or abnormal full blood count
Suspected haemolysis or haematological malignancy
Suspected sickle cell disease or red cell morphology abnormality
contraindications: None
equipment: EDTA tube or capillary sample equipment
Clean glass slides and spreader slide
steps: Confirm identity and the clinical question for the film.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and collect venous blood into an EDTA tube or a capillary drop.
Invert the EDTA tube gently to mix.
Make the smear within two to three hours of collection, or send the tube promptly for the laboratory to make it.
Place a small drop at one end of the slide and spread with a spreader at about 30-45 degrees in one smooth movement.
Check the film has a feathered edge and does not reach the slide edges.
Air dry the film and label it with pencil.
Send the slide and tube to the laboratory with clinical details.
aftercare: Review the film report together with the full blood count.
Refer to haematology if blasts or abnormal cells are reported.
