red_flags: Blasts or suspected leukaemia reported (urgent referral)
Evidence of severe haemolysis or schistocytes with low platelets
Severe anaemia with symptoms

form.label: Smear made by
options: Sent tube for laboratory to make

form.label: Labelling
options: Labelled and checked by second person

indications: Suspected lymphatic filariasis (lymphoedema, hydrocele, elephantiasis)
Eosinophilia in a resident of an endemic area
Mass drug administration surveillance
contraindications: None
equipment: Lancet or venepuncture equipment and EDTA tube
Gloves, alcohol swab and cotton wool
Filariasis antigen test kit if available
steps: Confirm identity and the suspected filarial infection, as timing differs by species.
Plan collection between 10 pm and 2 am for nocturnal Wuchereria, or around midday if Loa loa is suspected.
Explain why the sample is taken at night and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Collect a finger-prick or venous EDTA sample and record the exact time.
Make thick films with a measured volume of blood if the laboratory requires counting.
Air dry the slides, label them with pencil and send them with the EDTA tube.
Use an antigen rapid test as an alternative where available, as it does not need night sampling.
aftercare: Treat according to national filariasis programme guidelines.
Teach limb hygiene and skin care for lymphoedema.
Screen for onchocerciasis and Loa loa before treatment in co-endemic areas.
red_flags: Acute painful limb swelling with fever (acute adenolymphangitis)
Heavy Loa loa microfilaraemia reported before treatment (specialist advice)

form.label: Labelling
options: Labelled and checked by second person

indications: Screening for anaemia in antenatal or child clinics
Pre-donation donor screening
Rapid assessment of suspected severe anaemia or bleeding
contraindications: None; confirm unexpected results with a laboratory sample
equipment: Control cuvette or quality control material
steps: Confirm identity and check the meter has passed its daily quality control.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and warm the hand if cold.
Clean the side of the fingertip (heel in infants) and allow it to dry.
Prick firmly, wipe away the first two drops and let a large drop form without squeezing hard.
Fill the cuvette in one continuous action and wipe excess blood from the outside.
Check the cuvette for air bubbles and refill a new cuvette if present.
Place the cuvette in the meter and read the result within the time stated by the manufacturer.
Apply pressure to the puncture site and dispose of sharps and cuvette safely.
Record the result with units and act on it or refer.
aftercare: Treat or investigate anaemia according to local guidelines.
Repeat or send a laboratory full blood count if the result is unexpected.
red_flags: Very low haemoglobin or symptoms of heart failure (urgent review for transfusion)
Low haemoglobin in pregnancy or in a child with fever
Result inconsistent with the clinical picture (repeat or send laboratory sample)

indications: Monitoring glycaemic control in diabetes
Screening for diabetes where the method is validated for diagnosis
contraindications: Sickle cell disease or other haemoglobin variants (result may be unreliable)
Recent blood transfusion, haemolysis, severe anaemia or pregnancy (use other measures)
equipment: HbA1c analyser with in-date test cartridges
Capillary sampling device supplied with the kit
steps: Confirm identity, diabetes history and any haemoglobin variant, transfusion or anaemia.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Check the analyser quality control and that cartridges are at room temperature.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the fingertip.
Prick the finger, wipe away the first drop and collect the sample with the kit device.
Load the cartridge into the analyser immediately as instructed by the manufacturer.
Apply pressure to the finger and dispose of sharps safely.
Record the result with units and discuss it with the patient.
aftercare: Adjust the diabetes management plan with the patient.
Plan the next HbA1c in about three months.
red_flags: Very high HbA1c with symptoms of hyperglycaemia or ketosis (check glucose and ketones)
Result inconsistent with glucose readings (consider haemoglobin variant)

indications: High blood glucose in a person with diabetes
Suspected diabetic ketoacidosis
Monitoring treatment of DKA
Unwell child with diabetes, vomiting or abdominal pain
contraindications: None
equipment: Ketone meter with in-date ketone strips
Lancet and alcohol swab or water
steps: Confirm identity and check the meter and strips are in date and coded if required.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and wash or clean the fingertip and let it dry.
Insert the ketone strip into the meter.
Prick the side of the fingertip (heel in infants) and form a drop.
Apply the drop to the strip until the meter signals enough sample.
Read and record the result with units together with blood glucose.
Apply pressure and dispose of sharps safely.
Act on the result according to the local DKA or sick-day protocol.
aftercare: Repeat ketone checks at the interval set by the treatment protocol.
Teach sick-day rules to patients with diabetes.
red_flags: Blood ketones 3.0 mmol/L or more, or rising despite treatment (start DKA protocol and escalate)
Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep sighing breathing or drowsiness
Child with diabetes and any ketones who is unwell

indications: Screening for gestational diabetes
Diagnosis of diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance when fasting glucose is borderline
Screening in high-risk patients such as those with previous gestational diabetes
contraindications: Known diabetes or fasting glucose already in the diabetic range
Acute illness, vomiting or recent surgery
Previous gastric surgery (relative)
equipment: Standard glucose load for the test per local protocol (weight-based in children)
Water to dissolve the glucose and a cup
Fluoride oxalate (grey) tubes or glucose meter per local practice
Chair for the patient to rest during the test
steps: Confirm identity and that the patient has fasted overnight for 8 to 14 hours with only water.
Confirm normal carbohydrate intake in the preceding days and no acute illness.
Explain the test, the waiting time and the need to rest without smoking or eating, and obtain verbal consent.
Take the fasting blood sample, check a fasting glucose by meter first and do not give the glucose load if it is in the diabetic range.
Give the glucose load dissolved in water to drink within five minutes and note the start time.
Ask the patient to stay seated and rest for the duration of the test.
Take the timed samples (usually at two hours, and at one hour in pregnancy per local protocol).
Label each sample with the exact time and send all samples to the laboratory together.
Offer food and drink once the final sample is taken.
aftercare: Interpret results against national or WHO criteria for the population tested.
Refer positive results to the diabetes or antenatal clinic.
red_flags: Patient vomits the glucose drink (stop the test and rebook)
Symptoms of hypoglycaemia or fainting during the test
Fasting glucose already in the diabetic range (stop and do not give glucose)

indications: Newborn screening for sickle cell disease or other conditions
Early infant HIV diagnosis
Programme testing such as viral load where venous samples are impractical
contraindications: Do not prick the back of the heel, previous puncture sites or an infected or oedematous heel
equipment: Filter paper card within expiry and with request details
Sterile heel lancet of the correct depth for the infant's size
steps: Confirm infant identity with the carer and complete the card details without touching the filter circles.
Explain the test to the carer and obtain verbal consent.
Warm the heel, position the infant with the leg lower than the heart and offer breastfeeding for comfort.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the outer or inner side of the plantar heel and let it dry.
Puncture with the heel lancet and wipe away the first drop.
Let a large drop form and touch it to the circle from one side only until it soaks through completely.
Fill each circle with a single application and do not layer drops or touch the card to the skin.
Apply pressure to the heel and dispose of the lancet safely.
Dry the card horizontally at room temperature away from sunlight and heat for at least three hours.
Pack the dry card in a bag with desiccant and send it with the programme register.
aftercare: Tell the carer when and how results will be returned.
Record the card number in the infant's record and follow up the result.
red_flags: Positive screening result (recall the infant and refer promptly)
Card rejected for poor quality (recall for a repeat sample)
Prolonged bleeding or heel infection

indications: Suspected urinary tract infection
Urinalysis abnormality needing microscopy or culture
Antenatal screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria
contraindications: None; use a catheter or suprapubic sample when a clean catch is not possible
equipment: Sterile wide-mouthed urine container with lid
Water or saline for cleaning the genital area
Urine collection bag or clean-catch pot for young children
steps: Confirm identity and record symptoms and any antibiotics already taken.
Explain the clean-catch method and obtain verbal consent.
Ask the patient to wash hands and clean the genital area with water from front to back.
Ask a woman to separate the labia, or a man to retract the foreskin, while passing urine.
Pass the first part of the stream into the toilet without stopping.
Collect the middle part of the stream into the sterile container without touching the inside.
Pass the remaining urine into the toilet and close the lid firmly.
In infants use a clean-catch technique while the nappy is off, or a sterile bag only if no other method is possible.
Label the container with patient details, date, time and method of collection.
Send to the laboratory within two hours or refrigerate if delayed.
aftercare: Start treatment if indicated and review the culture result.
Advise fluids and return if symptoms worsen.
red_flags: Fever, loin pain or rigors suggesting pyelonephritis
Infant or young child with fever and a positive urine (same-day medical review)
Pregnant woman with urinary infection
Visible blood in urine without infection

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Suspected urinary tract infection
Antenatal visit screening for protein and glucose
Hypertension, diabetes or kidney disease assessment
Unexplained abdominal pain or haematuria
contraindications: None
equipment: In-date reagent strips stored in the closed original container
Fresh urine in a clean container
steps: Confirm identity and that the urine sample is fresh, ideally within an hour.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Check the strip expiry date and replace the container lid straight away.
Put on gloves and mix the urine gently.
Dip the strip briefly so all pads are wet and remove it at once.
Run the edge of the strip on the container rim to remove excess urine and hold it horizontally.
Read each pad against the colour chart at the time specified by the manufacturer.
Record each result and send the urine for culture or microscopy if needed.
Dispose of the strip and urine safely and perform hand hygiene.
aftercare: Act on abnormal results and send a sample for culture when infection is suspected.
Repeat abnormal protein or blood on a fresh sample.
red_flags: Proteinuria in pregnancy with raised blood pressure (assess for pre-eclampsia)
Glucose and ketones in an unwell patient (check blood glucose and ketones)
Blood in urine without infection (investigate)

indications: Missed period or suspected pregnancy
Before imaging, surgery or medicines that may harm a pregnancy
Abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding in a woman of reproductive age
contraindications: None
equipment: In-date hCG test cassette or strip
steps: Confirm identity and record the date of the last menstrual period.
Explain the test, its purpose and confidentiality, and obtain verbal consent, with age-appropriate safeguarding for adolescents.
Use an early-morning urine sample if possible as it is more concentrated.
Put on gloves and check the kit expiry date.
Add the stated number of drops to the sample well or dip the strip to the marked line.
Read the result at the time stated by the manufacturer and not later.
Confirm a control line is present, otherwise the test is invalid and must be repeated.
Treat any visible test line, however faint, as positive.
Share the result privately and record it.
aftercare: Arrange antenatal booking or counselling as appropriate.
Repeat in a few days if negative but pregnancy is still suspected.
red_flags: Positive test with abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or bleeding (exclude ectopic pregnancy urgently)
Adolescent pregnancy with safeguarding concerns

indications: Quantifying protein loss in kidney disease or pre-eclampsia
Creatinine clearance estimation
Investigation of kidney stones or hormone excess
contraindications: Patient unable to collect reliably without catheter (consider spot protein-creatinine ratio instead)
equipment: Labelled 24-hour urine container with preservative if required by the test
Smaller jug or pot for collecting each void
steps: Confirm identity and the tests requested, and check with the laboratory whether a preservative is needed.
Explain the method and obtain verbal consent, warning about any preservative in the container.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder into the toilet at the start time and record that time.
Collect every void for the next 24 hours into the container using the jug.
Ask the patient to pass urine into the container at the same time the next day to finish.
Keep the container closed and cool during the collection.
Record any missed voids, as the collection must be restarted if urine is lost.
Label the container with start and finish times and send it to the laboratory promptly.
Send a blood creatinine sample at the same time if creatinine clearance is requested.
aftercare: Review the result against the total urine volume.
Repeat the collection if it was incomplete.
red_flags: Very low urine output during the collection (assess for acute kidney injury)
Heavy proteinuria in pregnancy with hypertension
Preservative spilled on skin or eyes (wash immediately)

indications: Visible or microscopic haematuria in a resident of an endemic area
School-age children with history of swimming or wading in fresh water
Programme surveillance
contraindications: None
equipment: Filtration kit or centrifuge tubes in the laboratory
steps: Confirm identity and exposure history to fresh water.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Collect the sample between 10 am and 2 pm, when egg output is highest.
Ask the patient to do some light exercise such as walking or climbing stairs before collection.
Ask the patient to pass urine and collect the last part of the stream, or the whole void, into the container.
Test a portion with a dipstick for blood and record the result.
Label and send the sample to the laboratory within a few hours for filtration or sedimentation.
Send repeat samples on different days if the first is negative and suspicion remains.
aftercare: Treat according to national schistosomiasis programme guidelines.
Advise avoiding contact with infested fresh water.
red_flags: Heavy haematuria with clots or urinary retention
Loin pain or symptoms of obstructive uropathy
Long-standing haematuria in adults (investigate for bladder cancer)

indications: Suspected poisoning or overdose
Altered consciousness or behaviour of unknown cause
Monitoring in addiction or mental health services
Pre-employment or legal requests (use chain-of-custody procedure)
contraindications: Refusal by a competent patient for non-emergency testing
equipment: Immunoassay urine drug test cup or cassettes within expiry
Clean urine container with temperature strip
Chain-of-custody form and tamper-evident seal for legal samples
steps: Confirm identity, the reason for testing and current prescribed medicines that may cause positives.
Explain the test and who will see the result, obtain consent (written if the result may be used legally), or act in best interests if the patient lacks capacity.
Provide the container and ensure privacy, with supervision only if required by policy.
Check the temperature strip and appearance soon after the sample is passed to detect tampering.
Put on gloves, check the kit expiry and run the test as the manufacturer instructs.
Read each drug panel at the stated time and confirm the control lines are present.
Record results as presumptive, as positives must be confirmed by laboratory testing.
Seal the sample and complete the chain-of-custody form if the result may be used legally.
Send a sample for laboratory confirmation when results will affect care or legal decisions.
aftercare: Interpret results with the clinical picture and prescribed medicines.
Offer support or referral to addiction services where relevant.
red_flags: Reduced consciousness, seizures, arrhythmia or breathing problems (treat as poisoning emergency)
Child with a positive screen (safeguarding referral)
Suicidal intent or self-harm (mental health assessment)

indications: Diarrhoea, especially bloody or persistent
Suspected intestinal parasites or worms
Suspected cholera or typhoid outbreak investigation
contraindications: None
equipment: Clean dry wide-mouthed stool container with spoon in lid
Clean bedpan, potty or plastic sheet to pass stool onto
Cary-Blair transport medium if cholera or delay is expected
steps: Confirm identity, symptoms, travel and any antibiotics or antiparasitic medicine taken.
Explain the method and obtain verbal consent.
Ask the patient to pass stool onto a clean dry surface without mixing with urine or water.
Use the spoon to transfer a portion about the size of a walnut, or several spoonfuls of liquid stool, into the container.
Include any blood, mucus or worms seen.
Close the lid firmly and wipe the outside if soiled.
In infants collect fresh stool from the nappy or use a rectal swab if needed.
Label with patient details, date and time of collection.
Send to the laboratory within one to two hours, or within thirty minutes for amoebic trophozoites.
aftercare: Give oral rehydration and zinc for children with diarrhoea as per local guidelines.
Teach hand hygiene and safe water and food handling.
Follow up results and treat accordingly.
red_flags: Signs of dehydration, shock or reduced consciousness
Bloody diarrhoea with fever or in a young child
Suspected cholera (notify public health)

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Colorectal cancer screening in eligible adults
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or change in bowel habit where colonoscopy is not immediately available
contraindications: Visible rectal bleeding (needs direct investigation, not FOBT)
Active menstruation or bleeding haemorrhoids (defer)
equipment: FIT kit with sampling stick and tube, or guaiac test cards
Clean paper or container to catch stool
steps: Confirm identity and the reason for testing, and check there is no visible rectal bleeding.
Explain the test, including that a positive result needs colonoscopy, and obtain verbal consent.
Give dietary and medicine advice if a guaiac test is used, as FIT does not need diet changes.
Ask the patient to pass stool onto clean paper away from urine and toilet water.
Scrape the sampling stick across several areas of the stool as the kit instructs.
Return the stick to the tube and close it firmly, or apply the sample to the card windows.
Label the kit with name and date of collection.
Return the kit to the clinic or laboratory within the time stated by the manufacturer.
aftercare: Refer positive results for colonoscopy.
Advise a repeat according to the screening interval if negative.
red_flags: Positive test (refer for colonoscopy; do not repeat to disprove)
Weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or abdominal mass regardless of result

indications: Presumptive pulmonary tuberculosis
Monitoring of TB treatment response
Pneumonia or bronchiectasis needing culture
contraindications: Do not collect inside crowded or poorly ventilated rooms
equipment: Respirator mask (N95 or equivalent) for staff
Well-ventilated or outdoor collection area away from others
Request form noting new or follow-up case
steps: Confirm identity and whether this is a diagnostic or follow-up sample.
Explain the method and obtain verbal consent.
Take the patient to a well-ventilated or outdoor area away from others and wear a respirator.
Ask the patient to rinse the mouth with water to remove food particles.
Ask the patient to take two or three deep breaths and cough deeply from the chest.
Collect the sputum, not saliva, into the container, ideally 3-5 mL in volume.
Close the lid tightly without contaminating the outside.
Give a second container for an early-morning sample if microscopy needs two samples.
For young children who cannot produce sputum, arrange induced sputum or gastric aspirate per local protocol.
Label the container and send it to the laboratory promptly or refrigerate if delayed.
aftercare: Teach cough hygiene and advise mask use until TB is excluded.
Follow up results and link positive patients to the TB programme.
Screen household contacts if TB is confirmed.
red_flags: Haemoptysis, especially large volume (urgent review)
Respiratory distress or low oxygen saturation
Rifampicin resistance detected (refer to drug-resistant TB services)

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Sore throat with suspected streptococcal infection
Suspected diphtheria
Outbreak investigation or carrier screening
contraindications: Suspected epiglottitis or airway obstruction (do not examine the throat; call for airway help)
steps: Confirm identity and check for drooling, stridor or tripod posture before examining.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, warning that it may cause gagging.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves and mask.
Seat the patient with the head tilted back, with a child held securely on a carer's lap.
Depress the tongue and swab both tonsils and the posterior pharyngeal wall with a firm rotating motion.
Avoid touching the tongue, cheeks and teeth.
Swab any membrane or exudate edge if diphtheria is suspected and alert the laboratory.
Place the swab in transport medium, label it and send it promptly.
aftercare: Start treatment if indicated without waiting where diphtheria is suspected.
Advise fluids, analgesia and return if breathing difficulty develops.
red_flags: Stridor, drooling or difficulty breathing
Grey adherent membrane or bull neck (suspected diphtheria - isolate and notify)
Inability to swallow or open the mouth (peritonsillar abscess)

form.label: Swab type
options: Flocked swab in viral transport medium

indications: Suspected respiratory viral infection such as influenza or COVID-19
Suspected pertussis
Outbreak or surveillance testing
contraindications: Suspected base of skull fracture or recent facial trauma
Recent nasal surgery or severe nasal obstruction
Severe bleeding disorder (relative; consider nasal or throat swab)
equipment: Respirator mask, eye protection, gown and gloves
steps: Confirm identity and check for contraindications.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, warning it is uncomfortable but brief.
Perform hand hygiene and put on full personal protective equipment.
Ask the patient to blow the nose, then tilt the head back slightly, with a child held securely.
Insert the swab along the floor of the nose parallel to the palate, not upwards.
Advance gently to a depth about the distance from the nostril to the ear tragus until resistance is felt.
Rotate the swab gently and leave it in place for a few seconds to absorb secretions.
Withdraw slowly, place the swab in the transport medium and snap the shaft at the break point.
Close and label the tube and place it in a biohazard bag.
Remove personal protective equipment safely and perform hand hygiene.
Send to the laboratory promptly, refrigerated if delayed.
aftercare: Advise isolation and infection control measures while awaiting results.
Follow up results and notify public health for notifiable infections.
red_flags: Persistent nosebleed after swabbing
Breathing difficulty or low oxygen saturation
Notifiable infection suspected (inform public health)

form.label: Swab type
options: Flocked swab in viral transport medium

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Abnormal vaginal discharge, itching or odour
Suspected bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis or trichomoniasis
Postpartum or post-abortion fever
contraindications: Heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy until placenta praevia is excluded
Refusal of speculum examination (offer a self-taken low vaginal swab)
equipment: Swab in transport medium and a dry swab or slide for wet mount
Gloves, drape and couch with privacy screen
steps: Confirm identity and take a brief history including symptoms, pregnancy and last menstrual period.
Explain the examination, offer a chaperone and obtain verbal consent.
Ensure privacy and position the patient in the lithotomy or dorsal position.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and inspect the vulva.
Insert the speculum gently and open it to view the vaginal walls and cervix.
Swab the posterior fornix and lateral walls, rotating the swab to collect discharge.
Place the swab in transport medium and prepare a wet mount or pH test if available.
Take endocervical samples at the same time if sexually transmitted infection is suspected.
Remove the speculum gently and allow the patient to dress in private.
Label the sample and send it to the laboratory promptly.
aftercare: Treat syndromically per national guidelines if results will be delayed.
Offer HIV and syphilis testing and partner treatment where STI is suspected.
Advise return if pain, fever or heavy bleeding develops.
red_flags: Fever with pelvic pain or offensive discharge after delivery or abortion (sepsis)
Heavy bleeding in pregnancy
Disclosure of sexual assault (follow forensic and safeguarding procedure)

form.label: Swab type
options: Flocked swab in viral transport medium

indications: Suspected gonorrhoea or chlamydia
Mucopurulent cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease
Screening of contacts of a partner with STI
contraindications: Heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy until placenta praevia is excluded
Refusal of speculum examination (offer a self-taken vaginal NAAT swab)
equipment: NAAT collection swab and transport medium for culture as needed
Large cotton swab to clean the cervix
steps: Confirm identity, symptoms, pregnancy status and sexual history.
Explain the examination, offer a chaperone and obtain verbal consent.
Position the patient in the lithotomy or dorsal position with privacy.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and insert the speculum to view the cervix.
Remove excess mucus and discharge from the cervix with a large swab.
Insert the collection swab one to two centimetres into the cervical os.
Rotate the swab for the time stated by the kit and withdraw it without touching the vaginal walls.
Place the swab in the correct medium and break the shaft if required.
Remove the speculum gently and allow the patient to dress in private.
Label the sample and send it to the laboratory promptly.
aftercare: Treat syndromically per national STI guidelines if indicated.
Offer HIV and syphilis testing and arrange partner notification.
Advise abstinence or condom use until treatment is completed.
red_flags: Fever, severe pelvic pain or cervical motion tenderness (pelvic inflammatory disease)
Possible ectopic pregnancy
Disclosure of sexual assault or a minor at risk (safeguarding)

form.label: Swab type
options: Flocked swab in viral transport medium

indications: Urethral discharge or dysuria suggesting urethritis
Suspected gonorrhoea or chlamydia
Partner of someone with a sexually transmitted infection
contraindications: None; first-void urine NAAT is an acceptable less painful alternative
equipment: Thin urethral swab in transport medium or NAAT swab
steps: Confirm identity and check the patient has not passed urine for at least one to two hours.
Explain the procedure, offer a chaperone and obtain verbal consent, warning of brief discomfort.
Ensure privacy, perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Retract the foreskin and wipe away external discharge at the meatus.
Collect any visible discharge on a swab and make a slide for Gram stain.
Insert the thin swab gently two to three centimetres into the urethra.
Rotate the swab once and withdraw it gently.
Place the swab in transport medium, label it and send it promptly.
aftercare: Treat syndromically per national STI guidelines where indicated.
Offer HIV and syphilis testing and partner notification.
Advise drinking fluids and that passing urine may sting briefly.
red_flags: Testicular pain or swelling (epididymo-orchitis or torsion)
Fever, joint pain or rash (disseminated gonococcal infection)
Urinary retention after the procedure

indications: Clinically infected wound or ulcer
Surgical site infection
Non-healing chronic wound with signs of infection
contraindications: Clean wound without signs of infection (swab adds little)
equipment: Sterile swab in bacterial transport medium
Sterile saline and gauze for cleaning
Sterile gloves or non-touch technique supplies
steps: Confirm identity and record wound site, duration and antibiotic history.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, offering analgesia if the wound is painful.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and remove the old dressing.
Clean the wound with sterile saline to remove surface pus, slough and debris.
Moisten the swab with transport medium or saline if the wound is dry.
Rotate the swab with gentle pressure over about one square centimetre of viable tissue to express fluid.
Avoid swabbing pus on the surface, slough, eschar or surrounding skin.
Place the swab in transport medium and label it with the site.
Apply a fresh dressing and send the sample promptly.
aftercare: Continue wound care and review the culture result.
Adjust antibiotics to sensitivities where they are needed.
red_flags: Spreading redness, crepitus or severe pain out of proportion (necrotising infection)
Fever, rigors or signs of sepsis
Exposed bone or tendon

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Abscess or collection where an aspirate gives better culture than a swab
Suspected septic arthritis or pyomyositis (collect at drainage)
Suspected anaerobic or tuberculous infection
contraindications: Collection close to major vessels or deep spaces without imaging guidance
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Sterile gloves and antiseptic skin preparation
Sterile capped container or blood culture bottle as advised by the laboratory
steps: Confirm identity, site and indication, and review imaging if the collection is deep.
Explain the procedure and risks and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the skin with antiseptic.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic over the point of maximum fluctuance.
Insert the needle into the collection and aspirate pus while maintaining sterility.
Remove the needle safely and transfer the pus to a sterile container, or cap the syringe without the needle.
Note the volume, colour and smell of the aspirate.
Apply a dressing and arrange incision and drainage if needed.
Label the sample and send it promptly, requesting AFB or fungal culture if suspected.
aftercare: Review the culture result and adjust antibiotics.
Check for reaccumulation and refer for formal drainage if needed.
red_flags: Spreading infection, sepsis or a collection near the airway or joint
Blood rather than pus on aspiration (stop; consider vascular lesion)
Reaccumulation after aspiration

indications: Diarrhoea when a stool sample cannot be obtained, especially in infants
Screening for resistant organisms or infection control
Suspected rectal gonorrhoea or chlamydia
contraindications: Recent rectal or anal surgery
Severe neutropenia (relative)
equipment: Swab in transport medium (Cary-Blair for enteric pathogens)
steps: Confirm identity and the indication.
Explain the procedure, offer a chaperone and obtain verbal consent.
Ensure privacy and position the patient on the left side with knees drawn up, or an infant on the back with legs raised.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Moisten the swab with sterile saline or transport medium.
Insert the swab gently about two to three centimetres past the anal sphincter (less in infants).
Rotate the swab gently against the rectal wall and withdraw it.
Check for visible faecal material on the swab.
Place the swab in transport medium, label it and send it promptly.
aftercare: Continue rehydration and treatment as indicated.
Follow up results and apply infection control precautions if needed.
red_flags: Rectal bleeding after the swab
Signs of dehydration or sepsis in a child with diarrhoea

form.label: Swab type
options: Flocked swab in viral transport medium

form.label: Transport
options: Kept at room temperature before dispatch

indications: Purulent conjunctivitis, especially in neonates (ophthalmia neonatorum)
Conjunctivitis not responding to treatment
Suspected chlamydial or gonococcal eye infection
contraindications: Suspected penetrating eye injury (do not swab; refer urgently)
steps: Confirm identity and record onset, discharge and treatment so far.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, with a carer holding an infant's head steady.
Collect the sample before any eye drops are instilled.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Ask the patient to look up and gently pull down the lower eyelid.
Moisten the swab with sterile saline and wipe it along the lower fornix from the inner to outer corner.
Avoid touching the eyelashes and lid margins.
Make a slide for Gram stain if gonococcal infection is suspected.
Use a separate swab for each eye and label each with the side.
Send the samples to the laboratory promptly.
aftercare: Start treatment according to the clinical picture and guidelines.
Teach eye hygiene and hand washing to prevent spread.
Treat the mother and partner if neonatal chlamydial or gonococcal infection is confirmed.
red_flags: Neonate with purulent conjunctivitis (same-day treatment and review)
Reduced vision, severe pain, photophobia or corneal haze
Swelling and redness around the eye (periorbital cellulitis)

indications: Chronic or recurrent ear discharge
Otitis externa not responding to treatment
Discharge after grommet or ear surgery
contraindications: Do not insert the swab deep into the canal or beyond direct vision
equipment: Thin sterile swab in transport medium
steps: Confirm identity and record duration of discharge and any ear drops used.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent, with a carer holding a child's head still.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Inspect the ear canal and drum with the otoscope.
Straighten the canal by pulling the pinna up and back in adults or down and back in young children.
Insert the swab gently into the outer canal under direct vision and rotate it in the discharge.
Withdraw the swab without touching the outer ear.
Place it in transport medium, label it with the side and send it.
aftercare: Teach dry mopping of the ear and to keep water out.
Follow up results and refer to ENT if discharge persists.
red_flags: Swelling or tenderness behind the ear (mastoiditis)
Facial weakness, severe headache, dizziness or reduced consciousness
Severe pain with granulation in diabetic or elderly patients (malignant otitis externa)

indications: Suspected onchocerciasis with itching, rash or nodules
Eye symptoms in an endemic area
Programme evaluation of onchocerciasis control
contraindications: Infected skin at the chosen site
Bleeding disorder (relative)
equipment: Sterile corneoscleral punch or sterile needle and scalpel blade
Microtitre plate or glass slide with normal saline
steps: Confirm identity, symptoms and residence in an endemic area.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Choose sites such as both iliac crests, buttocks or calves, or scapulae per local protocol.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean each site with antiseptic and let it dry.
Take a bloodless superficial skin snip with the punch, or lift the skin with a needle and shave it with the blade.
Place each snip in a well or drop of saline and label it with the site.
Apply pressure and a plaster to each site.
Incubate the snips at room temperature and examine under the microscope for emerging microfilariae as advised by the laboratory.
Dispose of single-use blades and sterilise reusable punches before any reuse on another patient, then perform hand hygiene.
aftercare: Keep the sites clean and dry until healed.
Treat per national onchocerciasis programme guidance, checking for Loa loa co-infection first.
Refer eye symptoms for ophthalmology review.
red_flags: Signs of infection at a snip site
Visual loss or eye inflammation (urgent eye review)
Heavy Loa loa co-infection suspected before treatment (specialist advice)

indications: Palpable lump in the breast, thyroid, lymph node or salivary gland
Suspected tuberculous lymphadenitis
Recurrent cyst needing aspiration and cytology
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Suspected vascular lesion or pulsatile mass
Uncooperative patient where the lump cannot be stabilised
equipment: Clean labelled glass slides and spreader slide
Saline or culture container for AFB or culture
Cytology request form with clinical details
steps: Confirm identity, the lump site and the indication, and review any imaging.
Explain the procedure, risks and what happens to results, and obtain written consent.
Perform hand hygiene, label the slides and prepare fixative.
Position the patient, clean the skin and put on gloves.
Stabilise the lump firmly between the fingers of the non-dominant hand.
Insert the needle into the lump and apply suction while making several passes in different directions.
Release suction before withdrawing the needle from the lump.
Detach the needle, draw air into the syringe, reattach and expel the material onto the slides.
Spread the material gently, fix some slides immediately in alcohol and air dry others as the laboratory requests.
Rinse the needle in saline for culture or cell block if TB or infection is suspected.
Apply firm pressure to the site and a plaster.
Repeat a pass with a fresh needle if the material is inadequate, up to the local limit.
Send slides and samples with the request form to the laboratory.
aftercare: Advise the patient that mild bruising or soreness is expected.
Arrange a review appointment for results.
Refer for core biopsy or excision if the result is inconclusive.
red_flags: Expanding swelling or bleeding at the site
Breathing difficulty after neck aspiration
Malignant result (refer promptly to the relevant team)

indications: Investigation of couple infertility
Confirmation of success after vasectomy
Suspected male reproductive tract infection
contraindications: Recent fever or illness within the last few weeks (results may be falsely low; consider deferring)
equipment: Sterile wide-mouthed container from the laboratory
Request form recording abstinence and collection time
steps: Confirm identity and the reason for testing.
Explain the method and obtain verbal consent, giving clear written or verbal instructions.
Advise abstinence from ejaculation for two to seven days before collection.
Ask the patient to pass urine and wash hands and penis before collection.
Collect the whole ejaculate by masturbation directly into the sterile container.
Advise not to use condoms, lubricants or saliva as they can harm sperm.
Record if any part of the sample was lost, especially the first part.
Keep the sample close to body temperature and deliver it to the laboratory within one hour.
Label the container with name, date, collection time and abstinence days.
aftercare: Arrange a repeat sample if the result is abnormal.
Review results with the couple and refer to a fertility clinic where needed.
red_flags: No sperm on repeated samples (refer to a specialist)
Blood in semen with pain, fever or a testicular lump

indications: Suspected poisoning or overdose
Unexplained reduced consciousness, seizures or metabolic acidosis
Suspected alcohol intoxication affecting management
contraindications: None in an emergency; do not delay resuscitation to collect samples
equipment: Plain or serum tubes, fluoride oxalate (grey) tube for alcohol and EDTA tube as advised
Non-alcohol skin cleanser when blood alcohol is requested
Container for gastric aspirate or vomitus if relevant
Request form recording time of ingestion
Sealed bags for the substance or packaging brought in
steps: Stabilise airway, breathing and circulation first and call for help as needed.
Confirm identity and record the suspected substance, amount and time of exposure.
Explain and obtain consent, or act in the patient's best interests if they lack capacity.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the skin without alcohol if blood alcohol is required and perform venepuncture.
Fill the tubes requested by the laboratory and time drug-level samples correctly after ingestion.
Collect urine for toxicology screening where available.
Keep any vomitus, gastric aspirate, tablets or packaging in sealed labelled containers.
Label every sample with the exact collection time and send it urgently.
Contact the poisons information service or toxicology unit for advice where available.
aftercare: Repeat timed samples if required by the toxicology protocol.
Observe for delayed effects and arrange mental health assessment after self-harm.
red_flags: Reduced consciousness, seizures, arrhythmias or respiratory depression
Paediatric ingestion or suspected non-accidental poisoning (safeguarding)
Toxic level reported (start antidote or specific treatment urgently)

name: Forensic sample collection with chain of custody

indications: Sexual assault examination
Request by police or court for medico-legal samples
Assault, suspected poisoning or impaired driving with legal implications
contraindications: Refusal by a competent adult (document and offer care anyway)
Untrained examiner where a trained forensic examiner or referral centre is available
equipment: Forensic sample kit or sterile swabs, tubes and containers
Paper bags for clothing and tamper-evident seals
Body diagram and camera if local policy permits
Gloves, mask and clean paper sheet
steps: Ensure the patient's medical needs and safety are addressed first.
Explain the purpose, what will be collected and who will receive it, and obtain written consent from the patient or guardian.
Involve a chaperone and, for children, follow safeguarding procedures and use a specialist examiner.
Wear gloves and mask and change gloves between each sample site to avoid contamination.
Ask the patient to undress over a clean paper sheet and place each clothing item in a separate paper bag.
Collect swabs and samples in the order set by the kit and air dry swabs before packaging.
Seal each sample, label it with patient details, site, date, time and your signature.
Document injuries on a body diagram with measurements, and photograph if permitted.
Complete the chain-of-custody form and sign each time samples change hands.
Store samples securely until handed to police, recording the recipient's name and signature.
Offer emergency contraception, post-exposure prophylaxis and counselling where relevant.
aftercare: Arrange follow-up for medical care, HIV and STI testing and psychological support.
Refer to a sexual assault referral centre or social services where available.
Keep all documentation secure and confidential.
red_flags: Serious injuries or bleeding needing urgent treatment
Child or vulnerable adult at continuing risk (immediate safeguarding action)
Break in the chain of custody (document and inform police)
Suicidal thoughts or severe distress

indications: Tissue removed at surgery or biopsy that needs histological diagnosis
Products of conception, excised lesions or lymph nodes
contraindications: Do not put specimens needing culture, frozen section or lymphoma studies into formalin
equipment: Leak-proof specimen container of suitable size
10% neutral buffered formalin (about ten times the specimen volume)
Sterile saline or dry sterile container for fresh specimens
Specimen labels and histology request form
steps: Confirm the patient identity and specimen details with the operating team before the patient leaves.
Label the container itself, not the lid, with patient details, specimen type, site and side.
Decide whether the specimen needs to be fresh for culture, frozen section or lymphoma studies.
Place the specimen in formalin covering it completely, using enough fixative for its size.
Mark orientation with sutures where the surgeon requests it and record this on the form.
Close the lid tightly and check for leaks.
Complete the request form with clinical history, operation findings and the clinical question.
Record the specimen in the register and place it in a biohazard bag with the form.
Send to the laboratory promptly, or record storage and dispatch time if delayed.
Handle formalin in a ventilated area and wash off any skin or eye contact immediately.
aftercare: Track the specimen until the laboratory confirms receipt.
Follow up the histology report and discuss results with the patient.
red_flags: Specimen lost, unlabelled or mislabelled (report as an incident immediately)
Malignant result (ensure prompt review and referral)
Formalin splash to eyes (irrigate and seek eye review)

indications: Voluntary or family replacement blood donation
Autologous pre-deposit donation where offered
contraindications: Donor fails selection criteria for age, weight, haemoglobin, blood pressure or pulse
Recent illness, high-risk behaviour, pregnancy or recent delivery
Known transfusion-transmissible infection or other deferral reason in the donor questionnaire
equipment: Donor questionnaire and written consent form
Haemoglobin meter, blood pressure machine and weighing scale
Sterile closed blood collection bag system with anticoagulant and 16 G needle
Blood collection mixer scale or manual scale
Tourniquet or blood pressure cuff and antiseptic skin preparation
Sample tubes for donor infection screening and grouping
Donor couch, gauze, plaster and refreshments
steps: Confirm donor identity and complete the donor questionnaire in private.
Check weight, haemoglobin, blood pressure and pulse against national blood service criteria.
Explain the process and infection screening, and obtain written consent.
Position the donor comfortably on the couch and label the bag and sample tubes with the same donation number.
Perform hand hygiene, apply the cuff or tourniquet and select a large antecubital vein.
Disinfect the site thoroughly and allow it to dry.
Insert the collection needle and secure it, then release the cuff to the collection pressure.
Mix the bag continuously and stop at the target collection volume on the scale.
Collect screening samples from the diversion pouch or line.
Release the cuff, clamp the tubing, remove the needle and apply firm pressure with the arm straight.
Seal the tubing and store the unit at the correct temperature promptly.
Keep the donor lying for a few minutes, then sitting, and offer fluids and a snack.
aftercare: Advise extra fluids, avoiding heavy lifting with that arm and strenuous activity for the rest of the day.
Tell the donor to lie down with legs raised if faint and to contact the centre if unwell.
Inform the donor how screening results will be communicated.
red_flags: Fainting, vomiting or seizure during or after donation
Arterial puncture or rapidly expanding haematoma
Arm numbness, tingling or severe pain (nerve injury)
Positive infection screen (confidential donor notification and referral)

indications: Any patient presenting with psychiatric symptoms or behavioural change
Baseline and follow-up review of a known mental disorder
Assessment of confusion, delirium or reduced cognition on medical wards
Medico-legal or fitness assessments
contraindications: Immediate medical emergency that must be stabilised first
equipment: Quiet private room with safe exits for patient and staff
Interpreter if the patient's language is not shared
MSE recording template or note form
steps: Confirm the patient's identity, explain the purpose of the interview and obtain verbal agreement.
Ensure a safe setting with an unobstructed exit and inform a colleague if risk is suspected.
Observe appearance and behaviour, including self-care, eye contact, motor activity and rapport.
Note speech rate, volume, tone and quantity.
Ask about mood in the patient's own words and observe affect for range, reactivity and congruence.
Assess thought form for coherence, flight of ideas, loosening of association or thought block.
Explore thought content, including delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions and preoccupations.
Ask directly about thoughts of self-harm, suicide and harm to others.
Ask about perceptual disturbances such as hallucinations, illusions and depersonalisation.
Test orientation to time, place and person, attention and short-term memory.
Assess insight into illness and need for treatment, and judgement.
Collect a collateral history from family where available and with the patient's agreement.
Summarise the findings to the patient in plain language and agree the next steps.
aftercare: Document findings promptly and compare with previous examinations.
Act on any risk identified the same day.
Arrange review according to clinical need.
red_flags: Stop and seek help if the patient becomes threatening, agitated or attempts to leave while at high risk.
Escalate urgently for active suicidal intent, homicidal ideation or command hallucinations to harm.
Treat fluctuating attention or disorientation as possible delirium and look for a medical cause.

indications: Self-harm or suicide attempt
Expressed suicidal thoughts or hopelessness
Depression, psychosis, substance use or recent major loss
Before discharge from a psychiatric or emergency admission
contraindications: Medical instability after self-harm that must be treated first
equipment: Private, safe room cleared of ligature points and sharp objects
Structured risk assessment and safety plan form
Contact details of family, crisis lines and on-call team
steps: Treat any physical injury or poisoning first and ensure the patient is medically stable.
Confirm identity, explain the purpose and assure confidentiality with its limits where there is risk to life.
Remove or secure means of harm in the room and keep the patient under observation if risk is high.
Ask directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts, as asking does not increase risk.
Explore the details of any current attempt, including intent, planning, lethality and whether rescue was expected.
Ask about current plans, access to means such as pesticides, drugs, ropes or firearms, and timing.
Identify risk factors including previous attempts, mental illness, substance use, chronic pain, debt and social isolation.
Identify protective factors such as family, faith, children, future plans and reasons for living.
For children and adolescents, assess for abuse, bullying and safeguarding concerns and involve a parent or guardian appropriately.
Obtain collateral information from family or carers with consent where possible.
Formulate the overall risk level and the immediate safety needs.
Develop a written safety plan with the patient, including warning signs, coping steps and people to contact.
Agree means restriction with the family, such as removing pesticides and stockpiled medicines.
Decide on admission, close community follow-up or referral, and document the reasoning.
aftercare: Give the patient and family a copy of the safety plan and crisis contacts.
Arrange follow-up within days for any patient discharged after self-harm.
Inform the treating team and record risk on the patient's record.
red_flags: Do not leave a patient with imminent risk alone; arrange continuous observation.
Escalate immediately for an ongoing plan with access to means, command hallucinations or refusal of help while at high risk.
Tell the family to return or call for help if the patient talks of dying, gives away belongings or withdraws suddenly.

indications: Severe depression with psychotic features, high suicide risk or refusal of food and fluids
Catatonia not responding to first-line treatment
Treatment-resistant depression, mania or schizophrenia
Previous good response to ECT
contraindications: Raised intracranial pressure or recent intracranial bleed
Recent myocardial infarction or unstable cardiac disease
Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
No anaesthetist available (unmodified ECT should not be given)
equipment: ECT machine with EEG and ECG monitoring, checked and calibrated
Anaesthetic machine, oxygen, suction and airway equipment
Pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor and defibrillator
Anaesthetic induction agent and muscle relaxant per anaesthetist
steps: Confirm written informed consent, or the legal authority to treat a patient lacking capacity, and the prescription for the course.
Confirm the patient has fasted, voided and had a pre-ECT medical and anaesthetic review.
Perform the time-out with the anaesthetist and ECT team confirming identity, electrode placement and stimulus settings.
Remove dentures, hairpins and jewellery and clean the electrode sites on the scalp.
Insert an IV cannula and attach ECG, pulse oximetry and blood pressure monitoring.
The anaesthetist pre-oxygenates and gives the induction agent and muscle relaxant.
Confirm muscle relaxation, then insert the bite block to protect the teeth and tongue.
Apply electrodes in the agreed position, check impedance and deliver the stimulus.
Time the motor seizure and EEG seizure and record their duration.
If the seizure is absent or too short, restimulate at a higher setting, limiting the number of attempts per the unit protocol.
Support the airway and ventilation until spontaneous breathing returns.
Transfer the patient to recovery in the recovery position with continuous monitoring.
aftercare: Observe vital signs and conscious level until fully alert and oriented.
Give simple analgesia for headache or muscle pain.
Assess memory and mood between treatments and review progress against the course plan.
Do not allow the patient to drive or make major decisions on treatment days.
red_flags: Stop and call for help for prolonged seizure, arrhythmia, hypoxia or failure to resume breathing.
Escalate for prolonged confusion, agitation on waking or severe memory complaints.
Return or report for chest pain, severe headache, new weakness or worsening confusion.

form.label: Legal basis for treatment
options: Second opinion under mental health law

indications: Severe agitation or violence with risk to the patient or others after de-escalation has failed
Acute disturbed behaviour preventing urgent assessment or treatment
contraindications: De-escalation or oral medication not yet attempted when time allows
Known allergy or previous severe reaction to the intended medicine
Untreated medical cause such as hypoglycaemia, hypoxia or head injury that should be addressed first
equipment: Medicines for rapid tranquillisation per local protocol and drug list
Pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor and thermometer
Oxygen, suction, bag-valve-mask and resuscitation trolley
Reversal agent for benzodiazepines and medicine for acute dystonia available per local protocol
steps: Attempt verbal de-escalation first, using a calm voice, space and one lead staff member.
Check blood glucose and look for medical causes such as hypoxia, intoxication, withdrawal, infection or head injury.
Offer oral medication first and explain what it is for.
If oral medication is refused or ineffective and risk remains high, decide on intramuscular medication with the senior clinician.
Review previous medicines, allergies, ECG if available, recent substance use and physical health before choosing the medicine.
Gather enough trained staff to hold the patient safely for the injection if required, avoiding pressure on the chest, neck or back.
Give the chosen medicine by the intramuscular route into a large muscle such as the deltoid, thigh or buttock.
Explain to the patient what has been given and why, even if they are agitated.
Release any holding as soon as it is safe and place the patient in a quiet area.
Monitor pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature and level of consciousness at regular intervals.
Increase monitoring to continuous observation if the patient falls asleep or becomes over-sedated.
Debrief the patient and staff after the event and record it.
aftercare: Continue physical observations until the patient is alert and walking.
Encourage oral fluids and check for dystonia, low blood pressure and breathing problems.
Review the treatment plan to reduce the need for further tranquillisation.
Inform the family where appropriate.
red_flags: Call for urgent help for respiratory rate below normal limits, falling oxygen saturation or unrousable patient.
Escalate for acute dystonia, severe hypotension, arrhythmia, high fever or muscle rigidity.
Seek senior review if a second dose is being considered or the patient remains agitated.

indications: Imminent risk of serious harm to the patient or others that cannot be managed by de-escalation
Holding to give urgent treatment to a patient lacking capacity
contraindications: Use as punishment, for staff convenience or to replace adequate staffing
Chaining or tying to fixed objects (not acceptable practice)
equipment: Enough trained staff (usually at least three)
Padded mechanical restraints only if allowed by local policy
steps: Use restraint only as a last resort after de-escalation has failed and the risk is immediate.
Call for help and appoint one lead person to coordinate and talk to the patient throughout.
Remove other patients and hazards from the area.
Hold the patient using trained techniques that keep the airway clear and avoid pressure on the chest, neck, back or abdomen.
Avoid the face-down (prone) position, or keep it as brief as possible if unavoidable.
Keep one staff member monitoring the patient's breathing, colour and level of consciousness.
For children, use the least force possible, involve staff trained in paediatric holding and inform the parent or guardian.
Use the shortest possible duration and review continuously whether restraint is still needed.
If mechanical restraint is used under local policy, apply padded devices, check circulation regularly and never leave the patient unattended.
Release restraint in a planned, gradual way as the patient calms.
Check the patient for injuries and record physical observations after release.
Debrief the patient and staff and record the event and its reasons.
aftercare: Continue observations and check for injury, pain or breathing difficulty.
Review the care plan to prevent recurrence, including medication and triggers.
Report the incident according to the facility's policy and inform the family.
red_flags: Release immediately if the patient has difficulty breathing, becomes limp, vomits or loses consciousness, and start resuscitation if needed.
Escalate for injury, limb swelling, numbness or colour change in a restrained limb.
Seek senior review if restraint lasts longer than a few minutes or is repeated.

indications: Severe disturbed behaviour with serious risk of harm to others that cannot be managed by other means
contraindications: High suicide or self-harm risk without continuous direct observation
Medical instability, recent rapid tranquillisation with over-sedation, or delirium
Use as punishment or because of staff shortage
equipment: Purpose-built seclusion room, free of ligature points, with viewing window, ventilation and light
Mattress, blanket and tear-resistant clothing if required
steps: Confirm that less restrictive options have failed and the seclusion is authorised by the responsible clinician per local policy.
Check the room is safe, clean, ventilated, at a comfortable temperature and free of hazards.
Search the patient respectfully for dangerous items, with same-sex staff where possible.
Explain to the patient why they are being secluded and what is needed for it to end.
Place the patient in the room and record the start time.
Maintain continuous observation by a staff member who can see the patient at all times.
Record behaviour, breathing and level of consciousness on the observation chart at short intervals.
Offer fluids, food and toilet access at regular intervals.
Arrange medical and nursing reviews at the intervals set by local policy.
End the seclusion as soon as the risk has reduced, and record the end time.
Debrief the patient after the seclusion ends.
aftercare: Check physical health and observations after release.
Update the care plan to reduce the need for further seclusion.
Inform the family and report the episode as required by policy.
red_flags: Enter immediately with enough staff if the patient self-harms, collapses, has breathing difficulty or cannot be seen.
Escalate if seclusion is needed for longer than local policy allows or repeatedly.
Seek medical review for signs of physical illness, dehydration or over-sedation.

form.label: Authorised by
options: Nurse in charge pending doctor review

indications: Maintenance treatment of schizophrenia or related psychosis
Poor adherence to oral antipsychotics or patient preference
Bipolar disorder maintenance where depot is prescribed
contraindications: No valid prescription or patient refusal without legal authority to treat
Known hypersensitivity to the prescribed depot
Signs of serious adverse effects such as neuroleptic malignant syndrome or severe movement disorder at review
Patient who has never taken the antipsychotic and has not first shown tolerance to the oral form
equipment: Prescribed depot medicine with prescription and administration record
Appropriate syringe and needle (e.g. 21-23 G for deltoid or gluteal, length suited to body habitus)
Alcohol swabs, gloves, gauze and sharps container
steps: Confirm identity, prescription, due date, product, route and site rotation against the administration record, and that the patient has previously tolerated this antipsychotic.
Ask about side effects such as stiffness, tremor, restlessness, sexual problems, weight change and sedation.
Check for movement disorders, signs of relapse and adherence with any oral medication.
Explain the injection and obtain the patient's agreement.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the injection per the product instructions.
Choose the site, rotating between sides and between deltoid and gluteal where the product allows.
Clean the skin and give the injection deep intramuscularly using the Z-track technique where recommended.
Do not massage the site, and apply light pressure with gauze.
Dispose of sharps safely and record the product, batch, site and next due date.
Observe the patient for a period after injection where the product requires it.
aftercare: Give the patient a card or note with the next due date.
Advise to report pain, swelling or lumps at the site.
Trace missed appointments promptly by phone or community worker.
red_flags: Withhold and seek medical review for fever with rigidity and confusion, severe movement problems or jaundice.
Escalate for signs of relapse, suicidal thoughts or excessive sedation after injection.
Return for an abscess, severe pain at the site or difficulty breathing.

indications: Memory complaints or suspected dementia
Monitoring of known cognitive impairment
Confusion after stroke, head injury or illness once delirium is excluded or treated
contraindications: Acute delirium (screen for delirium instead and treat the cause)
Severe sensory loss or language barrier without suitable adaptation (interpret with caution)
equipment: Validated cognitive screening tool suited to education and language (e.g. IDEA cognitive screen, MoCA, CSI-D)
Pen, paper, watch and clock-drawing sheet
Spectacles and hearing aid if the patient uses them
steps: Confirm identity, explain the purpose of the test and obtain verbal agreement.
Ensure the patient can see and hear, and that the room is quiet.
Record the patient's years of education, literacy and preferred language.
Screen for delirium by checking attention and recent change in alertness.
Administer the chosen tool exactly as per its instructions, without coaching.
Score each item and calculate the total score.
Adjust the interpretation for education, literacy and culture where the tool allows.
Take a collateral history from a family member about daily function and change over time.
Check for reversible causes such as depression, hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, HIV, syphilis and medicines.
Explain the results sensitively and agree the next steps with the patient and family.
aftercare: Arrange investigations and specialist referral where indicated.
Provide carer information and safety advice, for example about cooking, wandering and medicines.
Repeat the test at intervals to monitor change.
red_flags: Escalate for sudden onset or fluctuating confusion, which suggests delirium or a new medical problem.
Refer urgently for rapid decline, new neurological signs or young-onset cognitive impairment.
Report safeguarding concerns such as neglect, financial abuse or accusations of witchcraft against an older person.

indications: Doubt about a patient's ability to make a specific decision about treatment, admission or discharge
Refusal of urgent or recommended treatment
Decisions about finances, property or care placement where capacity is questioned
contraindications: Assumption of incapacity based only on diagnosis, age, appearance or disagreement with the clinician
equipment: Interpreter and communication aids if needed
Information about the decision in simple language
steps: Define the specific decision and the time it needs to be made.
Start from the presumption that the patient has capacity.
Look for a mental or brain condition that could be affecting decision-making.
Give the relevant information in simple language, including risks, benefits and alternatives, using an interpreter if needed.
Treat reversible causes such as intoxication, pain or delirium and reassess when possible if the decision can wait.
Check whether the patient understands the information.
Check whether the patient can retain the information long enough to decide.
Check whether the patient can weigh up the information as part of the decision.
Check whether the patient can communicate a decision by any means.
Record the patient's answers in their own words as evidence.
If capacity is lacking, decide in the patient's best interests involving family, and follow national mental health and consent law.
aftercare: Reassess capacity if the patient's condition changes.
Inform the treating team and family of the outcome.
Seek a second opinion or legal advice for serious or disputed decisions.
red_flags: Seek senior or legal advice when an incapacitated patient refuses life-saving treatment.
Escalate concerns of coercion or abuse influencing the decision.
Reassess promptly if capacity is fluctuating.

form.label: Condition affecting the mind or brain
Outcome
options: Referred for legal or second opinion

indications: Severe mental disorder with serious risk to the patient or others and refusal of voluntary admission
Patient lacking capacity to consent to needed inpatient treatment
contraindications: Patient willing and able to accept voluntary admission or community treatment
Behaviour fully explained by a medical condition needing medical admission instead
equipment: Statutory forms required by the National Mental Health Act and the facility
Private safe room and security support if needed
steps: Confirm the patient's identity and gather the referral information, history and risk concerns.
Ensure a safe setting with adequate staff and, if needed, security or police support.
Introduce yourself, explain the purpose of the assessment and the patient's rights.
Perform a full mental state examination and risk assessment.
Exclude or treat medical causes such as delirium, intoxication, infection and hypoglycaemia.
Assess capacity to consent to admission and treatment.
Consider all less restrictive alternatives, including voluntary admission and home treatment.
Interview the family or next of kin and record their views.
Decide whether the criteria for involuntary admission under national mental health law are met.
Obtain the required second opinion or independent professional where the law requires it.
Complete the statutory forms and inform the patient and family of the decision, rights and appeal process.
Arrange safe transport and handover to the admitting team.
aftercare: Review the need for detention regularly and discharge from it as soon as criteria are no longer met.
Ensure the patient receives written information on their rights.
Protect the patient's dignity and prevent chaining or other abusive practices.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for imminent violence, self-harm or attempts to abscond during assessment.
Seek medical admission if there is a physical illness causing the behaviour.
Report any coercion, abuse or unlawful detention observed.

form.label: Rights explained to patient and family

indications: Depression and anxiety disorders
Panic disorder, phobias and obsessive-compulsive disorder
Insomnia, substance use and adjunct in psychosis
contraindications: Acute psychosis, severe intoxication or high suicide risk needing urgent care first
Severe cognitive impairment preventing engagement
equipment: Worksheets, thought records and homework sheets
Symptom measures such as PHQ-9 or GAD-7
steps: Confirm identity, review risk briefly and obtain agreement to continue.
Complete a symptom measure and review the score with the patient.
Set the agenda for the session together.
Review the homework from the previous session and what was learned.
Work on the session target, such as identifying and challenging unhelpful thoughts.
Use behavioural techniques where appropriate, such as activity scheduling, exposure or problem solving.
For children, adapt the language, use play or drawings and involve parents in parts of the session.
Summarise the key learning points in the patient's words.
Agree homework for the coming week.
Ask for feedback on the session and book the next appointment.
aftercare: Encourage the patient to practise the skills between sessions.
Provide crisis contacts in case of worsening.
Review progress against goals every few sessions.
red_flags: Pause therapy and complete a risk assessment if suicidal thoughts emerge or worsen.
Refer for medical review if symptoms worsen despite therapy or psychosis appears.
Raise a safeguarding concern if abuse is disclosed.

name: Brief intervention for alcohol or substance use

indications: Hazardous or harmful alcohol use identified on screening
Cannabis, tramadol, codeine or other substance use identified on screening
Alcohol or drug-related injury or illness
contraindications: Severe intoxication at the time of the visit (rebook)
Dependence with withdrawal risk needing medical management (refer instead)
equipment: Validated screening tool (AUDIT, AUDIT-C, ASSIST or CRAFFT for adolescents)
Standard drink chart and information leaflets
steps: Confirm identity, ask permission to talk about alcohol or substance use and assure confidentiality.
Complete the screening tool and calculate the score.
Give feedback on the score and its risk level in a non-judgemental way.
Link the substance use to the patient's own health or social concerns.
Explore the patient's views on the pros and cons of their use.
Assess readiness to change using a simple scale.
Give clear advice to reduce or stop use and offer a menu of options.
Agree a specific goal and plan with the patient.
For adolescents, explore family, school and peer factors and involve a parent or guardian when safe and appropriate.
Refer for specialist treatment if the score indicates possible dependence.
Arrange follow-up to review progress.
aftercare: Provide written information and helpline contacts.
Review progress at the next visit and repeat screening.
Screen for depression, anxiety and suicide risk if indicated.
red_flags: Refer urgently for withdrawal symptoms, seizures or confusion.
Assess risk if the patient reports suicidal thoughts or drug injection.
Return for chest pain, vomiting blood, jaundice or severe abdominal pain.

indications: Alcohol dependence with planned or unplanned stopping
Alcohol withdrawal symptoms in hospital or clinic
contraindications: Community withdrawal for patients with history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or serious illness (admit instead)
equipment: CIWA-Ar or similar withdrawal scale chart
Thermometer, blood pressure monitor and pulse oximeter
Benzodiazepine and parenteral thiamine per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity and obtain consent, explaining the plan and possible symptoms.
Take an alcohol history including amount, pattern, last drink and previous withdrawals or seizures.
Examine for intoxication, dehydration, infection, liver disease, head injury and Wernicke encephalopathy.
Check blood glucose and send blood tests such as electrolytes, liver function and full blood count.
Give parenteral thiamine per local protocol before any glucose-containing fluid.
Score withdrawal using the CIWA-Ar or local scale at regular intervals.
Give withdrawal medication according to the score or a fixed schedule per local protocol.
Correct dehydration and electrolyte problems and encourage oral fluids and nutrition.
Nurse in a calm, well-lit area with fall precautions.
Monitor vital signs, consciousness and hallucinations, and increase monitoring if scores rise.
Reduce and stop withdrawal medication over several days as symptoms settle.
Offer brief intervention and plan relapse prevention and follow-up.
aftercare: Continue oral thiamine and vitamins per local protocol.
Link to a treatment programme, support group or family support.
Advise against driving while taking sedating medicines.
red_flags: Escalate urgently for seizures, confusion, hallucinations, fever, rapid pulse or high blood pressure (possible delirium tremens).
Call for help for ataxia, eye movement problems or confusion (possible Wernicke encephalopathy).
Return for vomiting blood, yellow eyes, black stools or relapse with withdrawal symptoms.

indications: Child and adolescent emotional or behavioural problems
Family conflict affecting a patient's mental health
Family psychoeducation in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or eating disorders
contraindications: Ongoing domestic violence where joint sessions would increase risk
Family members acutely intoxicated or threatening
equipment: Room large enough for the family with seating in a circle
Toys or drawing materials for young children
steps: Confirm who is attending, explain confidentiality and obtain each member's agreement.
Agree ground rules such as one person speaking at a time and respect.
Ask each family member to describe the problem and what they hope to change.
Draw a genogram to map relationships, losses and important events.
Observe communication patterns, alliances and conflicts during the session.
Help the family to see the problem as shared rather than blaming one member.
Teach and practise skills such as active listening, problem solving and positive communication.
Address stigma, cultural and religious beliefs about the illness respectfully.
Agree a task for the family to practise before the next session.
Screen privately for abuse or violence if concerns arise.
aftercare: Share a short summary of the plan with the family.
Book the next session and give contacts for crises.
red_flags: Stop the joint session and see members separately if there is threat, violence or disclosure of abuse.
Follow child safeguarding procedures when a child is at risk.
Escalate if any member reports suicidal thoughts or relapse.

indications: Depression, anxiety and adjustment problems
Substance use recovery and relapse prevention
Chronic mental illness skills and support groups
contraindications: Acute psychosis, active intoxication or behaviour that disrupts the group
High suicide risk needing individual care first
equipment: Private room with chairs in a circle
Session materials, flip chart or handouts
steps: Confirm the attendance list and check briefly on each member's safety.
Remind the group of confidentiality and ground rules.
Begin with a check-in where each member shares briefly.
Introduce the session theme or skill.
Facilitate discussion, encouraging all members to take part and preventing any one member from dominating.
Practise the skill in pairs or as a group where appropriate.
Manage conflict or distress calmly and offer individual time after the session if needed.
Summarise the key points and agree any tasks for the week.
End with a check-out and note any member needing follow-up.
aftercare: Follow up members who were distressed or absent.
Record attendance and progress for each member.
red_flags: See a member individually and assess risk if suicidal thoughts or relapse are disclosed.
Remove a member safely from the session if their behaviour threatens others.
Escalate breaches of confidentiality that put members at risk.

indications: Depression linked to grief, role disputes, role transitions or social isolation
Perinatal depression
contraindications: Psychotic depression or high suicide risk needing urgent care first
Severe intoxication or cognitive impairment preventing engagement
steps: Confirm identity, review risk and complete the symptom measure.
In early sessions, explain depression as a treatable illness and give the patient the sick role.
Complete an interpersonal inventory of important relationships.
Agree the focus problem area, such as grief, dispute, life change or isolation.
In middle sessions, link mood changes in the week to interpersonal events.
Work on the focus area, for example exploring feelings about a loss or options for resolving a dispute.
Use role play to practise new ways of communicating.
In group IPT, encourage members to support each other and share strategies.
In final sessions, review progress, prepare for ending and plan for warning signs of relapse.
Agree the task for the coming week and book the next session.
aftercare: Encourage the patient to use the skills in daily relationships.
Provide crisis contacts and review risk at each session.
red_flags: Complete a risk assessment and escalate if suicidal thoughts appear or worsen.
Refer for medical review if depression worsens or psychotic symptoms appear.
Follow safeguarding steps if domestic violence is disclosed.

indications: Mild to moderate depression or anxiety
Common mental disorders linked to life stressors, delivered by trained lay or primary care workers
contraindications: Psychosis, high suicide risk or severe depression needing specialist care first
Intoxication at the time of the session
equipment: Private space (a bench in a quiet area is acceptable)
Screening tool such as SSQ-14 or PHQ-9
steps: Confirm identity, explain the session and obtain agreement.
Complete the screening tool and check for suicide risk.
