Fluid overload with shock or raised intracranial pressure
contraindications: No suitable vascular access
Lack of trained staff or ICU monitoring
equipment: CRRT machine or haemodialysis machine set up for SLED
Replacement and dialysate fluids per prescription
Anticoagulation per unit protocol (citrate or other)
steps: Confirm identity, prescription (modality, dose, fluid removal target, anticoagulation) and written consent.
Check access function and baseline observations, electrolytes, calcium and coagulation.
Prime the circuit following the machine instructions and run the alarm checks.
Perform hand hygiene and connect the catheter aseptically.
Start the blood pump slowly and increase to the prescribed flow while watching blood pressure.
Start effluent, replacement and dialysate flows and the fluid removal rate.
Start anticoagulation per protocol and monitor its effect.
Record pressures, fluid balance and observations hourly.
Check electrolytes, calcium and acid-base at the protocol intervals and adjust fluids.
Change bags and filters as needed, documenting downtime.
At the end, return blood and disconnect aseptically, then lock the catheter.
aftercare: Continue strict fluid balance and electrolyte monitoring.
Review daily for kidney recovery and the need to continue.
red_flags: Stop and escalate for severe hypotension, circuit air or blood leak alarm, or suspected haemolysis.
Escalate for bleeding or signs of citrate accumulation.
Escalate for repeated filter clotting.

indications: Fluid overload with acceptable electrolytes, for example heart failure resistant to diuretics or between dialysis sessions
contraindications: Hyperkalaemia or severe uraemia needing diffusive dialysis
Haemodynamic instability
No usable vascular access
equipment: Vascular access needles or catheter set
Weighing scale and blood pressure monitor
steps: Confirm identity, target volume, duration and written consent.
Weigh the patient and record baseline observations and electrolytes.
Prime the circuit and set the machine to ultrafiltration only (no dialysate flow).
Perform hand hygiene, connect the access aseptically and start the blood pump.
Start anticoagulation per protocol.
Set the ultrafiltration rate to remove the target volume over the planned time.
Monitor blood pressure, pulse and symptoms frequently.
Reduce or pause ultrafiltration if blood pressure falls or cramps occur.
Return blood and disconnect at the end.
Weigh the patient and record the volume removed.
aftercare: Follow fluid and salt restriction.
Daily weights where possible.
red_flags: Stop for symptomatic hypotension, chest pain or arrhythmia.
Escalate if breathlessness persists or worsens after the session.

indications: Nephrotic syndrome in adults, or steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children
Unexplained acute kidney injury or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Glomerular haematuria with proteinuria or reduced function
Lupus or systemic disease with kidney involvement
contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension
Uncorrected bleeding tendency or ongoing antiplatelet or anticoagulant effect
Single functioning native kidney (relative)
Small shrunken kidneys
Uncooperative patient without sedation
Kidney infection or hydronephrosis
equipment: Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover
Automated spring-loaded biopsy gun with needles of suitable gauge
Sterile gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Local anaesthetic, syringes and spinal needle for track infiltration
Specimen containers for light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy as available
Saline-soaked gauze and dissecting microscope or magnifier
steps: Confirm identity, indication, blood pressure, platelet count, clotting, haemoglobin, group and save, and written consent.
Confirm antiplatelet and anticoagulant medicines have been held per protocol.
Position the patient prone (supine oblique if more suitable) and scan to choose the lower pole of the kidney.
Perform the time-out, prepare the skin and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the kidney capsule under ultrasound.
Make a small skin nick and advance the biopsy needle under real-time ultrasound to the capsule.
Ask the patient to hold breath, fire the needle into the cortex and withdraw.
Inspect the core for cortex and glomeruli and repeat passes as needed, limiting passes to what is necessary.
Divide and place the cores in the correct fixatives.
Scan for perinephric haematoma, apply pressure and a dressing.
aftercare: Bed rest for several hours with frequent blood pressure, pulse and site checks.
Check each urine sample for visible blood.
Recheck haemoglobin per protocol before discharge.
Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for about two weeks.
red_flags: Stop after the planned passes or if a haematoma enlarges on scanning.
Escalate urgently for falling blood pressure, rising pulse, severe loin pain or heavy haematuria with clots.
Escalate for urinary retention from clots.
Return after discharge for loin pain, visible blood in the urine, dizziness or fever.

indications: End-stage kidney disease in a medically suitable recipient with a compatible donor
contraindications: Active infection or untreated malignancy
Severe uncorrectable cardiac or vascular disease
Positive crossmatch without a desensitisation plan
Non-adherence or lack of follow-up support likely
equipment: Major vascular surgery set and retractors
Ureteric stent and bladder catheter with three-way irrigation
Cold preservation solution and ice for the graft
steps: Confirm identity, donor-recipient compatibility, final crossmatch, viral screening and written consent.
Complete the transplant checklist and time-out, with immunosuppression and prophylaxis per protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and insert central and urinary catheters.
Bench-prepare the donor kidney, keeping it cold.
Make a curved lower abdominal incision and expose the iliac vessels extraperitoneally.
Anastomose the renal vein to the external iliac vein.
Anastomose the renal artery to the external iliac artery.
Release clamps, check perfusion and haemostasis, and record ischaemia times.
Implant the ureter into the bladder over a stent.
Check graft position, place a drain and close in layers.
aftercare: Hourly urine output and fluid replacement per protocol.
Daily kidney function, drug levels and blood counts.
Early ultrasound with Doppler of the graft.
Lifelong adherence to anti-rejection medicines and clinic review.
Stent removal per protocol, usually within six weeks.
red_flags: Escalate urgently for a sudden fall in urine output (thrombosis, obstruction, leak).
Escalate for bleeding, swelling over the graft or haemodynamic instability.
Return urgently after discharge for fever, graft pain, reduced urine or rising creatinine.

indications: Fully assessed, voluntary living kidney donor with a compatible recipient
contraindications: Inadequate kidney function or abnormal kidney anatomy on imaging
Uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes or significant medical disease
Evidence of coercion or payment against national law and ethics approval
Age under 18
equipment: Laparoscopy stack and instruments or open nephrectomy set
Cold preservation solution, ice and sterile bowl for the back table
steps: Confirm identity, independent donor advocate assessment, ethics approval, imaging and written consent.
Complete the transplant checklist and time-out with the recipient team coordinated.
Give general anaesthesia, catheterise and position the donor laterally.
Enter the abdomen laparoscopically or through a flank incision.
Mobilise the colon and expose the kidney, ureter, renal artery and vein.
Divide the ureter low, preserving its blood supply.
Maintain good urine output, then clamp and divide the artery and vein with secure closure.
Remove the kidney quickly and pass it to the back table for cold flush.
Check haemostasis of the vascular stumps and close the wounds.
Record warm ischaemia time and complete the sign-out.
aftercare: Pain control and early mobilisation.
Monitor urine output and creatinine.
Lifelong annual check of blood pressure, kidney function and urine protein.
red_flags: Convert to open surgery for uncontrolled bleeding.
Escalate urgently for hypotension, falling haemoglobin or abdominal distension.
Return after discharge for fever, wound problems or reduced urine.

indications: Graft dysfunction or rising creatinine without clear cause
Suspected rejection or drug toxicity
Delayed graft function beyond expected time
Protocol biopsy per transplant centre policy
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding tendency or uncontrolled hypertension
Graft hydronephrosis or perigraft collection not assessed
equipment: Automated biopsy gun and needles of suitable gauge
Specimen containers for histology, immunofluorescence and C4d staining as available
steps: Confirm identity, indication, blood pressure, clotting, platelets and written consent.
Confirm antiplatelet and anticoagulant medicines are held per protocol.
Position the patient supine and scan the graft to plan an upper or lower pole route avoiding the hilum and bowel.
Perform the time-out, prepare the skin and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the graft capsule.
Advance the biopsy needle under real-time ultrasound and fire into the cortex.
Check each core for cortex and repeat passes only as needed.
Place cores in the correct fixatives.
Scan for haematoma and apply pressure and a dressing.
aftercare: Bed rest for several hours with observations and urine checks for blood.
Recheck haemoglobin before discharge per protocol.
Continue immunosuppression unless told otherwise.
red_flags: Escalate for hypotension, rising pulse, graft pain or heavy haematuria.
Escalate for urinary retention from clots.
Return for fever, graft tenderness or reduced urine output.

indications: Intravenous fluids, medicines or blood products needed
Anticipated emergency need for venous access
Contrast or procedural sedation
contraindications: Limb with infection, burn, fistula or lymphoedema on the chosen side
Limb on the side of axillary node clearance where avoidable
Venous access possible by a less invasive route for a single dose
equipment: Cannula of appropriate gauge (smallest that meets the need)
Flush syringe with sterile saline and extension set or bung
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and verbal consent, and check allergies including to tape or chlorhexidine.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare equipment on a clean tray.
Choose a straight vein away from joints, starting distally, avoiding the dominant hand if possible.
Apply the tourniquet above the site and let the vein fill, using gentle tapping or warmth if needed.
Put on gloves and clean the skin with antiseptic, letting it dry completely without touching the site again.
Anchor the vein by stretching the skin below the site.
Insert the cannula bevel up at a shallow angle until flashback is seen in the chamber.
Advance slightly further, then slide the cannula off the needle into the vein while holding the needle still.
Release the tourniquet, press on the vein above the tip and withdraw the needle straight into the sharps container.
Attach the bung or extension and flush with saline, watching for swelling or pain.
Secure with a sterile dressing and label it with date and time of insertion.
Splint the limb in infants and young children, keeping fingers or toes visible.
Limit attempts per operator and escalate to a more experienced colleague after two failures.
aftercare: Inspect the site at least once a shift and score for phlebitis.
Flush before and after each use and keep the dressing clean and dry.
Remove the cannula when no longer needed or according to local policy.
Tell the patient to report pain, swelling or redness at the site.
red_flags: Stop if the patient has severe pain or swelling on flushing (possible extravasation).
Remove the cannula and inform the doctor if there is redness tracking up the arm, pus or fever.
Escalate if access fails in a shocked patient; consider intraosseous access.

indications: Routine site inspection and flushing of an existing cannula
Cannula no longer needed
Phlebitis, infiltration, blockage or dislodgement
Cannula has reached the local re-site time
equipment: Sterile gauze or cotton wool and tape or plaster
Replacement sterile dressing if keeping the cannula
steps: Confirm patient identity and explain the procedure.
Perform hand hygiene and put on clean gloves.
Inspect the site and score it with the visual infusion phlebitis (VIP) score.
If keeping the cannula, clean the hub with antiseptic, flush with saline and check for pain or resistance.
Replace the dressing if it is loose, wet or soiled, and re-label it.
If removing, stop any infusion and close the clamp.
Remove the dressing gently, holding the cannula in place.
Withdraw the cannula slowly along the line of the vein and apply gauze with firm pressure for at least one minute.
Check the cannula tip is intact.
Cover the site with a plaster once bleeding has stopped.
Discard waste safely and document the reason for removal.
aftercare: Recheck the site later for bleeding or haematoma.
Continue to observe a phlebitic site until signs settle.
Ask the patient to report pain, swelling or redness after removal.
red_flags: Send the tip for culture and inform the doctor if there is pus or fever.
Inform the doctor at once if the cannula tip is missing or broken.
Escalate a VIP score of 3 or more, or tracking redness.

indications: Prescribed intravenous fluids
Prescribed intermittent or continuous intravenous medicine infusion
contraindications: No valid prescription
Cannula not patent or site phlebitic
equipment: Prescribed fluid bag (checked for name, expiry, clarity and leaks)
Administration set (macro-drip, or burette or micro-drip set for children)
Watch with second hand, or infusion pump
Fluid balance chart and medication label
steps: Check the prescription, patient identity and allergies against the fluid and any added medicine.
Perform hand hygiene and inspect the fluid bag for expiry, colour, particles and leaks.
Close the roller clamp and spike the bag aseptically without touching the spike.
Squeeze the chamber to half full and prime the line slowly, removing all air bubbles.
Label the bag with any additive, the start time and the nurse's name.
Clean the cannula port and check patency with a saline flush.
Connect the line and open the clamp.
Calculate the drip rate from the prescribed volume, time and the set's drop factor, and count drops for a full minute.
For children, use a burette or pump and fill only one or two hours of fluid at a time.
Record the start time and volume on the fluid balance chart.
Check the rate, site and remaining volume at least hourly.
aftercare: Record intake hourly and total at the end of each bag.
Change the administration set according to local policy or if contaminated.
Watch the patient for signs of fluid overload or dehydration.
red_flags: Stop the infusion and inform the doctor for breathlessness, crackles, raised JVP or new oedema.
Stop if the site is swollen, painful or blanched (infiltration).
Stop and escalate if a reaction (rash, rigors, wheeze) occurs during a medicine infusion.
Report if the infusion is well ahead of or behind the prescribed schedule.

name: Infusion pump or syringe driver setup

indications: Accurate delivery of fluids or medicines where gravity is unsafe
Infusions for neonates and small children
Continuous medicine infusions (for example inotropes, insulin, sedation, analgesia)
contraindications: Pump not serviced, alarms faulty or battery not charged
Staff not trained on the model in use
equipment: Serviced infusion pump or syringe driver with charged battery
Prescribed fluid or prepared medicine with label
Extension line, preferably with an anti-siphon or one-way valve
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies and the prepared medicine with a second nurse for high-risk infusions.
Perform hand hygiene and check the pump is clean, charged and within its service date.
Prime the line or syringe and extension, removing air.
Load the set or syringe into the pump exactly as the manufacturer directs, ensuring the syringe plunger is engaged.
Switch on, select the correct syringe or set type and any drug library entry.
Enter the rate and volume to be infused and have a second nurse confirm settings for high-risk medicines.
Clean the port, confirm cannula patency and connect the line.
Start the pump and confirm it is running and the line is free of kinks.
Position the syringe driver level with the patient to avoid siphoning.
Record the start time, rate and settings on the chart.
Check the rate, volume infused, site and alarms at least hourly.
aftercare: Never silence an alarm without finding the cause.
Label lines clearly when several infusions run together.
Keep the pump plugged in when possible.
red_flags: Stop and recheck if the volume infused does not match the expected amount.
Escalate at once if a high-risk medicine was given at the wrong rate.
Stop for site swelling, pain or an occlusion alarm that does not clear.

indications: Prescribed red cells, whole blood, platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate
contraindications: Unlabelled or mislabelled unit, or mismatch with the patient or compatibility form
Unit expired, leaking, discoloured or with clots
Patient refusal (respect religious objections and inform the doctor)
equipment: Patent cannula (18-20 G in adults; smaller acceptable in children)
Normal saline only, if a flush is needed
Observation chart, thermometer, BP machine and pulse oximeter
steps: Confirm a valid prescription, documented indication and written consent.
Take baseline temperature, pulse, BP, respiratory rate and SpO2 within an hour before starting.
Collect only one unit at a time from the blood bank and start within 30 minutes of collection.
At the bedside, two staff check the patient's name, number and date of birth against the unit, form and wristband.
Check blood group, unit number, expiry and that the unit is intact.
Perform hand hygiene, prime the blood set and connect it to the cannula.
Start slowly and stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes.
Repeat observations at 15 minutes, then at least hourly and at the end of the unit.
Complete each unit within 4 hours of it leaving cold storage.
Do not add any medicine to the blood or its line.
Record the unit number, start and finish times and observations.
aftercare: Check observations 15 minutes after the transfusion ends.
Return empty bags to the blood bank if local policy requires.
Warn patients going home to report fever, rash, dark urine or breathlessness within 24 hours.
red_flags: Stop at once and keep the line open with saline for fever, rigors, rash, wheeze, back pain, low BP or breathlessness.
Call the doctor urgently and recheck the identity of the unit if a reaction is suspected.
Send the bag and post-reaction blood and urine samples to the blood bank after a reaction.
Watch for fluid overload in the elderly, children and those with heart disease.

indications: Prescribed parenteral nutrition when the gut cannot be used adequately
contraindications: No dedicated lumen or appropriate venous access
Bag damaged, emulsion separated (cracked) or past expiry
equipment: Prescribed PN bag stored as directed and brought to room temperature
Dedicated central or suitable peripheral line lumen
Filtered administration set and infusion pump
Sterile gloves, antiseptic and dressing pack
Capillary glucose meter and fluid balance chart
steps: Check the prescription, patient identity and bag label, contents and expiry with a second nurse.
Inspect the bag for leaks, particles or separation of the emulsion.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique throughout.
Prime the filtered set and load it into the pump.
Clean the dedicated lumen hub with antiseptic and allow it to dry.
Connect the line and start at the prescribed rate, using any prescribed step-up.
Never use the PN lumen for blood sampling, medicines or other fluids.
Monitor capillary glucose as prescribed, especially at the start and end.
Record weight, fluid balance and observations as per protocol.
At the end, stop or taper as prescribed and lock or flush the lumen.
aftercare: Change the set with each new bag.
Check the line site and temperature every shift.
Send scheduled blood tests (electrolytes, glucose, liver function, triglycerides).
red_flags: Stop and escalate for fever or rigors (possible line infection).
Escalate high or low glucose readings.
Stop if the emulsion separates or the line is not the dedicated one.

indications: Mild to moderate dehydration when IV access is difficult or unwanted
Palliative or elderly patients needing fluids on the ward or at home
contraindications: Severe dehydration or shock (needs IV or IO access)
Severe electrolyte disturbance needing rapid correction
Bleeding disorder, generalised oedema or skin infection at the site
equipment: Fine butterfly needle or small subcutaneous cannula
Antiseptic swab, clean gloves and transparent dressing
steps: Confirm identity, prescription and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and prime the set.
Choose a site with good subcutaneous tissue such as the abdomen, upper chest, thigh or over the scapula.
Clean the skin and allow it to dry.
Pinch the skin and insert the needle at 30-45 degrees into the subcutaneous tissue.
Check that no blood is drawn back, then secure with a transparent dressing.
Start the infusion at the prescribed slow rate.
Check the site for swelling, redness or leaking at least every 4 hours.
Re-site the needle if the site becomes hard, red or painful.
aftercare: Expect some soft swelling that settles as the fluid is absorbed.
Record intake on the fluid balance chart.
Change the site according to local policy.
red_flags: Stop if the site is very painful, red, hard or leaking heavily.
Escalate if dehydration is worsening or the patient becomes drowsy.

indications: Prescribed medicine or vaccine for the intramuscular route
contraindications: Known allergy to the medicine
Infection, scarring or wound at the site
Severe bleeding disorder or low platelets (check with the prescriber)
equipment: Prescribed medicine with label and expiry checked
Syringe of appropriate size and needle with length suited to site and patient size
Alcohol swab if local policy requires, and cotton wool
steps: Check the prescription, patient identity, allergies and the five rights of medicine administration.
Explain the injection and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and draw up the medicine aseptically.
Choose the site; use vastus lateralis in infants and the deltoid or ventrogluteal in older children and adults.
Avoid the dorsogluteal site where possible because of the risk of sciatic nerve injury, and never use it in infants or young children.
Position the patient so the muscle is relaxed, and clean the skin if required.
Stretch the skin or use the Z-track technique and insert the needle at 90 degrees.
Inject slowly and steadily, then withdraw the needle and apply light pressure.
Discard the needle immediately into the sharps container without recapping.
Observe for at least 15 minutes after vaccines or medicines with an allergy risk.
aftercare: Record medicine, site, time and batch number where applicable.
Advise that mild soreness is expected.
Rotate sites for repeated injections.
red_flags: Treat as anaphylaxis and call for help for wheeze, swelling, collapse or widespread rash.
Report numbness, shooting pain or foot drop after a buttock injection.
Report a hot, swollen, painful site days later (possible abscess).

indications: Prescribed subcutaneous medicine (for example insulin, anticoagulant, some vaccines)
Teaching self-injection
contraindications: Known allergy to the medicine
Oedema, lipohypertrophy, bruising or infection at the site
equipment: Prescribed medicine, pen device or vial with checked label and expiry
Insulin syringe or fine short needle as appropriate
Cotton wool, clean gloves and sharps container
Capillary glucose meter when giving insulin
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies and the five rights.
For insulin, check a recent capillary glucose and that the patient will eat.
Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the dose aseptically, priming a pen device as directed.
Choose a site, rotating from the last injection.
Pinch a fold of skin and insert the needle at 90 degrees, or 45 degrees in thin patients.
Inject slowly, wait a few seconds, then withdraw the needle.
Do not rub the site; apply light pressure if it bleeds.
Discard the needle into the sharps container without recapping.
aftercare: Record medicine, site and time.
Teach site rotation and safe sharps disposal to patients who self-inject.
Watch for hypoglycaemia after insulin.
red_flags: Treat hypoglycaemia promptly if glucose is low or the patient is sweaty or confused.
Report a large spreading bruise or bleeding after an anticoagulant injection.
Call for help for signs of allergy or anaphylaxis.

indications: Tuberculin skin testing
BCG vaccination by trained staff
Allergy or sensitivity skin testing as prescribed
contraindications: Previous severe reaction to the same agent
Skin infection, burn or eczema at the site
For BCG, known or suspected immunosuppression (including symptomatic HIV)
equipment: Prescribed agent with checked label and expiry
Tuberculin or 1 mL syringe with a fine short needle (25-27 G)
Cotton wool, clean gloves and sharps container
Skin marker and ruler for reading tests
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies and any previous reactions.
Explain the procedure, including any need to return for reading, and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and draw up the exact amount without air bubbles.
Use the inner forearm for skin tests or the left upper arm over the deltoid insertion for BCG.
Stretch the skin taut and insert the needle bevel up almost parallel to the skin, just under the surface.
Inject slowly; a pale raised bleb should form and resistance should be felt.
If no bleb forms the injection is too deep; note it and follow local policy.
Withdraw the needle without massaging the site and discard it safely.
Mark the site if a reading is needed.
aftercare: Tell the patient not to scratch, rub or cover the site tightly.
Book tuberculin readings at 48-72 hours and measure induration, not redness.
For BCG, explain that a small ulcer and scar forming over weeks is normal.
red_flags: Call for help for signs of anaphylaxis.
Refer for a large discharging abscess or swollen armpit glands after BCG.

indications: Prescribed medicine for direct intravenous injection
contraindications: Medicine not licensed or not safe for bolus (check the drug information)
Cannula not patent, phlebitic or infiltrated
Known allergy to the medicine
equipment: Prescribed medicine with label and expiry checked
Watch or clock to time the injection
Sharps container and access to the emergency trolley
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies and five rights, with a second checker where policy requires.
Confirm the medicine can be given as a bolus and the required dilution and injection time.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the medicine aseptically, labelling the syringe.
Inspect the cannula site and clean the port with antiseptic, letting it dry.
Flush with saline to confirm patency, watching for pain or swelling.
Inject the medicine at the recommended speed, timing it and watching the patient and site.
Flush with saline at the same speed to clear the line.
Separate incompatible medicines with a flush between each.
Observe the patient for immediate reactions.
Discard sharps safely and sign the chart immediately.
aftercare: Monitor for delayed reactions as appropriate to the medicine.
Recheck the cannula site.
red_flags: Stop and call for help for rash, wheeze, hypotension, chest pain or collapse.
Stop if the site swells or the patient reports burning (extravasation).
Report any medicine given too fast or to the wrong patient at once.

indications: Prescribed oral medicine
contraindications: Nil by mouth status or unsafe swallow (seek an alternative route)
Reduced consciousness
Persistent vomiting
equipment: Medicine cups, oral syringes for liquids
Tablet crusher if crushing is approved for that medicine
steps: Perform hand hygiene and check the prescription is complete, legible and current.
Check patient identity with wristband and by asking name and date of birth.
Confirm allergies and any medicine-specific checks (for example pulse, BP or glucose).
Check the medicine name, strength, expiry and the five rights.
Prepare doses without touching tablets, using an oral syringe for liquids.
Sit the patient upright and check they can swallow.
Give the medicine and stay until it is swallowed.
Do not crush modified-release or enteric-coated tablets without pharmacist advice.
For children, use age-appropriate formulations and involve the caregiver.
Sign the chart immediately and record any refused or omitted doses with the reason.
aftercare: Watch for expected effects and side effects.
Tell the prescriber about repeated refusals or missed doses.
Explain to the patient what each medicine is for.
red_flags: Stop and seek help if the patient coughs, chokes or has a changed voice after swallowing.
Call for help for signs of allergic reaction.
Report any medicine error immediately.

indications: Prescribed rectal medicine (for example for fever, seizures, constipation or nausea)
Oral route not possible
contraindications: Recent rectal or anal surgery or trauma
Neutropenia or severe low platelets
Rectal bleeding of unknown cause
steps: Check prescription, identity, allergies and five rights.
Explain the procedure, gain verbal consent and ensure privacy with a chaperone if needed.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves and apron.
Position the patient on the left side with knees bent; infants may lie on their back with legs raised.
Lubricate the tip of the suppository.
Separate the buttocks and insert the suppository gently past the anal sphincter, using a finger in adults and the little finger in infants.
Hold the buttocks together briefly to help retention.
Wipe the area, remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Ask the patient to stay lying for at least 15 minutes if possible.
aftercare: Record the time given and any result.
Check whether the suppository was expelled and inform the prescriber if so.
red_flags: Stop if there is resistance, severe pain or bleeding.
Watch for a vasovagal reaction (slow pulse, fainting).

indications: Prescribed eye medicine
Teaching patients or caregivers to instil eye medicines
contraindications: Known allergy to the medicine
Suspected penetrating eye injury (do not instil, refer)
equipment: Prescribed drops or ointment, labelled for one patient and within its opened date
Sterile gauze or cotton wool and clean water or saline
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies, which eye and the opened date of the bottle.
Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Clean any discharge from the lid, wiping from inner to outer corner with a fresh swab each time.
Ask the patient to tilt the head back and look up.
Gently pull down the lower lid to form a pocket.
Instil one drop, or a thin line of ointment from inner to outer corner, without touching the eye with the tip.
Ask the patient to close the eye gently and press on the inner corner for a minute to reduce systemic absorption.
Wait at least 5 minutes between different drops, and give ointment last.
Wipe away excess and perform hand hygiene.
aftercare: Warn that ointment blurs vision briefly.
Discard bottles after the period stated by the manufacturer once opened.
red_flags: Refer urgently for sudden loss of vision, severe eye pain or a fixed red eye.
Stop and report redness, swelling or itching that worsens after the medicine.

indications: Prescribed ear medicine (for example for otitis externa or wax softening)
contraindications: Suspected perforated eardrum unless the medicine is safe for perforation
Grommets in place unless the medicine is approved for them
equipment: Prescribed ear drops warmed to body temperature in the hand
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies and which ear.
Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and warm the bottle in the hands to avoid dizziness.
Ask the patient to lie on the side or tilt the head with the affected ear up.
Straighten the canal by pulling the pinna up and back in adults, or down and back in young children.
Instil the prescribed drops without touching the ear with the tip.
Press gently on the tragus to help the drops enter.
Ask the patient to stay in position for a few minutes.
Wipe away excess and perform hand hygiene.
aftercare: Advise keeping the ear dry during treatment.
Advise not to insert cotton buds or objects into the ear.
red_flags: Refer for severe pain, swelling behind the ear, facial weakness or fever.
Stop if dizziness or new hearing loss occurs.

indications: Symptomatic relief of nasal congestion in older children and adults
contraindications: Infants and young children (high scald risk; use saline drops and fluids instead)
Confused, drowsy or unsupervised patients
Severe asthma or breathing difficulty (needs medical assessment)
equipment: Bowl of hot (not boiling) water on a stable surface
steps: Explain the procedure and its scald risk, and gain verbal consent.
Place the bowl on a firm, stable surface at table height, never on the lap.
Allow the water to cool from boiling before use.
Ask the patient to sit upright with the face about 30 cm above the bowl.
Drape a towel over the head and bowl if tolerated, keeping eyes closed.
Ask the patient to breathe slowly through the nose for a few minutes, stopping if uncomfortable.
Stay with children and frail patients throughout.
Remove the bowl safely after use.
aftercare: Encourage fluids and nose blowing.
Teach caregivers that home steam is not advised for young children.
red_flags: Treat any scald immediately with cool running water and report it.
Seek medical review for fast breathing, chest indrawing, wheeze or high fever.

indications: Enteral feeding when oral intake is unsafe or inadequate
Gastric decompression in bowel obstruction or ileus
Medicine administration when swallowing is not possible
contraindications: Suspected base of skull fracture or severe facial trauma (use the oral route)
Recent oesophageal surgery, known varices or stricture without senior advice
Unsafe airway in a drowsy patient without airway protection
equipment: Nasogastric tube of correct size (fine-bore for feeding, wider Ryle's for drainage)
Water-based lubricant and a glass of water if the patient can swallow
Clean gloves, apron, tissues and a vomit bowl
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent, and agree a stop signal.
Perform hand hygiene and sit the patient upright with the head neutral.
Measure the tube from the nose tip to the earlobe and down to the xiphisternum (NEX) and mark it.
Check the nostrils and choose the clearer side.
Lubricate the tip and pass it gently back along the floor of the nose.
When the tube reaches the throat, ask the patient to swallow sips of water or dry swallow as you advance.
Advance to the marked length and stop if the patient coughs, struggles or becomes breathless.
Secure the tube to the nose and note the external length.
Aspirate gastric contents and test with a pH strip; pH 5.5 or less confirms gastric placement.
If no aspirate or pH above 5.5, reposition the patient, wait and retry, then request an X-ray before use.
Never confirm position by air whoosh test, by bubbling in water or by litmus paper.
Document the tube type, size, external length and confirmation method.
aftercare: Recheck the position before every feed, medicine or flush and after vomiting or coughing.
Check the external length mark each shift.
Provide nasal and mouth care and change tape when soiled.
red_flags: Remove the tube at once for coughing, choking, cyanosis or breathlessness during insertion.
Do not use the tube if placement cannot be confirmed; get an X-ray.
Report nosebleeds, pressure sores on the nostril or a displaced tube.

indications: Prescribed enteral feed via an NG or orogastric tube
contraindications: Tube position not confirmed
Bowel obstruction, ileus or high gastric aspirates as defined by local protocol
Active vomiting or reduced consciousness without airway protection
equipment: Prescribed feed (formula, expressed breast milk or blended feed per dietitian)
Enteral syringes or giving set and feeding pump
steps: Check the feeding plan, patient identity and feed type, volume and expiry.
Perform hand hygiene and sit the patient up at least 30-45 degrees.
Check the tube's external length mark and confirm placement by aspirate pH before feeding.
Flush the tube with water as per local protocol.
Give a bolus feed slowly by gravity using the syringe barrel, or start a pump feed at the set rate.
Never push the feed under pressure with the plunger.
Watch for coughing, distress or abdominal distension during the feed.
Flush the tube with water after the feed and after each medicine.
Keep the patient upright for at least 30 minutes after bolus feeds.
Record the volume given on the fluid balance chart.
aftercare: Clean or change syringes and sets according to local policy.
Weigh the patient regularly and review the plan with the dietitian or doctor.
Give mouth care regularly.
red_flags: Stop the feed if the patient coughs, vomits, becomes breathless or the tube appears displaced.
Report abdominal distension, diarrhoea or repeated high aspirates.
Check blood glucose and electrolytes in malnourished patients starting feeds (refeeding risk).

form.label: Placement checked before feed
options: X-ray confirmed earlier and length unchanged

indications: Daily stoma site care for a gastrostomy tube
Prescribed feeding or medicines via gastrostomy
contraindications: Suspected tube displacement, leakage of feed into the abdomen or peritonitis
equipment: Cooled boiled water or saline and gauze
Prescribed feed and water for flushes
Dressing only if the site is leaking
steps: Confirm identity and the feeding plan, and explain the procedure.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Inspect the stoma site for redness, swelling, leaking, overgranulation or pain.
Clean around the site with water or saline and dry thoroughly.
Once the tract is healed, rotate the tube 360 degrees daily and move it gently in and out unless told otherwise.
Check the external length marker or fixation plate position.
Sit the patient up 30-45 degrees and flush the tube with water.
Give the feed by gravity bolus or pump as prescribed.
Flush after the feed and after each medicine, giving medicines one at a time.
Record the site condition, volume given and any problems.
aftercare: Keep the patient upright for at least 30 minutes after a feed.
Teach the caregiver site care, flushing and what to do if the tube falls out.
Check the balloon water volume weekly on balloon tubes per manufacturer.
red_flags: If the tube falls out, cover the site and get it replaced urgently because the tract closes within hours.
Stop feeds and escalate for pain on feeding, leakage around the tube, fever or a rigid abdomen.
Report bleeding, spreading redness or pus at the site.

indications: Acute urinary retention
Accurate urine output monitoring in critical illness
Peri-operative bladder drainage
Urine sample in a child who cannot void when clean catch is not possible
contraindications: Suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, pelvic fracture) - refer, do not attempt
Recent urethral surgery without specialist advice
equipment: Sterile catheter pack with drapes, gauze and gallipot
Foley catheter of appropriate size (12-16 Fr adults; smaller in children)
Sterile saline or water for cleaning and sterile water for the balloon
Sterile lubricating gel, with local anaesthetic gel where available
Specimen container if a sample is needed
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent, and ensure privacy with a chaperone.
Perform hand hygiene, open the pack aseptically and put on sterile gloves.
Position the patient supine, with knees bent and apart for females.
Clean the meatus with saline, retracting the foreskin in males and separating the labia in females.
Instil lubricating gel into the urethra in males, or apply it to the catheter tip in females, and wait for it to act.
Insert the catheter gently with a no-touch technique until urine flows.
Advance a little further in females, and almost to the hub in males, before inflating the balloon.
Inflate the balloon with sterile water to the volume printed on the catheter, stopping if the patient has pain.
Withdraw gently until resistance is felt and connect the drainage bag.
Replace the foreskin in males to prevent paraphimosis.
Secure the catheter to the thigh and hang the bag below bladder level off the floor.
Record the residual volume, catheter size, balloon volume and batch number.
aftercare: Keep the drainage system closed and the bag below the bladder.
Give daily meatal hygiene with soap and water.
Review the need for the catheter every day and remove it as soon as possible.
red_flags: Stop and seek senior help if resistance is met, there is bleeding or no urine flows in males.
Never inflate the balloon until urine has drained.
Report fever, flank pain, blood or debris in the urine, or a sudden drop in output.

indications: Catheter no longer needed
Planned trial without catheter after retention
Catheter blocked or due for change
contraindications: Removal not agreed after urological surgery or trauma (check the surgical plan)
equipment: Measuring jug and bladder scanner if available
steps: Check the plan for removal, confirm identity and gain verbal consent.
Remove early in the morning where possible so voiding can be monitored during the day.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Empty the drainage bag and record the volume.
Attach the syringe to the balloon port and let the balloon deflate passively, drawing back gently only if needed.
Check the volume withdrawn matches the volume recorded at insertion.
Ask the patient to breathe out and withdraw the catheter gently.
Inspect the catheter tip is intact and clean the meatus.
Encourage oral fluids and ask the patient to measure each void.
Record the time of removal and the time and volume of first void.
aftercare: Expect some burning or frequency on the first few voids.
Scan the bladder or check for retention if not voided within 6 hours or voids are small.
red_flags: Stop if the balloon will not deflate or the catheter will not come out; do not cut the catheter, seek senior help.
Re-catheterise or escalate if the patient is in retention, distressed or the bladder is palpable.
Report fever, haematuria or severe pain.

indications: Daily care of an indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheter
Drainage bag change
steps: Explain the care and gain verbal consent, ensuring privacy.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Wash the meatus and catheter from the body outward with soap and water and dry, retracting and replacing the foreskin in males.
Check the catheter is secured to the thigh without tension.
Check the tubing is not kinked and the bag is below bladder level and off the floor.
Empty the bag into a clean jug when two-thirds full, without letting the tap touch the jug.
Change the bag as per manufacturer or local policy, without breaking the closed system unnecessarily.
Record urine volume and appearance.
Review and document whether the catheter is still needed.
aftercare: Encourage oral fluids unless restricted.
Teach patients going home how to care for the catheter and bags.
red_flags: Report fever, rigors, confusion, flank pain or cloudy offensive urine (possible infection).
Check for blockage and escalate if urine output falls suddenly or urine bypasses the catheter.
Report blood clots or frank blood in the bag.

indications: Neurogenic bladder (for example spina bifida, spinal cord injury)
Chronic incomplete bladder emptying
Caregiver to catheterise a child
contraindications: Unable to perform the technique and no trained caregiver available
Suspected urethral stricture or injury before specialist review
equipment: Single-use or reusable nelaton catheters of suitable size
Container to measure urine, and a bladder diary
Clean storage container for reusable catheters
steps: Confirm the plan with the doctor and explain the purpose to the patient or caregiver.
Teach hand washing with soap and water before and after.
Teach the patient to find a comfortable position (sitting on the toilet, standing or lying).
Teach cleaning of the meatus with water or a wipe, front to back in females.
Show how to find the meatus, using a mirror for females at first.
Lubricate the catheter and insert it gently until urine flows, then a little further.
Let the bladder drain fully, then withdraw slowly, pausing if urine flows again.
Show how to measure and record the volume in the diary.
Teach cleaning, drying and storage of reusable catheters where single-use ones are not affordable.
Watch the patient or caregiver perform the technique and correct errors.
Agree the catheterisation schedule set by the doctor.
aftercare: Give written instructions and a supply plan.
Book a review to check technique and the bladder diary.
red_flags: Seek help for fever, flank pain, bloody urine or cloudy offensive urine.
Stop and seek help if the catheter cannot be passed or causes bleeding.
Report volumes repeatedly above the limit set by the doctor.

indications: Suspected urinary retention
Post-void residual measurement after catheter removal
Deciding whether catheterisation is needed
contraindications: Open wound or dressing over the suprapubic area
Pregnancy (results unreliable; use clinical assessment)
equipment: Portable bladder scanner, charged and calibrated, or point-of-care ultrasound
steps: Explain the scan and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and position the patient supine with the abdomen exposed.
Select the correct patient setting (male, female or child) on the scanner.
Apply gel about 3 cm above the pubic bone in the midline.
Place the probe pointing towards the bladder and scan, adjusting until the bladder is centred.
Repeat the scan and take the highest reliable reading.
Wipe off the gel and clean the probe.
Record the volume and the time since the last void.
aftercare: Act on the result according to the plan or inform the doctor.
Repeat the scan as planned if voiding is being monitored.
red_flags: Escalate a large residual volume or a painful, palpable bladder for catheterisation.
Interpret with caution in obesity, ascites or after pelvic surgery and correlate clinically.

indications: Surgical wound, laceration, abrasion or minor burn needing cleaning and cover
Soiled, wet or loose dressing
equipment: Sterile dressing pack (gauze, gallipot, forceps or sterile gloves)
Sterile saline or clean drinking-quality water
Prescribed or appropriate dressing (gauze, non-adherent, absorbent)
Clean gloves, apron and clinical waste bag
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Give analgesia beforehand if the dressing is likely to be painful.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the trolley and position the patient comfortably.
Remove the old dressing with clean gloves, soaking it if stuck, and discard it.
Perform hand hygiene again and open the sterile pack using aseptic non-touch technique.
Assess the wound for size, wound bed, exudate, odour, edges and surrounding skin.
Clean the wound gently with saline from the cleanest to the dirtiest area, or irrigate.
Take a swab only if there are signs of infection.
Dry the surrounding skin and apply the chosen dressing.
Secure the dressing without constricting the limb.
Dispose of waste, perform hand hygiene and document the assessment.
aftercare: Advise keeping the dressing clean and dry and when it will next be changed.
Give advice on nutrition and on not touching the wound.
Check tetanus status for traumatic wounds.
red_flags: Report spreading redness, increasing pain, pus, foul smell or fever.
Report wound breakdown or sudden heavy bleeding.
Refer wounds not healing as expected.

indications: Open cavity after abscess drainage or surgical wound breakdown
Deep wound healing by secondary intention
contraindications: Undrained abscess or unexplored sinus tract of unknown depth (refer for review)
equipment: Sterile dressing pack and sterile gloves
Sterile saline for irrigation and a syringe
Packing material (ribbon gauze, alginate or other cavity dressing)
Analgesia given in advance where needed
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Give analgesia 30 minutes before if packing is painful.
Perform hand hygiene and remove the old packing, soaking it with saline if stuck.
Count the pieces of old packing removed and compare with the last record.
Irrigate the cavity with saline using a syringe.
Measure length, width and depth with a sterile probe.
Pack the cavity loosely to fill the dead space without forcing, leaving a tail visible.
Use one continuous piece where possible and record the number of pieces left in.
Cover with a secondary absorbent dressing.
Document measurements, wound bed, exudate and packing used.
aftercare: Change the packing as planned, usually daily or when soaked.
Reduce packing as the cavity fills with granulation tissue.
red_flags: Report bleeding that does not stop with pressure.
Report spreading redness, fever, a foul smell or a cavity getting bigger.
Escalate if a piece of packing cannot be found.

indications: Healed wound at the planned time for suture removal
contraindications: Wound not healed or gaping on inspection (seek review before removing all sutures)
equipment: Sterile suture removal pack (forceps and stitch cutter or fine scissors)
Clean gloves and clinical waste bag
steps: Confirm identity, the plan for removal and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and remove the dressing.
Inspect the wound for healing, gaping, discharge or redness.
Clean the suture line with saline.
Lift each knot with forceps, cut the suture close to the skin on one side and pull it out towards the wound.
Never pull the exposed, contaminated part of the suture through the skin.
Remove alternate sutures first if healing is uncertain, and stop if the wound starts to gape.
Count the sutures removed and check they are complete.
Apply skin closure strips if there is any tension.
Document the number removed and the state of the wound.
aftercare: Advise avoiding strain on the wound for some weeks.
Advise protecting the scar from strong sun.
red_flags: Stop and seek review if the wound gapes or opens.
Report pus, spreading redness or fever.

indications: Healed wound closed with skin staples at the planned time
contraindications: Wound not healed or gaping (seek review)
equipment: Sterile dressing pack, saline and gauze
steps: Confirm identity, the plan for removal and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and remove the dressing.
Inspect the wound for healing, gaping, discharge or redness.
Clean the wound with saline.
Slide the lower jaw of the remover under the centre of the staple.
Squeeze the handles fully so the staple bends and its ends lift out of the skin.
Lift the staple away and place it in the sharps container.
Remove alternate staples first if healing is uncertain, and stop if the wound gapes.
Count the staples removed against the number recorded at closure.
Apply skin closure strips if needed and document.
aftercare: Advise avoiding strain on the wound for some weeks.
Explain that small red dots at the staple sites fade.
red_flags: Stop and seek review if the wound gapes or opens.
Report pus, spreading redness or fever.

indications: Surgical drain no longer needed as instructed by the surgical team
contraindications: No instruction from the surgical team to remove
High or bloody drainage in the last 24 hours (check with the surgeon)
equipment: Sterile dressing pack, saline and gauze
Specimen container if the tip is to be sent
steps: Confirm the instruction to remove, identity and verbal consent, and give analgesia if needed.
Record the drainage volume in the last 24 hours.
Release the vacuum on a suction drain by clamping and releasing the bottle as per the device.
Perform hand hygiene, remove the dressing and clean around the drain site.
Cut and remove the securing suture.
Ask the patient to breathe out and withdraw the drain steadily, stopping if there is strong resistance.
Check the drain is intact and the tip complete.
Apply pressure, then cover the site with a dressing.
Measure and record the final drainage and the appearance of the fluid.
aftercare: Check the site for leakage over the next few hours.
Change the dressing if it becomes soaked.
red_flags: Stop and seek senior help if the drain will not come out with gentle traction.
Report a drain that is not intact.
Report swelling, fever or heavy leakage after removal (possible collection).

indications: Pressure ulcer of any category needing assessment and dressing
contraindications: Heel ulcer with stable dry black eschar and poor circulation should not be debrided (seek review)
equipment: Appropriate dressing (hydrocolloid, foam, alginate, hydrogel or gauze as available)
Wound measuring tape or ruler and camera if allowed by policy
Clean gloves, apron and waste bag
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Give analgesia beforehand if needed.
Perform hand hygiene and position the patient to expose the ulcer, with help.
Remove the old dressing and assess the ulcer category, size, wound bed, exudate, odour and edges.
Clean the ulcer and surrounding skin with saline.
Remove loose slough gently only if trained; refer deep or necrotic ulcers for debridement.
Protect the surrounding skin from moisture and choose a dressing to match the wound bed and exudate.
Apply the dressing and secure it without tension.
Reposition the patient off the ulcer and on a pressure-relieving surface.
Document the assessment and update the pressure care plan.
aftercare: Continue regular repositioning and pressure-area checks.
Optimise nutrition and hydration and control incontinence.
Review the ulcer at least weekly with measurements.
red_flags: Report fever, spreading redness, foul smell or exposed bone (possible osteomyelitis).
Report an ulcer that is getting larger or deeper.
Inform the doctor of any new category 3 or 4 ulcer.

indications: Immobile, bedbound, sedated or paralysed patients
Patients at risk on a pressure risk score (for example Braden or Waterlow)
Existing pressure ulcer
contraindications: Unstable spinal injury (log roll with a trained team only)
steps: Explain repositioning to the patient and involve them where possible.
Perform hand hygiene and check the pressure risk score at admission and as policy requires.
Inspect skin over bony areas (sacrum, heels, hips, elbows, occiput, ears) for redness that does not blanch.
Check under devices such as tubes, masks, splints and catheters.
Move the patient with enough staff and a slide sheet, avoiding dragging.
Change position at the set interval, alternating left side, back and right side.
Use a 30-degree tilt and pillows between knees and ankles.
Float the heels off the bed with a pillow under the calves.
Keep the head of bed at 30 degrees or less unless medically required.
Keep the skin clean and dry and manage incontinence promptly.
Record each position change and skin findings on the chart.
aftercare: Encourage nutrition, fluids and mobility as able.
Teach caregivers to turn the patient at home.
red_flags: Report any new non-blanching redness, blister or broken skin.
Report pain on turning or pressure damage under a device.

indications: Routine appliance change for colostomy, ileostomy or urostomy
Leaking appliance or sore peristomal skin
Teaching self-care
equipment: New appliance (one- or two-piece, drainable or closed) and stoma measuring guide
Curved scissors to cut the flange
Warm water, soft wipes or gauze and a towel
Adhesive remover and skin barrier if available
Clean gloves, apron and disposal bag
steps: Explain the procedure, gain verbal consent and ensure privacy.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and empty a drainable bag first.
Remove the old appliance gently from top to bottom, supporting the skin.
Clean the stoma and skin with warm water and pat dry; avoid soap residue and alcohol.
Inspect the stoma colour, size, height and the surrounding skin.
Measure the stoma and cut the flange to fit with a gap of about 2-3 mm.
Apply skin barrier if the skin is sore, and let it dry.
Apply the appliance from the bottom up, pressing around the stoma for a good seal.
Close the outlet of a drainable bag.
Dispose of waste in a sealed bag and document stoma and skin findings and output.
aftercare: Teach the patient or caregiver to empty, change and order supplies.
Advise on diet, fluids and signs of dehydration with ileostomy.
Refer to a stoma nurse where available.
red_flags: Report a dark red, purple, black or pale stoma (poor blood supply) urgently.
Report no output with vomiting and abdominal swelling (possible obstruction).
Report a stoma that retracts, prolapses or bleeds heavily, or very high output.

indications: Routine cleaning of the tracheostomy stoma and inner cannula
Tie or dressing change
contraindications: Fresh tracheostomy in the first days without an experienced nurse present
equipment: Spare tracheostomy tubes (same size and one smaller) and obturator at the bedside
Suction machine with catheters, and oxygen with a tracheostomy mask
Sterile saline, gauze and keyhole tracheostomy dressing
Clean gloves, apron and eye protection
Bag-valve device and emergency tracheostomy algorithm
steps: Explain the procedure, gain consent and check that emergency equipment is at the bedside.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves, apron and eye protection.
Pre-oxygenate if needed and suction if secretions are present.
Remove and replace the inner cannula with a clean one, then clean the removed one as per manufacturer.
Remove the old dressing and clean the stoma with saline, from inside outwards.
Inspect the stoma for redness, granulation, bleeding or pus.
Dry the skin and place a new keyhole dressing.
Change ties with a second person holding the tube, leaving one finger space under the ties.
Check the cuff pressure on cuffed tubes as per local policy.
Check humidification and that the patient is comfortable and breathing easily.
Document stoma condition, secretions and tube details.
aftercare: Check the inner cannula at least every 4 hours and more often with thick secretions.
Keep humidification and suction ready at all times.
Teach caregivers before discharge where the tube is long-term.
red_flags: Treat sudden breathlessness, no airflow, or failure to pass a suction catheter as a blocked or displaced tube emergency.
Call the airway team immediately if the tube comes out and follow the emergency algorithm.
Report bleeding from the stoma or tube, or surgical emphysema.

indications: Secretions the patient cannot clear by coughing
Noisy, gurgling breathing or falling SpO2 from secretions
contraindications: Nasal route with base of skull fracture, severe nosebleed or bleeding disorder
Stridor or epiglottitis (do not stimulate the airway; call senior help)
equipment: Working suction unit with set pressure, or a manual suction device
Yankauer sucker for the mouth and soft suction catheters of correct size
Clean gloves, apron and eye protection
Sterile water to clear the tubing
steps: Explain the procedure, gain consent where possible and position the patient semi-upright or on the side.
Perform hand hygiene and put on PPE.
Check suction works and set the pressure to the lowest effective level for age.
Give oxygen beforehand if SpO2 is low.
For the mouth, sweep the Yankauer around the cheeks and floor of the mouth, avoiding the back of the throat.
For the nose, measure from nose tip to earlobe, lubricate and insert without suction.
Apply suction only while withdrawing, with each pass under 10-15 seconds.
Allow recovery and re-oxygenation between passes and limit the number of passes.
Clear the tubing with water and discard the catheter.
Record secretion type, amount and the patient's response.
aftercare: Reassess breathing, colour and SpO2.
Give mouth care and encourage coughing and fluids if able.
red_flags: Stop at once for falling SpO2, slow heart rate, vomiting or bleeding.
Call senior help if secretions keep re-accumulating or breathing worsens.

indications: Visible or audible secretions in an intubated or tracheostomised patient
Rising airway pressures or falling SpO2 from secretions
contraindications: Routine suction at fixed times without clinical need
equipment: Suction unit with pressure set for age
Sterile suction catheters no wider than half the tube's internal diameter, or closed in-line suction
Sterile gloves, apron and eye protection
Sterile water for clearing the tubing
steps: Explain the procedure to the patient even if sedated.
Perform hand hygiene and put on PPE.
Pre-oxygenate with increased oxygen as per local protocol.
Choose the correct catheter size and set the suction pressure.
Insert the catheter with a sterile technique and without suction to the pre-measured depth, just beyond the tube tip.
Withdraw while applying suction, with each pass lasting no longer than 10-15 seconds.
Allow recovery between passes and limit to the fewest passes needed.
Do not instil saline routinely.
Reconnect the ventilator promptly and return oxygen to baseline when stable.
Clear the tubing and discard the catheter, or rinse closed suction as directed.
Record secretion type, amount and the patient's response.
aftercare: Check chest movement, breath sounds, SpO2 and ventilator pressures.
Ensure humidification is adequate.
red_flags: Stop for desaturation, bradycardia, arrhythmia or hypotension.
Call the doctor for bloodstained secretions or if the tube may be blocked or displaced.
Call for help if the catheter will not pass down the tube.

indications: Patient with an intercostal chest drain in place
equipment: Two large clamps at the bedside (for emergencies and bottle change only)
Sterile water for the underwater seal bottle
steps: Explain the checks to the patient.
Perform hand hygiene and check observations including respiratory rate and SpO2.
Keep the drain bottle upright and below chest level at all times.
Check the tubing is not kinked, looped below the bottle or disconnected.
Check the water seal tube is under water to the marked level.
Look for swinging of the fluid level with breathing and for bubbling.
Measure and record drainage and its colour.
Inspect the insertion site for leaking, redness or surgical emphysema.
Check the drain is secured and the dressing is clean and dry.
Do not clamp a bubbling drain unless directed.
Encourage deep breathing, coughing and mobility with the bottle kept below the chest.
Change the bottle only as per local procedure with a second nurse.
aftercare: Give regular analgesia so the patient can breathe deeply.
Inform the doctor when drainage or bubbling stops, for review of removal.
red_flags: Call the doctor urgently for sudden breathlessness, falling SpO2, chest pain or hypotension.
Report drainage of fresh blood above the local threshold per hour.
If the drain disconnects, put the tube end under sterile water and call for help; if it falls out, cover the hole and call for help.

indications: External fixator or skeletal traction pins in place
equipment: Sterile dressing pack and sterile gloves
Antiseptic or sterile saline as per local protocol
Sterile gauze or pin site dressings
steps: Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Give analgesia beforehand if needed.
Perform hand hygiene and remove old pin site dressings.
Inspect each pin site for redness, swelling, discharge, pain or loosening.
Clean each pin site with a separate swab using the agreed solution, moving away from the pin.
Remove crusts only if they block drainage.
Apply new dressings around each pin with light compression.
Check the frame for loose clamps and the traction weights hang freely if present.
Record findings for each pin.
aftercare: Repeat care as per protocol, usually daily or weekly once settled.
Teach the patient or caregiver pin care before discharge.
red_flags: Report redness, pus, increasing pain or a loose pin (possible pin site infection).
Report fever or numbness, tingling or coldness of the limb.

indications: Central venous catheter or PICC in place
Dressing due, loose, wet or soiled
equipment: Sterile dressing pack and sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antiseptic (or alternative per policy)
Needle-free connectors if due for change
steps: Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, wear a mask and apron and position the patient with the head turned away.
Remove the old dressing towards the insertion site, taking care not to pull the line.
Inspect the site for redness, swelling, tenderness or discharge and check the external length.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves.
Clean the skin with antiseptic in a back-and-forth motion and let it dry completely.
Apply a new transparent dressing and label it with the date.
Scrub each hub with antiseptic before access and flush each lumen with a pulsatile push-pause technique.
Lock lumens as per policy and clamp them.
Document site findings, external length and lumens flushed.
aftercare: Review daily whether the line is still needed.
Change transparent dressings as per policy or when not intact.
red_flags: Report fever, rigors, or pus or redness at the site (possible line infection).
Stop and report if a lumen will not flush; never force a flush.
Report arm or neck swelling, or an increased external length.

indications: Constipation or faecal impaction not responding to oral treatment
Bowel preparation before a procedure as prescribed
contraindications: Suspected bowel obstruction, perforation or acute abdomen
Recent rectal or colonic surgery
Severe dehydration or kidney failure for phosphate enemas
Phosphate enemas in infants and children under 2 years, or with Hirschsprung disease or megacolon (risk of dangerous electrolyte disturbance)
Neutropenia or very low platelets
equipment: Prescribed enema warmed to body temperature
Rectal tube or nozzle and lubricant
Clean gloves, apron and protective pads
steps: Check the prescription, identity, allergies and gain verbal consent, ensuring privacy.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves and apron.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder, then lie on the left side with knees bent.
Place pads under the buttocks.
Lubricate the nozzle and insert gently into the rectum, directed towards the umbilicus.
Instil the solution slowly, stopping if there is pain or resistance.
Withdraw the nozzle and ask the patient to hold the enema for the recommended time.
Help the patient to the commode or toilet and stay nearby.
Record the result, including stool type and amount.
aftercare: Encourage fluids and review the cause of constipation.
Clean the perianal skin.
red_flags: Stop for pain, bleeding, resistance or a vasovagal reaction.
Report no result, severe cramps or abdominal distension.

indications: Admission, routine ward observations and before and after procedures
Any patient who appears unwell or has deteriorated
contraindications: BP cuff on a limb with a fistula, lymphoedema or IV infusion
equipment: BP machine with cuffs of correct size for the arm
Observation chart with early warning score
steps: Explain the observations to the patient or caregiver.
Perform hand hygiene and ensure the patient has rested for a few minutes.
Count the respiratory rate for a full minute without the patient noticing.
Measure SpO2 and note whether the patient is on oxygen.
Count the pulse for a full minute and note rhythm and strength.
Measure BP with the correct cuff size, arm supported at heart level.
Measure temperature by the appropriate route for age.
Assess level of consciousness using AVPU or ACVPU.
Check capillary refill time in children.
Calculate the early warning score (adult or paediatric) and plot it on the chart.
Escalate according to the score and record the action taken.
aftercare: Set the frequency of the next observations according to the score.
Clean the equipment between patients.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for a high early warning score or any single very abnormal value.
Call for help for new confusion, reduced consciousness, SpO2 falling or signs of shock.
Escalate if staff or family are worried even if the score is low.

form.label: Escalation
options: Rapid response or emergency team called

indications: Assessment of oxygenation in respiratory illness, sepsis or after sedation
Titrating oxygen therapy
Continuous monitoring of high-risk or sedated patients
equipment: Pulse oximeter with probe of correct size (adult, paediatric, neonatal wrap)
Alcohol wipe for cleaning the probe
steps: Explain the purpose to the patient or caregiver.
Perform hand hygiene and clean the probe.
Choose a warm, well-perfused finger, toe or earlobe, or the hand or foot in neonates.
Remove nail polish or false nails from the chosen finger.
Attach the probe and keep the patient still for at least 30 seconds.
Read the SpO2 only when the waveform or signal bar is steady and the pulse rate matches the palpated pulse.
Note whether the patient is on room air or oxygen and the flow or device.
For continuous monitoring, set alarm limits and rotate the probe site every few hours.
Record the reading with oxygen details.
aftercare: Check the skin under the probe for pressure marks.
Clean the probe between patients.
red_flags: Escalate SpO2 below the target range for the patient, or a falling trend.
Do not rely on a normal SpO2 in carbon monoxide poisoning or severe anaemia; treat the patient, not the number.
Recheck readings with poor signal, cold hands, shivering or very dark nail polish.

form.label: Escalation
options: Rapid response or emergency team called

indications: Head injury, stroke, meningitis, seizures or reduced consciousness
After neurosurgery or procedures with neurological risk
Cerebral malaria or poisoning
equipment: Neurological observation chart (adult or paediatric GCS, or Blantyre coma scale for young children)
BP machine, thermometer and pulse oximeter
steps: Explain the observations to the patient or caregiver.
Perform hand hygiene.
Assess eye opening, speaking to the patient first and then using a central painful stimulus only if needed.
Assess the best verbal response, using the age-appropriate scale for young children.
Assess the best motor response, asking the patient to obey a command first.
Add the scores to give the total GCS and record each component separately.
Check pupil size and reaction to light in each eye.
Test limb power in all four limbs and note any weakness.
Record pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature and SpO2 at the same time.
Compare with previous scores and escalate any deterioration.
aftercare: Repeat at the frequency set by the doctor or protocol.
Keep the patient safe from falls and position the unconscious patient on the side.
red_flags: Escalate immediately a drop in GCS of 2 or more points, or of 1 point in the motor score.
Escalate a new unequal or non-reacting pupil, new limb weakness or a seizure.
Escalate rising BP with slowing pulse and irregular breathing (possible raised intracranial pressure).
Protect the airway and call for help if GCS is 8 or less.

form.label: Escalation
options: Rapid response or emergency team called

indications: IV fluids, NG feeds, diuretics, kidney or heart failure
Dehydration, sepsis, burns, pre-eclampsia or post-operative care
Children with diarrhoea or poor intake
equipment: Measuring jug and graduated urine bag or urometer
Weighing scale for nappies or patients
steps: Explain the chart to the patient and family and ask them to report all drinks and losses.
Record every oral, IV, NG and medicine fluid intake with the time and volume.
Measure all urine output, using a urometer hourly in critically ill patients.
Weigh nappies and subtract the dry weight to estimate urine output in infants.
Record vomit, stool, drain, NG aspirate and other losses.
Total intake and output at the set times and at the end of 24 hours.
Calculate the balance and compare with the target set by the doctor.
Calculate urine output per kilogram per hour where needed.
Weigh the patient daily at the same time if requested.
aftercare: Hand over the running totals at each shift change.
Review the chart with the doctor at ward rounds.
red_flags: Escalate low urine output for age and weight (for example under 0.5 per kilogram per hour in adults).
Escalate a large positive balance with breathlessness or oedema.
Escalate large ongoing losses from diarrhoea, vomiting or drains.

form.label: Escalation
options: Rapid response or emergency team called

indications: Diabetes, insulin or steroid therapy
Reduced consciousness, seizures, confusion or suspected hypoglycaemia
Sick or malnourished children, severe malaria, sepsis
Neonates at risk of hypoglycaemia
contraindications: Poor peripheral perfusion or shock (readings unreliable; send a venous sample)
equipment: Glucometer with in-date strips matched to the meter, quality-controlled as per policy
steps: Explain the test and gain verbal consent.
Ask the patient to wash and dry the hands, or clean with water; let alcohol dry fully if used.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Choose the side of a fingertip, or the heel side in infants, rotating sites.
Prick with the lancet and wipe away the first drop if local policy advises.
Apply a drop of blood to the strip without squeezing hard.
Apply pressure to the site and discard the lancet into the sharps container.
Read and record the result, time and relation to meals.
Act on the result according to the hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia protocol.
aftercare: Repeat at the frequency in the care plan.
Teach self-monitoring to patients with diabetes.
red_flags: Treat low glucose immediately as per protocol and recheck after treatment.
Escalate very high readings, readings shown as HI, or ketones in a patient with diabetes.
Send a laboratory sample if the reading does not match how the patient looks.

indications: Hyperthermia (for example heat stroke) as an adjunct to medical treatment
Comfort in high fever when the patient finds it soothing, after antipyretic treatment
contraindications: Shivering, cold peripheries or shock
Routine fever control in children (not recommended; it causes discomfort and shivering)
Use of cold water or alcohol rubs
equipment: Basin of lukewarm (tepid) water, not cold
Sponges or soft cloths and towels
steps: Explain the purpose and gain verbal consent.
Check the temperature and that fever medicine has been given as prescribed.
Perform hand hygiene and ensure privacy and a draught-free room.
Remove heavy clothing and cover the patient with a light sheet.
Sponge the face, limbs and trunk gently with tepid water, one area at a time.
Let the water evaporate from the skin rather than rubbing dry.
Stop if the patient shivers or becomes uncomfortable.
Recheck the temperature after 30 minutes.
Dress the patient in light clothing and offer fluids.
aftercare: Encourage fluids and monitor temperature.
Teach caregivers that light clothing, fluids and fever medicine are preferred for children.
red_flags: Stop if shivering, mottled skin or cold hands and feet develop.
Escalate fever with drowsiness, neck stiffness, rash, convulsions or fast breathing.

indications: Patients unable to wash themselves or mobilise to the bathroom
contraindications: Unstable patient where moving causes deterioration (defer or limit to essential care)
equipment: Two basins of warm water, soap or wash solution
Disposable cloths, towels, clean linen and gown
steps: Explain the bath, ask about preferences and ensure privacy and a warm room.
Perform hand hygiene, put on PPE and check the water temperature with the elbow or a thermometer.
Encourage the patient to do as much as they can.
Wash the face first without soap unless preferred, then the neck, arms, chest and abdomen, drying each area.
Keep the patient covered except for the area being washed.
Change the water and wash the legs and feet.
Turn the patient safely with help and wash the back and buttocks, inspecting pressure areas.
Wash the genital area last with fresh water and a separate cloth, front to back.
Apply moisturiser to dry skin and change the gown and linen.
Check lines, drains and catheters are secure and the patient is comfortable.
Record skin condition and any concerns.
aftercare: Provide mouth care, nail and hair care as needed.
Leave the call bell and personal items within reach.
red_flags: Report new pressure damage, rashes, bruises or wounds found.
Stop and seek help if the patient becomes breathless, faint or in pain.

indications: Patients who cannot clean their own mouth (unconscious, nil by mouth, frail)
Ventilated patients, oral thrush, mucositis or dry mouth
equipment: Soft toothbrush and toothpaste, or foam sticks or gauze
Water or mouthwash as per local protocol
Suction available for patients who cannot swallow
Pen torch, clean gloves and towel
steps: Explain the care and position the patient upright, or on the side if unconscious.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Inspect the lips, tongue, gums, teeth and mucosa with a pen torch.
Remove and clean dentures, and store them labelled in water.
Brush teeth, gums and tongue gently with a soft brush and a small amount of paste.
Use foam sticks or gauze moistened with water where brushing is not possible.
Suction the mouth in patients who cannot swallow, so fluid is not aspirated.
Apply moisturiser to the lips.
Record the condition of the mouth and any problems.
aftercare: Repeat as per care plan, at least twice daily and more often if nil by mouth.
Encourage fluids if allowed.
red_flags: Report white plaques (thrush), ulcers, bleeding gums or a painful mouth.
Stop if the patient coughs or chokes during care.

indications: Unconscious, sedated or paralysed patients
Incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos), for example facial palsy
equipment: Sterile saline and sterile gauze or eye pads
Polyethylene film or moisture chamber dressing if available
steps: Explain the care even if the patient appears unconscious.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Check whether the eyelids fully close.
Inspect the eyes for redness, discharge, swelling or a cloudy cornea.
Clean each eye with a separate saline-soaked gauze from inner to outer corner.
Instil prescribed lubricant into each eye.
If the lids do not close, tape them gently closed or apply a polyethylene film cover as per protocol.
Never put tape directly onto the cornea or press on the eyeball.
Record findings for each eye.
aftercare: Repeat at the frequency in the care plan, usually every 2-4 hours.
Keep the head of the bed raised if allowed to reduce eyelid swelling.
red_flags: Report redness, discharge, a cloudy or white patch on the cornea, or swelling.
Report exposure of the cornea despite care.

indications: Perineal pain or swelling after childbirth or episiotomy
Haemorrhoids, anal fissure, or after anorectal surgery
Perianal abscess after drainage
contraindications: Fresh wound with active bleeding
Patient too unsteady to sit safely without help
equipment: Clean basin or sitz bath bowl that fits the toilet, or a clean bath
Warm water (comfortable to the elbow) with salt if advised
steps: Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Clean the basin and fill it with warm water, checking the temperature.
