Help the patient to sit so the perineum is immersed, with feet supported.
Ensure privacy and that the call bell is within reach.
Let the patient soak for 10-20 minutes, adding warm water if it cools.
Help the patient stand slowly, as they may feel faint.
Pat the area dry with a clean towel and apply a clean pad or dressing.
Clean and disinfect the basin after use.
aftercare: Repeat two to three times a day or after bowel movements as advised.
Teach the patient to do it safely at home.
red_flags: Stop if the patient feels faint or dizzy.
Report increasing pain, foul discharge, fever or heavy bleeding.

indications: Prevention of venous thromboembolism in surgical patients where prescribed
Chronic venous insufficiency or after deep vein thrombosis as prescribed
contraindications: Peripheral arterial disease, absent foot pulses or low ankle-brachial pressure index
Severe leg oedema from heart failure, leg deformity or fragile skin
Recent skin graft, dermatitis or cellulitis of the legs
Peripheral neuropathy with loss of sensation
equipment: Stockings of the correct type and size
Clean gloves if skin is broken
steps: Check the prescription and assess the legs for contraindications, including foot pulses.
Explain the purpose and gain verbal consent.
Measure the legs (ankle and calf circumference, and leg length or thigh for thigh-length) as per the manufacturer's chart.
Choose the correct size and length.
Turn the stocking inside out down to the heel.
Slide the foot section over the foot and position the heel pocket.
Ease the stocking up the leg without folds, wrinkles or rolled tops.
Check the toe hole is under the toes and the top band is not tight.
Record the size and the leg check.
aftercare: Remove the stockings daily for skin inspection and hygiene.
Re-measure if the legs swell or shrink.
Encourage early mobilisation and fluids.
red_flags: Remove and report if the toes become pale, blue, cold, numb or painful.
Report skin marks, blisters or breakdown.
Report calf pain or swelling, or chest pain and breathlessness (possible thromboembolism).

indications: Securing dressings or splints
Support of sprains and soft tissue injuries
Pressure to control bleeding
Slings for arm support
contraindications: Tight compression on a limb with suspected compartment syndrome or arterial insufficiency
equipment: Roller bandages of suitable width (crepe, cotton, elastic) or triangular bandage
steps: Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and check the limb's circulation, sensation and movement first.
Place the limb in a functional position and pad bony areas.
Start below the injury, working from distal to proximal.
Anchor the bandage with two turns, then wrap overlapping each turn by about half to two-thirds.
Use a figure-of-eight pattern over joints.
Apply even, firm but not tight tension.
Leave fingers or toes visible to check circulation.
Secure the end with tape or clips, not over the wound or a bony prominence.
Recheck circulation, sensation and movement and record.
aftercare: Teach the patient to keep the limb raised and check fingers or toes.
Explain when and how to reapply or remove the bandage.
red_flags: Loosen or remove the bandage at once if fingers or toes go pale, blue, cold, numb or tingling.
Seek urgent review for severe or increasing pain, especially on stretching the fingers or toes.

indications: Cold for acute soft tissue injury, swelling or pain in the first 48 hours
Warm for muscle spasm, phlebitis or a localised collection as advised, and breast engorgement
contraindications: Reduced sensation, poor circulation, or unconscious or confused patients unless closely supervised
Warm compress over acute bleeding, swelling or malignancy
Cold in Raynaud's phenomenon or sickle cell disease (can trigger crisis)
equipment: Ice pack, cold pack or ice in a plastic bag, or a warm pack or clean cloth soaked in warm water
Thermometer for water temperature where available
steps: Explain the procedure and gain verbal consent.
Check skin integrity and sensation at the site.
Wrap the compress in a cloth so it never touches the skin directly.
Check warm water is comfortably warm, not hot, before soaking the cloth.
Apply to the area for 10-20 minutes.
Check the skin every few minutes for redness, blistering or blanching.
Remove the compress and dry the skin.
Repeat at the advised interval, leaving the skin to recover between applications.
aftercare: Advise elevation and rest for injuries.
Teach safe use at home, especially with children.
red_flags: Stop if the skin blisters, becomes very red, white or numb.
Seek review if pain or swelling worsens, or fever or spreading redness develops.

indications: Suspected or confirmed infectious disease (for example TB, Lassa fever, cholera, measles, MRSA, COVID-19)
Protective isolation for neutropenic or immunosuppressed patients
equipment: Single room or cohort area with door and signage
PPE suited to the precautions (gloves, gowns or aprons, surgical masks or respirators, eye protection)
Hand-hygiene station or alcohol hand rub at the door
Clinical waste bins and linen bags
steps: Identify the type of precautions needed (contact, droplet, airborne or protective) and inform infection prevention.
Explain isolation to the patient and family, gain verbal agreement and offer support.
Place the patient in a single room or cohort, with the door closed for airborne precautions.
Put signage on the door and limit visitors and staff.
Keep dedicated equipment in the room.
Perform hand hygiene and put on PPE in the correct order before entering.
Take off PPE in the correct order at the door, performing hand hygiene between steps.
Handle linen, waste and specimens as infectious, in sealed bags and labelled.
Clean the room and surfaces daily and at discharge with the agreed disinfectant.
For viral haemorrhagic fever, follow the national protocol and use a trained team only.
Report notifiable diseases as per national rules.
aftercare: Review the need for isolation daily with the infection prevention team.
Provide activities and reassurance to reduce loneliness.
red_flags: Report any PPE breach or needlestick immediately for post-exposure management.
Escalate when isolation cannot be provided for an airborne or high-consequence infection.

form.label: Reason
options: Lassa or other viral haemorrhagic fever

form.label: Infection prevention or public health notified

indications: Any patient going for surgery or a procedure under anaesthesia or sedation
equipment: Pre-operative checklist and WHO surgical safety checklist
Skin marker for site marking (by the surgeon)
Clippers for hair removal if needed (not razors)
Observation equipment and capillary glucose meter
steps: Confirm patient identity, procedure, side and site against the consent form and notes.
Check that written consent for the operation is signed and valid.
Check allergies and apply an allergy band if needed.
Confirm fasting times as per the anaesthetic instructions, and that clear fluids were allowed as advised.
Check that the surgical site has been marked by the surgeon where applicable.
Record baseline observations, weight and capillary glucose if diabetic or a child.
Confirm blood results, group and save or crossmatch, pregnancy test and imaging are available as required.
Check which regular medicines were given or withheld as instructed.
Remove jewellery, make-up, nail polish, dentures and prostheses, or tape and record them.
Ensure the patient has washed, and clip hair only if needed and close to the time of surgery.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder, and put on the theatre gown.
Complete the checklist and hand over to the theatre nurse with the notes.
aftercare: Reassure the patient and family and explain what will happen next.
Keep the patient fasting until theatre.
red_flags: Stop and inform the surgeon if identity, site, side or consent do not match.
Inform the anaesthetist of fever, abnormal observations, recent food intake or a positive pregnancy test.
Inform the team of loose teeth, abnormal glucose or a missing result.

indications: Care of the body after death has been confirmed by an authorised clinician
contraindications: Death not yet confirmed
Coroner or police case (do not remove lines, tubes or clothing; preserve evidence)
equipment: Clean gloves, apron and other PPE as for infection risk
Basin, water, soap, towels and clean sheet or shroud
Gauze, tape and dressings to cover wounds and line sites
Body bag if infection risk or local policy
steps: Confirm death has been verified and documented by an authorised clinician.
Inform the family sensitively, offer them time with the body and ask about religious and cultural wishes.
Respect Islamic, Christian and traditional practices, including washing by family and early burial, within safety rules.
Perform hand hygiene and put on PPE.
Lay the body flat, close the eyes and support the jaw with a rolled towel.
Remove lines, tubes and drains unless the case is for the coroner or police, and cover sites with dressings.
Wash the body unless the family or faith wish to do it, and comb the hair.
Remove jewellery in the presence of a witness, record it and return it to the family, or tape it if they wish it left.
Attach identification labels to the wrist and ankle.
Wrap the body in a clean sheet or shroud, and in a body bag if there is an infection risk.
Record the time of death, the people informed and the property handed over.
Arrange transfer to the mortuary or release to the family as per policy.
aftercare: Offer support to the family and staff.
Give the family information on death certification and collection of the body.
red_flags: Use full PPE and the national protocol for high-consequence infections (for example Lassa or Ebola); do not allow family washing.
Stop and inform the senior clinician if there are unexplained injuries or the death may need a coroner or police report.

indications: Second stage of labour with cephalic presentation and progress
Woman in labour with no indication for operative delivery
contraindications: Placenta praevia covering the cervix
Transverse lie or other non-deliverable presentation
Previous classical caesarean scar
equipment: Sterile delivery pack (2 artery forceps, cord scissors, episiotomy scissors)
Sterile gloves, apron and eye protection
Clean warm towels and a cap for the baby
Uterotonic drawn up ready for third stage
Newborn resuscitation area with bag-valve-mask and suction
Kidney dish and receptacle for placenta
steps: Confirm the woman's identity, explain the delivery and obtain verbal consent.
Check the partograph, maternal observations and fetal heart rate before pushing.
Prepare a warm delivery area and check newborn resuscitation equipment is ready.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves and protective wear.
Help the woman into a position of her choice and encourage pushing with contractions.
Clean the vulva and perineum with antiseptic or clean water from front to back.
Support the perineum and flex the head as it crowns to allow slow delivery between contractions.
Feel for a cord around the neck and loosen it over the head or deliver through it.
Allow restitution and external rotation, then deliver the anterior and posterior shoulders with gentle traction.
Deliver the body, place the baby skin to skin on the mother and dry thoroughly.
Assess breathing and start newborn resuscitation if the baby is not breathing.
Give a uterotonic and manage the third stage actively.
Inspect the perineum, vagina and placenta for completeness and repair any tears.
Record time of birth, sex, Apgar scores and estimated blood loss.
aftercare: Observe the mother's pulse, blood pressure, uterine tone and bleeding every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours.
Start breastfeeding within the first hour.
Give newborn care including eye care, cord care and vitamin K per protocol.
Encourage the woman to pass urine within 6 hours.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding or a soft uterus after delivery
Baby not breathing or with poor tone after drying
Shoulder dystocia or failure to deliver the shoulders
Maternal collapse, convulsions or severe headache
Retained placenta beyond 30 minutes

name: Active management of third stage of labour

indications: All vaginal births to prevent postpartum haemorrhage
contraindications: Undiagnosed second twin in the uterus (exclude before uterotonic)
Controlled cord traction without a skilled attendant or without a uterotonic
equipment: Uterotonic in a syringe ready to give
Kidney dish or receptacle for the placenta
Measuring container or calibrated drape for blood loss
steps: Palpate the abdomen to exclude another baby before giving the uterotonic.
Give a uterotonic within one minute of birth per local protocol.
Clamp and cut the cord after one to three minutes unless the baby needs resuscitation.
Wait for a contraction and signs of separation such as lengthening of the cord.
Hold the cord with a clamp close to the perineum in one hand.
Place the other hand above the pubic bone and apply counter-pressure upward on the uterus.
Apply gentle downward controlled cord traction during the contraction only.
Stop and wait for the next contraction if the placenta does not descend within 30 to 40 seconds.
Deliver the placenta with both hands, turning it gently to deliver the membranes intact.
Massage the uterus until it is firm and check tone every 15 minutes.
Examine the placenta and membranes for completeness.
Estimate and record the blood loss.
aftercare: Check uterine tone and bleeding every 15 minutes for 2 hours.
Teach the woman to feel her uterus and rub it if it becomes soft.
Keep the mother and baby together and support breastfeeding.
red_flags: Placenta not delivered within 30 minutes
Bleeding of 500 mL or more, or signs of shock
Cord snaps or the uterus appears to invert
Incomplete placenta or ragged membranes

indications: Fetal distress needing expedited delivery in the second stage
Instrumental delivery where the perineum is tight
Rigid perineum preventing delivery
Shoulder dystocia needing access for internal manoeuvres
contraindications: Routine use in uncomplicated births
Woman's refusal
equipment: Local anaesthetic, 10 mL syringe and 21 G needle
steps: Explain the need for the episiotomy and obtain verbal consent.
Clean the perineum with antiseptic solution.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic along the planned line unless an epidural is working, aspirating first.
Wait for the anaesthetic to take effect and test the area.
Insert two fingers between the fetal head and the perineum to protect the head.
At the height of a contraction, cut a mediolateral incision at about 60 degrees from the midline.
Control the head and deliver the baby, supporting the perineum.
Apply pressure with gauze to any bleeding points.
Inspect the episiotomy for extension after delivery and repair it promptly.
aftercare: Repair the episiotomy after the third stage.
Advise perineal hygiene and pain relief.
red_flags: Extension into the anal sphincter or rectum
Heavy bleeding from the incision
Haematoma or increasing perineal pain

indications: Episiotomy after vaginal delivery
contraindications: Third- or fourth-degree extension (repair in theatre by a skilled operator)
equipment: Repair pack with needle holder, toothed forceps, scissors and artery forceps
Absorbable synthetic suture on a taper needle (or chromic catgut if unavailable)
Local anaesthetic, 10 mL syringe and needle
Sterile gloves, gauze swabs and a vaginal tampon or rolled swab
steps: Explain the repair and obtain verbal consent.
Position the woman in lithotomy with good light and clean the area.
Insert a tampon or rolled swab high in the vagina to keep the field clear and count it.
Check that the anal sphincter is intact with a rectal examination.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the wound edges if not already effective.
Place the first stitch about 1 cm above the apex of the vaginal cut.
Close the vaginal mucosa with a continuous suture to the hymenal ring.
Close the perineal muscle with interrupted or continuous sutures without leaving dead space.
Close the skin with a subcuticular or interrupted suture.
Remove the vaginal tampon and confirm the swab and needle count.
Perform a rectal examination to make sure no stitches pass through the rectum.
aftercare: Advise perineal hygiene, regular washing and changing pads.
Offer pain relief and advise on sitting and walking.
Explain that the stitches dissolve and do not need removal.
Review at postnatal visits for healing.
red_flags: Increasing pain, swelling or a mass suggesting haematoma
Fever, foul discharge or wound breakdown
Passage of stool or wind from the vagina
Inability to pass urine

name: Repair of first- or second-degree perineal tear

indications: First-degree tear that is bleeding or with poorly aligned edges
Second-degree tear involving perineal muscle
contraindications: Involvement of the anal sphincter or rectal mucosa (needs third- or fourth-degree repair)
equipment: Repair pack with needle holder, toothed forceps, scissors and artery forceps
Absorbable synthetic suture on a taper needle
Local anaesthetic, 10 mL syringe and needle
Sterile gloves, gauze swabs and vaginal tampon
steps: Explain the repair and obtain verbal consent.
Position the woman with good light and clean the perineum.
Examine the whole tear and perform a rectal examination to classify it correctly.
Insert and count a vaginal tampon or rolled swab to keep the field clear.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the wound edges.
Leave small first-degree tears that are aligned and not bleeding unsutured.
Start above the apex and close the vaginal mucosa with a continuous suture to the hymenal ring.
Close the perineal muscle in one or two layers to obliterate dead space.
Close the skin with a subcuticular suture or leave well-aligned skin unsutured.
Remove the tampon, check the count and repeat the rectal examination.
aftercare: Advise perineal hygiene and pain relief.
Encourage early passage of urine.
Check healing at postnatal review.
red_flags: Perineal swelling, severe pain or haematoma
Fever or foul discharge
Faecal incontinence or stool from the vagina

name: Repair of third- or fourth-degree perineal tear

indications: Tear involving the external or internal anal sphincter
Tear involving the anorectal mucosa
contraindications: Repair by an untrained operator (refer to an experienced obstetrician)
equipment: Theatre with good light, assistant and lithotomy stirrups
Repair pack with Allis forceps, fine toothed forceps and needle holders
Absorbable synthetic and long-lasting absorbable sutures
steps: Explain the injury, its implications and the repair, and obtain written consent.
Move the woman to theatre and provide regional or general anaesthesia.
Perform the surgical time-out and confirm the swab count.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Classify the tear carefully with a rectal examination under good light.
Repair torn anorectal mucosa with interrupted absorbable sutures.
Identify and repair the internal anal sphincter separately if torn.
Grasp the torn ends of the external anal sphincter with Allis forceps and repair by overlap or end-to-end technique.
Repair the perineal muscles and vaginal mucosa as for a second-degree tear.
Close the skin and confirm the swab and needle count.
Perform a final rectal examination and insert a urinary catheter.
aftercare: Continue antibiotics and give stool softeners per local protocol.
Remove the catheter when mobile, usually after 12 to 24 hours.
Advise pelvic floor exercises and arrange review at 6 to 12 weeks.
Discuss mode of delivery in future pregnancies.
red_flags: Faecal or flatus incontinence
Wound breakdown, fever or foul discharge
Rectovaginal fistula symptoms
Severe pain or urinary retention

indications: Bleeding cervical laceration after delivery with a well-contracted uterus
contraindications: Tear extending into the lower segment or above the vaginal vault (needs laparotomy)
equipment: Two sponge-holding forceps or ring forceps
Sims or right-angle vaginal retractors and an assistant
Long needle holder and absorbable synthetic suture
Good light, sterile gloves and gauze
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Resuscitate as needed with intravenous access and blood sent for crossmatch.
Give analgesia, sedation or anaesthesia, and position the woman in lithotomy.
Have an assistant retract the vaginal walls to expose the cervix fully.
Grasp the cervix with ring forceps on each side of the tear and inspect it all around.
Identify the apex of the tear and place the first suture above the apex.
Close the tear with a continuous or interrupted absorbable suture toward the cervical edge.
Leave small tears that are not bleeding unsutured.
Check haemostasis and the swab and needle count.
aftercare: Monitor pulse, blood pressure and vaginal bleeding closely for 2 hours.
Check haemoglobin if blood loss was significant.
red_flags: Apex cannot be reached or tear extends into the uterus (laparotomy)
Continued bleeding or shock after repair

indications: Bleeding vaginal wall laceration after delivery
Deep sulcus tears
contraindications: Large expanding haematoma (treat as haematoma evacuation)
equipment: Needle holder, toothed forceps and scissors
Good light, gauze swabs and vaginal tampon
steps: Explain the repair and obtain verbal consent.
Position the woman in lithotomy with good light and clean the area.
Retract the vaginal walls and inspect to find the full extent and apex of the tear.
Give local anaesthetic, or regional or general anaesthesia for deep tears.
Place the first stitch above the apex.
Close the laceration with a continuous absorbable suture, avoiding the urethra.
Check haemostasis and perform a rectal examination for stitches through the rectum.
Confirm the swab and needle count.
aftercare: Observe bleeding and vital signs for 2 hours.
Advise perineal hygiene and pain relief.
red_flags: Swelling or pain suggesting haematoma
Urinary retention or haematuria
Continued bleeding

indications: Prolonged second stage with maternal exhaustion
Suspected fetal compromise in the second stage
Maternal conditions where pushing should be shortened
contraindications: Cervix not fully dilated or membranes intact
Head more than one-fifth palpable abdominally or above station 0
Face, brow or breech presentation
Gestation under 34 weeks
Suspected cephalopelvic disproportion
equipment: Vacuum device (hand-held or with pump) and correct cup
Sterile gloves, antiseptic and urinary catheter
Local anaesthetic or pudendal block equipment
Newborn resuscitation equipment and a person skilled in resuscitation
steps: Confirm the indication, check prerequisites and obtain informed consent.
Check the head is no more than one-fifth palpable abdominally and the cervix is fully dilated.
Determine the position of the fetal head precisely by vaginal examination.
Empty the bladder with a catheter and give analgesia.
Place the cup over the flexion point, about 3 cm in front of the posterior fontanelle on the sagittal suture.
Check that no maternal tissue is trapped under the cup rim.
Raise the vacuum to the working pressure recommended for the device.
Pull with each contraction along the axis of the pelvis while the woman pushes.
Stop and abandon if there is no descent after three pulls or the cup detaches three times.
Release the vacuum once the head is delivered and complete the delivery.
Examine the baby for scalp injury and the mother for tears.
aftercare: Observe the baby for cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage and jaundice.
Monitor the mother for postpartum haemorrhage and urinary retention.
Debrief the woman about the delivery.
red_flags: No descent with correct traction (move to caesarean section)
Rapidly enlarging boggy scalp swelling or pallor in the baby
Maternal heavy bleeding or retention of urine

indications: Prolonged second stage
Fetal compromise in the second stage
After-coming head in breech delivery
Need to avoid maternal pushing
contraindications: Cervix not fully dilated
Head more than one-fifth palpable or unknown position
Suspected cephalopelvic disproportion
Operator not trained in the type of forceps needed
equipment: Obstetric forceps (outlet or low-cavity) checked as a pair
Sterile gloves, antiseptic and urinary catheter
Pudendal block or regional anaesthesia equipment
steps: Confirm the indication and prerequisites and obtain informed consent.
Confirm full dilatation, station and exact position of the head.
Ensure adequate anaesthesia and empty the bladder.
Assemble the forceps outside the vagina to check they lock correctly.
Insert the left blade first between the head and the left pelvic wall, guided by the fingers.
Insert the right blade in the same way and lock the handles without force.
Check the application is correct with the sagittal suture midway between the blades.
Apply traction during contractions along the pelvic axis, combined with maternal effort.
Perform an episiotomy if the perineum is tight as the head distends it.
Remove the blades once the head is delivered and complete the birth.
Abandon and proceed to caesarean section if there is no descent with three pulls.
Examine the perineum, vagina and cervix and repair any tears.
aftercare: Observe the baby for facial nerve palsy and skin marks.
Monitor the mother for haemorrhage, urinary retention and perineal pain.
Offer debriefing.
red_flags: Blades do not lock or no descent with traction
Severe perineal tear or cervical tear
Baby with poor tone, seizures or facial palsy

indications: Breech presentation in advanced labour where caesarean is not possible or declined
Selected frank or complete breech with adequate pelvis after counselling
contraindications: Footling breech or knee presentation
Estimated fetal weight over 3.8 kg or growth restriction
Hyperextended fetal neck
Clinically inadequate pelvis or previous caesarean section
equipment: Delivery pack with episiotomy scissors and cord clamps
Obstetric forceps (Piper or standard) for the after-coming head
Newborn resuscitation equipment and skilled assistant
steps: Counsel the woman, confirm the type of breech and obtain consent.
Ensure a skilled assistant and newborn resuscitation are ready.
Confirm full dilatation and encourage pushing only when the breech is on the perineum.
Perform an episiotomy if needed as the buttocks distend the perineum.
Keep hands off and let the breech deliver until the umbilicus appears.
Flex the knees to free the legs if they do not deliver spontaneously.
Hold the baby by the bony pelvis only and keep the back anterior.
Deliver the arms by sweeping them across the face, or use the Loveset manoeuvre if they are extended.
Let the baby hang until the nape of the neck is visible.
Deliver the head with the Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre or forceps, keeping the head flexed.
Ask the assistant to apply suprapubic pressure to keep the head flexed.
Resuscitate the baby if needed and manage the third stage actively.
aftercare: Examine the baby for hip dysplasia, fractures and brachial plexus injury.
Monitor the mother for haemorrhage and perineal tears.
Arrange hip ultrasound for the baby if available.
red_flags: Entrapped after-coming head
Cord prolapse
Arms not delivering or nuchal arm
Baby not breathing after birth

form.label: Interval from umbilicus to head delivery

indications: Twin pregnancy in labour with the first twin cephalic
contraindications: First twin non-cephalic
Monoamniotic twins
Other indication for caesarean section
equipment: Two delivery packs and two sets of cord clamps labelled for each twin
Two newborn resuscitation areas and skilled staff
Intravenous access and uterotonics including oxytocin infusion
Portable ultrasound or Doppler for the second twin
steps: Confirm presentations by ultrasound and obtain consent for the plan.
Secure intravenous access, send blood for group and crossmatch, and alert the team.
Monitor both fetal hearts during labour.
Deliver the first twin as a normal birth and clamp the cord with one clamp to identify it.
Do not give a uterotonic until the second twin is delivered.
Palpate the abdomen immediately to check the lie of the second twin and listen to its heart.
Correct the lie to longitudinal by external version if needed while an assistant stabilises it.
Start or increase an oxytocin infusion if contractions do not resume within 10 minutes.
Rupture the second sac once the presenting part is in the pelvis and check for cord prolapse.
Deliver the second twin, by breech extraction or internal version if needed and skilled.
Give a uterotonic and manage the third stage actively, anticipating postpartum haemorrhage.
Label both babies and record the times of each birth.
aftercare: Continue an oxytocin infusion for several hours to prevent haemorrhage.
Observe the mother closely for bleeding for at least 2 hours.
Assess both babies for prematurity and growth problems.
red_flags: Fetal distress in the second twin
Cord prolapse after rupture of the second sac
Delay of more than 30 minutes before the second twin
Postpartum haemorrhage

form.label: Second twin presentation after first birth

name: Internal podalic version and breech extraction

indications: Second twin with transverse lie when external version fails
Second twin with fetal distress needing rapid delivery
contraindications: Singleton pregnancy at term with intact uterus (use caesarean section)
Ruptured membranes with little liquor and contracted uterus
Previous uterine scar
Operator not trained in the manoeuvre
equipment: Anaesthesia (general or regional) and uterine relaxant per local protocol
Delivery pack and newborn resuscitation equipment
steps: Explain the urgency and obtain consent from the woman.
Provide anaesthesia and uterine relaxation if available.
Perform hand hygiene and put on a long sterile glove.
Insert the hand into the uterus with membranes intact if possible and identify a fetal foot.
Confirm it is a foot by finding the heel, not a hand.
Grasp the foot and pull it down gently while the other hand pushes the head up abdominally.
Rupture the membranes once the foot is in the vagina.
Continue traction to deliver the legs and buttocks, keeping the back anterior.
Deliver the arms and the after-coming head as in breech delivery.
Give a uterotonic and explore the uterus for rupture after delivery.
aftercare: Monitor for postpartum haemorrhage and signs of uterine rupture.
Assess the baby for birth injury.
red_flags: Pain, bleeding or shock suggesting uterine rupture
Failure to bring down a foot (move to caesarean)
Baby not breathing after birth

name: Manual rotation of the fetal head

indications: Persistent occipito-posterior or transverse position in the second stage
contraindications: Cervix not fully dilated
Head high or suspected cephalopelvic disproportion
Face or brow presentation
equipment: Vacuum or forceps available to complete delivery
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Confirm full dilatation and determine the exact position by palpating the sutures and fontanelles.
Ensure adequate analgesia and empty the bladder.
Insert the hand matching the direction of rotation, with fingers behind the lambdoid suture.
Flex the head and rotate it to occipito-anterior between contractions.
Hold the head in position through the next contractions while the woman pushes.
Complete delivery spontaneously or with an instrument.
aftercare: Monitor for postpartum haemorrhage and cervical or vaginal tears.
Examine the baby for birth injury.
red_flags: Head does not rotate or descend
Fetal heart abnormalities during the manoeuvre
Cord prolapse

indications: Failure of the shoulders to deliver with gentle traction after the head is born
Turtle sign
contraindications: Fundal pressure (never use)
Excessive or lateral traction on the head
equipment: Step or wedge to reposition the woman
steps: Call for help immediately including a senior midwife, obstetrician and neonatal resuscitator.
Note the time the head was delivered and tell the woman to stop pushing.
Lie the woman flat and perform the McRoberts manoeuvre by sharply flexing her thighs onto her abdomen.
Apply suprapubic pressure from the side of the fetal back for 30 seconds, continuous then rocking.
Consider an episiotomy to make room for internal manoeuvres.
Deliver the posterior arm by flexing the elbow and sweeping the forearm across the chest.
Attempt internal rotation with Rubin II or Woods screw manoeuvres if the arm cannot be reached.
Move the woman onto all fours and repeat the manoeuvres if still undelivered.
Avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction on the head at all times.
Hand the baby to the resuscitation team and manage the third stage actively.
Record the timing, manoeuvres used, staff present and which shoulder was anterior.
aftercare: Examine the baby for brachial plexus injury and fractures of the clavicle or humerus.
Watch the mother for postpartum haemorrhage and severe perineal tears.
Debrief the woman and her family.
red_flags: Head-to-body interval over 5 minutes
Baby floppy, not breathing or with absent arm movement
Postpartum haemorrhage

indications: Obstructed labour or cephalopelvic disproportion
Fetal distress not amenable to rapid vaginal delivery
Placenta praevia or abruption with ongoing bleeding
Malpresentation, previous caesareans or other planned indications
contraindications: Dead fetus with a stable mother where safe vaginal delivery is possible (relative)
equipment: Prophylactic antibiotics and uterotonics per local protocol
steps: Confirm the indication and urgency category, and obtain written consent.
Send blood for crossmatch and secure intravenous access.
Provide spinal or general anaesthesia with left lateral tilt.
Insert a urinary catheter and give prophylactic antibiotics before skin incision.
Scrub, gown and glove, then clean the abdomen with antiseptic and drape.
Check the fetal heart, perform the surgical time-out and an initial swab count.
Make a transverse lower abdominal incision unless a midline incision is needed.
Open the abdomen, reflect the bladder and make a transverse lower uterine segment incision.
Deliver the baby, clamp the cord and hand the baby to the resuscitation team.
Give a uterotonic and deliver the placenta by controlled cord traction.
Check the uterine cavity is empty and close the uterus in one or two layers.
Check haemostasis, the tubes and ovaries, and confirm swab and instrument counts.
Close the abdomen in layers.
Record the indication, findings, blood loss and any intraoperative problems.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, uterine tone, vaginal bleeding and urine output.
Give pain relief and thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Encourage early mobilisation, oral fluids and breastfeeding.
Advise on wound care and the interval and mode of the next delivery.
red_flags: Heavy vaginal bleeding or a soft uterus
Rising pulse, falling blood pressure or reduced urine output
Fever, wound discharge or abdominal distension
Calf pain or breathlessness

indications: Maternal cardiac arrest with the uterus at or above the umbilicus and no return of circulation after 4 minutes of CPR
contraindications: Uterus below the umbilicus (no haemodynamic benefit)
equipment: Caesarean or basic surgical set if immediately available
steps: Call the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams as soon as arrest is recognised.
Start CPR with manual left uterine displacement.
Prepare to perform the delivery by 4 minutes and aim to deliver within 5 minutes of arrest.
Do not move the woman to theatre and do not wait for full asepsis.
Inform the family if present, without delaying the procedure.
Make a midline vertical incision from below the umbilicus to the pubis while CPR continues.
Open the uterus with a vertical incision and deliver the baby and placenta.
Hand the baby to the neonatal team.
Continue maternal resuscitation and give a uterotonic if circulation returns.
Close the uterus and abdomen in theatre if circulation returns.
Document the timing of arrest, incision and delivery.
aftercare: Transfer to critical care if circulation returns.
Provide bereavement and staff debriefing support as needed.
red_flags: Massive haemorrhage after return of circulation
Need for intensive care for mother or baby

indications: Life-threatening postpartum haemorrhage not controlled by conservative measures
Placenta accreta spectrum
Irreparable uterine rupture
Severe uterine sepsis
contraindications: Bleeding controllable by uterotonics, tamponade or compression sutures
equipment: Crossmatched blood and blood products, ideally massive transfusion protocol
steps: Obtain written consent from the woman or next of kin as the situation allows, explaining loss of fertility.
Call for senior help and activate massive transfusion arrangements.
Perform the surgical time-out and confirm counts.
Clamp, cut and ligate the round ligaments and open the broad ligament.
Clamp, cut and ligate the utero-ovarian ligaments or tubes, preserving the ovaries where possible.
Push the bladder down well below the lower segment.
Clamp, cut and ligate the uterine vessels on each side close to the uterus.
Decide on subtotal or total hysterectomy depending on bleeding and stability.
Remove the uterus and close the cervical stump or vaginal vault.
Check haemostasis, ureters and bladder integrity.
Place a drain if needed, confirm counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Admit to high-dependency or intensive care.
Correct blood loss and clotting, and monitor urine output.
Give thromboprophylaxis and antibiotics per local protocol.
Provide psychological support about loss of fertility.
red_flags: Continued bleeding from the vault or drain
Falling urine output or haematuria (ureteric or bladder injury)
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation

indications: Placenta not delivered 30 minutes after birth despite active management
Retained placenta with heavy bleeding
contraindications: Suspected placenta accreta (prepare for laparotomy)
equipment: Uterotonics and prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Secure intravenous access, send blood for crossmatch and give analgesia or anaesthesia.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and empty the bladder.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the perineum and put on long sterile gloves.
Hold the cord with a clamp and pull it gently until horizontal.
Insert the gloved hand into the vagina and uterus along the cord.
Support the fundus through the abdomen with the other hand.
Find the edge of the placenta and separate it with the side of the hand in a slicing movement.
Withdraw the hand with the placenta once fully separated.
Explore the cavity to make sure no tissue remains.
Give a uterotonic and massage the uterus.
Examine the placenta for completeness.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, uterine tone and bleeding every 15 minutes for 2 hours.
Continue a uterotonic infusion if needed.
Watch for fever or foul lochia over the following days.
red_flags: No cleavage plane found (suspect accreta)
Uterine inversion or continued heavy bleeding
Fever or offensive discharge after the procedure

indications: Postpartum haemorrhage with suspected retained tissue
Suspected uterine rupture after vaginal delivery
Incomplete placenta or membranes
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability without resuscitation under way
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Resuscitate and give analgesia or anaesthesia.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and empty the bladder.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the perineum and put on long sterile gloves.
Insert the gloved hand into the uterus while the other hand steadies the fundus.
Sweep the whole cavity systematically for clots, retained tissue and defects in the wall.
Remove any clots or tissue found.
Feel the lower segment and previous scar for rupture.
Withdraw the hand, give a uterotonic and massage the uterus.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, tone and bleeding closely.
Watch for signs of infection.
red_flags: Defect in the uterine wall (laparotomy)
Continued bleeding with a contracted uterus (check for tears)

indications: Postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony not responding to massage and uterotonics
Temporary measure while awaiting theatre or transfer
contraindications: Uterine rupture suspected (go to laparotomy)
equipment: Help to call for theatre and blood
steps: Call for help and start resuscitation with intravenous fluids and uterotonics.
Explain to the woman what you are about to do.
Put on sterile gloves and insert one hand into the vagina, forming a fist in the anterior fornix.
Place the other hand on the abdomen behind the uterus and press it firmly against the fist.
Maintain compression until bleeding stops and the uterus contracts.
Use external aortic compression above the umbilicus if bleeding continues while awaiting help.
Release slowly and check whether bleeding recurs.
Proceed to tamponade or surgery if bleeding does not stop.
aftercare: Continue uterotonics and monitor vital signs and bleeding every 15 minutes.
Check haemoglobin and transfuse if needed.
red_flags: Bleeding restarts once compression is released
Signs of shock or clotting failure

indications: Postpartum haemorrhage from atony not responding to uterotonics and massage
contraindications: Uterine rupture or retained placenta
Bleeding from genital tract trauma not yet repaired
equipment: Commercial balloon device or condom tied over a 16-18 Fr Foley catheter
Sterile saline or clean water and a 50 mL syringe or giving set
Prophylactic antibiotics and uterotonics per local protocol
steps: Explain the procedure to the woman and continue resuscitation.
Exclude retained placenta and genital tract tears.
Empty the bladder and leave an indwelling catheter.
Insert the balloon or condom-catheter fully into the uterine cavity with forceps.
Fill the balloon with fluid until bleeding stops, usually 300 to 500 millilitres in total.
Pack the vagina with gauze to keep the balloon in place.
Mark the fundal height and continue uterotonic infusion.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Observe that bleeding through the catheter lumen has stopped.
aftercare: Keep the balloon in for 12 to 24 hours with close observation.
Deflate gradually before removal and watch for further bleeding.
Monitor fundal height, pulse, blood pressure and urine output.
red_flags: Continued bleeding through the drainage tube or around the balloon (laparotomy)
Rising fundal height or signs of shock
Fever or offensive discharge

indications: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage at laparotomy or caesarean not responding to uterotonics
contraindications: Bleeding from placenta accreta or rupture needing other surgery
equipment: Large curved needle with long-lasting absorbable suture
steps: Obtain written consent and perform the surgical time-out.
At laparotomy, exteriorise the uterus and test bimanual compression to see if it controls bleeding.
Open or reopen the lower segment incision if needed.
Enter the uterus below the incision on one side and exit above it.
Take the suture over the fundus and enter the posterior wall at the level of the incision.
Bring the suture across the back and out on the other side posteriorly.
Take it back over the fundus and enter and exit the anterior wall on the other side as on the first side.
Have an assistant compress the uterus while the suture is tightened and tied.
Close the lower segment incision and check for bleeding per vaginam.
Confirm counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Monitor in high-dependency care for bleeding.
Continue uterotonics and correct blood loss.
red_flags: Continued bleeding (consider vessel ligation or hysterectomy)
Signs of uterine necrosis or infection later

indications: Postpartum haemorrhage at laparotomy not controlled by uterotonics or compression sutures
Bleeding from lateral extension of the uterine incision
contraindications: Haemodynamic collapse where hysterectomy is faster and safer
equipment: Absorbable suture on a large curved needle
steps: Obtain written consent and perform the surgical time-out.
Exteriorise the uterus and push the bladder down.
Identify the uterine vessels at the level of the lower segment on one side.
Pass the needle through the myometrium medial to the vessels, about 2 cm from the edge.
Bring the needle out through an avascular area of the broad ligament lateral to the vessels.
Tie the ligature firmly and repeat on the other side.
Check for reduced bleeding and good uterine colour.
Confirm counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Monitor closely for bleeding and urine output.
Correct blood loss and clotting.
red_flags: Continued bleeding (internal iliac ligation or hysterectomy)
Haematuria or anuria suggesting ureteric injury

indications: Intractable pelvic or postpartum haemorrhage when other measures fail
Desire to preserve fertility where the surgeon is experienced
contraindications: Surgeon not trained in retroperitoneal pelvic dissection (choose hysterectomy)
equipment: Major laparotomy set with long instruments and right-angle forceps
steps: Obtain written consent and perform the surgical time-out.
Call the most experienced surgeon available.
Identify the bifurcation of the common iliac artery and the ureter crossing it.
Open the posterior peritoneum over the common iliac bifurcation and keep the ureter attached to the medial peritoneal leaf.
Identify the internal iliac artery and follow it about 3 cm below the bifurcation.
Pass a right-angle forceps carefully under the anterior division, avoiding the internal iliac vein.
Tie the artery with two ligatures without dividing it.
Check pulses in the external iliac and femoral arteries.
Repeat on the other side.
Check haemostasis, confirm counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Monitor in high-dependency care for bleeding and limb perfusion.
Monitor urine output for ureteric injury.
red_flags: Cold or pulseless leg (external iliac ligated in error)
Venous injury with major bleeding
Anuria or haematuria

indications: Uterine rupture where the edges are repairable and the woman is stable enough
Scar dehiscence found at caesarean section
contraindications: Extensive or irregular rupture involving vessels (hysterectomy may be safer)
steps: Resuscitate, crossmatch blood and obtain written consent including possible hysterectomy.
Perform laparotomy under general or regional anaesthesia after the time-out.
Deliver the baby and placenta and give a uterotonic.
Inspect the extent of the tear including the broad ligament, bladder and vessels.
Trim ragged edges if needed and close the tear in one or two layers.
Check the bladder for injury and repair it if found.
Offer tubal ligation if the woman requested it before surgery.
Check haemostasis, confirm counts and close the abdomen.
aftercare: Monitor closely in high-dependency care.
Leave a urinary catheter in if the bladder was repaired.
Counsel about the high risk of rupture in future pregnancy and need for early elective caesarean.
red_flags: Continued bleeding or broad ligament haematoma
Haematuria or urine leak (bladder injury)
Fever or abdominal distension

indications: Acute uterine inversion after delivery
contraindications: Giving a uterotonic before the uterus is replaced
equipment: Intravenous access, fluids and analgesia or anaesthesia
Warm sterile fluid, giving set and a silastic ventouse cup or the woman's hand seal for the hydrostatic method
steps: Call for help and stop any uterotonic infusion.
Explain to the woman and start resuscitation for shock.
Give analgesia or anaesthesia and a uterine relaxant if available.
Leave the placenta attached if not yet separated.
Grasp the inverted uterus and push it up through the cervix, replacing the part that came out last first.
Push the fundus up toward the umbilicus with the fist until it reverts.
Use the hydrostatic method by running warm fluid into the vagina with the introitus sealed if manual reduction fails.
Keep the hand inside until the uterus contracts after giving a uterotonic.
Remove the placenta manually once the uterus is replaced if still attached.
Proceed to laparotomy if vaginal reduction fails.
aftercare: Continue uterotonics and observe closely for haemorrhage and re-inversion.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
red_flags: Re-inversion
Persistent shock or haemorrhage
Failed reduction (laparotomy)

name: Evacuation of vulval or perineal haematoma

indications: Enlarging or painful vulval, perineal or vaginal haematoma after birth
Haematoma over about 5 cm or with signs of blood loss
contraindications: Small stable haematoma (manage conservatively)
equipment: Repair pack, scalpel and suction if available
steps: Explain the procedure, resuscitate if needed and obtain written consent.
Provide regional or general anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Incise the haematoma at its most dependent point through the vaginal or skin side.
Evacuate the clot and irrigate the cavity.
Ligate any obvious bleeding vessels.
Close the cavity with absorbable sutures to obliterate dead space, or leave a drain.
Pack the vagina and insert a urinary catheter.
Confirm swab and needle counts.
aftercare: Remove the vaginal pack after 12 to 24 hours.
Monitor haemoglobin, pain and urine output.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
red_flags: Re-accumulation of the haematoma
Signs of shock out of proportion to visible loss (retroperitoneal extension)
Fever or offensive discharge

indications: Obstetric haemorrhage with signs of shock while awaiting definitive treatment or transfer
contraindications: Viable pregnancy in utero (relative)
Bleeding above the diaphragm, such as from the chest
Mitral stenosis or heart failure
steps: Explain the garment to the woman and continue resuscitation.
Lay the open garment under the woman with the top segment at the lowest rib.
Close the ankle segments first, tightly, then the calves and thighs.
Close the pelvic segment with the lower edge at the symphysis pubis.
Close the abdominal segment with the pressure ball over the umbilicus.
Check that two fingers can fit under the top edge and breathing is not restricted.
Proceed with treatment of the cause or transfer with the garment in place.
Remove only when the bleeding source is controlled and the woman has been stable for 2 hours.
Remove from the ankles upward, one segment at a time, checking pulse and blood pressure between segments.
aftercare: Monitor pulse, blood pressure and urine output during and after removal.
Clean and dry the garment for reuse per manufacturer instructions.
red_flags: Fall in blood pressure or rise in pulse during removal (stop and reapply)
Breathlessness when the abdominal segment is closed

indications: History of mid-trimester losses or preterm births suggesting cervical insufficiency
Short cervix on ultrasound with a history of preterm birth
Painless cervical dilatation in the second trimester (rescue cerclage)
contraindications: Active labour, bleeding or ruptured membranes
Chorioamnionitis
Fetal anomaly incompatible with life or fetal death
equipment: Vaginal surgery set with speculum, retractors and sponge forceps
Non-absorbable tape or braided suture on a large needle
steps: Confirm viability and gestation by ultrasound and obtain written consent.
Provide spinal or general anaesthesia and position in lithotomy.
Perform the surgical time-out and clean the vagina.
Expose the cervix with retractors and grasp it with sponge forceps.
Insert a purse-string suture high around the cervix at the cervico-vaginal junction in four or more bites.
Avoid the bladder anteriorly and the vessels at 3 and 9 o'clock.
Tie the suture anteriorly and leave long ends for later removal.
Check the fetal heart after the procedure.
aftercare: Advise pelvic rest and avoid heavy strenuous activity as advised.
Plan removal at about 36 to 37 weeks or earlier if labour starts.
Record the stitch type and knot position in the antenatal notes.
red_flags: Contractions, bleeding or fluid leakage (remove stitch if labouring)
Fever or offensive discharge

indications: Planned removal at 36 to 37 weeks
Onset of labour, ruptured membranes or infection with a stitch in place
contraindications: Shirodkar or transabdominal stitch needing theatre removal or caesarean
equipment: Sponge-holding forceps and stitch cutter or fine scissors
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Position the woman in lithotomy and insert a speculum.
Identify the knot and the long ends of the suture.
Hold the ends with forceps and cut the suture below the knot.
Pull the suture out completely and check it is intact.
Check the fetal heart after removal.
aftercare: Explain that labour may follow but may not start immediately.
Advise to return if contractions, bleeding or fluid loss occur.
red_flags: Stitch cannot be found or removed (theatre)
Heavy bleeding or fever

indications: Breech presentation at 36 weeks or more in a nullipara, or 37 weeks or more in a multipara
contraindications: Placenta praevia or recent antepartum haemorrhage
Abnormal fetal heart rate tracing
Ruptured membranes or multiple pregnancy
Major uterine anomaly or other indication for caesarean section
equipment: CTG or Doppler for fetal heart monitoring
Access to theatre for emergency caesarean
steps: Confirm breech presentation, liquor volume and placental site by ultrasound.
Obtain written consent explaining the success rate and small risk of emergency caesarean.
Record a normal fetal heart tracing before the procedure.
Give a tocolytic per local protocol if used.
Lie the woman supine with slight lateral tilt.
Lift the breech out of the pelvis with one hand.
Guide the head forward or backward around the uterus with the other hand to encourage a forward roll.
Stop if the woman has significant pain or the fetal heart is abnormal.
Confirm the new presentation by ultrasound.
Monitor the fetal heart for at least 30 minutes after the procedure.
aftercare: Give anti-D to rhesus-negative women per protocol.
Advise to return with bleeding, pain, reduced movements or leaking fluid.
red_flags: Persistent fetal bradycardia (emergency caesarean)
Vaginal bleeding or abdominal pain after ECV
Reduced fetal movements

indications: Induction of labour with a favourable cervix
Augmentation of slow labour
Need to assess liquor or apply a fetal scalp electrode
contraindications: Unengaged or high presenting part
Placenta praevia or vasa praevia
HIV with high viral load or active genital herpes (relative)
steps: Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Check the fetal heart rate and confirm the head is engaged by abdominal palpation.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the vulva.
Perform a vaginal examination and feel for pulsating vessels or cord.
Guide the amnihook along the fingers and hook the membranes between contractions.
Keep the fingers in the vagina to let liquor drain slowly and check for cord prolapse.
Note the colour and amount of liquor.
Check the fetal heart rate immediately after.
aftercare: Monitor fetal heart and contractions and record on the partograph.
Start oxytocin if contractions do not establish within the time set by local protocol.
red_flags: Cord prolapse
Fresh bleeding (vasa praevia or abruption)
Thick meconium or fetal heart abnormality

indications: To reduce the need for formal induction from 39 to 41 weeks
contraindications: Placenta praevia or unexplained antepartum bleeding
Ruptured membranes
Preterm pregnancy
equipment: Sterile or clean examination gloves and lubricant
steps: Explain the procedure, its benefits and possible discomfort, and obtain verbal consent.
Check the fetal heart rate and the presentation abdominally.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Perform a vaginal examination and insert a finger through the cervical os if possible.
Sweep the finger in a circle to separate the membranes from the lower segment.
Massage the cervix if the os is closed.
Assess and record the Bishop score.
aftercare: Warn of possible cramping and light bleeding.
Advise to return with heavy bleeding, ruptured membranes, regular contractions or reduced movements.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding
Rupture of membranes with meconium
Reduced fetal movements

indications: Induction of labour with an unfavourable cervix
Ripening where prostaglandins are unavailable or a uterine scar is present
contraindications: Placenta praevia or unexplained vaginal bleeding
Ruptured membranes (relative)
Active genital infection
equipment: Sterile water or saline and a 50 mL syringe
Tape to secure the catheter to the thigh
steps: Confirm the indication for induction and obtain verbal consent.
Check the fetal heart rate and presentation.
Position the woman and insert a sterile speculum to see the cervix.
Clean the cervix with antiseptic.
Pass the catheter through the cervix with forceps until the balloon is above the internal os.
Inflate the balloon with sterile water or saline, usually 30 to 60 millilitres.
Pull the catheter back gently until it sits against the internal os.
Tape the catheter to the inner thigh with gentle traction if used locally.
Check the fetal heart rate after insertion.
aftercare: Check the fetal heart and contractions regularly.
Remove the catheter after 12 to 24 hours if not expelled.
Reassess the Bishop score and plan amniotomy or further induction.
red_flags: Vaginal bleeding or ruptured membranes with abnormal fetal heart
Fever or offensive discharge
Strong frequent contractions with fetal distress

indications: Post-term pregnancy at 41 weeks or more
Hypertensive disorders, diabetes or other maternal conditions
Prelabour rupture of membranes at term
Fetal growth restriction or intrauterine fetal death
contraindications: Placenta praevia, vasa praevia or transverse lie
Previous classical caesarean or more than one previous caesarean (relative)
Cord presentation
Cephalopelvic disproportion
equipment: Ripening agents or Foley catheter per local protocol
Oxytocin and infusion pump or a counted-drip giving set
CTG or Doppler for fetal monitoring
steps: Confirm the indication, gestational age and absence of contraindications.
Obtain consent after explaining the methods, risks and possible need for caesarean.
Assess the cervix and record the Bishop score.
Ripen an unfavourable cervix with a prostaglandin or Foley catheter per local protocol.
Monitor the fetal heart and contractions after each ripening dose.
Perform amniotomy once the cervix is favourable.
Start an oxytocin infusion and increase it gradually per local protocol until effective contractions.
Monitor contractions and fetal heart closely, and stop oxytocin if there is hyperstimulation.
Start the partograph once active labour is established.
Reassess and plan caesarean section if induction fails.
aftercare: Monitor for postpartum haemorrhage after delivery, especially after prolonged oxytocin.
Record the induction method and interval to delivery.
red_flags: More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes or a contraction longer than 2 minutes
Abnormal fetal heart rate
Signs of uterine rupture (pain, bleeding, loss of contractions)

indications: All women in active labour
contraindications: None (do not delay emergency action to complete the chart)
equipment: Partograph or WHO labour care guide form
steps: Start the partograph when active labour is confirmed.
Record patient details, parity, gestation, time of admission and time membranes ruptured.
Record the fetal heart rate every 30 minutes in the first stage and every 5 minutes in the second.
Record liquor colour and moulding at each vaginal examination.
Plot cervical dilatation and descent of the head at each vaginal examination, usually every 4 hours.
Record the number and length of contractions in 10 minutes every 30 minutes.
Record pulse every 30 minutes and blood pressure and temperature every 4 hours.
Record urine volume, protein and ketones and any drugs or fluids given.
Act promptly when the alert line or action line is crossed.
Sign each entry and hand over the chart at shift change.
aftercare: File the completed partograph in the delivery record.
red_flags: Alert or action line crossed
Fetal heart under 110 or over 160 beats per minute
Thick meconium, severe moulding or no descent
Maternal fever, hypertension or tachycardia

indications: High-risk pregnancy in labour
Abnormality heard on intermittent auscultation
Reduced fetal movements or antenatal assessment
Oxytocin use, meconium or maternal fever
contraindications: None absolute
equipment: CTG machine with ultrasound and tocodynamometer transducers
steps: Explain the purpose and obtain verbal consent.
Check the date, time and paper speed on the machine.
Position the woman in left lateral or semi-recumbent position.
Palpate to find the fetal back and place the ultrasound transducer over the fetal heart.
Place the contraction transducer on the fundus.
Check the maternal pulse to make sure the fetal heart, not the maternal, is recorded.
Record for at least 20 minutes antenatally or continuously in labour.
Classify the trace using baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations.
Sign and date the trace with the classification and plan.
aftercare: Act on suspicious or pathological traces per local guidance.
File the trace in the patient's record.
red_flags: Prolonged bradycardia over 3 minutes
Reduced variability with late decelerations
Sinusoidal pattern

indications: Low-risk labour
Antenatal checks from the second trimester
contraindications: High-risk labour where continuous monitoring is available and indicated
steps: Explain what you are doing to the woman.
Palpate to find the fetal back and place the Pinard or Doppler over it.
Feel the maternal pulse at the same time to differentiate it.
Listen during and for at least 1 minute after a contraction.
Count the fetal heart rate for a full minute.
Listen every 15 to 30 minutes in the first stage and every 5 minutes in the second stage.
Record the rate and any decelerations on the partograph.
aftercare: Increase monitoring or start CTG if an abnormality is heard.
red_flags: Fetal heart under 110 or over 160 beats per minute
Decelerations after contractions
Fetal heart not heard

indications: Confirming labour and assessing progress
Before amniotomy or analgesia decisions
Suspected cord prolapse or full dilatation
contraindications: Known or suspected placenta praevia before ultrasound
Preterm ruptured membranes without labour (use speculum)
equipment: Sterile gloves and lubricant or antiseptic
steps: Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent with a chaperone present.
Ask the woman to empty her bladder and palpate the abdomen first.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves.
Clean the vulva and part the labia.
Insert two fingers gently between contractions.
Assess cervical dilatation, effacement, position and consistency.
Assess the presenting part, its position, station, caput and moulding.
Check the membranes and note the liquor colour if ruptured.
Exclude cord presentation or prolapse.
Record findings and the Bishop score on the partograph.
aftercare: Limit examinations to about every 4 hours unless indicated.
Explain findings to the woman.
red_flags: Cord felt in the vagina
Bleeding during examination
Malpresentation or severe moulding

indications: Suspected cephalopelvic disproportion
Assessment before trial of labour or breech delivery
Short stature or history of pelvic fracture or rickets
contraindications: Placenta praevia
steps: Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent with a chaperone present.
Ask the woman to empty her bladder and position her in lithotomy.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves.
Try to reach the sacral promontory with two fingers to estimate the diagonal conjugate.
Feel the curve of the sacrum and the sacrospinous ligaments.
Assess the prominence of the ischial spines.
Assess the subpubic angle with two fingers.
Assess the intertuberous diameter with the knuckles of a closed fist.
Record the pelvis as adequate, borderline or contracted.
aftercare: Discuss the plan for delivery with the woman.
Remember that labour is the best test of pelvic adequacy in a cephalic presentation.
red_flags: Contracted pelvis with a large baby (plan caesarean section)

indications: Prenatal diagnosis of chromosomal or genetic disorders
Suspected intra-amniotic infection
Assessment or treatment of polyhydramnios
contraindications: Active maternal infection at the site
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Procedure before 15 weeks
Maternal HIV or hepatitis B or C with high viral load (relative; counsel and refer)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with a sterile probe cover
5 mL and 20 mL syringes and sterile sample tubes
steps: Counsel about indication, risks including miscarriage, and limits of the test, and obtain written consent.
Check blood group and rhesus status.
Scan to confirm viability, placental site and a clear pool of liquor.
Clean the skin with antiseptic and apply sterile drapes.
Insert the needle under continuous ultrasound guidance into the pool, avoiding the placenta if possible.
Discard the first few drops, then aspirate the required sample.
Withdraw the needle and confirm the fetal heart beat.
Label the samples and send them to the laboratory.
aftercare: Give anti-D to rhesus-negative women.
Advise to rest and to report pain, bleeding, leaking fluid or fever.
Explain when and how results will be given.
red_flags: Leakage of fluid or vaginal bleeding
Abdominal pain, fever or contractions
Reduced fetal movements

indications: Obstructed labour with a confirmed dead fetus where caesarean carries high maternal risk
Hydrocephalus with a dead fetus
contraindications: Live fetus
Uterine rupture or imminent rupture (laparotomy)
Operator without training in the technique
Cervix less than fully dilated (except for decompression of hydrocephalus)
equipment: Craniotomy instruments (perforator, cranioclast) or embryotomy set
Heavy scissors and strong toothed forceps
Regional or general anaesthesia or sedation
steps: Confirm fetal death by ultrasound or absent fetal heart on two checks.
Counsel the woman and family and obtain written consent.
Resuscitate and correct dehydration, and give prophylactic antibiotics.
Provide anaesthesia, empty the bladder and position in lithotomy.
Perform the surgical time-out.
Steady the fetal head abdominally and perforate the skull at the most accessible point with care.
Evacuate the brain tissue and apply traction with strong forceps to deliver the head.
Perform cleidotomy if needed to deliver the shoulders.
Deliver the placenta and give a uterotonic.
Explore the uterus and genital tract for rupture or tears.
Leave an indwelling catheter for at least 7 to 14 days after obstructed labour.
aftercare: Monitor for haemorrhage, infection and urinary fistula.
Provide bereavement counselling.
Plan follow-up and advise on mode of future deliveries.
red_flags: Uterine rupture found at exploration
Continuous urine leakage (vesicovaginal fistula)
Fever or offensive lochia

form.label: Fetal death confirmed by
options: Absent fetal heart on repeated checks

indications: All births where the baby does not need immediate resuscitation
contraindications: Baby needing resuscitation where it cannot be given with the cord intact
Placental abruption or cord avulsion
equipment: Two sterile cord clamps or sterile ties
steps: Dry the baby and place it skin to skin on the mother after birth.
Assess breathing while the cord is intact.
Wait at least 1 to 3 minutes, or until pulsation stops, before clamping.
Place the first clamp about 2 to 3 cm from the baby's abdomen.
Place the second clamp a few centimetres further toward the mother.
Cut between the clamps with sterile scissors, shielding with gauze.
Check the cord stump for bleeding and count the vessels.
Apply chlorhexidine or keep the cord clean and dry per local protocol.
aftercare: Teach the mother to keep the cord clean and dry and look for infection.
Check the stump at each newborn review.
red_flags: Bleeding from the cord stump
Redness, swelling or pus around the umbilicus
Single umbilical artery (needs newborn assessment)

indications: Eclampsia
Severe pre-eclampsia to prevent convulsions
contraindications: Myasthenia gravis
Absent patellar reflexes, respiratory depression or very low urine output (withhold maintenance)
equipment: Magnesium sulphate per local protocol with prepared dilutions
Syringes, needles or an infusion pump or counted-drip set
Calcium gluconate as antidote, drawn up and ready
Urinary catheter with hourly urine measuring bag
Monitoring chart, pulse oximeter and reflex hammer
steps: Call for help, protect the airway and place the woman in left lateral position during a fit.
Explain the treatment to the woman or her relatives.
Secure intravenous access and insert a urinary catheter for hourly urine output.
Give the loading dose per the local regimen (Pritchard or Zuspan), checking the prescription with a second person.
Start the maintenance dose by the intramuscular or intravenous route per the local regimen.
Check respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output before every maintenance dose or hourly on infusion.
Withhold or delay the next dose if reflexes are absent, breathing is slow or urine output is low.
Give calcium gluconate per protocol if there is respiratory depression.
Treat severe hypertension alongside per local protocol.
Continue treatment for 24 hours after delivery or the last convulsion.
Plan delivery once the woman is stable.
aftercare: Continue close monitoring of blood pressure, reflexes, breathing and urine output.
Refer early to a higher-level facility if needed after the loading dose.
red_flags: Respiratory rate under 16 per minute
Absent patellar reflexes
Urine output under 30 mL per hour
Recurrent convulsions

indications: Rhesus-negative non-sensitised woman after birth of a rhesus-positive baby
Sensitising events such as bleeding, miscarriage, ectopic, trauma, ECV or amniocentesis
Routine antenatal prophylaxis in the third trimester where available
contraindications: Rhesus-positive woman
Woman already sensitised (anti-D antibodies present)
Previous severe reaction to immunoglobulin
equipment: Syringe and needle for intramuscular injection
Blood sample tubes for group, antibody screen and Kleihauer test if available
steps: Confirm the woman's identity and rhesus-negative status with a current group and antibody result.
Explain that anti-D is a blood product and obtain consent.
Check the product, batch number, expiry and dose prescribed per local protocol.
Take a sample for a Kleihauer test after delivery or a large sensitising event if available.
Give by deep intramuscular injection into the deltoid within 72 hours of the event.
Record batch number and time in the notes and the blood product register.
Observe the woman for 20 minutes for reactions.
aftercare: Give an extra dose if the Kleihauer test shows a large bleed.
Give the woman a card or record of the anti-D given.
red_flags: Allergic reaction or anaphylaxis
More than 72 hours since the event (still give, up to 10 days)

name: Sterile speculum examination for ruptured membranes

indications: History of fluid leakage per vaginam in pregnancy
Suspected preterm or prelabour rupture of membranes
contraindications: Digital vaginal examination in suspected preterm rupture (avoid)
equipment: Nitrazine paper or a commercial amniotic fluid test if available
Swabs for culture including high vaginal and group B streptococcus
steps: Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent with a chaperone present.
Ask the woman to lie flat for 20 to 30 minutes beforehand if possible to allow pooling.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves.
Insert a sterile speculum without lubricant gel.
Look for pooling of liquor in the posterior fornix and ask her to cough.
Note the colour of any fluid and any cord or fetal parts.
Test the fluid with nitrazine or a commercial test if available.
Take swabs for culture and assess the cervix visually.
Remove the speculum and check the fetal heart.
aftercare: Plan management according to gestation and findings.
Advise the woman to report fever, offensive discharge, reduced movements or contractions.
red_flags: Cord visible or felt
Meconium or blood-stained liquor
Maternal fever or tachycardia (chorioamnionitis)

indications: Every antenatal visit from about 20 weeks
Admission in labour
contraindications: None
steps: Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent.
Ask the woman to empty her bladder and lie semi-recumbent with slight tilt.
Inspect for size, shape, scars, striae and fetal movements.
Measure the symphysis-fundal height in centimetres from the fundus to the top of the pubic bone.
Palpate the fundus to identify which fetal pole lies there.
Palpate both sides to find the fetal back and limbs and determine the lie.
Palpate the lower pole to determine the presentation.
Assess engagement in fifths palpable above the pelvic brim.
Listen to the fetal heart over the anterior shoulder and count for a full minute.
Record findings and plot fundal height on a chart if available.
aftercare: Explain findings to the woman.
Arrange ultrasound if size is not consistent with dates or presentation is uncertain.
red_flags: Fundal height smaller or larger than expected for dates
Malpresentation after 36 weeks
Fetal heart not heard or abnormal rate
Abdominal tenderness

indications: Routine postnatal visits within 24 hours, at day 3, at 1 to 2 weeks and at 6 weeks
contraindications: None
equipment: Haemoglobin and urine test strips if available
steps: Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent.
Ask about bleeding, pain, passing urine and stool, breastfeeding, mood and sleep.
Check pulse, blood pressure and temperature.
Examine the breasts for engorgement, cracked nipples or mastitis.
Palpate the abdomen for uterine involution and tenderness, and check any caesarean wound.
Inspect the perineum for healing, infection or haematoma.
Assess the lochia for amount and smell.
Examine the legs for calf tenderness or swelling.
Screen for postnatal depression with a validated tool if available.
Discuss and offer family planning.
Check the baby's feeding, weight and immunisations at the same visit.
aftercare: Give advice on danger signs, nutrition and hygiene.
Arrange the next postnatal visit.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding or passing clots
Fever, foul lochia or abdominal tenderness
Severe headache, visual disturbance or high blood pressure
Calf pain, breathlessness or chest pain
Thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby

indications: Every new eye presentation and follow-up visit
Before and after eye surgery or treatment
Screening (school, driving, occupational, diabetes)
Eye injury, before any other examination
contraindications: None; defer only if irrigation for chemical injury is needed first
equipment: Snellen, tumbling E or LogMAR chart at the correct distance (usually 6 m) with good lighting
Picture or Lea symbol chart for young children
Occluder or palm of the patient's hand
steps: Confirm identity and ask whether the patient normally wears glasses for distance.
Seat or stand the patient at the marked distance from a well-lit chart.
Test the right eye first with the left eye fully covered, using current distance glasses if worn.
Ask the patient to read from the top down and record the smallest line read with most letters correct.
Repeat for the left eye, then both eyes together if needed.
If acuity is worse than 6/9, repeat each eye through a pinhole and record the pinhole acuity.
If the top line cannot be read, walk the patient closer (e.g. 3 m, 1 m) and record as 3/60 or 1/60.
If still unable, test counting fingers, then hand movements, then perception of light with a torch.
For preverbal children, assess fixing and following or use preferential-looking or picture charts.
Test near vision with the near chart at reading distance if relevant.
Record results for each eye, with or without correction and with pinhole.
aftercare: Explain the result and the need for refraction or further examination if reduced.
red_flags: Refer urgently for sudden loss of vision, or vision reduced after injury.
Refer a child who cannot fix and follow, or has unequal vision between eyes (amblyopia risk).
Vision not improving with pinhole suggests eye disease rather than refractive error and needs examination.

indications: Red eye, eye pain or discharge
Reduced vision
Eye injury or suspected foreign body
Pre-operative and post-operative assessment
Glaucoma, uveitis and diabetic eye review
contraindications: Patient unable to sit or position at the slit lamp (use loupe and torch or portable slit lamp)
equipment: Alcohol wipes for chin and forehead rests
Lid retractor or cotton bud for eversion
steps: Confirm identity, explain the examination and record visual acuity first.
Clean the chin and forehead rests and perform hand hygiene.
Seat the patient with chin on the rest and forehead against the band, at eye level with the canthal mark.
Focus the beam and examine the lids, lashes and lid margins at low magnification.
Examine the conjunctiva and sclera, everting the upper lid if a foreign body is suspected.
Examine the cornea with a narrow slit beam for clarity, opacities, foreign bodies and epithelial defects.
Assess anterior chamber depth and look for cells, flare, hypopyon or hyphaema with a short narrow beam.
Examine the iris and pupil, then the lens for opacity or displacement.
Instil fluorescein and use the cobalt blue light to look for staining or wound leak if indicated.
Repeat for the other eye and record findings for each eye.
aftercare: Advise not to rub the eye if topical anaesthetic was used until it wears off.
red_flags: Refer urgently for hypopyon, hyphaema, corneal ulcer, suspected penetrating injury or very shallow anterior chamber.
Stop if a globe rupture is suspected; do not press on the eye and shield it.

indications: Diabetic retinopathy screening
Hypertension, raised intracranial pressure or unexplained headache
Unexplained reduced vision or floaters and flashes
Glaucoma assessment of the optic disc
Retinopathy of prematurity screening in at-risk infants
contraindications: Known narrow angles or previous angle-closure without iridotomy (assess angle first)
Patient needing pupil observation for neurological monitoring (agree with the treating team)
Iris-fixated lens implant (check before dilating)
equipment: Direct ophthalmoscope, or indirect ophthalmoscope with condensing lens, or slit lamp with fundus lens
Short-acting mydriatic eye drops per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, record visual acuity and ask about glaucoma, eye surgery and driving home.
Estimate anterior chamber depth with a torch from the side or at the slit lamp before dilating.
Explain the drops and that vision will be blurred and light-sensitive for several hours.
Instil mydriatic drops in each eye to be examined and wait until the pupils are well dilated.
Darken the room and ask the patient to look at a distant target.
Examine the red reflex, then the optic disc for colour, cup-to-disc ratio and margins.
Follow the vessels out to each quadrant looking for haemorrhages, exudates, new vessels or detachment.
Examine the macula last by asking the patient to look at the light.
Repeat for the other eye and record findings, including diabetic retinopathy grade if relevant.
aftercare: Do not drive or operate machinery until vision clears.
Wear sunglasses or a hat in bright light.
red_flags: Return immediately for eye pain, red eye, haloes, headache or vomiting after dilation (acute angle closure).
Refer urgently for retinal detachment, vitreous haemorrhage, swollen optic disc or proliferative retinopathy.

indications: Glaucoma screening (age over 40, family history, Black African ancestry)
Glaucoma follow-up
Red painful eye with suspected acute angle closure
