Steroid use, uveitis or after eye surgery
contraindications: Suspected open globe injury (do not touch the eye)
Active corneal infection for contact tonometry (use a disposable tip or non-contact method)
equipment: Goldmann or Perkins applanation tonometer, rebound tonometer or Schiotz tonometer
Topical anaesthetic and fluorescein strips for applanation
Slit lamp with cobalt blue light
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and check there is no suspicion of globe rupture.
Perform hand hygiene and confirm the tonometer tip is disinfected or new and calibrated.
Instil topical anaesthetic and fluorescein for applanation tonometry.
Seat the patient at the slit lamp, ask them to look straight ahead and keep both eyes open.
Hold the lids without pressing on the globe and bring the tip gently onto the central cornea.
Adjust the dial until the inner edges of the semicircles just touch and read the pressure.
For rebound tonometry, take the series of readings per the device without anaesthetic.
Repeat for the other eye and record each pressure with the method and time.
Disinfect or discard the tip per protocol.
aftercare: Do not rub the eye until the anaesthetic wears off.
red_flags: Treat or refer the same day for pressure of 30 mmHg or more, or raised pressure with pain, haloes or vomiting.
Stop if the cornea is abraded during measurement and stain to check.

indications: Glaucoma diagnosis and monitoring
Suspected pituitary, optic nerve or brain lesion
Unexplained visual loss or headache with visual symptoms
Driving or occupational assessment
contraindications: Patient too unwell or unable to concentrate (use confrontation testing)
equipment: Automated perimeter, or red-topped pin and target for confrontation testing
Near correction lens for the perimeter if needed
steps: Confirm identity, record visual acuity and explain the test.
For confrontation, sit facing the patient at arm's length with one eye each covered.
Bring a target in from the periphery in each quadrant and ask the patient to say when they first see it.
Compare with your own field and test central field with a red target for desaturation or scotoma.
For automated perimetry, enter patient details and select the test programme.
Fit the correct near lens, occlude the other eye and position the patient comfortably at the bowl.
Explain to press the button whenever a light is seen while looking at the central target.
Monitor fixation and reliability during the test and encourage the patient.
Repeat for the other eye and print or save the results with reliability indices.
aftercare: Explain that a first test is often less reliable and may need repeating.
red_flags: Refer urgently for a new hemianopia or bitemporal field defect (possible stroke or pituitary lesion).
Refer for progressive field loss in glaucoma.

indications: Reduced vision that improves with pinhole
Headaches or eye strain with near work
Presbyopia
Children with squint, amblyopia or failed school screening
contraindications: Cycloplegic drops in narrow angles or known allergy to the drops
equipment: Trial frame and trial lens set, or phoropter
Cycloplegic eye drops for children per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, take a visual history and record unaided and current spectacle acuity.
For children and suspected latent hyperopia, instil cycloplegic drops and wait for full effect.
Perform retinoscopy in a dim room at a known working distance to obtain an objective result.
Refine sphere for each eye using plus and minus lenses to the best acuity with the most plus.
Refine cylinder axis and power using a cross-cylinder if astigmatism is present.
Balance the two eyes and check binocular acuity.
Measure near addition for patients with presbyopia at their working distance.
Measure pupillary distance and write the prescription clearly for each eye.
Check the final prescription in a trial frame for comfort before issuing it.
aftercare: Explain how and when to wear the spectacles and that adaptation may take a few days.
Advise review at the recommended interval, sooner in children.
red_flags: Refer if best-corrected vision remains reduced (cataract, glaucoma, retinal or optic nerve disease).
Refer a child with suspected amblyopia or squint to an ophthalmologist.

indications: Any chemical splash to the eye (alkali, acid, solvents, cement, lime, battery fluid)
Particulate contamination of the eye
contraindications: None in chemical injury; start immediately, even before visual acuity
Suspected open globe (irrigate gently without pressure)
equipment: Normal saline or Ringer's lactate (clean tap water if nothing else is available)
Lid speculum or retractor, cotton buds
steps: Start irrigation immediately on arrival and ask about the chemical while irrigating.
Instil topical anaesthetic to allow the patient to open the eye.
Lie the patient down with the head turned to the affected side over a kidney dish.
Hold the lids open and run fluid from the inner corner across the eye, asking the patient to look in all directions.
Evert the upper lid and sweep the fornices with a moist cotton bud to remove particles such as lime or cement.
Continue for at least 30 minutes or until several litres have been used.
Wait 5 minutes then check the pH in the lower fornix and continue irrigating until it is neutral.
Record visual acuity once the pH is neutral and examine for corneal haze and limbal whitening.
Instil fluorescein to assess epithelial loss.
aftercare: Use prescribed lubricant, antibiotic and other drops exactly as instructed.
Do not rub the eye and attend review the next day.
red_flags: Refer urgently to an ophthalmologist for alkali injury, corneal haze, limbal whitening or reduced vision.
Recheck pH again after 20 minutes as alkali can leach out; repeat irrigation if it rises.

indications: Superficial foreign body embedded in the cornea
Rust ring after metallic foreign body
contraindications: Deep or penetrating foreign body, or suspected intraocular foreign body (refer)
Uncooperative patient (consider examination under anaesthesia, especially in children)
equipment: Sterile 25G or 23G needle on a cotton bud or syringe, or a foreign-body spud
Ophthalmic burr for rust ring if available
steps: Confirm identity, record visual acuity and take a history of the mechanism (hammering or grinding suggests high velocity).
Examine at the slit lamp to confirm the depth and that the anterior chamber is formed and quiet.
Obtain verbal consent and instil topical anaesthetic.
Position the patient at the slit lamp with the head firmly against the band and ask them to fix on a target.
Rest your hand on the patient's cheek and approach the cornea tangentially with the needle bevel up.
Lift the foreign body out gently, keeping strictly within the superficial cornea.
Remove a loose rust ring with the needle or burr; leave a deep rust ring for later review.
Stain with fluorescein and confirm no wound leak (Seidel negative).
Instil topical antibiotic and pad the eye only if comfort requires.
aftercare: Use antibiotic drops as prescribed and do not rub the eye.
Never give topical anaesthetic drops to take home; repeated use damages the cornea.
Wear protective eyewear for grinding and hammering work.
Return for review in 1–2 days if a rust ring remains or the eye is not improving.
red_flags: Stop and refer if the foreign body is deep, the anterior chamber is shallow, or Seidel test is positive.
Obtain X-ray or refer if an intraocular foreign body is possible after high-velocity injury.
Return urgently for increasing pain, discharge, white spot on the cornea or reduced vision.

indications: Foreign body on the conjunctiva or under the upper lid
Linear vertical corneal scratches suggesting a subtarsal foreign body
contraindications: Suspected penetrating injury or intraocular foreign body (refer)
equipment: Slit lamp or torch with loupe
Sterile cotton buds moistened with saline
steps: Confirm identity and record visual acuity.
Instil topical anaesthetic.
Examine the conjunctiva and fornices, asking the patient to look in each direction.
Ask the patient to look down and evert the upper lid over a cotton bud.
Wipe the foreign body away with a moist cotton bud or irrigate it out with saline.
Sweep the upper and lower fornices for further particles.
Stain with fluorescein to look for corneal abrasion.
Instil topical antibiotic if there is an abrasion.
aftercare: Do not rub the eye; use drops as prescribed.
Wear protective eyewear for dusty work.
red_flags: Refer for any suspected penetration, hyphaema, irregular pupil or reduced vision.
Return if pain or discharge worsens or vision drops.

indications: Suspected corneal abrasion or ulcer
Foreign body sensation or eye injury
Dry eye assessment
Checking for wound leak (Seidel test)
Contact lens related red eye
contraindications: Known allergy to fluorescein
Soft contact lens in the eye (remove first)
equipment: Sterile fluorescein strips or single-use drops
Slit lamp with cobalt blue filter, or blue-light torch
steps: Confirm identity, record visual acuity and remove contact lenses.
Moisten the fluorescein strip with a drop of sterile saline.
Ask the patient to look up and touch the strip gently to the lower conjunctiva.
Ask the patient to blink to spread the dye.
Examine the cornea with cobalt blue light for areas of green staining and note size and shape.
Note dendritic, punctate, linear or round patterns and measure the defect.
For Seidel test, apply concentrated dye over the wound and watch for a stream of diluted dye.
Record findings and draw the defect in the notes.
aftercare: Explain that tears may be yellow-green for a short time.
Do not reinsert soft contact lenses for several hours.
red_flags: Refer urgently for a dendritic ulcer, large or central ulcer, or positive Seidel test.
Refer contact lens wearers with a corneal ulcer the same day.

indications: Visually significant cataract affecting daily life
Mature, hypermature or white cataract
Lens-induced glaucoma or uveitis
Cataract preventing view of the fundus for treatment of retinal disease
contraindications: Active ocular or periocular infection
Uncontrolled systemic disease (blood pressure, diabetes) until optimised
Eye with no perception of light (unless for pain or lens-induced disease)
equipment: MSICS instrument set (crescent and keratome blades, cystitome, irrigating vectis, Simcoe cannula, forceps)
Povidone-iodine for skin and conjunctival sac
Posterior chamber IOL of calculated power, plus anterior chamber IOL as backup
steps: Confirm identity, eye to be operated (marked), biometry, IOL power and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Check blood pressure and blood glucose and review the anaesthetic plan.
Give the local anaesthetic block and achieve akinesia and anaesthesia.
Prepare the skin and instil povidone-iodine into the conjunctival sac, then drape and insert the speculum.
Make a fornix-based conjunctival flap and apply light cautery.
Create a frown or straight scleral incision about 2 mm behind the limbus and tunnel forward into clear cornea.
Enter the anterior chamber with the keratome and fill it with viscoelastic.
Perform a capsulotomy (capsulorhexis or can-opener) with the cystitome.
Hydrodissect and prolapse the nucleus into the anterior chamber.
Deliver the nucleus through the tunnel with the irrigating vectis or viscoexpression.
Aspirate the remaining cortex with the Simcoe cannula.
Fill the capsular bag with viscoelastic and implant the posterior chamber IOL.
Remove viscoelastic, form the chamber and check the tunnel is self-sealing; suture if it leaks.
Reposition the conjunctiva, give antibiotic per local protocol and apply a pad and shield.
aftercare: Use prescribed drops exactly as instructed and keep the shield on at night for the first weeks.
Avoid rubbing the eye, heavy lifting and dusty or dirty water exposure.
Attend review the next day and at the planned follow-up for refraction.
red_flags: Stop and manage per protocol for posterior capsule rupture, vitreous loss or suprachoroidal haemorrhage.
Return immediately for increasing pain, worsening vision, discharge or a red swollen eye (endophthalmitis).
Return for flashes, floaters or a curtain over vision.

indications: Visually significant cataract
Refractive lens surgery where indicated
Cataract with glaucoma or diabetic eye disease needing a clear view
contraindications: Active ocular infection
Very dense brunescent cataract or poor corneal endothelium (consider MSICS or ECCE)
Uncontrolled systemic disease until optimised
equipment: Phacoemulsification machine with handpieces checked and primed
Keratome and side-port blades, capsulorhexis forceps or cystitome, chopper
Foldable IOL of calculated power and injector
Povidone-iodine, sterile drapes and lid speculum
steps: Confirm identity, operative eye (marked), biometry, IOL power and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Give topical or block anaesthesia per plan.
Instil povidone-iodine, drape to isolate the lashes and insert the speculum.
Make the side-port and main clear corneal incisions.
Fill the anterior chamber with viscoelastic and perform a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis.
Hydrodissect and confirm the nucleus rotates freely.
Emulsify the nucleus with a chosen technique while protecting the posterior capsule and endothelium.
Remove the cortex with irrigation and aspiration.
Fill the bag with viscoelastic and inject the foldable IOL into the capsular bag.
Remove viscoelastic and hydrate the wounds until watertight.
Give antibiotic per local protocol and apply a shield.
aftercare: Use prescribed drops exactly as instructed and wear the shield at night.
Avoid rubbing the eye, swimming and dusty environments for the period advised.
Attend review the next day and at follow-up for refraction.
red_flags: Stop and convert or manage per protocol for posterior capsule rupture, dropped nucleus or wound burn.
Return immediately for pain, worsening vision, discharge or red eye (endophthalmitis).
Return for flashes, floaters or a shadow over vision.

indications: Visually significant cataract where MSICS or phaco is not suitable
Very hard or brunescent nucleus
Poor endothelium or small pupil where a large incision is safer
contraindications: Active ocular infection
Uncontrolled systemic disease until optimised
equipment: ECCE instrument set (blades, corneal scissors, cystitome, lens loop, Simcoe cannula)
Rigid posterior chamber IOL of calculated power
Fine nylon sutures and needle holder
steps: Confirm identity, operative eye (marked), biometry, IOL power and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Give the local anaesthetic block and check akinesia.
Instil povidone-iodine, drape and insert the speculum, and place a superior rectus bridle suture if needed.
Make a limbal-based or fornix-based conjunctival flap and apply light cautery.
Make a partial-thickness limbal groove and enter the anterior chamber.
Perform a can-opener capsulotomy with viscoelastic support.
Extend the incision with corneal scissors to fit the nucleus.
Express the nucleus with gentle pressure or a lens loop.
Place preplaced sutures, then aspirate the cortex.
Implant the IOL in the bag or sulcus under viscoelastic.
Close the wound with interrupted or continuous sutures and check it is watertight.
Give antibiotic per local protocol and apply pad and shield.
aftercare: Use prescribed drops and keep the shield on at night.
Expect suture-related astigmatism; selective suture removal may be needed later.
Attend review the next day and as scheduled.
red_flags: Manage per protocol for vitreous loss or expulsive haemorrhage and close the wound quickly.
Return immediately for pain, discharge or falling vision (endophthalmitis).

indications: Congenital or developmental cataract obscuring the visual axis
Traumatic cataract in a child
Dense cataract with absent red reflex in an infant (operate early to prevent amblyopia)
contraindications: Child not fit for general anaesthesia until optimised
Active ocular infection
equipment: General anaesthesia with paediatric airway equipment
Paediatric speculum, blades and capsulorhexis forceps
IOL of calculated power (if implanting) or aphakic plan
steps: Confirm identity with the parent or guardian, operative eye (marked) and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Induce general anaesthesia and perform biometry and examination under anaesthesia.
Prepare with povidone-iodine, drape and insert the paediatric speculum.
Make small corneal or scleral tunnel incisions.
Stain the capsule if needed and perform an anterior capsulorhexis.
Aspirate the soft lens matter with irrigation-aspiration.
Perform a primary posterior capsulotomy and anterior vitrectomy in young children per plan.
Implant the IOL in the bag or sulcus if planned.
Close all incisions with absorbable sutures as children's wounds do not self-seal.
Give antibiotic and anti-inflammatory treatment per local protocol and apply a shield.
aftercare: Give drops exactly as instructed and keep the shield on to prevent rubbing.
Start spectacles or contact lenses and patching as soon as advised; vision depends on this.
Attend every follow-up for refraction, pressure checks and amblyopia treatment.
red_flags: Return immediately for a red, painful or swollen eye, discharge or child very irritable (endophthalmitis).
Refer for raised pressure or loss of red reflex at follow-up (glaucoma or visual axis opacity).

indications: Glaucoma progressing or pressure uncontrolled on maximal tolerated treatment
Poor access to or adherence with long-term drops
Advanced glaucoma at presentation
contraindications: Active ocular inflammation or infection
Neovascular glaucoma without prior treatment (higher failure)
Eye with no perception of light (consider cyclodestruction)
equipment: Trabeculectomy set (crescent blade, punch or Vannas scissors, fine forceps)
Antimetabolite applied by local protocol with sponges, and safe disposal
steps: Confirm identity, operative eye (marked), pre-operative pressure and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Give local anaesthetic block and place a corneal traction suture.
Prepare with povidone-iodine, drape and insert the speculum.
Create a fornix-based conjunctival flap and apply light cautery.
Apply the antimetabolite on sponges under the conjunctiva per local protocol, then irrigate thoroughly.
Fashion a partial-thickness scleral flap into clear cornea.
Make a paracentesis and remove a block of trabecular tissue under the flap.
Perform a peripheral iridectomy.
Close the scleral flap with releasable or fixed sutures and titrate flow through the paracentesis.
Close the conjunctiva watertight and check for a raised bleb and no leak.
Give antibiotic and anti-inflammatory treatment per local protocol and apply a shield.
aftercare: Use drops exactly as instructed and stop glaucoma drops in the operated eye unless told otherwise.
Attend frequent early reviews for pressure checks and suture adjustment.
Never rub the eye; return at once if it becomes red or sticky, even years later.
red_flags: Return immediately for a red, painful, sticky eye or drop in vision (blebitis or endophthalmitis).
Review urgently for a very low pressure with shallow chamber or choroidal detachment.
Review for a bleb leak (positive Seidel) or high pressure.

indications: Primary angle closure or angle-closure glaucoma
Primary angle closure suspect with occludable angles
Fellow eye after acute angle closure
Pupil block
contraindications: Cloudy cornea preventing a clear view (clear first or consider surgical iridectomy)
Flat anterior chamber
Uncooperative patient
equipment: Nd:YAG laser (with argon laser if available for thick irides)
Iridotomy contact lens with coupling gel
Miotic and pressure-lowering drops per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, eye, gonioscopy findings and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Instil miotic and pressure-lowering drops per local protocol and allow the pupil to constrict.
Instil topical anaesthetic and seat the patient at the laser.
Place the iridotomy lens with coupling gel.
Choose a site in the superior or temporal peripheral iris, ideally in a crypt and covered by the lid.
Focus precisely on the iris surface and apply laser shots until a full-thickness opening is seen.
Confirm patency by seeing pigment and aqueous flow or the lens capsule through the opening.
Remove the lens and check pressure after about one hour.
aftercare: Use anti-inflammatory drops as prescribed.
Expect mild blur; report any persistent glare or ghost images.
Attend review for gonioscopy to confirm the angle has opened.
red_flags: Treat and recheck if pressure rises significantly after laser.
Stop and apply lens pressure if iris bleeding occurs, until it stops.
Return urgently for eye pain, haloes or vomiting.

indications: Posterior capsule opacification reducing vision after cataract surgery
Capsular opacity preventing fundus view or treatment
contraindications: Corneal opacity preventing focus
Uncooperative patient or uncontrolled nystagmus
Active intraocular inflammation
equipment: Capsulotomy contact lens with coupling gel (optional)
steps: Confirm identity, eye, visual acuity and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Dilate the pupil and instil pressure-lowering drops per local protocol.
Seat the patient at the laser and place the contact lens if used.
Focus slightly behind the posterior capsule to avoid pitting the IOL.
Open the capsule with a cruciate or circular pattern using the lowest effective energy.
Make an opening similar in size to the undilated pupil.
Remove the lens and check pressure after about one hour.
aftercare: Use anti-inflammatory drops if prescribed.
Floaters are common for a few days.
red_flags: Return urgently for flashes, a shower of floaters or a curtain over vision (retinal detachment).
Return for eye pain or haloes (pressure rise).

indications: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy where follow-up is uncertain
Neovascular glaucoma or iris new vessels
Ischaemic retinal vein occlusion with new vessels
contraindications: Media opacity preventing an adequate view (consider vitrectomy or cataract surgery first)
Uncooperative patient
equipment: Retinal laser (slit lamp or indirect delivery)
Wide-field fundus contact lens with coupling gel
Laser safety goggles and warning sign
steps: Confirm identity, eye, indication and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Dilate the pupil fully and instil topical anaesthetic.
Post the laser safety sign and ensure everyone in the room wears goggles.
Seat the patient comfortably and place the contact lens.
Set spot size, duration and power to produce a light grey-white burn, starting in the periphery.
Place burns about one burn-width apart outside the arcades, avoiding vessels and the macula.
Complete the planned number of burns in one or several sessions to reduce pain and macular oedema.
Record the number of burns and settings and draw the treated area.
aftercare: Expect blur and glare for the rest of the day; do not drive.
Continue good diabetes and blood pressure control.
Attend for the next session and review as planned.
red_flags: Stop if the burns are too white or cause a bubble, or the patient cannot keep still.
Return urgently for sudden loss of vision (vitreous haemorrhage) or severe pain.

indications: Diabetic macular oedema
Neovascular age-related macular degeneration
Macular oedema from retinal vein occlusion
Endophthalmitis (intravitreal antibiotics)
Proliferative retinopathy adjunct per specialist plan
contraindications: Active ocular or periocular infection (except endophthalmitis treatment)
Known allergy to the agent
Uncontrolled raised pressure
equipment: Sterile lid speculum, calipers and gloves
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked), agent and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Check for any eye infection and record visual acuity and pressure.
Instil topical anaesthetic and povidone-iodine into the conjunctival sac.
Wear sterile gloves and mask, avoid talking over the field, and insert a sterile speculum.
Measure 3.5–4 mm behind the limbus in phakic eyes (3–3.5 mm in pseudophakic) inferotemporally.
Inject the prescribed agent slowly through the pars plana, aiming toward the centre of the eye.
Withdraw the needle and press briefly with a sterile cotton bud.
Check perfusion of the optic disc or that the patient can count fingers, and check pressure.
Remove the speculum and rinse the povidone-iodine.
aftercare: Some grittiness and a small red patch on the white of the eye are expected.
Do not rub the eye or swim for the period advised.
Attend the next planned injection or review.
red_flags: Treat immediately if the disc is not perfused or vision is no light perception after injection.
Return immediately for increasing pain, redness, discharge or falling vision in the days after (endophthalmitis).
Return for flashes or a curtain over vision.

indications: Pterygium encroaching on the visual axis or progressing
Induced astigmatism reducing vision
Recurrent irritation or restricted eye movement
Cosmetic concern after counselling about recurrence
contraindications: Active ocular surface infection
Uncertain diagnosis of a conjunctival lesion (biopsy to exclude neoplasia)
equipment: Pterygium set (blades, Westcott scissors, fine forceps, calipers)
Fibrin glue or fine absorbable sutures
Local anaesthetic for subconjunctival or topical use
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked) and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Give topical and subconjunctival local anaesthetic.
Prepare with povidone-iodine, drape and insert the speculum.
Dissect the pterygium head off the cornea and excise the body with underlying Tenon's tissue.
Smooth the corneal bed and apply light cautery to bleeding points.
Measure the bare scleral defect with calipers.
Harvest a thin conjunctival graft from the superior bulbar conjunctiva, keeping its limbal orientation.
Place the graft on the defect with limbus to limbus and secure with fibrin glue or sutures.
Send the excised tissue for histology if atypical.
Apply antibiotic and anti-inflammatory treatment per local protocol and pad the eye.
aftercare: Use drops as prescribed and wear sunglasses or a hat outdoors.
Avoid rubbing the eye; return for suture removal if non-absorbable sutures were used.
red_flags: Return urgently for severe pain, discharge or reduced vision.
Review if the graft appears displaced or lost.

indications: Chalazion persisting despite warm compresses and lid hygiene
Large chalazion causing ptosis, astigmatism or amblyopia risk in a child
contraindications: Recurrent lesion at the same site or atypical lesion in an adult (biopsy to exclude malignancy)
Acute cellulitis (treat first)
equipment: Antibiotic ointment per local protocol and eye pad
steps: Confirm identity, eye and lid (marked) and consent; use general anaesthesia or sedation in young children.
Instil topical anaesthetic and inject local anaesthetic around the lesion.
Place the chalazion clamp and evert the lid.
Make a vertical incision through the tarsal conjunctiva over the chalazion, avoiding the lid margin.
Curette out the contents and break down loculations.
Send tissue for histology if recurrent or atypical.
Remove the clamp and press with a pad until bleeding stops.
Apply antibiotic ointment per local protocol and a firm pad.
aftercare: Remove the pad after a few hours and continue warm compresses and lid hygiene.
Use ointment as prescribed.
red_flags: Return for increasing swelling, redness spreading over the lid or fever (cellulitis).
Review for recurrence at the same site (biopsy needed).

indications: Suspected ocular surface squamous neoplasia (common with HIV)
Pigmented or enlarging conjunctival lesion
Conjunctival cyst, papilloma or granuloma
Diagnostic biopsy for inflammatory or infiltrative disease
contraindications: Lesion with suspected orbital or intraocular extension (image and refer)
equipment: Fine forceps, Westcott scissors and blades
Cryotherapy probe if available for neoplasia margins
Absolute alcohol and sponges if corneal component per local protocol
Absorbable sutures, fibrin glue or graft material
Labelled specimen pot with orientation marker
steps: Confirm identity, eye, lesion site and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Offer HIV counselling and testing if OSSN is suspected.
Give topical and local anaesthetic, prepare with povidone-iodine and drape.
Mark a margin of about 3–4 mm of clear tissue around suspected neoplasia.
Excise the lesion with a no-touch technique, avoiding handling the tumour directly.
Remove any corneal component with alcohol-assisted epitheliectomy per local protocol.
Apply double freeze-thaw cryotherapy to the conjunctival margins if available.
Close the defect, or cover with a conjunctival graft or leave bare as planned.
Place the specimen flat, orientate it and send for histology.
aftercare: Use drops as prescribed and attend for histology results.
Attend long-term follow-up as recurrence can occur.
red_flags: Refer to an oncology-capable eye unit if margins are involved or invasive carcinoma is reported.
Return for a new lump, bleeding or redness at the site.

indications: Trachomatous trichiasis with one or more lashes touching the globe
Recurrent trichiasis after previous surgery (experienced surgeon)
contraindications: Active lid infection
Severe lid deformity or cicatricial entropion beyond the surgeon's competence (refer)
equipment: Trichiasis surgery set (lid clamp or plate, blade, scissors, forceps, needle holder)
Absorbable sutures for the tarsus and non-absorbable or absorbable sutures for skin per protocol
Antibiotic ointment per local protocol and eye pad
steps: Confirm identity, eye and lid (marked), count lashes touching the globe and obtain written consent.
Check visual acuity and look for corneal opacity.
Clean the lid with povidone-iodine and drape.
Inject local anaesthetic along the upper lid.
Apply the lid clamp or plate and make a full-thickness incision 3 mm from and parallel to the lid margin.
Extend the incision along the full length of the lid, avoiding the lacrimal punctum.
Pass everting mattress sutures through the distal and proximal tarsus and skin.
Tie the sutures to evert the lash-bearing margin slightly away from the globe.
Close the skin with interrupted sutures and check the lid contour and closure.
Apply antibiotic ointment per local protocol and pad the eye.
aftercare: Keep the eye clean, use ointment as prescribed and return for suture removal if non-absorbable.
Keep the face clean and wash daily to reduce trachoma spread in the household.
Attend follow-up for recurrence checks.
red_flags: Return for lid swelling with fever, discharge or severe pain.
Return if lashes touch the eye again (recurrence) or the lid will not close.

indications: Few trichiatic lashes (often peripheral) touching the eye
Patient declining or awaiting trichiasis surgery
Misdirected lashes from other lid disease
contraindications: Many lashes or central trichiasis where surgery is better (offer surgery)
equipment: Torch and loupe or slit lamp
steps: Confirm identity and explain that surgery is the definitive treatment for trachomatous trichiasis.
Count and locate the lashes touching the globe with the patient looking in each direction.
Instil topical anaesthetic if needed.
Grasp each offending lash close to the lid margin with the forceps.
Pull it out firmly in the direction of growth to remove the whole lash.
Recheck that no lashes are left touching the eye.
Train the patient or a family member on safe epilation with good forceps if appropriate.
aftercare: Lashes regrow within weeks; repeat epilation or return for surgery.
Do not cut lashes, as short stubs scratch more.
red_flags: Refer for surgery if many lashes, corneal opacity or recurrent trichiasis.
Return for a painful red eye or reduced vision (corneal ulcer).

indications: Exposure keratopathy (facial palsy, proptosis, lagophthalmos)
Persistent corneal epithelial defect or neurotrophic ulcer
Protection of the cornea in unconscious or intensive care patients
contraindications: Active corneal infection needing frequent drops and examination (temporary only with access)
equipment: Fine forceps, scissors, needle holder and blade
Non-absorbable double-armed sutures and bolsters (tubing pieces)
steps: Confirm identity, eye and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Clean the lids with povidone-iodine and drape.
Inject local anaesthetic into the upper and lower lids at the planned site.
For permanent tarsorrhaphy, split the grey line and remove a strip of marginal epithelium on both lids.
Pass a mattress suture through a bolster, the upper lid, the lower lid and a second bolster.
Tie the suture to bring the lid margins together over the intended width.
Check that the cornea is covered and the lids are apposed without tension.
Apply antibiotic ointment per local protocol.
aftercare: Keep the area clean and use ointment as prescribed.
Return for review and suture removal as planned.
red_flags: Return for pain, discharge, swelling or redness of the lids.
Review if the tarsorrhaphy opens or sutures cut through.

indications: Partial or full-thickness eyelid laceration
Lid margin laceration
Canalicular laceration (medial lid)
contraindications: Suspected open globe injury (repair the globe first and do not press on the eye)
equipment: Fine plastic or lid surgery set
Absorbable sutures for tarsus and subcutaneous layers, fine sutures for skin
Silk or absorbable suture for the lid margin
Pigtail probe and silicone stent if the canaliculus is cut
steps: Confirm identity and examine the globe first, including visual acuity, to exclude penetrating injury.
Obtain consent and check tetanus status; use general anaesthesia in children or complex injuries.
Clean and irrigate the wound, removing foreign material, and preserve all viable tissue.
Probe the medial lid wounds for canalicular involvement.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and drape.
Align the lid margin first with a vertical mattress suture through the grey line.
Close the tarsal plate with partial-thickness absorbable sutures.
Repair the canaliculus over a stent if divided.
Close skin and muscle with fine sutures, leaving margin suture ends long and tied away from the cornea.
Apply antibiotic ointment per local protocol.
aftercare: Clean the wound gently and use ointment as prescribed.
Return for suture removal (skin in about 5–7 days, margin later) and stent removal if placed.
red_flags: Refer urgently for reduced vision, suspected globe injury, or tissue loss needing reconstruction.
Return for spreading redness, fever, pus or swelling (cellulitis).

indications: Full-thickness corneal, corneoscleral or scleral laceration
Globe rupture after blunt trauma
contraindications: None absolute; patient must be fit for anaesthesia (stabilise life-threatening injuries first)
equipment: General anaesthesia (avoid pressure on the eye)
Corneal suture set with fine nylon sutures and absorbable sutures for sclera
Rigid eye shield for pre-operative protection
Systemic and intracameral antibiotics per local protocol
Orbital X-ray or CT if intraocular foreign body suspected
steps: Confirm identity, record visual acuity and relative afferent pupil defect, and shield the eye without pressure.
Keep the patient fasted, give antiemetic and analgesia, start antibiotics per protocol and check tetanus.
Image for intraocular foreign body when the mechanism suggests it.
Obtain written consent, discussing the possibility of evisceration if repair is impossible.
Tell the anaesthetist the globe is open so that agents and manoeuvres that raise eye pressure are avoided (no pressure from the mask).
Induce general anaesthesia and complete the time-out.
Clean the periocular skin with povidone-iodine, avoiding the open wound, and insert a speculum without pressure.
Reposit or excise prolapsed uvea depending on viability, and remove exposed vitreous.
Close the limbus first, then the cornea with fine interrupted nylon sutures.
Explore and close scleral wounds from front to back, extending the conjunctival peritomy as needed.
Reform the anterior chamber with balanced salt solution and check the wound is watertight.
Bury suture knots and give antibiotics per protocol.
Apply a shield and plan secondary surgery for lens, retina or foreign body as needed.
aftercare: Use drops exactly as instructed and wear the shield at all times initially.
Attend frequent reviews; further surgery may be needed.
Report any change in the other eye (sympathetic ophthalmia is rare but serious).
red_flags: Refer to a vitreoretinal unit for intraocular foreign body, retinal detachment or posterior rupture.
Return immediately for increasing pain, discharge or falling vision (endophthalmitis).
Return urgently for redness, pain or blurred vision in the uninjured eye.

indications: Painful blind eye
Endophthalmitis or panophthalmitis not responding to treatment
Severely damaged unrepairable globe
Cosmetically unacceptable blind eye
contraindications: Suspected or unexcluded intraocular tumour (enucleate instead)
Eye with potential for useful vision
equipment: Evisceration set (blade, corneal scissors, evisceration spoon, forceps)
Orbital implant of appropriate size if used
Local anaesthetic block or general anaesthesia
Specimen pot for histology or culture
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked on the lid and checked twice) and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Confirm there is no suspicion of intraocular tumour, using B-scan if the fundus cannot be seen.
Give general anaesthesia or a block and prepare and drape.
Perform a 360-degree peritomy and remove the cornea (or make a scleral incision if keeping the cornea).
Remove all uveal tissue from the scleral shell with the evisceration spoon.
Wipe the inside of the shell to ensure no uveal tissue remains.
Place an implant within the shell only if planned and the eye is not actively infected (omit or delay it in endophthalmitis), then close the sclera in layers.
Close Tenon's and conjunctiva and insert a conformer.
Send contents for histology or culture and apply a pressure dressing.
aftercare: Keep the pressure dressing on for the time advised and use prescribed ointment.
Keep the conformer in place and attend for prosthesis fitting after healing.
red_flags: Return for severe swelling, bleeding, fever or discharge.
Return if the implant becomes exposed or the conformer falls out.

indications: Intraocular tumour (retinoblastoma, choroidal melanoma)
Painful blind eye with possible tumour
Severely injured eye at risk of sympathetic ophthalmia per specialist judgement
contraindications: Tumour with orbital extension (needs oncology planning, may need exenteration or chemotherapy first)
Eye with useful vision
equipment: Enucleation set (scissors, muscle hooks, enucleation scissors or snare, forceps)
Specimen pot with formalin, labelled with orientation
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked and checked against imaging and notes) and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Re-examine the eye after induction to confirm the correct eye (dilated fundus view for tumours).
Perform a 360-degree peritomy and separate Tenon's capsule from the globe.
Hook each rectus muscle, secure it with a suture and detach it from the globe.
Detach the oblique muscles.
Cut the optic nerve with enucleation scissors, taking a long stump for tumours.
Remove the globe gently without squeezing and control bleeding with pressure.
Place the implant, attach the rectus muscles to it and close Tenon's and conjunctiva in layers.
Insert a conformer and apply a pressure dressing.
Send the globe for histology with the optic nerve length recorded.
aftercare: Keep the dressing on as advised and use ointment as prescribed.
Attend for histology results, oncology follow-up and prosthesis fitting.
red_flags: Return for severe swelling, bleeding, fever or discharge.
Return if the implant becomes exposed.
For retinoblastoma, ensure siblings are screened and the other eye is followed up.

indications: Malignant tumour involving the orbit (eyelid, conjunctival or lacrimal carcinoma, melanoma)
Life-threatening orbital infection (mucormycosis) per multidisciplinary decision
contraindications: Distant metastases where surgery will not help (palliative discussion)
Patient unfit for general anaesthesia
equipment: Orbital surgery set with periosteal elevators, enucleation scissors and bone instruments
Haemostatic packing or skin graft materials
Specimen pot with formalin and orientation markers
steps: Confirm identity, side (marked), imaging, histology and written consent with counselling about disfigurement, and complete the time-out.
Confirm the multidisciplinary plan and group and save or cross-match blood.
Induce general anaesthesia, prepare and drape.
Incise the skin around the orbital rim (sparing the lids if planned).
Elevate the periosteum from the orbital walls back to the apex.
Divide the orbital apex contents and remove the orbital contents en bloc.
Achieve haemostasis with diathermy and pressure.
Line the socket with a split-skin graft or leave to granulate, or close with lid skin.
Orientate and send the specimen with margins marked.
Apply a pressure dressing.
aftercare: Follow wound care instructions and attend dressing changes.
Attend for histology, oncology review and prosthesis planning.
Seek support for body image and mental well-being.
red_flags: Return for bleeding, fever, foul discharge or clear fluid leakage (possible CSF leak).
Return for a new lump or non-healing area in the socket.

indications: Child who cannot be examined awake (suspected glaucoma, cataract, retinoblastoma, trauma)
Uncooperative adult needing full eye examination
Retinoblastoma staging and follow-up
Paediatric biometry before surgery
contraindications: Patient not fit for anaesthesia until optimised
equipment: General anaesthesia or sedation with monitoring
Handheld slit lamp or operating microscope
Calipers, keratometer and A-scan as needed
Camera for fundus photography if available
steps: Confirm identity with the parent or guardian, indication and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Dilate the pupils before induction if the fundus is to be examined.
Measure intraocular pressure immediately after induction, as anaesthesia lowers it.
Insert the speculum and examine the lids, cornea, anterior chamber, iris and lens.
Measure corneal diameter and keratometry and axial length if needed.
Examine the fundus with the indirect ophthalmoscope, including the periphery with indentation.
Photograph and draw the findings.
Perform any planned minor procedure (suture removal, syringing) under the same anaesthetic.
Recover the patient and explain findings to the family.
aftercare: Follow the anaesthetic recovery and feeding advice.
Attend the next planned review or surgery.
red_flags: Stop if anaesthetic complications occur.
Refer urgently for retinoblastoma or congenital glaucoma confirmed at EUA.

indications: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction persisting after about 12 months of age despite massage
Recurrent dacryocystitis in a child
contraindications: Acute dacryocystitis (treat infection first)
Adult acquired obstruction (consider syringing and DCR)
equipment: General anaesthesia or sedation for children
Bowman lacrimal probes of graded sizes
Lacrimal cannula, syringe and saline with fluorescein
Nasal suction or catheter to confirm patency
steps: Confirm identity with the parent or guardian, eye and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Dilate the upper or lower punctum with the punctum dilator.
Pass the probe vertically 2 mm, then horizontally along the canaliculus with the lid stretched laterally until a hard stop is felt.
Rotate the probe vertically and pass it down the nasolacrimal duct, feeling for a give as the obstruction opens.
Confirm the probe in the nose with a second probe (metal-on-metal) or by direct view.
Irrigate with fluorescein-stained saline and confirm it is recovered from the nose.
Place silicone intubation if planned for complex or repeat cases.
Record the level of obstruction and any false passage.
aftercare: Use prescribed drops as advised.
Expect slight blood-stained tears or nasal discharge for a day.
Return for review; continue massage if advised.
red_flags: Stop if the probe meets abnormal resistance or bleeding suggests a false passage.
Return for swelling, redness or pus over the tear sac, or a persistently watery eye.

indications: Watery eye to assess patency of the lacrimal drainage system
Before cataract or other intraocular surgery to exclude dacryocystitis
Mucocele or recurrent sticky eye
contraindications: Acute dacryocystitis
Recent canalicular laceration repair (unless advised)
equipment: Lacrimal cannula on a 2 mL or 5 mL syringe
steps: Confirm identity and explain the procedure.
Instil topical anaesthetic and seat the patient with the head supported.
Press over the lacrimal sac to check for regurgitation of mucus or pus.
Dilate the lower punctum.
Pass the cannula vertically then horizontally along the lower canaliculus while stretching the lid laterally.
Note whether a hard stop (reaches the sac) or soft stop (canalicular block) is felt.
Inject saline gently and ask whether the patient tastes or feels fluid in the throat.
Note any regurgitation from the same or opposite punctum and whether it is clear or mucopurulent.
Repeat through the upper punctum if needed and record the result.
aftercare: Some fluid in the nose or throat is normal.
red_flags: Stop if there is pain, swelling of the lid (false passage) or bleeding.
Defer intraocular surgery if mucopus regurgitates; treat the infection first.

form.label: Result
options: Blocked with regurgitation from opposite punctum
Blocked with regurgitation from same punctum

indications: Acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction with watering or discharge
Chronic or recurrent dacryocystitis or mucocele
Failed probing in older children (specialist decision)
contraindications: Acute dacryocystitis (treat first)
Lacrimal sac tumour suspected (biopsy first)
Uncontrolled bleeding disorder
equipment: General or local anaesthesia with nasal packing for vasoconstriction per local protocol
DCR set (Rollet retractors, periosteal elevator, bone punches or drill, lacrimal probes)
Absorbable sutures for flaps and fine sutures for skin
steps: Confirm identity, side (marked) and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Pack the nose on the operative side per protocol to reduce bleeding.
Make a curved skin incision medial to the angular vessels (external approach) or proceed endoscopically.
Elevate the periosteum and reflect the lacrimal sac laterally.
Create a bony ostium through the lacrimal fossa into the nose.
Open the lacrimal sac and nasal mucosa to form anterior and posterior flaps.
Pass a probe through the canaliculi to confirm entry into the sac.
Place silicone intubation if needed and suture the mucosal flaps together.
Close the muscle and skin and confirm haemostasis.
aftercare: Avoid blowing the nose hard and do not lift heavy objects for the period advised.
Use nasal and eye drops as prescribed.
Return for skin suture and silicone tube removal as planned.
red_flags: Return urgently for heavy nosebleed that does not stop with pressure.
Return for swelling, redness, fever or recurring watering.

indications: Manifest squint not corrected by glasses or amblyopia treatment
Squint causing double vision or abnormal head posture
Cosmetic and psychosocial impact of squint
contraindications: Uncorrected refractive error or untreated amblyopia (treat first)
Squint from untreated neurological or orbital disease (investigate first)
equipment: Strabismus set (muscle hooks, calipers, Westcott scissors, fine forceps, needle holder)
steps: Confirm identity, eye(s), muscles and planned measurements, and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Perform forced duction testing after induction.
Warn the anaesthetist about the oculocardiac reflex; release muscle traction at once if the heart rate falls.
Make a fornix or limbal conjunctival incision over the muscle.
Isolate the muscle on a hook and clear intermuscular attachments.
Secure the muscle with double-armed absorbable sutures near its insertion.
Disinsert the muscle and reattach it at the measured position (recession) or shorten and reattach (resection).
Check the measurements with calipers and that the sutures are secure.
Close the conjunctiva and repeat on other muscles as planned.
Apply antibiotic and anti-inflammatory treatment per local protocol.
aftercare: Expect redness and some discomfort for a few weeks; use drops as prescribed.
Avoid swimming for the period advised.
Continue glasses and patching as instructed and attend orthoptic review.
red_flags: Return immediately for increasing pain, swelling, discharge or reduced vision (infection or scleral perforation).
Return for a sudden large change in eye position (slipped muscle).

indications: Congenital ptosis covering the visual axis or risking amblyopia
Acquired ptosis limiting vision or causing brow strain
Cosmetic concern
contraindications: Untreated myasthenia, third nerve palsy or Horner's syndrome without assessment
Poor Bell's phenomenon or dry eye at high risk of exposure (caution)
equipment: General anaesthesia for children, local for adults
Oculoplastic set (blades, scissors, forceps, needle holder, lid guards)
Frontalis sling material (autologous fascia or synthetic) if needed
steps: Confirm identity, eye, measurements (margin reflex distance, levator function) and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Mark the lid crease and give anaesthesia.
For levator surgery, incise the lid crease and expose the levator aponeurosis.
Advance or resect the levator and fix it to the tarsal plate with partial-thickness sutures.
Check lid height and contour (sitting up if under local) and adjust sutures.
For poor levator function, place a frontalis sling between the tarsus and brow through stab incisions.
Close the skin and reform the lid crease.
Apply lubricant ointment and protect the cornea.
aftercare: Use lubricant frequently, especially at night, as the lid may not close fully at first.
Use cold compresses for swelling and attend suture removal.
red_flags: Return urgently for a painful red eye or blurred vision (exposure keratopathy).
Return for bleeding, swelling with pain or loss of vision (orbital haemorrhage).

indications: Involutional, cicatricial or spastic entropion with lashes rubbing the eye
Ectropion causing watering, exposure or chronic conjunctivitis
Lid malposition after facial palsy or scarring
contraindications: Active lid or conjunctival infection
Cicatricial disease needing grafting beyond local capability (refer)
equipment: Oculoplastic set (blades, Westcott scissors, forceps, needle holder, lid guard)
steps: Confirm identity, eye and lid (marked), type of malposition and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Assess lid laxity, lash position and lower lid retractors before marking.
Clean, drape and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
For lid laxity, perform a lateral tarsal strip with canthotomy and refix the tarsus to the lateral orbital rim.
For involutional entropion, add everting sutures or retractor reattachment as needed.
For medial ectropion, add a medial spindle excision if needed.
Check lid position, tension and closure, and adjust before tying.
Close the skin and apply antibiotic ointment per local protocol.
aftercare: Use ointment and cold compresses as advised.
Return for suture removal and review.
red_flags: Return for pain, increasing swelling, bleeding or reduced vision.
Return if the lid turns in or out again.

indications: Delivery of antibiotic or anti-inflammatory medicine at the end of eye surgery
Severe anterior uveitis or scleritis per specialist plan
Severe corneal ulcer where drops are not enough per local protocol
Local anaesthesia for minor conjunctival procedures
contraindications: Scleral thinning or scleritis with necrosis (risk of perforation)
Known allergy to the agent
equipment: 1 mL or 2 mL syringe with 27G or 30G needle
steps: Confirm identity, eye, prescribed agent and consent.
Instil topical anaesthetic and povidone-iodine into the conjunctival sac.
Insert a speculum or hold the lids open and ask the patient to look away from the injection site.
Grasp or tent the conjunctiva with a cotton bud or forceps away from the limbus.
Insert the needle bevel up into the subconjunctival space, parallel to the globe, avoiding vessels.
Inject slowly to raise a bleb and withdraw the needle.
Press with a cotton bud briefly and check for any leak or bleeding.
aftercare: A red swelling on the white of the eye is expected and settles over days.
Use any other drops as prescribed.
red_flags: Stop if the globe is penetrated (sudden loss of resistance, fall in pressure) and refer urgently.
Return for severe pain, reduced vision or discharge.

indications: Anaesthesia and akinesia for cataract, glaucoma, vitreoretinal or other intraocular surgery
Analgesia for painful eye procedures
contraindications: Patient refusal, inability to lie still or communicate
Local infection at the injection site
Long axial length or staphyloma (higher perforation risk, consider sub-Tenon)
Uncontrolled coagulopathy (consider sub-Tenon or topical)
equipment: 25G peribulbar needle (short, about 25 mm) on a 5 mL or 10 mL syringe
Monitoring (pulse oximetry, ECG, blood pressure) and IV access
Resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion available
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked), axial length and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Secure IV access and attach monitoring.
Instil topical anaesthetic and clean the lower lid skin.
Ask the patient to look straight ahead in primary gaze.
Insert the needle at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of the inferior orbital rim, just above the rim.
Advance tangentially to the globe, staying outside the muscle cone and not beyond the equator depth.
Aspirate, then inject slowly while watching for globe movement or rising lid tension.
Add a medial canthal injection if akinesia is incomplete.
Apply gentle ocular compression and reassess akinesia and pressure before surgery.
Monitor the patient continuously until surgery and after.
aftercare: Keep the eye covered until the block wears off as the lid may not close.
Double vision or a droopy lid for some hours is expected.
red_flags: Stop and manage immediately for globe perforation, retrobulbar haemorrhage (tense proptosis), or brainstem anaesthesia (drowsiness, apnoea).
Treat local anaesthetic toxicity per protocol (seizures, arrhythmia).
Perform lateral canthotomy urgently for retrobulbar haemorrhage with raised pressure.

indications: Suspected microbial keratitis (bacterial, fungal, acanthamoeba)
Large, central or atypical corneal ulcer
Ulcer not responding to initial treatment
contraindications: Impending or actual corneal perforation (do not scrape; refer)
Very thin cornea at the ulcer base
equipment: Topical anaesthetic without preservative if possible
Sterile 21G or 23G needle, scalpel blade or spatula
Glass slides for Gram and KOH stains
Culture media (blood agar, chocolate agar, Sabouraud) or transport medium
steps: Confirm identity, eye and verbal consent, and record visual acuity and ulcer size.
Stop topical antibiotics before scraping if possible, per local protocol.
Instil topical anaesthetic and seat the patient at the slit lamp.
Scrape the leading edge and base of the ulcer with the needle held tangentially, avoiding deep pressure.
Smear the material on slides for Gram and KOH staining.
Take fresh scrapes for each culture medium, inoculating in rows without breaking the agar.
Label all samples and send promptly with a clear request.
Start empirical treatment per local protocol straight after sampling.
aftercare: Use drops exactly as prescribed, including through the night if instructed.
Return daily or as advised until the ulcer is improving.
red_flags: Stop if the cornea is very thin or Seidel positive and refer urgently.
Return immediately for increasing pain, enlarging white patch, hypopyon or reduced vision.

indications: Emergency lowering of very high pressure (central retinal artery occlusion, acute angle closure per specialist)
Aqueous sampling for infective uveitis or endophthalmitis
Diagnostic PCR for viral retinitis or uveitis
contraindications: Very shallow or flat anterior chamber without experienced operator
Active external eye infection (unless sampling for it)
equipment: 30G or 27G needle on a 1 mL syringe (or tuberculin syringe)
Fine forceps for stabilising the globe
Specimen tubes for PCR or culture
steps: Confirm identity, eye and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Instil topical anaesthetic and povidone-iodine and insert a sterile speculum.
Stabilise the globe with forceps at the limbus if needed.
Enter the anterior chamber at the temporal limbus with the bevel up, parallel to the iris.
Keep the needle tip over the iris and away from the lens.
Aspirate or allow gentle egress of a small volume of aqueous.
Withdraw the needle and check the chamber remains formed and the wound is not leaking.
Label samples and send promptly; recheck pressure.
Instil antibiotic per local protocol.
aftercare: Use drops as prescribed and attend review as advised.
red_flags: Stop if the lens is touched or the chamber collapses, and refer.
Return immediately for pain, redness or falling vision (infection).

indications: Non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage
Tractional or complex retinal detachment
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with traction
Endophthalmitis
Macular hole or epiretinal membrane
Dropped lens fragment or intraocular foreign body
contraindications: Active external eye infection (except endophthalmitis)
Patient unable to posture when gas tamponade is planned
equipment: Vitrectomy machine with cutter, light pipe and trocar cannulas
Operating microscope with wide-angle viewing system
Tamponade agents (air, gas, silicone oil) as planned
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked), plan, tamponade and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Give block or general anaesthesia and prepare with povidone-iodine.
Insert trocar cannulas through the pars plana (3.5–4 mm behind the limbus) and confirm the infusion is inside the eye.
Perform core vitrectomy, then induce or confirm posterior vitreous detachment.
Remove peripheral vitreous and treat haemorrhage, membranes or traction as indicated.
Identify and treat retinal breaks with endolaser or cryotherapy.
Perform fluid-air exchange and inject the planned tamponade if needed.
Remove cannulas and check for wound leak, suturing if necessary.
Check pressure and give antibiotic per local protocol.
aftercare: Follow the posturing instructions exactly if gas or oil was used.
Do not fly or travel to high altitude, and warn anaesthetists about nitrous oxide while gas is in the eye.
Use drops as prescribed and attend all reviews; oil removal may be needed later.
red_flags: Return immediately for severe pain, vomiting or haloes (pressure rise).
Return immediately for redness, discharge or falling vision (endophthalmitis).
Return for a new curtain or shadow in vision (redetachment).

indications: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Retinal dialysis or detachment in young phakic patients (buckle often preferred)
contraindications: Thin sclera at the buckle site (consider vitrectomy)
Severe proliferative vitreoretinopathy (vitrectomy needed)
equipment: Silicone buckle elements (explant bands or sponges) and scleral sutures
Needle for subretinal fluid drainage if planned
Gas for injection if pneumatic retinopexy
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked), retinal drawing of breaks and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Give anaesthesia, prepare and drape.
Perform a conjunctival peritomy and sling the rectus muscles.
Localise all retinal breaks with indirect ophthalmoscopy and scleral indentation.
Apply cryotherapy around each break until the retina just whitens.
Place scleral sutures and position the buckle element beneath them to support the breaks.
Drain subretinal fluid through a small sclerotomy if needed.
Tighten the sutures and check that the breaks sit on the buckle and the optic disc is perfused.
Inject gas if needed and check pressure.
Close the conjunctiva and give antibiotic per local protocol.
aftercare: Follow any posturing advice and do not fly if gas was used.
Expect pain and swelling for a few days; use drops as prescribed.
Attend all reviews; spectacle changes are common after buckling.
red_flags: Return immediately for severe pain, vomiting or loss of vision (pressure rise or ischaemia).
Return for a new shadow or curtain in vision (redetachment).
Return for redness and discharge over the buckle (infection or extrusion).

indications: Corneal scarring reducing vision (trachoma, infection, trauma)
Keratoconus not corrected by contact lenses
Corneal endothelial failure (bullous keratopathy, Fuchs dystrophy)
Therapeutic graft for non-healing infection or perforation
contraindications: Active ocular surface disease or severe dry eye (graft failure risk)
Uncontrolled glaucoma
No access to donor tissue of acceptable quality or to long-term follow-up
equipment: Donor cornea from an eye bank with screening documentation
Trephines (donor punch and recipient), corneal scissors
Fine nylon sutures and needle holder
steps: Confirm identity, eye (marked), donor tissue details and written consent, and complete the time-out.
Check the donor cornea's screening, expiry and quality before starting.
Give anaesthesia, prepare and drape, and place a fixation ring if needed.
Punch the donor cornea from the endothelial side to the planned size.
Mark the recipient centre and trephine to the planned depth.
Complete the excision with corneal scissors under viscoelastic protection.
Place the donor button and secure it with cardinal sutures.
Complete interrupted or running sutures and adjust tension to reduce astigmatism.
Reform the chamber and check the wound is watertight.
Give antibiotic and anti-inflammatory treatment per local protocol and apply a shield.
aftercare: Use drops exactly as prescribed for a long period; do not stop without advice.
Wear eye protection and never rub the eye.
Attend all reviews; sutures are removed gradually over months.
red_flags: Return immediately for redness, sensitivity to light, reduced vision or pain (RSVP signs of rejection).
Return for a loose suture, discharge or a white spot on the graft.

indications: Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage (tense proptosis, reduced vision, high pressure)
Orbital haemorrhage after trauma or peribulbar block with sight threatened
contraindications: Suspected open globe injury (repair globe first; seek senior help)
equipment: Straight blunt-tipped scissors (Stevens or iris scissors)
steps: Confirm identity and eye, and obtain consent quickly as this is sight-saving and time-critical.
Record visual acuity, pupil reaction and pressure if possible without delaying treatment.
Clean the lateral canthus and inject local anaesthetic if time allows.
Clamp the lateral canthus horizontally with the haemostat to the orbital rim for about one minute.
Cut along the crushed line about 1 cm laterally with scissors (canthotomy).
Pull the lower lid down and away, identify the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon and cut it (cantholysis).
Check the lower lid now moves freely away from the globe.
Reassess pressure, proptosis and vision, and cut the superior crus if still tight.
Leave the wound open and dress with gauze.
aftercare: The wound usually heals without stitches; formal repair can be planned later.
Keep the area clean and follow up with ophthalmology.
red_flags: Refer urgently to ophthalmology and image the orbit after decompression.
Escalate if vision or pressure does not improve after cantholysis.

indications: Loose or broken sutures
Suture with vascularisation, infiltrate or mucus
Selective removal to reduce astigmatism after cataract or graft surgery
Planned removal after wound healing
contraindications: Unhealed wound where removal could cause dehiscence
steps: Confirm identity, eye and which sutures to remove, and obtain verbal consent.
Instil topical anaesthetic and povidone-iodine.
Seat the patient at the slit lamp, stabilise your hand on the cheek and ask the patient to fix a target.
Cut the suture with the needle tip or blade, away from the buried knot.
Grasp the end on the knot side and pull it out along its track so the knot does not drag through the wound.
Check for wound leak with fluorescein (Seidel test).
Instil topical antibiotic per local protocol.
aftercare: Use antibiotic drops as prescribed for a few days.
Attend review for refraction or further suture removal.
red_flags: Stop and review if the wound gapes or the Seidel test is positive.
Return for pain, redness or discharge.

indications: Comfort after corneal abrasion or foreign body removal (when needed)
Protection after eye surgery
Exposure protection in an unconscious patient or facial palsy
Rigid shield (no pad) for suspected open globe
contraindications: Suspected open globe for a soft pad (use a rigid shield without pressure)
Bacterial keratitis or contact lens-related ulcer (do not pad)
Young child with a normal other eye for more than a few hours (amblyopia risk)
equipment: Rigid eye shield (for surgery or suspected open globe)
steps: Confirm identity, eye and the reason for padding, and explain to the patient.
Perform hand hygiene.
Instil any prescribed ointment.
Ask the patient to close both eyes.
Place the pad over the closed lid; fold a second pad underneath for a pressure pad if ordered.
Tape the pad diagonally from the forehead to the cheek so the lid cannot open, avoiding the mouth and hair.
For a shield, tape it to the bony orbital rim so it does not press on the eye.
Check the patient is comfortable and record the time and type of pad.
aftercare: Do not drive while one eye is padded.
Remove or keep the pad as instructed and return for review.
red_flags: Remove and review if pain increases under the pad.
Return urgently for discharge, worsening vision or increasing redness.

indications: Opaque media (dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, corneal opacity) preventing a fundus view
Suspected retinal detachment
Suspected intraocular tumour or foreign body
Before evisceration to exclude tumour
contraindications: Open globe injury for a contact scan (scan only gently through closed lids if essential, by an experienced operator)
equipment: Ophthalmic B-scan probe (about 10 MHz) or high-frequency linear probe
steps: Confirm identity, eye and indication, and explain the scan.
Disinfect the probe and position the patient lying back or reclined.
Apply gel to the closed upper lid (or to the probe for direct corneal contact with topical anaesthetic).
Set gain high initially to detect vitreous opacities, then reduce to assess dense structures.
Scan with transverse and longitudinal sections through all four quadrants and the posterior pole.
Ask the patient to move the eye to perform kinetic scanning and assess membrane mobility.
Measure lesion height and base, and note reflectivity and any shadowing.
Save images and record findings for each eye.
Wipe off the gel and disinfect the probe.
aftercare: No special care is needed.
red_flags: Refer urgently for retinal detachment, suspected tumour or intraocular foreign body.
Stop and avoid pressure if globe rupture is suspected.

indications: Glaucoma diagnosis and classification (open versus closed angle)
Shallow anterior chamber or angle-closure suspect
Before and after laser iridotomy
Suspected angle recession, neovascularisation or angle tumour
contraindications: Corneal abrasion, infection or recent corneal surgery
Suspected open globe
equipment: Coupling fluid if required by the lens
steps: Confirm identity, eye and indication, and explain the examination.
Disinfect the lens and instil topical anaesthetic.
Dim the room light and use a short narrow slit beam that does not pass through the pupil.
Ask the patient to look straight ahead and place the lens gently on the cornea.
Examine each quadrant of the angle, identifying the deepest visible structure.
Use indentation to differentiate appositional from synechial closure.
Note pigmentation, peripheral anterior synechiae, new vessels or recession.
Remove the lens, check the cornea and disinfect the lens.
Record the grade of each quadrant on a diagram.
aftercare: Do not rub the eye until the anaesthetic wears off; blur from coupling fluid clears soon.
red_flags: Treat or refer promptly for occludable angles or angle neovascularisation.
Stop if the cornea is abraded and treat the abrasion.

indications: Displaced or angulated closed fracture outside acceptable limits
Fracture causing skin tenting or neurovascular compromise from deformity
Displaced distal radius, forearm, ankle or paediatric long-bone fractures
contraindications: Open fracture needing debridement first
Unstable fracture pattern that will need internal fixation
Fracture more than 2-3 weeks old with callus (consider open reduction)
Patient unfit for sedation or anaesthesia without monitoring
equipment: Analgesia, local anaesthetic or sedation and monitoring equipment
Cast padding, plaster of Paris or backslab material and water bucket
steps: Confirm patient identity, injury side and consent and review the X-rays.
Examine and document skin and distal neurovascular status before reduction.
Give analgesia and anaesthesia such as haematoma block, Bier's block, sedation or general anaesthesia, with monitoring.
Prepare and pre-measure the cast or backslab before manipulation.
Apply steady longitudinal traction with counter-traction from an assistant.
Disimpact the fragments by briefly recreating the deformity if needed.
Correct angulation, rotation and displacement by reversing the mechanism of injury.
Hold the reduction while the cast or backslab is applied and moulded with three-point pressure.
Check the reduction with image intensifier or check X-ray in two planes.
Re-examine and document distal neurovascular status after reduction.
Elevate the limb and observe until recovered from sedation.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and move uninvolved joints regularly.
Check circulation, swelling and cast tightness within 24 hours.
Repeat X-ray at about 1 and 2 weeks to detect loss of reduction.
Give analgesia per local protocol and written cast care advice.
red_flags: Increasing pain, especially on passive stretch of fingers or toes, suggesting compartment syndrome.
Pale, cold, numb or blue fingers or toes.
Loss of reduction on follow-up X-ray.
Cast too tight, wet, cracked or causing pressure sores.

indications: Definitive immobilisation of a stable or reduced fracture once swelling has settled
Immobilisation after tendon or ligament injury or surgery
Serial casting for clubfoot or contracture
contraindications: Acute fracture with marked or expected swelling (use a backslab first)
Open wound needing regular inspection without a window
Suspected compartment syndrome
equipment: Plaster of Paris or fibreglass rolls of suitable width
Plaster scissors or cast saw for trimming
steps: Confirm patient identity, limb and indication and explain the procedure.
Inspect the skin and document distal neurovascular status.
Position the limb in the required position, with an assistant holding it.
Apply stockinette and two to three layers of padding evenly, with extra over bony prominences.
Dip the plaster roll in lukewarm water until bubbling stops and squeeze gently.
Roll the plaster on smoothly with half overlap, without tension or reverse folds.
Fold back the stockinette at the ends and incorporate it for smooth edges.
Mould the cast with the palms (not fingertips) to hold position as it sets.
Trim the edges to allow full movement of fingers or toes and uninvolved joints.
Check the cast is not tight and re-examine distal circulation, sensation and movement.
Check X-ray if the cast holds a reduced fracture.
aftercare: Keep the limb elevated for the first 48-72 hours.
Keep the cast dry and do not insert objects under it.
Move fingers or toes and free joints often.
Review in clinic as planned, usually within 1-2 weeks for fractures.
red_flags: Severe or increasing pain, numbness, tingling or colour change in fingers or toes.
Swelling that does not settle with elevation.
Burning or rubbing under the cast, foul smell or discharge.
Cast cracked, soft or loose.

indications: Acute fracture with swelling expected
Temporary immobilisation before definitive treatment or referral
Soft tissue injury needing rest
After reduction where swelling is likely
contraindications: Suspected compartment syndrome without senior review
Open wound not yet dressed
equipment: Plaster of Paris rolls or slab of suitable width
Tape measure or the uninjured limb as template
steps: Confirm patient identity, limb and indication and explain the procedure.
Inspect the skin and document distal neurovascular status.
Measure the slab length against the uninjured limb and lay out 8-12 layers of plaster.
Apply padding over the limb with extra padding over bony prominences.
Wet the slab, squeeze out excess water and smooth the layers together.
Place the slab on the correct surface of the limb, covering at least half the circumference.
Hold the slab in place with a bandage applied without tension.
Mould the slab to hold the limb in the required position as it sets.
Re-examine distal circulation, sensation and movement.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and move free fingers or toes often.
Keep the slab dry.
Loosen the bandage if fingers or toes swell or go numb.
Attend fracture clinic for definitive cast or further treatment, usually within 1 week.
red_flags: Increasing pain or pain on moving fingers or toes.
Numbness, pale or blue fingers or toes.
Slab broken or slipping.

indications: End of planned immobilisation
Cast too tight, damaged, wet or soiled
Suspected pressure sore, infection or compartment syndrome under the cast
contraindications: Fracture not yet healed clinically or radiologically when removal is routine (re-check plan)
equipment: Oscillating cast saw with sharp blade, or plaster shears for manual removal
Gloves, eye protection and dust mask
Water or vinegar to soften plaster for manual removal
steps: Confirm patient identity and that removal is planned or indicated.
Explain the noise and vibration of the saw and reassure, especially children.
Mark cutting lines along both sides of the cast, avoiding bony prominences.
Cut with an up-and-down motion of the saw, never dragging the blade along the skin.
Check blade temperature often and pause to let it cool.
Open the cast with the spreader and cut the padding with blunt scissors.
Remove the cast gently while supporting the limb.
Inspect the skin for sores, burns, cuts or infection and document findings.
Assess the limb clinically and arrange X-ray if fracture union is to be checked.
aftercare: Wash the skin gently and apply moisturiser; do not scratch.
Expect stiffness and mild swelling; start gentle range-of-motion exercises.
Refer to physiotherapy if stiffness is marked.
Avoid high-impact or contact activity until cleared.
red_flags: Skin burn, cut or pressure sore found.
Pain or tenderness at the fracture site suggesting non-union.
Rapidly increasing swelling, calf pain or breathlessness.

indications: Temporary immobilisation of a femoral fracture awaiting surgery (benefit for hip fracture pain is limited; use a nerve block where available)
Femoral shaft fracture in a child under 2 years and light enough for the frame (Gallows traction)
Femoral shaft fracture in older children where surgery is not available
Reduction of hip or knee flexion contracture
contraindications: Skin wounds, ulcers, dermatitis or fragile skin at the application site
Peripheral vascular disease or diabetic neuropathy of the limb
Need for traction weight greater than skin can tolerate (use skeletal traction)
equipment: Skin traction kit or adhesive strapping with spreader bar
Traction cord, pulley and weights (or water-filled containers)
Bed blocks or frame to elevate the foot of the bed
steps: Confirm patient identity, limb, indication and verbal consent.
Inspect and clean the skin and document distal neurovascular status.
Pad the malleoli and any bony prominences.
Apply the traction strips to the medial and lateral sides of the limb, leaving a loop beyond the foot.
Secure the strips with a crepe bandage from ankle upwards without excess tension.
Attach the spreader bar and cord and pass the cord over the pulley.
Attach the weight set by the surgeon, usually about one-tenth of body weight in a child and in adults no more than the skin tolerates (about 4-5 kg).
For Gallows traction, suspend both legs vertically so the buttocks just clear the bed.
Elevate the foot of the bed to provide counter-traction.
Re-check distal circulation, sensation and movement after setting up.
aftercare: Check circulation, skin and bandage every 4 hours and reapply the bandage daily.
Ensure weights hang freely and do not rest on the floor or bed.
Pressure area care, chest physiotherapy and calf exercises for adults.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
red_flags: Pale, cold or numb toes or loss of foot movement.
Skin blistering or sores under the strapping.
Pain over the common peroneal nerve or foot drop.
Calf swelling or breathlessness.

indications: Femoral shaft fracture where surgical fixation is delayed or unavailable
Acetabular fracture or central hip dislocation
Unstable pelvic or femoral fractures needing more weight than skin tolerates
Tibial fracture needing traction (calcaneal pin)
contraindications: Infection or open wound at the pin site
Fracture or ligament injury involving the pin site bone or knee
Open proximal tibial physis in young children (choose a site away from the growth plate)
equipment: Steinmann or Denham pin and hand drill or T-handle chuck
Skin antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Cord, pulleys, weights and Thomas or Braun frame
steps: Confirm patient identity, limb, pin site and written consent.
Mark the pin site, usually about 2.5 cm below and behind the tibial tuberosity, entering from the lateral side to avoid the peroneal nerve.
For a distal femoral pin, enter from the medial side to avoid the femoral vessels.
Perform hand hygiene, wear sterile gloves and gown, clean and drape the site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the periosteum on both sides.
Make a small stab incision and insert the pin perpendicular to the long axis of the limb, parallel to the knee joint.
Drill or hand-insert the pin through both cortices until it tents the skin on the other side, then make a stab incision to let it out.
Ensure the pin protrudes equally on both sides and the skin is not tethered.
Apply pin site dressings, attach the stirrup and cap the sharp ends.
Set up the cord, pulleys and frame and apply a weight of about one-seventh to one-tenth of body weight.
Elevate the foot of the bed and check distal neurovascular status.
Obtain a check X-ray once traction is established.
aftercare: Daily pin site care and look for discharge or redness.
Check alignment and leg length with X-ray in the first week and adjust weight.
Quadriceps, ankle and breathing exercises; pressure area care.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
red_flags: Pin site discharge, spreading redness or fever.
Foot drop or numbness on the top of the foot.
Pin loosening or sliding.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.

indications: Femoral shaft fracture for pain relief and transport
Definitive treatment of femoral shaft fracture with traction where surgery is unavailable
contraindications: Hip, pelvic or knee fractures (splint not effective)
