Injury to the groin or perineum where the ring would press
Ankle or foot injury that prevents skin traction (use skeletal traction)
equipment: Thomas splint with ring sized to the thigh and length to the uninjured leg
Skin traction kit or skeletal traction pin
Calico or crepe slings to support the limb
Windlass stick or traction cord and weights
Bed blocks and Balkan beam if used in ward traction
steps: Confirm patient identity, limb and indication and explain the procedure.
Give adequate analgesia or nerve block before handling the limb.
Measure the ring size at the upper thigh and the splint length on the uninjured leg.
Apply skin traction strips or confirm skeletal pin is in place.
Prepare the splint with slings across the bars to support the thigh and calf.
With gentle manual traction, slide the splint up the leg until the ring sits against the ischial tuberosity.
Tie the traction cords to the end of the splint and tighten with a windlass, or attach to weights for sliding traction.
Place padding under the fracture to restore the anterior bow of the femur.
Secure the limb in the splint with bandages without compressing the calf or peroneal nerve.
Check distal neurovascular status and obtain a check X-ray.
aftercare: Check the ring and groin skin every shift and keep it clean and dry.
Adjust traction and slings to maintain alignment.
Pressure area care, quadriceps and ankle exercises.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
red_flags: Pressure sore at the groin, ischium or heel.
Numbness or weakness of the foot.
Pale, cold or swollen foot.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.

indications: Support of the arm after shoulder, clavicle, humerus, elbow or forearm injury
Elevation of the hand or forearm to reduce swelling
Proximal or shaft humeral fracture (collar and cuff to allow gravity traction)
Support after upper limb surgery or cast application
contraindications: Collar and cuff for unstable supracondylar fracture where elbow flexion compromises circulation
steps: Confirm patient identity and indication and explain the purpose.
Check distal circulation and sensation of the hand.
Support the injured arm across the chest at the required elbow angle.
For a broad arm sling, place the triangle under the arm and tie the ends at the side of the neck over padding.
For a high arm sling, keep the hand raised towards the opposite shoulder.
For a collar and cuff, loop the strap around the wrist and neck so the elbow hangs free.
Ensure the fingertips remain visible and the knot does not press on the spine or neck.
Re-check hand circulation and teach the patient how to remove and reapply it.
aftercare: Remove for washing as advised and move fingers, wrist and shoulder as instructed.
Sleep semi-upright for humeral fractures.
Attend follow-up as planned.
red_flags: Fingers becoming numb, cold, pale or blue.
Neck skin soreness from the strap.
Increasing pain or deformity.

indications: Clavicle shaft fracture where the patient prefers it to a sling for comfort
Birth or childhood clavicle fracture needing support (sling usually preferred)
contraindications: Open clavicle fracture or skin tenting
Neurovascular injury to the arm
Displaced fracture needing surgical fixation
equipment: Commercial figure-of-eight clavicle brace or padded stockinette
steps: Confirm patient identity and indication and check the arm for neurovascular injury.
Explain that a sling gives similar results and the brace is for comfort.
Sit the patient upright with hands on hips and shoulders braced back.
Pad both axillae well.
Pass the bandage around the front of one shoulder, through the axilla, across the back and around the other shoulder.
Tighten enough to brace the shoulders without compressing the axillae.
Secure the bandage at the back and check radial pulses and hand sensation on both sides.
Teach the patient how to check and adjust it.
aftercare: Check the axillae daily for soreness and the hands for tingling.
Tighten the bandage as it loosens over the first days.
Use for about 2-4 weeks, then start gentle shoulder movement.
red_flags: Tingling, numbness or swelling of the hands.
Skin breakdown in the axillae.
Skin over the fracture becoming tight or broken.

indications: Displaced intra-articular fracture
Unstable fracture not controllable by closed means
Forearm shaft fractures in adults
Failed closed reduction or loss of reduction
Fracture with vascular injury needing stable fixation
contraindications: Active infection at the operative site
Severe soft tissue swelling or blisters (delay surgery)
Patient unfit for anaesthesia
Lack of required implants, image intensifier or sterile instruments
equipment: Full orthopaedic set and sterile drapes
Implants (plates, screws) of appropriate system with complete sizes
Drill, drill bits, taps, depth gauge and screwdriver
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, implant availability and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol before skin incision or tourniquet inflation.
Position the patient, apply a tourniquet if used, prepare and drape the limb.
Expose the fracture through a standard approach, protecting nerves and vessels.
Clean the fracture ends of haematoma and soft tissue while preserving periosteal blood supply.
Reduce the fracture anatomically for articular fractures and restore length, alignment and rotation for shaft fractures.
Hold the reduction with clamps or K-wires.
Apply lag screws and a plate of suitable length using correct drilling, measuring and tapping technique.
Confirm reduction, implant position and screw lengths with image intensifier or X-ray.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and irrigate the wound.
Close in layers with a drain if needed and apply a sterile dressing and splint.
Check and document distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and give analgesia per local protocol.
Post-operative X-ray in two planes.
Wound check at 48 hours and suture removal at 10-14 days.
Physiotherapy and weight-bearing plan as instructed by the surgeon.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for lower limb surgery in adults.
red_flags: Fever, wound redness, discharge or wound breakdown.
Pain out of proportion or on passive stretch suggesting compartment syndrome.
New numbness or weakness.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.

indications: Femoral or tibial shaft fracture in adults
Humeral shaft fracture where operative fixation is indicated
Pathological or impending fracture of a long bone
Paediatric femoral fracture in older children (flexible nails)
contraindications: Active infection or contaminated wound not yet debrided
Open physes for rigid nails (use flexible nails in children)
Medullary canal too narrow or deformed
Patient unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Nail system (e.g. SIGN) with nails of suitable length and diameter and locking screws
Fracture table or manual traction team
Image intensifier if available (SIGN technique allows nailing without it)
Full orthopaedic set and sterile drapes
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, nail sizes available and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol before incision.
Position the patient supine or lateral with traction, prepare and drape the limb.
Make the entry incision and open the canal at the correct entry point with an awl.
Reduce the fracture closed or through a small open incision.
Pass the guide wire or reamer across the fracture into the distal fragment.
Ream the canal progressively until the chosen nail diameter fits.
Measure and insert the nail of correct length across the fracture.
Insert proximal and distal locking screws using the targeting device or freehand technique.
Check length, alignment and rotation clinically against the other leg.
Confirm nail and screw position with image intensifier or X-ray.
Irrigate and close the wounds and apply sterile dressings.
Check and document distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Early mobilisation and weight-bearing as instructed by the surgeon.
Post-operative X-ray in two planes.
Watch for fat embolism in the first 72 hours after femoral nailing.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
Wound check and suture removal at 10-14 days.
red_flags: Breathlessness, confusion or petechial rash suggesting fat embolism.
Severe pain or tight swelling of the leg suggesting compartment syndrome.
Wound discharge, fever or redness.
Limb shortening or rotation deformity noted on walking.

name: Closed reduction and percutaneous K-wire fixation

indications: Displaced supracondylar humerus fracture in children
Unstable distal radius fracture
Metacarpal or phalangeal fractures
Paediatric fractures that will not hold in a cast
contraindications: Open fracture needing debridement
Failure of closed reduction (convert to open reduction)
No image intensifier for fractures where wire position cannot be confirmed
equipment: K-wires of suitable diameter and wire driver or hand drill
Wire cutter and bender and wire caps
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Document pre-operative neurovascular status, including radial pulse and nerve function.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol, then under anaesthesia prepare and drape the limb.
Reduce the fracture by traction and manipulation and confirm with image intensifier.
Insert K-wires percutaneously in a pattern that gives stable fixation, avoiding known nerve paths.
For medial wires at the elbow, make a small incision and protect the ulnar nerve.
Confirm reduction and wire position in two planes and test stability.
Bend and cut the wires outside the skin or bury them, and dress the pin sites.
Apply a backslab or cast in a position that does not compromise circulation.
Re-check and document distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Elevate and monitor circulation closely for the first 24 hours.
Pin site care and keep the cast dry.
X-ray at about 1 week and remove wires usually at 3-6 weeks.
Start range-of-motion exercises after wire removal.
red_flags: Absent radial pulse with a cold or pale hand.
Pain on passive finger extension or increasing pain suggesting compartment syndrome.
New numbness or weakness in the hand.
Pin site discharge or fever.

indications: Open fracture with soft tissue injury (Gustilo II-III)
Damage control fixation in the polytrauma patient
Pelvic fracture with haemodynamic instability
Infected fracture or non-union
Temporary spanning fixation of periarticular fractures
contraindications: Infection at planned pin sites
Patient unfit for anaesthesia (consider splint and resuscitation first)
equipment: External fixator set (pins, clamps, rods or tubes)
Power or hand drill and drill sleeve
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and debride open wounds first if present.
Plan pin sites away from the zone of injury, joints and neurovascular structures.
Make stab incisions, spread to bone and insert two or more pins in each main fragment through a drill sleeve.
Confirm pins engage both cortices without excessive protrusion.
Reduce the fracture, restoring length, alignment and rotation.
Connect pins with clamps and rods, keeping rods a hand's breadth from the skin to allow swelling and wound care.
Tighten all clamps and check stability.
Confirm alignment with image intensifier or X-ray.
Release skin tension around pins and dress pin sites and wounds.
Check and document distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Daily pin site care per local protocol.
Elevate the limb and start joint exercises as allowed.
Plan wound coverage and definitive fixation if the fixator is temporary.
Check clamp tightness at each review.
red_flags: Pin site redness, pus, pain or loosening.
Fever or wound breakdown.
Loose frame or loss of alignment.
New numbness, weakness or circulation problems.

indications: Infected non-union or bone defect needing bone transport
Limb lengthening or deformity correction
Complex tibial plateau or pilon fractures
Neglected clubfoot or other complex deformity
contraindications: Patient or family unable to manage long frame treatment and follow-up
Severe uncontrolled systemic disease
Inadequate soft tissue or vascular supply for wire placement
equipment: Ilizarov rings, rods, wire fixation bolts and hinges as planned
Tensioned wires, half pins and wire tensioner
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, frame plan and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and prepare and drape the limb.
Mount the pre-built frame around the limb centred on the bone.
Insert reference wires at the proximal and distal rings in safe corridors, avoiding nerves and vessels.
Tension the wires and fix them to the rings.
Add further wires and half pins to each ring for stability.
Perform osteotomy (corticotomy) if lengthening or bone transport is planned.
Adjust the frame to correct alignment and confirm with image intensifier.
Tighten all connections and check joints move freely where required.
Dress pin and wire sites and check distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Daily pin and wire site care and teach the family to do it.
Start distraction after the latency period per the surgeon's schedule.
Physiotherapy to prevent joint contracture.
Regular clinic review with X-ray to check regenerate and alignment.
red_flags: Pin or wire site infection, loosening or broken wire.
Numbness, tingling or weakness during lengthening.
Joint stiffness or contracture developing.
Fever or severe pain.

indications: Displaced transverse olecranon fracture
Displaced transverse patella fracture
Medial malleolus or greater tuberosity avulsion fractures
contraindications: Comminuted fracture where the wire would collapse the joint surface (use plating)
Active infection at the site
Patient unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Stainless steel cerclage wire and wire tightener
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and apply the tourniquet.
Expose the fracture through a longitudinal incision and clear the fracture ends.
Reduce the fracture anatomically and hold with a clamp.
Insert two parallel K-wires across the fracture.
Drill a transverse hole in the distal fragment or pass the wire under the tendon insertion.
Pass the cerclage wire in a figure-of-eight around the K-wire ends over the tension surface.
Tighten the wire evenly to compress the fracture.
Bend and impact the K-wire ends to prevent backing out.
Check reduction and stability through a range of motion and with imaging.
Close in layers and apply a dressing and splint.
aftercare: Early gentle range-of-motion exercises as advised by the surgeon.
Post-operative X-ray.
Wound check and suture removal at 10-14 days.
Warn the patient that wires may irritate and may need removal later.
red_flags: Wound discharge or fever.
Wire ends felt under the skin or poking through.
Loss of extension or sudden pain suggesting fixation failure.

indications: Stable intertrochanteric (extracapsular) hip fracture
Basicervical femoral neck fracture
contraindications: Reverse oblique or subtrochanteric fracture (use an intramedullary device)
Displaced intracapsular fracture in an older patient (consider arthroplasty)
Patient unfit for anaesthesia after optimisation
equipment: DHS set with guide wire, triple reamer, tap, lag screw and side plate
Full orthopaedic set and sterile drapes
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position on the fracture table and reduce the fracture by traction and internal rotation, confirming with image intensifier.
Prepare and drape and make a lateral incision over the proximal femur.
Insert the guide wire through the angle guide into the femoral head, centre-centre on both views.
Measure, ream and tap to the chosen depth, keeping a tip-apex distance under 25 mm.
Insert the lag screw and side plate and seat the plate on the femoral shaft.
Fix the plate to the shaft with cortical screws and apply a compression screw if used.
Confirm final position on image intensifier in two planes.
Irrigate, close in layers and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Mobilise full weight-bearing as tolerated from day 1 unless told otherwise.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Check haemoglobin and watch for delirium.
Falls and bone health assessment.
red_flags: Sudden pain or shortening suggesting fixation failure.
Wound discharge or fever.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.
New confusion.

name: Cannulated screw fixation of femoral neck

indications: Undisplaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture
Displaced femoral neck fracture in a young adult (urgent reduction and fixation)
contraindications: Displaced intracapsular fracture in an older patient (arthroplasty preferred)
Pathological fracture or established arthritis of the hip
Patient unfit for anaesthesia after optimisation
equipment: Cannulated screw set with guide wires and parallel guide
Sterile drapes and basic orthopaedic set
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position on the fracture table and reduce the fracture if displaced, confirming with image intensifier.
Prepare and drape and make a small lateral incision.
Insert three parallel guide wires in an inverted triangle, the lowest along the calcar.
Confirm wire positions on both views without breaching the joint.
Measure, drill and insert cannulated screws of correct length over the wires.
Confirm screw position and compression on final images.
Close the wound and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Weight-bearing as instructed by the surgeon.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Follow-up X-rays to watch for non-union or avascular necrosis.
red_flags: Groin pain or limp increasing over weeks or months suggesting avascular necrosis or non-union.
Wound discharge or fever.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.

indications: Infected implant
Prominent or painful implant after fracture union
Broken implant or non-union needing revision
Implant in a growing child where removal is planned
Removal of K-wires or external fixator pins
contraindications: Fracture not yet united when removal is elective
Routine removal where risks outweigh benefit (asymptomatic adult implants)
equipment: Correct screwdrivers and extraction set for the implant system
Nail extractor and slap hammer for nails
Sterile drapes and basic orthopaedic set
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, implant type from records and X-ray, and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Confirm the correct removal instruments are available before anaesthesia.
Prepare and drape and use the previous incision where possible.
Expose the implant, clearing bone and soft tissue from screw heads.
Remove screws, then the plate, or remove locking screws and extract the nail.
Use the extraction set for stripped or broken screws.
Send tissue and implant swabs for culture if infection is suspected.
Debride and irrigate infected tissue.
Confirm complete removal with imaging if available.
Close the wound and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Protect the limb from heavy impact for about 6 weeks as screw holes fill.
Wound check and suture removal at 10-14 days.
Antibiotics guided by culture if infected.
red_flags: New pain after a fall suggesting refracture.
Wound discharge or fever.
New numbness or weakness.

indications: Any open fracture
Contaminated wound communicating with bone or joint
Repeat debridement of an open fracture wound
contraindications: None absolute; resuscitate and stabilise life-threatening injuries first
equipment: Large volumes of sterile normal saline (clean drinkable water if saline unavailable)
Debridement set with scalpels, curettes, rongeurs and scissors
Specimen containers if infection is present
steps: Give antibiotics per local protocol as soon as possible after injury and check tetanus status.
Photograph the wound if possible, cover with a saline-soaked dressing and splint the limb.
Confirm patient identity, side, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Wash the limb with soap and water, then prepare and drape.
Extend the wound along the limb axis as needed to see the full zone of injury.
Excise devitalised skin, fat, fascia and non-contractile or non-bleeding muscle.
Remove loose bone fragments without soft tissue attachment and all foreign material.
Irrigate with large volumes of saline at low pressure.
Stabilise the fracture with splint, traction or external fixator.
Leave the wound open or loosely closed and plan a second look in 48-72 hours.
Document the wound size, contamination and Gustilo grade.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and monitor neurovascular status.
Continue antibiotics per local protocol.
Return to theatre for second look and plan soft tissue cover early.
Analgesia and nutrition support.
red_flags: Fever, foul smell or spreading redness.
Crepitus or grey discharge suggesting gas gangrene.
Pain on passive stretch suggesting compartment syndrome.
Cold or pulseless limb.

indications: Displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture in an older or low-demand patient
Femoral head avascular necrosis in low-demand patients
contraindications: Active infection
Pre-existing significant hip arthritis (consider total hip replacement)
Patient unfit for anaesthesia after optimisation
equipment: Prosthesis (Austin Moore, Thompson, modular unipolar or bipolar) in a range of sizes
Head extractor, rasps and trial heads
Bone cement and cement gun if a cemented stem is used
Hip retractors and full orthopaedic set
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, prosthesis sizes and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position lateral, prepare and drape.
Approach the hip through a posterior or lateral approach, protecting the sciatic nerve.
Open the capsule, cut the femoral neck to the planned level and remove the head.
Measure the head diameter and trial the head size in the acetabulum.
Prepare the femoral canal with rasps.
Warn the anaesthetist before cementing, then insert the stem, cemented or uncemented, with correct version.
Reduce the hip and check stability, leg length and range of motion.
Repair the capsule and short external rotators where possible.
Close in layers with or without a drain and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Mobilise with physiotherapy from day 1 if possible.
Follow hip precautions advised for the approach used.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Check haemoglobin, watch for delirium and assess bone health.
red_flags: Sudden pain, shortening or rotation of the leg suggesting dislocation.
Wound discharge, redness or fever.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.
Drop in oxygen saturation or blood pressure during cementing.

indications: Severe hip osteoarthritis or inflammatory arthritis with pain and loss of function
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head with collapse (including sickle cell disease)
Displaced femoral neck fracture in a fit, active patient
contraindications: Active local or systemic infection
Neuropathic joint or severe neuromuscular disease
Patient unfit for major surgery
Lack of implants, sterile theatre conditions or post-operative rehabilitation
equipment: Total hip system with acetabular cup, liner, femoral stem and head in a range of sizes
Acetabular reamers, femoral rasps and trials
Bone cement and cement gun if cemented
Hip retractors and full orthopaedic set
Laminar flow or clean-air theatre where available
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, implant availability and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and an antifibrinolytic per local protocol if used.
Position lateral, prepare and drape with strict asepsis.
Approach the hip, release the capsule and dislocate the hip.
Cut the femoral neck at the planned level.
Ream the acetabulum to bleeding subchondral bone and insert the cup in correct inclination and version.
Prepare the femoral canal with rasps and trial the components.
Check stability, leg length and range of motion with trials.
Warn the anaesthetist before cementing, then insert the definitive stem and head, cemented or uncemented.
Reduce the hip and recheck stability and leg length.
Repair the capsule and external rotators and close in layers.
Apply a dressing and check distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Mobilise with physiotherapy from day 1.
Follow hip precautions for the approach used.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Post-operative X-ray and follow-up at 6 weeks.
red_flags: Sudden pain, shortening or rotation of the leg suggesting dislocation.
Wound discharge, redness or fever.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.
Foot drop or numbness of the foot.

indications: Severe knee osteoarthritis or inflammatory arthritis with pain and loss of function despite non-operative care
Post-traumatic arthritis of the knee
contraindications: Active local or systemic infection
Non-functioning extensor mechanism
Severe peripheral vascular disease of the limb
Patient unfit for major surgery
equipment: Total knee system with femoral, tibial and patellar components and trials in a range of sizes
Cutting jigs, alignment guides and oscillating saw
Knee retractors and full orthopaedic set
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent, implant availability and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and an antifibrinolytic per local protocol if used.
Apply a thigh tourniquet, prepare and drape with strict asepsis.
Expose the knee through a midline incision and medial parapatellar arthrotomy.
Make the distal femoral and proximal tibial cuts using alignment guides.
Balance the flexion and extension gaps with soft tissue releases as needed.
Size and finish the femoral cuts and prepare the tibia.
Trial the components and check alignment, stability and patellar tracking.
Cement the definitive components and remove excess cement.
Resurface the patella if planned.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close in layers.
Apply a compression dressing and check distal neurovascular status.
aftercare: Mobilise and start knee bending with physiotherapy from day 1.
Aim for full extension and progressive flexion.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol.
Post-operative X-ray and follow-up at 6 weeks.
red_flags: Wound discharge, redness, increasing pain or fever.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.
Foot drop or numbness.
Knee stuck and not bending despite physiotherapy.

indications: Anterior shoulder dislocation confirmed clinically and on X-ray
Posterior shoulder dislocation
contraindications: Associated displaced fracture of the humeral neck (refer for reduction under general anaesthesia)
Dislocation older than about 3 weeks (refer)
Unstable patient with other priorities
equipment: Analgesia, sedation and monitoring equipment as needed
Broad arm sling or shoulder immobiliser
steps: Confirm patient identity and side, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Review the X-ray to confirm the direction of dislocation and exclude fracture.
Examine and document axillary nerve (regimental badge area sensation) and distal neurovascular status.
Give analgesia, intra-articular local anaesthetic or procedural sedation with monitoring.
For anterior dislocation choose a gentle method such as external rotation, FARES, Cunningham or traction-countertraction.
Avoid Kocher and Hippocratic methods where possible because of the higher risk of fracture and nerve injury.
For posterior dislocation use in-line traction with gentle internal rotation, never external rotation, and refer if it does not reduce.
Apply gentle, slow, steady movement and avoid sudden force or leverage.
Feel for a clunk and confirm restored shoulder contour and range of motion.
Place the arm in a sling or immobiliser.
Re-examine and document axillary nerve and distal neurovascular status.
Obtain a post-reduction X-ray.
aftercare: Sling for comfort for 1-3 weeks depending on age.
Start gentle pendulum exercises and refer to physiotherapy.
Avoid abduction and external rotation for several weeks.
Follow up in fracture clinic, especially young patients at risk of recurrence.
red_flags: Numbness over the shoulder or arm weakness.
Cold or pale hand.
Repeat dislocation.
Failed reduction after two attempts (refer for general anaesthesia).

indications: Posterior or posterolateral elbow dislocation confirmed on X-ray
contraindications: Associated fracture needing open reduction (complex dislocation, refer)
Absent pulse not restored by gentle reduction (urgent vascular review)
steps: Confirm patient identity and side, explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Review the X-ray and look for associated fractures, including the medial epicondyle in children.
Examine and document radial pulse and median, ulnar and radial nerve function.
Give procedural sedation or analgesia with monitoring.
Apply gentle in-line traction on the forearm with counter-traction on the upper arm.
Correct any medial or lateral displacement first.
Push the olecranon forwards with the thumbs while flexing the elbow until it reduces.
Test stability through flexion and extension and note the angle at which it re-dislocates.
Apply an above-elbow backslab at about 90 degrees and a sling.
Re-examine neurovascular status and obtain a post-reduction X-ray.
aftercare: Elevate and monitor circulation for swelling.
Begin gentle movement within 1-2 weeks to avoid stiffness.
Fracture clinic review within 1 week.
red_flags: Absent radial pulse, cold or pale hand.
Numbness or weakness in the hand.
Increasing forearm pain or tight swelling.
Repeat dislocation.

indications: Traumatic native hip dislocation (reduce within 6 hours to reduce avascular necrosis risk)
Dislocated hip prosthesis
contraindications: Associated femoral neck fracture (needs open reduction and fixation)
Irreducible dislocation after appropriate attempts (proceed to open reduction)
equipment: Pre-reduction X-ray of pelvis and hip
Procedural sedation or general anaesthesia with full monitoring
steps: Confirm patient identity, side and consent and complete a pre-procedure check.
Review X-rays to confirm direction and exclude femoral neck fracture.
Examine and document sciatic nerve function and distal pulses.
Give deep sedation with muscle relaxation or general anaesthesia with monitoring.
Have an assistant stabilise the pelvis by pressing down on both anterior superior iliac spines.
For posterior dislocation, flex the hip and knee to 90 degrees and apply steady upward traction with gentle rotation, never sudden force or leverage and with a limited number of attempts.
Feel for a clunk and check the hip moves freely.
Test stability gently in flexion.
Re-examine sciatic nerve function and distal pulses.
Obtain post-reduction X-ray and arrange CT if fragments or acetabular fracture are suspected.
aftercare: Bed rest or protected weight-bearing as advised by the orthopaedic team.
Keep knee immobiliser or abduction pillow to avoid flexion and adduction.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
Follow-up imaging to watch for avascular necrosis.
red_flags: Foot drop or numbness suggesting sciatic nerve injury.
Re-dislocation or leg shortening.
Groin pain or limp developing over months.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.

indications: Lateral patellar dislocation with the knee locked in flexion
contraindications: Intra-articular or intercondylar patellar dislocation (refer)
Associated displaced fracture needing surgery
equipment: Analgesia such as inhaled or IV analgesia, or sedation with monitoring
steps: Confirm patient identity and side, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Check distal neurovascular status.
Give analgesia or sedation as needed.
Flex the hip to relax the quadriceps.
Slowly extend the knee while pushing the patella gently medially.
Confirm the patella has reduced and the knee extends fully.
Check for a haemarthrosis and test patellar stability gently.
Apply a knee splint or cylinder backslab in extension.
Obtain X-rays after reduction to look for osteochondral fracture.
aftercare: Walk with crutches, weight-bearing as tolerated in the splint.
Physiotherapy for quadriceps strengthening.
Review in fracture clinic within 1-2 weeks.
red_flags: Knee locking or giving way repeatedly.
Large tense swelling.
Osteochondral fragment on X-ray (refer).

indications: Dorsal interphalangeal joint dislocation
Simple metacarpophalangeal joint dislocation
Thumb interphalangeal or metacarpophalangeal dislocation
contraindications: Complex MCP dislocation with volar plate entrapment (dimpled skin, needs open reduction)
Open dislocation needing washout
Large intra-articular fracture fragment
equipment: Local anaesthetic for digital block, syringe and fine needle
Aluminium finger splint or buddy-strapping tape
steps: Confirm patient identity, finger and side, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Review the X-ray and check for fracture.
Check and document digital sensation and capillary refill.
Perform a digital nerve block with local anaesthetic.
For an interphalangeal joint, apply gentle longitudinal traction, exaggerate the deformity slightly, then push the base of the distal bone back into place.
For an MCP joint, avoid strong traction (it can trap the volar plate); flex the wrist, push the base of the proximal phalanx over the metacarpal head, and refer if it does not reduce easily.
Check full active and passive movement and joint stability.
Re-check digital sensation and capillary refill.
Buddy-strap or splint the finger as appropriate.
Obtain a post-reduction X-ray.
aftercare: Buddy strapping for 2-3 weeks with early movement.
Elevate the hand to reduce swelling.
Hand therapy referral if stiffness persists.
red_flags: Finger pale, cold or numb.
Joint re-dislocates or will not straighten.
Increasing swelling or wound infection.

indications: Clinical acute compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment)
Raised compartment pressure where measurement is available
Prophylactic after revascularisation of a prolonged ischaemic limb
contraindications: Established compartment syndrome with dead muscle and late presentation, where amputation may be safer (senior decision)
equipment: Major set with scalpel, scissors and retractors
Sterile saline-soaked dressings or negative pressure dressing
steps: Recognise compartment syndrome clinically and remove all circumferential casts and dressings to skin immediately.
Keep the limb at heart level, not elevated, and call the senior surgeon urgently.
Confirm patient identity, side, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
For the leg, make two long incisions (anterolateral and posteromedial) to release all four compartments.
For the forearm, make a volar curvilinear incision and release the carpal tunnel and dorsal compartment if needed.
Divide the fascia along the full length of each compartment.
Inspect the muscle for colour, contraction, consistency and bleeding.
Excise clearly dead muscle.
Stabilise any associated fracture.
Leave the wounds open and apply bulky dressings without constriction.
Plan return to theatre in 48-72 hours for re-inspection and delayed closure or grafting.
aftercare: Monitor urine output and kidney function for rhabdomyolysis.
Keep the wounds covered and return to theatre for second look.
Splint the limb in a functional position.
Analgesia per local protocol.
red_flags: Dark urine or falling urine output.
Persistent pain or tense compartments after release.
Wound infection or foul smell.
Signs of sepsis.

indications: Unsalvageable limb trauma
Diabetic foot sepsis or gangrene not controllable by local surgery
Critical limb ischaemia with gangrene
Malignant tumour of the foot or ankle
contraindications: Gangrene or infection extending above the planned level (choose a higher level)
Fixed knee flexion contracture that would prevent prosthetic use
equipment: Amputation set with amputation knife, saw (Gigli or power), bone file and rongeurs
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and apply a tourniquet unless ischaemic.
Mark a long posterior myocutaneous flap, with the bone cut about 12-15 cm below the knee joint line.
Incise skin and fascia and divide the anterior and lateral compartment muscles.
Identify, ligate and divide the anterior tibial, posterior tibial and peroneal vessels.
Pull the nerves gently, divide them sharply and let them retract.
Divide the tibia and bevel its anterior edge, then divide the fibula 1-2 cm shorter.
Shape the posterior flap and remove the limb, then label it and handle it per hospital policy and the family's wishes.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and irrigate.
Close the fascia and skin over a drain without tension, or leave open if infected.
Apply a stump dressing and keep the knee extended.
aftercare: Keep the knee straight; avoid pillows under the knee to prevent contracture.
Wound check at 48 hours and remove sutures at 2-3 weeks.
Early physiotherapy, stump shaping and prosthesis referral.
Control diabetes and treat infection per culture.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
red_flags: Wound discharge, dusky flap or wound breakdown.
Fever or signs of sepsis.
Bleeding soaking the dressing.
Severe phantom or stump pain not controlled.

indications: Unsalvageable limb where below-knee amputation is not possible
Gangrene or infection extending above the knee
Knee flexion contracture or non-ambulant patient
Malignant tumour of the lower leg or knee
contraindications: Viable tissue allows a lower amputation level with better function
equipment: Amputation set with amputation knife, saw (Gigli or power), bone file and rongeurs
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Mark equal anterior and posterior fish-mouth flaps, aiming for as long a femur as possible.
Incise skin and fascia and divide the muscles.
Identify, ligate (double for the femoral artery) and divide the femoral vessels.
Pull the sciatic nerve gently, ligate and divide it sharply so it retracts.
Divide the femur, remove the limb and label it for handling per hospital policy and the family's wishes, then smooth the bone edges.
Perform myodesis or myoplasty of the adductors to the femur where possible.
Achieve haemostasis and irrigate.
Close the fascia and skin over a drain without tension, or leave open if infected.
Apply a stump dressing.
aftercare: Lie prone for periods daily to prevent hip flexion contracture.
Wound check at 48 hours and remove sutures at 2-3 weeks.
Early physiotherapy, transfers training and prosthesis referral.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for adults.
red_flags: Wound discharge, dusky flap or wound breakdown.
Fever or signs of sepsis.
Bleeding soaking the dressing.
Severe phantom or stump pain not controlled.

indications: Gangrene of a toe or finger (diabetic, ischaemic)
Osteomyelitis of a phalanx or metatarsal
Severe crush or traumatic amputation of a digit needing revision
Tumour of a digit
contraindications: Ischaemia or infection extending into the foot or hand beyond the planned level
Adequate blood supply for healing not confirmed in ischaemic limbs
equipment: Minor orthopaedic set with bone nibblers, small saw or bone cutter
Digital or ring block local anaesthetic, or regional anaesthesia
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, digit, site marking, consent and complete the time-out.
Assess circulation and infection extent and confirm the planned level.
Give anaesthesia such as a digital, ankle or wrist block.
Prepare and drape and apply a digital tourniquet if not ischaemic.
Design flaps (often a longer plantar or palmar flap) or a racquet incision for a ray.
Divide the soft tissues, identify and ligate digital vessels, and divide digital nerves sharply so they retract.
Divide the bone at the planned level, removing infected bone, and smooth the ends.
Send bone for culture and histology where infection or tumour is present.
Remove the tourniquet and achieve haemostasis.
Close the skin loosely or leave open if infected.
Apply a dressing.
aftercare: Dressing changes and wound review every 2-3 days.
Offloading footwear for foot wounds in diabetics.
Control blood glucose and treat infection per culture.
Suture removal at 10-14 days.
red_flags: Wound turning black or spreading redness.
Foul discharge or fever.
Pain and swelling spreading into the foot or hand.

indications: Unsalvageable upper limb trauma
Gangrene, for example from tight traditional bone-setter splints or ischaemia
Life-threatening infection such as necrotising fasciitis or gas gangrene
Malignant tumour of the arm
contraindications: Viable tissue allows a lower level with better function (preserve as much length as possible)
equipment: Amputation set with amputation knife, saw (Gigli or power), bone file and rongeurs
steps: Confirm patient identity, side, site marking, consent and complete the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and apply a tourniquet unless ischaemic or infected.
Choose the most distal viable level and mark equal anterior and posterior flaps.
Incise skin and fascia and divide the muscles.
Identify, ligate and divide the main vessels.
Pull nerves gently, divide them sharply and let them retract.
Divide the bone or bones, remove the limb and label it for handling per hospital policy and the family's wishes, then smooth the edges.
Perform myodesis or myoplasty where possible to cover the bone end.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and irrigate.
Close over a drain without tension, or leave open if infected.
Apply a stump dressing.
aftercare: Elevate the stump and mobilise the shoulder and elbow early.
Wound check at 48 hours and suture removal at 2-3 weeks.
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and prosthesis referral.
Psychological support and return-to-work planning.
red_flags: Wound discharge, dusky flap or wound breakdown.
Fever or signs of sepsis.
Bleeding soaking the dressing.
Severe phantom or stump pain not controlled.

indications: Chronic osteomyelitis with radiological sequestrum
Persistent discharging sinus from infected bone
Failure of antibiotic therapy with dead bone present
contraindications: Sequestrum present before an adequate involucrum has formed (risk of fracture or bone loss)
Patient unfit for anaesthesia until anaemia and sepsis are corrected
equipment: Major orthopaedic set with osteotomes, gouges and bone nibblers
Pneumatic or rubber tourniquet if limb site
Specimen pots for culture and histology
Antibiotic beads or cement if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and site, and review current X-rays showing sequestrum and involucrum.
Correct anaemia and ensure blood is grouped and saved or cross-matched.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia, apply a tourniquet if on a limb, and prepare and drape the limb.
Excise the sinus tract and approach the bone through healthy tissue along the line of the sinus or standard approach.
Open a window in the involucrum (cortical window) just large enough to remove the sequestrum.
Remove all sequestra and send samples for culture and histology.
Curette granulation tissue and pus until healthy bleeding bone is seen.
Saucerise the cavity by bevelling the edges so that soft tissue can fall in and dead space is reduced.
Irrigate copiously with saline.
Place antibiotic beads or fill the dead space with muscle if available and appropriate.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis, and close loosely over a drain or leave the wound open for dressings.
Protect the weakened bone with a backslab or cast to reduce the risk of pathological fracture.
aftercare: Elevate the limb and check circulation regularly
Continue antibiotics guided by culture per local protocol
Wound dressing changes as planned
Protected weight bearing until bone has remodelled
Serial X-rays to monitor healing and fracture risk
Nutrition and anaemia correction
red_flags: Fever, spreading redness or pus after surgery
Severe pain or deformity suggesting pathological fracture
Cold, pale or numb limb
Heavy bleeding soaking through dressings

indications: Septic arthritis confirmed or strongly suspected
Pus on joint aspiration
Infected joint failing to settle after aspiration
Contaminated penetrating joint wound
contraindications: Uncorrected shock (resuscitate first, then operate urgently)
equipment: Basic orthopaedic or minor operating set
Large-bore syringe and needle for confirmation aspirate
Several litres of warm saline and irrigation set
Culture bottles and sterile specimen pots
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and joint, and review aspirate results if available.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and position for the standard approach to the joint.
Prepare and drape, and apply a tourniquet if appropriate.
Aspirate the joint first to confirm the entry point and send fluid for Gram stain and culture.
Make the arthrotomy through a standard approach that avoids neurovascular structures.
Take synovial fluid and tissue samples before irrigating.
Break down loculations and remove fibrin and debris.
Irrigate the joint copiously with warm saline until the effluent is clear.
Inspect the cartilage and bone for erosion or adjacent osteomyelitis.
Close the capsule loosely or leave it open and insert a drain if needed.
Close the skin and apply a bulky dressing and splint in a position of function.
Start or continue intravenous antibiotics per local protocol after samples are taken.
aftercare: Elevate and splint the limb for comfort
Intravenous antibiotics then oral according to culture and local protocol
Monitor temperature, pain and inflammatory markers
Remove drain when output is low
Start gentle range-of-motion exercises once pain settles
Plan repeat washout if not improving
red_flags: Persistent fever or worsening pain after 48 hours
Signs of sepsis or shock
Reaccumulation of joint swelling
In children, new limp, deformity or limb-length change at follow-up

indications: Suspected septic arthritis
Suspected crystal arthritis
Diagnosis of unexplained joint effusion
Relief of a tense effusion or haemarthrosis
contraindications: Cellulitis or broken skin over the entry site
Prosthetic joint (refer to orthopaedic team)
Uncorrected severe coagulopathy (relative)
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Position the patient with the joint relaxed (knee extended and supported for knee aspiration).
Identify landmarks or the deepest pocket of fluid with ultrasound and mark the entry site.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the skin widely with antiseptic.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the skin and soft tissues along the track.
Insert the aspiration needle along the planned track, aspirating gently as you advance.
Aspirate fluid, changing syringes with the needle held still if a large volume is present.
Note the volume and appearance of the fluid.
Withdraw the needle and apply pressure and a sterile dressing.
Send fluid promptly for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals as indicated.
aftercare: Rest the joint for 24 hours
Simple analgesia as needed
Check the dressing and site the next day
Act on Gram stain and culture results
red_flags: Purulent fluid (treat as septic arthritis and refer for washout)
Fever, increasing redness or swelling after the procedure
Rapid reaccumulation of blood in the joint

indications: Painful osteoarthritis not controlled by simple measures
Inflammatory arthritis flare in a single joint
Frozen shoulder or adhesive capsulitis
contraindications: Suspected or possible joint infection
Skin infection over the injection site
Prosthetic joint
Injection into the same joint within the last 3 months or more than 3 per year
Uncontrolled diabetes (relative; warn about raised glucose)
equipment: Corticosteroid suitable for intra-articular use with local anaesthetic, per prescriber
steps: Confirm identity, the joint and side, and check allergies, diabetes and anticoagulant use.
Explain benefits and risks (flare, infection, skin changes, raised blood glucose) and obtain consent.
Position the patient comfortably with the joint relaxed and mark the entry point.
Perform hand hygiene and clean the skin with antiseptic, using a no-touch technique.
Insert the needle along the chosen approach into the joint space.
Aspirate any effusion first and inspect it; stop and send for culture if it looks cloudy.
Inject the prescribed medicine slowly; it should flow with little resistance.
Withdraw the needle and apply a plaster.
Move the joint gently through its range to spread the injectate.
Observe the patient for a short period for vasovagal or allergic reactions.
aftercare: Relative rest of the joint for 24–48 hours
Expect possible pain flare for 1–2 days
Diabetic patients to monitor blood glucose for several days
Review effect at follow-up
red_flags: Hot, swollen joint or fever after injection (possible infection; return urgently)
Worsening pain beyond 48 hours
Signs of allergic reaction

indications: Trigger finger or thumb
De Quervain's tenosynovitis
Lateral or medial epicondylitis not settling with rest and physiotherapy
Plantar fasciitis
Trochanteric or other bursitis
Carpal tunnel syndrome as a temporary measure
contraindications: Local skin infection
Injection directly into a tendon or near the Achilles or patellar tendon
Repeated injections at the same site within 3 months
Bleeding disorder (relative)
equipment: Corticosteroid with local anaesthetic, per prescriber
steps: Confirm identity, the site and side, and check allergies, diabetes and anticoagulant use.
Explain benefits and risks including skin thinning, depigmentation and tendon rupture, and obtain consent.
Position the patient and palpate to mark the point of maximum tenderness or the tendon sheath.
Perform hand hygiene and clean the skin with antiseptic.
Insert the needle at the planned angle into the sheath, bursa or tissue around the lesion, not into the tendon itself.
Withdraw slightly and reposition if there is high resistance, which suggests the needle is in tendon.
Inject slowly and watch for blanching of the skin, which suggests too superficial a placement.
Withdraw the needle and apply a plaster.
Observe for a short period for vasovagal or allergic reactions.
aftercare: Avoid heavy use of the area for one to two weeks
Expect possible pain flare for 1–2 days
Diabetic patients to monitor blood glucose
Continue stretching or physiotherapy programme
red_flags: Redness, heat, swelling or fever (possible infection)
Sudden loss of tendon function or a snap (possible rupture)
Persistent numbness after the local anaesthetic wears off

indications: Carpal tunnel syndrome failing splinting or injection
Thenar wasting or constant numbness
Nerve conduction study confirming moderate to severe compression
Acute carpal tunnel syndrome after wrist trauma
contraindications: Uncertain diagnosis (consider cervical radiculopathy or neuropathy)
Active infection of the hand
equipment: Hand surgery set with fine retractors and McIndoe scissors
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side, and mark the operative hand.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local or regional anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet.
Prepare and drape the hand and forearm.
Make a longitudinal palmar incision in line with the radial border of the ring finger, starting at Kaplan's line and not extending distal to it.
Divide the palmar fascia to expose the transverse carpal ligament.
Divide the transverse carpal ligament under direct vision, protecting the median nerve and its motor branch.
Extend the release proximally to the distal forearm fascia and distally until fat around the palmar arch is seen.
Inspect the nerve for compression and the canal for masses.
Release the tourniquet and achieve haemostasis.
Close the skin with interrupted sutures and apply a bulky dressing.
aftercare: Elevate the hand in a sling for 48 hours
Encourage finger movements from day one
Keep the wound dry and remove sutures at 10–14 days
Avoid heavy gripping for 4–6 weeks
red_flags: Increasing pain, swelling or redness of the wound
New numbness or weakness of the thumb
Tight dressing with swollen fingers

indications: Trigger finger or thumb not responding to injection
Locked digit
Recurrence after two injections
contraindications: Active hand infection
Triggering due to inflammatory arthritis needing different surgery (refer)
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and digit, and mark the digit.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet.
Prepare and drape the hand.
Make a small incision over the A1 pulley at the level of the distal palmar crease or thumb MCP crease.
Spread bluntly, retracting and protecting the digital nerves on each side.
Identify the A1 pulley and divide it fully along its length.
Ask the patient to flex and extend the digit to confirm triggering has resolved.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close the skin.
Apply a light dressing that allows finger movement.
aftercare: Move the finger fully from the first day
Elevate the hand for 48 hours
Keep the wound dry and remove sutures at 10–14 days
red_flags: Numbness on either side of the digit
Wound redness or discharge
Persistent triggering or bowstringing

indications: De Quervain's tenosynovitis not responding to splinting and injection
contraindications: Active infection at the site
Diagnosis uncertain (exclude thumb base arthritis)
equipment: Light dressing or thumb spica splint
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and mark the wrist.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local or regional anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet.
Prepare and drape the hand and forearm.
Make a transverse or longitudinal incision over the first dorsal compartment.
Spread bluntly and protect the superficial branches of the radial nerve.
Divide the sheath of the first dorsal compartment along its dorsal side.
Identify and release any separate sub-compartment for extensor pollicis brevis.
Confirm free gliding of the tendons with thumb movement.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close the skin.
Apply a dressing and soft support.
aftercare: Elevate the hand for 48 hours
Begin gentle thumb movement early
Remove sutures at 10–14 days
red_flags: Numbness or burning over the back of the thumb (radial nerve irritation)
Wound infection
Painful snapping of tendons

form.label: Radial sensory nerve identified and protected

indications: Painful or enlarging ganglion
Ganglion causing nerve compression
Recurrence after aspiration
Patient preference for removal after counselling
contraindications: Asymptomatic ganglion in a child (often resolves spontaneously)
Uncertain diagnosis of a solid or vascular mass (image first)
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side, and mark the swelling.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet.
Prepare and drape the limb.
Make an incision over the ganglion in line with skin creases where possible.
Dissect the cyst wall free, protecting nearby arteries, nerves and tendons.
Follow the stalk to the joint capsule or tendon sheath.
Excise the cyst with its stalk and a small cuff of capsule.
Send the specimen for histology.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close the skin.
Apply a compression dressing and splint if needed.
aftercare: Elevate and rest the limb for a few days
Gentle movement after 48 hours
Remove sutures at 10–14 days
Warn of possible recurrence
red_flags: Numbness or coldness of the hand or foot
Wound bleeding or infection
Persistent stiffness

indications: Complete flexor tendon laceration
Partial laceration greater than half the tendon width
Closed flexor tendon avulsion (jersey finger)
contraindications: Grossly contaminated wound (debride and delay repair)
Severe crush with loss of skin cover (needs staged reconstruction or referral)
No access to hand therapy follow-up (consider referral)
equipment: Hand surgery set with fine instruments and loupes if available
Non-absorbable core suture (3-0 or 4-0) and fine epitendinous suture (5-0 or 6-0)
Tendon retrieval instruments or paediatric feeding tube
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and digits, and document preoperative sensation and tendon function.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give regional or general anaesthesia, apply a tourniquet and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Prepare and drape the hand and forearm.
Debride and irrigate the wound thoroughly.
Extend the wound with zig-zag (Bruner) incisions to expose the tendon ends.
Retrieve the proximal tendon end atraumatically and hold it with a transverse needle.
Preserve the A2 and A4 pulleys as far as possible.
Perform a core suture repair of at least four strands and add an epitendinous running suture.
Check that the repair glides smoothly through the sheath without gapping.
Repair any divided digital nerves under magnification.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close the skin.
Apply a dorsal blocking splint with the wrist and MCP joints flexed and fingers extended.
aftercare: Elevate the hand
Start early protected mobilisation under a hand therapist within days
Keep the splint on for about 6 weeks
No forceful gripping for 12 weeks
red_flags: Sudden loss of finger flexion (repair rupture)
Wound infection or increasing pain
Cold or pale finger

indications: Laceration of extensor tendon of the hand, wrist or foot
Open mallet finger or boutonniere injury
contraindications: Human bite wound over the knuckle (wash out and treat infection first)
Grossly contaminated wound (debride and delay repair)
equipment: Hand surgery set or minor set
Non-absorbable or slowly absorbable tendon sutures
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and document which digit cannot extend.
Ask about how the wound happened and exclude a fight bite over the knuckle.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give local or regional anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet.
Prepare and drape the hand.
Irrigate and debride the wound and extend it as needed to see the tendon ends.
Inspect the underlying joint for capsule breach or foreign body.
Repair the tendon with figure-of-eight, mattress or core sutures according to tendon thickness.
Check the repair holds with gentle passive flexion.
Close the skin and apply a splint holding the repaired tendon relaxed.
aftercare: Elevate the hand
Keep the splint on as directed, usually 4–6 weeks
Hand therapy for graded movement
Remove sutures at 10–14 days
Tetanus status checked and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol for contaminated wounds
red_flags: Redness, swelling or pus, especially after a bite
Loss of extension again (repair failure)
Severe stiffness

indications: Acute Achilles tendon rupture in an active patient choosing surgery
Open laceration of the Achilles tendon
Re-rupture or delayed presentation with a gap
contraindications: Poor skin condition or uncontrolled diabetes (consider non-operative casting)
Peripheral vascular disease
Smoking and steroid use (relative; higher wound risk)
equipment: Strong non-absorbable suture for core repair
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and confirm rupture with a calf squeeze (Thompson) test or ultrasound.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give spinal or general anaesthesia and position the patient prone with both legs prepared for comparison of tension.
Apply a tourniquet and make a posteromedial incision avoiding the sural nerve.
Open the paratenon carefully and preserve it for closure.
Debride frayed tendon ends minimally.
Place a locking core suture in each end and tie with the foot in natural resting equinus compared with the other side.
Add a running epitendinous suture.
Close the paratenon and skin carefully without tension.
Apply a backslab with the foot in equinus.
aftercare: Elevate and keep non-weight bearing initially
Graduated reduction of equinus in a boot or casts over 6–8 weeks
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol
Physiotherapy for strengthening
red_flags: Wound breakdown or discharge
Calf swelling or pain (possible DVT)
Sudden loss of push-off (re-rupture)

indications: Nail bed laceration
Nail plate avulsion with nail bed injury
Large subungual haematoma with displaced nail or fracture
contraindications: Severe crush with tuft bone loss needing referral
equipment: Digital block materials and local anaesthetic without adrenaline unless local policy allows
Fine instruments and magnifying loupes if available
steps: Confirm identity and digit, check X-ray for tuft fracture, and obtain consent.
Perform a digital nerve block and wait for full numbness.
Clean the finger and apply a digital tourniquet, recording the time.
Remove the nail plate gently with a fine elevator and keep it if intact.
Irrigate the nail bed and remove debris and haematoma.
Repair the nail bed accurately with fine absorbable sutures.
Replace the cleaned nail plate (or a silicone or foil splint) under the nail fold to keep it open.
Remove the tourniquet and check capillary refill.
Apply a non-adherent dressing and protective splint.
aftercare: Elevate the hand
Change dressing after 3–5 days
Warn that the new nail may take months to grow and may be deformed
Prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol if fracture is open
red_flags: Pale or blue fingertip after tourniquet removal
Signs of infection or throbbing pain
Tourniquet left on (always check removal)

indications: Fingertip amputation with or without exposed bone
Crushed fingertip unsuitable for simple closure
contraindications: Thumb or multiple-digit amputation suitable for replantation (refer urgently)
equipment: Digital block materials and local anaesthetic
Hand surgery set with bone nibbler (rongeur)
steps: Confirm identity, digit and hand dominance, check X-ray, and obtain consent.
Discuss options including healing by dressings, local flap, graft or terminalisation.
Give a digital block and apply a digital tourniquet, recording the time.
Irrigate and debride devitalised tissue.
In children and small wounds without exposed bone, plan healing by secondary intention with dressings.
Where bone is exposed, trim it with a rongeur until it is below the soft tissue level.
Trim the digital nerves back so they retract away from the scar.
Close the skin without tension, or cover with a local advancement flap or graft.
Excise remaining nail matrix fully if the nail cannot be supported, to prevent a hook nail.
Remove the tourniquet and confirm perfusion of the remaining finger.
Apply a non-adherent dressing and protective splint.
aftercare: Elevate the hand
Dressing review at 2–5 days
Early finger movement and desensitisation
Tetanus status checked and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol
red_flags: Dusky or white flap or finger
Infection or increasing pain
Painful neuroma later

indications: Idiopathic congenital talipes equinovarus, ideally started in the first weeks of life
Neglected or relapsed clubfoot in a young child
Syndromic clubfoot (with modified expectations)
contraindications: Skin breakdown on the foot until healed
equipment: Plaster of Paris rolls (5–10 cm) and cast padding
Plaster knife or saw and scissors for removal
Foot abduction brace for after correction
steps: Confirm identity, explain the programme to the caregivers and obtain consent.
Record the Pirani score for each foot.
Remove the previous cast (soak and unwind or cut) and inspect the skin.
Settle the baby, ideally feeding during casting.
Locate the head of the talus and use it as the fulcrum for correction.
Correct the cavus first by elevating the first metatarsal, then abduct the foot around the talar head.
Never pronate the foot or press on the calcaneus.
Apply thin padding and a well-moulded below-knee cast while holding the correction.
Extend the cast above the knee with the knee flexed to 90 degrees.
Check the toes for colour and capillary refill when the cast is complete.
Plan weekly cast changes and tenotomy when abduction is adequate but equinus persists.
aftercare: Keep the cast dry and clean
Caregivers check toes several times a day
Return weekly for the next cast
After correction, brace full time then at night and naps until about 4 years
red_flags: Toes swollen, blue, pale or cold
Cast slipped so toes are hidden
Foul smell, fever or crying more than usual

form.label: Skin on removal of previous cast

indications: Persistent equinus after Ponseti casting with adequate abduction
Dorsiflexion less than about 10–15 degrees beyond neutral
contraindications: Abduction not yet adequate (continue casting)
Local skin infection
Bleeding disorder (exclude by history before cutting)
equipment: Plaster of Paris for post-tenotomy cast
steps: Confirm identity, side and consent from caregivers, and record the Pirani score.
Perform a time-out confirming side.
Have an assistant hold the leg with the foot dorsiflexed.
Clean the skin and infiltrate a small amount of local anaesthetic medial to the tendon.
Insert the blade from the medial side about 1–1.5 cm above the calcaneus, parallel to the tendon.
Turn the blade and divide the tendon fully, feeling a pop and a sudden gain in dorsiflexion.
Apply pressure with gauze to stop bleeding.
Apply a long-leg cast in maximum abduction and dorsiflexion.
Check toe colour and capillary refill.
aftercare: Keep the cast for 3 weeks
Fit the foot abduction brace when the cast is removed
Teach caregivers brace routine and check-ups
red_flags: Bleeding through the cast
Swollen, pale or cold toes
Fever or foul smell from the cast

indications: Femoral shaft fracture in a young child
After closed or open reduction of developmental dysplasia of the hip
After pelvic or hip osteotomy
contraindications: Unstable fracture with significant shortening better treated surgically
Polytrauma needing abdominal access
equipment: Plaster of Paris or fibreglass rolls
Image intensifier if reduction is performed
steps: Confirm identity, side, indication and caregiver consent.
In a child who is not yet walking, consider non-accidental injury and follow safeguarding procedures.
Give sedation or anaesthesia and position the child on the spica frame.
Apply stockinette and padding with a folded towel over the abdomen to leave space for breathing and feeding.
Reduce the fracture or position the hip as planned, checking with X-ray or image intensifier if available.
Apply the cast from the lower chest over the pelvis and down the affected leg and, as needed, the other thigh.
Hold the limb in the planned position of hip and knee flexion and abduction while the cast sets.
Mould well over the iliac crests and around the knee.
Trim the perineal opening widely and protect the edges with waterproof tape.
Remove the towel to leave abdominal space and check circulation in the toes.
Obtain a check X-ray of position.
aftercare: Teach caregivers nappy care, skin checks and cast hygiene
Turn the child two to four hourly
Adapted car seat or carrying position
Follow-up X-ray at one to two weeks
red_flags: Toes cold, pale, blue or swollen
Breathing difficulty or vomiting (cast too tight)
Foul smell, wet cast or skin breakdown at edges

indications: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in infants under about 6 months
Dislocatable or dislocated hip reducible on examination
contraindications: Infant older than about 6 months or too large
Irreducible or teratological dislocation
Neuromuscular conditions with stiff or weak legs
steps: Confirm identity, review clinical and ultrasound findings, and explain the plan to caregivers.
Undress the infant and lay them on a firm surface.
Fit the chest strap at nipple level with room for two fingers.
Fit the foot stirrups with the straps leaving the knees free.
Adjust the anterior straps to hold the hips in about 90–100 degrees of flexion.
Adjust the posterior straps loosely so the knees fall into gentle abduction, never forced.
Mark strap positions so caregivers can refit correctly.
Check that the hips reduce in the harness, with ultrasound if available.
Teach caregivers how to bathe, dress and change nappies while keeping the harness on as instructed.
aftercare: Wear full time as instructed
Review weekly at first with clinical or ultrasound check
Stop and review if hip not reduced by 3–4 weeks
Total treatment usually several months
red_flags: Infant not kicking the legs (possible femoral nerve palsy)
Skin breakdown in creases
Harness repeatedly slipping or straps changed by family

name: Corrective osteotomy for genu varum or valgum

indications: Progressive or severe bow legs or knock knees beyond physiological range
Blount's disease (tibia vara)
Rickets deformity persisting after medical treatment
Post-traumatic or post-infective angular deformity
contraindications: Active rickets not yet treated medically
Physiological bowing in a young child likely to correct
Deformity suitable for guided growth (consider less invasive option)
equipment: Major orthopaedic set with oscillating saw or osteotomes
Fixation (plate and screws, staples, Kirschner wires, or external fixator)
Goniometer and long-leg standing X-rays with deformity planning
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side, and review the preoperative deformity plan and angles.
Check that rickets has been treated medically and bone chemistry has improved.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Give anaesthesia, apply a tourniquet and prepare both legs if bilateral.
Perform fibular osteotomy first if doing a proximal tibial correction.
Expose the planned osteotomy site, protecting the physis and the common peroneal nerve.
Cut the bone (wedge, dome or opening osteotomy) according to the plan.
Correct the deformity and check alignment with a long cable or image intensifier.
Fix the osteotomy with the chosen device.
Perform prophylactic anterior compartment fasciotomy if the tibial correction is large.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close in layers.
Apply a well-padded cast or dressing and check foot pulses and movement.
aftercare: Elevate and monitor for compartment syndrome and foot drop
Protected weight bearing until union
Check X-ray at 2 and 6 weeks
Continue medical treatment of rickets
Follow up for recurrence until skeletal maturity
red_flags: Severe pain unrelieved by analgesia or pain on passive toe stretch
Foot drop or numbness on the top of the foot
Wound infection or pin-site infection

indications: Mechanical symptoms (locking) from a meniscal tear
Loose body removal
Diagnostic assessment when imaging is unavailable or unclear
Arthroscopic washout of septic knee
contraindications: Degenerative knee pain without mechanical symptoms (little benefit)
Skin infection over portal sites
equipment: Arthroscopy tower with camera, light source and monitor
Saline irrigation with pump or gravity
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and mark the knee.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia, apply a thigh tourniquet and position with a leg holder or lateral post.
Prepare and drape the knee and set up the arthroscopy equipment and fluid.
Make the anterolateral portal and introduce the arthroscope.
Make the anteromedial portal under direct vision.
Perform a systematic examination of all compartments, cruciates and patellofemoral joint.
Treat findings as planned (partial meniscectomy, repair, loose body removal or debridement).
Record photographs of key findings if possible.
Wash out the joint, remove instruments and close the portals.
Apply a compression dressing.
aftercare: Ice, elevation and simple analgesia
Early quadriceps exercises and weight bearing as allowed
Protected weight bearing and brace after meniscal repair
Remove sutures at 10–14 days
red_flags: Hot, swollen knee with fever (septic arthritis)
Calf swelling or pain (DVT)
Persistent bleeding or very tense knee

indications: Symptomatic knee instability after ACL rupture
Active patient wishing to return to pivoting sport or work
ACL tear with repairable meniscal tear
contraindications: Stiff or swollen knee not yet rehabilitated
Patient unable to complete prolonged rehabilitation
Open growth plates (needs specialist physeal-sparing technique)
equipment: Graft harvest instruments (hamstring stripper or bone-patellar tendon-bone set)
Graft fixation devices (interference screws or suspensory buttons)
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and examine the knee under anaesthesia.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Apply a tourniquet, prepare and drape the limb, and perform diagnostic arthroscopy, treating meniscal tears.
Harvest the chosen graft and prepare it on the back table, measuring diameter and length.
Clear the ACL stump and notch as needed.
Drill the femoral tunnel at the anatomical footprint.
Drill the tibial tunnel using the guide.
Pass the graft and fix it on the femoral side.
Cycle the knee, tension the graft and fix it on the tibial side.
Check graft position, tension and absence of impingement.
Close the wounds and apply a dressing and brace if used.
aftercare: Ice, elevation and analgesia
Structured physiotherapy programme from day one
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol
Return to sport usually not before 9 months
red_flags: Fever, hot swollen knee or wound discharge
Calf pain or swelling
Inability to straighten the knee

indications: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication failing conservative care
Cauda equina compression from stenosis
Progressive neurological deficit
Epidural abscess or tumour causing compression
contraindications: Symptoms not matching imaging levels
Significant instability needing fusion as well (plan fusion)
equipment: Spinal set with Kerrison rongeurs and pituitary rongeurs
Image intensifier or X-ray for level localisation
steps: Confirm identity, consent and levels against MRI or myelogram, and record neurological examination.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Give general anaesthesia and position prone on bolsters with the abdomen free.
Confirm the level with an X-ray marker before incision.
Prepare and drape the back.
Make a midline incision and strip the paraspinal muscles off the laminae subperiosteally.
Confirm the level again on X-ray with an instrument on the lamina.
Remove the spinous process and laminae at the affected levels.
Excise the ligamentum flavum and undercut the facets to decompress the lateral recesses, preserving facet joints.
Decompress the foramina and check each nerve root is free.
Check for dural tears and repair if present.
Achieve haemostasis, place a drain if needed and close in layers.
aftercare: Neurological observations of legs and bladder
Early mobilisation with physiotherapy
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol
Avoid heavy lifting for 6 weeks
red_flags: New leg weakness or numbness
Urinary retention or saddle numbness
Clear fluid leak from the wound or positional headache (CSF leak)
Fever or wound discharge

indications: Lumbar disc prolapse with sciatica failing 6–12 weeks of conservative care
Cauda equina syndrome from central disc prolapse (emergency)
Progressive motor deficit
contraindications: Back pain without matching radicular symptoms or imaging
equipment: Spinal set with Kerrison and pituitary rongeurs
Operating microscope or loupes and headlight
Image intensifier or X-ray for level localisation
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and level against the MRI, and record neurological examination.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general anaesthesia and position prone with the abdomen free.
Mark the level with an X-ray before incision.
Prepare and drape the back.
Make a small incision and strip the muscles from the lamina on the symptomatic side.
Confirm the level again with an X-ray.
Open the ligamentum flavum and remove a small amount of lamina as needed.
Retract the nerve root medially and identify the disc prolapse.
Remove the sequestrated and loose disc fragments.
Check that the nerve root is free and mobile.
Achieve haemostasis and close in layers.
aftercare: Early mobilisation on the day of or day after surgery
Neurological and bladder observations
Avoid heavy lifting and prolonged sitting for several weeks
Physiotherapy for core strengthening
red_flags: New leg weakness, numbness or saddle anaesthesia
Urinary retention or incontinence
Clear wound leak or positional headache
Fever or severe back pain (discitis)

indications: Unstable spinal fracture
Spondylolisthesis with instability or after decompression
Spinal tuberculosis or tumour with instability
Progressive spinal deformity
contraindications: Poor bone quality without augmentation plan
Active uncontrolled infection at the operative site (relative)
Lack of image intensifier for screw placement
equipment: Spinal set and pedicle screw-rod system with correct screw sizes
Bone graft harvest tools or bone substitute
Bipolar diathermy and cell salvage if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, levels and implant availability, and record neurological examination.
Ensure blood is cross-matched and perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general anaesthesia, prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol, and position prone with pressure areas padded.
Confirm levels with image intensifier before incision.
Prepare and drape the back.
Expose the posterior elements to the tips of the transverse processes at the planned levels.
Identify entry points and prepare pedicle tracks with a probe, checking for breaches with a feeler.
Insert pedicle screws and confirm positions on image intensifier in two planes.
Perform any decompression needed.
Contour and seat the rods, and reduce or correct deformity carefully.
Decorticate the fusion bed and lay bone graft.
Check final implant position on imaging and test the neurology if monitoring is available.
Achieve haemostasis, insert a drain and close in layers.
aftercare: Hourly neurological observations initially
Drain and haemoglobin monitoring
Thromboprophylaxis and early mobilisation per local protocol
Postoperative X-ray of implant position
Brace if advised
red_flags: New weakness or numbness in the legs
Bladder or bowel dysfunction
Wound discharge or fever
Signs of major bleeding or shock

indications: Spinal tuberculosis with neurological deficit not improving on anti-TB treatment
Large abscess or sequestra compressing the cord
Progressive kyphosis or instability
Diagnostic uncertainty needing tissue
contraindications: Patient unfit for thoracotomy or major surgery (consider posterior or extrapleural approach)
No plan to start anti-TB treatment promptly
No thoracic surgical, anaesthetic and intensive care backup (stabilise with brace and refer)
equipment: Major spinal and thoracotomy or retroperitoneal set
Strut graft (rib or iliac crest) or cage
Specimen pots for TB culture, GeneXpert and histology
