steps: Confirm identity, consent and levels, record neurological examination, and confirm anti-TB treatment plan.
Correct anaemia and nutrition, cross-match blood, and perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give general anaesthesia, with lung isolation if transthoracic, give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol after samples are planned, and position lateral, then prepare and drape.
Approach the spine through a thoracotomy, thoracoabdominal or retroperitoneal route as appropriate to the level.
Confirm the level on imaging.
Drain the abscess and send pus and tissue for TB culture, molecular testing and histology.
Remove caseous material, sequestra and diseased disc and bone back to bleeding bone.
Decompress the cord anteriorly until the dura is seen pulsating.
Insert a strut graft or cage spanning the defect, with additional fixation if needed.
Achieve haemostasis, insert a chest or wound drain and close in layers.
aftercare: Continue anti-TB treatment for the full course per national guidelines
Chest drain care and chest physiotherapy
Neurological observations
Brace and graduated mobilisation
Nutrition support and HIV testing if not done
red_flags: Worsening leg weakness or sensory level
Breathing difficulty or air leak
Wound discharge or graft displacement on X-ray

indications: Cervical spine fracture or dislocation needing reduction
Temporary stabilisation of an unstable cervical injury pending surgery
Cervical spine tuberculosis with deformity (selected cases)
contraindications: Skull fracture at the pin sites
Atlanto-occipital dislocation (traction is dangerous)
Uncooperative patient for awake reduction without monitoring (relative)
No experienced team or lateral imaging available (immobilise in a collar or sandbags and refer)
equipment: Gardner-Wells or similar tongs with pins
Lateral cervical X-ray or image intensifier
Razor for hair at pin sites
steps: Confirm identity and consent, and record a full neurological examination.
Review imaging to confirm injury type and exclude contraindications.
Position supine with the head supported and maintain in-line immobilisation.
Mark pin sites one finger-breadth above the pinna in line with the external auditory meatus, below the skull equator.
Shave, clean with antiseptic and infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the periosteum.
Insert the pins together, tightening evenly until the spring-loaded indicator protrudes.
Attach the rope over the pulley and apply a small starting weight.
Add weight in small increments with neurological checks and a lateral X-ray after each increase.
Stop increasing weight and reduce it if the neurology worsens or the X-ray shows over-distraction.
Once reduced, reduce to maintenance weight and document the final weight and position.
Retighten the pins the next day.
aftercare: Neurological observations at least four-hourly
Daily pin-site care
Pressure area care and turning with log-roll
Check X-ray after any change and plan definitive treatment
red_flags: New or worsening weakness, numbness or breathing difficulty
Pin loosening, slippage or pin-site infection
Severe headache or clear fluid from pin sites

indications: Non-union or delayed union
Bone defect after trauma, tumour curettage or infection
Spinal or joint fusion
contraindications: Infection at the donor site
Active infection at the recipient site not yet controlled
equipment: Kidney dish with saline-soaked swab for graft
Local anaesthetic for donor site infiltration
steps: Confirm identity, consent, recipient site and donor site, and mark both.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia and position to allow access to both donor and recipient sites.
Prepare and drape the donor site separately or together as planned.
Incise along the iliac crest, staying behind the anterior superior iliac spine to protect the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
In children, avoid damaging the iliac apophysis (split it rather than strip it).
Elevate the muscles from the outer or inner table as needed.
Harvest cancellous or corticocancellous bone with gouges or osteotomes without breaching both tables.
Keep the graft moist in a saline-soaked swab.
Achieve haemostasis at the donor site with bone wax and close in layers.
Prepare the recipient bed to bleeding bone and pack the graft into the defect.
Close the recipient wound and apply dressings.
aftercare: Donor site analgesia and early mobilisation
Watch for donor site haematoma
Recipient site protection as per the main procedure
Serial X-rays to assess incorporation
red_flags: Expanding swelling at donor site
Numbness on the outer thigh persisting
Fever or wound discharge at either site

indications: Suspected primary bone tumour
Suspected metastatic bone disease without a known primary
Suspected bone infection or tuberculosis needing tissue diagnosis
contraindications: Suspected sarcoma where this centre will not do the definitive surgery (discuss and refer first)
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Specimen pots for histology (formalin) and culture (sterile, dry)
steps: Confirm identity, consent and site, and review all imaging with the surgeon who will do the definitive surgery if possible.
Plan the biopsy track so it can be excised with the later tumour resection.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia, prepare and drape, and apply a tourniquet without exsanguination if a tumour is suspected.
Make a small longitudinal incision in line with the definitive incision, through a single muscle compartment.
Avoid neurovascular structures and do not raise flaps.
Take tissue from the soft-tissue component or the edge of the lesion, and make a small round cortical window if needed.
Send tissue for histology and, unless sure it is a tumour, for culture.
Achieve meticulous haemostasis and plug any cortical window with bone wax or cement.
Close tightly in layers; if a drain is used, bring it out in line with the incision.
Protect the limb with a splint if the bone is weakened.
aftercare: Protect the limb from fracture with reduced weight bearing
Wound care and suture removal
Follow up histology results promptly and discuss at a multidisciplinary meeting
red_flags: Sudden pain or deformity (pathological fracture)
Wound haematoma or infection
Rapidly growing swelling

indications: Benign aggressive bone tumour such as giant cell tumour
Symptomatic or large bone cyst at fracture risk
Enchondroma or other benign lesion with a confirmed diagnosis
contraindications: Malignant tumour needing wide resection
Diagnosis not confirmed by imaging and, where needed, biopsy
equipment: Basic orthopaedic set with curettes of several sizes
Bone graft, bone substitute or bone cement
Fixation implants if prophylactic fixation planned
steps: Confirm identity, consent, site and histological diagnosis.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia, apply a tourniquet if on a limb, and prepare and drape.
Approach the lesion through a planned incision that incorporates any biopsy track.
Open a cortical window large enough to see the whole cavity.
Curette the lesion thoroughly and send tissue for histology.
Extend the curettage with a burr into healthy bone if available.
Use a local adjuvant for aggressive lesions per local protocol.
Wash out the cavity and fill it with bone graft, bone substitute or cement.
Add prophylactic fixation if the bone is at risk of fracture.
Close in layers and protect the limb.
aftercare: Protected weight bearing until healing seen on X-ray
Wound review and suture removal
Serial X-rays for recurrence over several years
red_flags: Pain or deformity suggesting fracture
Wound infection
Return of pain or swelling (recurrence)
Histology unexpectedly malignant (refer to a sarcoma team)

indications: End-stage arthritis of ankle, wrist, foot or small joints where replacement is unsuitable
Painful post-infective or post-traumatic joint destruction
Unstable flail or paralytic joint
Severe deformity not correctable by soft-tissue surgery
contraindications: Active infection not controlled (consider staged surgery)
Poor skin or vascular supply at the site
Adjacent joint arthritis that would make fusion intolerable
equipment: Major orthopaedic set with osteotomes, curettes and saw
Fixation (screws, plates, nail or external fixator)
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and joint, and agree the position of fusion with the patient.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out and give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Give anaesthesia and apply a tourniquet.
Expose the joint through the planned approach protecting neurovascular structures.
Remove all remaining cartilage and sclerotic bone to expose bleeding surfaces.
Shape the bone ends to achieve good contact in the planned position of function.
Add bone graft if there are gaps.
Hold the joint in position and fix it with compression screws, plate, nail or external fixator.
Check position and implant placement on image intensifier.
Release the tourniquet, achieve haemostasis and close in layers.
Apply a well-padded backslab or cast.
aftercare: Elevate and monitor circulation
Non- or partial weight bearing in a cast for about 6–12 weeks
Serial X-rays for union
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol for lower-limb fusions
Stop smoking
red_flags: Severe pain or tight cast with numb toes or fingers
Wound infection or pin-site infection
Persistent pain at fusion site after 3 months (non-union)

indications: Fixed joint contracture from polio, cerebral palsy or other neuromuscular disease
Post-burn or post-traumatic contracture limiting function
Contracture preventing walking, sitting, hygiene or bracing
contraindications: Contracture still responding to physiotherapy and stretching
Poor skin cover without a plan for grafting or flap
No access to postoperative splinting and physiotherapy
equipment: Basic orthopaedic or plastic surgery set
Plaster of Paris or splint materials
steps: Confirm identity, consent, side and joints, and measure the contracture angles with a goniometer.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia, apply a tourniquet where possible, and prepare and drape.
Re-examine under anaesthesia to separate fixed contracture from spasticity.
Approach the contracted structures through planned incisions, using Z-plasty for skin bands.
Release or lengthen tight tendons, fascia and capsule step by step, rechecking the angle after each step.
Protect nerves and vessels, which are often shortened and at risk with sudden full correction.
Accept partial correction if pulses weaken or nerves are tight, and plan serial casting.
Close the skin without tension, using grafts or flaps for defects.
Apply a padded cast or splint in the corrected position and check distal circulation.
aftercare: Elevate and check circulation and sensation regularly
Serial casting or splinting to maintain or improve correction
Physiotherapy and long-term bracing
Night splints to prevent recurrence
red_flags: Pale, cold or numb limb after correction
Severe pain under the cast
Wound breakdown or graft failure

indications: Established non-union with persistent pain or movement at the fracture site
Failed or broken implant with no healing
Malunion causing functional problems (combined with osteotomy)
contraindications: Unrecognised infected non-union (investigate and plan staged treatment)
Uncorrected nutritional, metabolic or smoking factors (optimise first where possible)
equipment: Implant removal set including broken screw and nail extraction tools
New fixation implants (plate, nail or external fixator) in suitable sizes
Bone graft harvest tools or substitute
Specimen pots for multiple culture samples
steps: Confirm identity, consent and side, and review X-rays, inflammatory markers and nutrition.
Ensure the right removal tools and new implants are available and blood is grouped.
Perform the surgical safety checklist time-out.
Give anaesthesia, position for access and imaging, and prepare and drape.
Expose the non-union through the previous or a suitable approach.
Remove the failed implants.
Take several deep tissue samples for culture before giving antibiotics where infection is possible.
Debride fibrous tissue and sclerotic bone ends back to bleeding bone, and open the medullary canal.
Correct alignment, length and rotation.
Fix stably with a new implant, exchange nail or external fixator.
Pack autologous bone graft around the non-union.
Check alignment and implant position on image intensifier.
Close in layers over a drain if needed.
aftercare: Elevate and monitor circulation
Weight bearing as allowed by fixation
Act on culture results
Serial X-rays for union
Optimise nutrition and stop smoking
red_flags: Fever, wound discharge or redness
Severe pain or new deformity (fixation failure)
Numb or cold limb

indications: Infant or child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally
Heart rate below 60 per minute with signs of poor perfusion despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation
Witnessed or unwitnessed cardiac arrest
contraindications: Valid documented do-not-attempt-resuscitation or treatment-limitation decision
Obvious signs of irreversible death (rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition)
equipment: Paediatric bag-valve-mask with infant and child masks
Suction with Yankauer and soft catheters
Oropharyngeal airways in a range of sizes
Defibrillator or AED with paediatric pads or attenuator
Paediatric resuscitation drug and dose chart or length-based tape
Clock or timer and resuscitation record sheet
steps: Ensure scene safety, check responsiveness, shout for help and activate the resuscitation team.
Open the airway with head tilt-chin lift (neutral position in infants, sniffing in children) or jaw thrust if trauma is suspected.
Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
Give 5 initial rescue breaths with bag-valve-mask and high-flow oxygen, watching for chest rise.
Check for signs of life and a central pulse (brachial in infants, carotid or femoral in children) for no more than 10 seconds.
If there are no signs of life or the pulse is below 60 per minute with poor perfusion, start chest compressions at 100-120 per minute.
Compress the lower half of the sternum by at least one third of chest depth, using two-thumb encircling in infants and one or two hands in children.
Give 15 compressions to 2 breaths, minimise interruptions and change the compressor about every 2 minutes.
Attach the defibrillator or monitor as soon as available and check the rhythm every 2 minutes.
For a shockable rhythm (VF or pulseless VT), give a weight-based shock and restart CPR immediately without a pulse check.
Obtain IV or intraosseous access and give adrenaline and other resuscitation drugs at the weight-based dose from the chart.
Look for and treat reversible causes (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis).
Check blood glucose and treat hypoglycaemia per protocol.
If a skilled provider places an advanced airway, give continuous compressions with asynchronous ventilation.
On return of spontaneous circulation, start post-resuscitation care; otherwise stop only on the team leader's decision and record the time and reason.
aftercare: Reassess ABCDE and keep oxygen saturation in the normal range without hyperoxia
Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, saturation, temperature and glucose closely
Treat seizures and avoid fever
Arrange HDU/ICU care or urgent escorted referral
Debrief the team and speak with the family, documenting the conversation
red_flags: Recurrent arrest or bradycardia after ROSC
Persistent hypotension or poor perfusion after fluid
Seizures or deteriorating consciousness after ROSC
Recurrent hypoglycaemia
No ICU available for a ventilated child - arrange urgent escorted transfer

indications: Infant needing IV fluids, antibiotics or other IV medicines when limb veins are not accessible
Infant needing blood transfusion when limb access has failed
contraindications: Infection, haematoma or injury of the scalp at the intended site
Inability to distinguish the vein from an artery
Shock needing immediate access (use intraosseous access instead)
equipment: 24G or 26G cannula or 23-25G scalp vein (butterfly) set
Rubber band with a tape tab as tourniquet
Razor or scissors for a small area of hair
Antiseptic (chlorhexidine-alcohol or per local policy) and gauze
Saline flush in a 2 mL or 5 mL syringe
Transparent dressing, tape and a protective cover
steps: Confirm the infant's identity and indication, explain to the parent (including any hair shaving) and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Swaddle the infant and have an assistant hold the head steady; offer breastfeeding or oral sucrose for comfort.
Choose a straight superficial temporal, frontal or posterior auricular vein.
Palpate the vessel and reject it if it pulsates, as it is an artery.
Shave only a small area around the vein after the parent agrees.
Place the rubber band around the head below the vein as a tourniquet, with a tape tab so it can be cut off safely.
Clean the skin with antiseptic and allow it to dry.
Insert the needle at a shallow angle in the direction of blood flow (towards the heart) until flashback is seen.
Advance the cannula off the needle, then cut or release the band.
Flush gently and watch for blanching of the skin (arterial placement) or swelling (extravasation).
Secure with a dressing and tape so the site stays visible, and protect it from knocks.
Dispose of sharps and record the site, size and time.
aftercare: Inspect the site at least hourly while fluids run
Flush and check patency before each medicine
Tell the parent to report swelling, redness or crying when fluids run
Remove the cannula when no longer needed or if any problem develops
red_flags: Blanching or skin colour change on flushing - remove immediately (arterial)
Swelling, hardness or pain around the site (extravasation)
Redness, pus or fever (phlebitis or infection)
Line will not flush

indications: Sterile urine sample for culture in an infant under 2 years with suspected UTI or sepsis
Clean-catch or catheter sample not possible or repeatedly contaminated
contraindications: Empty bladder on ultrasound or void within the last hour
Bleeding disorder or severe thrombocytopenia
Skin infection over the puncture site
Abdominal distension, organomegaly or known genitourinary or abdominal anomaly
equipment: Chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine and sterile gauze
steps: Confirm identity, explain to the parent and obtain verbal consent.
Confirm the infant has not voided in the last hour and the bladder is full, ideally on ultrasound or by percussion.
Lay the infant supine in frog-leg position held by an assistant; give oral sucrose or breastfeed for comfort.
Have a sterile container ready, as the infant may void during the procedure.
Ask the assistant to occlude the urethra (gentle penile pinch in boys, pressure on the urethra in girls).
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the suprapubic skin.
Insert the needle in the midline 1-2 cm above the pubic symphysis, perpendicular or angled slightly towards the head.
Advance while gently aspirating and stop as soon as urine appears.
Withdraw the needle and press on the site with gauze.
Limit to two attempts; if dry, wait an hour, rehydrate and recheck the bladder before trying again.
Transfer urine into the sterile container, label it and send it to the laboratory promptly.
aftercare: Apply a plaster and observe for a few minutes
Tell the parent transient pink urine can occur
Keep the sample refrigerated if it cannot reach the laboratory within an hour
red_flags: Persistent or heavy blood in the urine
Abdominal distension, vomiting or worsening irritability after the procedure
Aspirate looks like bowel content (suspect bowel puncture - inform senior, observe)

indications: Urine dipstick or microscopy screen in a child not toilet-trained
Urine output measurement where catheterisation is not wanted
contraindications: Urgent culture needed in an unwell infant (use clean-catch, catheter or suprapubic sample)
Broken or inflamed perineal skin
equipment: Sterile paediatric urine collection bag of the right size
Warm water, soap and clean gauze (no antiseptic needed)
steps: Confirm identity and explain the purpose to the parent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Wash the genital and perineal area with soap and water, rinse and pat dry.
Remove the backing and apply the bag, covering the penis in boys or the labia in girls, starting from the perineum.
Press the adhesive firmly with no creases so urine cannot leak.
Put a loose nappy over the bag or leave it uncovered and check every 15 minutes.
Remove the bag as soon as urine is passed, peeling gently from the top.
Transfer the urine into a sterile container, label it and send it promptly.
Replace the bag with a fresh one if no urine after about an hour, rather than leaving it on.
aftercare: Check and clean the skin after removing the bag
Explain that a bag sample is useful to rule out infection but a positive culture needs a cleaner sample to confirm
red_flags: Positive dipstick or culture in a bag sample - confirm with clean-catch, catheter or suprapubic sample before treating as proven UTI where possible
Skin breakdown under the adhesive
Infant becomes unwell while waiting - do not delay treatment for the sample

indications: Acute diarrhoea with no dehydration (Plan A) or some dehydration (Plan B)
Prevention of dehydration in a child with diarrhoea or vomiting
contraindications: Severe dehydration with shock or inability to drink (needs IV or IO rehydration, Plan C)
Persistent vomiting of all fluids
Abdominal distension with suspected ileus or surgical abdomen
Reduced consciousness with unsafe swallow
equipment: Safe drinking water and a measuring container of the volume stated on the sachet
ORT corner chart or WHO dehydration chart
steps: Assess the degree of dehydration and danger signs, and weigh the child.
For Plan B, work out the ORS amount for the first 4 hours from the WHO chart by weight or age; for Plan A, plan the ORS to give after each loose stool.
Show the caregiver how to mix one sachet in the exact volume of clean water stated on the packet.
Ask the caregiver to give small frequent sips by cup or spoon (a teaspoon every 1-2 minutes for a small child).
If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and then continue more slowly.
Encourage breastfeeding to continue throughout.
Reassess hydration, intake, output and vomiting at least every hour.
After 4 hours reassess fully and choose Plan A, repeat Plan B, or move to NG or IV rehydration.
Start zinc per national protocol.
Before discharge, teach Plan A at home, how much ORS to give after each loose stool, and the danger signs.
aftercare: Continue feeding with the usual diet and breast milk
Give ORS after every loose stool at home
Complete the zinc course
Discard mixed ORS after 24 hours
Return for review if not improving in 2-3 days
red_flags: Unable to drink or breastfeed, or vomiting everything
Lethargy or reduced consciousness
Sunken eyes or very slow skin pinch despite ORS
Blood in stool, convulsions or high fever
Puffy eyelids during ORT (overhydration - stop ORS and reassess)

form.label: Caregiver taught Plan A and danger signs
Outcome
options: Changed to NG or IV fluids

indications: Some dehydration when the child will not or cannot drink enough ORS
Severe dehydration when IV or IO access is not possible and while arranging referral
Rehydration of a malnourished child per national protocol using the recommended solution
contraindications: Shock where IV or IO access is available
Reduced consciousness without airway protection
Abdominal distension, suspected ileus or surgical abdomen
Suspected basal skull fracture or facial trauma
equipment: Nasogastric tube 6-10 Fr according to size
Low-osmolarity ORS (or malnutrition rehydration solution per protocol)
Giving set, burette or enteral syringe for drip or bolus delivery
steps: Confirm identity, weigh the child, assess dehydration and explain to the caregiver.
Perform hand hygiene and measure the tube from nose to earlobe to midway between xiphisternum and umbilicus.
Insert the tube gently through the nostril with the head slightly flexed, advancing as the child swallows.
Confirm position by aspirating gastric content with pH 5.5 or below, or by X-ray if no aspirate.
Secure the tube to the cheek and mark the length at the nostril.
Calculate the ORS volume and rate from the protocol for the child's weight and degree of dehydration.
Give ORS by slow continuous drip or small regular boluses via the tube.
Reassess hydration, abdomen, vomiting and output every hour.
Slow the rate if there is repeated vomiting or abdominal distension.
Move to oral ORS once the child drinks well, or to IV fluids if not improving.
aftercare: Check tube position before each bolus and after vomiting or coughing
Continue breastfeeding where possible
Record intake and output on the fluid chart
Start zinc per national protocol
red_flags: Signs of shock or deteriorating consciousness - change to IV or IO fluids
Abdominal distension or bilious vomiting
Respiratory distress or coughing during feeds (possible misplacement or aspiration)
Puffy eyelids, fast breathing or crackles in a malnourished child (fluid overload - stop)

indications: Routine well-child visits at recommended ages
Parental or carer concern about development, speech, hearing or vision
Risk factors such as prematurity, birth asphyxia, neonatal jaundice, meningitis, cerebral malaria or malnutrition
contraindications: Acutely ill or distressed child (defer screening)
equipment: Validated screening tool or national milestone checklist for age
Age-appropriate toys (cubes, ball, picture book, small objects, crayon and paper)
Growth chart and tape for head circumference
steps: Confirm identity and explain to the carer that this checks how the child is developing.
Calculate the child's age, using corrected age for infants born preterm until 2 years.
Ask the carer about concerns and about skills the child does at home.
Measure weight, length or height and head circumference and plot them.
Observe and test gross motor skills for age.
Observe and test fine motor and problem-solving skills with toys.
Assess speech, language and response to sound.
Assess social and emotional behaviour and play.
Check for vision and hearing concerns and any loss of skills already gained.
Score the tool and compare with age-expected milestones.
Explain the result to the carer and give play and stimulation advice.
Refer for full developmental, hearing or vision assessment if delay is suspected.
aftercare: Schedule rescreening for children at risk or borderline
Give the carer simple home stimulation activities
Refer early to physiotherapy, speech therapy or developmental clinic when indicated
red_flags: Loss of previously acquired skills (regression)
No social smile by 3 months, not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months
No words by 18 months or no two-word phrases by 2 years
Asymmetric movements, persistent fisting or abnormal tone
Head circumference crossing centiles or carer concern about hearing or vision

indications: Child 6-59 months with severe acute malnutrition being assessed for outpatient therapeutic care
Follow-up visits in outpatient care to confirm appetite remains good
contraindications: Danger signs or medical complications needing inpatient stabilisation (assess first, do not delay referral)
Bilateral pitting oedema grade +++ or child too ill to eat
Known allergy to peanut or milk in RUTF
equipment: Safe drinking water and a cup
National CMAM appetite test table by weight
steps: Confirm identity, take weight, height or length, MUAC and check for bilateral pitting oedema.
Check for danger signs and medical complications before the test.
Explain the purpose to the caregiver and ask them to wash their hands and the child's hands.
Seat the caregiver and child in a quiet place away from distractions.
Open the sachet and let the caregiver offer it gently, without forcing the child.
Offer safe drinking water to drink with the RUTF.
Allow up to 30 minutes, then estimate the amount eaten by sachet fraction or weighing.
Compare the amount eaten with the minimum required for the child's weight in the national table.
Record pass if the child eats at least the minimum, fail if less or refused.
Admit to outpatient care if passed with no complications; refer for inpatient stabilisation if failed or complicated.
aftercare: Explain RUTF is medicine for this child only and should not be shared
Teach the caregiver to give RUTF in small amounts through the day with water and continue breastfeeding
Book the weekly outpatient review
red_flags: Failed appetite test - refer for inpatient care
Vomiting, convulsions, lethargy, hypothermia or not able to drink
Fast breathing, chest indrawing or severe dehydration
Increasing oedema or skin lesions

indications: Failed or incomplete hydrostatic or pneumatic enema reduction
Enema reduction contraindicated or not available
Peritonitis, perforation or pneumoperitoneum
Suspected pathological lead point or recurrent intussusception
contraindications: Uncorrected shock (resuscitate first, then operate without delay)
equipment: Paediatric laparotomy set and bowel clamps
Absorbable sutures for anastomosis and layered closure
Warm saline packs and warm IV fluids
Warming mattress or blanket and temperature probe
Stoma appliance if a stoma may be needed
steps: Resuscitate with IV fluids, decompress the stomach with a nasogastric tube and correct electrolytes.
Confirm identity, written consent (including possible resection or stoma), site and fasting, and cross-match blood.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and complete the WHO surgical safety checklist and time-out.
Under general anaesthesia, keep the child warm and insert a urinary catheter if needed.
Open the abdomen through a right transverse incision at or just above the umbilicus.
Deliver the intussusception and reduce it by gentle retrograde squeezing from the distal end, never by pulling.
Wrap the reduced bowel in warm packs and assess colour, peristalsis and mesenteric pulsation.
Resect bowel that is non-viable, perforated or cannot be reduced, with primary anastomosis or stoma as the child's condition allows.
Look for a pathological lead point such as Meckel diverticulum, polyp, duplication cyst or lymphoma, and send tissue for histology.
Perform appendicectomy if the appendix is compromised or per surgeon's practice, and record it.
Wash out any contamination with warm saline.
Close the abdomen in layers and count swabs, instruments and needles.
Record findings, procedure and postoperative instructions.
aftercare: Continue nasogastric drainage and IV fluids until bowel function returns
Give analgesia and monitor temperature, pulse, blood pressure and urine output
Start feeds gradually when bowel sounds return and drainage falls
Follow up histology and arrange oncology referral if lymphoma is found
red_flags: Fever, increasing abdominal distension or tenderness (anastomotic leak or abscess)
Persistent bilious aspirate or vomiting
Bleeding per rectum after day 2
Poor urine output or signs of shock
Wound discharge or dehiscence

indications: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis confirmed clinically (palpable olive) or on ultrasound
contraindications: Uncorrected dehydration or metabolic alkalosis (correct before surgery; this is not an emergency operation)
equipment: Paediatric minor laparotomy set or laparoscopic set
Pyloric spreader and fine dissecting forceps
steps: Rehydrate with IV fluids and correct electrolytes and alkalosis before theatre, confirming with repeat blood tests.
Empty the stomach with a nasogastric tube and keep it on free drainage.
Confirm identity, written consent, fasting and normal electrolytes, then complete the WHO checklist and time-out.
Under general anaesthesia with airway protection against aspiration, keep the infant warm.
Make a right upper quadrant or supraumbilical incision, or use laparoscopic ports.
Deliver the pylorus and identify the avascular area on its anterior surface.
Incise the serosa and muscle longitudinally from the pyloric vein to the gastric antrum, avoiding the duodenal end.
Split the muscle with the pyloric spreader until the submucosa bulges along the full length.
Check that the two halves move independently and test for mucosal perforation by insufflating air through the nasogastric tube.
Repair any mucosal perforation and record it.
Return the pylorus, check haemostasis and close the wound in layers.
aftercare: Start feeds within a few hours per local feeding protocol
Reassure parents that small vomits in the first day are common
Give simple analgesia and monitor glucose and temperature
Most infants go home within 24-48 hours
red_flags: Persistent forceful vomiting beyond 48-72 hours (incomplete myotomy)
Fever, abdominal distension or irritability (suspect missed perforation)
Wound redness, discharge or dehiscence
Lethargy or poor feeding at home

indications: Undescended testis persisting beyond 6 months of age (ideally operate by 18 months)
Ectopic testis
Retractile testis that has ascended and cannot be brought to the scrotum
Undescended testis with associated hernia
contraindications: Acute illness or local skin infection (postpone)
Bilateral impalpable testes with hypospadias (investigate for disorder of sex development first)
equipment: Paediatric minor surgical set with fine instruments
Laparoscopic set if the testis is impalpable and available
Local anaesthetic for wound or caudal block
steps: Confirm identity, side and written consent (including possible orchidectomy or staged procedure), mark the side and complete the WHO checklist.
Under general anaesthesia with caudal or local block, examine again to confirm testis position before incision.
Make an inguinal skin crease incision.
Open the external oblique and find the testis and cord.
Separate and ligate the patent processus vaginalis (hernia sac) high at the internal ring.
Mobilise the cord to gain length, dividing cremasteric fibres and lateral bands.
Create a dartos pouch through a separate scrotal incision.
Bring the testis into the pouch without twisting or tension on the vessels.
If the testis is intra-abdominal, use laparoscopy and a staged (Fowler-Stephens) or single-stage approach per surgeon.
Remove an atrophic or nubbin testis and send it for histology.
Close the wounds in layers and record the testis size and final position.
aftercare: Give regular simple analgesia
Keep wounds dry and avoid straddle toys for 2 weeks
Review at 6 weeks and again later to check testis position and size
Teach testicular self-examination at puberty
red_flags: Increasing scrotal swelling or bruising
Fever or wound discharge
Testis no longer felt in the scrotum on review
Severe pain not controlled by analgesia

indications: Inguinal hernia in an infant or child (repair soon after diagnosis because of incarceration risk)
Incarcerated hernia after successful manual reduction (repair within 24-48 hours)
Irreducible or strangulated hernia (emergency)
contraindications: Acute intercurrent illness (postpone elective repair)
Preterm infant not fit for anaesthesia without postoperative apnoea monitoring
equipment: Paediatric minor surgical set with fine instruments
Local anaesthetic for wound or caudal block
Laparoscopic set if laparoscopic repair is used
steps: Confirm identity, side and written consent, mark the side and complete the WHO checklist and time-out.
Under general anaesthesia with caudal or local block, make a small skin crease incision over the internal ring.
Open the external oblique if needed (not in small infants) and identify the cord.
Separate the sac gently from the vas deferens and vessels without grasping them.
Open the sac, check contents and reduce them, inspecting bowel or ovary for viability.
Twist and transfix the sac high at the internal ring and excise the excess.
In girls, check the sac for a gonad and consider disorder of sex development if a testis is found.
Make sure the testis lies in the scrotum at the end.
Close the wound in layers with absorbable sutures.
Record findings, contents and any contralateral exploration.
aftercare: Give simple analgesia
Monitor preterm and ex-preterm infants for apnoea overnight
Keep the wound dry for 48 hours
Review in 2-6 weeks
red_flags: Recurrent groin swelling
Scrotal swelling, discolouration or high testis
Vomiting, abdominal distension or fever
Apnoea or colour change in an ex-preterm infant

indications: Communicating hydrocele persisting beyond 1-2 years of age
Hydrocele that varies in size or is associated with a hernia
Large or tense hydrocele causing discomfort
contraindications: Hydrocele in infancy that is likely to resolve (observe first)
Acute illness or local skin infection
Uncertain diagnosis of scrotal swelling (scan first to exclude tumour or torsion)
equipment: Paediatric minor surgical set with fine instruments
Local anaesthetic for wound or caudal block
steps: Confirm identity, side and written consent, mark the side and complete the WHO checklist and time-out.
Under general anaesthesia with caudal or local block, make an inguinal skin crease incision.
Identify the cord and find the patent processus vaginalis on its anteromedial side.
Separate the processus from the vas and vessels gently.
Divide the processus and ligate the proximal end high at the internal ring.
Drain the hydrocele fluid by opening the distal sac widely or pressing the fluid out.
Do not excise the distal sac extensively in children.
Make sure the testis lies in the scrotum.
Close the wound in layers and record findings.
aftercare: Give simple analgesia
Explain that some scrotal swelling can persist for a few weeks
Review in 4-6 weeks
red_flags: Increasing or tense scrotal swelling
Fever or wound discharge
High or absent testis on review
Persistent hydrocele beyond 3 months

indications: Umbilical hernia persisting beyond 4-5 years of age
Large defect unlikely to close spontaneously, per surgeon
Incarceration, strangulation or skin ulceration
contraindications: Small hernia in a child under 4 years without complications (observe; most close)
Acute illness or local skin infection
equipment: Absorbable or non-absorbable sutures for the fascia per surgeon
Local anaesthetic for wound infiltration or rectus sheath block
steps: Confirm identity and written consent and complete the WHO checklist and time-out.
Under general anaesthesia, make a curved infraumbilical incision in the skin crease.
Dissect around the hernia sac and separate it from the underside of the umbilical skin without making a hole.
Open or reduce the sac and return any contents.
Excise excess sac and identify the fascial edges of the defect.
Close the fascial defect transversely with interrupted sutures.
Tack the umbilical skin down to the fascia to recreate the umbilicus.
Close the skin with subcuticular absorbable sutures.
Apply a pressure dressing to reduce haematoma.
Record defect size and repair method.
aftercare: Keep the pressure dressing on for 48 hours
Give simple analgesia
Avoid heavy straining or contact sport for 2 weeks
Review in 2-4 weeks
red_flags: Swelling, bruising or bleeding under the dressing
Fever, wound redness or discharge
Vomiting or abdominal pain
Recurrent bulge at the umbilicus

indications: Anorectal malformation needing definitive repair, after colostomy or as a primary repair in suitable cases
Perineal or vestibular fistula suitable for primary repair in the neonatal period or infancy per surgeon
contraindications: Child not fit for prolonged anaesthesia
Distal colostogram not done when colostomy is present (needed to define the fistula)
Associated cardiac, renal or spinal anomalies not yet screened
equipment: Paediatric major set with fine instruments and self-retaining retractor
steps: Review the distal colostogram and screening for VACTERL anomalies, and plan the repair.
Confirm identity and written consent (including continence expectations) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and insert a urinary catheter.
Under general anaesthesia, position prone with the pelvis raised.
Map the external sphincter and muscle complex with the electrical stimulator and mark the centre.
Make a midline posterior sagittal incision from the coccyx towards the anal dimple, dividing the muscle exactly in the midline.
Identify the rectum, place traction sutures and separate it from the urethra or vagina, closing the fistula.
Mobilise the rectum enough to reach the perineum without tension.
Place the rectum within the limits of the muscle complex and reconstruct the muscles behind it.
Perform the anoplasty with interrupted sutures to the skin at the marked centre.
Close the wound in layers and record the anatomy, fistula level and sacral and muscle quality.
aftercare: Keep the urinary catheter for the time advised for the fistula level
Nurse with legs apart or prone and keep the wound clean
Start an anal dilatation programme about 2 weeks after surgery as taught by the surgeon
Plan colostomy closure after the dilatation programme, and long-term bowel management follow-up
red_flags: Wound breakdown or perineal infection
Urine leaking from the wound or perineum
Difficulty passing urine after catheter removal
Anal stenosis or bleeding during dilatation
Abdominal distension or fever

name: Divided sigmoid colostomy for anorectal malformation

indications: Newborn with anorectal malformation without a perineal fistula after 24 hours of observation
High or intermediate malformation, cloaca, or unclear anatomy
Associated anomalies or poor condition making primary repair unsafe
contraindications: Low malformation with perineal fistula suitable for primary repair (colostomy not needed)
Uncorrected shock or hypothermia (stabilise first)
equipment: Saline for washing out the distal loop
steps: Resuscitate, keep warm, decompress with a nasogastric tube and screen for associated anomalies.
Confirm identity and written consent, explain stoma care and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Under general anaesthesia, make a left lower quadrant oblique incision.
Identify the sigmoid colon where it leaves the retroperitoneum and choose a point allowing a long distal limb.
Divide the colon, bringing the proximal end out as the colostomy and the distal end as a separate small mucous fistula.
Place the stomas far enough apart for a bag to fit over the colostomy alone.
Wash out meconium from the distal loop to reduce urinary infection.
Mature both stomas with interrupted absorbable sutures.
Close the wound between the stomas and apply a stoma bag.
Record anatomy and stoma sites.
aftercare: Start feeds when the stoma works
Teach parents stoma care and bag changes before discharge
Monitor for urinary infection and dehydration
Arrange distal colostogram before definitive repair
red_flags: Dusky, black or retracted stoma
No stoma output with abdominal distension or vomiting
Stoma prolapse or bleeding
Fever or offensive urine (rectourinary fistula infection)
High stoma output with dehydration

indications: Hirschsprung disease confirmed on rectal biopsy (absent ganglion cells)
Child with levelling colostomy ready for definitive repair
contraindications: Active enterocolitis (treat and decompress first)
Diagnosis not confirmed histologically
Severe malnutrition or unfit for anaesthesia (decompress with washouts or stoma first)
equipment: Paediatric major set and transanal retractor (or stay sutures)
Access to frozen-section histology or marked serial biopsies
steps: Prepare the bowel with rectal washouts per protocol and review the contrast enema.
Confirm identity and written consent (including stoma and continence risks) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and insert a urinary catheter.
Under general anaesthesia, take seromuscular biopsies to map the transition zone.
Confirm ganglion cells at the planned level by frozen section or reliable intraoperative histology.
For transanal endorectal pull-through, start the mucosal dissection above the dentate line and continue to the peritoneal reflection.
Mobilise the aganglionic rectum and colon, dividing mesenteric vessels, until normal ganglionated bowel reaches the anus without tension.
For Duhamel, bring ganglionated colon behind the rectum and create a side-to-side anastomosis.
Resect the aganglionic bowel and send it for histology with the proximal margin marked.
Perform the coloanal anastomosis with interrupted absorbable sutures, preserving the dentate line.
Check haemostasis, close any abdominal wounds and record level and technique.
aftercare: Keep nil by mouth or start feeds per surgeon and monitor abdomen
Protect perianal skin with barrier cream as stools are frequent
Calibrate or dilate the anastomosis if advised
Teach parents enterocolitis warning signs and arrange long-term bowel follow-up
red_flags: Abdominal distension, fever, explosive or foul diarrhoea (enterocolitis - urgent review and washouts)
Bleeding per rectum
Constipation or obstructive symptoms returning
Perianal wound breakdown or abscess

indications: Suspected Hirschsprung disease in an infant (delayed meconium, distension, chronic constipation from birth)
Abnormal contrast enema suggesting a transition zone
contraindications: Active enterocolitis (treat first)
Bleeding disorder or low platelets
Older child with thick submucosa (use full-thickness biopsy under anaesthesia)
equipment: Rectal suction biopsy device with capsule
Suction source or syringe for the device
Specimen containers per laboratory (formalin and fresh or frozen as required)
steps: Confirm identity and written consent, check clotting or platelets if indicated, and label specimen containers.
Position the infant supine with legs held flexed, or in the left lateral position.
Lubricate the device and insert it gently into the rectum with the capsule window on the posterior wall.
Take biopsies at about 2, 3 and 5 cm above the anal verge, avoiding the anal canal.
Apply suction, fire the blade and withdraw the device for each biopsy.
Check each specimen contains enough submucosa before sending.
Place specimens in the correct containers for routine and special stains.
Check for bleeding after the last biopsy.
aftercare: Observe for 30-60 minutes for bleeding
Allow normal feeds
Explain a little blood in the next stool is common
Arrange review with histology result
red_flags: More than streaks of blood in the stool
Abdominal distension, fever or vomiting (possible perforation or enterocolitis)
Inadequate samples - repeat or take full-thickness biopsy

form.label: Highest biopsy level above anal verge

indications: Decompression in suspected or confirmed Hirschsprung disease while awaiting surgery
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (with IV fluids and antibiotics)
Bowel preparation before pull-through surgery
contraindications: Suspected perforation or peritonitis
Recent rectal or anastomotic surgery unless the surgeon advises
equipment: Soft rectal tube 12-20 Fr according to size
steps: Confirm identity, explain to the parent and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and apron, and warm the saline to body temperature.
Position the child supine with legs raised or in the left lateral position on a waterproof pad.
Lubricate the tube and insert it gently past the transition zone, rotating without force.
Allow gas and stool to drain first.
Instil a small volume of warm saline by syringe, then let it drain back by gravity.
Repeat, gently moving the tube and massaging the abdomen, until the return is clear or the agreed total volume is reached.
Record the volume instilled and returned, checking that most of the fluid comes back.
Remove the tube, clean the child and reassess the abdomen.
aftercare: Repeat washouts as prescribed, usually once or twice daily
Teach parents to do washouts at home if planned
Monitor fluid balance in small infants
red_flags: Fresh bleeding or severe pain during the washout - stop
Much less fluid returned than instilled (risk of fluid absorption)
Fever, worsening distension, lethargy or foul diarrhoea (enterocolitis)
Abdominal rigidity or tenderness (possible perforation)

indications: Malrotation with midgut volvulus (emergency)
Malrotation with symptoms of intermittent obstruction or bilious vomiting
Malrotation found incidentally per surgeon's judgement
contraindications: None absolute when volvulus is suspected (resuscitate during preparation, do not delay)
equipment: Paediatric laparotomy set or laparoscopic set
Warm saline packs and warm IV fluids
steps: Resuscitate with IV fluids, decompress with a nasogastric tube and cross-match blood.
Confirm identity and written consent (including possible bowel resection, stoma or second-look) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Under general anaesthesia, open the abdomen through a right upper transverse incision and eviscerate the small bowel.
Untwist the volvulus by rotating the bowel counter-clockwise until the mesentery is flat.
Wrap the bowel in warm packs and assess viability.
Divide Ladd's bands crossing the duodenum and straighten the duodenum along the right side.
Widen the base of the small bowel mesentery by separating the duodenum and caecum.
Perform appendicectomy, as the appendix will lie in an abnormal position.
Place the small bowel on the right side and the colon on the left side of the abdomen.
Resect clearly dead bowel; if viability is doubtful, close temporarily and plan a second look within 24-48 hours.
Close the abdomen and record findings and bowel length remaining.
aftercare: Continue nasogastric drainage and IV fluids until bowel function returns
Monitor perfusion, urine output, lactate and blood gases where available
Start feeds gradually
Plan nutrition support if short bowel is likely
red_flags: Worsening acidosis, shock or abdominal distension (ischaemic bowel - consider second look)
Bloody stools
Persistent bilious aspirate
Recurrent obstructive symptoms later

name: Biopsy and staging for Burkitt lymphoma

indications: Rapidly growing jaw, orbital, abdominal or nodal mass suspicious of Burkitt lymphoma
Tissue diagnosis and staging before chemotherapy
contraindications: Airway compromise from a large mass under anaesthesia (involve anaesthetist; prefer least invasive sample)
Uncorrected tumour lysis or severe metabolic derangement (start hydration and correct first)
Extensive surgical debulking (not indicated; biopsy only)
equipment: Fine needle aspiration set (21-23G needles, syringes, slides, fixative)
Core biopsy needle or minor surgical set for incisional biopsy
Local anaesthetic and sedation or anaesthesia as needed
Lumbar puncture needle and sterile CSF containers
Specimen containers (formalin and fresh for flow cytometry if available)
steps: Confirm identity and written consent and explain the plan to the family, including the urgency of starting treatment.
Check full blood count, renal function, electrolytes, uric acid, LDH and HIV status, and start IV hydration to prevent tumour lysis.
Choose the most accessible, least invasive diagnostic sample (pleural or ascitic fluid, FNA, core or small incisional biopsy).
Perform hand hygiene, use aseptic technique and give local anaesthetic, sedation or anaesthesia as appropriate.
Take the sample, avoiding extensive dissection or tumour debulking.
Make air-dried and fixed smears and send tissue in formalin and fresh where flow cytometry is available.
Perform bone marrow aspiration for marrow involvement.
Perform lumbar puncture for CSF cytology, coordinating with the first intrathecal treatment where the protocol allows.
Arrange abdominal ultrasound and chest X-ray to stage disease.
Assign the stage (St Jude/Murphy) and refer to the oncology team promptly.
aftercare: Continue hydration and monitor urine output, electrolytes, uric acid and renal function
Check the biopsy site for bleeding
Chase histology and cytology urgently
Counsel the family and link with social support for treatment costs
red_flags: Falling urine output, rising potassium, creatinine or uric acid (tumour lysis)
Breathing difficulty or stridor from a jaw, neck or mediastinal mass
Paraplegia, cranial nerve palsy or headache (CNS involvement)
Bleeding from the biopsy site

indications: CNS prophylaxis or treatment in leukaemia or lymphoma as prescribed by the oncology protocol
contraindications: Raised intracranial pressure or focal neurological signs without imaging
Platelet count or coagulation below the threshold in the treatment protocol
Skin infection at the puncture site
Any doubt about the drug, route or patient identity (stop until resolved)
equipment: Spinal needles 22G of the right length for size
Sterile pack, gown, gloves, drapes and antiseptic
Local anaesthetic and sedation or anaesthesia as planned
Intrathecal drug syringes from pharmacy, labelled for intrathecal use only
steps: Give intrathecal chemotherapy only in a designated area by trained, authorised staff.
Confirm identity, written consent and the protocol prescription, and check the full blood count and clotting are within the protocol limits.
Collect the intrathecal drugs from pharmacy only at the time of the procedure.
Make sure no IV-only chemotherapy, especially vinca alkaloids (fatal if given intrathecally), is present in the area.
Do an independent two-person check of patient, drug, dose, route, expiry and label against the prescription and sign the register.
Position the child curled in the lateral or sitting position held by a trained assistant, with sedation or anaesthesia as planned.
Identify the L3-L4 or L4-L5 space, then clean and drape with full asepsis.
Give local anaesthetic and insert the spinal needle until CSF flows.
Collect CSF for cytology, cell count and protein before injecting.
Repeat the two-person verbal check at the bedside, then inject the drug slowly.
Remove the needle, apply a dressing and record drug, batch and time.
aftercare: Lie flat or as advised by the protocol after the injection
Monitor vital signs and neurological status while sedation wears off
Watch for headache, back pain or leg symptoms
Send CSF samples and chase results
red_flags: Any suspicion that the wrong drug or route was used - stop and escalate immediately
Severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness or fever
Leg weakness, numbness, seizures or confusion
Bleeding or CSF leak from the puncture site

indications: Symptomatic or progressive hydrocephalus confirmed on imaging
Hydrocephalus after myelomeningocele repair
Failed or unsuitable endoscopic third ventriculostomy
contraindications: Active CSF infection or ventriculitis (treat and clear CSF first)
Peritonitis, abdominal infection or necrotising enterocolitis
Very high CSF protein or blood in CSF (risk of blockage - consider temporary drainage)
Skin infection or breakdown along the shunt route
equipment: Shunt system (ventricular catheter, valve, peritoneal catheter) of the chosen pressure
steps: Review imaging, OFC trend and CSF results, and confirm there is no infection.
Confirm identity and written consent (including shunt failure and infection risk) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and minimise theatre traffic.
Under general anaesthesia, position supine with the head turned and shoulder raised, then prepare head, neck and abdomen together.
Make a curved scalp incision at the chosen frontal or parieto-occipital entry point and create a burr hole.
Make a small abdominal incision and open the peritoneum under direct vision.
Tunnel the shunt passer subcutaneously from scalp to abdomen and pull the catheter through.
Open the dura and insert the ventricular catheter to the planned depth, confirming CSF flow.
Send CSF for microscopy, protein and culture.
Connect the ventricular catheter to the valve and secure all connections.
Confirm spontaneous CSF drip from the distal catheter and place it in the peritoneal cavity.
Close both wounds in layers without the shunt lying under the incision line.
aftercare: Nurse flat or as advised and monitor OFC, fontanelle and neurological status
Check wounds daily and keep them dry
Teach parents signs of shunt blockage and infection
Arrange follow-up imaging and clinic review
red_flags: Vomiting, irritability, drowsiness, bulging fontanelle or sunset eyes (shunt blockage)
Fever, wound redness or fluid along the shunt track (infection)
Abdominal pain, distension or tube visible at the anus or wound (abdominal complication)
Headache or drowsiness on standing (over-drainage)

indications: Obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus, such as aqueductal stenosis or posterior fossa obstruction
Shunt malfunction in a child with obstructive hydrocephalus, per neurosurgeon
Infant hydrocephalus suitable for ETV with choroid plexus cauterisation, per neurosurgeon
contraindications: Communicating hydrocephalus (except selected infants for ETV with choroid plexus cauterisation, per neurosurgeon)
Active CSF infection or blood in CSF
Unfavourable anatomy on imaging (very narrow third ventricle or prepontine space)
equipment: Neuroendoscope with camera, light source and monitor
Fogarty balloon catheter or blunt probe for fenestration
steps: Review imaging and calculate the ETV success score, and confirm there is no infection.
Confirm identity and written consent (including possible failure and conversion to shunt) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Under general anaesthesia, position supine with the head slightly flexed and fixed.
Make a frontal burr hole at or just in front of the coronal suture.
Insert the endoscope into the lateral ventricle and send CSF for analysis.
Pass through the foramen of Monro into the third ventricle using landmarks.
Perforate the floor of the third ventricle in the midline between the mammillary bodies and infundibular recess, behind the clivus.
Enlarge the stoma with balloon dilatation and confirm free movement of the floor and a clear prepontine space.
Cauterise the choroid plexus where planned.
Irrigate, check for bleeding, withdraw the endoscope and close the dura and wound in layers.
aftercare: Monitor neurological status, fontanelle and OFC
Check electrolytes, as sodium disturbance can occur
Arrange follow-up clinical review and imaging
Teach parents signs of failure
red_flags: Vomiting, drowsiness, bulging fontanelle or rising OFC (ETV failure)
Fever or neck stiffness (infection)
New weakness, eye movement problems or seizures
CSF leak from the wound

indications: Open neural tube defect in a newborn (ideally close within 72 hours of birth)
Leaking or ruptured sac
contraindications: Unstable newborn not fit for anaesthesia (cover with sterile moist dressing and stabilise)
Severe associated anomalies where the family and team agree on comfort care
steps: At birth, nurse prone, cover the lesion with a sterile saline-moistened non-adherent dressing and plastic cover, and use latex-free equipment.
Examine for level of neurological deficit, hydrocephalus, club feet and bladder function and record OFC.
Confirm identity and written consent (including future hydrocephalus and continence issues) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Under general anaesthesia in the prone position, keep the baby warm.
Incise around the placode at the junction of skin and arachnoid membrane.
Free the neural placode and excise the epithelial remnants so no skin is left attached.
Reconstitute the neural tube by suturing the pial edges where possible.
Close the dura watertight over the placode.
Close the fascia where available and mobilise the skin to close without tension, using relaxing incisions or flaps if needed.
Apply a dressing and record level, defect size and closure method.
aftercare: Nurse prone or on the side and keep the wound free of stool and urine
Measure OFC daily and scan for hydrocephalus
Start clean intermittent catheterisation teaching if the bladder does not empty
Refer to physiotherapy, orthopaedics and urology follow-up and use latex precautions
red_flags: Wound breakdown or CSF leak
Fever, irritability or neck stiffness (meningitis)
Rising OFC, bulging fontanelle or vomiting (hydrocephalus)
Stridor, apnoea or swallowing problems (Chiari II)

indications: Encephalocele with thin or leaking covering (urgent)
Skin-covered encephalocele for elective repair once the baby is fit
contraindications: Unstable infant not fit for anaesthesia
Very large defect with most of the brain in the sac where the family and team agree on comfort care
steps: Review imaging to define sac contents, venous sinuses and hydrocephalus.
Confirm identity and written consent (including possible shunt and developmental outcome) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and cross-match blood.
Under general anaesthesia, position the baby (prone for occipital lesions) with the airway secured carefully.
Incise the skin around the neck of the sac, preserving enough skin for closure.
Open the sac and inspect the contents.
Excise non-functional, gliotic brain tissue in the sac, preserving functional tissue and avoiding venous sinuses.
Close the dura watertight, using a graft if needed.
Close the bony defect where needed and the skin in layers without tension.
Record location, contents and closure.
aftercare: Monitor OFC, fontanelle and neurological status
Check the wound for CSF leak
Scan for hydrocephalus and plan shunt or ETV if needed
Arrange developmental and eye follow-up
red_flags: CSF leak or wound breakdown
Fever, irritability or seizures
Rising OFC or bulging fontanelle
Apnoea or feeding difficulty

indications: Infant with ankyloglossia causing breastfeeding difficulty despite feeding support
Older child with tongue-tie affecting speech or oral function (usually under anaesthesia)
contraindications: Bleeding disorder or family history of bleeding not yet assessed
Micrognathia or neuromuscular disease where the tongue helps the airway
Thick vascular frenulum or older child needing general anaesthesia (refer)
Tongue-tie not causing any problem
equipment: Grooved director or gloved fingers to lift the tongue
steps: Confirm identity, assess the tongue function and feeding with the breastfeeding support person, and record the assessment.
Explain benefits and risks (bleeding, infection, recurrence) and obtain consent from the parent.
Check vitamin K was given at birth.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves.
Swaddle the infant, give comfort measures such as breastfeeding or oral sucrose, and have an assistant hold the head steady.
Lift the tongue with the grooved director or fingers to show the frenulum.
Divide the thin frenulum with one or two small cuts close to the tongue, avoiding the sublingual ducts and vessels.
Press with gauze for a minute if there is bleeding.
Give the infant to the mother to breastfeed immediately.
Watch a feed to check latch and comfort.
aftercare: Breastfeed straight away and often
A small white patch under the tongue is normal healing
Arrange breastfeeding review within a week
red_flags: Bleeding that does not stop with pressure
Fever, swelling or refusal to feed
Breathing difficulty
Feeding problems persisting after 2 weeks

indications: Labial adhesions causing urinary retention, dribbling, recurrent UTI or discomfort
Adhesions not resolving after a course of topical oestrogen
contraindications: Asymptomatic adhesions (usually resolve; reassure)
Thick dense adhesions (needs separation under anaesthesia - refer)
Concerns about sexual abuse not yet assessed (follow the safeguarding process first)
equipment: Cotton-tipped swabs or a fine probe
Petroleum jelly or bland barrier ointment
steps: Confirm identity, take a careful history and examine with a chaperone, considering safeguarding if there are concerns.
Explain to the parent and child (assent), and obtain verbal consent.
Apply topical anaesthetic to the adhesion and wait for it to work.
Position the child supine in frog-leg position with the parent comforting her.
Apply gentle lateral traction to the labia majora to show the fine line of adhesion.
Separate the adhesion gently with a cotton-tipped swab or probe along the midline, without force.
Stop if the adhesion is thick or the child is distressed, and refer for separation under anaesthesia.
Apply petroleum jelly to the raw edges.
Check that the urethra and vaginal opening are visible and the child can pass urine.
aftercare: Apply petroleum jelly to the separated edges daily for several weeks to prevent re-adhesion
Avoid bubble baths and irritant soaps
Explain that recurrence is common until puberty
red_flags: Unable to pass urine after the procedure
Bleeding or severe pain
Fever or burning on passing urine
Recurrence with urinary symptoms

indications: Child usually 1-5 years holding the arm still after a sudden pull on the hand or forearm, with no swelling or deformity
contraindications: Fall or direct injury, swelling, bruising, deformity or point bony tenderness (X-ray first to exclude fracture)
Neurovascular deficit
equipment: None needed beyond a calm environment
Toy or sticker to test arm use afterwards
steps: Confirm identity and take a history of the mechanism, checking for any fall or direct blow.
Examine the whole arm for swelling, bruising, deformity, bony tenderness and neurovascular status.
Explain the manoeuvre and brief discomfort to the parent and obtain verbal consent.
Seat the child on the parent's lap facing you.
Hold the child's elbow with your thumb over the radial head and the wrist with your other hand.
Hyperpronate the forearm firmly; if no click, supinate the forearm and flex the elbow fully.
Feel for a click over the radial head, which suggests reduction.
Distract the child and observe for 15-30 minutes for normal use of the arm, such as reaching for a toy.
If two attempts fail, or the child still does not use the arm, X-ray and review.
aftercare: Advise parents to avoid lifting or swinging the child by the hands or forearms
Explain that recurrence is common in young children
No sling needed if the child uses the arm normally
red_flags: Child still not using the arm after 30 minutes or two attempts
Swelling, bruising or tenderness suggesting fracture
Numbness, pale or cold hand
Recurrent episodes (review technique advice and consider other causes)

indications: Temporary bladder drainage in posterior urethral valves when primary valve ablation is not possible
Neurogenic bladder with high pressures or upper tract dilatation not manageable with catheterisation
Prune belly syndrome or severe reflux with poor drainage, per urologist
contraindications: Child who can be managed with clean intermittent catheterisation or primary valve ablation
Uncorrected sepsis or severe metabolic derangement (stabilise first)
steps: Stabilise renal function and electrolytes and treat infection with catheter drainage first.
Confirm identity and written consent (including that the stoma is temporary) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Under general anaesthesia, fill the bladder through the catheter.
Make a small transverse incision midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis.
Open the rectus sheath and expose the dome of the bladder, pushing the peritoneum up.
Bring the bladder dome up to the skin, fixing it to the rectus sheath to prevent prolapse.
Open the dome and suture the bladder mucosa to the skin to make a stoma that admits the agreed size.
Check that urine drains freely and remove the urethral catheter.
Record the stoma size and position.
aftercare: Urine drains into the nappy; change nappies often and protect the skin
Monitor renal function, electrolytes and urine output
Teach parents stoma care and signs of infection
Plan definitive surgery and closure with the urologist
red_flags: Stoma stops draining or child is in pain with a full bladder (stenosis)
Bladder mucosa prolapses through the stoma
Fever or offensive urine (UTI)
Bleeding or severe skin excoriation

indications: Posterior urethral valves confirmed on micturating cystourethrogram or cystoscopy
Boy with valves stabilised on catheter drainage with improving renal function
contraindications: Urethra too small for the available cystoscope (use vesicostomy or wait for growth)
Untreated urinary sepsis or severe metabolic derangement (stabilise on catheter first)
equipment: Paediatric cystoscope 7.5-9.5 Fr with working channel, or neonatal resectoscope
Cold knife, hook or Bugbee electrode, or laser fibre
Diathermy unit set for low power
Feeding tube or Foley catheter 6-8 Fr
Fogarty balloon catheter if endoscope unavailable for valve disruption
steps: Drain the bladder by catheter until renal function, electrolytes and infection are controlled.
Confirm identity and written consent and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol.
Under general anaesthesia, position in lithotomy and calibrate the urethra.
Pass the cystoscope gently and inspect the urethra, valves, bladder neck and bladder.
Identify the valve leaflets distal to the verumontanum.
Incise the leaflets at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions, and at 12 o'clock if needed, avoiding the external sphincter.
Check that the leaflets are disrupted and that suprapubic pressure produces a good stream.
Inspect for bleeding or urethral injury.
Leave a urethral catheter for the time advised by the surgeon.
Record the valve type, positions incised and catheter size.
aftercare: Monitor urine output, renal function and electrolytes, watching for post-obstructive diuresis
Remove the catheter as planned and observe voiding
Arrange repeat imaging or check cystoscopy to confirm adequate ablation
Lifelong follow-up of renal function, bladder function and growth
red_flags: Poor stream, straining or retention after catheter removal
Fever or offensive urine
Very high urine output with dehydration
Rising creatinine
Haematuria with clots

indications: Unilateral Wilms tumour after preoperative chemotherapy per protocol (or upfront surgery where the protocol advises)
Renal tumour in a child needing tissue diagnosis and local control
contraindications: Bilateral tumours (nephron-sparing approach in a specialist centre)
Tumour thrombus extending above the hepatic veins without cardiac surgical support
Unresectable tumour invading adjacent organs (more chemotherapy first)
Uncorrected anaemia, hypertension or poor nutrition (optimise first)
equipment: Paediatric major laparotomy set with self-retaining retractors
steps: Review imaging for the contralateral kidney, IVC and lungs, and confirm the chemotherapy given.
Confirm identity, side and written consent, mark the side and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and cross-match blood.
Under general anaesthesia, make a generous transverse upper abdominal transperitoneal incision.
Inspect the liver, peritoneum and contralateral kidney if not well imaged.
Mobilise the colon and expose the renal vessels, checking the renal vein and IVC for thrombus.
Ligate the renal artery before the vein where safe.
Remove the kidney, tumour, perinephric fat and ureter en bloc, handling the tumour gently to avoid rupture.
Sample hilar, para-aortic and paracaval lymph nodes even if they look normal.
Record any tumour spill or rupture and mark suspicious residual areas with clips.
Send the specimen fresh or fixed per oncology protocol with orientation.
Check haemostasis and close in layers.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output, blood pressure and haemoglobin
Give analgesia and continue nasogastric drainage until bowel function returns
Restart chemotherapy per protocol, usually within 2-3 weeks
Arrange oncology review with histology and stage
red_flags: Signs of bleeding (tachycardia, pallor, falling blood pressure)
Falling urine output or rising creatinine
Abdominal distension, vomiting or fever
Wound infection or dehiscence

indications: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis in a young child who cannot produce sputum
Follow-up sampling when other samples are unavailable
contraindications: Low platelets or bleeding disorder
Reduced consciousness without airway protection
Suspected basal skull fracture or facial trauma
equipment: Nasogastric tube 6-10 Fr according to size
steps: Explain to the caregiver the day before that the child must fast for the period in the national TB guideline (usually a few hours, shorter in young infants) and stay lying in bed in the morning.
On waking, before the child eats, drinks or gets up, confirm identity and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and measure the tube from nose to earlobe to midway between xiphisternum and umbilicus.
Insert the tube and confirm position by aspirating gastric content or with pH strips.
Aspirate the gastric content slowly with a syringe into the sterile container.
If little or no fluid is aspirated, instil a small volume of sterile water or saline and aspirate again.
Add neutralising buffer if the sample cannot reach the laboratory within an hour.
Remove the tube, label the sample and send it promptly for testing.
Allow the child to eat and drink.
Repeat on further mornings as requested, usually for 2-3 days.
aftercare: Give the child breakfast straight after
Record the volume and time sent
Use other sample types (induced sputum, stool) for Xpert testing where available
red_flags: Respiratory distress, coughing or cyanosis during insertion (remove tube)
Blood-stained aspirate
Child deteriorating clinically while awaiting results - do not delay empirical treatment if indicated

form.label: Fasted per protocol and still in bed
Sterile fluid instilled to obtain sample

indications: Hypospadias with abnormal meatal position, chordee or hooded foreskin affecting function or appearance
Ideally repaired between 6 and 18 months of age
contraindications: Circumcision before repair (the foreskin may be needed; advise families not to circumcise)
Proximal hypospadias with undescended testes not yet assessed for disorder of sex development
Active urinary or skin infection
equipment: Fine plastic surgery set with magnification loupes
Tourniquet for the penile base if used
Urethral stent or feeding tube 6-8 Fr
Local anaesthetic for penile or caudal block
steps: Examine meatal position, chordee, glans and testes, and plan the repair.
Confirm identity and written consent (including fistula and redo risk) and complete the WHO checklist.
Under general anaesthesia with caudal or penile block, place a glans traction suture.
Mark and make a circumcoronal incision and deglove the penis to the penoscrotal junction.
Perform an artificial erection test and correct any chordee.
Create the new urethra using the chosen technique (such as tubularised incised plate) over a stent.
Cover the neourethra with a vascularised dartos or tunica vaginalis flap.
Perform glansplasty to bring the meatus to the tip.
Reconstruct the skin cover with preputial or penile skin.
Secure the stent and apply a compressive dressing.
Record the meatal position before and after, technique and stent size.
aftercare: Keep the stent draining into a double nappy for the time advised
Give regular analgesia and treat bladder spasm per local protocol
Remove the dressing and stent on the planned day
Review after 6 weeks and at toilet training to check the stream
red_flags: Stent blocked or falls out early
Swelling, dark discolouration or bleeding of the penis
Urine leaking from another opening (fistula)
Thin stream or straining (meatal stenosis or stricture)
Fever or offensive urine

indications: Redundant foreskin after incomplete circumcision
Skin bridges, adhesions or cicatrix trapping the glans
Concealed or trapped penis after circumcision
Asymmetric or excess skin causing hygiene problems or recurrent infection
contraindications: Hypospadias or other penile anomaly found (refer for planned reconstruction)
Active infection (treat first)
Bleeding disorder not assessed (check family history; screen if positive)
equipment: Paraffin gauze or petroleum jelly dressing
Local anaesthetic for dorsal penile or caudal block
steps: Examine to define the problem and exclude hypospadias, buried penis or meatal stenosis.
Confirm identity and written consent and complete the WHO checklist and time-out.
Under anaesthesia with a dorsal penile or caudal block, free any adhesions between the glans and shaft skin.
Divide skin bridges and excise the scar tissue.
Mark and excise redundant skin, keeping enough shaft skin for erection without tethering.
For a trapped or concealed penis, release the cicatrix and anchor the skin at the base if needed.
Achieve careful haemostasis with bipolar diathermy only.
Approximate the skin edges with fine absorbable sutures.
Check the meatus and do a meatotomy if it is stenosed.
Apply petroleum jelly and a light dressing.
aftercare: Apply petroleum jelly to the wound at each nappy change for about a week
Give simple analgesia
Let the child pass urine before discharge
Review in 1-2 weeks
red_flags: Bleeding that does not stop with gentle pressure for 10 minutes
Unable to pass urine for more than 8 hours
Increasing swelling, discolouration or pus
Fever

indications: Lymphatic malformation of the neck, axilla or elsewhere causing pressure, deformity, infection or bleeding
Lesion not suitable for, or not responding to, sclerotherapy
contraindications: Macrocystic lesion suitable for sclerotherapy where available (consider first)
Active infection in the lesion (treat first)
Extensive involvement of the airway or mediastinum without specialist airway support
equipment: Paediatric major set with fine dissecting instruments
Bipolar diathermy and nerve stimulator if available
Difficult airway equipment and tracheostomy set
steps: Review imaging (ultrasound, CT or MRI) to define extent, cyst type and relation to airway and nerves.
Plan the airway with the anaesthetist and have a tracheostomy set ready.
Confirm identity and written consent (including nerve injury, recurrence and drain) and complete the WHO checklist.
Under general anaesthesia, make a skin crease incision over the lesion.
Raise flaps and dissect the cysts off surrounding structures, keeping them intact where possible.
Identify and preserve the marginal mandibular, spinal accessory, hypoglossal, vagus and phrenic nerves as relevant.
Avoid sacrificing vital structures; leave residual tissue on them and treat it later if needed.
Ligate lymphatic channels to reduce lymph leak.
Place a suction drain and close in layers.
Record extent of excision and nerves identified.
aftercare: Monitor the airway closely in the first 24 hours
Record drain output and remove when it is low
Watch for seroma, which may need aspiration
Follow up for recurrence
red_flags: Stridor, breathing difficulty or neck swelling (airway compromise)
Facial asymmetry, drooping shoulder or tongue deviation (nerve injury)
Fever, redness or tense swelling (infection or seroma)
Persistent high milky drain output

indications: Sacrococcygeal teratoma diagnosed antenatally or at birth (excise early in the neonatal period)
Recurrent sacrococcygeal mass
contraindications: Haemodynamically unstable newborn (resuscitate, correct coagulopathy, then operate urgently)
Large intrapelvic or abdominal component not yet imaged (plan combined approach)
equipment: Cross-matched blood and fresh frozen plasma available
Rectal tube or Hegar dilator to identify the rectum
