steps: Image the pelvis and abdomen to define the intrapelvic extent, and send alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG.
Confirm identity and written consent (including bleeding, continence and recurrence risk) and complete the WHO checklist.
Cross-match blood, place good IV access and keep the baby warm.
Under general anaesthesia, start with laparotomy to control the median sacral vessels if there is a large pelvic component.
Position prone and make a chevron incision over the sacrum, preserving skin for closure.
Place a tube or dilator in the rectum to identify it throughout the dissection.
Dissect the tumour from the gluteal muscles and rectum, keeping the capsule intact.
Ligate the median sacral vessels early to reduce bleeding.
Excise the tumour en bloc with the coccyx, as leaving the coccyx increases recurrence.
Reconstruct the pelvic floor and anal sphincter muscles and close the skin in layers.
Send the specimen for histology and record capsule rupture and blood loss.
aftercare: Nurse prone and keep the wound clean of stool and urine
Monitor haemoglobin, temperature and urine output
Check alpha-fetoprotein every few months for at least 3 years to detect recurrence
Follow up bowel and bladder function
red_flags: Signs of bleeding or shock
Wound infection or breakdown
New swelling or rising alpha-fetoprotein on follow-up
Constipation, urinary retention or leg weakness

indications: Classic bladder exstrophy (primary closure in a specialist centre)
Isolated epispadias causing incontinence or penile deformity
Staged reconstruction after earlier closure
contraindications: Bladder plate too small for closure (refer for delayed or alternative reconstruction)
Centre without paediatric urology, orthopaedic and anaesthetic support for this operation (refer)
Active infection or unstable infant
equipment: Paediatric major and fine reconstructive sets
Orthopaedic osteotomy set if osteotomy planned
Immobilisation equipment (spica cast, traction or mummy wrap)
Epidural or caudal catheter for analgesia
steps: Protect the bladder plate from birth with cling film, avoiding gauze that sticks, and refer to a specialist team.
Assess bladder plate size, pubic diastasis, genitalia and kidneys.
Confirm identity and written consent (including staged surgery and continence outlook) and complete the WHO checklist.
Give prophylactic antibiotics per local protocol and plan epidural or caudal analgesia.
Perform pelvic osteotomies first if planned, depending on age and diastasis.
Separate the bladder plate from the surrounding skin and mobilise it into the pelvis.
Close the bladder and posterior urethra over ureteric stents and a suprapubic catheter.
Repair the epispadias at the same time or later according to the chosen approach.
Bring the pubic bones together and close the abdominal wall and umbilicus.
Immobilise the pelvis and legs as planned.
Record the stage, technique and devices left in.
aftercare: Maintain immobilisation for the planned period with careful skin care
Keep all catheters and stents draining and never let them block
Give strong analgesia and treat bladder spasm
Arrange long-term follow-up for continence, kidneys and fertility
red_flags: Catheter or stent not draining
Fever or offensive urine
Wound breakdown or bladder dehiscence
Pressure sores or circulation problems under casts or traction

indications: Annual stroke risk screening in children with HbSS or HbSβ0 thalassaemia aged 2-16 years
Repeat scan after a conditional or abnormal result
Monitoring on a stroke prevention programme
contraindications: Acute illness, fever, crisis or recent transfusion (defer the routine scan)
Child asleep or sedated (velocities are lower; rescan awake)
equipment: TCD machine with 2 MHz probe (non-imaging) or imaging ultrasound with transcranial setting
steps: Confirm identity, genotype and age, explain the scan to the child and parent and obtain verbal consent.
Check the child is well, awake and has not had a recent transfusion, and note the haemoglobin if available.
Lay the child supine and calm, with the head on a pillow.
Apply gel and place the probe on the temporal window above the zygomatic arch.
Identify the middle cerebral artery and record the time-averaged mean of maximum velocity at several depths.
Record the distal internal carotid artery and its bifurcation, and the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries where possible.
Repeat on the other side.
Take the highest MCA or ICA velocity on either side as the result.
Classify non-imaging TCD by STOP criteria (normal below 170 cm/s, conditional 170-199, abnormal 200 or above; imaging TCD uses lower local cut-offs).
Note an inadequate window or abnormally low velocities, which may need imaging.
Explain the result and plan to the family and record it.
aftercare: Normal result - rescan in 12 months
Conditional result - rescan in 3-6 months
Abnormal result - repeat within 2-4 weeks and refer urgently to haematology for stroke prevention therapy
red_flags: Abnormal velocities on repeat scan - start stroke prevention (transfusion or hydroxyurea programme) without delay
Very low velocities or inadequate window in a child with symptoms (arrange MRI or MRA)
Any new weakness, speech difficulty, seizure or severe headache (urgent stroke assessment)

form.label: Highest left MCA or ICA velocity
Highest right MCA or ICA velocity
Plan
options: Refer to haematology for stroke prevention

indications: Child with a new gastrostomy before discharge
Change of device, feeding method or caregiver
Problems at home with feeding or stoma care
contraindications: Stoma not yet healed enough for the device to be handled as taught (follow surgeon's timing)
Signs of peritonitis or tube displacement in a new tract (urgent review instead)
equipment: Child's gastrostomy device and extension sets
Enteral syringes (ENFit or local type) and feed
Feeding bag or pump if used
pH strips if the device type requires them
Spare device or a catheter of the same size for emergency tract keeping
steps: Confirm identity, assess caregiver understanding and agree goals with the family.
Explain the device type, size and parts, and when it is due for change.
Show handwashing and preparation of feed and equipment.
Show how to check the device position and, for balloon devices, the balloon water at the set interval.
Show how to attach the extension set and flush with water before and after each feed and medicine.
Demonstrate bolus feeding with the child upright, letting feed run in slowly by gravity.
Demonstrate pump or gravity bag feeding if prescribed.
Show how to give medicines one at a time with flushes between them.
Teach daily stoma cleaning, drying and rotating the device where advised.
Teach what to do if the device falls out, including covering the tract and attending within an hour.
Ask the caregiver to demonstrate each step until competent.
Give the written plan and contact numbers, and record competencies.
aftercare: Arrange a home or clinic follow-up visit
Weigh the child regularly and review feed volume with the dietitian
Supply enough equipment and feed until the next visit
red_flags: Device falls out (attend immediately; the tract can close within hours)
Pain, fever, redness or leakage of feed around the stoma
Vomiting, abdominal distension or pain during feeds
Blocked tube not cleared by warm water flushes
Weight loss or dehydration

indications: Retained secretions in pneumonia, bronchiectasis or cystic fibrosis
Lobar collapse from sputum plugging
Post-operative sputum retention
Ventilated patients with secretion build-up
contraindications: Unstable haemodynamics or active cardiac arrhythmia
Undrained pneumothorax
Active haemoptysis or pulmonary haemorrhage
Rib fractures, flail chest or unstable spine (avoid percussion)
Raised intracranial pressure (avoid head-down positions)
Severe osteoporosis or bleeding disorder (avoid percussion)
equipment: Pillows, wedges or tilting bed for positioning
Thin towel to cover the chest
Suction unit with catheters (if patient cannot clear secretions)
steps: Confirm identity, review the chest X-ray and notes, and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and check vital signs and oxygen saturation before starting.
Auscultate the chest to locate the affected lobes.
Position the patient to drain the affected segment, modifying head-down tilt if not tolerated.
Perform rhythmic percussion with cupped hands over a towel on the affected area for a few minutes.
Apply vibrations or shaking during expiration to move secretions.
Ask the patient to take deep breaths and huff or cough to clear secretions.
Suction the airway if the patient cannot cough effectively.
Monitor saturation, breathing and colour throughout and stop if the patient deteriorates.
Reassess by auscultation and note the amount and colour of sputum.
aftercare: Return the patient to a comfortable upright position with oxygen as prescribed.
Teach the patient or carer airway clearance techniques to continue between sessions.
Encourage fluids unless restricted.
red_flags: Fall in oxygen saturation that does not recover with rest and oxygen
New chest pain, haemoptysis or sudden breathlessness
Arrhythmia or marked change in heart rate or blood pressure
Signs of pneumothorax

indications: Prevention of chest complications after surgery
Chronic lung disease with breathlessness
Reduced chest expansion from pain or immobility
Dysfunctional breathing or anxiety-related breathlessness
contraindications: Acute respiratory failure needing urgent medical care
Undrained pneumothorax (for incentive spirometry and breath-holds)
equipment: Chair or bed with pillows for supported sitting
steps: Confirm identity, review the indication and obtain verbal consent.
Check vital signs, oxygen saturation and pain level.
Position the patient upright or in supported sitting.
Teach relaxed diaphragmatic breathing with one hand on the abdomen.
Teach slow deep breaths with a short hold at full inspiration.
Teach pursed-lip breathing for breathlessness where appropriate.
Use an incentive spirometer or a simple bottle-and-straw device if available and appropriate.
Practise supported coughing or huffing, splinting any wound with a pillow.
Observe technique, correct errors and check the patient can repeat it alone.
aftercare: Advise practice of the exercises regularly through the day, usually each waking hour after surgery.
Ensure adequate pain relief so deep breathing is possible.
Encourage early sitting out and walking.
red_flags: Increasing breathlessness, chest pain or confusion
Fever with productive cough after surgery
Oxygen saturation falling below the target range

indications: Unconscious or paralysed patients to prevent contractures
Stroke, spinal cord injury or other neurological weakness
Prolonged bed rest or ICU stay
Maintenance of joint range when active movement is not possible
contraindications: Unstable or unfixed fracture of the limb
Suspected deep vein thrombosis in the limb
Recent surgery where the surgeon has restricted movement
Acutely inflamed or dislocated joint
Heterotopic ossification (gentle only, specialist guidance)
equipment: Bed or plinth at a safe working height
steps: Confirm identity, check for movement restrictions in the notes and obtain verbal consent from patient or carer.
Perform hand hygiene and explain each movement even if the patient is unconscious.
Position the patient supported and comfortable with the limb exposed.
Support the limb above and below the joint being moved.
Move each joint slowly and smoothly through its available range in all planes.
Repeat each movement several times, stopping at the point of resistance or pain.
Watch the face and vital signs for signs of discomfort.
Measure range with a goniometer where needed and note any loss.
Reposition the patient in a good position to prevent contractures.
aftercare: Teach carers or nurses to repeat the movements once or twice daily.
Use positioning, splints or pillows to keep joints in functional positions.
Review skin over pressure areas.
red_flags: New calf swelling, warmth or pain (possible DVT)
Sudden loss of range, swelling or deformity (possible fracture or dislocation)
Increasing joint stiffness despite treatment

indications: Muscle weakness after injury, surgery or illness
Chronic musculoskeletal pain such as low back pain or knee osteoarthritis
Reduced endurance or deconditioning
Joint instability needing strengthening
contraindications: Unstable cardiac condition or uncontrolled hypertension
Acute fracture or soft-tissue injury not yet ready to load
Acute systemic illness with fever
equipment: Resistance bands, free weights or sandbags (or improvised weights such as filled bottles)
Step, chair and wall for functional exercises
steps: Confirm identity, review the diagnosis and precautions and obtain verbal consent.
Assess pain, strength, range and function to set measurable goals with the patient.
Check blood pressure and heart rate in patients with cardiovascular risk.
Warm up with gentle active movements.
Teach each exercise with demonstration, correcting posture and technique.
Set the resistance, repetitions and sets so the last repetitions are challenging but pain does not rise sharply.
Include strengthening, stretching and functional tasks relevant to the patient's goals.
Cool down and reassess pain and response.
Give a written or picture home programme and agree how often to do it.
aftercare: Expect mild muscle soreness for one to two days, which is normal.
Progress the programme at each review as strength improves.
Encourage regular general activity such as walking.
red_flags: Chest pain, palpitations or severe breathlessness during exercise
Pain that is much worse and lasting more than a day after exercise
New numbness, weakness or loss of bladder or bowel control

indications: Day 0 to day 2 after surgery to reduce chest infection, clots and deconditioning
After joint replacement or fracture fixation per surgeon's weight-bearing instructions
Prolonged bed rest after illness
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability or active bleeding
Surgeon's instruction for bed rest
Uncontrolled pain or nausea (treat first)
Unstable spine or unfixed fracture
equipment: Walking aid appropriate to the patient
Chair with arms placed near the bed
Pulse oximeter and blood pressure monitor
Portable oxygen, drip stand and catheter bag holder as needed
steps: Confirm identity, check the operation note for weight-bearing and movement restrictions and obtain verbal consent.
Check vital signs, pain, nausea and drains and lines before starting.
Secure drains, catheters, drips and oxygen so they move with the patient.
Help the patient roll and sit over the edge of the bed, supporting any wound.
Allow a short rest while sitting and check for dizziness.
Stand the patient with the walking aid and appropriate assistance.
March on the spot, then walk a short distance as tolerated within weight-bearing limits.
Monitor colour, breathing, saturation and symptoms throughout.
Sit the patient out in the chair or return them to bed safely.
aftercare: Agree a plan with nursing staff to sit out and walk regularly each day.
Continue breathing exercises and calf pumping between walks.
Keep the call bell and walking aid within reach.
red_flags: Fainting, marked drop in blood pressure or new arrhythmia
Sudden breathlessness or chest pain (possible pulmonary embolism)
Fresh bleeding from the wound or drains
Calf pain and swelling

indications: Abnormal walking pattern after stroke, injury or surgery
Neurological conditions such as cerebral palsy or Parkinson disease
After lower limb fracture or joint replacement
Falls risk from unsteady gait
contraindications: Unable to bear weight safely as instructed by the surgeon
Unstable cardiovascular condition
Severe postural hypotension not yet controlled
equipment: Stopwatch and measured walkway for timed walk tests
steps: Confirm identity, check weight-bearing status and obtain verbal consent.
Observe the patient walking and identify the main gait faults.
Measure baseline walking speed or a timed up-and-go test where possible.
Practise the components of gait such as weight shift, step length and heel strike, starting in parallel bars if needed.
Give clear verbal, visual or hands-on cues to correct the pattern.
Progress from parallel bars to walking aid to independent walking as safety allows.
Practise turning, obstacles and different surfaces relevant to the patient's home.
Stay close to guard against falls throughout.
Reassess and record walking aid, assistance and distance achieved.
aftercare: Give a home walking plan with safe distance and frequency.
Advise on safe footwear and removing trip hazards at home.
Review progress at the next session.
red_flags: Falls or near falls at home
New weakness, numbness or sudden change in walking
Increasing joint pain or swelling with walking

indications: Restricted weight-bearing after lower limb injury or surgery
Unsteady walking with falls risk
Lower limb pain limiting walking
contraindications: Unable to follow instructions safely (use supervised walking or wheelchair)
Insufficient upper limb strength for the chosen aid (choose another aid)
equipment: Suitable walking aid (frame, rollator, elbow or axillary crutches, stick)
Spanner or key to adjust height
Stairs or a step for practice
steps: Confirm identity, check weight-bearing instructions and obtain verbal consent.
Choose the aid based on balance, strength, weight-bearing status and home setting.
Check the aid is intact with good rubber ferrules.
Adjust the height so the handgrip is level with the wrist crease with the elbow slightly bent.
Teach sit to stand and stand to sit using the chair arms, not the aid.
Teach the walking pattern that matches the weight-bearing status.
Practise walking and turning with close supervision.
Teach stairs if needed, going up with the good leg first, down with the bad leg and aid first.
Check the patient can use the aid safely and independently before discharge.
aftercare: Advise checking ferrules regularly and replacing worn ones.
Advise removing loose rugs and clutter at home.
Give the date the aid should be reviewed or returned.
red_flags: Falls or near falls with the aid
Pain or numbness in the armpit or hands (crutches set incorrectly)
Increasing pain or swelling in the injured limb

indications: Older adults with falls or fear of falling
Balance problems after stroke or neurological disease
Ankle instability after sprain
Peripheral neuropathy affecting balance
contraindications: Acute vertigo with vomiting needing medical review
Unstable cardiovascular condition or uncontrolled postural hypotension
equipment: Stable chair, rail or parallel bars for support
Firm and foam surfaces (folded mat or cushion)
steps: Confirm identity, take a falls history and obtain verbal consent.
Measure baseline balance with a simple test such as single-leg stance or timed up-and-go.
Set up a safe area with support within reach and stand close to the patient.
Start with static balance such as feet together and tandem stance, holding support if needed.
Progress to dynamic tasks such as weight shifting, reaching and stepping.
Add challenge by reducing hand support, closing eyes or using a soft surface as safety allows.
Include sit to stand practice and lower limb strengthening.
Teach how to get up from the floor safely if appropriate.
Reassess and give a home programme done near a stable support.
aftercare: Practise the home programme most days near a kitchen counter or sturdy chair.
Review home hazards, lighting, footwear and eyesight.
Ask the doctor to review medicines that may cause dizziness.
red_flags: Repeated falls or a fall with head injury
New dizziness, double vision or slurred speech
Blackouts or fainting

indications: Joint stiffness after immobilisation or injury
Frozen shoulder
Mechanical joint pain in the spine or limbs
contraindications: Fracture, bone tumour or infection at the joint
Acute inflammatory arthritis flare
Joint hypermobility or instability
Severe osteoporosis
Suspected cauda equina or spinal cord compression (spinal mobilisation)
equipment: Plinth or couch at adjustable height
steps: Confirm identity, screen for red flags and contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Assess pain, range of movement and joint end-feel.
Position the patient relaxed and supported with the joint accessible.
Stabilise the proximal segment with one hand.
Apply gentle oscillatory or sustained glides to the distal segment at the chosen grade.
Ask about symptoms during treatment and adjust grade or stop if pain increases sharply.
Reassess range and pain after each set.
Finish with active exercises to maintain the gain.
aftercare: Expect mild soreness for up to a day.
Continue home range of movement exercises.
Review at the next session.
red_flags: Severe or increasing pain after treatment
New numbness, tingling or weakness
Joint swelling, warmth and fever

indications: Acute or subacute mechanical low back pain without red flags
Mechanical thoracic pain
Mechanical neck pain (by trained practitioners after careful screening)
contraindications: Red flags for fracture, cancer, infection or cauda equina
Osteoporosis or long-term steroid use
Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis of the neck
Signs of spinal cord compression or progressive neurological deficit
Anticoagulant therapy or bleeding disorder
Signs of vertebral or carotid artery disease (cervical manipulation)
Practitioner not trained in manipulation
steps: Confirm identity and screen thoroughly for red flags, osteoporosis and anticoagulant use.
For the neck, screen for vascular symptoms such as dizziness, double vision or drop attacks.
Explain the benefits and risks, including rare serious risks, and obtain written consent.
Perform a neurological examination and record baseline findings.
Position the patient relaxed and take up the slack in the target segment.
Check for any symptoms in the pre-manipulative hold and abandon if any occur.
Deliver a single controlled small-amplitude high-velocity thrust.
Reassess pain, range of movement and neurological status.
Follow with active exercises and advice to stay active.
aftercare: Advise staying active and avoiding prolonged bed rest.
Expect mild soreness for one to two days.
Continue the home exercise programme.
red_flags: New weakness, numbness, saddle anaesthesia or bladder or bowel change (urgent review)
Dizziness, double vision, slurred speech or difficulty swallowing after neck manipulation (emergency)
Severe pain not settling within two days

indications: Muscle spasm or tightness
Scar tissue adhesion after healing
Relaxation and pain relief in chronic musculoskeletal pain
contraindications: Suspected deep vein thrombosis in the area
Open wounds, skin infection or burns at the site
Malignancy at the site
Acute inflammation or haematoma in the first days after injury
Bleeding disorder (firm massage)
equipment: Massage medium such as oil, cream or powder
steps: Confirm identity, check skin and contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Ask about allergies to oils or creams.
Position the patient comfortably with the area exposed and the rest draped.
Perform hand hygiene and apply a small amount of medium.
Start with light stroking, then progress to deeper kneading as tolerated.
Use frictions or sustained pressure over specific tight areas or scars.
Check comfort throughout and adjust pressure.
Remove excess medium and reassess pain and tissue tension.
aftercare: Expect mild tenderness for a day.
Combine with stretching and exercise for lasting benefit.
red_flags: Calf swelling, warmth or pain
Skin reaction or rash from the medium
Bruising or worsening pain

indications: Lymphoedema after breast cancer surgery or radiotherapy
Primary lymphoedema
Lymphatic filariasis-related lymphoedema (with hygiene care)
Post-traumatic or post-surgical oedema
contraindications: Acute cellulitis or infection in the limb (treat first)
Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Uncontrolled heart failure
Peripheral arterial disease or poor limb perfusion (no compression bandaging)
Active untreated cancer in the area without oncology advice
equipment: Short-stretch bandages, padding and tubular stockinette
steps: Confirm identity, screen for infection, DVT and heart failure and obtain verbal consent.
Inspect the skin and measure limb circumference at fixed points on both limbs.
Position the patient comfortably with the limb elevated.
Begin with gentle stimulation of lymph nodes in the neck and trunk.
Use light, slow, rhythmic skin-stretching strokes, working from the trunk towards the limb.
Move the fluid towards healthy lymph node areas, avoiding deep pressure.
Apply multilayer compression bandaging or a garment after treatment.
Teach skin care, simple self-massage and exercises.
aftercare: Keep the skin clean, dry and moisturised, and treat cuts promptly.
Wear compression as advised and remove it if the fingers or toes become numb or blue.
Elevate the limb and exercise regularly.
red_flags: Redness, heat, fever or spreading pain in the limb (cellulitis)
Numbness, pain or colour change under bandages
Sudden swelling with calf pain or breathlessness

indications: Acute or chronic musculoskeletal pain
Labour pain
Neuropathic pain as an adjunct
contraindications: Cardiac pacemaker or implanted defibrillator
Over the front of the neck, eyes or across the chest
Over the pregnant abdomen except for labour use
Broken or numb skin at the electrode site
Epilepsy (avoid head and neck)
equipment: Leads and self-adhesive or carbon electrodes with gel
steps: Confirm identity, screen for pacemaker and other contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Check skin sensation at the planned sites.
Clean the skin and place electrodes around or over the painful area.
Check the unit is switched off, then connect the leads.
Turn up the intensity slowly until a strong but comfortable tingling is felt.
Set the mode and pulse settings for the type of pain.
Check the skin and comfort after the session and reassess pain.
Teach the patient to use the unit at home if one is available.
aftercare: Check the skin under electrodes after each use.
Do not use while driving, operating machinery, sleeping or in water.
red_flags: Skin burn, rash or blistering under electrodes
Palpitations or dizziness during use

indications: Soft-tissue injury in the subacute stage
Tendinopathy
Scar tissue and soft-tissue tightness before stretching
contraindications: Over the pregnant uterus, eyes, gonads or heart
Over growing bone in children (epiphyses)
Malignancy, active infection or recent bleeding at the site
Over a pacemaker or deep vein thrombosis
Reduced sensation at the site (thermal settings)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with checked treatment head
steps: Confirm identity, screen for contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Check skin sensation over the area.
Test that the machine is producing output before treatment.
Apply coupling gel to the skin over the target area.
Select frequency, mode and intensity appropriate to the tissue depth and stage of healing.
Keep the treatment head moving slowly and in contact with the skin throughout.
Ask the patient to report any heat or pain and stop if it occurs.
Clean off the gel and inspect the skin.
aftercare: Combine with exercise and stretching for best effect.
Report any skin changes before the next session.
red_flags: Burning pain or skin burn
Increased pain or swelling after treatment

indications: Musculoskeletal pain such as back and knee pain
Soft-tissue swelling after injury
Muscle spasm
contraindications: Cardiac pacemaker or implanted electronic device
Over the pregnant abdomen
Over the anterior neck, eyes or chest in cardiac patients
Malignancy, infection, broken skin or thrombosis at the site
Reduced skin sensation
equipment: Electrodes (pads with damp sponges or suction cups)
Straps or weights to hold electrodes
steps: Confirm identity, screen for contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Check skin sensation and clean the skin.
Place four electrodes in a crossed pattern or two electrodes over the area.
Secure the electrodes with good skin contact.
Select frequency and sweep settings for the treatment goal.
Increase intensity slowly to a strong but comfortable tingling.
Stay within call and check the patient during treatment.
Turn intensity to zero before removing electrodes and inspect the skin.
aftercare: Inspect the skin at the next session.
Continue the exercise programme.
red_flags: Skin burn or blistering under electrodes
Dizziness, faintness or palpitations

indications: Chronic joint stiffness and pain such as osteoarthritis
Chronic soft-tissue conditions needing deep heating
Pulsed mode for soft-tissue healing
contraindications: Metal implants, jewellery or metal in the treatment field
Pacemaker, cochlear implant or other implanted device
Pregnancy and treatment over the pelvis during menstruation
Reduced sensation, poor circulation or ischaemia at the site
Malignancy, active tuberculosis, infection or bleeding at the site
Over the eyes, testes or growing bone
equipment: Capacitor plates or inductive drum with spacers
Wooden chair or couch without metal parts
steps: Confirm identity, screen carefully for metal, implants and other contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Remove all jewellery, hearing aids, phones and metal from the patient and the area.
Test skin thermal sensation with warm and cold tubes.
Position the patient on a non-metal couch and place a dry towel over the skin.
Place the electrodes with correct spacing and keep leads apart.
Tune the machine and set the dose to produce comfortable mild warmth or pulsed output.
Give the patient a call bell and warn them not to move or touch the machine.
Check the patient during treatment and stop if heat becomes uncomfortable.
Inspect the skin after treatment.
aftercare: Inspect skin for redness or burns at the next session.
Continue the exercise programme.
red_flags: Burn or blistering of the skin
Severe heat discomfort, faintness or headache

indications: Muscle spasm and superficial pain
Chronic joint stiffness before exercise
Relaxation before manual therapy
contraindications: Reduced skin sensation or impaired circulation
Acute inflammation or recent injury within the first days
Skin infection, dermatitis or recent radiotherapy to the area
Over the eyes or testes
Confused patient unable to report burning
equipment: Eye protection if lamp is near the face
steps: Confirm identity, screen for contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Test skin sensation to warm and cold.
Expose and clean the area, removing creams and oils.
Position the lamp at a safe distance, with the rays at right angles to the skin.
Warn the patient that they should feel only comfortable warmth.
Set a timer and keep the patient within call.
Check the skin and comfort regularly and move the lamp further away if too hot.
Turn off the lamp, move it away and inspect the skin.
aftercare: Expect mild even redness that fades within an hour.
Follow with stretching or exercise.
red_flags: Blistering, burning or patchy redness
Headache or faintness during treatment

indications: Stiffness and pain of the hands, wrists or feet in arthritis
Hand stiffness after fracture or immobilisation
Scleroderma or contractures of the hands (with caution)
contraindications: Open wounds, skin infection or rash on the area
Reduced sensation or poor circulation
Acute inflammation or swelling
Allergy to paraffin wax
equipment: Thermostatically controlled paraffin wax bath at the correct temperature
Plastic bags and towels or mitts
steps: Confirm identity, screen for contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Check the wax temperature on the thermometer before use.
Remove jewellery and wash and dry the hand or foot.
Check skin sensation.
Dip the part into the wax and lift it out, repeating to build several layers.
Wrap the part in a plastic bag and towel to keep the heat in.
Leave for the treatment time, then peel off the wax and discard it into the bath or bin per local practice.
Inspect the skin and follow with hand or foot exercises.
aftercare: Do exercises straight after treatment while the joints are warm.
Do not use a home wax bath without proper temperature control.
red_flags: Burn or blistering of the skin
Increased swelling or pain after treatment

indications: Arthritis and chronic pain limiting land-based exercise
Early rehabilitation after joint surgery or fracture once wounds have healed
Neurological conditions needing supported movement
contraindications: Open wounds, infections, diarrhoea or urinary incontinence without protection
Uncontrolled epilepsy
Unstable heart disease or severe breathlessness
Fear of water without adequate support
Tracheostomy or recent ear surgery
equipment: Heated therapy pool with steps, rails and hoist
Flotation aids and pool exercise equipment
Trained pool attendant and rescue equipment
Towels and changing area with non-slip floor
steps: Confirm identity, screen for contraindications and obtain verbal consent.
Check vital signs and that the pool temperature and water quality checks are recorded.
Ensure a second trained person is present and rescue equipment is ready.
Help the patient enter the pool safely by steps or hoist.
Start with warm-up walking or movement in the water.
Lead exercises using the buoyancy for support or resistance.
Watch for fatigue, dizziness or breathlessness throughout.
Help the patient leave the pool slowly and sit to rest.
Check vital signs and advise drinking water.
aftercare: Rest after the session as fatigue is common.
Shower and dry the skin thoroughly, especially between the toes.
red_flags: Dizziness, chest pain or breathlessness in the pool
Seizure or loss of consciousness (start pool emergency procedure)
Skin infection or rash after sessions

indications: Cervical radiculopathy with arm pain
Mechanical neck pain with nerve root symptoms
contraindications: Cervical fracture, instability, tumour or infection
Rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome affecting the upper neck
Signs of spinal cord compression (myelopathy)
Vertebral artery symptoms
Severe osteoporosis
Acute torticollis or acute whiplash
equipment: Mechanical traction unit or over-door traction kit
Head halter with chin and occipital straps
Couch with pillows or a chair
steps: Confirm identity, screen for red flags and myelopathy and obtain verbal consent.
Record baseline neck and arm symptoms and neurological findings.
Position the patient supine with the neck slightly flexed, or seated.
Fit the halter so the pull is mainly through the back of the head, not the jaw.
Apply a low trial force first and check symptoms.
Increase gradually to the chosen force and mode, staying within comfort.
Give the patient a stop switch and check them regularly.
Release the traction slowly, rest the patient briefly and reassess symptoms.
aftercare: Get up slowly after treatment.
Continue neck exercises and posture advice.
red_flags: Increasing arm pain, numbness or weakness
Dizziness, nausea or visual disturbance during traction
Jaw or temporomandibular joint pain

indications: Lumbar radiculopathy with leg pain not responding to exercise alone
Selected cases of mechanical low back pain with nerve root symptoms
contraindications: Red flags for fracture, tumour, infection or cauda equina syndrome
Pregnancy
Severe osteoporosis or spinal instability
Uncontrolled hypertension or abdominal hernia
Recent spinal surgery
equipment: Mechanical traction couch or split table
steps: Confirm identity, screen for red flags and obtain verbal consent.
Record baseline back and leg symptoms and neurological findings.
Fit the thoracic and pelvic harnesses firmly over clothing.
Position the patient supine with hips and knees flexed, or prone as chosen.
Apply a low trial force and check symptoms.
Increase to the chosen force and mode within comfort, giving the patient a stop switch.
Check the patient regularly throughout the session.
Release slowly, let the patient rest lying down, then reassess symptoms.
aftercare: Roll to the side and get up slowly after treatment.
Continue back exercises and stay active.
red_flags: Increasing leg pain, numbness or weakness
Saddle numbness or bladder or bowel change (emergency referral)
Breathing difficulty from the thoracic harness

indications: Musculoskeletal pain and support in sports injuries
Oedema or bruising after injury
Postural or muscle facilitation support
contraindications: Broken, fragile or infected skin
Known allergy to tape adhesive
Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Over a malignancy
equipment: Alcohol wipes or soap and water
Clippers for hair removal if needed
steps: Confirm identity, check skin and allergies and obtain verbal consent.
Clean and dry the skin, clipping hair if needed.
Measure and cut the tape to the required length and shape, rounding the corners.
Position the body part to stretch the target tissue.
Apply the anchor without stretch, then lay the tape with the chosen tension.
Apply the end anchor without stretch.
Rub the tape to activate the adhesive.
Check comfort, movement and circulation.
aftercare: The tape can usually stay on for a few days and can get wet; pat dry.
Remove slowly in the direction of hair growth, holding the skin.
red_flags: Itching, rash or blistering under the tape (remove it)
Numbness, swelling or colour change beyond the tape

indications: Myofascial trigger points causing pain
Chronic neck, shoulder or back muscle pain not responding to other treatment
contraindications: Needle phobia or patient unwilling
Anticoagulant therapy or bleeding disorder
Local skin infection, lymphoedema or wound at the site
Over the chest wall without training in safe depth (risk of pneumothorax)
First trimester of pregnancy
Practitioner not trained in dry needling
equipment: Sterile single-use solid filament needles of suitable length
Alcohol swabs, gloves and cotton wool
steps: Confirm identity, screen for bleeding risk and contraindications and obtain written consent.
Position the patient lying down to reduce the risk of fainting.
Identify the trigger point by palpation.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and clean the skin.
Insert the needle into the trigger point, keeping depth safe for the anatomy.
Seek local twitch responses with gentle movement of the needle.
Remove the needle and apply pressure to stop any bleeding.
Discard needles straight into the sharps container and count them.
Reassess pain and range of movement.
aftercare: Expect muscle soreness for one to two days.
Use gentle stretching and heat for soreness.
red_flags: Breathlessness or chest pain after needling near the chest (possible pneumothorax, urgent review)
Fainting, persistent bleeding or large bruising
Signs of infection at the needle site

indications: Weakness, poor balance or reduced function after stroke
Prevention of complications such as contractures, shoulder pain and chest infection
Carer training before discharge
contraindications: Medically unstable patient such as fluctuating consciousness or uncontrolled blood pressure
New neurological deterioration needing medical review first
equipment: Plinth or bed, chair and parallel bars
Pillows, positioning wedges and shoulder support
Blood pressure monitor and pulse oximeter
Simple objects for arm and hand tasks
steps: Confirm identity, review medical status and obtain verbal consent from patient or carer.
Check blood pressure, heart rate and alertness before starting.
Assess tone, strength, sensation, balance and function, and agree goals.
Position the patient correctly in bed and chair, protecting the weak shoulder.
Practise bed mobility and sit-to-stand with the right level of help.
Train sitting and standing balance, and walking when safe.
Practise task-specific arm and hand activities such as reaching and grasping.
Include stretches for muscles at risk of shortening.
Teach carers safe handling, positioning and the home programme.
Recheck vital signs and record progress against goals.
aftercare: Carers should repeat positioning and exercises daily.
Never pull on the weak arm when moving the patient.
Attend follow-up sessions; most recovery happens in the first months.
red_flags: New weakness, speech change, severe headache or drop in consciousness (urgent medical review)
Painful swollen shoulder or hand
Calf swelling or chest pain
Choking or coughing with meals

form.label: Walking ability
options: Walks with help of one or more people

indications: Cerebral palsy with delayed motor milestones
Spasticity or abnormal tone affecting movement and posture
Prevention of contractures and hip problems
Parent and carer training for home therapy
contraindications: Acute illness with fever or uncontrolled seizures on the day
Suspected hip dislocation or fracture with pain (review first)
equipment: Floor mat, therapy ball, rolls and wedges
Standing frame or corner seat if available (can be made locally)
Splints or orthoses the child uses
steps: Confirm identity, obtain verbal consent from the parent and ask about seizures and recent illness.
Assess motor level, tone, posture, range of movement and hip position.
Agree goals with the family that fit daily life, such as sitting, feeding or walking.
Use play to engage the child throughout.
Practise key movements such as head control, rolling, sitting, standing or walking at the child's level.
Use handling to guide better posture and movement, reducing support as the child improves.
Stretch tight muscles gently, especially calves, hamstrings and hip adductors.
Advise on positioning for sitting, sleeping and carrying.
Teach the parent the home programme and watch them do it.
aftercare: Parents should do the home programme daily as part of play.
Use positioning equipment and orthoses as advised.
Attend regular reviews and hip surveillance as arranged.
red_flags: New or worsening seizures
Hip pain, leg shortening or loss of skills
Feeding difficulty, choking or poor weight gain

indications: Congenital muscular torticollis in infants
Sternocleidomastoid tumour or tightness with head tilt
Plagiocephaly with neck tightness
contraindications: Head tilt not yet assessed for non-muscular causes such as spinal, eye or neurological problems
Suspected cervical spine abnormality or hip problem not yet assessed
equipment: Firm padded surface or parent's lap
Toys to attract the infant's gaze
steps: Confirm identity, obtain verbal consent from the parent and confirm medical assessment for other causes.
Assess head tilt, rotation range and any neck lump, and check the hips.
Position the infant supine with the shoulders gently stabilised.
Rotate the chin slowly towards the affected shoulder and hold the stretch.
Tilt the ear gently towards the unaffected shoulder and hold the stretch.
Stop if the infant becomes very distressed and resume when settled.
Teach positioning by placing toys and feeding on the side that encourages turning to the affected side.
Encourage supervised tummy time while awake.
Teach the parent the stretches and watch them perform them.
aftercare: Parents should do the stretches several times a day, often at nappy changes.
Review regularly until full range is achieved.
red_flags: No improvement after several months of stretching (refer to orthopaedics)
Head tilt with eye problems, vomiting or developmental delay
Infant in pain or very distressed with stretching

name: Physiotherapy for brachial plexus birth palsy

indications: Arm weakness from brachial plexus injury at birth
Prevention of shoulder and elbow contractures
Monitoring recovery to decide on surgical referral
contraindications: Unhealed clavicle or humerus fracture (gentle care only until healed)
Untreated shoulder dislocation
steps: Confirm identity, obtain verbal consent from the parent and check for fractures.
Assess active movement at the shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand and record it.
Perform gentle passive range of movement at each joint, especially shoulder external rotation.
Stabilise the shoulder blade when moving the shoulder to avoid overstretching.
Encourage active movement through play and touch to the affected arm.
Teach the parent the exercises and safe handling, including dressing the affected arm first.
Check for developing contractures at each review.
Arrange referral to a specialist surgeon if recovery is poor by the agreed age.
aftercare: Parents should do the exercises several times a day.
Avoid lifting the baby under the arms.
red_flags: No elbow bending or poor recovery by about three months of age (refer urgently)
Loss of shoulder movement or a fixed posture
Drooping eyelid on the affected side

indications: Foot drop after stroke, nerve injury or cerebral palsy
Prevention or correction of contractures
Joint support or protection after injury or surgery
Clubfoot maintenance after correction (foot abduction brace)
contraindications: Skin breakdown or wound at pressure points without a plan to protect it
Severe fixed deformity that the orthosis cannot accommodate (refer to orthotist)
equipment: Prefabricated or custom orthosis of correct size
Heat gun and tools for adjustment if thermoplastic
Suitable footwear for lower limb orthoses
steps: Confirm identity, check the prescription and obtain verbal consent.
Inspect the skin and check sensation and range of the joint.
Check the orthosis is the correct type, size and side.
Fit the orthosis and fasten straps snugly without being tight.
Check alignment, pressure areas and comfort in sitting, standing and walking as relevant.
Adjust trim lines or padding to remove pressure points.
Remove after a short trial and inspect the skin for red marks.
Teach the patient or carer how to put it on, wear it and care for it.
Give a wearing schedule that builds up over days.
aftercare: Check the skin every time the orthosis is removed.
Red marks that do not fade within about 20 minutes mean it needs adjusting.
Keep the orthosis away from direct heat.
red_flags: Blisters, sores or persistent red marks
Numbness, swelling or colour change of the limb
Orthosis broken or no longer fits (common in growing children)

indications: Lower limb amputation with a healed stump ready for a prosthesis
Gait problems with an existing prosthesis
New or replacement prosthesis delivery
contraindications: Unhealed stump wound or infection
Severe heart or lung disease limiting walking effort
Uncontrolled stump pain or swelling
equipment: Prosthesis with socket, liners and stump socks
steps: Confirm identity, review the stump and general health and obtain verbal consent.
Inspect the stump for wounds, swelling and pressure marks and measure its volume.
Teach correct donning of liner, socks and prosthesis.
Check the socket fit, prosthesis length and alignment in standing.
Start weight transfer and balance in parallel bars.
Progress to walking in the bars, then with walking aids, correcting the pattern.
Practise sit to stand, turning, slopes, stairs and getting up from the floor as able.
Remove the prosthesis and inspect the stump for red marks.
Teach stump care, sock adjustment and a gradual wearing schedule.
aftercare: Check the stump daily with a mirror and keep it clean and dry.
Add or remove stump socks as the stump changes size.
Return to the prosthetist if the fit changes.
red_flags: Stump wound, blister or skin breakdown
Increasing stump pain or swelling
Prosthesis feels loose, too tight or makes a noise
Falls when walking

indications: Stress or mixed urinary incontinence
During pregnancy and after childbirth
Pelvic organ prolapse symptoms (mild)
After prostate surgery with leakage
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection (treat first)
Internal assessment if the patient declines, with vaginal bleeding, active genital infection or in the early weeks after childbirth (teach by observation only)
Examiner not trained in internal assessment (teach without internal examination)
equipment: Private room with couch and screen
Gloves and lubricant if internal assessment is done
steps: Confirm identity, take a bladder and bowel history and obtain verbal consent, offering a chaperone.
Explain the pelvic floor using a diagram or model.
Teach the patient to squeeze and lift as if stopping wind and urine, without holding the breath.
Check the contraction by observation or, if consented and trained, by internal assessment.
Grade the strength and endurance of the contraction.
Set a programme of long holds and quick contractions repeated several times a day.
Teach the knack of squeezing before coughing, sneezing or lifting.
Give a bladder diary and advice on fluids, constipation and weight.
aftercare: Continue exercises daily for at least three months to see benefit.
Do not practise by stopping urine flow regularly.
red_flags: Blood in the urine or pain on passing urine
Bulge or heaviness getting worse
No improvement after three months (refer for review)

indications: After myocardial infarction or acute coronary syndrome
After coronary bypass or valve surgery
Stable heart failure
Stable angina
contraindications: Unstable angina, uncontrolled arrhythmia or decompensated heart failure
Resting systolic blood pressure very high or symptomatic low blood pressure
Acute illness or fever
Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis or acute myocarditis or pericarditis
New symptoms since the last session not yet reviewed
equipment: Blood pressure monitor, pulse oximeter and heart rate monitor
Exercise space, steps, bike or treadmill
Emergency trolley with defibrillator and trained staff
Patient's angina reliever spray if prescribed
steps: Confirm identity, ask about new symptoms and medicines and obtain verbal consent.
Check resting heart rate, blood pressure and saturation before exercise.
Confirm emergency equipment and trained staff are present.
Lead a gradual warm-up of at least several minutes.
Run the exercise circuit at the agreed target intensity using heart rate and perceived exertion.
Monitor symptoms, heart rate and exertion throughout.
Lead a gradual cool-down and do not let patients stop suddenly.
Recheck vital signs before the patient leaves.
Give education on risk factors, medicines, diet, smoking and return to activity.
aftercare: Do the home walking programme on most days at the agreed intensity.
Carry angina reliever medicine if prescribed.
red_flags: Chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations during exercise (stop and assess)
Chest pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes (call emergency help)
Increasing ankle swelling or weight gain over a few days

indications: COPD with breathlessness limiting activity
Bronchiectasis or interstitial lung disease
After treated pulmonary tuberculosis with residual lung damage
Before or after lung surgery
contraindications: Acute exacerbation or chest infection
Unstable heart disease
Infectious tuberculosis not yet treated
Severe resting desaturation without supplemental oxygen available
equipment: Pulse oximeter and blood pressure monitor
Measured walkway for the six-minute walk test
steps: Confirm identity, ask about recent exacerbations and obtain verbal consent.
Check vital signs and resting saturation.
Measure exercise capacity with a walk test at the start of the programme and at the end.
Lead a warm-up and teach breathing control during exercise.
Run endurance training such as walking or cycling at the agreed intensity.
Add upper and lower limb strength exercises.
Monitor saturation and breathlessness, using oxygen and rest periods as needed.
Cool down and recheck saturation.
Give education on inhaler technique, airway clearance, energy conservation and exacerbation plans.
aftercare: Do the home exercise programme on most days.
Use pacing and breathing control for daily tasks.
red_flags: Saturation that falls below the target and does not recover with rest
Chest pain, fever or change in sputum colour (possible exacerbation)
Increased ankle swelling

indications: Aphasia or dysarthria after stroke or brain injury
Speech and language delay in children
Stammering or voice disorders
Communication difficulty in autism or cerebral palsy
contraindications: Medically unwell or too drowsy to take part on the day
Hearing loss not yet assessed in a child with language delay (arrange hearing test)
equipment: Recording sheet or standardised assessment if available
steps: Confirm identity and obtain verbal consent from the patient or parent.
Ask about hearing, language used at home and communication concerns.
Assess understanding, expression, speech clarity and social communication.
Agree goals with the patient or family that matter in daily life.
Carry out therapy activities targeted to the goals, using familiar languages and materials.
Introduce alternative communication such as gestures or picture boards if speech is limited.
Teach the family or carers strategies to support communication.
Record progress and set home practice.
aftercare: Practise the activities daily in everyday routines.
Use the agreed strategies with all family members.
red_flags: Loss of speech or language skills already gained (urgent review)
Sudden new speech difficulty in an adult (possible stroke, emergency)
Coughing or choking with food or drink (refer for swallowing assessment)

indications: Dysphagia after stroke or brain injury
Swallowing difficulty in neurological or neuromuscular disease
Feeding and swallowing difficulty in children with cerebral palsy
After head and neck surgery or radiotherapy
contraindications: Reduced consciousness or unable to sit upright (no oral trials)
Absent cough and very wet voice at rest (no oral trials, keep nil by mouth and review)
Respiratory distress or high oxygen need
equipment: Water, thickened fluids and soft foods of different textures
steps: Confirm identity and obtain verbal consent from the patient or carer.
Check alertness, posture, breathing and saturation, and sit the patient fully upright.
Examine the mouth, oral hygiene, lip and tongue movement, voice and cough.
Give small trials starting with teaspoons of water if safe, watching for coughing, wet voice or desaturation.
Progress through textures as safe and stop at the first sign of aspiration.
Choose the safest diet and fluid texture and any posture or technique changes.
Teach swallowing exercises or strategies such as chin tuck and small mouthfuls.
Advise staff or carers on supervision, feeding technique and mouth care.
Recommend nil by mouth with alternative feeding if oral intake is unsafe and inform the doctor.
aftercare: Sit upright for meals and for a while after.
Follow the recommended textures and give mouth care regularly.
red_flags: Coughing, choking or wet voice with eating or drinking
Fever, chest infection or breathlessness (possible aspiration pneumonia)
Weight loss or dehydration

indications: Difficulty with self-care, work or school after illness or injury
Discharge planning for patients with reduced function
Hand injuries or conditions affecting hand use
Developmental coordination or sensory difficulties in children
contraindications: Medically unstable patient (defer functional tasks)
equipment: Assessment forms or functional scale such as the Barthel index
Kitchen, bathroom or practice area if available
Hand assessment tools such as a goniometer and dynamometer
steps: Confirm identity and obtain verbal consent from the patient or carer.
Take a history of home, work or school, roles and daily routines.
Identify the activities the patient finds difficult and their priorities.
Observe the patient performing key tasks such as dressing, washing, eating or toileting.
Assess physical, cognitive and sensory factors affecting performance.
Score function on an agreed scale such as the Barthel index.
Consider the home environment and the need for adaptations or equipment.
Agree goals and a plan with the patient and family.
aftercare: Practise the recommended strategies at home.
Arrange equipment or home adaptations before discharge where possible.
red_flags: Unsafe to be at home alone (for example falls, wandering or unable to use the toilet)
Signs of carer strain, neglect or abuse
Rapid decline in function

indications: Unable to walk or walk safely for functional distances
Spinal cord injury, amputation, stroke or cerebral palsy
Need for postural support in sitting
contraindications: Existing pressure sore needing treatment before long sitting (plan pressure care)
equipment: Range of wheelchairs and cushions to trial (or locally made options)
Postural supports such as lateral supports and headrest
steps: Confirm identity and obtain verbal consent from the patient or carer.
Assess mobility, posture, skin, transfers, home and community environment.
Check skin over the sitting bones and spine for pressure areas.
Measure seat width, seat depth, back height, footrest length and armrest height in sitting.
Choose the wheelchair type, cushion and supports to suit the needs and budget.
Fit the wheelchair and adjust it to the measurements.
Check posture, comfort and pressure in the chair.
Teach transfers, propulsion, braking, kerbs and folding.
Teach pressure relief every so often and daily skin checks.
Arrange follow-up for adjustments and growth in children.
aftercare: Check the skin daily and do pressure relief regularly while sitting.
Keep tyres inflated and brakes working.
Return for review if the chair no longer fits.
red_flags: Red marks or sores over the sitting bones, spine or heels
Sliding or leaning in the chair
Brakes or frame failing

indications: Child due or overdue for vaccines on the national immunisation schedule
Catch-up of missed vaccines at any visit
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the same vaccine or one of its components
Severe immunodeficiency for live vaccines (seek advice)
Moderate or severe acute illness (defer, do not miss the opportunity later)
equipment: Vaccines from the cold box with vaccine vial monitors
Auto-disable syringes of the correct size and diluent where needed
Child health card and immunisation register
steps: Greet the caregiver, confirm the child's identity and review the child health card.
Work out which vaccines are due or overdue using the national schedule and catch-up rules.
Screen for contraindications and previous reactions and explain the vaccines and common side effects.
Obtain verbal consent from the caregiver.
Check each vaccine name, expiry date and vaccine vial monitor and reconstitute only with its own diluent.
Perform hand hygiene and position the child securely on the caregiver's lap.
Give oral vaccines first, then injectable vaccines at separate sites using the correct route.
Use a new auto-disable syringe for each injection and discard immediately in the safety box without recapping.
Comfort the child and encourage breastfeeding after the injections.
Record each vaccine, batch number and site on the card, register and in the record.
Observe the child for at least 30 minutes for immediate reactions.
Tell the caregiver the date of the next visit and write it on the card.
aftercare: Expect mild fever, fussiness and soreness at the injection site for one to two days.
Keep the child cool, continue breastfeeding and fluids, and do not apply anything to the site.
Bring the card to every visit.
red_flags: Treat anaphylaxis immediately if breathing difficulty, swelling, pallor or collapse develops.
Return urgently for high fever, convulsions, inconsolable crying for more than three hours or limpness.
Report any serious or unusual reaction as an adverse event following immunisation.

form.label: Vaccine condition
options: VVM at discard point - not used

indications: Newborns and infants per the national schedule
Unvaccinated children without a BCG scar per national catch-up policy
contraindications: Symptomatic HIV infection or known severe immunodeficiency
Infant born to a mother with infectious TB until assessed for preventive therapy
Generalised skin disease at the injection site
equipment: BCG vaccine and its own diluent, kept cold
BCG syringe with fine short needle (auto-disable)
steps: Confirm the infant's identity, check the card and screen for contraindications.
Explain the vaccine and the expected scar and obtain verbal consent.
Check vaccine and diluent expiry and reconstitute only with the cooled diluent supplied.
Write the reconstitution time on the vial and discard it at the end of the session or after six hours.
Perform hand hygiene and draw up the correct volume for age.
Hold the infant's left arm firmly and stretch the skin over the insertion of the deltoid.
Insert the needle bevel up just under the surface of the skin, nearly parallel to it.
Inject slowly to raise a pale bleb with an orange-peel surface, then withdraw the needle.
Do not rub or cover the site and discard the syringe in the safety box.
Record the vaccine, batch and site and give the next appointment.
aftercare: Explain that a small lump, then an ulcer that heals to a scar, forms over two to six weeks.
Keep the site clean and dry and do not apply dressings, creams or herbs.
Check for a scar at the next visits.
red_flags: Stop and reassess technique if no bleb forms (injection given too deep).
Return for an abscess, an ulcer larger than expected or swollen glands in the armpit.
Refer for spreading lesions or a sick infant with possible disseminated BCG.

form.label: Vaccine condition
options: VVM at discard point - not used

indications: Girls in the national target age group, through school, outreach or clinic
Eligible older girls and young women per national catch-up policy
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous HPV dose or vaccine component (including yeast)
Known pregnancy (defer)
Moderate or severe acute illness (defer)
equipment: Chair or couch for sitting or lying
steps: Confirm identity and age and check eligibility and any previous HPV doses.
Explain the purpose, benefits and common side effects to the girl and her parent or guardian.
Obtain consent according to school or national policy and the girl's assent.
Ask about allergies, previous fainting with injections and possible pregnancy if relevant.
Check vaccine expiry and vial monitor and perform hand hygiene.
Seat the girl and expose the deltoid of the non-dominant arm.
Give the vaccine by intramuscular injection into the deltoid.
Discard the syringe in the safety box without recapping.
Keep her seated and observe for at least 15 to 30 minutes because fainting is common in adolescents.
Record the vaccine, batch and date and tell her if any further dose is due.
aftercare: Expect a sore arm, mild headache or fever for a day or two.
Explain that cervical screening is still needed later in adult life.
red_flags: Lie her flat with legs raised if she feels faint and observe until fully recovered.
Treat anaphylaxis immediately if breathing difficulty, swelling or collapse occurs.
Report serious or unusual events as an adverse event following immunisation.

indications: Pregnant women at antenatal booking or follow-up per the national Td schedule
Prevention of maternal and neonatal tetanus
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous tetanus- or diphtheria-containing vaccine
steps: Confirm identity and gestational age and review the antenatal card for previous Td or TT doses.
Decide which dose is due from documented history using the national schedule.
Explain that the vaccine protects both mother and newborn from tetanus and obtain verbal consent.
Check vaccine expiry and vial monitor and perform hand hygiene.
Expose the upper arm and give the vaccine intramuscularly into the deltoid.
Discard the syringe in the safety box without recapping.
Observe for immediate reactions.
Record the dose number and date on the antenatal card, Td card and register.
Give the date for the next dose if one is due.
aftercare: Expect mild soreness or swelling of the arm for a few days.
Keep the Td card safe for future pregnancies and injuries.
Encourage clean delivery in a health facility and clean cord care.
red_flags: Treat anaphylaxis immediately if it occurs.
Return for a large painful swelling, fever or any concern about the pregnancy.

indications: Health workers and students with exposure to blood
Household and sexual contacts of people with hepatitis B
People with HIV, on dialysis or with chronic liver disease, and other high-risk groups
Adults requesting protection after a negative HBsAg test
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or vaccine component (including yeast)
Known HBsAg-positive (vaccine gives no benefit)
equipment: Auto-disable or disposable syringe and needle for intramuscular injection
steps: Confirm identity and review previous hepatitis B doses and HBsAg result.
Offer HBsAg testing first where available if status is unknown.
Explain the schedule and common side effects and obtain verbal consent.
Check vaccine expiry and vial monitor and perform hand hygiene.
Give the vaccine intramuscularly into the deltoid, not the buttock.
Discard the needle in the safety box without recapping.
Observe for immediate reactions.
Record the dose number, batch and date and give dates for remaining doses.
Arrange an antibody check after the series for health workers where available.
aftercare: Expect a sore arm or mild fever for a day or two.
Complete the full series even if a dose is late; do not restart.
red_flags: Treat anaphylaxis immediately if it occurs.
Refer if HBsAg is positive for hepatitis B assessment instead of vaccination.

indications: Infants at nine months per the national schedule
Unvaccinated children and adults in Nigeria and travellers needing an international certificate
Outbreak response campaigns
contraindications: Age under six months
Severe egg allergy or anaphylaxis to a previous dose
Symptomatic HIV or other severe immunodeficiency, or immunosuppressive treatment
Thymus disorder
Pregnancy and breastfeeding of infants under six months unless the risk of exposure is high
equipment: Yellow fever vaccine and its own diluent, kept cold
Child health card or International Certificate of Vaccination
steps: Confirm identity and age and check that the vaccine has not already been given.
Screen for contraindications, including allergy, immune status and pregnancy.
Explain the vaccine and side effects and obtain verbal consent.
Reconstitute with the cooled diluent supplied, note the time and keep the vial on ice.
Perform hand hygiene and give the vaccine by subcutaneous injection into the upper arm or by the route stated by the manufacturer.
Discard the syringe in the safety box without recapping.
Observe for at least 30 minutes for immediate reactions.
Record vaccine, batch and date on the card, register or international certificate and stamp the certificate if issued.
Discard reconstituted vaccine at the end of the session or after six hours.
aftercare: Expect mild fever, headache or muscle aches five to ten days after vaccination.
Travellers should keep the certificate with their passport.
red_flags: Treat anaphylaxis immediately if it occurs.
Return urgently for high fever, jaundice, confusion, convulsions or weakness in the weeks after vaccination.
Report any serious event as an adverse event following immunisation.

form.label: Vaccine condition
options: VVM at discard point - not used

indications: Bite, scratch or lick on broken skin or mucosa from a dog, cat, monkey, bat or other animal that may carry rabies
Category II or III exposure under the WHO classification
contraindications: None absolute; rabies is fatal so pregnancy and infancy are not contraindications
equipment: Antiseptic such as povidone-iodine or alcohol
Syringes and needles for intramuscular or intradermal use
steps: Confirm identity and take the history of the exposure, animal, time, site and the animal's current status.
Classify the exposure as category I, II or III.
Wash every wound immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water for about 15 minutes.
Apply antiseptic after washing and avoid suturing the wound if possible; if needed, delay and loosely approximate.
Explain the course, the importance of completing it and possible side effects and obtain verbal consent.
For category III exposures, infiltrate rabies immunoglobulin into and around the wounds as far as anatomically possible.
Give the first vaccine dose by the intramuscular or intradermal route per the national regimen, at a site away from the immunoglobulin.
Assess tetanus status and give tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics where indicated.
Observe for immediate reactions.
Record the regimen and give a card with the dates of the remaining doses.
Advise the patient to report the animal to veterinary or public health officers for observation.
aftercare: Attend every scheduled vaccine dose on time even if well.
Keep the wound clean and watch for infection.
If the dog or cat stays healthy for ten days, the course may be stopped on clinical advice.
red_flags: Start prophylaxis without delay; do not wait for the animal's test result.
Return urgently for fever, tingling or pain at the bite site, fear of water, agitation or weakness.
Return for wound redness, swelling, pus or fever.
Refer category III exposures if immunoglobulin is not available locally.

form.label: Wound washed with soap and water

indications: Any wound or burn in a person whose tetanus immunisation is incomplete, unknown or not recent
Tetanus-prone wounds such as puncture wounds, soil contamination, devitalised tissue or delay over six hours
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous tetanus vaccine (immunoglobulin may still be given)
equipment: Tetanus-diphtheria or age-appropriate tetanus-containing vaccine kept cold
Tetanus immunoglobulin or anti-tetanus serum where available
Syringes and needles for intramuscular injection
steps: Confirm identity and assess the wound for tetanus risk.
Ask for and check documented tetanus vaccination history.
Decide whether vaccine, immunoglobulin, both or neither is needed using the national wound-management table.
Explain the plan and obtain verbal consent.
Clean and debride the wound thoroughly, as this is the most important step.
Perform hand hygiene and give the tetanus vaccine intramuscularly into the deltoid or anterolateral thigh.
Give human tetanus immunoglobulin, if indicated, intramuscularly at a different site with a separate syringe.
Use horse serum only if human immunoglobulin is unavailable; skin testing is unreliable, so have the anaphylaxis kit ready.
Observe for at least 30 minutes for immediate reactions.
Record what was given and when further doses to complete the primary series are due.
aftercare: Complete the remaining vaccine doses to finish the series.
Keep the wound clean and return for wound review.
red_flags: Treat anaphylaxis immediately, especially after horse serum.
Return urgently for jaw stiffness, difficulty swallowing, muscle spasms or stiffness near the wound.
Return for spreading redness, pus or fever.

indications: Serious AEFI such as death, hospital admission, disability or anaphylaxis
Clusters of AEFI or events causing community concern
Unusual or unexpected events after vaccination
contraindications: None
equipment: National AEFI reporting and investigation forms
Vaccination register, cards and vaccine stock records
Phone or transport to contact the LGA and state immunisation officers
steps: Ensure the affected person has received or is receiving appropriate treatment first.
Explain the purpose of the investigation to the patient or family and obtain verbal consent to the interview.
Record identity, vaccines given, dates and times, batch numbers and the person giving the vaccine.
Take a detailed history of the event, time from vaccination to onset, symptoms and treatment.
Examine the patient and review the clinical record and any test results.
Check vaccine storage, cold-chain records, reconstitution practice and injection technique at the site.
Identify any other people vaccinated from the same vials or batch and check them for similar events.
Collect and send samples of vaccine and diluent per national guidance if requested.
Notify the LGA immunisation officer and complete the AEFI reporting form within the national time limit.
Communicate calmly with the family and community without blaming individuals.
Agree follow-up and any corrective actions with the immunisation team.
aftercare: Follow up the patient until recovery or a final outcome is known.
Record the final causality classification when the review committee reports it.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for deaths, clusters or events causing panic in the community.
Suspend use of the suspected vial or batch pending advice if a programme error is suspected.

form.label: Other cases from same batch or session

indications: Fever now or in the past 48 hours, or other signs suggesting malaria
Confirmation of malaria before treatment as national policy requires
contraindications: None
equipment: Malaria RDT kit in date, stored per instructions
Sample transfer device supplied with the kit
steps: Confirm identity, take a brief history and explain the test.
Check the kit expiry and packaging and label the cassette with the patient's name.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Clean the fingertip (or heel in infants) and allow it to dry.
Prick the side of the fingertip, wipe away the first drop and collect blood with the transfer device.
Place the blood in the sample well and add the buffer drops as instructed.
Apply pressure to the puncture site and discard the lancet in the sharps container.
Start the timer and read the result at exactly the time stated by the manufacturer.
Interpret the control and test lines and record the result.
Treat or refer according to the result and national malaria guidelines.
aftercare: Explain the result and the plan to the patient.
If negative, look for another cause of fever.
Return if the fever continues for more than two to three days or symptoms worsen.
red_flags: Repeat with a new kit if there is no control line (invalid test).
Refer immediately for danger signs such as convulsions, lethargy, unable to drink, vomiting everything, breathing difficulty or jaundice.
Consider microscopy if the test is negative but malaria is still strongly suspected.

indications: Client-initiated testing or provider-initiated testing in clinics and antenatal care
Partners and family members of people living with HIV
Symptoms or conditions suggesting HIV, including TB and sexually transmitted infections
contraindications: Client declines after counselling
Children under 18 months need virological testing instead
equipment: National serial testing algorithm kits in date (screening, confirmatory and tie-breaker)
Lancets, alcohol swabs and capillary tubes or pipettes
HTS register and client intake form
steps: Confirm identity and give pre-test information in a private space.
Obtain informed verbal consent, including assent and caregiver consent for minors per national policy.
Check kit expiry and label the devices.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and take a fingerprick sample.
Run the first (screening) test and read it at the time stated by the manufacturer.
If reactive, run the second test and if needed the tie-breaker per the national algorithm.
Record the results and interpret the final status according to the algorithm.
Give the result in private with post-test counselling suited to the result.
For a positive result, arrange same-day linkage to antiretroviral therapy and offer partner and family testing.
For a negative result, discuss prevention, including condoms and PrEP, and retesting if exposure was recent.
Record the result in the HTS register and the patient record and keep results confidential.
aftercare: Retest per national guidance if in the window period or at ongoing risk.
Encourage partner testing and disclosure with support.
red_flags: Refer to the reference laboratory for inconclusive or discordant results.
Screen for intimate partner violence and suicide risk and refer if at risk.
Do not give a positive diagnosis based on a single test.

indications: HIV-exposed infants at the ages set by the national EID schedule
Sick infant of unknown HIV exposure with a reactive maternal or antibody test
Follow-up testing after breastfeeding stops
contraindications: None
equipment: Dried blood spot (DBS) card with filter paper
Gas-impermeable bag with desiccant and humidity card
steps: Confirm the infant's identity and HIV-exposed status and explain the test to the caregiver.
Obtain verbal consent and complete the request form and card label.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and warm the heel or toe.
Clean the site with alcohol and allow it to dry completely.
Puncture the lateral or medial plantar surface of the heel with an infant lancet.
Wipe away the first drop and let large drops fall onto each printed circle until fully filled from one side.
Do not touch the filter paper or layer blood on the same circle.
Apply pressure with gauze until bleeding stops and dispose of sharps safely.
Air-dry the card flat on the rack for at least three hours away from sunlight.
Package the dried card with desiccant and send it with the form by the sample transport system.
Record the sample and give the caregiver a return date for the result.
aftercare: Continue infant prophylaxis and breastfeeding counselling as per the plan.
Return on the given date for the result; positive results need prompt ART.
red_flags: Recollect if circles are underfilled, clotted, layered or smeared.
Start ART without waiting for confirmation if the PCR is positive, and send a confirmatory sample.
Refer a sick infant with signs of HIV disease urgently.

indications: Antenatal screening
Screening before hepatitis B vaccination or blood donation
Health workers, contacts of people with hepatitis B and people with HIV
Jaundice or abnormal liver tests
contraindications: None
equipment: HBsAg rapid test kit in date
Lancet, alcohol swab and transfer device or pipette
Buffer if required by the kit
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Check the kit expiry and label the device.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Take a fingerprick or venous sample as the kit requires.
Add the sample and buffer to the device as instructed.
Read the result at the time stated by the manufacturer and check the control line.
Give the result with counselling and record it.
If positive, arrange liver assessment and offer testing and vaccination to household and sexual contacts.
If negative and not immune, offer hepatitis B vaccination.
aftercare: Positive pregnant women need assessment for antiviral treatment and a plan for the baby's hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours of birth.
Advise avoiding alcohol and sharing razors or toothbrushes if positive.
red_flags: Repeat with a new device if the result is invalid.
Refer urgently for jaundice with confusion, bleeding or abdominal swelling.

indications: People who inject drugs, people with HIV, dialysis patients and those with past transfusion or unsafe injections
Abnormal liver tests or chronic liver disease
Health workers after occupational exposure
contraindications: None
equipment: Anti-HCV rapid test kit in date
Lancet, alcohol swab and transfer device
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and that a positive antibody test needs confirmation, and obtain verbal consent.
Check the kit expiry and label the device.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Take a fingerprick sample and add it with buffer to the device as instructed.
Read at the time stated by the manufacturer and check the control line.
Give the result with counselling and record it.
If reactive, request HCV RNA or core antigen testing to confirm current infection and refer for treatment.
Discuss prevention of transmission, including not sharing needles or razors.
aftercare: Return for the confirmatory result and treatment plan.
Retest people with ongoing risk at intervals.
