red_flags: Repeat with a new device if invalid.
Refer urgently for jaundice, confusion, vomiting blood or abdominal swelling.

indications: Antenatal screening at booking and again late in pregnancy where policy requires
Patients with sexually transmitted infections or genital ulcers
Key populations and partners of people with syphilis
contraindications: None
equipment: Treponemal rapid test or dual HIV-syphilis test kit in date
Lancet, alcohol swab and transfer device
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Check the kit expiry and label the device.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Take a fingerprick sample and add it with buffer to the device.
Read at the time stated by the manufacturer and check the control line.
Give the result with counselling and record it.
If positive, treat on the same day per national guidelines, especially in pregnancy, and notify partners for treatment.
Send RPR or VDRL where available to stage infection and monitor treatment response.
aftercare: Partners should be tested and treated to prevent reinfection.
Avoid sex until treatment of both partners is complete.
Return for follow-up testing as advised.
red_flags: Treat in pregnancy without delay to prevent congenital syphilis.
Observe for allergic reaction after treatment and refer if there is a penicillin allergy in pregnancy.
Refer for neurological or eye symptoms.

indications: Cervical screening of women in the national target age group
Women living with HIV, who need earlier and more frequent screening
Triage after a positive HPV test
contraindications: Menstruation (reschedule)
Pregnancy (defer routine screening unless policy allows)
Obvious cancerous growth (refer directly instead)
equipment: Examination couch and good light source
Freshly prepared dilute acetic acid (3–5% vinegar solution)
Lugol's iodine if VILI is used
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Take a brief gynaecological history and ask the client to empty her bladder.
Position her in lithotomy, perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Insert the speculum gently and fully expose the cervix.
Identify the squamocolumnar junction and note any discharge, polyps or growths.
Apply acetic acid to the cervix with a soaked swab and wait one minute.
Look for dense, well-defined acetowhite areas near the transformation zone.
If used, apply Lugol's iodine and look for mustard-yellow non-staining areas.
Classify the result as negative, positive or suspicious for cancer and note whether the transformation zone is fully visible.
Remove the speculum and decontaminate the instruments.
Explain the result and offer same-visit treatment if positive and eligible, or refer.
Record the findings with a cervix diagram in the register.
aftercare: If negative, rescreen at the interval set by national guidelines.
If treated, follow the post-treatment advice and return for review.
red_flags: Refer urgently for a growth, ulcer, contact bleeding or lesion suspicious for cancer.
Refer for colposcopy if the lesion is too large or extends into the canal.

form.label: Lesion extent
options: Less than 75% of cervix and ablation-eligible

indications: Primary cervical screening using HPV testing for women in the target age group
Women who decline a speculum examination or cannot easily attend a clinic
contraindications: Menstruation or heavy bleeding (reschedule)
Pregnancy (defer per local policy)
Abnormal symptoms such as postcoital bleeding needing a clinical examination instead
equipment: Self-sampling kit (swab or brush with transport tube)
steps: Confirm identity, explain the purpose of HPV testing and obtain verbal consent.
Label the tube with the client's details in her presence.
Explain how to collect the sample using the leaflet and wash hands.
Ask her to insert the swab into the vagina to the depth shown and rotate it for the time stated.
Ask her to place the swab into the tube, close it and hand it back.
Check the tube is labelled and sealed and complete the request form.
Store and transport the sample to the laboratory as instructed.
Record the sample and agree how she will receive the result.
aftercare: If HPV-negative, rescreen at the interval set by national guidelines.
If HPV-positive, return for VIA triage or treatment.
red_flags: Examine the client clinically instead if she reports abnormal bleeding, discharge or pain.
Recall and resample if the sample is rejected by the laboratory.

indications: VIA-positive or HPV-positive women with an ablation-eligible lesion
Lesion covering less than 75% of the cervix, fully visible and not entering the canal
contraindications: Suspected invasive cancer
Lesion extending into the canal or beyond the cryoprobe
Pregnancy
Active cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease (treat first)
Within 12 weeks after delivery
equipment: Carbon dioxide or nitrous oxide gas cylinder with adequate pressure
Dilute acetic acid and cotton swabs
steps: Confirm identity, eligibility, VIA findings and that she is not pregnant.
Explain the procedure, side effects and alternatives and obtain written consent.
Check the gas pressure and test the unit by freezing the probe briefly.
Position her in lithotomy, perform hand hygiene and insert the speculum.
Apply acetic acid to outline the lesion and confirm eligibility.
Place the probe tip firmly on the cervix centred on the os and covering the lesion.
Make sure the probe does not touch the vaginal walls.
Freeze for three minutes until an ice ball extends beyond the edge of the probe.
Thaw for five minutes, then freeze again for three minutes.
Allow the probe to thaw fully before removing it from the cervix.
Inspect the cervix, remove the speculum and decontaminate the probe.
Let her rest and check for cramping or faintness before she leaves.
aftercare: Expect watery discharge for up to four weeks and mild cramps.
Avoid sex, tampons and douching for four weeks, or use condoms.
Return for repeat screening at the time advised, usually after one year.
red_flags: Stop if the gas pressure drops or a full ice ball cannot be formed, and reschedule or refer.
Return urgently for fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe lower abdominal pain or heavy bleeding.

indications: VIA-positive or HPV-positive women with an ablation-eligible lesion
Lesion fully visible, not entering the canal and within reach of the probe
contraindications: Suspected invasive cancer
Lesion extending into the canal or too large for ablation
Pregnancy
Active cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease (treat first)
Within 12 weeks after delivery
equipment: Thermal ablation unit, charged, with sterile or high-level disinfected probes
Dilute acetic acid and cotton swabs
steps: Confirm identity, eligibility, screening findings and that she is not pregnant.
Explain the procedure, side effects and alternatives and obtain written consent.
Check the device is charged and heats to the treatment temperature.
Position her in lithotomy, perform hand hygiene and insert the speculum.
Apply acetic acid to outline the lesion and confirm eligibility.
Place the heated probe firmly on the cervix over the os for the time set by the device, usually 20 to 40 seconds.
Overlap further applications until the whole transformation zone and lesion are treated.
Remove the probe and inspect the cervix.
Remove the speculum and decontaminate the probe.
Let her rest and check for cramping or faintness before she leaves.
aftercare: Expect watery discharge and mild cramps for up to four weeks.
Avoid sex, tampons and douching for four weeks, or use condoms.
Return for repeat screening at the time advised, usually after one year.
red_flags: Stop and refer if the device fails to heat or the lesion cannot be fully covered.
Return urgently for fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe lower abdominal pain or heavy bleeding.

indications: Opportunistic breast screening in women, especially from age 40 or with risk factors
Breast lump, pain, nipple discharge or skin change
contraindications: Client declines
steps: Confirm identity, explain the examination, offer a chaperone and obtain verbal consent.
Take a brief history of symptoms, family history and menstrual and pregnancy history.
Perform hand hygiene and inspect both breasts with arms at the sides, raised and pressing on the hips.
Look for asymmetry, skin dimpling, peau d'orange, nipple retraction, ulceration or discharge.
Lay her down with her arm above her head and palpate each breast systematically with the flat of the fingers.
Cover the whole breast, including the axillary tail, using a vertical strip or circular pattern.
Gently examine the nipple for discharge.
Palpate the axillary, supraclavicular and infraclavicular lymph nodes.
Describe any lump by site (clock position and distance from nipple), size, consistency and mobility.
Explain the findings and refer for imaging or biopsy if abnormal.
Teach breast awareness and record the findings on a breast diagram.
aftercare: Encourage breast awareness and early reporting of any change.
Attend referral appointments promptly if abnormal.
red_flags: Refer urgently for a hard, fixed or irregular lump, skin changes, nipple retraction, bloody discharge or enlarged axillary nodes.
Refer any new lump in a woman over 30 for imaging.

indications: Testing for TB infection in contacts and people with HIV before preventive therapy where policy uses it
Supporting the diagnosis of TB in children
Screening of health workers
contraindications: Previous severe reaction such as blistering or ulceration to a tuberculin test
Extensive burns or eczema at the test site
equipment: Tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) kept cold
Tuberculin syringe with fine short needle
Ruler marked in millimetres and pen
steps: Confirm identity, explain the test and the need to return in 48 to 72 hours, and obtain verbal consent.
Check the PPD expiry and draw up the standard volume per the product instructions.
Perform hand hygiene and choose the inner surface of the forearm away from veins.
Stretch the skin and insert the needle bevel up just under the surface.
Inject slowly to raise a pale bleb with an orange-peel appearance and withdraw the needle.
Do not cover or rub the site and discard the syringe safely.
Book the reading visit 48 to 72 hours later.
At reading, feel for induration with the fingertips and mark its edges across the forearm.
Measure the transverse diameter of induration, not redness, in millimetres.
Interpret the result using the cut-off for the person's risk group and record it.
aftercare: Keep the site clean and do not scratch it; mild itching is normal.
Return on the reading day; results read after 72 hours may be unreliable.
red_flags: Repeat at a different site if no bleb forms.
Assess for active TB disease with symptoms, X-ray and sputum before starting preventive therapy.
Return if there is blistering, ulceration or a very large reaction.

indications: Household and close contacts of a person with pulmonary TB, especially bacteriologically confirmed
Contacts of drug-resistant TB
contraindications: None
equipment: TB contact register and screening tool
Access to GeneXpert or other rapid molecular test and chest X-ray
steps: Obtain the index patient's consent and list all household and close contacts.
Visit the household or invite contacts to the clinic and explain the purpose.
Obtain verbal consent from each contact or caregiver.
Screen each contact for cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats and, in children, poor growth.
Weigh children and check growth and HIV status where relevant.
Collect sputum from symptomatic contacts for rapid molecular testing and arrange chest X-ray where available.
Refer symptomatic children for clinical assessment for TB.
Offer TB preventive therapy to eligible contacts once active TB is excluded.
Give TB infection-control advice to the household.
Record each contact and the outcome in the contact register.
aftercare: Contacts should return at once if symptoms develop.
Follow up contacts on preventive therapy for adherence and side effects.
red_flags: Refer urgently any contact with severe illness, breathing difficulty or a child under five with symptoms.
Contacts of drug-resistant TB need specialist advice before preventive therapy.

form.label: Screening result
options: No TB - not eligible for preventive therapy

indications: Patients on TB treatment, especially during the intensive phase and for drug-resistant TB
Other treatment programmes using supervised dosing
contraindications: None
equipment: Phone for video-observed therapy where used
steps: Confirm the patient's identity and check the treatment card for the regimen and phase.
Ask about symptoms, side effects and any missed doses.
Check the correct medicines for the regimen and weight band from the patient's supply.
Watch the patient swallow all the medicines with water.
Record the dose as taken on the treatment card.
Screen for side effects such as jaundice, vomiting, rash, numbness or visual or hearing changes.
Check weight monthly and adjust weight band through the clinician if needed.
Arrange follow-up sputum tests at the times set by the programme.
Trace patients who miss a dose the same or next day.
aftercare: Take medicines at the same time each day and never stop early.
Cover the mouth when coughing and keep rooms ventilated.
red_flags: Stop the medicines and refer urgently for jaundice, persistent vomiting, severe rash or confusion.
Refer for worsening cough, coughing blood, breathlessness or weight loss despite treatment.
Escalate patients who interrupt treatment for two weeks or more.

indications: HIV-negative people at substantial ongoing risk of HIV
Serodiscordant partners, key populations and people requesting PrEP
contraindications: HIV-positive or suspected acute HIV infection
Reduced kidney function below the threshold in national guidelines
Known allergy to the PrEP medicine
equipment: HIV rapid test kits per the national algorithm
Hepatitis B and creatinine testing where available
steps: Confirm identity and assess HIV risk and the client's reasons for wanting PrEP in private.
Test for HIV on the same day using the national algorithm.
Screen for symptoms of acute HIV infection in the last month and defer if present.
Check hepatitis B status, kidney function and pregnancy status where available.
Explain how PrEP works, effective use, side effects and the need for regular testing.
Obtain verbal consent and agree the dosing approach recommended nationally.
Prescribe PrEP and give condoms and lubricant.
Discuss adherence support and when protection begins.
Record baseline results and book the first follow-up visit.
aftercare: Return after one month and then every three months for HIV testing and refills.
Continue condoms to prevent other sexually transmitted infections.
Do not stop suddenly if hepatitis B positive without medical advice.
red_flags: Defer PrEP and retest if there are flu-like symptoms suggesting acute HIV.
Stop and link to ART if any follow-up HIV test is positive.
Return for severe side effects or reduced urine output.

form.label: Risk group
options: Men who have sex with men

indications: Exposure to blood or body fluids from a person with HIV or unknown status within 72 hours
Needlestick and sharps injuries, mucosal splashes, sexual assault and unprotected sex
contraindications: More than 72 hours since exposure (PEP not effective; offer follow-up testing)
Exposed person already HIV-positive (link to ART)
equipment: Soap and running water and eyewash
PEP starter pack per national guidelines
Pregnancy test and hepatitis B testing where available
Emergency contraception and STI treatment for sexual assault
Exposure report form and PEP register
steps: Give first aid at once by washing skin with soap and water or flushing mucosa or eyes with water.
Confirm identity, the time and type of exposure and the source's HIV status if known.
Assess whether the exposure carries a risk of HIV transmission.
Obtain verbal consent and test the exposed person for HIV.
Test the source with consent where possible, without delaying PEP.
Start PEP as soon as possible and within 72 hours, using the national regimen.
For sexual assault, offer emergency contraception, STI treatment, forensic referral and psychosocial support.
Assess hepatitis B vaccination status and give vaccine or immunoglobulin as needed.
Explain the full course, side effects and adherence and give condoms.
Complete the exposure report and book follow-up testing.
aftercare: Complete the full course of PEP.
Use condoms and avoid blood donation until follow-up testing is negative.
Return for HIV testing at the intervals given.
red_flags: Do not delay PEP to wait for source test results.
Return for rash, jaundice, severe vomiting or flu-like illness during or after the course.
Refer survivors of sexual assault at risk of further harm or with severe distress.

indications: Routine growth monitoring of children under five at immunisation and child welfare visits
Nutrition screening of sick children and in community programmes
contraindications: None
equipment: Calibrated infant and child weighing scale or hanging scale with pants
Length board for children under two and height board for older children
Growth chart in the child health card
steps: Confirm the child's identity and date of birth and calculate age.
Remove heavy clothing and shoes and zero the scale.
Weigh the child and read the weight to the nearest 0.1 kg.
Measure length lying down for children under two and height standing for older children.
Measure MUAC on the left arm midway between shoulder and elbow for children aged 6 to 59 months.
Check both feet for pitting oedema by pressing for three seconds.
Plot the measurements on the growth chart and note the direction of the curve.
Classify nutritional status using the WHO standards.
Discuss the growth curve with the caregiver and give feeding advice suited to age.
Refer or enrol children with acute malnutrition according to the local protocol.
aftercare: Return for the next growth monitoring visit.
Follow the feeding advice given.
red_flags: Refer urgently for bilateral pitting oedema, MUAC under 115 mm with complications or a sick child.
Act early if weight falls, stays flat or crosses centile lines downward.

indications: Children aged 6 to 59 months every six months per the national schedule
Children with measles, severe acute malnutrition, persistent diarrhoea or xerophthalmia per treatment guidelines
contraindications: Supplementation received within the past month (except treatment of measles or xerophthalmia per protocol)
equipment: Vitamin A capsules of the correct strength for age, in date
Child health card and tally sheet
steps: Confirm the child's identity and age.
Check the card or ask when vitamin A was last given.
Explain the purpose to the caregiver and obtain verbal consent.
Select the capsule strength and number for the child's age band.
Perform hand hygiene and cut the narrow tip of the capsule with clean scissors.
Squeeze the contents into the child's mouth, not the whole capsule for young children.
Make sure the child swallows the liquid and does not spit it out.
Record the date on the child health card and tally sheet.
Tell the caregiver when the next dose is due.
aftercare: Return in six months for the next dose.
Encourage foods rich in vitamin A such as red palm oil, eggs, liver and dark green leafy vegetables.
red_flags: Do not give extra doses beyond the schedule because of the risk of toxicity.
Return for vomiting, headache or a bulging fontanelle after the dose.

indications: Children from 12 months in areas with soil-transmitted helminths, every six or twelve months
School-based deworming programmes
Pregnant women after the first trimester per national guidelines
contraindications: First trimester of pregnancy
Child under 12 months
Known allergy to the medicine
equipment: Child health card or tally sheet
steps: Confirm identity and age and check when deworming was last given.
Screen for pregnancy in women and girls of reproductive age.
Explain the purpose and common side effects and obtain verbal consent.
Select the medicine and number of tablets for the age group per national guidance.
Crush or break the tablet and mix with water for young children to prevent choking.
Observe the child or adult chewing and swallowing the tablet.
Record the treatment on the card or tally sheet.
Give advice on handwashing, wearing shoes and safe sanitation.
aftercare: Mild abdominal pain or nausea may occur and usually settles quickly.
Return for the next round as scheduled.
red_flags: Never force a tablet into a crying or struggling child because of choking risk.
Return for severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or allergic reaction.

indications: Children aged 3 to 59 months in SMC states during the high transmission season
Monthly cycles as set by the national malaria programme
contraindications: Child with fever or acute illness (test and treat instead)
Known allergy to sulfa drugs or amodiaquine
Child receiving co-trimoxazole prophylaxis
Child who received the same medicines in the past month
equipment: Malaria RDT kits for febrile children
SMC child record card and tally sheets
steps: Confirm the child's identity and age band and check the SMC card for previous cycles.
Ask about fever, illness, allergies and co-trimoxazole use.
Test febrile children with a malaria RDT and treat or refer instead of giving SMC.
Explain the medicines, side effects and the home doses and obtain verbal consent.
Give the first day's medicines from the blister pack for the age band, dispersed in water.
Observe the child for 30 minutes and repeat the dose once if the child vomits.
Give the caregiver the remaining doses for days two and three and show how to give them.
Record the cycle on the SMC card and tally sheet.
Tell the caregiver the date of the next cycle.
aftercare: Give the home doses at the same time on the next two days.
Bring the child to the facility if fever develops at any time.
red_flags: Refer for severe vomiting, rash, jaundice or a sick child.
Do not give SMC to a child who vomits the repeat dose; refer for assessment.

form.label: Fever or illness on the day

name: Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy

indications: Pregnant women from 13 weeks of gestation at each scheduled antenatal visit, at least a month apart
contraindications: First trimester
Allergy to sulfa drugs
Women taking co-trimoxazole prophylaxis (for example with HIV)
Last IPTp given less than a month ago
equipment: Insecticide-treated net for distribution where available
steps: Confirm identity and gestational age and review the antenatal card for previous IPTp.
Check for contraindications, including allergy, co-trimoxazole use and the date of the last dose.
Explain the purpose of IPTp and obtain verbal consent.
Give the tablets with water under direct observation in the clinic.
Record the dose number and date on the antenatal card and register.
Give or check an insecticide-treated net and advise sleeping under it every night.
Tell her the date of the next antenatal visit and IPTp dose.
aftercare: Continue folic acid and iron as prescribed (avoid high-dose folic acid on the day per national guidance).
Sleep under an insecticide-treated net every night.
red_flags: Stop and refer urgently for skin rash, peeling or mouth ulcers after the dose.
Return for fever, as malaria in pregnancy needs prompt testing and treatment.

name: Mass drug administration for neglected tropical diseases

indications: Community-wide treatment for onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths or trachoma in endemic areas
contraindications: Pregnancy and first week of breastfeeding for ivermectin, and first trimester of pregnancy for albendazole
Children below the height or age limit for each medicine
Severe illness on the day
Known allergy to the medicine
steps: Confirm community mobilisation and explain the campaign to the household.
Register each household member and confirm identity and age.
Screen for pregnancy, breastfeeding, severe illness and previous reactions.
Measure height with the dose pole to set the number of tablets where required.
Obtain verbal consent from each person or caregiver.
Give the tablets and observe the person swallowing them with water.
Record treatment in the register and tally sheet.
Explain possible side effects, such as itching or swelling, and where to report them.
Return to treat people who were absent.
aftercare: Mild itching, rash, dizziness or abdominal pain may occur for a day or two.
Report any side effects to the community drug distributor.
red_flags: Do not give ivermectin where loiasis is co-endemic without specialist programme guidance.
Refer urgently for severe reactions such as confusion, breathing difficulty, high fever or collapse.

indications: Opportunistic screening of adults at any visit or community event
Pregnant women at antenatal visits
Adults with diabetes, kidney disease or other risk factors
contraindications: Do not use an arm with an AV fistula, lymphoedema or on the side of a mastectomy
equipment: Cuffs of correct size (small, standard and large adult)
steps: Confirm identity, explain the check and obtain verbal consent.
Ask the person to avoid caffeine, smoking and exercise for 30 minutes and empty the bladder if possible.
Seat the person with back supported, feet flat and arm supported at heart level and rest for five minutes.
Choose a cuff whose bladder covers most of the arm circumference.
Wrap the cuff on the bare upper arm with the artery mark over the brachial artery.
Take the reading without talking and repeat after one to two minutes.
Record the average of the last two readings and the arm used.
Measure both arms at the first visit and use the higher arm thereafter.
Classify the result and explain it to the person.
Give lifestyle advice and refer or book repeat readings according to the result.
aftercare: Return for repeat measurement on another day if raised.
Reduce salt, stay active, maintain healthy weight and avoid smoking and excess alcohol.
red_flags: Refer urgently for blood pressure at or above 180/110 mmHg or raised readings with chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache or confusion.
Refer pregnant women with readings at or above 140/90 mmHg the same day.

indications: A confirmed or probable case of a notifiable infectious disease such as Lassa fever, cholera, measles, mpox, diphtheria or TB
Sexually transmitted infections needing partner notification
contraindications: None
equipment: Case investigation and contact listing forms (paper or electronic)
Personal protective equipment suited to the disease
steps: Prepare by reviewing the case details and the disease's incubation period and transmission route.
Wear PPE appropriate to the disease and keep a safe distance where needed.
Introduce yourself, explain the purpose and confidentiality, and obtain verbal consent.
Establish the period of infectiousness for the case.
List everyone the case was in contact with during that period, with type and date of last contact.
Collect each contact's name, age, address and phone number.
Classify each contact by exposure risk.
Agree how and when each contact will be reached without revealing the case's identity unnecessarily.
Give advice on symptoms, hygiene and when to seek care.
Report the contact list to the LGA disease surveillance and notification officer.
Arrange daily or periodic follow-up of contacts for the incubation period.
aftercare: Follow up contacts until the end of the monitoring period.
Refer symptomatic contacts for testing and isolation.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for viral haemorrhagic fever, cholera clusters or any outbreak signal.
Stop the interview and use full PPE if the person is unwell with a high-risk disease.
Protect the safety and confidentiality of the case, especially for stigmatised diseases.

indications: Group education in clinics, antenatal sessions, schools or communities
Campaign topics such as immunisation, malaria, nutrition, hygiene or family planning
contraindications: None
equipment: Flip chart, posters or demonstration materials
steps: Choose the topic from local needs and prepare simple key messages.
Arrange a comfortable space where everyone can see and hear.
Greet the group, introduce yourself and explain the topic and duration.
Use the local language and simple words, avoiding jargon.
Ask what people already know and believe about the topic.
Present the key messages using pictures, stories or demonstrations.
Invite questions and correct misconceptions respectfully.
Check understanding by asking participants to repeat the main points.
Tell people where to get services related to the topic.
Record the topic, number of attendees and any follow-up needs.
aftercare: Follow up individuals who need personal counselling or services.
red_flags: Refer anyone who reveals a medical emergency or abuse during the session.
Note and report rumours or misinformation that may harm uptake of services.

indications: Medical fitness assessment requested by an employer before starting work
Job-specific requirements such as driving, food handling, health care or work at height
contraindications: None
equipment: Employer's medical form and job description
Weighing scale, height measure and BP machine
Snellen chart and colour vision plates
Access to laboratory and chest X-ray as required
steps: Confirm identity with photo identification and review the employer's form and job demands.
Explain what the examination includes, who will receive the report, and obtain written consent.
Take a medical, occupational, medication and immunisation history.
Measure weight, height, BMI, blood pressure and pulse.
Test visual acuity and colour vision and screen hearing where required.
Perform a systematic physical examination.
Test urine with a dipstick.
Request tests required by the employer or indicated by findings, with consent for any HIV or pregnancy testing.
Decide fitness for the specific job and any restrictions or adjustments.
Discuss any findings with the candidate before reporting.
Complete the report, disclosing only fitness and restrictions, not diagnoses, unless the candidate agrees.
aftercare: Follow up any new findings such as raised blood pressure or diabetes with treatment or referral.
Update immunisations required for the job.
red_flags: Do not test for HIV or pregnancy without specific informed consent, and do not use them to bar employment.
Refer urgently any serious finding found during the examination.

indications: Food handlers in restaurants, hotels, schools, hospitals and markets needing certification by regulation
Return to work after diarrhoea, typhoid or other infectious illness
contraindications: None
equipment: Sputum containers and access to chest X-ray where required
Gloves and good light for examination
steps: Confirm identity, explain the screening and obtain verbal consent.
Ask about recent diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, cough, skin infections and typhoid.
Examine the hands, nails, skin, eyes and throat for infection or jaundice.
Check for discharging ears, boils or infected wounds.
Collect stool for microscopy and culture and other tests required by local regulation.
Screen for TB symptoms and arrange sputum testing if present.
Give food hygiene education, especially handwashing and covering wounds.
Decide fitness to handle food and issue or withhold the certificate.
Record results and any treatment or exclusion period.
aftercare: Stay away from food handling while ill with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or infected skin.
Renew the certificate at the interval required.
red_flags: Exclude from food handling and notify public health for typhoid, cholera, hepatitis A or dysentery.
Treat and recheck carriers before return to work.

indications: School entry and periodic school health checks
School health programme screening days
contraindications: None
equipment: Weighing scale, height board and MUAC tape
steps: Confirm the child's identity and that parental consent or school consent is in place.
Examine the child with a parent, teacher or chaperone present, respecting privacy and modesty.
Review the child's medical history and immunisation record from the parent or card.
Measure weight and height and calculate BMI-for-age.
Screen vision and, where possible, hearing.
Examine the eyes, ears, teeth, throat, skin and scalp.
Listen to the heart and chest and examine the abdomen.
Check for signs of anaemia, malnutrition, goitre and skin infections such as scabies or ringworm.
Note developmental, learning or behavioural concerns from the teacher or parent.
Identify missed vaccines and arrange catch-up.
Record the findings and send a summary with referral notes to the parent.
aftercare: Follow through referral for any problem found.
Repeat the check at the next scheduled school health visit.
red_flags: Refer urgently for a heart murmur with symptoms, severe anaemia, severe malnutrition or signs of abuse.
Refer for poor vision, hearing loss or dental infection.

indications: Routine screening of school children for reduced vision
Child with squint, headaches, poor school performance or reported difficulty seeing the board
contraindications: None
equipment: Snellen, tumbling E or LogMAR chart at the correct distance (usually 6 m)
Measuring tape to mark the distance
Occluder or card to cover each eye
steps: Confirm consent from the school or parent and the child's identity.
Set up the chart at eye level in good light and mark the testing distance.
Explain and demonstrate the test using the tumbling E or letters.
Test with glasses on if the child normally wears them.
Cover the left eye and test the right eye from the top line down.
Record the smallest line on which the child reads most letters correctly.
Repeat for the left eye, then both eyes together.
Retest any eye that does not reach the pass line through a pinhole.
Check eye alignment and look for redness, discharge or white pupil with a torch.
Refer children who fail the pass criteria and record the results.
aftercare: Attend the eye clinic referral and wear any glasses prescribed.
Sit near the front of the class until assessed.
red_flags: Refer urgently for a white pupil, sudden loss of vision, a painful red eye or a new squint.
Refer children who fail in one eye even if the other is normal.

indications: Confirmation of pregnancy viability and dating
Fetal anatomy survey in the second trimester
Assessment of fetal growth, presentation, liquor and placenta
Bleeding or pain in pregnancy
Reduced fetal movements or suspected multiple pregnancy
contraindications: None absolute for transabdominal ultrasound
equipment: Ultrasound machine with curvilinear abdominal probe
Tissue or towel for gel removal
steps: Confirm patient identity, gestation by dates and the clinical question on the request.
Explain the scan, obtain verbal consent and offer a chaperone.
Ask the patient to lie supine with a slight left tilt and expose the lower abdomen.
Perform hand hygiene, apply gel and select the obstetric preset.
Confirm the number of fetuses, fetal heart activity and presentation.
Take biometric measurements appropriate to gestation (CRL or BPD, HC, AC and FL).
Assess amniotic fluid volume by deepest pool or amniotic fluid index.
Locate the placenta and note its relation to the internal os.
Perform an anatomy survey when the gestation is suitable.
Save representative images and record measurements and estimated fetal weight.
Clean the probe and remove gel from the patient.
Explain findings within your role and refer urgent findings to the obstetric team the same day.
aftercare: File the report in the record and give the patient a copy if local practice allows.
Arrange a repeat or specialist scan where findings are uncertain.
Refer abnormal findings to the antenatal clinic or obstetrician.
red_flags: No fetal heart activity in a previously viable pregnancy
Suspected ectopic pregnancy or free fluid in the pelvis
Placenta praevia or suspected abruption with bleeding
Severe oligohydramnios or fetal growth restriction
Abnormal fetal lie in labour or preterm labour

indications: Abdominal pain or mass
Jaundice or abnormal liver tests
Suspected gallstones, renal stones or hydronephrosis
Ascites or suspected abscess
Pelvic mass or urinary symptoms
contraindications: None absolute
Open wound or dressing over the scan area (scan around it or use sterile cover)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with curvilinear probe (linear probe for small children)
steps: Confirm patient identity, the clinical question and fasting status where gallbladder assessment is needed.
Explain the scan, obtain verbal consent and offer a chaperone.
Ask the patient to drink water beforehand if a full bladder is needed for pelvic views.
Position the patient supine and expose the abdomen while maintaining privacy.
Perform hand hygiene, apply gel and select the abdominal preset.
Examine the liver, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas and spleen systematically.
Examine both kidneys in two planes and measure their lengths.
Examine the aorta, bladder and pelvic organs as appropriate.
Look for free fluid, collections and masses and measure any abnormality.
Save representative and abnormal images.
Clean the probe and remove gel from the patient.
Write the report and communicate urgent findings to the requesting clinician.
aftercare: The patient may eat and drink normally after the scan.
Arrange further imaging (CT) or referral where findings are indeterminate.
red_flags: Free intraperitoneal fluid in a trauma or unwell patient
Abdominal aortic aneurysm larger than expected or with symptoms
Obstructed infected kidney or bilateral hydronephrosis
Suspected appendicitis, intussusception or bowel obstruction in a child

indications: Suspected ectopic pregnancy or early pregnancy assessment
Abnormal uterine bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding
Pelvic pain or adnexal mass
Infertility work-up and follicle tracking
Cervical length assessment in pregnancy
contraindications: Patient declines or has never been sexually active (use transabdominal approach)
Ruptured membranes or placenta praevia with active bleeding (seek senior advice)
Vaginal atresia or recent vaginal surgery
equipment: Probe cover or condom and sterile gel
High-level disinfection for the probe per local protocol
Couch with privacy screen and drape
steps: Confirm patient identity, last menstrual period and the clinical question.
Explain the procedure, obtain verbal consent and ensure a chaperone is present.
Ask the patient to empty her bladder.
Position in lithotomy or with the pelvis raised on a pillow and drape for privacy.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and cover the probe with gel and a probe cover.
Insert the probe gently into the vagina with the patient's agreement.
Examine the uterus in sagittal and transverse planes and measure the endometrial thickness.
Examine both ovaries and adnexa and the pouch of Douglas for fluid.
In early pregnancy identify the gestational sac location, yolk sac, embryo and heartbeat.
Withdraw the probe, remove and discard the cover and clean the probe by high-level disinfection.
Save images, write the report and communicate urgent findings immediately.
aftercare: Mild spotting can occur and should settle.
Arrange serial scans or hCG follow-up for pregnancy of unknown location per local protocol.
red_flags: Empty uterus with positive pregnancy test and adnexal mass or free fluid
Haemodynamic instability during or after the scan
Heavy vaginal bleeding after the scan

indications: Prostate volume assessment
Raised PSA or abnormal digital rectal examination
Guidance for prostate biopsy
Suspected prostatic abscess or seminal vesicle pathology
contraindications: Painful anorectal conditions such as acute fissure or thrombosed haemorrhoids
Previous abdominoperineal resection
Patient declines
equipment: Ultrasound machine with endocavity or biplane rectal probe
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and any bleeding risk or anticoagulant use.
Explain the procedure, obtain verbal consent and offer a chaperone.
Position the patient in left lateral decubitus with knees drawn up.
Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves and perform a digital rectal examination.
Cover the probe with gel and a probe cover and lubricate it.
Insert the probe gently into the rectum.
Examine the prostate in transverse and sagittal planes and measure three diameters.
Calculate the prostate volume and note focal lesions, calcification and seminal vesicles.
Withdraw the probe, discard the cover and disinfect the probe.
Save images and write the report.
aftercare: Mild rectal discomfort may occur for a short time.
Arrange biopsy or urology review as indicated.
red_flags: Rectal bleeding that does not stop
Fever or rigors after the scan
Suspected prostatic abscess needing drainage

indications: Scrotal or testicular swelling or mass
Acute scrotal pain (only if it does not delay surgical exploration for suspected torsion)
Undescended testis localisation
Suspected varicocele or hydrocele
Infertility work-up or scrotal trauma
contraindications: Suspected testicular torsion where scanning would delay surgery
equipment: Ultrasound machine with high-frequency linear probe and colour Doppler
steps: Confirm patient identity, symptoms and duration of pain.
Escalate immediately to the surgical team if torsion is suspected rather than scanning first.
Explain the scan, obtain verbal consent (parental consent for children) and offer a chaperone.
Position supine and support the scrotum on a rolled towel with the penis covered.
Perform hand hygiene, apply warm gel and select the small parts preset.
Examine each testis and epididymis in two planes and measure the testes.
Compare blood flow in both testes with colour Doppler.
Assess for hydrocele, varicocele with Valsalva, hernia and masses.
Save images, clean the probe and write the report.
Communicate urgent findings directly to the surgical team.
aftercare: Refer solid testicular masses urgently to urology.
Arrange follow-up for benign findings as advised.
red_flags: Absent or reduced flow in a painful testis
Solid intratesticular mass
Testicular rupture after trauma
Abscess formation

indications: Palpable breast lump
Breast pain localised to one area
Nipple discharge or skin changes
Further assessment of a mammographic abnormality
Suspected breast abscess
contraindications: None absolute
equipment: Ultrasound machine with high-frequency linear probe
Couch with pillow and privacy screen
steps: Confirm patient identity, history and the site of the lump or symptom.
Explain the scan, obtain verbal consent and offer a chaperone.
Position supine with the arm raised behind the head, rolling slightly to the opposite side for outer quadrants.
Perform hand hygiene, apply gel and select the breast preset.
Scan the whole breast systematically in radial or overlapping strips including the axillary tail.
Examine the axilla for lymph nodes.
Measure any lesion in three dimensions and record clock position and distance from the nipple.
Classify the lesion using the BI-RADS categories.
Save images, clean the probe and write the report.
Refer suspicious lesions for biopsy and explain the next step to the patient.
aftercare: Arrange biopsy for BI-RADS 4 or 5 lesions.
Arrange short-interval follow-up for BI-RADS 3 lesions.
red_flags: Irregular solid mass or suspicious axillary nodes
Breast abscess needing drainage
Skin tethering or peau d'orange

form.label: Lesion clock position and distance from nipple

indications: Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Peripheral arterial disease or limb ischaemia
Carotid stenosis assessment after stroke or TIA
Varicose vein assessment
Assessment of dialysis access or vascular grafts
contraindications: None absolute
Open wound or fresh dressing at the scan site (scan around it)
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear and curvilinear probes and colour and spectral Doppler
steps: Confirm patient identity, the vessel to be studied and the clinical question.
Explain the scan and obtain verbal consent.
Position the patient appropriately (reverse Trendelenburg for leg veins, supine with head turned for carotids).
Perform hand hygiene, apply gel and select the vascular preset.
Image the vessel in transverse and longitudinal planes along its length.
For veins check compressibility, flow and augmentation at each level.
For arteries record waveforms and peak velocities and grade any stenosis.
Measure and save images of abnormal segments.
Clean the probe and remove gel.
Write the report and communicate a positive DVT or critical stenosis to the clinician immediately.
aftercare: Start treatment as directed by the requesting team for a confirmed DVT.
Repeat the scan as advised if an initial study is negative but suspicion remains.
red_flags: Proximal DVT or free-floating thrombus
Critical limb ischaemia or absent distal flow
Severe carotid stenosis in a symptomatic patient
Pseudoaneurysm after arterial puncture

indications: Reduced fetal movements
Post-term pregnancy
Hypertensive disorders or diabetes in pregnancy
Fetal growth restriction or oligohydramnios
Non-reassuring CTG
contraindications: None absolute
Gestation below viability (result not useful)
equipment: CTG machine if the non-stress test is included
steps: Confirm patient identity, gestational age and indication.
Explain the test and obtain verbal consent.
Position the patient semi-recumbent with a left lateral tilt.
Perform hand hygiene, apply gel and locate the fetus.
Observe for up to 30 minutes for fetal breathing movements, gross body movements and tone.
Measure the deepest vertical pool of amniotic fluid.
Score each component as 2 or 0 and add the non-stress test score if performed.
Record the total score and time taken.
Clean the probe and remove gel.
Communicate a low score to the obstetric team immediately.
aftercare: Repeat the test as advised by the obstetric team.
Advise the patient to report reduced fetal movements promptly.
red_flags: Score of 4 or less
Oligohydramnios regardless of total score
Absent fetal heart activity

name: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma

indications: Blunt or penetrating torso trauma
Unexplained hypotension after injury
Suspected haemothorax or pneumothorax (extended FAST)
Suspected pericardial effusion after trauma
contraindications: Need for immediate laparotomy should not be delayed by scanning
equipment: Portable ultrasound machine with curvilinear or phased array probe
steps: Perform the scan during the primary survey without interrupting resuscitation.
Explain to the patient if conscious; consent is implied in the emergency.
Perform hand hygiene, wear gloves and apply gel.
Examine the right upper quadrant for fluid in the hepatorenal pouch.
Examine the left upper quadrant for perisplenic and splenorenal fluid.
Examine the pelvis for fluid around the bladder.
Examine the pericardium from the subxiphoid window.
For eFAST examine both anterior chests for lung sliding and both bases for fluid.
Record each view as positive, negative or indeterminate.
Communicate results to the trauma team leader immediately.
Repeat the scan if the patient's condition changes.
aftercare: A negative FAST does not exclude injury; arrange CT or observation as indicated.
Repeat FAST after any change in haemodynamic status.
red_flags: Positive FAST in an unstable patient (surgery or transfer without delay)
Pericardial fluid with hypotension
Absent lung sliding with hypoxia or hypotension

indications: Acute breathlessness or hypoxia
Suspected pneumonia, pleural effusion or pneumothorax
Suspected pulmonary oedema
Monitoring of known lung disease where X-ray is not available
contraindications: None absolute
equipment: Ultrasound machine with curvilinear, phased array or linear probe
steps: Confirm patient identity and the clinical question.
Explain the scan and obtain verbal consent.
Position the patient supine or sitting depending on condition.
Perform hand hygiene and apply gel.
Scan each hemithorax in anterior, lateral and posterior zones.
Assess for lung sliding, A-lines and B-lines in each zone.
Look for consolidation, air bronchograms and pleural fluid at the bases.
Estimate the size of any effusion and look for septations.
Record findings by zone and save representative images.
Clean the probe and communicate findings to the treating team.
aftercare: Combine findings with clinical assessment and other tests.
Repeat the scan to monitor response to treatment.
red_flags: Absent lung sliding with a lung point (pneumothorax)
Large effusion with respiratory distress
Diffuse bilateral B-lines with hypoxia

indications: Abnormal uterine bleeding with suspected polyp or submucous fibroid
Infertility or recurrent miscarriage work-up
Thickened or poorly seen endometrium on transvaginal scan
Suspected intrauterine adhesions
contraindications: Pregnancy or possible pregnancy
Active pelvic infection or untreated cervicitis
Heavy active bleeding
equipment: Ultrasound machine with endocavity probe, probe cover and gel
Sonohysterography catheter or small paediatric Foley catheter
Sterile normal saline and 20 mL syringes
Sponge-holding forceps and tenaculum if needed
steps: Confirm identity, menstrual cycle day (ideally early follicular phase) and a negative pregnancy test.
Explain the procedure, obtain written consent and ensure a chaperone is present.
Offer simple analgesia before the procedure per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy and perform a baseline transvaginal scan.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, insert the speculum and clean the cervix with antiseptic.
Pass the catheter through the cervix into the uterine cavity and inflate the balloon if present.
Remove the speculum carefully leaving the catheter in place and reinsert the transvaginal probe.
Instil sterile saline slowly while scanning the cavity in sagittal and transverse planes.
Identify and measure any polyp, fibroid or adhesion outlined by the saline.
Deflate the balloon, remove the catheter and observe the patient briefly.
Disinfect the probe, save images and write the report.
aftercare: Expect mild cramping and watery discharge for a day.
Use simple analgesia as needed.
Return if fever, worsening pain or foul discharge develops.
red_flags: Fever or offensive discharge in the days after the procedure
Severe pelvic pain
Vasovagal collapse that does not settle

indications: Suspected fracture or dislocation
Chest symptoms, pneumonia or tuberculosis screening
Abdominal obstruction or perforation
Foreign body localisation
Line, tube or device position check
contraindications: Pregnancy for abdominal or pelvic films unless clinically essential (shield and justify)
equipment: X-ray machine (fixed or mobile) with digital or film cassette
Lead aprons, thyroid shields and gonad shields
Positioning aids and immobilisation devices for children
steps: Confirm patient identity against the request and the body part, side and views required.
Check the request is justified and ask women of reproductive age about possible pregnancy.
Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent.
Remove metal objects and clothing from the area and provide a gown.
Position the patient for the required projection using positioning aids.
Apply lead shielding where it does not obscure the area of interest.
Collimate the beam to the area of interest and set exposure factors for patient size.
Ensure staff are behind the protective screen and that carers holding children wear lead.
Instruct the patient to keep still and hold their breath if needed, then make the exposure.
Check image quality and repeat only if non-diagnostic.
Label the image with patient details, side marker and date and send for reporting.
aftercare: No specific aftercare; return to the referring clinician for results.
Record the number of exposures in the record.
red_flags: Unexpected tension pneumothorax, free gas under the diaphragm or misplaced tube (inform clinician immediately)
Unstable fracture or cervical spine injury
Possible non-accidental injury in a child

indications: Breast cancer screening in women of eligible age
Breast lump or symptom in women over about 35 years
Follow-up after breast cancer treatment
Further assessment of an ultrasound finding
contraindications: Pregnancy (use ultrasound first)
Women under about 35 years with a symptom (ultrasound first)
Recent breast surgery or open wound (defer)
equipment: Wipes to clean the paddle and detector
Previous mammograms for comparison if available
steps: Confirm patient identity, symptoms, previous breast surgery and implants.
Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Explain the examination including compression discomfort and obtain verbal consent.
Ask the patient to undress to the waist and remove deodorant or powder.
Place skin markers on palpable lumps or scars if used locally.
Position for the craniocaudal view and apply firm compression for the exposure.
Position for the mediolateral oblique view and apply compression for the exposure.
Repeat for the other breast and take additional views if needed.
Check images for positioning and quality.
Clean the equipment and send images for reporting with previous films.
aftercare: Mild breast tenderness may last a day.
Explain how and when results will be given.
Arrange ultrasound or biopsy for abnormal findings.
red_flags: Suspicious mass, architectural distortion or microcalcifications (BI-RADS 4 or 5)
Skin bleeding or bruising after compression

indications: Head injury, stroke or suspected intracranial bleeding
Major trauma
Acute abdomen or abdominal pathology not resolved by ultrasound
Suspected pulmonary embolism or aortic disease
Staging of cancer
contraindications: Pregnancy unless clinically essential
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast (for contrast studies)
Impaired kidney function (contrast studies need risk assessment)
Patient too unstable to leave resuscitation without a doctor escort
equipment: CT scanner with injector for contrast studies
Cannula of suitable size for contrast injection
Iodinated contrast medium and oral contrast if needed
Resuscitation trolley and anaphylaxis kit in the scanner room
Immobilisation aids and sedation equipment for children
steps: Confirm patient identity, the request, the region and whether contrast is needed.
Check pregnancy status, allergies, previous contrast reactions, kidney function and diabetes medicines.
Explain the scan and obtain verbal consent (written if sedation or local policy requires it).
Remove metal objects from the scan area and change into a gown.
Insert an intravenous cannula and check patency with saline if contrast is planned.
Give oral contrast in advance when required by the protocol.
Position the patient on the table and immobilise children safely or arrange sedation.
Select the protocol and use the lowest radiation dose that answers the question, especially in children.
Inject contrast with the pump while watching the cannula site for extravasation.
Observe the patient for contrast reactions during and after the scan.
Check images for quality and coverage before the patient leaves.
Remove the cannula after observation and send images for reporting.
aftercare: Observe for at least 30 minutes after contrast for delayed reactions.
Encourage oral fluids after contrast unless fluid-restricted.
Follow local guidance on restarting metformin after contrast.
red_flags: Contrast reaction with wheeze, hypotension or airway swelling (treat as anaphylaxis)
Large contrast extravasation with pain or swelling
Critical finding such as intracranial bleed or aortic dissection (inform clinician immediately)
Deterioration of a critically ill patient in the scanner

indications: Spinal cord compression or back pain with neurological signs
Brain tumours, seizures, demyelination or selected stroke cases
Joint and soft tissue injury
Pelvic staging of gynaecological or rectal cancer
Liver, biliary (MRCP) or cardiac assessment
contraindications: Non-MRI-conditional pacemaker, cochlear implant or neurostimulator
Metal fragments in the eye or ferromagnetic aneurysm clips
Gadolinium contrast with severe kidney impairment unless essential
Gadolinium contrast in pregnancy unless essential (check pregnancy status first)
Severe claustrophobia without sedation
equipment: MRI-safe or MRI-conditional monitoring equipment and trolley
Cannula and gadolinium contrast if required
Sedation equipment and trained staff for children
steps: Confirm patient identity, the request and whether contrast is needed.
Complete the MRI safety questionnaire with the patient and check implants against their documentation.
Take a plain radiograph of the orbits if metal in the eye is possible.
Explain the scan, its noise and duration, and obtain verbal consent.
Remove all metal objects, cards, phones and clothing with metal and change into a gown.
Insert a cannula and check kidney function if contrast is needed.
Arrange sedation or general anaesthesia for young children or claustrophobic patients as needed.
Position the patient with the correct coil and give ear protection and a call button.
Run the sequences while keeping in contact with the patient by intercom.
Give gadolinium contrast when required and watch for reactions.
Check images for quality before the patient leaves and send for reporting.
aftercare: Observe after contrast or sedation until recovered.
Sedated children go home only after full recovery and with a responsible adult.
red_flags: Any ferromagnetic object brought into the scanner room (stop immediately)
Heating or burning sensation during scanning
Contrast reaction or sedation-related breathing problems
Critical finding such as cord compression (inform clinician immediately)

indications: Suspected osteoporosis or fragility fracture
Long-term steroid or aromatase inhibitor use
Early menopause or hypogonadism
Monitoring of osteoporosis treatment
contraindications: Pregnancy
Contrast or nuclear medicine study within the last few days (defer)
steps: Confirm patient identity, height, weight and fracture history.
Ask about pregnancy and recent contrast or nuclear medicine studies.
Explain the scan and obtain verbal consent.
Remove metal objects and clothing with metal from the scan areas.
Position the patient supine for the lumbar spine with legs raised on the block.
Scan the lumbar spine.
Position the hip with internal rotation and scan the femoral neck and total hip.
Scan the forearm if the spine or hip cannot be used.
Check that the regions of interest are correctly placed.
Record T-scores and Z-scores and send for reporting.
aftercare: No aftercare needed.
Repeat the scan at the interval advised for monitoring.
red_flags: Very low bone density with recent fracture (refer for treatment)
Unexpected findings suggesting secondary causes

indications: Infertility work-up for tubal patency
Assessment of uterine cavity shape
Recurrent miscarriage
Confirmation of tubal occlusion after sterilisation
contraindications: Pregnancy or possible pregnancy
Active pelvic infection or recent pelvic inflammatory disease
Active uterine bleeding
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
equipment: Sterile speculum, tenaculum and sponge-holding forceps
Water-soluble iodinated contrast and 20 mL syringe
steps: Confirm identity, cycle day (after menses and before ovulation) and a negative pregnancy test.
Explain the procedure, obtain written consent and ensure a chaperone is present.
Give prophylactic antibiotic and simple analgesia per local protocol.
Position the patient in lithotomy on the fluoroscopy table.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, insert the speculum and clean the cervix.
Insert the cannula or balloon catheter into the cervical canal.
Remove the speculum if possible and take a scout image.
Inject contrast slowly under intermittent fluoroscopy and capture images of the cavity and tubes.
Confirm free spill into the peritoneum on each side or note the level of blockage.
Remove the catheter and observe the patient for pain or vasovagal reaction.
Record screening time and dose and send images for reporting.
aftercare: Expect cramping and spotting for a day or two.
Use simple analgesia and sanitary pads.
Return if fever, worsening pain or offensive discharge develops.
red_flags: Fever or offensive discharge after the procedure (possible infection)
Contrast reaction with wheeze or hypotension
Severe pain or heavy bleeding

indications: Haematuria where CT urography is not available
Suspected urinary tract stones or obstruction
Assessment of congenital urinary tract anomalies
Suspected ureteric injury after surgery
contraindications: Pregnancy
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
Significantly impaired kidney function
Severe dehydration
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication, kidney function, allergies and pregnancy status.
Explain the examination and obtain verbal consent.
Check bowel preparation and recent food intake per local protocol.
Ask the patient to empty the bladder and take a control film of the kidneys, ureters and bladder.
Insert an intravenous cannula.
Inject contrast and watch the patient closely for reactions.
Take timed films of the kidneys in the nephrogram and pyelogram phases.
Apply abdominal compression if used and release it for ureteric views.
Take a full-length film and a post-micturition film.
Take delayed films if there is obstruction.
Remove the cannula after observation and send films for reporting.
aftercare: Observe for 30 minutes for delayed contrast reactions.
Encourage oral fluids unless restricted.
red_flags: Contrast reaction with wheeze, hypotension or swelling
Obstructed kidney with fever (urgent urology referral)
Contrast extravasation from the urinary tract

indications: Suspected urethral stricture
Suspected urethral injury after pelvic fracture or perineal trauma
Assessment before or after urethroplasty
Suspected urethral fistula or diverticulum
contraindications: Active urinary tract infection or urethritis (defer if possible)
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
equipment: Small Foley catheter (8–12 Fr) or penile clamp
Water-soluble iodinated contrast and 50 mL bladder syringe
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, drapes and lubricant gel
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and allergy history.
Explain the procedure, obtain verbal consent and offer a chaperone.
Position the patient obliquely on the table with the lower hip flexed.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the glans and meatus.
Insert the catheter tip into the fossa navicularis and inflate the balloon gently with a little sterile water.
Take a scout image.
Inject contrast slowly under fluoroscopy while gently stretching the penis.
Capture images of the whole anterior and posterior urethra showing any stricture or leak.
Deflate the balloon and remove the catheter.
Record the stricture site and length and send images for reporting.
aftercare: Mild stinging on passing urine may occur for a day.
Drink plenty of fluids.
Return if unable to pass urine or if fever or heavy bleeding develops.
red_flags: Inability to pass urine after the study
Fever or rigors (possible urosepsis)
Contrast reaction

indications: Recurrent urinary tract infection in a young child
Suspected vesicoureteric reflux
Suspected posterior urethral valves in a boy
Assessment of neurogenic bladder
contraindications: Active urinary tract infection (treat first)
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
equipment: Feeding tube or urethral catheter (6–8 Fr for children)
Water-soluble iodinated contrast warmed to body temperature
Sterile gloves, antiseptic and lubricant gel
Lead aprons for staff and parent
steps: Confirm identity, indication, recent urine culture and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Explain the procedure to the child and parent and obtain verbal consent from the parent.
Position the child supine and keep them warm and calm with a parent present.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean the genitalia.
Insert the lubricated catheter into the bladder using aseptic technique and drain the urine.
Secure the catheter with tape.
Fill the bladder slowly with contrast by gravity drip under intermittent fluoroscopy.
Image the bladder, ureters and kidneys during filling for reflux.
Remove the catheter and image the urethra during voiding (lateral view in boys).
Take a post-void image and record screening time and dose.
Grade any reflux and send images for reporting.
aftercare: Continue prophylactic antibiotic as prescribed.
Encourage fluids and expect mild stinging on passing urine.
Return if fever, pain or not passing urine.
red_flags: Fever after the study (possible urinary infection)
Inability to pass urine
Posterior urethral valves seen (urgent paediatric urology referral)

indications: Dysphagia or odynophagia
Suspected oesophageal stricture, web, pouch or achalasia
Suspected tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Suspected leak after oesophageal surgery (water-soluble contrast)
contraindications: Suspected perforation or leak (use water-soluble contrast, not barium)
High aspiration risk without a speech or swallow assessment
Pregnancy unless essential
equipment: Cups and straws, feeding bottle for infants
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and fasting status per local protocol.
Check for suspected perforation and choose water-soluble contrast if present.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent (parental consent for children).
Ensure suction is available and position the patient upright at the fluoroscopy table.
Give a small test swallow and watch for aspiration.
Ask the patient to swallow contrast while imaging the pharynx and oesophagus in frontal and lateral views.
Image the oesophagus in oblique and prone positions as required.
Assess the gastro-oesophageal junction and look for reflux.
Record screening time and save images.
Send images for reporting and explain the next steps.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids to clear barium.
Stools may be pale for a day or two.
Return if constipated for more than two days or if chest pain develops.
red_flags: Aspiration of contrast into the airway (stop the study; water-soluble contrast is harmful in the lungs)
Contrast leak indicating perforation
Chest pain, fever or breathlessness after the study

indications: Suspected malrotation in an infant with bilious vomiting (urgent)
Gastric outlet obstruction
Suspected small bowel Crohn's disease or tuberculosis
Unexplained abdominal pain where endoscopy or CT is not available
contraindications: Suspected perforation (use water-soluble contrast)
Complete large bowel obstruction
Pregnancy unless essential
equipment: Effervescent granules for double contrast if used
Nasogastric tube for infants if needed
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and fasting status per local protocol (keep fasting short in infants).
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Give contrast by mouth or via nasogastric tube in infants.
Image the stomach and duodenum in several positions.
In infants confirm the position of the duodenojejunal flexure to exclude malrotation.
Take timed images of the small bowel as contrast passes to the terminal ileum.
Use compression views of the terminal ileum.
Record screening time and save images.
Send for reporting and communicate malrotation or obstruction immediately.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids and expect pale stools for a few days.
Return if constipation, abdominal pain or vomiting develops.
red_flags: Malrotation or volvulus in an infant (emergency surgical referral)
Contrast leak suggesting perforation
Complete obstruction

indications: Suspected Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus in a neonate
Large bowel obstruction or stricture
Anastomotic leak check before stoma closure
Colonic assessment where colonoscopy or CT is not available
contraindications: Suspected perforation or toxic megacolon (no barium)
Recent deep rectal biopsy (defer)
Pregnancy unless essential
equipment: Rectal catheter or soft Foley catheter (smaller sizes for infants)
Enema bag or syringe and tubing
Lubricant gel, gloves and incontinence pads
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and any recent biopsy; give no bowel preparation or rectal washout before a suspected Hirschsprung study.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent and offer a chaperone.
Position the patient in left lateral position and perform a digital examination if appropriate.
Insert the lubricated rectal catheter gently.
Run contrast in slowly under intermittent fluoroscopy.
Turn the patient to image each segment of the colon.
In neonates look for a transition zone and assess the rectosigmoid ratio.
Stop and drain if a leak is seen.
Take post-evacuation images and record screening time.
Remove the catheter and send images for reporting.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids and expect pale stools.
Monitor neonates for abdominal distension and feeding tolerance.
Return if abdominal pain, fever or no stool for two days.
red_flags: Contrast leak or free air (perforation)
Abdominal distension or collapse after the study
Water-soluble contrast fluid shifts in neonates causing dehydration

indications: Chronic discharging sinus or fistula of unknown extent
Suspected enterocutaneous fistula
Assessment of a perianal fistula where MRI is not available
Assessment of a drain tract or abscess cavity
contraindications: Acute cellulitis around the opening
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
equipment: Fine feeding tube, cannula sheath or small Foley catheter
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gauze and drapes
steps: Confirm patient identity, indication and allergy history.
Explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and clean around the opening with antiseptic.
Place a radio-opaque marker at the external opening and take a scout image.
Gently insert the catheter into the tract opening without force.
Inject contrast slowly under fluoroscopy while applying gentle pressure around the opening.
Image the tract in two planes to show its course, branches and any communication with bowel or bladder.
Remove the catheter and apply a dressing.
Record screening time and send images for reporting.
aftercare: Keep the dressing on and continue usual wound care.
Return if fever, increasing pain or redness develops.
red_flags: Spread of infection or fever after the study
Communication with bowel, bladder or joint needing surgical referral

indications: Ileocolic intussusception confirmed on ultrasound in a stable child
contraindications: Peritonitis or suspected perforation
Shock not responding to resuscitation
Pathological lead point or small bowel intussusception (surgery)
No surgeon available to manage failure or perforation
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear and curvilinear probes
Large Foley catheter or rectal tube suitable for child size
Warm normal saline in a bag with giving set raised to set height, or air insufflator with pressure gauge
Wide-bore needle for emergency decompression of tension pneumoperitoneum
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis on ultrasound, and that the child is resuscitated with intravenous access.
Inform the surgical team and confirm theatre availability before starting.
Explain the procedure, risks including perforation and failure, and obtain written consent from the parent.
Give analgesia or sedation per local protocol.
Insert the catheter into the rectum, inflate the balloon if used and seal the buttocks with tape.
Run warm saline (or air) at the set pressure while watching the intussusceptum under ultrasound.
Follow the intussusceptum back to the ileocaecal valve.
Confirm reduction by seeing fluid or air pass into the terminal ileum.
Limit each attempt to a few minutes and make no more than three attempts per local protocol.
Stop immediately if perforation is suspected and decompress a tension pneumoperitoneum with a needle.
Drain the bowel by removing the catheter and record the result.
aftercare: Observe in hospital for recurrence, usually for 24 hours.
Start feeds gradually once the child is comfortable.
Rescan if symptoms recur.
red_flags: Sudden distension, collapse or free fluid or air (perforation)
Failed reduction (urgent surgery)
Recurrence of pain, vomiting or bloody stool

indications: Thyroid nodule with suspicious ultrasound features
Enlarged or suspicious lymph node
Breast lump or cyst
Superficial soft tissue mass
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Skin infection at the puncture site
Uncooperative patient
equipment: Ultrasound machine with high-frequency linear probe and sterile probe cover
21–25 G needles and 10 mL or 20 mL syringes (aspiration gun if used)
Glass slides, fixative and specimen containers
steps: Confirm identity, the lesion, bleeding risk and anticoagulant use.
Explain the procedure and obtain written consent.
Scan the lesion to plan a safe route away from vessels.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, clean the skin and cover the probe.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, site and side.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic if needed.
Insert the needle under real-time ultrasound into the lesion.
Move the needle back and forth within the lesion with or without suction to collect cells.
Withdraw the needle and apply pressure.
Spread the sample onto slides, fix or air-dry as required, and place rinses in a container.
Repeat passes as needed and check sample adequacy if rapid on-site assessment is available.
Label specimens at the bedside and send with the request form.
aftercare: Apply pressure and a plaster.
Expect mild bruising or soreness.
Return if swelling, bleeding or fever develops.
red_flags: Rapidly enlarging neck swelling or breathing difficulty after thyroid FNA
Persistent bleeding
Pneumothorax symptoms after axillary or supraclavicular FNA

indications: Suspicious breast lesion
Liver lesion or diffuse liver disease
Kidney biopsy for medical kidney disease
Lymph node, soft tissue or abdominal mass needing histology
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder or low platelets
Uncontrolled hypertension (kidney biopsy)
No safe window on ultrasound
Uncooperative patient without sedation
equipment: Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover
Core biopsy needle (14–18 G) with or without coaxial guide
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Formalin specimen pots and saline for culture if needed
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting results and that anticoagulants have been stopped as advised.
Explain the procedure and risks and obtain written consent.
Scan to plan a safe route and mark the skin.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the skin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, site and side.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the capsule or lesion and make a small skin nick.
Advance the biopsy needle under real-time ultrasound to the edge of the target.
Fire the needle and withdraw to inspect the core.
Take further cores until adequate tissue is obtained.
Place cores in formalin, label at the bedside and send with the request.
Apply pressure and a sterile dressing and rescan for bleeding.
aftercare: Bed rest and observations per local protocol (often four to six hours for liver or kidney).
Monitor pulse, blood pressure and puncture site.
Check urine for blood after kidney biopsy.
Avoid heavy lifting for a few days.
red_flags: Falling blood pressure or rising pulse
Severe pain or abdominal distension
Frank haematuria with clots after kidney biopsy
Shortness of breath after a liver biopsy

indications: Lung mass or nodule needing tissue diagnosis
Bone lesion or deep retroperitoneal mass not seen on ultrasound
Suspected metastasis needing confirmation
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Severe emphysema, single lung or pulmonary hypertension (lung biopsy)
Patient unable to lie still or hold breath
Pregnancy
equipment: Coaxial introducer and core biopsy needle
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Chest drain kit and oxygen available for lung biopsy
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting results and anticoagulant plan.
Explain the procedure and risks including pneumothorax and obtain written consent.
Position the patient on the CT table and scan with a skin grid to plan the route.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the skin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, site and side.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and make a small skin nick.
Advance the introducer in steps with check scans until it reaches the lesion edge.
Take cores through the introducer and place them in formalin.
Remove the needle and apply pressure and a dressing.
Perform a check scan for pneumothorax or bleeding.
Label specimens at the bedside and send with the request.
aftercare: Observe pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and breathing for at least four hours.
Take a chest radiograph after lung biopsy per local protocol.
Avoid flying or strenuous activity for the period advised.
red_flags: Breathlessness, chest pain or falling saturation (pneumothorax)
Coughing up more than a small amount of blood
Falling blood pressure or rising pulse

indications: Large liver abscess or one at risk of rupture
Abscess not responding to antimicrobial treatment
Left lobe abscess near the pericardium
Diagnostic aspiration when the cause is uncertain
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Suspected hydatid cyst (specialist advice first)
No safe ultrasound window
Vascular lesion
equipment: Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover
18–16 G spinal or aspiration needle or sheathed cannula
20 mL and 50 mL syringes, three-way tap and extension tubing
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Sterile containers for microscopy and culture
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting results and abscess size and position on ultrasound.
Explain the procedure and obtain written consent.
Plan a route through liver tissue avoiding pleura, gallbladder, vessels and bowel.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the skin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, site and side.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the liver capsule.
Advance the needle under real-time ultrasound into the abscess cavity.
Aspirate pus, noting colour and volume, and send samples for microscopy and culture.
Aspirate until the cavity is nearly empty and confirm on ultrasound.
Withdraw the needle, apply pressure and a sterile dressing.
Place a drain instead if the cavity is large or refills (see image-guided drainage).
aftercare: Observe pulse, blood pressure and temperature per local protocol.
Continue antimicrobial treatment as prescribed.
Repeat ultrasound to check for reaccumulation.
red_flags: Falling blood pressure or rising pulse (bleeding)
Increasing abdominal pain or peritonism (leak)
Breathlessness or chest pain (pleural injury)
Persistent fever after aspiration

indications: Intra-abdominal or pelvic abscess
Large liver, splenic or psoas abscess
Infected fluid collection after surgery
Empyema or loculated pleural collection
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
No safe access route
Collection that needs surgical washout (multiloculated with necrotic tissue)
equipment: Pigtail drainage catheter (8–14 Fr) with trocar or Seldinger set
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Scalpel blade, suture and fixation device
Drainage bag and sterile containers for culture
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting results and imaging of the collection.
Explain the procedure and obtain written consent.
Plan a route that avoids bowel, vessels and pleura.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the skin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, site and side.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and make a small skin incision.
