Insert the catheter by trocar technique or by needle, guidewire and dilators under imaging.
Form the pigtail inside the collection and confirm position on imaging.
Aspirate pus, send samples for culture, and flush gently with sterile saline.
Fix the catheter to the skin and connect to a drainage bag.
Apply a sterile dressing and record catheter size and output.
aftercare: Record drain output daily and flush as instructed.
Continue antimicrobials as prescribed.
Repeat imaging before removal when output falls and the patient improves.
Teach the patient or carer drain care.
red_flags: Bleeding into the drain or falling blood pressure
Faecal or bile content suggesting fistula
Drain falls out or stops draining with return of fever
Increasing pain or peritonism

indications: Obstructed infected kidney (pyonephrosis)
Obstructive uropathy from stones, tumour or stricture with failing kidney function
Urinary diversion for leak or fistula
Access for later stone surgery or ureteric stenting
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Uncontrolled hypertension
Non-dilated system without specialist expertise
equipment: Ultrasound machine with sterile cover and fluoroscopy unit
Nephrostomy set with access needle, guidewires, dilators and pigtail catheter (8–12 Fr)
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Scalpel blade, suture or fixation device
steps: Confirm identity, indication, side, clotting results and kidney function.
Explain the procedure and risks and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and establish intravenous access and monitoring.
Position the patient prone or prone-oblique and confirm the dilated kidney on ultrasound.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the flank and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, side and site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and puncture a lower or mid-pole posterior calyx under ultrasound.
Confirm urine return, send a sample for culture and inject only a little contrast to outline the system, avoiding overdistension of an infected system.
Pass a guidewire into the collecting system or ureter under fluoroscopy.
Dilate the tract and insert the pigtail catheter over the wire.
Confirm position with contrast, lock the pigtail and fix the catheter to the skin.
Connect to a drainage bag and apply a sterile dressing.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs and urine output closely for 24 hours.
Watch for sepsis after drainage of infected urine.
Keep the bag below kidney level and secure the tube.
Plan definitive treatment of the obstruction.
red_flags: Rigors, hypotension or confusion (sepsis)
Heavy bleeding in the tube or falling blood pressure
Tube falls out or stops draining
Breathlessness after an upper pole puncture

indications: Obstructive jaundice where ERCP has failed or is not available
Cholangitis with biliary obstruction
Palliation of malignant biliary obstruction
Access for biliary stenting
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Large volume ascites (drain first)
Non-dilated ducts without specialist expertise
equipment: Fine access needle (21–22 G), guidewires, dilators and biliary drainage catheter (8–10 Fr)
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Suture or fixation device and drainage bag
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting results and imaging showing dilated ducts.
Explain the procedure and risks and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and establish intravenous access and monitoring.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the skin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient and access side.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic at the right intercostal or subxiphoid access site.
Puncture a dilated duct under ultrasound or fluoroscopy and inject contrast to confirm position.
Pass a guidewire into the bile duct and, if possible, across the obstruction.
Dilate the tract and place the drainage catheter as an external or internal-external drain.
Confirm position with contrast and fix the catheter to the skin.
Connect to a drainage bag, send bile for culture and apply a sterile dressing.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs and drain output closely for 24 hours.
Record daily bile output and replace fluid and electrolytes as needed.
Flush the catheter as instructed and keep the bag secured.
Check bilirubin to confirm improvement.
red_flags: Rigors, hypotension or confusion (cholangitis or sepsis)
Blood in the drain or falling haemoglobin
Bile leak around the catheter or peritonitis
Sudden drop in drain output with pain

indications: Peripheral arterial disease before intervention
Suspected arterial bleeding
Vascular malformations or aneurysms
Planning embolisation or angioplasty
contraindications: Uncorrected bleeding disorder
Previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
Significantly impaired kidney function without risk management
Pregnancy
equipment: Arterial access needle, sheath (4–6 Fr), guidewires and diagnostic catheters
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Closure device or manual compression supplies
steps: Confirm identity, indication, clotting results, kidney function and allergies.
Explain the procedure and risks and obtain written consent.
Establish intravenous access and monitoring and check distal pulses.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the groin or wrist and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient and access site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and puncture the artery under ultrasound guidance.
Insert the sheath using the Seldinger technique.
Advance the catheter over a guidewire to the target vessel under fluoroscopy.
Inject contrast and acquire images in the required projections.
Remove the catheter and sheath and achieve haemostasis by compression or a closure device.
Check distal pulses and the puncture site and record contrast volume and dose.
aftercare: Bed rest with the limb straight for the time advised.
Check puncture site, distal pulses and vital signs regularly.
Encourage fluids to protect kidney function.
red_flags: Swelling or bleeding at the puncture site
Cold, pale or pulseless limb
Back pain with hypotension (retroperitoneal bleed)
New neurological symptoms

indications: Symptomatic uterine fibroids in a woman wishing to avoid surgery
Adenomyosis with heavy bleeding
Postpartum haemorrhage not controlled by medical treatment
Uterine arteriovenous malformation
contraindications: Pregnancy
Active pelvic infection
Suspected gynaecological malignancy
Uncorrected bleeding disorder or severe contrast allergy
equipment: Arterial access needle, sheath, guidewires, diagnostic catheters and microcatheter
Embolic particles or agents per protocol
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Analgesia plan including patient-controlled analgesia if available
steps: Confirm identity, indication, recent pelvic imaging and gynaecology review.
Explain the procedure, effects on fertility and risks and obtain written consent.
Establish intravenous access, monitoring and a urinary catheter.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the groin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient and access site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and gain femoral or radial arterial access.
Select each uterine artery with a catheter or microcatheter under fluoroscopy.
Inject embolic particles slowly until flow slows to the planned endpoint.
Perform check angiography of both uterine arteries.
Remove catheters and sheath and achieve haemostasis.
Check distal pulses and start the post-embolisation analgesia plan.
aftercare: Expect pelvic pain, nausea and low-grade fever for several days (post-embolisation syndrome).
Give analgesia and antiemetics as prescribed.
Monitor the puncture site and pulses.
Arrange follow-up imaging at about three to six months.
red_flags: High fever, offensive discharge or worsening pain after the first week (infection or necrosis)
Passage of fibroid tissue with heavy bleeding
Groin swelling or cold limb

indications: Gastrointestinal bleeding not controlled endoscopically
Solid organ or pelvic bleeding after trauma
Massive haemoptysis (bronchial artery embolisation)
Bleeding after surgery, biopsy or delivery
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability needing immediate surgery where theatre is faster
Severe contrast allergy (relative; premedicate per protocol)
Uncorrected coagulopathy (correct alongside)
equipment: Arterial access needle, sheath, guidewires, catheters and microcatheter
Embolic agents (coils, particles, gelatin sponge, glue) per protocol
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
Blood products and resuscitation equipment with anaesthetic support
steps: Confirm identity, indication and the likely bleeding site from CT or endoscopy.
Ensure ongoing resuscitation with blood products and anaesthetic support.
Explain the procedure and obtain written consent, or follow emergency consent policy.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the groin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient and access site.
Gain arterial access under ultrasound guidance and insert a sheath.
Perform selective angiography to identify the bleeding vessel.
Advance a microcatheter close to the bleeding point.
Embolise with the chosen agent until bleeding stops on check angiography.
Remove catheters and sheath and achieve haemostasis.
Hand over to the critical care or ward team with a clear record of vessels embolised.
aftercare: Continue close monitoring of vital signs and haemoglobin.
Watch for signs of bowel or organ ischaemia.
Check the puncture site and distal pulses.
red_flags: Ongoing bleeding or falling haemoglobin
Abdominal pain, fever or raised lactate (bowel ischaemia)
New weakness or numbness after bronchial embolisation (spinal artery involvement)
Groin bleeding or cold limb

indications: Intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma not suitable for surgery or ablation
Bridging to liver transplant
Selected liver metastases per multidisciplinary decision
contraindications: Decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) or significant ascites
Main portal vein thrombosis
Severe kidney impairment or uncorrected coagulopathy
Extensive tumour burden or extrahepatic spread
equipment: Arterial access needle, sheath, guidewires, catheters and microcatheter
Chemotherapy agent prepared by pharmacy per oncology protocol
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, gown and drapes
steps: Confirm identity, multidisciplinary team decision, liver function, kidney function and clotting.
Explain the procedure and risks and obtain written consent.
Give prophylactic antiemetic, antibiotic and hydration per local protocol.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gown and gloves, clean the groin and drape.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, access site and target lesions.
Gain arterial access and perform coeliac and superior mesenteric angiography to map liver supply.
Advance a microcatheter selectively into the feeding artery of the tumour.
Deliver the chemotherapy emulsion or beads slowly under fluoroscopy to the planned endpoint.
Handle and dispose of cytotoxic material safely.
Perform check angiography, remove catheters and achieve haemostasis.
Record the agent, volume delivered and vessels treated.
aftercare: Expect post-embolisation syndrome with pain, nausea and fever for a few days.
Monitor liver function and kidney function after the procedure.
Arrange response imaging at about four to six weeks.
red_flags: Jaundice, confusion or ascites (liver failure)
High fever after the first week or rigors (liver abscess)
Severe abdominal pain or vomiting blood
Groin bleeding or cold limb

indications: Staging and follow-up of prostate, breast or lung cancer
Unexplained bone pain with suspected metastases
Suspected occult fracture or osteomyelitis
Metabolic bone disease or Paget disease
contraindications: Pregnancy
Breastfeeding (interrupt per nuclear medicine advice)
equipment: Radiopharmaceutical prepared in the hot lab
Shielded syringe and cannula or butterfly
Radiation monitoring equipment and waste bins
steps: Confirm identity, indication, pregnancy and breastfeeding status.
Explain the scan, the radiation precautions and the waiting time and obtain verbal consent.
Check the prescribed radiopharmaceutical activity against the request.
Inject the radiopharmaceutical intravenously using a shielded syringe.
Record the time of injection and the activity given.
Ask the patient to drink plenty of water and pass urine frequently while waiting.
Perform whole-body imaging after the required interval, with the bladder empty just before scanning.
Take additional spot or SPECT views as required.
Check images for quality and send for reporting.
Dispose of radioactive waste per regulations.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids and pass urine often for the rest of the day.
Avoid prolonged close contact with pregnant women and young children for the time advised.
Wash hands well after using the toilet.
red_flags: Extravasation of the injection with pain
Spinal metastasis with new weakness or numbness (urgent spinal cord compression pathway)

indications: Hyperthyroidism of uncertain cause
Distinguishing Graves disease, toxic nodular goitre and thyroiditis
Assessment of a thyroid nodule with low TSH
Planning radioactive iodine therapy
contraindications: Pregnancy
Breastfeeding (interrupt per nuclear medicine advice)
Recent iodinated contrast or amiodarone (falsely low uptake)
equipment: Gamma camera with pinhole collimator or uptake probe
Radiation monitoring equipment and waste bins
steps: Confirm identity, indication, pregnancy and breastfeeding status.
Check thyroid medicines, recent contrast and iodine intake and whether they were stopped as advised.
Explain the test and radiation precautions and obtain verbal consent.
Give the radiopharmaceutical orally or intravenously and record the time and activity.
Image the thyroid with the patient supine and the neck extended at the set interval.
Measure uptake with the probe or camera at the required time points.
Mark palpable nodules for correlation with the image.
Check images and calculate the uptake percentage.
Dispose of radioactive waste per regulations and send results for reporting.
aftercare: Restart thyroid medicines as instructed.
Follow radiation precautions advised by the nuclear medicine team.
red_flags: Cold nodule needing cytology (arrange FNA)
Symptoms of thyroid storm while off medicines

indications: Graves disease or toxic nodular goitre
Remnant ablation after thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid cancer
Treatment of iodine-avid thyroid cancer metastases
contraindications: Pregnancy or planned pregnancy within the advised interval
Breastfeeding
Unable to follow radiation protection instructions
Active thyroid eye disease (relative; specialist advice)
equipment: Radioiodine capsule or liquid prepared by nuclear medicine
Isolation room with shielding for high-activity treatment
Radiation monitoring equipment and waste bins
Written radiation protection instructions for the patient
steps: Confirm identity, indication and specialist prescription.
Confirm a negative pregnancy test in women of reproductive age on the day.
Check that thyroid medicines and iodine intake were stopped as advised.
Explain the treatment, side effects and radiation precautions and obtain written consent.
Check the prescribed activity against the dispensed dose with a second checker.
Have the patient swallow the capsule or liquid in the designated area.
Record the time and activity administered.
Admit to the isolation room for high-activity treatment until emissions fall below the release limit.
Measure dose rate before discharge.
Give written instructions on contact restrictions and follow-up.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids and pass urine often.
Keep distance from others, especially pregnant women and children, for the time advised.
Avoid pregnancy for the period advised by the specialist.
Check thyroid function at the interval set by the specialist.
red_flags: Neck swelling or breathing difficulty
Vomiting soon after the capsule (inform nuclear medicine)
Symptoms of thyroid storm such as fever, fast heart rate or confusion

form.label: Medicines and iodine stopped as advised

indications: Curative treatment of cancers such as cervix, head and neck, breast and prostate
Adjuvant treatment after surgery
Palliation of bone pain, bleeding or spinal cord compression
contraindications: Pregnancy (unless specialist decision)
Previous radiotherapy to the same area beyond tolerance
Patient unable to lie still in the treatment position
equipment: Immobilisation devices (mask, vacuum bag, breast board)
Emergency stop and patient monitoring cameras
steps: Confirm identity using two identifiers and check the treatment plan and prescription.
Confirm written consent is on file and check the fraction number.
Ask about new symptoms, skin reactions and pregnancy where relevant.
Position the patient on the couch using immobilisation devices and skin marks.
Align the patient using lasers and the reference marks.
Acquire verification imaging and correct position as needed.
Leave the room, monitor the patient on camera and deliver the planned fraction.
Stop treatment immediately if the patient moves or becomes unwell.
Help the patient off the couch and remove immobilisation.
Record the fraction delivered and any reactions.
aftercare: Wash the treated skin gently and avoid perfumed products.
Report side effects at each visit and attend weekly review.
Maintain nutrition and fluid intake.
red_flags: Moist skin breakdown or bleeding in the field
Severe diarrhoea, vomiting or inability to swallow
Fever with low blood counts
New weakness or numbness (spinal cord compression)

indications: Cervical cancer as part of curative chemoradiotherapy
Endometrial cancer vaginal vault treatment
Selected prostate, breast or oesophageal cancers
contraindications: Pregnancy
Uterine perforation not yet assessed
Patient unfit for anaesthesia or sedation where needed
equipment: High dose rate afterloader with shielded treatment room
Applicators (tandem and ovoids or ring, vaginal cylinder)
Speculum, uterine sound and cervical dilators
Imaging for applicator verification (ultrasound, X-ray, CT or MRI)
Anaesthesia or sedation and monitoring equipment
steps: Confirm identity, prescription, fraction number and written consent.
Perform pre-procedure checks including pregnancy test, fasting and blood counts.
Give anaesthesia or sedation per plan and insert a urinary catheter.
Position in lithotomy and perform hand hygiene, sterile gloving and vulvovaginal cleaning.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, applicator type and fraction.
Sound and dilate the cervix and insert the applicators under ultrasound guidance.
Pack the vagina to displace bladder and rectum and secure the applicator.
Verify applicator position with imaging and complete planning.
Connect the applicator to the afterloader and deliver the treatment with the patient monitored remotely.
Survey the patient and room with a radiation monitor after treatment.
Remove packing and applicators and check for bleeding.
aftercare: Expect mild vaginal discharge, spotting and cramping.
Encourage fluids and report urinary or bowel symptoms.
Use vaginal dilators as advised after the course ends.
red_flags: Heavy vaginal bleeding
Fever or severe abdominal pain (possible uterine perforation or infection)
Inability to pass urine

indications: Pleural effusion of unknown cause needing diagnosis
Breathlessness from a large pleural effusion
Suspected empyema or parapneumonic effusion
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or very low platelets (relative)
Skin infection at the puncture site
Very small effusion not safely accessible
Uncooperative patient unable to keep still
equipment: Sterile pack, drapes, gloves and gown
Aspiration needle or cannula (16-21 G) with three-way tap and 50 mL syringe, or pleural aspiration kit
Drainage bag or container and specimen bottles, including blood culture bottles
steps: Confirm identity, side, indication and consent, and check the chest X-ray and clotting where relevant.
Mark the side and confirm the effusion with ultrasound, choosing a site above a rib in the safe triangle or posterior chest.
Sit the patient upright leaning forward on a table, or position a child with a carer's help.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and gown, clean and drape the site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the pleura, aspirating to confirm fluid.
Insert the aspiration needle or cannula just above the upper border of the rib until fluid is aspirated.
Collect samples for protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, microscopy, culture, AFB or GeneXpert and cytology as indicated.
For therapeutic aspiration, drain slowly through the three-way tap or bag, stopping at the advised maximum volume.
Stop if the patient develops cough, chest pain or breathlessness.
Remove the needle at end of expiration and apply an occlusive dressing.
Record volume and appearance, and request a chest X-ray if indicated.
aftercare: Rest for a short period and report breathlessness.
Keep the dressing dry for 24 hours.
Attend for the results and follow-up.
red_flags: Stop if the patient coughs persistently, develops chest pain, becomes breathless or faint.
Escalate for frank blood, falling oxygen saturation or signs of pneumothorax.
Return for worsening breathlessness, chest pain, fever or leakage at the site.

indications: Exudative pleural effusion of unknown cause
Suspected tuberculous pleurisy
Suspected pleural malignancy or mesothelioma
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy
Very small or no effusion for blind biopsy (use image guidance)
Skin infection at the site
Respiratory failure or inability to cooperate
equipment: Abrams or Cope pleural biopsy needle, or cutting needle for image-guided biopsy
Sterile pack, drapes, gloves and gown
steps: Confirm identity, side, indication and consent and review imaging and clotting.
Sit the patient leaning forward and confirm the effusion and site with ultrasound.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and gown, clean and drape the site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic generously down to the pleura, confirming fluid on aspiration.
Make a small skin nick above the upper border of the rib.
Insert the biopsy needle into the pleural space and confirm fluid can be aspirated.
Engage the parietal pleura with the hook and take a biopsy, rotating the needle between bites.
Take several biopsies from different directions, avoiding the upward direction near the intercostal vessels.
Place samples in formalin for histology and saline for TB culture.
Aspirate fluid for analysis if needed, then remove the needle and close the incision.
Apply an occlusive dressing and arrange a chest X-ray.
aftercare: Rest and report breathlessness or chest pain.
Keep the dressing dry and return for suture removal.
Attend for the results.
red_flags: Stop for breathlessness, chest pain, falling oxygen saturation or bleeding.
Escalate for signs of pneumothorax or haemothorax on review.
Return for fever, wound discharge or worsening breathlessness.

indications: Recurrent symptomatic malignant pleural effusion
Recurrent pneumothorax where surgery is not suitable
contraindications: Trapped lung that does not re-expand on X-ray
Short expected survival where an indwelling catheter or aspiration is preferable
Active pleural infection
equipment: Chest drain already in place, or thoracoscopy setup for poudrage
Sterile sclerosant (e.g. graded talc) prepared per protocol
Normal saline and 50 mL bladder-tip syringes
Analgesia per protocol and local anaesthetic for intrapleural use per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, side, indication and consent, and confirm full lung re-expansion on chest X-ray.
Give analgesia before the procedure per protocol.
Perform hand hygiene and put on sterile gloves.
Instil intrapleural local anaesthetic through the drain per protocol if used.
Prepare the sclerosant slurry in saline per protocol.
Instil the slurry through the chest drain and flush the tube with saline.
Clamp the drain for the period stated in the protocol, unless the patient becomes breathless.
Ask the patient to change position periodically if the protocol requires.
Unclamp the drain and connect to the underwater seal, with suction if advised.
Remove the drain when drainage is low and the lung remains expanded on X-ray.
aftercare: Expect chest pain and fever for a day or two; take analgesia as prescribed.
Report breathlessness straight away.
Attend follow-up chest X-ray and clinic.
red_flags: Unclamp immediately and escalate for breathlessness, falling oxygen saturation or surgical emphysema.
Escalate for hypotension or hypoxia after talc (possible acute lung injury).
Return for recurrent breathlessness or fever after discharge.

indications: Recurrent malignant pleural effusion
Trapped lung with symptomatic effusion
Patient preference for ambulatory drainage over pleurodesis
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy
Skin infection or tumour at the insertion site
No carer or community support to perform drainage (relative)
equipment: Indwelling pleural catheter kit with tunneller, introducer and drainage bottles
Sterile pack, drapes, gloves and gown
steps: Confirm identity, side, indication and consent, and confirm the effusion and site with ultrasound.
Position the patient lateral or sitting, and mark the insertion and exit sites.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves and gown, clean and drape the area.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic at both sites and along the tunnel track.
Make the incisions and create the subcutaneous tunnel with the tunneller.
Insert the guidewire into the pleural space using a Seldinger technique and dilate the track.
Insert the catheter through the peel-away sheath into the pleural space and remove the sheath.
Check the cuff lies within the tunnel and that the catheter drains.
Close the insertion incision and secure the catheter at the exit site.
Drain fluid slowly with the bottle, stopping for chest discomfort or cough.
Apply a dressing and arrange a chest X-ray.
Teach the patient and carer how to drain at home and arrange community support.
aftercare: Drain as advised and keep a drainage diary.
Keep the exit site clean and dry and change the dressing as taught.
Return for suture removal.
red_flags: Stop drainage for chest pain, cough or breathlessness.
Return for fever, redness, pus at the exit site or cloudy fluid (possible infection).
Return if the catheter stops draining, falls out or leaks.

indications: Symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax
Selected small secondary pneumothorax in a stable patient
contraindications: Tension pneumothorax (decompress immediately)
Haemopneumothorax or traumatic pneumothorax needing a chest drain
Patient on positive pressure ventilation
steps: Confirm identity, side, indication and consent and review the chest X-ray.
Position the patient semi-recumbent or upright.
Choose the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line or the fourth or fifth space in the mid-axillary line.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, clean and drape the site.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the pleura, aspirating air to confirm the space.
Insert the cannula above the rib into the pleural space and remove the needle.
Attach the three-way tap and syringe and aspirate air, expelling it through the side port.
Stop when resistance is felt, the patient coughs excessively, or the maximum volume per protocol is reached.
Remove the cannula and apply an occlusive dressing.
Repeat the chest X-ray to check lung re-expansion.
Insert a chest drain if aspiration fails and the patient remains symptomatic.
aftercare: Do not fly or dive until cleared by the doctor.
Stop smoking.
Attend follow-up chest X-ray.
red_flags: Stop and insert a chest drain for worsening breathlessness or falling oxygen saturation.
Return immediately for new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain.

indications: Pneumothorax resolved with no air leak
Pleural drainage reduced to the protocol threshold with lung expanded
Blocked or misplaced drain that is no longer useful
contraindications: Ongoing bubbling (air leak) or high drainage
Lung not re-expanded on chest X-ray
steps: Confirm identity and that the decision to remove was made after review of drainage, bubbling and chest X-ray.
Give analgesia beforehand if needed.
Explain the breathing instructions (hold breath or Valsalva on command; children may breathe out or cry).
Position the patient semi-upright and perform hand hygiene.
Remove the dressing and cut the securing suture, leaving any closure suture in place.
Ask the patient to hold the breath at end of inspiration or perform a Valsalva manoeuvre.
Pull the drain out in one smooth, swift movement while an assistant ties the closure suture or the site is sealed.
Apply an occlusive dressing.
Check the drain tip is intact and dispose of the drainage safely.
Observe breathing and oxygen saturation and arrange a chest X-ray if indicated.
aftercare: Keep the dressing on for 48 hours.
Return for suture removal after 5-7 days.
Avoid heavy lifting for a week.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for breathlessness, chest pain or surgical emphysema after removal.
Return for fever, wound discharge or worsening breathlessness.

indications: Suspected lung cancer or endobronchial lesion
Haemoptysis of uncertain cause
Persistent lobar collapse or non-resolving pneumonia
Suspected TB or opportunistic infection with negative sputum
Suspected foreign body (rigid bronchoscopy preferred for removal in children)
contraindications: Severe hypoxia not correctable with oxygen
Recent myocardial infarction or unstable arrhythmia
Uncorrected coagulopathy if biopsies planned
Uncooperative patient without anaesthetic support
equipment: Flexible bronchoscope of suitable size, light source and suction
Topical local anaesthetic and sedation per protocol
Oxygen, pulse oximeter, cardiac and blood pressure monitor
N95 respirators where TB is suspected
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent, fasting status, imaging and clotting.
Insert IV access and attach monitoring and supplemental oxygen.
Perform a time-out confirming patient, side and planned samples.
Apply topical local anaesthetic to the nose or throat.
Give sedation per protocol where used and monitor continuously.
Insert the bronchoscope through the nose or mouth with a bite block and pass through the vocal cords.
Give topical anaesthetic to the airways as you advance.
Inspect all segments systematically, starting with the normal side.
Take washings, brushings or biopsies from the abnormal area as planned.
Suction blood and secretions and confirm haemostasis before withdrawal.
Withdraw the scope and recover the patient with monitoring.
Label samples and send them, and decontaminate the scope per protocol.
aftercare: Nothing to eat or drink until the throat numbness has worn off (about 2 hours).
Expect mild sore throat and small streaks of blood.
Do not drive for 24 hours after sedation.
red_flags: Stop for persistent desaturation, significant bleeding, arrhythmia or laryngospasm.
Escalate after biopsy for breathlessness or chest pain (possible pneumothorax).
Return for heavy haemoptysis, fever over 24 hours or worsening breathlessness.

indications: Suspected pneumocystis, TB or other opportunistic infection
Ventilator-associated pneumonia sampling
Interstitial lung disease assessment
Non-resolving pneumonia
contraindications: Severe hypoxia not correctable during the procedure
Haemodynamic instability
Contraindications to bronchoscopy
equipment: Flexible bronchoscope, suction and light source
Sterile saline warmed to body temperature
Topical local anaesthetic and sedation per protocol
N95 respirators where TB is suspected
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent and fasting status, and review imaging to choose the segment.
Attach monitoring and oxygen and perform a time-out.
Perform bronchoscopy and avoid suction before reaching the target to reduce contamination.
Wedge the bronchoscope tip in the chosen segmental bronchus.
Instil sterile saline in aliquots through the working channel.
Aspirate gently after each aliquot into the sterile trap, avoiding airway collapse.
Record the volume instilled and returned.
Withdraw the scope, recover the patient and monitor oxygen saturation.
Label samples and send them promptly for microbiology, cytology and other tests.
aftercare: Nothing to eat or drink until throat numbness has worn off.
Expect mild fever or cough for a day.
red_flags: Stop for persistent desaturation, bronchospasm or bleeding.
Return for high fever beyond 24 hours, breathlessness or chest pain.

indications: Mediastinal or hilar lymph node enlargement of unknown cause
Staging of lung cancer
Suspected sarcoidosis, lymphoma or TB lymphadenitis
contraindications: Severe hypoxia or haemodynamic instability
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Unable to tolerate sedation or anaesthesia
equipment: Topical local anaesthetic and sedation or general anaesthesia per protocol
steps: Confirm identity, consent, fasting, clotting and the target nodes on CT.
Attach monitoring and oxygen and perform a time-out.
Give topical anaesthesia and sedation or general anaesthesia per protocol.
Insert the EBUS scope orally and perform a quick airway inspection.
Identify target lymph node stations with ultrasound and Doppler to avoid vessels.
Advance the needle into the node under real-time ultrasound and agitate it with suction.
Make several passes per node as needed for adequate material.
Prepare slides and place material in containers for cytology, culture and other tests.
Stage nodes in order from N3 to N1 if staging for cancer, changing needles between stations.
Withdraw the scope and recover the patient with monitoring.
aftercare: Nothing to eat or drink until throat numbness has worn off.
Do not drive for 24 hours after sedation.
Attend for results.
red_flags: Stop for significant bleeding, persistent desaturation or arrhythmia.
Return for fever, chest pain, haemoptysis or breathlessness after the procedure.

indications: Diagnosis of asthma or COPD
Monitoring of chronic lung disease
Pre-operative assessment
Occupational lung disease screening
contraindications: Recent myocardial infarction, eye, chest or abdominal surgery, or pneumothorax
Haemoptysis of unknown cause
Active TB until treated for the advised period (infection control)
Child under about 5 years who cannot perform the manoeuvre
equipment: Height measuring stick and weighing scale
Short-acting bronchodilator and spacer for reversibility testing
steps: Confirm identity, indication and that bronchodilators have been withheld if required.
Check the spirometer calibration for the day.
Measure height and weight and enter age, sex and ethnicity for reference values.
Explain and demonstrate the manoeuvre and sit the patient upright with a nose clip.
Ask the patient to take a full breath in, seal the lips around the mouthpiece and blow out as hard and fast as possible for as long as possible.
Encourage the patient throughout the blow.
Repeat for at least three acceptable and repeatable blows.
For reversibility, give the short-acting bronchodilator via spacer and repeat the blows after the advised wait.
Select the best results and check quality grading.
Interpret FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC against reference values.
Clean the equipment and discard single-use parts.
aftercare: Restart usual inhalers.
Attend for the results and treatment review.
red_flags: Stop if the patient becomes dizzy, has chest pain or develops severe bronchospasm.
Escalate if testing reveals very severe obstruction with symptoms.

indications: Assessment of acute asthma severity
Asthma monitoring and diagnosis with a peak flow diary
Occupational asthma assessment
contraindications: Child too young to perform reliably (usually under 5 years)
Patient too breathless to attempt (treat first)
equipment: Peak flow meter (low-range for small children)
Height measuring stick and predicted peak flow chart
steps: Confirm identity and explain the test.
Set the meter pointer to zero and fit a clean mouthpiece.
Ask the patient to stand or sit upright.
Ask the patient to take a deep breath, seal the lips round the mouthpiece and blow out as hard and fast as possible.
Record the reading and reset the pointer.
Repeat twice more and record the best of three.
Compare with predicted or best personal value.
Teach home use and diary recording if monitoring is planned.
aftercare: Record peak flows in the diary as advised.
Follow your asthma action plan when readings fall.
red_flags: Treat as severe or life-threatening asthma if peak flow is very low with breathlessness and escalate immediately.
Return urgently if peak flow falls into the danger zone of the action plan.

indications: Acute asthma or COPD exacerbation needing bronchodilator
Croup or bronchiolitis when prescribed
Delivery of other prescribed nebulised medicines
contraindications: Spacer with inhaler is preferred and equally effective in mild to moderate asthma where available
Oxygen-driven nebulisers may worsen CO2 retention in COPD (use air or limit duration)
equipment: Nebuliser chamber, mask or mouthpiece and tubing
Compressor or oxygen or air supply with flowmeter
steps: Confirm identity, the prescription and allergies.
Record baseline pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and peak flow if able.
Perform hand hygiene and assemble the nebuliser.
Add the prescribed medicine to the chamber.
Sit the patient upright and fit the mask or mouthpiece; a carer may hold a child on their lap.
Connect to oxygen or air at the flow advised by the manufacturer, or switch on the compressor.
Encourage normal breathing until the chamber is empty or misting stops.
Monitor the patient during treatment.
Repeat observations after treatment and record the response.
Wash, dry and store the chamber, or discard single-use parts.
aftercare: Rinse the mouth after steroid nebules.
Follow the asthma or COPD action plan.
red_flags: Escalate immediately for worsening breathlessness, exhaustion, silent chest, cyanosis or confusion.
Escalate for chest pain, very fast heart rate or arrhythmia after treatment.

indications: New inhaler prescription
Poorly controlled asthma or COPD
Routine annual review or change of device
contraindications: None
equipment: Spacer with mouthpiece or mask of suitable size (or a home-made bottle spacer if none is available)
steps: Confirm identity, the inhalers prescribed and current symptoms.
Ask the patient to show how they use their inhaler and note errors.
Explain the difference between reliever and preventer inhalers.
Demonstrate shaking the inhaler, removing the cap and fitting it to the spacer.
Show breathing out fully, sealing the lips on the mouthpiece or mask, pressing once and taking slow deep breaths or several tidal breaths.
Show waiting about 30 seconds before repeating a puff.
For dry powder inhalers, teach a fast deep inhalation without shaking or blowing into the device.
Ask the patient or carer to demonstrate back and correct errors.
Teach spacer cleaning and the dose counter or how to know when the inhaler is empty.
Give an action plan and record the technique score.
aftercare: Rinse the mouth after preventer inhalers.
Wash the spacer monthly and let it air-dry.
Bring inhalers and spacer to every review.
red_flags: Seek urgent care if the reliever is needed more often than every 4 hours or does not help.
Seek urgent care for difficulty speaking, blue lips or exhaustion.

indications: Hypoxaemia below the target saturation
Severe respiratory distress, shock or emergency signs (as per triage protocols)
Carbon monoxide poisoning
contraindications: None in hypoxaemia; use controlled oxygen with lower targets in patients at risk of CO2 retention
No open flames or smoking near oxygen
equipment: Oxygen source (cylinder, concentrator or piped supply) with flowmeter
Delivery device of suitable size (nasal prongs, face mask, Venturi mask, non-rebreather mask)
Humidifier if high flow or long duration
Pulse oximeter with adult and paediatric probes
steps: Confirm identity, assess airway, breathing and circulation and measure oxygen saturation on air.
Set the target saturation range for the patient and record it on the chart.
Check the oxygen source is full or working and set up the flowmeter and humidifier if needed.
Choose the delivery device based on oxygen need, age and risk of CO2 retention.
Fit nasal prongs just inside the nostrils or the mask over nose and mouth and secure comfortably.
Start at the flow suited to the device and age, then adjust to keep within the target range.
Recheck oxygen saturation, respiratory rate and work of breathing within minutes.
Check blood gases where CO2 retention is a risk or the patient is deteriorating.
Monitor saturation regularly and record oxygen flow and device on the chart.
Wean oxygen as the patient improves and stop when saturation is maintained on air.
aftercare: Keep the prongs or mask on and do not change the flow yourself.
Never smoke or allow flames near the oxygen.
For home oxygen, use as prescribed and keep the concentrator in a ventilated place.
red_flags: Escalate for saturation below target despite oxygen, rising respiratory rate, exhaustion or drowsiness.
Escalate for drowsiness or confusion in patients at risk of CO2 retention.
Act at once if the oxygen supply runs out or the concentrator stops (power failure).

indications: Acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure not responding to standard oxygen
Bronchiolitis or pneumonia in children with increased work of breathing
Post-extubation support
contraindications: Need for immediate intubation (apnoea, falling consciousness, inability to protect airway)
Nasal obstruction, facial trauma or base of skull fracture
Untreated pneumothorax
equipment: High-flow device with air-oxygen blender and heated humidifier
Nasal cannula of correct size (should not fill more than half the nostril)
Oxygen and air supply or device with internal turbine
steps: Confirm identity and indication and assess airway, breathing and circulation.
Set the target saturation range.
Assemble the circuit, fill the humidifier and allow it to warm to temperature.
Choose the cannula size and set initial flow by weight or age and FiO2 per protocol.
Clear the nose with suction if needed and position the cannula.
Start the flow and allow the patient to settle, holding a child with a carer if helpful.
Adjust FiO2 to keep saturation in the target range.
Reassess respiratory rate, heart rate, work of breathing and saturation within the first hour.
Escalate to NIV or intubation if there is no improvement per protocol.
Check nose skin, humidifier water and condensation in the tubing regularly.
Wean FiO2 first, then flow, as the patient improves.
aftercare: Keep the cannula in place and feed carefully or by tube if breathing is fast.
Report noisy tubing or water in the line.
red_flags: Escalate for rising FiO2 need, worsening work of breathing, apnoeas, exhaustion or drowsiness.
Escalate for sudden deterioration (consider pneumothorax or blocked cannula).

indications: Hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD exacerbation
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Obesity hypoventilation or neuromuscular disease with respiratory failure
Bubble CPAP for children or neonates with respiratory distress
contraindications: Respiratory arrest or need for immediate intubation
Unable to protect airway, vomiting or copious secretions
Untreated pneumothorax
Facial trauma or recent upper gastrointestinal surgery
Severe agitation or haemodynamic instability
equipment: NIV ventilator or CPAP device (bubble CPAP setup where resources are limited)
Interface of correct size (full face mask, nasal mask or nasal prongs)
Pulse oximeter, cardiac monitor and blood gas access
Pressure-relief dressings for the nose bridge
Nasogastric tube for gastric decompression in children if needed
steps: Confirm identity, indication and the ceiling of treatment, and record the escalation plan.
Obtain a baseline arterial or venous blood gas and observations.
Explain the treatment and sit the patient upright.
Choose and size the interface and apply protective dressings to pressure points.
Set initial pressures and FiO2 per protocol and connect the circuit.
Hold the mask gently to the face before securing the straps to help the patient adjust.
Increase pressures stepwise to effect as tolerated per protocol.
Adjust oxygen to keep saturation within the target range.
Repeat blood gas within 1-2 hours and reassess.
Escalate to intubation if gases or clinical state are not improving per the agreed plan.
Monitor observations, mask leak, skin and comfort regularly.
Plan breaks for mouth care and drinks and wean as the patient improves.
aftercare: Keep the mask on as advised and call staff if it is uncomfortable.
For home NIV or CPAP, use nightly and clean the mask and tubing daily.
red_flags: Escalate for worsening acidosis, falling consciousness, exhaustion or haemodynamic instability.
Escalate for vomiting, sudden chest pain or deterioration (possible pneumothorax).
Return for morning headaches or increasing sleepiness on home NIV.

indications: Respiratory failure not responding to oxygen or NIV
Inability to protect the airway or reduced consciousness
Post-operative ventilation or controlled ventilation in raised intracranial pressure
contraindications: Advance decision or agreed ceiling of care declining intubation
equipment: Ventilator checked, with circuit, filters and humidifier
Oxygen supply and backup cylinder with self-inflating bag
Airway trolley with endotracheal tubes, laryngoscopes and bougie
Capnography, pulse oximeter, cardiac and blood pressure monitoring
Sedation and induction medicines per anaesthetic protocol
steps: Confirm identity, indication and the escalation plan, and obtain consent from the patient or family where possible.
Check the ventilator and complete a pre-intubation checklist.
Preoxygenate and perform intubation per the airway protocol.
Confirm tube placement with capnography, chest movement and auscultation, and secure the tube.
Connect the ventilator and choose the mode (volume or pressure control).
Set tidal volume by predicted body weight, rate, PEEP and FiO2 per lung-protective protocol.
Set alarm limits for pressure, volume and disconnection.
Check plateau pressure and adjust settings to keep within safe limits.
Obtain a chest X-ray to confirm tube position and an arterial blood gas within 30 minutes.
Start sedation, analgesia, head-of-bed elevation, mouth care and pressure care bundles.
Record settings and plan daily sedation breaks and weaning assessment.
aftercare: Explain to the family what the ventilator does and the care plan.
Review daily for weaning and complications.
red_flags: Use DOPES checks (displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment, stacking) for sudden desaturation or high pressures, and bag by hand if needed.
Escalate for hypotension after intubation or high airway pressures.
Act at once for power or oxygen failure by switching to bag ventilation and backup supply.

indications: Moderate to severe ARDS on mechanical ventilation
Awake proning for hypoxaemia in a cooperative non-ventilated patient
contraindications: Unstable spine, pelvis or open chest or abdomen
Raised intracranial pressure
Severe haemodynamic instability
Late pregnancy (relative, needs specialist adaptation)
equipment: Enough trained staff for the turn (usually 4-6 for ventilated patients)
Pillows, gel pads or foam for pressure areas
ECG electrodes for placement on the back
steps: Confirm identity, indication and absence of contraindications, and explain to the patient or family.
Pre-oxygenate and suction the airway and mouth before turning ventilated patients.
Secure the endotracheal tube, lines and drains and check their lengths.
Assign a team leader at the head to control the airway and the turn.
Turn the patient in a coordinated log-roll onto the front using a slide sheet.
Position the head turned to one side and arms in swimmer's position, changing sides regularly.
Pad the face, chest, pelvis and knees to protect pressure points.
Recheck tube position, ventilation, lines and monitoring after the turn.
Maintain the prone position for the period in the protocol, monitoring oxygenation.
Return the patient supine with the same team process and recheck all devices.
aftercare: Check skin and eyes for pressure injury at every turn.
For awake proning, change position as tolerated and call staff if breathless.
red_flags: Return supine immediately for cardiac arrest, accidental extubation, severe desaturation or haemodynamic collapse.
Escalate for pressure injury to the face, eyes or chest.

indications: Suspected pulmonary TB in a patient unable to produce sputum
Suspected pneumocystis pneumonia
Children with suspected TB (with or without gastric aspirate)
contraindications: Severe asthma or FEV1 markedly reduced
Haemoptysis or severe respiratory distress
Recent nasal, eye, chest or abdominal surgery
equipment: Suction catheter and suction for children
N95 respirators and a well-ventilated or negative-pressure room or outdoor space
steps: Confirm identity and indication and explain the test.
Perform in a well-ventilated room or outdoors with staff wearing N95 respirators.
Give the short-acting bronchodilator first per protocol, especially in asthma.
Ask the patient to rinse the mouth with water.
Nebulise the hypertonic saline while monitoring oxygen saturation.
Encourage deep breathing and coughing at intervals and collect sputum into the container.
In young children, suction the nasopharynx after nebulisation to collect the sample.
Stop if wheeze, breathlessness or desaturation develops.
Label the sample and send it for GeneXpert, smear, culture or PCP testing.
Clean equipment and air the room before the next patient.
aftercare: Cough into a tissue or elbow and wear a mask until TB results are known.
Attend for results.
red_flags: Stop and give bronchodilator for wheeze, breathlessness or falling oxygen saturation.
Return for haemoptysis or worsening breathlessness.

indications: After chest or upper abdominal surgery to prevent atelectasis
Rib fractures or immobile patients at risk of chest infection
Sickle cell disease with chest pain to help prevent acute chest syndrome
contraindications: Patient unable to understand or cooperate
Untreated pneumothorax
equipment: Incentive spirometer (or blowing bottle or balloon as low-cost alternative)
steps: Confirm identity and that pain is controlled enough for deep breathing.
Sit the patient upright on the bed or in a chair.
Explain and demonstrate the device and set the target marker.
Ask the patient to breathe out normally and seal the lips round the mouthpiece.
Ask them to breathe in slowly and deeply to raise the indicator and hold the breath for 3-5 seconds.
Rest, then repeat for about ten breaths each hour while awake.
Encourage a supported cough after each set, splinting any wound with a pillow.
Record the volume achieved and progress.
aftercare: Use the device about ten times every hour while awake.
Keep moving and walking as advised.
red_flags: Report increasing breathlessness, chest pain, fever or coloured sputum.
Stop and report dizziness or tingling from over-breathing.

indications: Functional assessment in COPD, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension or heart failure
Assessment for oxygen need on exertion or pulmonary rehabilitation
contraindications: Unstable angina or recent myocardial infarction
Resting heart rate or blood pressure outside safe limits per protocol
Unable to walk safely
equipment: Flat corridor of measured length (usually 30 m) with turnaround cones
steps: Confirm identity, indication and that the patient is stable, wearing comfortable shoes.
Rest the patient seated for 10 minutes and record pulse, blood pressure, saturation and Borg score.
Explain that they should walk as far as possible in six minutes, back and forth, and may slow or rest.
Start the timer and walk behind the patient, giving standard phrases of encouragement each minute.
Monitor saturation and pulse during the walk if possible.
Stop the test if the patient develops chest pain, severe breathlessness, staggering or very low saturation.
At six minutes, stop the patient and mark the spot.
Record total distance, lowest saturation, pulse and Borg score at the end.
Let the patient rest and recover with observations.
aftercare: Rest until you feel recovered.
Attend for the results and treatment plan.
red_flags: Stop for chest pain, severe breathlessness, leg cramps, staggering, pallor or very low saturation.
Escalate if symptoms persist after rest.

indications: Suspected obstructive sleep apnoea
Snoring with witnessed apnoeas or daytime sleepiness
Children with snoring and tonsillar hypertrophy before surgery where indicated
Suspected hypoventilation in neuromuscular disease or obesity
contraindications: Acute illness (defer until recovered)
equipment: Polysomnography system or home sleep apnoea test device or overnight oximeter
EEG, EOG and EMG electrodes for full study
steps: Confirm identity, indication and the sleep questionnaire, and record weight, neck size and medicines.
Explain the study and ask the patient to avoid caffeine and alcohol on the day.
Attach the sensors per the study type and secure them for the night.
Check all signals are working before lights out.
Record overnight sleep, noting position changes and events.
Attend to loose sensors during the night in an attended study.
Remove the sensors in the morning and ask how the night's sleep compared with usual.
Score the study for apnoeas, hypopnoeas, oxygen desaturation and sleep stages.
Report the apnoea-hypopnoea index and severity and recommend treatment.
aftercare: Do not drive if you are very sleepy.
Attend for the results and treatment plan.
red_flags: Escalate if the study shows severe desaturation or hypoventilation needing urgent treatment.
Advise the patient not to drive while waiting if they are excessively sleepy.

indications: Early-stage lung cancer
Localised bronchiectasis or destroyed lobe after TB not controlled medically
Aspergilloma with recurrent haemoptysis
Benign tumours or lung abscess not responding to treatment
contraindications: Inadequate lung function for the planned resection
Distant metastases or unresectable disease
Unfit for general anaesthesia
equipment: Double-lumen endotracheal tube or bronchial blocker
Staplers and energy device where available
Chest drains and underwater seal bottles
Epidural or regional block equipment per anaesthetic plan
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, lung function, staging and blood availability.
Complete the surgical safety checklist and time-out, confirming the side and lobe.
Give general anaesthesia with lung isolation and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position the patient lateral with the operative side up.
Enter the chest by thoracotomy or VATS ports.
Inspect the pleura and lung to confirm resectability.
Dissect and divide the pulmonary vein, artery branches and bronchus to the lobe.
Complete the fissures and remove the lobe in a bag.
Sample or dissect mediastinal lymph nodes for staging.
Test the bronchial stump for air leak under saline and check haemostasis.
Insert chest drain(s) and close the chest in layers.
Send the specimen for histology and record findings.
aftercare: Do breathing exercises and walk early to protect the lungs.
Take analgesia regularly to allow deep breathing and coughing.
Avoid heavy lifting for six weeks.
red_flags: Escalate for heavy drain bleeding, hypotension, large air leak or rising oxygen need.
Escalate for new atrial fibrillation, fever or purulent sputum.
Return after discharge for breathlessness, chest pain, wound discharge or coughing blood.

name: Pulmonary function test with diffusion capacity

indications: Interstitial lung disease diagnosis and monitoring
Unexplained breathlessness
Pre-operative assessment for lung resection
Monitoring for drug toxicity affecting the lungs
contraindications: Recent myocardial infarction, pneumothorax or eye, chest or abdominal surgery
Haemoptysis of unknown cause
Active TB (infection control)
equipment: Pulmonary function system with diffusion and lung volume modules (body box or gas dilution)
Height measuring stick and weighing scale
steps: Confirm identity and indication, and ask the patient to avoid smoking on the day.
Check equipment calibration and record height, weight and latest haemoglobin.
Perform spirometry first to standard quality criteria.
Explain the diffusion test and fit the nose clip.
Ask the patient to breathe out fully, then inhale the test gas rapidly to full capacity.
Ask them to hold the breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out steadily.
Repeat after the recommended rest for at least two acceptable tests.
Measure lung volumes by body box or gas dilution per protocol.
Correct DLCO for haemoglobin and interpret against reference values.
Clean equipment and discard single-use parts.
aftercare: Resume usual activities and inhalers.
Attend for the results.
red_flags: Stop for dizziness, chest pain or severe coughing.
Escalate if results show severe impairment with symptoms.

indications: Acute urinary retention where urethral catheterisation has failed or is contraindicated
Urethral stricture or urethral injury
Long-term bladder drainage where a urethral catheter is unsuitable
contraindications: Bladder not palpable or not confirmed full on ultrasound
Previous lower abdominal surgery with possible bowel adhesions (use ultrasound guidance or open cystostomy)
Known or suspected bladder cancer
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
equipment: Suprapubic catheter trocar kit or Foley catheter with trocar
Sterile gloves, gown, drapes and antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity, indication and written consent and perform a time-out.
Confirm a full bladder by palpation, percussion or ultrasound.
Position supine and identify the site two finger-breadths above the pubic symphysis in the midline.
Perform hand hygiene, put on sterile gloves, prepare the skin with antiseptic and drape.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the bladder and aspirate urine to confirm depth and direction.
Make a small stab incision at the site.
Advance the trocar perpendicular to the skin or slightly caudal along the line of the needle until urine flows.
Pass the catheter through the trocar or sheath and inflate the balloon with sterile water.
Withdraw the trocar or peel away the sheath while holding the catheter in place.
Secure the catheter with a skin suture or fixation device and apply a dressing.
Connect to a closed drainage bag and record the urine volume and appearance.
aftercare: Monitor urine output and colour hourly for the first few hours.
Watch for decompression haematuria and hypotension after large-volume retention.
Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and the system closed.
Plan the first catheter change at 6–8 weeks or as per catheter type.
Teach the patient or carer site care and bag emptying.
red_flags: Abdominal pain, guarding or distension suggesting bowel injury or peritonitis
Heavy haematuria or clot retention
No drainage after insertion
Fever or rigors
Urine leaking around the site with signs of cellulitis

indications: Urinary retention with failed urethral and percutaneous suprapubic catheterisation
Urethral injury or complex stricture needing diversion
Bladder not safely accessible percutaneously (previous surgery, small bladder)
contraindications: Known bladder cancer (seeding risk)
Patient unfit for anaesthesia without first trying percutaneous drainage
equipment: Sterile drapes, gowns, gloves and antiseptic
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent and site and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position supine, prepare the lower abdomen with antiseptic and drape.
Make a short lower midline or transverse incision above the pubic symphysis.
Separate the recti and sweep the peritoneum upwards to expose the bladder.
Place two stay sutures on the anterior bladder wall and confirm by aspirating urine.
Open the bladder between the stay sutures and inspect the interior for stones or tumour.
Insert the catheter through a separate stab or through the wound and inflate the balloon.
Close the bladder around the catheter with absorbable sutures in one or two layers.
Secure the catheter to the skin, close the wound in layers and connect to closed drainage.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output and wound.
Keep the catheter secured and the drainage closed.
Mobilise early and give analgesia.
Arrange definitive treatment of the underlying cause and plan catheter changes.
red_flags: Catheter blocked or dislodged in the early postoperative period
Urine leak from the wound
Fever, wound infection or peritonitis
Heavy haematuria with clots

indications: Routine scheduled change of a long-term suprapubic catheter
Blocked, leaking or damaged suprapubic catheter
contraindications: Recently formed tract (under 4–6 weeks) unless done by an experienced clinician
equipment: New catheter of the same size and type
Sterile catheterisation pack, gloves and antiseptic
Sterile lubricating gel with or without local anaesthetic
10 mL syringe and sterile water for the balloon
steps: Confirm identity, explain the procedure and obtain verbal consent.
Check the size, type and date of the current catheter and have the new catheter ready.
Perform hand hygiene, position supine and expose the site.
Clean around the catheter site with antiseptic using an aseptic technique.
Deflate the balloon fully and note the volume withdrawn.
Remove the old catheter steadily, noting the angle and length of the tract.
Insert the lubricated new catheter promptly along the same tract to a similar depth.
Wait for urine to drain before inflating the balloon with sterile water.
Pull back gently until resistance is felt and connect to a closed drainage bag.
Apply a dressing if needed and record the catheter details and next change date.
aftercare: Check drainage over the next hour.
Advise on site care, fluid intake and bag management.
Schedule the next change per catheter type.
red_flags: Unable to reinsert the catheter (tract closes quickly, so escalate at once)
No urine drains after insertion
Bleeding that does not settle
Abdominal pain or fever after the change

indications: Short anterior urethral stricture where definitive surgery is not available or not wanted
Maintenance dilatation of a known stricture
Access for catheterisation through a narrow urethra
contraindications: Active urinary tract infection or urethritis
Recent urethral trauma
False passage from previous attempts
equipment: Graduated urethral sounds or filiform and followers
steps: Confirm identity, indication and written consent.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol and perform hand hygiene.
Position supine, clean the genitalia with antiseptic and drape.
Instil local anaesthetic gel into the urethra and wait several minutes for it to act.
Hold the penis upright and stretched and pass the lubricated sound gently without force.
Follow the curve of the urethra by lowering the penis as the sound passes into the bulbar urethra.
Progress through increasing sizes one at a time, stopping at resistance.
Note the calibre reached and any bleeding.
Insert a catheter if planned and connect to drainage.
aftercare: Expect mild burning and slight blood on voiding for a day or two.
Encourage oral fluids.
Arrange the next dilatation interval or referral for urethrotomy or urethroplasty.
red_flags: Fever or rigors after the procedure (urosepsis)
Heavy bleeding or clot retention
Unable to pass urine
Perineal or scrotal swelling suggesting extravasation

indications: Short single anterior or bulbar urethral stricture
Recurrent stricture where urethroplasty is not available
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection
Long, dense or multiple strictures (urethroplasty preferred)
Unfit for anaesthesia
equipment: Urethrotome with cold knife and optical sheath
Irrigation fluid (sterile water or saline per local protocol)
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent and urine culture and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Place in lithotomy, prepare and drape the genitalia.
Pass the urethrotome under vision to the stricture.
Pass a guidewire through the stricture lumen into the bladder.
Incise the stricture with the cold knife at the 12 o'clock position until healthy tissue is reached.
Advance the scope into the bladder and inspect for stones or other pathology.
Pass a Foley catheter over the guidewire or directly and inflate the balloon.
Record stricture site, length and the result of the incision.
aftercare: Keep the catheter for the period set by the surgeon, usually several days.
Monitor for bleeding and fever.
Arrange uroflowmetry and follow-up to detect recurrence.
red_flags: Fever, rigors or hypotension (urosepsis)
Heavy bleeding or clot retention
Perineal or scrotal swelling
Poor stream returning after catheter removal

indications: Bulbar or penile urethral stricture unsuitable for or failed after urethrotomy
Pelvic fracture urethral distraction defect
Long or obliterative stricture
contraindications: Active urinary tract infection
Unfit for prolonged anaesthesia
Untreated lichen sclerosus affecting graft choice (relative)
equipment: Urethroplasty set with fine instruments and retractor
Buccal mucosa harvest set if a graft is planned
steps: Confirm identity, consent, imaging of the stricture and sterile urine and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy with careful padding of pressure points.
Prepare and drape the perineum, genitalia and mouth if a graft is planned.
Make a perineal or penile incision and expose the corpus spongiosum over the stricture.
Identify the stricture with a sound and open or excise the scarred segment.
Perform a tension-free anastomosis or place and quilt a graft to widen the urethra.
Pass the urethral catheter across the repair before completing closure.
Close the tissues in layers with a drain if needed.
Record stricture site, length, technique and graft details.
aftercare: Keep the urethral catheter for the period set by the surgeon, often 2–3 weeks.
Perform a pericatheter urethrogram before removal if indicated.
Care for the buccal donor site with mouth rinses and soft diet.
Arrange flow rate follow-up to detect recurrence.
red_flags: Catheter falls out early (do not reinsert blindly; contact the surgeon)
Fever, perineal swelling or wound discharge
Heavy bleeding
Leg numbness or compartment symptoms after prolonged lithotomy

indications: Visible haematuria or unexplained non-visible haematuria
Suspected bladder tumour or surveillance after bladder tumour
Lower urinary tract symptoms with suspected stricture, stone or fistula
Removal of stents or foreign bodies
contraindications: Active untreated urinary tract infection
equipment: Flexible or rigid cystoscope with appropriate sheath
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent and check urine dipstick or culture.
Give prophylactic antibiotic if indicated per local protocol and perform hand hygiene.
Position supine (flexible) or lithotomy (rigid), clean with antiseptic and drape.
Instil local anaesthetic gel into the urethra and wait for it to act.
Pass the scope under direct vision, inspecting the urethra and prostate.
Enter the bladder and fill with irrigation fluid to distend it.
Inspect the whole bladder systematically, including the trigone, ureteric orifices and dome.
Take biopsies or perform planned minor procedures as indicated.
Drain the bladder and withdraw the scope while inspecting the urethra.
Document findings with a bladder diagram where possible.
aftercare: Expect mild burning and pink urine for a day or two.
Encourage oral fluids.
Give results and arrange follow-up of biopsies.
red_flags: Fever or rigors
Unable to pass urine
Heavy bleeding or clots

indications: Benign prostatic enlargement with refractory retention or failed medical treatment
Recurrent urinary retention, haematuria, bladder stones or upper tract dilatation from prostatic obstruction
Channel TURP for obstructing prostate cancer
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection
Uncorrected coagulopathy or antithrombotic not managed per protocol
Very large gland better treated by open prostatectomy
Urethral stricture not yet treated
equipment: Diathermy machine with matched irrigation fluid
Irrigation set for continuous bladder irrigation
steps: Confirm identity, consent, urine culture, blood count, electrolytes and group and save and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia (usually spinal) and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy, prepare and drape.
Perform urethrocystoscopy to assess the prostate, bladder and ureteric orifices.
Identify the verumontanum as the distal limit of resection to protect the external sphincter.
Resect the prostatic adenoma systematically down to the capsule.
Control bleeding with diathermy as you go.
Evacuate all chips with the evacuator and check haemostasis with the irrigation off.
Insert a three-way catheter and start continuous bladder irrigation.
Record resection time and fluid used and send chips for histology.
aftercare: Run continuous bladder irrigation titrated to light pink outflow.
Watch for TUR syndrome (confusion, bradycardia, hypertension then hypotension) and check sodium if suspected.
Remove the catheter after urine clears, usually day 2–3, and check voiding and residual.
Advise on retrograde ejaculation, temporary frequency and avoiding straining.
red_flags: Confusion, nausea, visual disturbance or seizures (TUR syndrome)
Clot retention or blocked catheter
Heavy bleeding or falling haemoglobin
Fever or hypotension (urosepsis)
Retention after catheter removal

indications: Large benign prostatic enlargement with retention or refractory symptoms
Prostatic enlargement with large bladder stone or diverticulum needing open surgery
TURP not available
contraindications: Suspected or proven prostate cancer (needs different management)
Untreated infection
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Small fibrous gland
equipment: Major open prostatectomy set with bladder retractor
steps: Confirm identity, consent, sterile urine, haemoglobin and cross-matched blood and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position supine, catheterise, prepare and drape.
Make a lower midline or Pfannenstiel incision and expose the bladder extraperitoneally.
Open the bladder (transvesical) or prostatic capsule (retropubic) and inspect the ureteric orifices.
Incise the mucosa at the bladder neck and enucleate the adenoma with the finger in the correct plane.
Control bleeding with pressure, haemostatic sutures at the bladder neck and trigonisation as needed.
Insert a three-way catheter with or without a suprapubic catheter and start irrigation.
Close the bladder or capsule in layers, place a drain and close the wound.
Send the adenoma for histology and record weight and blood loss.
aftercare: Run continuous bladder irrigation and monitor haemoglobin and vital signs.
Keep the catheter for the period set by the surgeon, usually 5–7 days.
Remove the drain when output is low and check voiding after catheter removal.
Advise about retrograde ejaculation and avoiding heavy lifting for several weeks.
red_flags: Persistent heavy bleeding or clot retention
Urine leak from the wound or drain
Fever, wound sepsis or hypotension
Leg swelling or chest pain (venous thromboembolism)

indications: Localised prostate cancer in a patient with good life expectancy
contraindications: Metastatic disease
Limited life expectancy or unfit for major surgery
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Major pelvic surgery set or laparoscopic set
Diathermy, suction and vessel sealing device if available
steps: Confirm identity, consent, staging results and cross-matched blood and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia, prophylactic antibiotic and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis per local protocol.
Position supine (open) or steep Trendelenburg (laparoscopic), catheterise, prepare and drape.
Develop the retropubic space and perform pelvic lymph node dissection if indicated.
Control the dorsal venous complex.
Divide the urethra and dissect the prostate and seminal vesicles off the rectum, preserving neurovascular bundles where oncologically safe.
Divide the bladder neck and remove the specimen.
Perform the vesicourethral anastomosis over a new catheter and test it for leaks.
Place a drain and close.
Send the prostate and nodes for histology and record blood loss.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, haemoglobin and drain output.
Keep the catheter for 1–2 weeks or as directed, and secure it well.
Start pelvic floor exercises after catheter removal.
Check PSA at follow-up and discuss continence and erectile recovery.
red_flags: Catheter falls out before the planned date (do not reinsert blindly)
High drain output suggesting urine leak or lymphocele
Bleeding or falling haemoglobin
Leg swelling or chest pain
Rectal bleeding or faecaluria

indications: Raised PSA for age
Abnormal digital rectal examination
Suspicious lesion on imaging
contraindications: Active urinary tract infection or prostatitis
Uncorrected bleeding disorder or antithrombotic not managed per protocol
Painful anorectal condition preventing probe insertion
equipment: Transrectal ultrasound probe with biopsy guide
Automated biopsy gun and core needles 18 G
Local anaesthetic and spinal needle for periprostatic block
steps: Confirm identity, indication, consent, urine culture and antithrombotic status.
Give prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in left lateral with knees drawn up.
Perform a digital rectal examination.
Insert the covered, lubricated ultrasound probe and measure prostate volume.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic around the prostate as a periprostatic block.
Take systematic cores from each side plus targeted cores from any lesion.
Place each core in a labelled pot by site.
Apply pressure if there is rectal bleeding and observe before discharge.
aftercare: Expect blood in urine, stool or semen for days to weeks.
Encourage fluids and advise on warning signs of infection.
Arrange results and follow-up appointment.
red_flags: Fever, rigors or feeling unwell within days of the biopsy (urosepsis, attend urgently)
Heavy rectal bleeding or clots in urine
Unable to pass urine

indications: Androgen deprivation for advanced or metastatic prostate cancer
contraindications: Patient has not had full counselling or declines permanent castration
Uncorrected bleeding disorder
steps: Confirm identity, diagnosis, written consent covering permanent effects and perform a time-out.
Give anaesthesia (local, spinal or general) per patient and setting.
Position supine, clean the scrotum with antiseptic and drape.
Make a midline raphe or bilateral scrotal incision and deliver the first testis.
Incise the tunica albuginea and scrape out the testicular tissue, leaving the capsule and epididymis.
Secure haemostasis carefully and close the tunica.
Repeat on the other side.
Close the dartos and skin with absorbable sutures and apply a scrotal support.
Send tissue for histology if required.
aftercare: Apply ice and scrotal support and give analgesia.
Check PSA at follow-up to confirm response.
Counsel on hot flushes, loss of libido and bone health monitoring.
red_flags: Rapidly enlarging scrotal swelling (haematoma)
Fever, wound discharge or spreading redness
Severe pain not controlled by analgesia

indications: Non-viable testis after torsion or trauma
Chronic painful or infected testis not responding to treatment
Atrophic testis
contraindications: Suspected testicular cancer (use radical inguinal approach)
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and exclusion of malignancy and perform a time-out with site marking.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic if indicated per local protocol.
Clean the scrotum with antiseptic and drape.
Make a scrotal incision on the marked side and deliver the testis.
Doubly ligate and divide the spermatic cord.
Remove the testis and check haemostasis carefully.
Close the dartos and skin with absorbable sutures.
Send the testis for histology and apply a scrotal support.
aftercare: Give analgesia, ice and scrotal support.
Offer a prosthesis discussion if wanted.
Review the wound at one to two weeks.
red_flags: Expanding scrotal haematoma
Fever or wound discharge
Severe pain

indications: Suspected testicular cancer
contraindications: None absolute; stabilise life-threatening metastatic disease first if needed
equipment: Soft non-crushing clamp for the cord
Non-absorbable ligature for the cord stump
steps: Confirm identity, side marking, tumour markers drawn, consent including fertility (sperm banking) and perform a time-out.
Give anaesthesia and position supine, prepare and drape the groin and scrotum.
Make an inguinal incision and open the external oblique aponeurosis.
Mobilise the spermatic cord and clamp it at the deep ring before handling the testis.
Deliver the testis from the scrotum into the wound without opening the scrotum.
Ligate the cord high at the deep ring with a non-absorbable ligature left long for later identification.
Remove the testis and cord as one specimen.
Check haemostasis, insert a prosthesis if consented, and close in layers.
Send the specimen fresh or in formalin per laboratory protocol.
aftercare: Give analgesia and review the wound.
Repeat tumour markers after surgery and arrange staging CT.
Refer to oncology with histology.
red_flags: Expanding groin or scrotal haematoma
Fever or wound infection
New breathlessness, cough or back pain (metastatic disease)

indications: Symptomatic adult vaginal hydrocele
Filarial hydrocele
contraindications: Paediatric communicating hydrocele (needs inguinal herniotomy)
Untreated scrotal infection
Testicular tumour not excluded when the testis cannot be felt (scan first)
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and perform a time-out with site marking.
Give anaesthesia and position supine; prepare the scrotum with antiseptic and drape.
Make a scrotal incision over the hydrocele and deliver the sac.
Open the sac, drain the fluid and inspect the testis and epididymis.
Perform plication of the sac (Lord's) for a thin sac, or excision and eversion (Jaboulay) for a large thick sac.
Achieve meticulous haemostasis of the sac edges.
Return the testis to the scrotum, place a drain if needed and close in layers.
Apply a scrotal support or pressure dressing.
aftercare: Expect scrotal swelling for several weeks; use scrotal support and ice.
Give analgesia and review the wound and drain.
Avoid heavy lifting for two weeks.
red_flags: Rapidly enlarging tense scrotum (haematoma)
Fever, wound discharge or redness
Severe pain

indications: Symptomatic hydrocele in a patient unfit for or declining surgery
Temporary relief pending surgery
contraindications: Children
Hernia not excluded
Testicular tumour not excluded (ultrasound first)
Overlying skin infection
equipment: Syringe and three-way tap or drainage tubing
Sclerosant only if per local protocol
steps: Confirm identity, side and verbal consent and check that hernia and tumour are excluded.
Perform hand hygiene and position supine.
Transilluminate to confirm the fluid and locate the testis, usually posterior.
Clean the scrotum with antiseptic and infiltrate local anaesthetic at an anterior avascular site.
Hold the hydrocele tense and insert the needle away from the testis and visible vessels.
