Aspirate the fluid fully and note its volume and colour.
Inject sclerosant only if this is the local protocol and the clinician is trained.
Withdraw the needle, apply pressure, a dressing and a scrotal support.
aftercare: Advise that recurrence is common.
Use a scrotal support and analgesia.
Send fluid for analysis if it is bloodstained or cloudy.
red_flags: Rapid refilling with blood (haematocele)
Fever, redness or severe pain

indications: Symptomatic varicocele with pain or heaviness
Varicocele with abnormal semen analysis and infertility
Adolescent varicocele with testicular growth arrest
contraindications: Sudden-onset right or non-reducing varicocele not yet investigated for a renal or retroperitoneal mass
Untreated scrotal or groin infection
equipment: Loupes or operating microscope if available
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and perform a time-out with site marking.
Give anaesthesia and position supine; prepare and drape.
Make a subinguinal or inguinal incision and deliver the spermatic cord.
Open the cord coverings and identify the testicular artery, lymphatics and vas.
Ligate and divide the dilated internal spermatic veins while preserving the artery, lymphatics and vas.
Check that no significant veins remain and that haemostasis is good.
Return the cord and close in layers.
aftercare: Give analgesia and advise scrotal support.
Avoid heavy exercise for two weeks.
Repeat semen analysis after three months if done for infertility.
red_flags: Scrotal swelling that increases (hydrocele or haematoma)
Fever or wound infection
Testis becomes painful or shrinks

indications: Suspected testicular torsion (clinical diagnosis; do not delay for imaging)
Acute scrotum where torsion cannot be excluded
contraindications: None; this is an emergency and delay costs the testis
steps: Confirm identity, side, time of pain onset and consent including possible orchidectomy (parent or guardian for a child) and perform a time-out.
Attempt manual detorsion (outward rotation) only as a temporising step while preparing theatre.
Give anaesthesia and prepare and drape the scrotum.
Make a midline raphe or transverse incision on the affected side and open the tunica vaginalis.
Untwist the cord and wrap the testis in warm saline swabs for several minutes.
Assess viability by colour and bleeding from a small incision in the tunica albuginea if needed.
Fix a viable testis with non-absorbable sutures, or remove a clearly necrotic testis.
Explore and fix the opposite testis through the same or a separate incision.
Close in layers and apply a scrotal support.
aftercare: Give analgesia and review the wound.
Explain the result and possible later atrophy.
Review at six weeks to assess testicular size.
red_flags: Expanding scrotal swelling
Fever or wound infection
New pain in the fixed testis

form.label: Time from pain onset to surgery

indications: Suspected testicular rupture after blunt trauma
Penetrating scrotal injury
Large or expanding scrotal haematoma
contraindications: Life-threatening injuries elsewhere take priority
steps: Resuscitate per trauma protocol and confirm identity and consent.
Perform a time-out and give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Clean and drape the scrotum and explore through a scrotal incision.
Evacuate haematoma and irrigate the wound.
Inspect both testes, epididymides and cords.
Debride non-viable seminiferous tubules and close the tunica albuginea with absorbable sutures.
Remove the testis only if it is unsalvageable.
Check haemostasis, place a drain if needed and close.
Give tetanus prophylaxis per local protocol.
aftercare: Give analgesia, scrotal support and ice.
Remove the drain when dry.
Review testicular size at follow-up.
red_flags: Re-accumulating swelling
Fever or wound sepsis
Urinary symptoms suggesting urethral injury

indications: Symptomatic or large epididymal cyst or spermatocele
contraindications: Man who wishes to preserve fertility on that side (risk of epididymal obstruction, counsel first)
Untreated infection
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent including fertility risk and perform a time-out with site marking.
Give anaesthesia and prepare and drape the scrotum.
Make a scrotal incision and deliver the testis and epididymis.
Dissect the cyst carefully off the epididymis, preserving the epididymal tubule and vas.
Ligate the neck of the cyst and excise it.
Check haemostasis and return the testis.
Close in layers and apply a scrotal support.
Send the cyst for histology if indicated.
aftercare: Give analgesia, ice and scrotal support.
Review the wound at one to two weeks.
red_flags: Expanding scrotal swelling
Fever or wound discharge

indications: Cultural or religious request
Phimosis not responding to conservative treatment
Recurrent balanoposthitis
HIV prevention programme (voluntary medical male circumcision)
contraindications: Hypospadias, epispadias, chordee or buried penis (refer; foreskin may be needed for repair)
Bleeding disorder until assessed and corrected
Unwell or premature neonate
Active local infection
equipment: Circumcision set (or Plastibell or clamp device of correct size)
Local anaesthetic without adrenaline for penile block
Bipolar diathermy if available (avoid monopolar with clamp devices)
steps: Confirm identity, consent (parent or guardian for a child) and check for penile anomalies and bleeding history.
Perform a time-out, hand hygiene and prepare the genitalia with antiseptic.
Give a dorsal penile or ring block with local anaesthetic without adrenaline, or general anaesthesia.
Free adhesions between the foreskin and glans gently.
Mark the line of excision at the corona, leaving adequate shaft skin.
Excise the foreskin by sleeve, dorsal slit or device technique.
Secure haemostasis, especially the frenular artery.
Approximate the skin edges with interrupted absorbable sutures where needed.
Check the glans and urethral meatus are intact and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Check that the child passes urine before discharge or within a few hours.
Keep the area clean and apply petroleum jelly to prevent sticking.
Give simple analgesia.
Review if a Plastibell ring has not separated by about 10 days.
red_flags: Bleeding that soaks the dressing or does not stop with pressure
No urine passed within 8–12 hours
Glans darkens or becomes swollen
Fever, pus or spreading redness
Plastibell ring stuck or migrated onto the shaft

indications: Paraphimosis that cannot be reduced manually
Severe phimosis with retention or balanoposthitis when circumcision is not possible now
contraindications: Penile anomalies such as hypospadias (refer)
Bleeding disorder until corrected
equipment: Minor surgical set with straight artery forceps
steps: Confirm identity and consent (parent or guardian for a child) and perform a time-out.
Perform hand hygiene, clean with antiseptic and give a dorsal penile block or anaesthesia.
Place straight forceps on the dorsal midline of the foreskin for a short while to crush it for haemostasis.
Divide the crushed foreskin in the dorsal midline with scissors, short of the corona.
Retract the foreskin to relieve the constriction or expose the glans.
Suture the cut edges of inner and outer layers with absorbable sutures.
Check the glans and meatus and apply a dressing.
aftercare: Keep clean and apply petroleum jelly.
Give simple analgesia.
Plan formal circumcision later if wanted.
red_flags: Bleeding that does not stop with pressure
Unable to pass urine
Glans discolouration or worsening swelling

indications: Retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans with swelling
contraindications: Glans necrosis (needs urgent surgical care)
equipment: Local anaesthetic gel or penile block
Fine needle for puncture technique if needed
steps: Confirm identity, explain and obtain verbal consent (parent or guardian for a child).
Perform hand hygiene and give analgesia, local anaesthetic gel or a penile block.
Reduce oedema by firm steady compression of the glans with a gauze-wrapped hand for several minutes, with ice if available.
Place both index fingers behind the trapped ring and both thumbs on the glans.
Push the glans back with the thumbs while pulling the foreskin forward with the fingers.
If oedema prevents reduction, make several needle punctures in the swollen foreskin and squeeze out fluid, then retry.
If still unsuccessful, proceed to dorsal slit.
Check the glans colour and the patient's ability to pass urine after reduction.
aftercare: Advise not to retract the foreskin for several days.
Teach correct foreskin hygiene and to always return the foreskin.
Discuss circumcision if recurrent.
red_flags: Recurrence of the trapped foreskin
Unable to pass urine
Darkening of the glans

indications: Symptomatic meatal stenosis with a thin deflected stream, straining or dysuria
contraindications: Hypospadias needing formal repair
Active infection
equipment: Fine surgical set with straight artery forceps
Local anaesthetic gel or penile block
steps: Confirm identity and consent (parent or guardian for a child) and perform a time-out.
Give anaesthesia and clean the glans with antiseptic.
Calibrate the meatus with a probe or dilator.
Crush the ventral meatal web with straight forceps briefly.
Incise the crushed tissue ventrally to open the meatus.
Suture the urethral mucosa to the glans skin on each side for a meatoplasty if needed.
Recalibrate to confirm an adequate opening.
aftercare: Apply petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment to the meatus to stop it re-closing.
Expect stinging on voiding for a few days.
Review the stream at follow-up.
red_flags: Bleeding that does not stop
Unable to pass urine
Return of a thin stream

indications: Ischaemic (low-flow) priapism lasting more than four hours
Priapism in sickle cell disease not resolving with initial measures
contraindications: Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism (bright red blood gas, painless; refer for imaging)
Overlying skin infection
Uncontrolled hypertension, heart disease or monoamine oxidase inhibitor use (do not give an alpha-agonist)
equipment: Diluted alpha-agonist prepared per local protocol by a senior clinician
steps: Confirm identity, duration of erection, cause (including sickle cell disease) and written consent.
For sickle cell disease, start hydration, oxygen and analgesia and involve haematology in parallel.
Perform hand hygiene, clean the penis with antiseptic and give a dorsal penile block.
Insert a needle into one corpus cavernosum at the 2 or 10 o'clock position of the lateral shaft.
Aspirate dark blood and send a sample for blood gas to confirm ischaemic priapism.
Continue aspiration with saline irrigation until bright red blood returns and detumescence occurs.
If the erection persists, inject a diluted alpha-agonist in small aliquots per protocol with blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.
Remove the needle, apply firm pressure and a light compressive dressing.
Escalate to shunt surgery if aspiration and alpha-agonist fail.
aftercare: Observe for recurrence for several hours.
Monitor blood pressure and pulse after alpha-agonist use.
Counsel about the risk of erectile dysfunction and treat the underlying cause.
red_flags: Recurrence of erection
Chest pain, palpitations, severe headache or hypertension after alpha-agonist
Penile haematoma or skin necrosis
Duration over 24 hours (high risk of erectile dysfunction; involve a urologist)

indications: Ischaemic priapism not resolved by aspiration, irrigation and alpha-agonist injection
contraindications: Non-ischaemic priapism
steps: Confirm identity, failed conservative treatment and written consent covering erectile dysfunction risk and perform a time-out.
Give anaesthesia and clean and drape the penis.
Create a distal shunt between the glans and the tips of the corpora cavernosa (Winter needle, T-shunt or Al-Ghorab excision).
Squeeze dark blood out through the shunt until the corpora soften.
Repeat on the other side if needed.
Close the glans incision with absorbable sutures, leaving the shunt open.
If distal shunts fail, consider proximal shunt or refer to a specialist unit.
Apply a light compressive dressing.
aftercare: Check for recurrence regularly over the next day.
Counsel about erectile dysfunction and future treatment options such as prosthesis.
Manage the underlying cause, such as sickle cell disease.
red_flags: Recurrence of erection
Glans or skin necrosis
Fever or wound infection
Urethral injury (blood at meatus or difficulty voiding)

indications: Clinical penile fracture (crack, sudden detumescence, swelling and bruising during erection)
contraindications: Unfit for anaesthesia (rare; surgery should not be delayed)
equipment: Slowly absorbable sutures for the tunica
Flexible cystoscope if urethral injury is suspected
steps: Confirm identity, history and consent and check for blood at the meatus or retention.
Perform a time-out and give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Assess the urethra by cystoscopy or urethrography if injury is suspected.
Make a subcoronal degloving incision or a direct incision over the defect.
Evacuate the haematoma and identify the tear in the tunica albuginea.
Close the tunical tear with slowly absorbable sutures, burying the knots.
Repair any urethral injury over a catheter.
Check with artificial erection if available, then close the skin.
Apply a light compressive dressing.
aftercare: Advise no sexual activity for 6 weeks.
Keep the catheter if a urethral repair was done for the time set by the surgeon.
Review erectile function and curvature at follow-up.
red_flags: Expanding haematoma
Unable to pass urine or blood at the meatus
Wound infection or skin necrosis

indications: Desire for fertility after previous vasectomy
Obstructive azoospermia from vasal obstruction
contraindications: Partner fertility not assessed or reversal unlikely to succeed where assisted reproduction is preferred
Active genital infection
equipment: Glass slides and microscope for vasal fluid
steps: Confirm identity, consent including success rates and alternatives and perform a time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prepare and drape the scrotum.
Expose the vas on each side and identify the vasectomy site.
Excise the scarred segment and examine the testicular-end fluid for sperm.
Perform a two-layer microsurgical vasovasostomy if sperm or clear fluid is present.
Perform a vasoepididymostomy if there is no sperm and thick fluid suggests epididymal obstruction and the surgeon is trained.
Achieve haemostasis and close in layers.
aftercare: Wear scrotal support and avoid sexual activity and heavy lifting for 2–3 weeks.
Check semen analysis at intervals starting around six weeks.
red_flags: Scrotal haematoma
Fever or wound infection

indications: Azoospermia (obstructive or non-obstructive) for assisted reproduction (ICSI)
Failed ejaculation where sperm are needed for assisted reproduction
contraindications: No access to an embryology laboratory to process and freeze the sample
Active genital infection
equipment: Fine needle and syringe for PESA or TESA
Minor surgical set for open or micro-TESE
Sperm culture medium and sterile containers from the laboratory
steps: Confirm identity, consent and laboratory readiness and perform a time-out.
Give a spermatic cord block or general anaesthesia and prepare the scrotum.
For PESA, aspirate the epididymis with a fine needle and pass the fluid to the embryologist.
For TESA, aspirate testicular tissue with a needle under negative pressure.
For TESE or micro-TESE, open the tunica and take tubules, using the microscope to select dilated tubules.
Have the embryologist check the sample for sperm before finishing.
Close the tunica and skin and apply a scrotal support.
Send a separate testicular sample for histology if indicated.
aftercare: Give analgesia and scrotal support.
Review laboratory results and plan assisted reproduction.
red_flags: Expanding scrotal swelling
Fever or wound infection

indications: Azoospermia to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive causes
Suspected intratubular germ cell neoplasia in high-risk testis
contraindications: Suspected testicular tumour (needs inguinal orchidectomy, not scrotal biopsy)
Active infection
equipment: Bouin's or other fixative (not formalin) as advised by the laboratory
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and perform a time-out.
Give a spermatic cord block or general anaesthesia and prepare the scrotum.
Make a small scrotal incision and open the tunica vaginalis.
Incise the tunica albuginea in an avascular area.
Remove a small piece of extruding tissue with sharp scissors without crushing.
Place it immediately in the correct fixative; send a sample for sperm search if planned.
Close the tunica albuginea and skin.
aftercare: Give analgesia and scrotal support.
Review histology and plan further management.
red_flags: Expanding scrotal swelling
Fever or wound discharge

indications: Large or multiple bladder stones
Bladder stones in children
Bladder stone with need for open prostatectomy or diverticulectomy
Endoscopic equipment not available
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection (treat first where possible)
steps: Confirm identity, consent and imaging and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Catheterise and fill the bladder with saline, then prepare and drape.
Make a low transverse or midline incision and expose the bladder extraperitoneally.
Place stay sutures and open the bladder.
Remove the stones with forceps and inspect for further stones, diverticula or outflow obstruction.
Send stones for analysis where available.
Close the bladder in two layers with absorbable sutures over a urethral catheter, with or without a suprapubic tube.
Place a drain in the retropubic space and close the wound.
aftercare: Monitor urine output, haematuria and drain output.
Remove the drain when dry and the catheter after about a week or as directed.
Investigate and treat the cause of stone formation (obstruction, infection, diet).
red_flags: Urine leak from the wound or high drain output
Blocked catheter or clot retention
Fever or wound infection

indications: Bladder stones suitable for endoscopic fragmentation
contraindications: Very large stone burden better removed by open surgery
Urethral stricture preventing scope passage (treat first)
Untreated urinary tract infection
equipment: Lithotrite, pneumatic, ultrasonic or laser lithotripter
steps: Confirm identity, consent and imaging and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy, prepare and drape.
Pass the scope and assess the stone, bladder and outlet.
Fragment the stone with the available energy source, keeping the bladder moderately filled.
Evacuate fragments with the evacuator and check that none remain.
Treat any outlet obstruction at the same sitting if planned.
Insert a catheter and send fragments for analysis.
aftercare: Monitor haematuria and remove the catheter when urine is clear.
Treat the cause of stone formation.
red_flags: Fever or rigors
Clot retention
Abdominal pain or distension (bladder perforation)

indications: Ureteric stone not passing or causing persistent pain or obstruction
Renal stones suitable for flexible ureteroscopy
Diagnostic ureteroscopy for filling defects
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection (obstructed infected kidney needs drainage first)
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Guidewires, ureteric access sheath and stone basket
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, sterile urine and imaging and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out with site marking.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy, prepare and drape.
Perform cystoscopy and pass a safety guidewire up the ureter under fluoroscopy.
Advance the ureteroscope alongside the wire to the stone.
Fragment the stone and extract fragments with a basket as needed.
Inspect the ureter for injury and residual stones.
Place a double-J stent if there is oedema, injury or residual fragments.
Record stone position, size, clearance and stent details.
aftercare: Expect stent discomfort and haematuria if a stent is placed.
Give analgesia and fluids.
Record and book the stent removal date before discharge.
Arrange imaging to confirm clearance.
red_flags: Fever or rigors (urosepsis)
Severe loin pain
Unable to pass urine
Forgotten stent (must be removed by the booked date)

indications: Renal stones larger than about 2 cm
Staghorn calculi
Lower pole stones unsuitable for other approaches
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Pregnancy
Interposed bowel or other organs on the planned tract
equipment: Nephrostomy tube and or double-J stent
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, sterile urine, imaging and cross-matched blood and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Place a ureteric catheter cystoscopically for retrograde contrast.
Position prone or supine, prepare and drape the flank.
Puncture the target calyx under fluoroscopy or ultrasound and pass a guidewire.
Dilate the tract and place the access sheath.
Fragment and remove the stone through the nephroscope.
Check for residual fragments with nephroscopy and imaging.
Place a nephrostomy tube and or stent, or finish tubeless if suitable.
Record access, stone burden, clearance and drainage.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, haemoglobin and urine colour.
Manage the nephrostomy and remove it when urine clears.
Arrange imaging to confirm stone clearance and stent removal.
red_flags: Heavy bleeding from nephrostomy or haematuria with falling haemoglobin
Fever or hypotension (urosepsis)
Breathlessness or chest pain (pleural injury)
Abdominal pain or distension (bowel injury)

indications: Renal stones up to about 2 cm suitable for fragmentation
Selected upper ureteric stones
contraindications: Pregnancy
Uncorrected coagulopathy or antithrombotic not managed per protocol
Untreated urinary tract infection
Obstruction distal to the stone
Aortic or renal artery aneurysm near the stone
equipment: Lithotripter with fluoroscopy or ultrasound targeting
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, pregnancy status, urine and clotting results and perform a time-out.
Give analgesia or sedation per local protocol.
Position the patient on the lithotripter with good coupling to the treatment head.
Locate the stone with fluoroscopy or ultrasound.
Start at low energy and increase gradually, checking targeting regularly.
Monitor pain, heart rate and rhythm throughout.
Stop when the planned number of shocks is reached or the stone is fragmented.
Record shocks, energy level and fragmentation.
aftercare: Drink plenty of fluids and strain urine to collect fragments.
Expect haematuria and colicky pain as fragments pass.
Arrange follow-up imaging and repeat sessions if needed.
red_flags: Fever or rigors
Severe loin pain or flank swelling (perirenal haematoma)
Unable to pass urine

indications: Renal pelvic or staghorn stones where endoscopic options are unavailable or unsuitable
Combined stone removal and pyeloplasty
contraindications: Untreated infection or pyonephrosis (drain first)
Unfit for major surgery
equipment: Double-J stent and or nephrostomy tube
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, imaging and cross-matched blood and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lateral flank position, prepare and drape.
Make a flank incision and expose the kidney and renal pelvis.
Open the renal pelvis and remove the stone intact where possible.
Retrieve calyceal fragments and irrigate the collecting system.
Check for residual stones by palpation or imaging.
Place a stent or nephrostomy as needed and close the pelvis with fine absorbable sutures.
Leave a drain and close the wound in layers.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, haemoglobin and drain output.
Remove the drain when output is low.
Arrange stent removal and stone prevention advice.
red_flags: Persistent urine leak from drain or wound
Bleeding or falling haemoglobin
Fever or wound infection
Breathlessness (pleural injury)

indications: Obstructed kidney from stone, stricture, tumour or external compression
Obstructed infected kidney needing urgent drainage
After ureteroscopy, pyeloplasty or ureteric repair
Ureteric injury or leak
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection without urgent drainage need (treat first)
Inability to pass a wire past the obstruction (consider nephrostomy)
equipment: Double-J stent of correct length and size (e.g. 4.8–6 Fr)
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent and imaging and perform a time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy, prepare and drape.
Perform cystoscopy and identify the ureteric orifice.
Pass a guidewire up to the kidney under fluoroscopy.
Perform retrograde pyelography if needed to assess the obstruction.
Advance the stent over the wire until the upper coil is in the renal pelvis.
Withdraw the wire and confirm the lower coil in the bladder.
Record the stent size and length and book the removal or change date.
aftercare: Expect frequency, urgency, haematuria and loin pain on voiding.
Give stent card or written removal date and enter it in the stent register.
Encourage fluids.
red_flags: Fever or rigors after insertion (urosepsis)
Severe pain or no drainage
Stent not removed or changed by the booked date

indications: Planned removal at end of stent dwell time
Stent symptoms or complications when the stent is no longer needed
contraindications: Ongoing obstruction still needing drainage (change instead)
Active urinary tract infection (treat first)
steps: Confirm identity, side, stent insertion date and verbal consent (written if under general anaesthesia).
Review recent imaging for encrustation if the stent is overdue.
Perform hand hygiene, position, clean with antiseptic and instil local anaesthetic gel.
Pass the cystoscope and identify the lower coil of the stent.
Grasp the stent and withdraw it steadily with the scope.
Stop if there is resistance and image for encrustation before further attempts.
Check that the stent is complete and record its removal in the stent register.
aftercare: Expect mild pain and haematuria for a day or two.
Encourage fluids.
Arrange follow-up imaging if planned.
red_flags: Severe loin pain after removal (obstruction)
Fever or rigors
Stent fragment retained

indications: Renal tumour (radical or partial)
Non-functioning kidney with infection, pain or hypertension
Pyonephrosis or xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis not responding to drainage
Severe renal trauma not controlled otherwise
contraindications: Inadequate function in the contralateral kidney (check before surgery)
Unfit for major surgery
equipment: Major open or laparoscopic renal set
Vascular clamps and non-absorbable ligatures or vascular staplers
Diathermy and vessel sealing device if available
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent, contralateral kidney function and cross-matched blood and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out with site marking.
Give anaesthesia, prophylactic antibiotic and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis per local protocol.
Position in flank or supine position for the chosen approach, prepare and drape.
Expose the kidney through a flank, subcostal, midline or laparoscopic approach.
Mobilise the colon and identify the ureter and renal hilum.
Ligate and divide the renal artery first, then the renal vein.
Ligate and divide the ureter.
Remove the kidney (with adrenal and perinephric fat for a radical procedure as indicated).
Check haemostasis, place a drain if needed and close in layers.
Send the specimen for histology.
aftercare: Monitor vital signs, urine output, haemoglobin and renal function.
Mobilise early with chest physiotherapy and analgesia.
Review histology and plan follow-up.
red_flags: Hypotension, tachycardia or falling haemoglobin (bleeding)
Low urine output or rising creatinine
Fever, wound infection or ileus
Breathlessness (pneumothorax after flank approach)

indications: Pelviureteric junction obstruction with symptoms, falling function or infection
Worsening hydronephrosis on serial imaging in children
contraindications: Untreated infection
Non-functioning kidney (nephrectomy may be more appropriate)
equipment: Double-J stent or nephrostomy and stent
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent (parent or guardian for a child) and imaging and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position, prepare and drape for flank, anterior or laparoscopic approach.
Expose the renal pelvis and pelviureteric junction and look for a crossing vessel.
Excise the narrowed junction and redundant pelvis.
Spatulate the ureter and fashion a tension-free anastomosis to the pelvis anterior to any crossing vessel.
Place a stent across the anastomosis before completing it.
Leave a drain and close.
aftercare: Monitor drain and urine output.
Remove the drain when dry and the stent at 4–6 weeks as booked.
Repeat imaging at 3–6 months to confirm improvement.
red_flags: Persistent urine leak
Fever or loin pain
Stent not removed by the booked date

indications: High-grade vesicoureteric reflux with breakthrough infections or renal scarring
Obstructed megaureter
Distal ureteric injury or stricture (including after pelvic surgery)
Ectopic ureter
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection
Neurogenic bladder not yet managed
steps: Confirm identity, side, consent (parent or guardian for a child) and imaging and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position supine, catheterise, prepare and drape.
Expose the bladder through a low transverse incision.
Mobilise the distal ureter (intravesical, extravesical or both) and excise any diseased segment.
Create a submucosal tunnel of adequate length and bring the ureter through it.
Anastomose the ureter to the bladder mucosa with fine absorbable sutures, adding a psoas hitch if length is short.
Place a ureteric stent and a urethral or suprapubic catheter.
Close the bladder and wound with a drain.
aftercare: Keep catheter and drain for several days and remove the stent as planned.
Continue prophylaxis per local protocol in children until follow-up.
Arrange follow-up ultrasound to exclude obstruction.
red_flags: Urine leak or high drain output
Fever or loin pain (obstruction or infection)
Bladder spasms with blocked catheter

indications: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture
Extraperitoneal rupture involving the bladder neck, with bone fragments, or needing laparotomy for other injuries
Iatrogenic bladder injury during surgery or obstetric procedures
contraindications: Uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture manageable with catheter drainage alone
equipment: Methylene blue or saline for leak test
steps: Resuscitate per trauma protocol and confirm identity and consent.
Perform a WHO surgical safety time-out and give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Explore through a lower midline laparotomy and treat other injuries by priority.
Identify the full extent of the bladder tear and inspect the trigone and ureteric orifices.
Debride non-viable edges.
Close the bladder in two layers with absorbable sutures.
Fill the bladder to check that the repair is watertight.
Leave a urethral catheter with or without a suprapubic catheter and a pelvic drain.
Close the abdomen.
aftercare: Keep the catheter for 7–14 days and consider a cystogram before removal.
Monitor drain and urine output.
Watch for pelvic and abdominal sepsis.
red_flags: Persistent urine in the drain or wound
Fever or peritonitis
Blocked catheter

indications: Bladder tumour seen on imaging or cystoscopy
Diagnosis and staging of bladder cancer
contraindications: Untreated urinary tract infection
Uncorrected coagulopathy
equipment: Specimen pots labelled for tumour and base
steps: Confirm identity, consent and imaging and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and prophylactic antibiotic per local protocol.
Position in lithotomy, prepare and drape.
Perform cystoscopy and map the number, size and site of tumours.
Resect the tumour in pieces down to and including detrusor muscle.
Send the tumour and base separately for histology.
Coagulate the resection bed and check for perforation.
Perform bimanual examination under anaesthesia for staging.
Insert a catheter with irrigation if needed and record a bladder diagram.
Give a single post-operative intravesical chemotherapy instillation only per local protocol if no perforation.
aftercare: Monitor haematuria and remove the catheter when urine clears.
Review histology at a multidisciplinary meeting.
Arrange surveillance cystoscopy.
red_flags: Clot retention or heavy bleeding
Abdominal pain or distension (perforation)
Fever or urosepsis

indications: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer
High-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer failing intravesical treatment
Advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder (including schistosomiasis-related)
contraindications: Metastatic disease
Unfit for major surgery
equipment: Major pelvic and bowel surgical set
steps: Confirm identity, staging, consent, stoma marking and stoma nurse review, and cross-matched blood and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia, prophylactic antibiotic and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis per local protocol.
Position supine (or Lloyd-Davies), catheterise, prepare and drape.
Open through a lower midline incision and assess for unresectable or metastatic disease.
Perform pelvic lymph node dissection.
Divide the ureters and send distal margins if needed.
Remove the bladder with prostate and seminal vesicles in men, or with uterus and anterior vaginal wall in women as indicated.
Isolate an ileal segment, restore bowel continuity and anastomose the ureters to the segment over stents.
Bring the conduit out as a stoma at the marked site.
Place drains, close and apply the stoma appliance.
aftercare: Monitor in high dependency with fluid balance, haemoglobin, electrolytes and renal function.
Check stoma colour and output regularly.
Start enhanced recovery feeding and mobilisation as tolerated.
Teach stoma care before discharge.
red_flags: Dusky or black stoma
Falling urine output from the stoma
Fever, abdominal distension or peritonitis (bowel or urine leak)
Leg swelling or chest pain

indications: Haematuria after TURP, TURBT or open prostatectomy
Haematuria with clots from bladder or prostate bleeding
contraindications: No three-way catheter in place
Suspected bladder perforation or recent bladder repair without surgeon approval
equipment: Irrigation solution (sterile saline) and Y-type irrigation set
steps: Confirm identity, the prescription for irrigation and verbal consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves.
Check the catheter is draining and not blocked before starting.
Connect the irrigation set to the inflow port using an aseptic technique.
Run the irrigation at a rate that keeps the outflow light pink.
Record input and output volumes and subtract irrigation from output to get true urine output.
Check the colour and flow at least hourly and change bags before they are full.
Stop the inflow and perform a manual bladder washout if outflow stops or the patient has pain.
Reduce and stop irrigation when the outflow is clear, per prescription.
aftercare: Continue fluid balance and catheter care.
Encourage oral fluids.
Plan catheter removal once urine stays clear.
red_flags: Outflow less than inflow or no outflow (blocked catheter, risk of bladder rupture)
Lower abdominal pain or distension
Heavy bleeding not improving or falling haemoglobin
Confusion or low sodium after TURP

indications: Clot retention
Blocked catheter from clots or debris
Ongoing haematuria needing cystoscopic control
contraindications: Recent bladder repair or anastomosis without surgeon approval
equipment: Sterile dressing pack, gloves and gown
Resectoscope and Ellik evacuator for theatre evacuation
steps: Confirm identity, indication and consent (written if in theatre) and perform hand hygiene.
Change to a large-bore three-way catheter if the existing one is small.
Using aseptic technique, instil sterile saline gently with the bladder syringe.
Aspirate firmly to pull out clots and repeat until returns are clear.
Do not use force if the patient has pain or the bladder is distended.
Move to theatre for cystoscopic evacuation and diathermy if clots cannot be cleared or bleeding continues.
Start continuous bladder irrigation if bleeding persists.
Record the volumes and nature of returns.
aftercare: Monitor catheter drainage and colour closely.
Check haemoglobin and clotting if bleeding is heavy.
Treat the cause of bleeding.
red_flags: Lower abdominal pain or distension after washout (bladder perforation)
Ongoing heavy bleeding or haemodynamic instability
Fever or rigors

indications: Lower urinary tract symptoms before surgery where the cause is unclear
Urinary incontinence not responding to treatment or before surgery
Neurogenic bladder assessment (spina bifida, spinal cord injury)
Voiding dysfunction in children
contraindications: Active untreated urinary tract infection
Recent lower urinary tract surgery
equipment: Filling line and sterile saline at room temperature
Bladder scanner or catheter for residual volume
steps: Confirm identity, indication and verbal consent and check the urine dipstick is negative.
Review the bladder diary and symptom questionnaire.
Perform free uroflowmetry with the patient arriving with a comfortably full bladder.
Measure post-void residual volume by scan or catheter.
Using aseptic technique, insert the bladder and rectal pressure lines and zero the transducers.
Fill the bladder at a set rate, recording sensations, compliance and detrusor activity.
Perform provocation tests (cough, Valsalva) to assess stress leakage.
Record a pressure-flow study during voiding.
Remove the catheters and summarise the findings.
aftercare: Expect mild burning on voiding and encourage fluids.
Review results with the patient and plan treatment.
red_flags: Fever or dysuria after the test (urinary infection)
Autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injury (headache, high blood pressure; stop and drain the bladder)
Unable to pass urine

indications: Necrotising soft tissue infection of the perineum, scrotum or penis
contraindications: None; surgery must not be delayed beyond initial resuscitation
equipment: Swabs and tissue pots for culture
steps: Resuscitate with fluids and start broad-spectrum antibiotics per local protocol without waiting for theatre.
Confirm identity and consent and perform a WHO surgical safety time-out.
Give anaesthesia and position in lithotomy; catheterise if possible.
Incise widely and excise all necrotic skin and fascia back to bleeding healthy tissue.
Send tissue and pus for culture.
Preserve the testes, which are usually viable, and protect them in a thigh pouch or moist dressing if exposed.
Assess for rectal or urethral involvement and arrange diversion (colostomy or suprapubic catheter) if needed.
Irrigate thoroughly and apply bulky moist dressings.
Plan a relook in theatre within 24–48 hours.
aftercare: Care in high dependency with monitoring for sepsis and fluid balance.
Control blood sugar in diabetes and give nutrition support.
Change dressings daily or as planned and return to theatre for further debridement.
Plan skin grafting or flap reconstruction once the wound is clean.
red_flags: Spreading redness, crepitus or new necrosis
Hypotension, confusion or low urine output (septic shock)
High blood sugar not controlled
